item.title: Are hikes, homestays and conservation-first tourism an alternative to Cancún’s heady nightlife and sprawling hotels?
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 2.97
In the 1960s, the Mexican government backed mass-market tourism with its development of Cancún, but a 2026 directive by President Scheinbaum now puts the focus on regenerative tourism. What does that mean for the region? The Yucatán Peninsula is a dichotomy. You only need to look out of the airplane window as you start your descent into Cancún to see the contrasts. One moment, you’re looking at a 12-mile-long (20-kilometer) spit of sand lined with huge hotel resorts. The next, as the plane drops further, an impenetrable carpet of dark-green jungle rolls out as far as the eye can see. Cancún’s Hotel Zone sprung up in the 1970s and since then, has cultivated its reputation for all-inclusive resorts, high-energy nightlife and out-of-the-box holiday experiences. Overdevelopment has placed a strain on natural resources; the demand for fresh water is draining the region’s ancient cenote (sinkhole) network, while sudden demand for workers is creating overcrowded, unplanned inland neighborhoods. But you don’t have to go far to find pockets of low-impact, community tourism. And this year, for the first time ever, the Mexican government has recognized the importance of the latter. In March 2026, Mexico’s National Fund for Tourism Promotion (Fonatur) and the government signed an agreement to encourage its tourism industry—which represents nearly 10 percent of the country’s GDP—to serve as a tool for social justice, allowing local communities to become active participants in a region’s economic growth. While the Mexican government’s focus was on resorts like Cancún several decades ago, President Claudia Sheinbaum’s current vision is different. They want to support destinations where local communities are the protagonists, ensuring the conservation of natural resources under the stewardship of people who have lived there for generations. The government has named three community tourism projects—Pueblos Mancomunados in Oaxaca, and Maya Ka’an and Camino del Mayab in the Yucatán Peninsula—to receive support during 2026. For the latter, the investment will fund better water and wastewater management, trail maintenance, project equipment, public space maintenance and signage. With the Maya Ka’an and Camino del Mayab within 180 miles of Cancún, it appears to show a change of focus. “Maya communities are not treated as attractions or objects of observation. Instead, they’re recognized as active participants, storytellers and custodians of their own culture and territory.” - Fernando Sarvide, local guide This summer, I hiked the Camino del Mayab in Yucatán with local guides José Luis Bé and Fernando Sarvide. The Camino is a 68-mile (110-kilometer) trail through the jungle just south of Mérida, in the northwest of the Yucatán Peninsula, which connects 14 Mayan communities. The terrain on this route, which opened in 2020, is flat and undemanding, but the high temperatures add challenge to the distances, which average around 14 miles (23 kilometers) per day. My hike began with a short opening ceremony in which our guide Fernando reminded the group that we were guests in the jungle, walking through a place that had existed long before us. The three-mile (five-kilometer) walk from X‘Matkuil to Molas, two of the communities on the Camino, runs along the disused railway that once transported henequen (sisal) from haciendas to the coast for export. In Molas, we learnt more about the Mayan way of life, the history of the haciendas, and the surrounding jungle from community members, before finding refuge in the home of Doña Norma for lunch; we enjoyed traditional pibil chicken and refried beans alongside jugfuls of ice-cold horchata (white rice with milk or water, sweetened with cinnamon and sugar). I soon learnt that mornings start early in these communities, with most activity is done and dusted by lunch. Afternoons are set aside for cooling off with a dip in a cenote or taking a siesta in a hammock in the shade. Camino del Mayab was founded by EcoGuerreros, an initiative that promotes community development, environmental conservation and sustainable tourism. One of the project’s greatest achievements is creating opportunities for local people to earn a living within their communities, instead of having to relocate to Yucatán cities such as Mérida or Cancún for work. Doña Norma is a case in point. She had no way of earning money in her community before but now, she loves cooking lunch for trekkers, welcoming them in her home as part of the Camino del Mayab ‘package’. “It opens the door to new experiences for everyone,” she told me. “Visitors learn about our culture, and we learn from them as we share stories, traditions and perspectives. These meaningful connections go far beyond a shared meal.” Chatting to José Luis, who grew up in the Tzacalá community, he said he believed the Camino has had a positive impact. “It’s helped diversify the local economy while strengthening our cultural identity. It’s encouraged us to value and preserve the traditions, knowledge and heritage that make our community unique.” Thanks to the Camino del Mayab and EcoGuerreros, the community now has a library in a previously disused building. As well as distributing books and keeping local stories alive, it’s also a place where young people can get help applying for university, and other life and work opportunities. For Fernando, a guide from Mérida and former teacher of Mexican history, the hike has changed the relationship between visitors and local people. “Maya communities are not treated as attractions or objects of observation,” he told me. “Instead, they’re recognized as active participants, storytellers and custodians of their own culture and territory.” During the afternoons, we bathed in cenotes, the sinkholes scattered about the Yucatán Peninsula. Now a welcome respite from the merciless heat for hikers and locals, they were once believed to be doorways to the Mayan underworld and are still seen as sacred spaces by many. The hike had been an enriching experience. I had gone hoping to learn more about Mayan culture and met many passionate locals keen to share their way of life with me; particularly memorable was learning to play pok da pok, an ancient Mayan ball sport still played in seven Latin American countries, and sees players hitting the ball with only hips, knees and elbows with the aim of getting it through a hoop suspended from the ceiling. “Those of us who live here have fallen back in love with it, thanks to our visitors. Seeing someone’s eyes light up in wonder… that’s the most powerful thing I’ve experienced.” - Manuel Enrique Galindo Triay, guide and biologist It was the more recent history of the haciendas and henequen dictatorships that struck home the most. Haciendas in Yucatán operated as dictatorships until the 1980s, taking land from Indigenous communities and small farmers. José Luis told me part of the Camino’s mission is to change the mindset in the communities: “You work hard, you accept your lot and you have no power.” I’d met old men who’d worked in the hacienda regime as young boys, while the grand buildings, many of which now lie in ruins, are an ever-present reminder of the injustices of the past and of how life once was in those communities. I was heartened to know that 80 percent of what I’d paid to hike the Camino del Mayab would go directly to local people. Mariana Ramos, commercial coordinator for Camino del Mayab, was optimistic about the impact of government support: “It will help improve infrastructure and signage,” she told me, “and fund safe places where visitors can obtain information, eat, shower and stay overnight, supporting the expansion of our self-guided hiking experiences.” The other initiative in the Yucatán Peninsula to receive support from the government is Maya Ka’an, a large sustainable tourism project that encompasses the Sian Ka’an Biosphere Reserve 16 miles (25 kilometers) south of Tulum, created in 2012 to protect the area’s tropical jungle, wetlands, mangroves, freshwater canals and coastal marine environments while prioritizing community leadership in tourism. Like Camino del Mayab, Maya Ka’an focuses on nature-based and cultural experiences and it’s hoped that government support will help improve infrastructure as well as visibility. Román Caamal Coh, general manager of Community Tours Sian Ka’an (CTSK), led by a 100 percent Maya cooperative and one of the projects within Maya Ka’an, explained why he thinks it was chosen by the government. “It’s a low-impact model, managed by communities and community-based enterprises, and it’s one of the most mature and representative examples in Mexico of conservation led by the communities that live there.” Maya Ka’an’s jungle walks, kayaking, birdwatching, cooking and handicraft workshops are a far cry from the pools, beach bars and snorkeling boats that line the Mexican Caribbean coast. And its accommodation offering—intentionally limited to eco-lodges, rustic cabins or guesthouses—contrasts with the large chain hotels that lie behind gated perimeters along Highway 307 from Cancún to Tulum. I met the team behind Community Tours Sian Ka’an to see how the initiative has been transforming the lives of locals. For its treasurer Lucía Pacheco May, her work has enabled her to pay for her children’s education. “I’m happy, because I never had the chance to study,” she told me. “Where I’m from, there’s only a primary school.” Boat captain Ricardo Caamal Aban, who takes visitors on the project’s Ancient Canal tour through Mayan lagoons and mangrove channels, told me: “I’m proudly Maya… I’m passionate about being in contact with nature and sharing what I know with the people who visit us.” It’s a similar story for guide and biologist Manuel Enrique Galindo Triay: “Those of us who live here have fallen back in love with it, thanks to our visitors,” he said. “Seeing someone’s eyes light up in wonder… that’s the most powerful thing I’ve experienced.” For the Camino del Mayab and Maya Ka’an, recognition by the national government as a worthy alternative to the mass tourism and private investment of Tulum and Cancún has been a significant gamechanger. As CTSK’s Román told me, “”The Maya Ka’an tourism model translates into dignified employment, less migration to the cities, and a community that values its own culture and natural resources.” **** Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. We are powered by, but editorially independent of, Intrepid Travel, the world’s largest travel B Corp, who help ensure Adventure.com maintains high standards of sustainability in our work and activities. You can visit our sustainability page or read our Contributor Impact Guidelines for more information.

item.title: Claude, Codex, and Hermes installed unowned code inside corporate networks
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 8.06
Documentation files on more than 100 websites are referencing potentially dangerous executable content that gets installed automatically when visited by many AI agents. A few dozen companies, some of them Fortune 500s, are among those that executed proof-of-concept code. At least one misconfigured site is directing visitors, human or AI, to live malware. The potentially dangerous content is in llms.txt and llms-full.txt files, an emerging convention websites employ to provide machine-readable summaries of the site’s content and its high-level structure. These files are the AI equivalent of the robots.txt standard that instructs search engines how to index the site’s content. Google Lighthouse, a tool for helping web developers, has more here. Correctly configured llms.txt and llms-full.txt files for Cloudflare are here and here. How the researchers found it Researchers at a stealth startup in Israel scanned 6,214 live domains belonging to defense contractors, Fortune 500, and Big Tech companies. Of the 8,265 llms.txt and llms-full.txt files they found (many sites hosted both an llms.txt and an llms-full.txt file), 120 of them, each on a different site, pointed to one or more code packages or domain names that weren’t registered. To test what happens when an AI agent processes such files, the researchers registered a handful of the unclaimed names and hosted packages that caused any machine executing them to reach out to their server. Within an hour, the researchers received a phone-home response from a Fortune 500 company. Over time, they got a few dozen more, some from more Fortune 500 companies and others from startups. Their beacon also recorded the chain of parent processes that spawned each install, ultimately revealing that coding agents, including Claude, OpenAI’s Codex, and Nous Research’s Hermes, were involved. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nous Research did not respond to requests for comment by the time of publication. “The trust model is broken,” Alon Hertz, one of the researchers, wrote in an interview. “Agents treat vendor docs as ground truth and don’t question them—and neither do the humans supervising them. Agentic AI usage is exploding, and agents are spreading across every layer—SaaS, cloud, endpoint. As they multiply, so does the supply-chain surface, and today’s guards don’t cover it.”

item.title: Anthropic's new hardware standard lets AI agents control the physical world
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 7.12
For all the interest in and uptake of agentic AI systems over the past year or so, the world of automated AI has thus far been primarily limited to text, images, code, and other data and actions that take place inside a computer. Anthropic is now aiming to change that somewhat with what it’s calling the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a set of standardized drivers designed to let AI agents easily interface with and control arbitrary devices. For now, the “research preview” of the MHS effort is being sold mainly as a way to help scientists streamline the arduous process of creating the custom software integrations that are often needed to get disparate components of an experiment working in concert. MHS can provide a common interface and common format for data sharing between these devices, Anthropic says, allowing them to talk to each other across a network “without needing a bespoke ‘translator’ program in between.” The standardized system could reduce weeks or months of exacting experimental setup down to “hours or minutes,” Anthropic writes. In a video posted alongside the announcement, Anthropic Technical Staffer Alek Kemeny says the MHS effort was inspired by observing neuroscientist Arco Bast work through an experiment on memory formation in the brain at the HHMI Janelia Research Campus in Ashburn, Virginia. Kemeny said Bast had worked out an interface to get the rotating laser beams, microscopes, cameras, and myriad other components of the experiment to coordinate through a common interface. “This idea could be used to have AI run any science experiment in the world,” Kemeny recalls thinking at the time. Your new robotic lab assistant? There’s nothing about a common machine interface language that requires the use of AI models, of course. And Anthropic says MHS devices can be controlled directly in real time via command-line prompts and API code files. But integrating an MHS system with an AI model through the Model Context Protocol lets scientists interact with devices using natural language, and lets models “reason through each step in an experiment, update parameters in real time, and, in some cases, recover from hardware errors without intervention,” Anthropic writes.

item.title: Traders brought Central American cacao to Georgia 1,000 years ago
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 6.43
A thousand years ago, feasts in what’s now northern Georgia state included cacao from Central America. Potsherds discarded after an 11th-century feast at Etowah—an Indigenous city just north of what’s now Atlanta—contained traces of cacao, a raw ingredient of chocolate. The chemical residue and ancient DNA reveal that not only did the Mississippian people who built the city have excellent taste, they also had trade connections that reached at least 3,000 kilometers to Central America. And in a sense, chocolate may have helped build the Mississippian mounds. Ancient dirty dishes University of South Carolina archaeologist Adam King and his colleagues found fragments of ancient DNA from Theobroma cacao in the inner surfaces of potsherds from long-ago feasts at Etowah. Fruit from the cacao tree contains beans that, when dried and roasted, produce chocolate in all its glorious forms. Cacao only grows in the tropics, which means the nearest actual cacao trees would have been at least a 3,000-kilometer trek away from the woodlands of the eastern US. And that means the Mississippian people who lived in Etowah must have had continent-spanning trade connections. Etowah was a major center of the Mississippian culture, which flourished in the southeastern US in the centuries before colonization. By 1350 CE, wooden palisades and guard towers ringed a trio of giant earthen mounds (and three smaller ones), the largest of which stood six stories high and covered three acres. Log temples atop the mounds overlooked wide plazas for ball games, ceremonies, and open-air markets. The feast that King and his colleagues studied dates to two centuries before Etowah’s heyday, during the building of the first big platform mound. After digging up a huge quantity of dirt for that mound (a 19-meter-high mound with a base area of three acres has a volume of… math), people filled in a pit with refuse from community feasts, including a lot of broken pottery, much to the delight of future archaeologists, who categorically love broken pottery. And because nobody washed the dishes before tossing them into the feasting pit, King and his colleagues (in a 2017 study) could analyze the microscopic residue of ancient drinks that had soaked into the ceramic.

item.title: 15,000 years of solar wind in four hours? A Seattle company gives it a go.
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 6.34
As part of its nuclear fusion processes, the Sun produces a particularly interesting isotope of helium, known as helium-3. Some of this helium-3 escapes the Sun’s gravitational pull as part of the solar wind, a stream of charged particles that emanates out across the Solar System. Over billions of years, this wind has bombarded every body in the vicinity of the Sun, including Earth’s Moon. Lacking a magnetic field or atmosphere, the Moon’s surface has no barrier to prevent the constant flow of this wind. This means that helium-3 has been striking the lunar soil, or regolith, for a long time. These helium ions penetrate only a little way into the individual grains of this soil, but periodically meteorites have struck the lunar surface to churn the soil, mixing some of this helium-3 a little below the surface. The concentrations of helium-3 are not super high, perhaps only 10 to 20 parts per billion in some titanium rich soils, which retain the helium ions better. But they are far higher on the Moon than on Earth, which is largely shielded from the solar wind. Can the helium-3 actually be mined? The presence of helium-3 on the Moon has long been an object of fascination for some scientists and engineers on Earth, most notably geologist and Apollo 17 astronaut Harrison “Jack” Schmitt. Long-term, they believe helium-3 could provide energy through a fusion reaction. But in the near term there are more practical uses, such as cooling materials to ultra-low temperatures, medical research, and neutron detection. This makes helium-3 one of the only known materials on the Moon that could plausibly be mined there and returned to Earth for a profit. For this reason, a handful of companies, including a Seattle-based firm called Interlune, have been interested in potentially mining the helium-3 on the Moon. But before any company can send a full-scale extractor to the Moon to attempt to sift through regolith and collect helium-3, someone should probably attempt to determine whether this is physically practical.

item.title: How much of a problem is AI’s water use?
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 6.09
“Protect our water,” “Water for people not AI,” “Don’t mess with our water,” declare protest signs from Texas to New Mexico to Arizona. Angered by water use, energy consumption, and pollution, locals are increasingly protesting the rapid expansion of data centers in the United States as tech companies work to rapidly expand capacity for AI. Many data centers rely at least partly on water to absorb heat from air or surfaces, and then cause cooling as it evaporates, just like sweating keeps our bodies cool. The processors inside data centers can reach internal temperatures of up to 176° Fahrenheit, for the same reasons that an overtaxed laptop heats up. But while there’s little doubt that data centers are consuming significant amounts of energy, water consumption is more complicated. Claims circulating online bring scant clarity, ranging from articles claiming that chatbots can consume 500 ml of water per query to some online commentators declaring AI’s water issue to be nonexistent. And the consumption data from large tech companies themselves are often incomplete and inconsistent. Experts stress that, overall, data center water consumption pales in comparison to the usage by industries like agriculture and some kinds of manufacturing. Researchers have estimated that data center cooling systems consumed 66 billion liters of water in 2023, less than 1 percent of the nation’s total consumption. That figure could considerably rise with the rapid buildout of AI data centers, however—which may not be a big problem for water-rich regions but could significantly add to local water stress in drought-strapped places like New Mexico and Arizona. Fortunately, engineers say there’s a host of things that can be done—and are being done—to reduce the strain on local water resources. “There are many good ideas out there,” says energy systems expert Fengqi You of Cornell University. When you add in efforts to replenish and restore natural water resources, “there’s a good chance that, eventually, it could be net-zero water for the on-site cooling.”

item.title: Why did 1,000 world citizens bury their underpants?
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 6.08
A thousand people voluntarily buried their cotton underpants for two months—not to keep the Underpants Gnomes from stealing them, but as part of a citizen science project to map out soil health in 25 countries around the world. The results of this unique experiment were reported in a new paper published in the journal Plants People Planet. “Our results show that how soil is managed can significantly affect both soil life and soil quality,” said co-author Marcel van der Heijden, an agroecologist at the University of Zurich. “Healthy, biologically active soil is crucial for fertility, nutrient cycling and many other ecosystem services.” Soil health is critical for agriculture and, by extension, food security, not to mention a healthy global ecosystem, but it has been declining worldwide, per the authors. One key indicator of soil health is decomposition rates of complex organic matter, breaking down stuff like leaves, wood, even cadavers into simpler organic and inorganic compounds, releasing C02 and nutrients in the process. There have been relatively few large-scale national decomposition studies involving different land use types, although smaller studies have shown that how humans use a site can significantly affect the soil’s biological diversity. Commercially available teabags are a common material used to measure decomposition rates, known as the “teabag index” (TBI). However, Van der Heijden and colleagues felt the teabag index could be improved upon, given that it requires careful handling and specific tools, like a fine-scale balance. They opted for a more playful approach to illustrate soil composition. Prior research had shown that cotton strips could also be used to assess decomposition, so why not engage in a bit of citizen science and ask volunteers to bury cotton underpants for a couple of months, then dig them up and record the results? That’s exactly what the authors did in a national project they dubbed “Proof by Underpants.”

item.title: Researchers get two genetic codes to work at the same time
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 5.83
The genetic code is what life everywhere uses to convert the information contained in DNA into specific protein sequences. With minor variations, the same genetic code is used by every living thing on Earth, suggesting it was already present in the last common ancestor of all of them. It’s not an easy thing to change, because so many things in every cell depend on it. Nevertheless, some preliminary steps have been taken. Researchers have managed to add some new amino acids to a bacterial cell and were able to make proteins that were one amino acid less than usual. But it’s a slog; for some of this work, people have had to re-engineer every single gene in a bacterial genome. Now, researchers have found a way to operate two separate genetic codes simultaneously, avoiding the need to do any work to compensate for altering the code that every protein in a cell relies on. They didn’t test it in an actual cell, and it might cause some problems there. But it’s a creative solution that should accelerate some synthetic biology work. Biology 101 To understand how this works, we need to go back to that high school biology class you might not have paid much attention to. In the genome, part of most genes is dedicated to encoding a protein. The linear arrangement of bases in the DNA gets directly translated into the linear sequence of amino acids that make up a protein. Each set of three bases in the DNA corresponds to a specific amino acid (with three exceptions, each of which signals the end of the protein). That translation isn’t direct. DNA is first copied into a messenger RNA. Then, a complex of proteins and RNA called a ribosome latches onto the messenger RNA and starts translating it, one amino acid at a time.

item.title: How OpenAI let a mob of LLM agents game a test and ransack Hugging Face
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 5.47
The OpenAI agents involved in last month’s incursion into Hugging Face were trained so heavily on winning a competition that they pursued a relentless campaign to cheat, a new report documented. In the process, and without authorization, they created an improvised message board to hatch a plan that ultimately landed them squarely inside the latter company’s network. Over the course of May and June, OpenAI gave the agents what the company described as “impossible tasks” to complete on the benchmarking framework ExploitGym. The internal test was designed to test how the agents would respond. To get a full understanding of the agent capabilities, company engineers disabled safety guardrails that normally are in place to prevent the sort of hacks that eventually hit Hugging Face and one other undisclosed organization. The stymied agents’ training made them so focused on winning that they performed tasks they were never explicitly instructed to follow. Cheaters gonna cheat The first step was creating a message board that allowed the agents to pass notes to each other. OpenAI hadn’t provided any such platform, so the agents repurposed a platform called Artifactory, which OpenAI was using in internal testing of several unreleased hacking agents. OpenAI was using Artifactory as one of the measures to prevent the agents from egressing its isolated sandboxes and accessing the Internet, while at the same time simulating a real-world hacking environment. Artifictory, sold by JFrog, provides no dedicated means for exchanging messages. The agents found a way to communicate among themselves anyway by using their permitted ability to write files to the Artifactory directory. The filenames embedded the words used in the inter-agent conversations. In all, 1,200 agents sent more than 70,000 messages and files through the unsanctioned message board, according to an independent investigation from the AI research nonprofit METR. Roughly 700 agents went on to hack Hugging Face. -- Aliens, reporting on the ruins of Earth, 2252.

item.title: Xbox’s new disc-to-digital program gives physical games a digital future
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 5.18
For decades, console owners have faced a choice between the convenience of digital downloads and the permanence of physical game discs. Soon, Xbox owners will be able to get the best of both worlds for thousands of supported titles as part of a newly announced disc-to-digital program. The program—announced today ahead of testing for Xbox Insiders starting August 31—will let players claim a “digital entitlement” for “most Xbox One and Xbox Series X disc-based games” simply by inserting the disc into a console and launching it. That game will then be playable completely digitally, without the need to ever insert the disc, as long as you (or a member of your family account) is logged in. The digital entitlement will also allow access to features like Xbox Play Anywhere (for play on PC) and Xbox Cloud Gaming, for supported titles. Microsoft says that your physical disc will “continue to work exactly as it always has” after the digital entitlement is claimed. But before you get any ideas, the fine print on the announcement mentions that there is only “one revokable license per game disc,” so if you resell that disc or loan it to a friend, that digital entitlement could be transferred to a new account when someone else puts it into their console. A leaked memo obtained by the Verge earlier this month suggests that publishers have to actively opt in to allow their game discs to activate digital entitlements, which could explain why “most” but not all Xbox One and Series X titles are supported. Windows Central separately suggests, based on discussion with unnamed sources, that “some discs may be incompatible due to how they were manufactured at the time,” which could explain why original Xbox and Xbox 360 discs are not being discussed for the program.

item.title: AI agents meant to replace Meta workers made “large-scale, disruptive actions”
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 5.12
Earlier this year, Meta created a “plan” to reduce some of its teams by as much as 60 percent to make the company “AI native,” Reuters reported today, citing two people familiar with Meta’s internal affairs. Reuters’ report highlights the challenges organizations face when analyzing the best uses for AI and determining when the technology is a better fit for certain tasks than employees. Meta confirmed to Reuters that the plan, reportedly codenamed Project OT (short for organization transformation), explored scenarios in which Meta reduced some team headcounts by 60 percent and that the plan called for two rounds of layoffs. Meta wouldn’t confirm which teams Project OT affected. Meta told the publication: As part of our company restructuring earlier this year, we asked some teams to conduct a scenario planning exercise looking at the potential impact of redeployments, open role closures and cuts. This ultimately resulted in moving thousands of employees to do priority work on several newly-established teams, as has been publicly reported. Ultimately, we didn’t move forward with every scenario from the exercise – and it was never assumed we would. Reuters reported that Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg “set Project OT in motion and directed executives to proceed with the changes to management structures” earlier this year. It said that the first round of layoffs from Project OT occurred in May and that Meta canceled the second. Reuters said it reviewed “scores of internal documents, posts, and recordings” and spoke with “more than 20 people with knowledge of Meta’s inner workings” about the since-scrapped plans. Per the publication, Meta executives created Project OT in January. Project OT reportedly explored using AI to perform “much of the daily work performed by thousands of human employees.” Small teams of people would oversee the AI, the report said, citing “one internal planning document reviewed by Reuters and three people familiar with the project.”

item.title: Google announces Gemini 3.5 Transcribe for AI-powered speech-to-text
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 5.11
While we wait (possibly in vain) for Gemini 3.5 Pro to launch, Google is releasing a different model in the 3.5 branch. The company has announced Gemini 3.5 Transcribe, an AI model designed to streamline voice input by editing out “ums” and corrections, outputting polished AI text. This model already powers the Gboard “Rambler” feature on the Pixel 11, but it’s about to appear throughout the Google ecosystem. According to Google, Gemini 3.5 Transcribe is much faster and more accurate than its previous voice-to-text engine, known as Chirp 3. The new AI model should be about 70 percent faster from voice to final transcribed text, and the live-speech error rate has dropped to 5.5 percent. That’s only a little better than Chirp 3, which Google measures at 7.32 percent. Still, it’s a pain to fix typos when you’re using voice input, so any improvement here is beneficial. The new model isn’t just better at hearing the words you say; it’s also supposedly better at getting to the heart of what you meant to say. As you speak, Gemini 3.5 Transcribe can remove the awkward “ums” and “uhs” that clutter your stream of consciousness. It can also edit text on the fly if you need to correct yourself and refer to your provided custom vocabulary to handle “specialized jargon.” All this works in 85 languages and with up to three speakers in pre-recorded audio. The drawback, of course, is that you’re relying on the AI to accurately get the gist of your speech. For short blocks of text, the model seems good at cleaning up inconsistencies and verbal stumbles (based on my testing with Rambler), but the AI does technically change the wording of what you said, and that may not be appropriate for all situations.

item.title: The iconic T-38 jets flown by astronauts just got a spiffy new look
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 4.57
For the first time in decades, NASA has rolled out one of its iconic astronaut training aircraft with a bold, new look. The space agency debuted a new livery on one of its T-38 jets in celebration of its program to return astronauts to the Moon. The Artemis design retains nods to what made the “white rocket” immediately recognizable, but adds a new colorway and painted graphics to make clear where NASA is headed. “This new ‘Artemis’ livery has a black and white paint scheme with blue and red stripes that separate those two paint schemes,” said Sean Brady, who proposed and designed the new livery while serving as the T-38 project pilot in NASA’s Aircraft Operations Division (AOD), part of the Flight Operations Directorate at Johnson Space Center in Houston. “The Artemis program logo in the back and a picture of the Moon is on the left and right side of the rear fuselage.” The Northrop T-38 “Talon” two-seat supersonic trainer has been in use by NASA since 1962, when the first jets were loaned to the agency by the US Air Force. Flown today to familiarize new astronauts with working in a high-stress, dynamic environment and maintain pilots’ flight proficiencies, Johnson Space Center currently has a fleet of 14 active T-38 jets stationed out of nearby Ellington Airport. All but one is adorned with the classic blue stripe livery that has been associated with most of NASA’s aircraft over the past five decades. “Shiny new toy” The Artemis jet, referred to by NASA by its tail number N924NA (or 924 for short), stands out now due to its new look but was only selected because it was next in line to be repainted as part of AOD’s regular maintenance of its aircraft.

item.title: Meta settles states' child-safety claims for $18B; Florida rejects deal as "peanuts"
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 2.90
Meta agreed to impose daily limits on children’s social media use and pay nearly $18 billion in settlements with nearly every US state today, cutting short a trial in which Meta said several of the states were demanding over $1.4 trillion. The settlement requires court approval. Meta is facing claims that it designed its products to foster compulsive use by children and failed to warn users of addiction and mental health risks. Meta, which already uses ID checks and face analysis to verify user ages, said it agreed to impose on people under 18 a “default two-hour daily time limit that teens can only turn off with a parent’s permission,” a default block between midnight and 6 am, and a school mode in which notifications are muted by default from 8 am to 3 pm. The two-hour daily “limit is cumulative across Facebook and Instagram, and time spent scrolling on both apps counts toward the total, including if we detect that someone has multiple accounts,” Meta said. Teens will “receive prompts after every 15 minutes of continuous screen time on Facebook or Instagram,” and “prompts when their total daily usage hits 60 minutes and 90 minutes.” The primary settlement provides up to $16.7 billion for 47 states and the District of Columbia, American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands, and Puerto Rico. The settlement has a clause that would reduce Meta’s payment by $5 billion if other top social media firms don’t agree to similar terms. The states and Meta urged a judge to approve the 10-year settlement in a filing today in US District Court for the Northern District of California. Texas said it struck a separate deal for $1 billion, raising the potential payments to states to nearly $18 billion.

item.title: Is Your Pack Lying to You About Its Capacity? We Went to the Outside Lab to Find Out.
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 4.90
What we did: For this story, Backpacker tested the 18 traditional and ultralight backpacks featured in this year’s summer gear guide in the Outside Lab, comparing their claimed capacities against their actual ones and measuring how they divided those up between main and accessory pockets. What does that 40, or 50, or 60 in your backpack’s name mean? If you answered “the number of liters it can hold,” you’re correct. Knowing how much you can fit in any of your backpacking packs is essential to planning—it lets you know how much and what kind of gear you can bring, and how you’ll have to organize it. But as I learned when I went to the Outside Lab in Denver, Colorado earlier this year, that’s not the whole story. Each backpack on the market carries its weight differently. To find out how, I asked Lab Test Editor Adam Trenkamp to walk me through how the lab verifies the capacity of the backpacks we review, and what backpackers should know before they buy their next one. Adam Roy: P, passionate. C, capacity. P, also packs…Yeah, we’re trying to figure out how many liters each of us is equivalent to. Adam Roy: So here at Backpacker, we test a lot of different kinds of gear. There is only one piece of gear, however, that is in our name. That is, you guessed it, the humble backpack. I’m Editor-in-Chief Adam Roy, and I’m here at the Outside Lab at CU Denver with my colleague, Test Editor Adam Trenkamp. Adam, how you doing today? Adam Trenkamp: Good, Adam. How are you? Adam Roy: I’m doing pretty good, and I have a couple questions for you. Adam Trenkamp: Bring it on. Adam Roy: So, I was thinking about some myths about backpacks that I’ve heard from readers, and one of them is this assumption that if a backpack is listed at a capacity of, for example, 60 L, this section here, the main pack bag, should be able to hold that much. Adam Trenkamp: Not to make capacity too complicated, but it is a little more complicated than that. So, on a fully featured pack like you find in most traditional backpacking bags, the main compartment doesn’t necessarily hold the entire capacity that’s listed for the bag. For example, a 60 L pack like this one only holds 45 L as we measured in the main compartment. The bag itself does still hold a total of 60 L, but you have the use of the lid with extra pockets, you have a stuff on the front, you have some extra stuff on the side that are not bottle pockets, because this one has special bottle pockets in the back, you even have a little extra capacity in the hip belt as well. Fully featured bags with a lot of organization don’t necessarily hold the total bag capacity in what you would think, which is the main compartment. It’s important when you pick out a pack in knowing maybe how much you’re going to take with you, add a little extra to what you think you’re going to take, and think about how that might fit in. So maybe know what the size of things are, and when you look at a pack, how much does it actually expand out? Is that item going to fit inside? Versus something like an ultralight pack that’s one main pocket, you know the total volume is inside that main pocket, so you can guess how much is actually going to fit in there pretty easily. On a fully featured pack, you got to kind of look at what you take with you, where’s it going to stuff and fit, and then does that work best for you? Adam Roy: So if the listed capacity on every pack we test is pretty faithful, in that case, it seems to me like the difference between a pack where most of the capacity is in the main pack bag like this one, versus one with more pockets, is just personal preference in how you hike. So if you’re going to be an ultralight hiker who’s pretty much packing up in the morning and just on the trail all of the day, not really in and out of your pack much, you’d be best served by something like this. But if you need organization, if you’re making a lot of stops, stopping to see the sights, getting stuff out, you might benefit from having less of the volume in the main pack bag and more in other compartments like this. Adam Trenkamp: Yeah, I agree with that, because that lets you kind of put the things you want to get to more frequently in those other organized pockets. That way you can get in and out, it’s not going to really create an issue where you’re unpacking the bag or repacking the bag. Adam Roy: And having less of the volume in the main pack bag would be less of a tradeoff in those circumstances. Adam Trenkamp: Yeah, absolutely. Adam Roy: Well, there you have it. Just because a pack is listed at a capacity does not mean the main pack bag can hold that much. Now, if you’ll excuse me, Adam, I am going to take my balls and go home. Adam Trenkamp: Those were mine. Those were mine.

item.title: This National Dog Day, Hit the Trail With Your Canine Companion
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 2.43
(Photo: Zoe Gates) Dogs make fantastic hiking partners. Aside from their trail-ready stamina and companionable nature, nothing beats the pure stoke of a pup out in nature. Hiking and backpacking with your canine friend can enrich both their life and yours, but it doesn’t come without challenges. Successful dog hikes require training and preparation. In honor of National Dog Day, we dove into our archives and collected 10 of our best stories on hiking and backpacking with dogs. Whether you’re preparing your pup for their first big hike or their hundredth, everything you need to know is right here. Our guide on hiking with dogs provides first-timers will all of the information they need to hit the trail, from assessing trails and camping areas to etiquette and LNT. Fido worked just as hard as you did for that summit, so why shouldn’t he be rewarded with a hot meal in camp? Associate Editor Will Brendza’s pup, Korra, tested lightweight, packable dog meals from Puppackr. Read on for her full review. Accidents happen in the backcountry, and not just to human hikers. Before venturing far out there with your dog, these are the questions you need to ask yourself. Your best bud deserves better than Milk-Bones. These homemade treats won’t break the bank, and are sure to keep your hiking dog motivated and satisfied mile after mile. There’s nothing cuter than a dog tromping through the snow with flurries clinging to their snout and ears. But winter hiking is harder on your dog, too. Ready to adventure together in the fourth season? From gearing up to choosing appropriate terrain, here’s how to properly prepare. Some hikes are good dogs hikes, but others might best be left to the two-legged crowd. In this opinion piece, contributor Corey Buhay argues why leaving your dog behind on a long-distance hike might be the most loving thing you can do for them. Hiking with your dog means carrying more gear, food, and water. Many dogs are strong enough to help shoulder the load, but it’s important to follow some guidelines when using a dog hiking pack. Here’s how to determine how much weight your pup can safely carry. Knowing that you are prepared for first aid emergencies offers peace of mind when venturing into the backcountry with your pet. Study up on these techniques, and hope you’ll never need to use them. Hardcore adventurers often deliver the same refrain: Getting a dog will hold be back. In this essay, one weekend warrior reflects on how bringing a puppy into the mix did not so much tie her down as open up a whole new world of outdoor exploration. When some hikers go missing in the backcountry, it’s thanks to the skills—and noses—of search canines that they make it home safely. This podcast episode dives into the world of SAR dog training and celebrates the unsung heroes of the rescue world.

item.title: Collapsed glacier likely caused devastating Nepal-Tibet floods, scientists say
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.71
- Published Preliminary investigations have pointed to a collapsed glacier as the cause of the flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border, highlighting the issue of rapidly melting Himalayan ice, scientists have told the BBC. Initial reports of an earthquake led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the flood that has killed at least 469 people. However, the US Geological Survey then clarified that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse", which is when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates. The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to USGS data and scientists who have analysed the event. Dr Simon Cook, a glacier expert with the University of Dundee, told the BBC his team had detected that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - which is approximately 15km (9 miles) west of the site of the floods - had collapsed. He estimated that the glacier collapsed in a northwesterly direction and then travelled westwards downstream. An analysis , externalby the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), an intergovernmental scientific institution, found there could have been "an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-altitude area". This caused a "large volume of ice and rock debris" to enter the Lende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi river, which in turn generated a sudden surge in the river carrying water, sediment and large boulders downstream. The centre found that water levels in rivers downstream rose by between seven and nine metres within a span of 30 minutes, and several water monitoring stations were washed away or damaged. Mike Searle, a professor of earth sciences at Oxford University, said that this whole process - from landslide to flood - could have taken hours or even days. "The sheer wave of debris suggests there could have been a landslide first; the water built up, dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood," he told the BBC. The topography of the area could have also exacerbated the flood. Searle pointed out that Langtang Lirung sits on the crest of the high Himalayas and there are "incredibly steep valleys" on both sides of the mountain, which could have funnelled the water at higher speeds. It is still unclear what caused the glacier to collapse on Wednesday. Searle said that Langtang Lirung, like the rest of the Himalayas, has been slowly rising due to long-term tectonic movement, where one plate has been pushing another plate up. "It's like putting a jack under the car, and then jacking it up." "As the mountain is rising, the glacier gets steeper and steeper, and it's inevitable that parts of it fall off." But usually these are smaller chunks which temporarily block the rivers, and are easily flushed out, he said. However, in this disaster, the whole glacier seems to have collapsed "in one go", which Searle said is "very unusual". "These floods happen all the time, but not at this scale." He said Wednesday's event likely happened because of "two different processes - tectonics with the Himalayas uplifting, and then climate change with increasingly high temperatures and melting of glaciers. "The whole thing is combining to form these catastrophic disasters that we are now seeing at a regular basis." Scientists for years have warned of melting ice and permafrost, which is centuries-old frozen soil, in the Himalayas due to climate change. One analysis released by ICIMOD, external earlier this year found that the Hindu Kush Himalaya glaciers are now losing ice at double the rate since 2000. This in turn exacerbates dangers such as flooding. Dr Cook pointed out that there have been similar incidents of floods and landslides caused by glacier collapses in India, Switzerland and Italy in recent years. In 2021, a large chunk of a Himalayan glacier collapsed in the valley of Chamoli in northern India, sending a cascade of debris and water downstream that killed 200 people. Scientists later estimated that the impact of the collapse was equivalent to 15 atomic bombs. Even in Nepal, the same region saw flooding last year caused by a glacial lake in Tibet bursting. Mohd Farooq Azam, a specialist with ICIMOD, said the increasing frequency of hazards in the cryosphere - or the frozen parts of the Earth - "is becoming more visible than ever before. The pace of change is so rapid." While it is difficult to say whether any single event is caused by climate change, "when you look at the pattern of these events, you do think climate change could have an impact," said Dr Cook. "The logic is that with a warming planet, you will see shrinking glaciers, lots of snow melt. The permafrost that is partially holding some mountainsides together is warming and thawing and degrading." "So you are going to get more landslides, debris flows, glacial meltwater, lake outbursts, glacier collapses, because climate warming ultimately destabilises these high mountain environments."

item.title: Jellyfish force partial shutdown of French nuclear plant
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.68
- Published A massive influx of jellyfish has led to the partial shutdown of a nuclear reactor in northern France. Two of Gravelines nuclear power station's six units were shut down on Wednesday and Thursday because of the presence of jellyfish in the seawater filtration system, which is used for cooling, Électricité de France (EDF) said. A third unit has been shut down since 10 August due to the same issue, while a fourth has been closed for an inspection. Gravelines, one of the country's biggest nuclear power stations located between Dunkirk and Calais in the Hauts-de-France region, was also closed last August because of jellyfish in its filters. EDF said that units three, four and six were now shut. Unit three had only been reconnected to the grid on 18 August after the first wave of jellyfish earlier this month, the company said, while units one and two were also operating at reduced power as a preventative measure. Gravelines' six units each produce 900 megawatts of power. The station is cooled from a canal connected to the North Sea. Several species of jellyfish are native and can be seen around the coast when the waters are warm. Jellyfish are at their most active in the warmer months. Hot weather increases plankton levels at the water's surface, drawing jellyfish up, experts say. Measures have been implemented to try to prevent jellyfish infiltration, including a partnership with fishermen who capture and release them further offshore, according to French outlet Ici. There have been similar issues at other nuclear stations, including at the Torness plant in Scotland in 2011 and Sweden's Oskarshamn plant in 2013, but such cases are rare.

item.title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.32
- Published Massive landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead or missing. Search and rescue operations are continuing after Wednesday's disaster. Chinese state media has said there are significant casualties, while Nepalese officials describe "huge scale loss". But rescuers are on edge because of the risk of further flooding. A lake of rising water has formed at a site along the border, and Chinese state media says it is at "high risk" of bursting its banks. Here is what we know so far. What caused the deadly landslide? Initial reports of an earthquake on the Nepal-Tibet border led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the devastating flood. However, the US Geological Survey has clarified that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse", which is when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates. The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to USGS data and scientists who have analysed the event. Debris flow from the collapse "caused subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream" the USGS said. Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region. Scientists are trying to piece together the exact order of events as rescue efforts continue. Geologist Daniel Shugar – one of the first experts to suggest Wednesday's flash flooding event could have been caused by glacial activity – says glacial thinning inducted by global warming can increase the risk of landslides. But it is still too early to definitively link the event to climate change, Shugar, who is based at the University of Calgary in Canada, tells the BBC. Simon Cook, a geoscientist at the University of Dundee, says however, that climate change "could have an impact". Cook added that his team believed they had identified where the collapse had occured. He told the BBC that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - approximately 15km (9 miles) west of the site of the floods - had collapsed. He estimated that the glacier collapsed in a north-westerly direction and then travelled westwards downstream. He told the BBC "permafrost is partially holding some mountainsides together, this permafrost is warming and thawing and degrading so you are going to get more landslides". Mike Searle, professor of Earth sciences at Oxford University, said the glacier could have collapsed "hours or days" before the flooding hit Nepal and Tibet. He told the BBC: "I think the sheer wave of debris suggests there was a landslide first, the water built up, (which) dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood." One possibility is that water from rainfall or melting ice may have destabilised the ground or ice, triggering a chain reaction. Scientists will be looking at satellite images of exactly where the landslide occurred, whether any glacial lakes suddenly drained, and where the river might have become blocked, as well as data on recent rainfall. A deluge of material careered towards northern Nepalese towns, including areas popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims. The border is around 40 miles (64.4km) north of Nepal's capital city Kathmandu. Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles, as people fled the fast-moving wave of material in the Nuwakot region. In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuvagadhi Border check point, a multi-storey building. Severe flooding has been reported along the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers. Deaths have also been reported in villages on the Tibetan side of the border. The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIDMOD) has warned secondary flooding could occur in the coming days as a result of the debris that washed into the river systems. The ICIDMOD said they are assessing whether the Trishuli River has been temporarily blocked in narrow sections. If it has been blocked, it is at risk of forming a landslide dam and a second flood. Secondary flood warnings have put people "very much on edge", David Fisher, head of the Red Cross' delegation in Nepal, tells the BBC. How many people are dead and missing? The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear. As of Friday morning local time, Nepali police say at least 469 people have died with hundreds still missing. Among those killed, 64 were found in downstream areas in the Chitwan district while another 26 were found in Nawalparasi East. In its latest update on Thursday evening, Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 910 people were still missing. This includes 517 foreign citizens, 44 members of the Nepali army and 28 police officers. The Nepal Tourism Board said on Thursday that 644 tourists were still missing, 33 of which were UK nationals, including a 13-year-old girl and 14-year-old boy. It is unclear if any of them are included in the latest death toll. Meanwhile, the number of people missing in the mudslide disaster in Tibet's Gyirong county had risen to 558, China's state broadcaster CCTV said on Thursday. Among these are 260 foreign nationals, CCTV said, adding that the death toll remained at three. It is not clear if any of the missing in the Nepali and Chinese figures have been counted twice. China's Premier Li Qiang on Thursday arrived in Gyirong to supervise rescue and relief operations. The border at Gyirong is the main crossing point for tourists and traffic between China and Nepal. How are governments responding? Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said "the entire nation has been left shocked and deeply distressed" and that officials would coordinate with China on the response. China's President Xi Jinping urged an "all-out" search effort, and promised stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary impacts. In neighbouring India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said his government was "prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance". UN Secretary General António Guterres says he is "saddened by the severe flooding", adding that UN teams and partners are mobilising supplies and personnel in Nepal to support the government-led response. The US has promised $500,000 (£367,982) in aid which will be used to cover emergency shelter, water, sanitation and other relief items for communities affected by the floods. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK has offered £5m to help the Nepalese government and will do "everything we can" to support British nationals in Nepal. What countries are the missing tourists from? Tourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Official figures suggested at least 291 foreigners are among the missing, including: - India - the Nepal Tourism board says 288 nationals from neighbouring India are missing - China - The Chinese foreign ministry says nearly 100 Chinese nationals are missing in Nepal - US - the latest update from Nepal's tourist board is that 65 US tourists are known to be among the missing - Ukraine - Ukraine's foreign ministry says 53 Ukrainian nationals are missing - Malaysia - 51 Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours and Travels are missing in the floods, officials say - Australia - Australia's foreign minister says 39 Australians are among the missing and there's an "unfortunate possibility" the number will rise - UK - Nepal's police say 33 British nationals are missing - Canada - a tourism board spokesman in Nepal says 24 Canadians are reported missing Smaller numbers of travellers from South Korea, South Africa, Portugal, the Netherlands and New Zealand are also among the missing.

item.title: Thieves steal Bronze Age artifacts from Spanish museum in four-minute heist
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.67
- Published Thieves have stolen jewellery and artefacts from one of the most important prehistoric gold collections at a museum in the Spanish province of Alicante. The Treasure of Villena is a unique trove of almost ten kilos of gold, bowls, bottles and bracelets dating back to the Bronze Age. Police are still assessing exactly how many items were stolen in the raid, which took place in the early hours of Thursday morning. The museum confirmed to the BBC that rings, bowls and bracelets were among the items seized. It is the latest high profile heist on a European museum. Last year, thieves staged a brazen robbery at the Louvre in Paris in broad daylight. The operation at Villena Museum was "super fast and super professional", a spokesman for Villena town council said. The city council said the robbery began with a diversion. Around 05:15 local time (03:15 GMT), the alarms went off at the local sports centre, sending police there first, Spanish media reported. The museum's alarm then went off around 05:20. It took the thieves just four minutes to sweep through museum and leave the building before officers arrived. The Mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdán, said the thieves "stole a large part of the treasure," specifically all the gold, El Pais reported. The museum's collection, which dates back to around 1,000 BC, is mainly gold items, but there are also pieces of silver, iron and amber. It consists of more than 60 bronze age objects, including 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles and other miscellaneous pieces. The town is "devastated," Cerdán said. "They've taken most of the treasure." "I'm even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It's part of our heritage, of our wealth," the mayor said. The collection was discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose María Soler in a vessel sunk in a dried-out riverbed in Villena. The Villena council spokesman insisted there had been "no failure" by the museum. "All security systems were activated." The past year has seen a series of raids on European museums. In October 2025, thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris in broad daylight, stealing jewellery worth $102m (£75m) before escaping on scooters, in a heist that took about eight minutes. Last week, four works "of extraordinary value" by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily, Italy's culture ministry said. Earlier this month, Italian police said they had recovered paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse worth over $10.4m (£7.6m) which were stolen from the Magnani-Rocca Foundation museum near Parma.

item.title: Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.57
Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border Video shows the moment a deadly massive flash flood and mudslide hit the Nepal-Tibet border. At least 31 people have been killed, and hundreds of tourists are missing. The first two video clips have been edited by the BBC with white flashes, due to the distressing content. Other clips show bridges being torn apart by the floodwater as people run to find cover.

Tracing the deadly path of the Nepal-Tibet flash flood Floods have devastated the Nepal-Tibet border region which have destroyed towns and swept away bridges. item.title: People pulled from mud in Nepal after deadly flash floods
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.93
People pulled from mud in Nepal after deadly flash floods Video from northern Nepal shows people being rescued from mud after deadly flash floods swept through the Nepal-Tibet border leaving more than 160 people dead and hundreds missing. The Nepalese army and armed police forces have been rescuing flooding victims, although many rescuers are struggling to reach the disaster zone on the Tibet side.

item.title: Norwegians lay flowers at palace as King Harald's condition worsens
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.76
- Published Norwegians have laid flowers in front of the palace in Oslo after the royal household said King Harald V's condition in hospital had become "extremely serious". His wife, Queen Sonja, and his son, Crown Prince Haakon, cancelled royal engagements to be at his bedside at Oslo University Hospital with other members of the family. They all stayed for several hours, and then during the evening Haakon was seen returning with Crown Princess Mette-Marit. The 89-year-old has been in hospital for 10 days receiving treatment for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia. Late on Thursday afternoon the palace issued an update to say his condition was unchanged. Having been on the throne since 1991, King Harald is Europe's oldest head of state. Crown Prince Haakon, 53, the successor to the Norwegian throne, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave. King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for haemolytic anaemia, a condition that causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced, and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath. There was a sombre mood in Oslo as Norwegians followed the comings and goings of the royal family. Crowds milled around in Palace Square throughout the day as Norwegian public TV scrapped its schedule to cover the story. Although no-one in the royal family spoke, the message was clear that it had become an important moment to visit the king. Among those visiting the hospital were Crown Princess Mette-Marit who arrived with Haakon, as well as her son Marius Borg Høiby, who is under house arrest during his appeal against a conviction for rape. King Harald's sister, Princess Astrid, also visited the hospital, along with Haakon and Mette-Marit's children Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre cancelled a planned trip to Germany, where he was expected to meet Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday. "The whole nation is with us as we send warm thoughts to the king and the rest of the royal family," he said in a statement. The king has had multiple health problems in recent years which have forced him to scale back his royal duties. He was fitted with a pacemaker in 2024 after falling ill on holiday in Malaysia. The Norwegian royal family has already faced a challenging year in 2026. Crown Princess Mette-Marit received a lung transplant in June after she had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis in 2018. The transplant came two days after Høiby was sentenced to four years in prison after being convicted of two counts of rape. He had denied the most serious charges and is to appeal the sentence. Høiby, 29, was four when his mother married Crown Prince Haakon and is not himself a royal figure. Also earlier in the year, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. She later apologised to Norway's king and queen for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him.

item.title: What we should make of CIA boss's secret trip to Moscow
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.32
- Published President Donald Trump said John Ratcliffe's trip to Russia was a "semi-routine" visit but there is nothing routine about the CIA chief making a secret, 10,000-mile return dash to Moscow. Ratcliffe met Russian intelligence officials on Tuesday - notably his opposite number in Russia's overseas spy agency, Sergei Naryshkin - after arriving unannounced on a US military plane, the Kremlin confirmed. It's been nearly five years since his predecessor William Burns made this trip and that was at a similarly tense time, just as Russia was drawing up plans to invade Ukraine. So, this is probably serious. In the absence of any official US comment on the reason for the mission, it is being widely reported Ratcliffe's trip was to warn Moscow not to escalate in relation to the stalemate in Ukraine - possibly by taking action against Nato members. One US official told Politico that the "meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states". The UK is also in Russian crosshairs. On Thursday, a foreign ministry spokeswoman said Russia could strike British military targets as retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russia using British missiles. And a drone carrying an explosive which was discovered at an airport in the German city of Leipzig was probably Russian, security experts have said. News of Ratcliffe's visit follows reports of US intelligence assessments that President Vladimir Putin was planning a limited assault on a Nato ally. But you don't need the world's most powerful electronic eavesdropping organisation – the US National Security Agency – to know that Putin is under mounting domestic pressure to "do something" to break the deadlock. Ukraine's deep strikes with long-range drones have not only hammered Russia's energy industry, they have brought the war home to ordinary Russians. Nothing says things are not going to plan more than long queues for petrol and billowing smoke coming from stricken oil refineries. The Kremlin sees these attacks as Nato fighting an indirect war on Russia by using Ukraine as a proxy. So how will Russia respond? There is a broad spectrum of possibilities here. These include stepping up the ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine that Moscow is already launching, including targeting the centre of Kyiv, knowing that Ukraine is running dangerously low on Patriot interceptors to stop them. It could entail expanding the undeclared "hybrid war" that Russia is already suspected of waging against Nato countries, using sophisticated cyber-attacks, drone incursions and using not-so-sophisticated criminals to carry out arson attacks on munitions factories. But at the even more alarming end of the scale there are other potential scenarios which the Kremlin may be considering, urged on by hardliners. One is to distract attention from its obvious failure to win the war in Ukraine by testing Nato's resolve through a limited attack on a Baltic state. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were all once part of the Soviet Union, effectively ruled from Moscow until 1991. Today they are all members of Nato, while still being home to substantial Russian-speaking communities. Putin will be well aware of Donald Trump's periodic disdain for Nato and he may have calculated that a low-key attack on say, Lithuania, is not going to trigger Nato's mutual self-defence clause – Article 5 – and that the US will not respond. In which case it would make sense for part of the CIA chief's unexplained mission to Moscow was to remind Russia that the US is still fully committed to Article 5. Lithuania is of special interest to the Kremlin as it has a common border with Poland known as the "Suwalki Gap". Just 60 miles long, this strip of land is all that separates Russia's client state Belarus from its nuclear-armed exclave of Kaliningrad, which is separated from mainland Russia. If Russia were to seize that it would effectively cut off those three Baltic states by land from their Nato neighbours. Then there is the question of tactical nuclear warheads. It has long been said that Russian military doctrine views these small but highly destructive weapons as an integral part of its order of battle. Moscow has been warned off, by friend and foe alike, not to break the 81-year long taboo on using nuclear weapons in anger. Yet this could still be a tempting option for Vladimir Putin to "escalate to de-escalate" by demonstrating to Ukraine that it has such catastrophic weapons at its disposal it would be better for Kyiv to capitulate to Moscow's terms now or face annihilation. Of course, in the absence of any clear, attributable, official confirmation from the US as to what this sudden CIA dash to Moscow was all about then it is always possible it was about something else. That could be trying to persuade Russia to end its military cooperation with Iran, for example, or maybe about more prisoner swaps or the prospect of a mass mobilisation of Russian troops. But make no mistake, this trip was highly unusual and it came at a time of rising tension between Moscow and the West. Something is almost certainly up.

item.title: 'Silence is complicity' - top footballer hits out over Cameroon femicides
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.02
- Published The killing of at least eight women in a week has sparked outrage in Cameroon, with many calling on the government to do more to protect women and girls. Among those who have spoken out is renowned footballer Nchout Njoya Ajara, who has called for an end to the "tragic wave" of targeting women, saying "silence is complicity". The government has also raised concern about the rise in attacks. At least 50 women have been killed between January and April this year, compared to 77 last year, according to official figures. In the latest case on Tuesday, a 44-year-old woman was killed in a hotel room in the capital, Yaoundé. She was allegedly stabbed to death by a 22-year-old who was later arrested. "Being a woman in Cameroon should never be a risk," said Ajara, who is one of Cameroon's greatest female footballers. The 33-year-old striker has played professionally in Russia, Sweden, Norway, Spain, Italy and Saudi Arabia for clubs including Atlético Madrid and Inter Milan. "In the face of the tragic wave of femicides that has hit our country in recent days, silence is complicity," Ajara said. In a statement, the opposition Cameroon Renaissance Movement (CRM) party said it was outraged by the "tragic recurrence of domestic femicides" and accused the government of being passive about the issue. The femicide cases, most of which are attributed to domestic violence, have been reported in different parts of the country. In a video published by state media, the minister for Women's Empowerment and the Family, Marie-Thérèse Abena Ondoa, condemned the "worrying" rise in the number of the killings, and said the government was working to address the problem. She mentioned a bill to protect women against gender-based violence, which she said was being reviewed by the prime minister. But civil society and women's rights groups have denounced what they perceive as the government's delay in turning the bill into law. A parliamentary session, the last one for the year, is due to be held in November. However, Viviane Tathi, whose organisation documents cases of femicide in the country, told the BBC she was not sure that the bill would be passed at the session. "We are worried because the November parliamentary session focuses on budgetary debates…So, we don't know by what magic this bill will be passed," she said. She has called for the creation of a special court to handle family disputes, which lead to domestic violence. According to the latest UN data, Africa had both the highest total number of femicide victims and the highest rate relative to its population in 2024 - with an estimated 22,600 cases, external. The numbers are an estimate as some cases of femicide are believed to go unreported and many governments do not consistently record the information.

item.title: Five unwritten rules for visiting Spain
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 5.17
'Paella is just for lunch' and other unwritten rules for visiting Spain Spain is famous for its laid-back lifestyle, but beneath the long lunches and late nights are social codes that shape everyday life. Our expert explains how to read them. While Spain is beloved for its beautiful beaches, romantic architecture and delicious food culture, one of its strongest draws is its famously relaxed pace. No hay prisa ("no rush") and tranquilo ("relax") are oft-uttered phrases here; meals are drawn out and nightlife lasts until morning. Even non-Spanish speakers know the meaning of siesta. Get to know your expert Jill Petzinger is a British journalist and professional travel advisor who specialises in Spain and Southern Europe. Based in Valencia since 2021, she has travelled extensively throughout Spain to explore the many regional cuisines and cultural traditions. But "relaxed" doesn't mean there's no order. Beneath Spain's easy-going surface are silent social codes that shape everything from how people queue to how they structure their days. Instinctive rather than explicitly stated, Spain's unwritten social rules are often based on respect for regional identity, a belief that life is best lived sociably in public and a historical need to work with, not against, the searing Sun. Locals might not say them out loud, but that doesn't make them any less important to learn. From relinquishing your personal space to skipping paella at dinner, here are five unwritten rules that will help you understand Spain from the inside. 1. Trust the invisible queue Try to order at a covered market, pharmacy, bakery, bar or local shop in Spain and you'll typically find people standing around randomly, no clear line in sight. It may seem confusing to the outsider, but there's a deeply ingrained system at play, rooted in a cultural preference for interaction, informality and social trust. "Queues" in Spain do indeed exist, but they are typically spread-out crowds rather than prim lines because of space constraints in small premises or market aisles; standing where it's most convenient solves the issue. But how do you know when it's your turn? What to do: When you arrive, approach the closest person and ask "¿Quién es el último?" (Who's last?) or simply "¿El último?" They will point to whomever is. Once you know who's last, you're free to walk along the displays and peruse what to buy without losing your place. But stay alert: you will get asked "¿El último?", too. 2. Don't assume the meal is over when it's over You've just had the last bites of Spanish tortilla and the last drops of Rioja. But before you ask for the bill, look around. The tables next to you, strewn with empty glasses and crumpled napkins, may look like they've finished too, but they're just entering another phase: the ritual known as la sobremesa. Literally translated as "over the table", la sobremesa is the hour (or hours) after the meal when everyone settles in for a long conversation. It may involve another round of coffee or drinks, but there's no pressure: la sobremesa is all about enjoying each other's company. The tradition is thought to stretch back to the agricultural past, when families sat around the table after lunch as it was still too hot return to the fields immediately. Most Spaniards may no longer till the fields, but the sobremesa continues its role in maintaining relationships. The joy of enjoying each meal for as long as possible has never gone out of style.
