What to do: Simply relax, put away your phone and keep chatting away. Waiters are used to letting people enjoy their conversations, so just raise a hand to ask for the bill when you're (really) ready to leave. And feel free to linger even longer. 3. Follow the Sun Spain's famously late rhythm can bewilder visitors, with dinners that last until midnight and shops that close for hours after lunch. But there's a logic behind the seemingly languorous rhythm. In Spain, people work with, not against, the Sun. Historically, Spanish farmers started the day early to get their work done before the Sun grew too hot, saving lunch until they were through. Then, in the 1940s, General Franco moved the clocks forward to align with Nazi Germany. Though the country now found itself in the Central European time zone, many stuck to the traditional solar schedule: lunch at 13:00 became lunch at 14:00 as the sun reached its zenith an hour later than before, and dinner happened later, too, as the light now lasted longer. More like this: In Spain, the workday is also slightly longer than the EU average: 36.3 hours per week versus 35.9 hours. Perhaps that's why Spain's famous "siesta" is increasingly less the norm, since 80% of its population now lives in cities. Unable to head home at lunchtime and have a nap, workers now often return to the office or use the post-lunch time to tackle chores. What to do: Shape your day around avoiding the worst of the afternoon Sun between 13:00 and 18:00 – a light breakfast. Check shop hours to avoid slogging through the heat to a shuttered destination, and keep in mind that only tourist restaurants open at 19:00. If you can hold off until 20:30 or 21:00 you'll be able to eat at better establishments. Consider a strategic siesta to help you stave off the hunger, or prepare for a long night. 4. Make room for the crowd Spain is a tactile nation, where touching an arm for emphasis, greeting with hugs and (lots of) kisses, bumping shoulders in a bar and standing close to strangers in a line are all everyday aspects of social behaviour – though they can surprise visitors from places with stricter norms around personal proximity. Furthermore, whether you find yourself in the city or the village, Spanish social life has traditionally been lived in public places like plazas, bars and streets. These shared spaces can get quite closely packed, meaning you end up very close to your neighbours by default. What to do: Don't automatically read physical closeness as rudeness. Stake out your own (little) space but accept that you'll still catch accidental bumps and jostles in busy areas. If you need to squeeze past someone, a simple "perdón" (sorry) suffices, and almost always elicits "no pasa nada" (no problem) from the other person. 5. Don't order paella for dinner or sangria at a bar Thanks to Spain's thriving tourist industry, you'll find the same supposed Spanish staples – sangria, paella and tapas – wherever you go. But Spain is a huge country, with 17 autonomous communities on the mainland, and an equal number of regional cuisines. Traditionally, people ate what was produced locally, and that love for and loyalty towards regional identity when it comes to food is still strong today. Embrace the opportunity to enjoy the beloved dishes of the city you're visiting. Paella is revered as a native dish of Valencia and Catalonia, but wherever you try it, do it like the Spanish and order it just at lunchtime, as it is considered a heavy meal to digest. Tapas bars will serve regional specialties depending on the city, but the sheer creative variety of pintxos is best enjoyed in their Basque homeland. If you're in Madrid in the colder months, don't miss the famous meaty chickpea cocido stew; enjoy gazpacho in Andalusia and most of Spain in the summer. Year-round, consider swerving the sangria. Locals do drink it, but it's not regarded a bar drink: it's more commonly consumed as a punch at parties. What to do: If a restaurant has a photo menu, it will likely be a tourist trap. To explore regional dishes, try a three-course menú del dia in local restaurants during weekdays. These menus are dying out in Spain partly because of shorter lunch breaks and the rise of new, trendier eateries, so look out for places full of locals with daily chalkboard menus, generally indicating fresh, seasonal food. To drink at the bar like a local, order the nationally adored tinto de verano, a mix of red wine and lemonade that contains no hard liquor, or tiny caña draft beers, which stay colder longer. --

item.title: Why Is Loonen Water So Hyped?
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.15
To every generation, an expensive, hype-driven water is bestowed. Or at least, that’s what it’s felt like for the last quarter of a century. See: Fiji water, the status symbol bottle of the early 2000s, later replaced by millennial La Croix, itself usurped by the Gen Z cult of Liquid Death in the early 2020s. In 2026, Loonen is part of a new vanguard of what’s being dubbed as “wellness waters,” bottled waters that appeal to people hoping to optimize their health. Some of these waters are infused with oxygen, others with hydrogen, and still others advertise that they’re alkaline and filled with electrolytes. In an era where companies are built off what they infuse and add, Loonen does the opposite. The brand goes hard on what’s not in each bottle. Namely microplastics, the highly discussed health risk quickly becoming the scourge of the 2020s. The brand hit the market in November of 2025, but it has quickly become something of a phenomenon. Loonen’s tall, wavy bottle began making appearances in the feeds of influencers like Brooks Marks and celebrities like Dua Lipa. It popped up in viral grocery stores like Meadow Lane, Happier Grocer and Erewhon. Then it was everywhere. “What the fuck is Loonen Water,” one thread in r/NYCinfluencersnark asked. The answer, in short: It’s a luxury bottled water brand that sells for nearly $6 per bottle (the high-end of the price scale for similar products) and markets itself as perfectly pure—but that’s only part of the story. Why is Loonen so popular? Some of Loonen’s success can be attributed to the company’s clever influencer marketing. “We send water to people who we think might love the product,” cofounder Clara Sieg says of Loonen’s strategy. She also says people love Loonen for its bottle. “It’s thin, it feels nice in hand. It has a wide spout. You can [dump] your electrolyte powders into it,” Sieg says. Influencer approval and a luxe bottle have made Loonen feel like a high-end product; one of many signifiers that gesture toward someone’s wealth and status—you’re not just staying hydrated, you’re living better. But Loonen’s success also speaks to a larger consumption trend: Buying water is now about more than quenching your thirst—it’s about more than hydrating, even. Consumers want water that feels like it helps optimize their health. It’s the same thinking that’s behind the protein-maxxing trend, the MAHA movement, and even the wave of raw milk lovers. People are distrustful of our foodways, and they’ll pay a premium for products that hold the promise of promoting wellness. For its part, Loonen leans on its purity claims. In a world where it’s increasingly difficult (or, perhaps, impossible) to avoid microplastics, Loonen has built a brand touting being microplastic-free, with frequent lab testing to back it up. Still, some water experts aren’t impressed with Loonen’s water, dubbing it simply processed spring water with a catchy label. “Americans love marketing stories with a sprinkle of fear mongering,” says water sommelier Martin Riese. “I am too hydrated for that.” What risks do microplastics in bottled water pose? To stand apart in a crowded luxury water field, Loonen extols its purity and transparency around testing. It’s processed and bottled without touching any plastic, and each batch is tested by a third-party laboratory for organic and inorganic compounds, including microplastics, pesticides, and forever chemicals. Those results are posted on Loonen’s website and regularly updated. According to a review of studies published in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology, microplastics are basically everywhere. They’re in bodies of water, soil, the atmosphere, and food systems. A study published in Frontiers in Chemistry suggests there’s evidence, too, that bottled water contains more microplastic than tap water. Microplastics are linked to a range of pretty bad health outcomes—cancer, respiratory disease, reproductive health, and “may also systematically accelerate the aging process and increase the risk of age-related diseases,” according to the review. There’s also research that indicates microplastics cause disruptions to our endocrine system, which regulates our hormones. That disruption may affect our development, metabolism, immunity, and brain development, according to experts. Is Loonen really more pure than other waters? Here’s the thing: Most bottled waters are actually just processed tap water that originate in the municipal system. Companies like Coca-Cola and Pepsi—who own Dasani and Aquafina, respectively—take tap water, treat it (which typically means removing some minerals deemed impurities), bottle it, and sell it at a markup. Other bottled water companies often process water using plastic, which would increase the risk of contamination. Yes, tap water is lower in microplastics than most bottled water, but bottling that tap water in plastic means microplastics leech into it. One recent study found nearly 250,000 plastic particles in a liter of bottled water. Because Loonen is bottled in glass instead of plastic or plastic-coated aluminum; sealed with a cap that the company says is unpainted, uncoated, and PFAs- and BPA-free; and not processed using plastic, the risk of microplastic contamination is negligible.

item.title: BA's Best Apple Pie
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.06
As cookbook author Claire Saffitz notes, this apple pie recipe is “something you can’t rush.” It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if you’re making it for Thanksgiving. The good news is, the trouble is worth it; first published in 2016, it’s been a reader (and staff) favorite for a decade. The glossy, warmly spiced filling gets its concentrated flavor from simmering fresh apple cider with a fragrant vanilla bean and the juices released by the sugared and spiced apples. (No vanilla bean? Stir in 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract after removing the reduced cider mixture from the heat.) You’ll toss the intensely appley syrup with the sliced fruit just before assembling your pie and sliding it into the oven. Pink Lady apples are our first choice here. Their firm texture and bright flavor make them exceptional for balancing the sweetness. Honeycrisp, Braeburn, Jonagold, and Granny Smith are excellent alternatives. Using a mix of apple varieties will give your apple pie even more complexity. For more options, see our guide to the best apples for baking. Apple pie FAQ Can I use apple cider vinegar instead of apple cider? No. The filling calls for fresh, unfiltered apple cider—the kind you drink—not apple cider vinegar. Cider vinegar is used only in the pie dough. Substituting it for the fresh cider in the filling will make your pie extremely sour. Do I have to peel the apples? Not necessarily. Peeling the apples creates a more uniform filling, but leaving them unpeeled won’t make or break your pie. If you don’t mind the texture of cooked apple skins, feel free to skip that step. Why is there a gap between my apple filling and the top crust? As the pie bakes, the crust will puff and set. Meanwhile, the apples soften and shrink, which can leave some space between the crust and filling. To minimize the gap, cut the apples into thin slices rather than wedges and pack them evenly and snugly into the bottom crust before adding the top crust. How do I know when apple pie is done? The top should be deeply golden brown, but don’t judge by the crust alone. The pie’s juices should be thick and bubbling. This pie takes 1½–2 hours at 375°F. If the crust is getting too dark before the filling is ready, tent the pie loosely with foil and continue baking. Can I use store-bought pie crust? Most store-bought pie dough is sized for a standard pie dish and may not fit a deep-dish one. It may also brown more quickly than homemade dough, which could cause the crust to get too dark during this pie’s long bake. If using store-bought dough, watch the pie closely and tent it loosely with foil as needed. Watch Claire make apple pie here: Recipe information - Total Time 3 hours plus cooling - Yield 8 Servings Ingredients Dough 3½ 2 1½ 1½ 2 Filling and Assembly 4 ⅓ ¼ 2 2 ½ ¼ ¼ 1½ 1 2 1 2 Special Equipment Need to make a substitution? Preparation - DoughStep 1Pulse 3½ (438 g) cups all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in food processor to combine. Add 1½ cups (3 sticks) chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and process until largest pieces of butter are pea-size. Transfer to a large bowl. Step 2Combine 2 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar and ½ cup ice-cold water in a small bowl and drizzle over flour mixture, mixing with a fork to combine. Mix until shaggy pieces form, then knead in bowl a couple of times with your hands to bring together (dough will look very clumpy, dry, with loose bits). Transfer large clumps of dough to work surface, drizzle 1 Tbsp. cold water over remaining flour mixture in bowl and knead again to bring it together. Place on top of dough on work surface. Working with half of the dough, press into a single mass, incorporating dry bits, then pat down to make a ¾"-thick square. Using a bench scraper or knife, divide dough into 4 pieces. Stack pieces on top of one another, placing any unincorporated dry bits in between layers, and press down to combine. Form dough into a ¾"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic wrap. Repeat with remaining dough. Chill at least 2 hours. Do Ahead: Pie dough can be made 5 days ahead. Keep chilled, or freeze up to 1 month. - Filling and AssemblyStep 3Toss 4 lb. Pink Lady or other firm, sweet-tart apples, peeled, cored, thinly sliced, ⅓ cup (packed; 68 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 2 tsp. ground cinnamon, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. plus ⅛ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. ground allspice, and ¼ tsp. ground cardamom in a large bowl to coat. Let apples sit until they start to release their juices, at least 1 hour and up to 3 hours. Step 4Let pie dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes to soften. Working one at a time, roll out disks of dough on a lightly floured surface ⅛" thick. Stack on a parchment-lined baking sheet, separating layers with a sheet of parchment, and chill while you prepare the filling. Step 5Place 1½ cups unfiltered apple cider in a medium saucepan and scrape in seeds from 1 vanilla bean, split lengthwise; add pod. Bring to a boil and cook, whisking occasionally, until reduced by two-thirds. Pour off juices that have accumulated in bowl of apples and add to apple cider. Return to a boil and cook until reduced to about ½ cup; remove vanilla pod. Stir 2 Tbsp. cornstarch into 3 Tbsp. cold water in a small bowl to dissolve, then whisk into apple cider. Cook, whisking constantly, until cider mixture is very thick and bubbling, about 1 minute. Let cool slightly, then scrape over apples; toss to coat. Step 6Carefully transfer dough round to pie dish. Lift up edges and allow dough to slump down into dish (if too cold to be pliable, let it warm up slightly first). Press dough firmly against sides and bottom of plate. Trim, leaving about 1" overhang. Beat 1 large egg with 1 tsp. cold water in a small bowl and brush over edges of dough. Scrape apple mixture into bottom crust, arranging apples in an even, compact layer; dot filling with 2 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Place remaining dough round over filling. Trim edges of top round, leaving a ½" overhang. Fold edge of bottom round up and over; press together to seal. Crimp edge and brush top with remaining egg wash. Sprinkle with demerara sugar and use a sharp knife to cut a few vents in top. Place pie pan on a foil-lined rimmed baking sheet and chill in freezer 10 minutes. Place oven rack in lower third of oven; preheat oven to 375°. Step 7Bake pie until top crust is deep golden brown and juices are thick and bubbling, 1½–2 hours (yes: 2 hours!). Transfer pie to a wire rack; let pie cool at least 4 hours before serving. Serve slices with a dollop of whipped cream or a scoop of vanilla ice cream (if using). Do Ahead: Pie can be made 1 day ahead. Let cool; store covered with foil at room temperature. Editor’s note: This recipe was originally published in our October 2016 issue as “BA’s Best Apple Pie” and has been updated for style with additional guidance. Head this way for more of our favorite Thanksgiving desserts →

item.title: BA’s Best Snickerdoodle Cookies
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.04
Snickerdoodles should be soft in the center, lightly crisp at the edges, and unmistakably tangy from cream of tartar (yes, it adds flavor!). Melted butter—not softened—encourages the cookies to spread and gives them a denser, chewier texture, while brown sugar helps keep the centers soft. A roll in cinnamon sugar provides the classic finish. The dough will look quite soft when first mixed—that’s expected with melted butter. Letting it rest for 30 minutes gives the flour time to hydrate and makes the dough easier to scoop. Give the cookies plenty of room on the baking sheet, and pull them while the centers are still puffed and soft. Can I make snickerdoodles without cream of tartar? Cream of tartar gives snickerdoodles their signature tang and works with baking soda to help the cookies puff. While other acids can technically take its place, they can alter the cookies’ flavor, texture, and spread. For the best results, we recommend sticking to cream of tartar. Read more about cream of tartar at Epicurious → Why did my snickerdoodles spread too much? The dough may have been too warm. Make sure the melted butter has cooled slightly before mixing and let the dough rest for the full 30 minutes before scooping. If the dough is still very soft, chill it briefly until easier to handle. Leave about 3 inches between cookies—they’re supposed to spread. Do I really need to beat the eggs for 3 minutes? Yep! And set a timer; it’s longer than you think. Beating the eggs for the full 3 minutes aerates the mixture, helping the cookies puff and develop their characteristic crackly tops. Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour - Yield Makes about 32 Ingredients 3 2 1 ¾ 1 1 ½ 1 2 1 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Whisk 3 cups (375 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. cream of tartar, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Step 2Using an electric mixer on medium speed, beat 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter, melted, cooled slightly, 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar, and ½ cup (packed; 100 g) light brown sugar in a large bowl, stopping and scraping down sides as needed, until combined. Scrape in seeds from 1 vanilla bean, split lengthwise (reserve pod for another use) or add 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, add 2 large eggs, room temperature, and beat until mixture is pale yellow and starting to thicken and falls from beaters in a ribbon-like stream when lifted out of the bowl, about 3 minutes. Step 3Reduce mixer speed to low and, with motor running, gradually add dry ingredients to butter mixture; beat, stopping and scraping down sides and bottom of bowl as needed, until just combined. Let dough sit at room temperature at least 30 minutes to allow flour to hydrate. (Dough will be very loose but will thicken as it sits.) Step 4Place racks in upper and lower thirds of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 1 Tbsp. ground cinnamon and remaining 2 Tbsp. (25 g) granulated sugar in a small bowl. Step 5Using a #30 cookie scoop or 2 (heaping) tablespoonfuls, portion out dough and roll into 1½" balls. Working with a few at a time, toss in cinnamon sugar to coat. Arrange 10–12 cookies each on 2 parchment-lined baking sheets (use 3 if you have them), spacing about 3" apart. (Do not flatten; cookies will spread and crack as they bake.) Step 6Bake cookies, rotating top to bottom and front to back, until edges are golden and firm but centers are still soft and puffed, 8–10 minutes. Let cool on baking sheets 10 minutes, then transfer to a wire rack and let cool completely. Repeat baking process with remaining cookies. Do Ahead: Dough can be made 3 days ahead. Cover and chill. Bring to room temperature before portioning and coating in cinnamon-sugar. Editor’s note: This snickerdoodle recipe was first published in April 2017; it was updated in 2026 in response to reader feedback. We increased the amount of flour for a more controlled texture and spreading, added a weight measurement for the flour, clarified the instructions, and added vanilla extract and vanilla bean paste as alternatives to a whole vanilla bean. Head this way for more of our favorite cookies for the holidays→

item.title: Best Kitchen Scales, Tested Over a Decade of Baking (2026)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.61
I’ve been an avid home baker for well over a decade (my first stint in “food media” was a baking blog I started in middle school!), and I can confirm that there is no single tool quite as important to the outcome of your baked goods as a simple kitchen scale. Bon Appétit’s Test Kitchen team agrees, which is why you’ll see gram measurements in the baking recipes on our site. Our top picks - Best kitchen scale overall: Escali Primo Digital Food Scale - Best budget kitchen scale: Amazon Basics Kitchen Scale - For bakers who are also coffee nerds: Fellow Tally Scale For the skeptics, try this actual experiment, which I did with senior editor Noah Kaufman: Make one batch of cookies with flour scooped directly from the bag and weighed, and another with flour spooned and leveled into a measuring cup. The two batches will turn out completely different. Scooped flour packs more densely into the cup, so you end up with more flour than the recipe calls for, and that will have a major impact on your finished product. A scale is the secret to staying true to the recipe every single time. Instagram content Another bonus of a kitchen scale? In most cases, you can kiss measuring cups and spoons goodbye, which means far fewer dishes to clean once your bakes are in the oven. Scales aren’t just for bakers, either. They make portioning burger patties and meatballs easier, streamline meal prep, and keep your Sunday morning pancake routine cleaner. I’ve tested 16 models over several years and consulted Shilpa Uskokovic, BA senior Test Kitchen editor and co-owner of Hani’s Bakery, to find the best kitchen scale for home cooks. The winner is just $27. New in this update: I tested the new ThermoWorks Gravitas Precision Kitchen Scale, but ultimately, while it can serve a real purpose for larger projects, I didn’t think its performance matched its price tag. You can read my full review below. Best kitchen scale overall: Escali Primo Digital Food Scale Pros and cons Pros: - Inexpensive - Comes in an array of colors - Lightweight and compact - Very accurate Cons: - Only measures in 1-gram increments - Display isn’t backlit Specs Size: 8.5 x 6 x 1.5" Capacity: 11 lb. Gradation: 1 g Auto shut-off: 4 minutes 30 seconds Power: AA batteries (included) This Escali Primo has held the top spot in our testing for over six years and has been a favorite in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen for far longer than that. “This scale has been with me for more than a decade of my career, staying faithfully by my side through 12-hour shifts in pastry kitchens, bouts of religious recipe testing, and weekly sessions of casual baking,” says senior Test Kitchen editor and resident baking whiz Shilpa Uskokovic. It’s durable, accurate, intuitive to use, and affordable—pretty much everything we could ask of a kitchen scale. What we love: The Escali Primo is lightweight, comes in a variety of fun colors, and has a simple two-button interface to turn it on, tare it, and toggle between ounces, pounds, and grams. In testing, it was responsive and precise, quick to tare, and delivered accurate readings every time. Its 4.5-minute auto shut-off is among the longest of any model we tested, so you won’t lose your measurements mid-bake. Plus, its 11-pound capacity is large enough to accommodate any task a home cook might ask of it. Performance aside, the Escali Primo has several design features that helped it stand out. For one, the fact that the weighing platform is elevated and offset from the base means you can easily read the display or use the buttons even when measuring into a large, wide mixing bowl. The plastic body and sealed control panel make it a breeze to wipe down after a floury baking session and also keep stray crumbs from getting stuck in any crevices. Another detail we like? The four rubberized feet keep it stable on your kitchen counter. The Escali Primo has proven quite durable as we’ve continued to test it long-term, another reason why it’s a perennial favorite among our Test Kitchen editors. Shilpa again: “It’s compact and easy to store, it’s easy to wipe clean, it toggles between grams and ounces seamlessly, and it’s reliably accurate." What we’d leave: The Escali can only measure in 1-gram increments. While this was typical of most scales we tested, those looking to use their kitchen scale for dialing in their coffee routine will want something more precise (though coffee scales are kind of their own thing). Unlike some pricier models, the Escali’s display is not backlit, but we didn’t find this to be an issue. It’s also worth noting that the Escali is not a touchscreen device, so you’ll need to use a bit of pressure on the buttons. Best budget kitchen scale: Amazon Basics Kitchen Scale Pros and cons Pros: - Very inexpensive - Lightweight and compact - Pretty accurate Cons: - Not quite as accurate as our top pick - Buttons can be prone to collecting crumbs and grime Specs Size: 8.3 x 7 x 1.3" Capacity: 11 lb. Gradation: 1 g Auto shut-off: NA Power: AAA batteries (included) Amazon Basics products are not consistent across the board, but this scale is a certifiable hit. At about half the price of the Escali, it’s a good option if you’re not positive about this scale thing and want to spend as little as humanly possible to do so. What we love: There are a lot of similarities between the Amazon Basics scale and the overall winner. The Amazon Basics scale has the same two-button setup, a similar elevated weighing platform that makes it easy to see the display, and the same 11-pound maximum capacity. It’s made of plastic with a stainless-steel platform that’s easy to wipe down and is just a touch larger than the Escali at 7 inches across. In testing, I was impressed by the Amazon scale’s accuracy, considering its price point. It responded to weight addition or removal almost as quickly as the Escali and provided an accurate readout about 99% of the time. That 1% weight change inaccuracy happened when someone repeatedly added weight or switched back and forth between units of measurement, and when it did happen, the reading was off by a minor amount. The problem could be fixed by removing what was on the scale, taring it, and starting over. For $10 (at the time of writing), you’d be hard-pressed to find a better model. What we’d leave: Unlike the Escali, the Amazon scale’s buttons lack any kind of laminated sealing to prevent crumbs or liquid from entering the crevices around them. As mentioned, this scale isn’t quite as accurate as the winner and it tended to overshoot an item’s actual weight at first (before correcting itself relatively quickly). And last, the stainless-steel platform is more prone to scratching or smudging than Escali’s plastic one. For bakers who are also coffee nerds: Fellow Tally Scale You’ll notice there aren’t any other scales marketed as coffee scales on this list, and that’s because the Fellow Tally was the only coffee scale we thought could plausibly work as an all-purpose model too. What we love: The Fellow Tally is one of our favorite coffee scales (especially for pour-over) thanks to features like a built-in timer and a “brew assist” that directs you on the proper ratio of coffee to water—but its 5.5-pound maximum capacity means it works for most home baking projects too. If you’re the kind of person who likes to nerd out over your brewing and baking techniques, this is your best bet unless you want to invest in two separate scales. In testing, we quite liked the Tally’s design for its tactile controls and easy-to-read OLED display, and appreciated its ability to measure grams, ounces, pounds, and milliliters (that milliliter measurement is calibrated for water, so one milliliter equals one gram; if you're measuring a heavier liquid like milk it will be slightly off). The elevated 6-inch platform is large enough to comfortably hold a mixing bowl while allowing easy visibility of the display. What we’d leave: This is undeniably a pricey scale, so unless you’re interested in its special coffee-making features, it's overkill. And while the 5.5-pound capacity should be enough for most things the average person would bake at home, if you see giant batches of sourdough or holiday cookies in your future, opt for the Escali. How we tested kitchen scales Calibration weight accuracy test To find out how accurate each scale was, I used a set of calibration weights. I tested each scale’s ability to give an accurate reading for the minimum amount of weight it claimed to be able to accommodate (usually 1 or 2 grams), and its ability to detect small changes when there was already weight on the platform. I also placed weights in various places on each scale’s platform to determine whether they could give an accurate reading regardless of whether the weight was in the center or at the edge. Cleaning test I coated each scale in a mixture of flour, water, and oil and let them sit overnight. I cleaned the residue off and noted which scales were easy to clean and resistant to any scratching or staining. Long-term testing I distributed winning scales to staffers to see how they fared after long-term use in our homes and in the Test Kitchen and added any long-term testing notes to reviews as they came in. What makes a good kitchen scale Accuracy and precision I looked for consistently accurate measurements and a short response time when adding and removing items of varying sizes and materials from each scale. I took into account how weight distribution affected the readings, looking for scales that delivered spot-on results regardless of where on the platform we placed the weights. I also took note of how precise each scale could be in its measurements, but found our favorite all-around options tended to measure in 1-gram increments. Ease of use I looked for scales that were intuitive to use without picking up a manual. Capacity I tested scales with weight capacities ranging from 1.65 to 16 pounds, but found that a maximum capacity of 11 pounds was more than enough for the tasks one might try to accomplish in a home kitchen. Construction I wanted a scale that felt durable, well-made, and stable on the counter and was also designed to be easy to clean. Size Unlike a stand mixer, a scale isn’t the kind of kitchen gadget most home cooks are looking to keep permanently on their counter. Lightweight, compact models that could be easily stashed in a cabinet were better. Price I took into account the relative price of each scale. After years of testing, we’ve found that you really don’t need to spend much to get a high-quality, highly accurate kitchen scale, so any models that were pricey needed to wow us with their design or extra features. Other kitchen scales we like These scales didn’t quite make our list of top picks, but they still impressed us in testing and might fit your needs depending on what you’re looking for. Escali Arti Glass Kitchen Scale This is another scale from the makers of our top overall pick. It’s sleeker and slightly more advanced, with a four-button control panel that includes the typical on-off, unit change, and tare functions, plus a “hold” feature that keeps your measurement on the screen rather than automatically shutting off after a given amount of time. We ultimately didn’t think the added feature and upgraded design merited spending an extra $10, but this is undoubtedly a good scale (and the rainbow of colorways available makes it easy to find a match for your kitchen decor). Oxo Good Grips Stainless-Steel Food Scale This Oxo scale is a favorite among professional chefs for its easy-to-clean stainless-steel weighing platform, handy pull-out display design (great for measuring into extra-large bowls), and accuracy. We liked it a lot, but didn’t feel it merited its price tag, which is about double that of the winning Escali at the time of writing. Editor’s note: This is a newer version of the model we tested. Kitchen scales we don’t recommend True to its name, this precision scale from Etekcity provides measurements in 0.1-gram increments as well as the option to measure in milliliters and fluid ounces (along with the typical grams and pounds/ounces). That said, we didn’t love that the instructions recommended using this scale with only the included plastic bowl and found that the stainless steel weighing platform scratched easily. This rechargeable digital kitchen scale seemed promising, with its 22-pound maximum weight, easy-to-clean weighing platform, Bluetooth-enabled app connectivity, customizable auto-off function, and host of premium features. However, it was one of the least accurate scales we tested: Our 5-gram nickel weighed in at a low of 2 grams and high of 6. For that reason, we don’t recommend it unless you’re buying a scale primarily for meal tracking reasons. The Zwilling Enfinigy Digital Food Scale was another promising option. It’s rechargeable via USB cord and has a sleek, buttonless design and 22-pound capacity. However, it wasn’t as accurate as we’d have liked, and despite how cool it looks, the lack of buttons turned out to be frustrating. We also disliked how the tab that switches the units of measurement is located underneath the scale. This scale is heavy-duty. It’s got a 16-pound max capacity, it can be charged with a plug-in A/C adapter, and it’s the size of a small kitchen appliance. It works well (and even allows you to measure using baker’s percentages), but unless you’re in a professional bakery setting, it’s overkill. At less than 3-by-3 inches, this scale is truly tiny. It’s an impressive little kitchen tool, able to provide measurements in 0.1 gram increments, but its maximum capacity of 1.65 pounds is just too small for most cooking or baking projects besides making coffee. This scale from Cuisinart has a glass weighing platform and removable stainless-steel bowl, but we ultimately didn’t love the idea of the bowl adding yet another piece of clutter to our kitchens. Besides that, this scale was less accurate than our top picks, had a short, 1-minute auto-off time, and was nearly double the price of the winning Escali. This scale lost for a couple reasons: It was less accurate than our winners and one of the most difficult scales to clean in our most recent round of testing. The display panel was prone to trapping crumbs and bits of flour, and the scale itself required intensive scrubbing to remove leftover residue. Like many of Joseph Joseph’s products, this scale has an interesting design. It’s made up of three prongs that fold into a small rectangle, making it easy to stash away when not in use. That said, this scale struggled in testing; it couldn’t detect small amounts of weight and was prone to reading the weight of your finger when you tapped its buttons. I had high hopes for this dual platform scale from the makers of some of our favorite pizza ovens. It’s got a sleek, low-profile design, wide capacity range (0.1–22 grams if you take into account both platforms), and handy light-up display. Unfortunately, we found both the small and big platforms inaccurate: The small platform struggled with picking up small changes and was often off by multiple tenths of a gram, and the big platform was inconsistent, often fluctuating between two readings or off by a couple grams. We noticed inaccuracies and inconsistencies with both of the KitchenAid’s platforms. The small scale is meant to be precise down to the hundredth of a gram, but it struggled to detect our .02-gram calibration weight and fluctuated between .19 and .20 when we weighed a 0.2-gram weight. The big scale was decidedly more inaccurate, off by 3–4 grams when we tested it with a 100-gram weight. Like all of Smeg’s products, the brand’s take on a kitchen scale is very cute. Unfortunately, while the design is aesthetically pleasing, it didn’t prove to be very functional. The scale is very bulky because of the built-in bowl, which can’t be removed from the base (though the stainless-steel bowl insert can be removed for cleaning). The scale’s base itself is sensitive to weight, which means pressing on the buttons with force can cause a temporary spike in the reading—and, more important, if you drop any ingredients on the base, the weight of said ingredient will be added to the total. We also found that this scale struggled to accurately report small (1- or 2-gram) changes in weight. I was very excited to test this scale from the brand behind our favorite cooking thermometers, but unfortunately it failed to impress me enough to merit a recommendation. The scale boasts the capability to measure down to the tenth of a gram, but according to ThermoWorks' product description, it does so with ±0.7 g accuracy. In testing, I found this to be true—readings were rarely accurate to the exact tenth. After testing the scale in his home kitchen for several weeks, senior commerce editor Noah Kaufman also noted that readings came in on the slow side, which made measuring ingredients that pour out quickly (like flour or liquids) tricky. I did appreciate the detachable display (helpful when using a large, wide bowl that might otherwise obscure the screen), but it wasn’t enough to outweigh the negatives—and besides, I’m of the opinion that there’s no reason for the average home cook to pay $120 for a scale when a $25 one performs incredibly well. We also tested the Ozeri Pronto, Etekcity Multifunction Food Kitchen Scale, and GDealer Tempered Glass Kitchen Scale, all of which have been discontinued. FAQ How do you use a kitchen scale? To use a kitchen scale, you’ll have to familiarize yourself with the concept of “tare.” Taring a scale allows you to reset the weight back to zero when you already have something on the weighing platform. This is particularly useful if you want to measure ingredients into a bowl (just place the bowl on the platform, click the tare button, and go on adding your ingredients), or if you want to measure multiple ingredients into that bowl without needing to add or subtract the existing weight in your head. What should you use a kitchen scale for? Baking is the obvious answer here, but the use cases for kitchen scales go far beyond the world of flour and butter. Use a scale to perfectly portion out meat for meatballs or burgers, aid in your meal prep for the week, or for any recipe where precise quantities are of the utmost importance. Get to know the expert Alaina Chou: Alaina has been testing products at Bon Appétit for over three years, which means she’s used dozens of air fryers, toasters, rice cookers, and—you guessed it—kitchen scales. She’s an avid baker who’s been a proponent of measuring by weight for the better part of a decade.

item.title: After Testing 16 Pizza Ovens, These Are the 5 I Recommend For Perfect Pies at Home (2026)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.59
Ever since I started testing pizza ovens four years ago, pizza night has become my family’s favorite excuse to get together. I’ll bring whatever in-season produce I find at the farmers market; my mom stops at our local cheesemonger for fresh mozzarella; my brother queues up an Italian playlist; and my sister pours the wine. If it’s a last-minute affair, my dad swings by our hometown pizzeria for dough. We crowd around the kitchen counter, stretching dough, piling on toppings, and catching up as we build one pie after another. Once the oven is fired up, the pizzas come out so quickly that we barely bother with plates. That's the magic of a backyard pizza oven. It turns making dinner into an occasion. Everyone gets involved, and suddenly a few humble ingredients have become the reason your family and friends are standing around the kitchen for three hours. But great homemade pizza does require a few things: good dough, good toppings, and an oven capable of getting much hotter than a standard home oven. Our top picks - Best outdoor pizza oven overall: Gozney Arc XL - Best budget pizza oven: Gozney Arc Lite - A great larger pizza oven: Ooni Koda Max 2 - Best electric pizza oven for outdoor use: Current Model P Smart Pizza Oven - A professional-level, dual-fuel splurge: Fontana Forni Volta After testing 16 pizza ovens for this story, I’ve learned that getting hot is only the beginning. The best ones hold their heat, recover quickly between pizzas, and produce the blistered, charred crust you’d expect from a great Neapolitan pizzeria. Just as important, they’re easy enough to use that you’ll want to fire one up even in the dead of winter, when the temperature is sub-freezing outside. (Yes, I’ve done this.) Ahead are the pizza ovens that impressed us most in testing, whether you’re looking to upgrade your weeknight pizza or feed a crowd at your next backyard party. New in this update: We tested two new outdoor pizza ovens this round. The Gozney Arc Lite, which is a smaller version of our best overall pick, became our new budget pick, unseating the Solo Stove Pi Prime. We also tested the Fontana Forta Volta 70, a pricey dual-fuel option with smart features, that we recommend if you're interested in shelling out a few thousand dollars for a luxe pizza-making experience. Best outdoor pizza oven overall: Gozney Arc XL Pros and cons Pros - Built-in digital thermometer shows you exact temperature at a glance - Single burner gives more control over cooking - Rolling flame arcs over the top of oven, allowing for bubbly cheese - Large cooking area Cons - Expensive Specs Size: 20.9" W x 24.8" L x 13.5" H Size of pizza accommodated: 16" Weight: 58.5 lb. Fuel source: Gas What we love: After testing over a dozen outdoor pizza ovens, Gozney’s Arc XL is the one I use regularly. It’s why we named it one of the best new products of 2025 in our Gear of the Year awards. The thing about the Arc XL—and all Gozney products, for that matter—is that you can tell it’s designed by people who think about every small detail. For example, it comes with a tiny metal tool that lets you adjust the pizza stone’s position by fractions of an inch until it’s exactly where you want it. And while some ovens require you to buy a separate infrared thermometer to measure temperature, this one has a built-in digital thermometer. The Arc XL’s signature feature is its namesake flame that arcs over the top of the oven. Most pizza ovens have long lines of side or rear burners, but this design mimics a traditional wood-fired oven. The single burner gave us way more control over the cook; whereas leaving a pie a little too long in one spot in other double-burner ovens would result in half the pie charring, it was much easier to recover from mistakes in the Arc XL. And with over 300 square inches of cooking space, there’s plenty of room on the stone to move a pie away from the direct flame. During our testing, we got far fewer burnt crusts and a perfect Neapolitan-style char every time. The rolling flame also allowed us to lift each pie to the flame to get blistered, bubbling cheese on top without worrying about burning the crust—something trickier to accomplish with shorter flame rows. While compact enough to live on a backyard table, the Arc XL also looks beautiful sitting on its custom stand, which keeps everything at the right height for a seamless pizza-making experience. What we’d leave: It's hard to find faults with the Arc XL. The only thing we can say is that it’s on the pricier end of our recommendations, but we think it’s well worth the investment. Long-term testing: After a year of testing, the Arc XL has held up great. I’ve gotten better at dialing in the flame and moving a pizza around the spacious stone, positioning it closer to or farther from the fire depending on whether I want more char on the crust or blistering on the cheese. But what keeps me coming back to the Arc XL is that it’s much more than a pizza oven. I’ve fire-roasted mushrooms and chicken thighs in it, and even baked a whole focaccia. It’s big enough that I keep finding new things to cook in it, which is a big part of why it remains my favorite. Best budget pizza oven: Gozney Arc Lite Pros and cons Pros - Same precise single-flame design as our top pick - Lightweight - Durable Cons - Slower heat-up (30 min to 800°F) Specs Size: 16.9” x 18.9” x 11.7” Size of pizza accommodated: 12" Weight: 26.4 lb. Fuel source: Gas Gozney's new Arc Lite carries the same design as our top-pick pizza oven, the Arc XL, for $400. That's $600 less, which puts our favorite pizza-making setup within reach at under half the price. What we love: One of the reasons the Arc XL is our top pick is because of its precise single-burner flame, which arcs over the top of the oven to get that desirable browning on top of the pie. The Arc Lite uses that same design. It's easy to dial in, and the mouth is wide and open enough that launching and turning a pie never feels cramped, even though you max out at a 12-inch pie. We ran it through our standard testing and then handed it to a few novice pizza makers, who pulled off evenly cooked pies with no burnt patches on their first attempts. That makes it one of the more forgiving ovens we've used for beginners. What we'd leave: There are some concessions. The 12-inch stone (versus 16 inches on the XL) runs a little small for our liking, and there's no built-in thermometer, so budget another $50 for an infrared thermometer to read your stone temp before you launch. Our test unit was also finicky to light, taking a few tries to catch, and when it was up and running it took 28 minutes to hit 800°F, a bit slower than we've seen with other small ovens. Even so, you're getting that arcing flame, which is the whole reason we love the XL. A great larger pizza oven: Ooni Koda 2 Max Pros and cons Pros - Quick heat up - Enormous opening - Two zone temperature control Cons - A little heavy if you're trying to store in between uses Specs Size: 36.5" x 32" x 15" Size of pizza accommodated: 20" Weight: 95 lb. Fuel source: Gas Tested by: Jeff Akin, contributor What we love: If you have the budget and space to upgrade, the 24-inch Ooni Koda 2 Max is as good as it gets without committing to some sort of immovable brick oven. At $1,199, the Koda 2 Max is on the pricey side for our tests, but it’s still less expensive than most professional-grade pizza ovens. The Koda 2 Max shares the same basic design as other ovens in the Koda line, with one big exception: two separately controlled burners, one on each side of the oven. This dual-burner functionality gives you greater control of the temperature and enables two-zone cooking. Because of its size, this oven takes longer to heat up, but thanks to the dual-burner setup, once it does it stays very hot. It continues to fire in even the coldest, windiest conditions. What we’d leave: As we said, it’s big, and as such, it burns through propane at approximately twice the rate as the smaller ovens we tested, so always be sure to have a backup tank in hand. Best electric pizza oven for outdoor use: Current Model P Smart Pizza Oven Pros and cons Pros - Quick heat up - Indoor/outdoor utility - Easy temperature control - Wide temperature range Cons - Quite large to keep on counter Specs Size: 17.5" x 21.2" x 14.21" Size of pizza accommodated: 12" Weight: 31 lb. Fuel source: Electric What we love: Electric pizza ovens have improved significantly over the past few years, and the Current Model P is an example of an electric oven that produces results rivaling those of gas ovens. Electric pizza ovens are quite large if you think of them as countertop appliances (as big as some outdoor models), which makes them particularly hard to store inside. That’s why we appreciate that the Model P can be kept outside year-round as long as you use a cover. The controls are intuitive and helpful. It has presets so you can pick the style of pizza you want and the corresponding temperature the oven should reach—for example, 850℉ for Neapolitan or 635℉ for New York—along with an estimated cook time. We made both Neapolitan and New York style in the Model P, and the bottoms came out evenly cooked with just the right amount of browning and bubbling on top, with no rotating required. The Model P is also a more versatile appliance than many electric pizza ovens. Thanks to a recent firmware update, the temperature settings can dip down to 350℉ so you can bake bread, roast vegetables, or even reheat pizza you previously made in it. What we’d leave: Although the presets are a nice touch, they can be a bit restrictive. At the moment, it's not possible to adjust the oven temperature once it reaches the set temperature. You have to turn the oven off and then back on to set a new temperature, which can be frustrating. Long-term testing: “I was especially drawn to the Current Model P's preset cooking modes that I could simply set and let preheat (ie: Neapolitan cooks at 800-850℉ for just a couple of minutes while New York-style needs a far lower temp around 500℉ for about 15 minutes). I appreciated the ample pizza stone that doesn't require turning (but you can if you'd like), and the cart and accessories bundle that truly streamlines the pizza-making experience when the party's on. Not only is the Current oven technically sound, but its user-friendly features are also ample enough to actually increase my likelihood of using it (near weekly, as of this writing), and that, perhaps, is its strongest feature.” —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor A professional-level, dual-fuel splurge: Fontana Forni Volta Pros and cons Pros - Dual fuel options - Incredible temperature control - Huge temperature range Cons - Almost industrial-level pricing - So, so heavy Specs Size: 34.6" x 28.9" x 21" Size of pizza accommodated: 24” x 20” cooking area; two 12" pizzas Weight: 238 lb. Fuel source: Electric and wood Tested by: Noah Kaufman, senior shopping editor What we loved: A problem budding home pizza makers run into frequently is that they either can’t or don’t know how to properly control the temperature of their ovens, resulting in such a hot stone that pies don’t get cooked all the way through before getting carbonized. That is the problem the Volta was designed to solve. With thermostatically programmable temperatures, it gets as close to dialing in 750℉ as anything else we’ve tried. And not only that, but the settable temperature range goes down as low as 300℉, meaning this really can act as a versatile second oven for roasting vegetables, proteins, even baking bread (although the way the burner throws heat over the top of the oven gives a broiling effect that’s not ideal for the job). It was ready to cook in less than half an hour, and even the smaller of the two models, the Volta 70, is luxuriously large, capable of holding two 12-inch pizzas easily. It’s so easy to use the gas burner in the oven that most people will probably not be interested in the feature, but the Volta has one of the easiest transitions from a gas oven to a wood-burning one (note that if you go the wood-burning route, you won’t be able to set the temperature). And finally, this is an oven of incredible quality. The steel and insulation make for a bulletproof cooking experience. The brand has been making ovens for 50 years and, no knock on the other recommendations in this piece, produces cooking equipment that would be right at home in a professional pizzeria. What we'd leave: The downsides of this oven are mostly what you’d expect: It’s quite expensive and requires a permanent commitment of your space. It weighs almost 250 pounds, and you’ll need to set it up either on a heavy-duty cart (Fontana sells one that adds $800 to the total price) or a well-built outdoor kitchen. And once you set it up, it’s not moving. It also comes with app connectivity that feels superfluous. Pizza ovens are generally quick, hands-on experiences, and of all the appliances that have been made “smart” with apps in the last decade, they are amongst the least valuable. Read Noah's full review of the Fontana Forni Volta 70. How we tested and evaluated pizza ovens We made a lot of pizza. For each oven, we started by cooking a basic Neapolitan-style Margherita at the maximum temperature of each oven (between 800–900℉), as well as a simple New York–style pie with raw sausage cooked between 600–700℉. From there, we tested a variety of pizza doughs (e.g., sourdough, pre-frozen, gluten-free, etc.), temperatures, and toppings to determine overall ease of use, finished-product quality, and value for the price. What to look for in a pizza oven Maximum temperature The thing that makes a pizza oven different from your regular oven is that it can get almost twice as hot. At least it can if it’s a good pizza oven. We looked for ovens that could hit close to 900℉ relatively quickly. Heat retention Though any individual Neapolitan pizza will only need about 90 seconds of cook time, we want an oven that will hold the temperature on its stone for longer pizza parties. Heat control It should be possible to adjust the temperature of the oven relatively easily, because we don’t always want to be cooking with the heat of 1,000 suns. Design Pizza ovens can be frustrating to use. We looked for versions with smart features like a wide opening to easily accommodate pies or burners oriented for consistent cooking. Other pizza ovens we liked Solo Stove Pi Prime The Solo Stove Pi Prime was our previous budget pick until it was unseated by the Gozney Arc Lite, which is also priced at $400. We still think it's a great pizza oven—particularly for beginners, thanks to the well-distributed flame along the back of the oven that covers half the pie and means less turning to get an even cook compared to the Lite's single flame. While the Pi Prime doesn’t have the bells and whistles of more expensive ovens, it does its most important job very well: It gets hot fast. In just 15 minutes, the stone preheats to more than 900℉ and is able to cook a Neapolitan-style pizza in 90 seconds. Weighing in at just 30 pounds, the Pi Prime is also relatively portable. The simple, familiar stainless-steel design requires no setup or additional accessories, and it’s easy to clean and store. The one thing it doesn't have that the Arc Lite does is a bespoke Booster that puts your countertop oven at a more comfortable height for making pizza—not a dealbreaker at all; the booster is just a nice-to-have. All-Clad 16" Outdoor Rotating Stone Gas Pizza Oven One of the most important skills you need to develop when making pizza in an outdoor oven is understanding when to rotate the pie. Wait too long, and you burn half the pie. Turn it too quickly, and you may not get the crispy bottom you're looking for. That problem is solved with All-Clad’s Outdoor Rotating Stone Pizza Oven. The battery-operated rotating pizza stone is timed so that when you set the flame height and launch your pie, all you have to do is sit back and wait until the crust is done to your liking. Not only is it nice to be hands-off, but it also means you don't have to invest in a separate pizza-turning peel. The All-Clad pizza oven is also powerful. Its curved flame lines the back of the oven and generates impressive heat. It was one of the fastest to come to temperature and easily exceeded 900℉. If you don’t get the placement on the stone just right, the pie won’t rotate properly and can cook unevenly, which happened to us the first time we tried it. If you're just starting out in your pizza-making journey, we’d recommend starting with smaller pies and really nailing your launch before graduating to larger doughs in this oven. While the oven comes with its own peel, we’d recommend buying Gozney’s Pro Placement Peel, which we’ve found lets dough slide off as easily as a hockey puck on ice. Ooni 18" Koda 2 Pro (2nd Generation) Ooni’s second-generation Koda 2 Pro got some upgrades that really improved the cooking experience compared to the first generation. For starters, the flames are now on opposite sides of the oven rather than in an L-shape in the back, which we found not only helped with heat retention but also cooked the top of the pie more evenly. It also has a larger 18-inch cooking stone, giving it 33% more capacity than gen one. Although it comes with a Bluetooth-enabled digital temperature hub, it was finicky and disconnected when we went inside (but were still within range), so it didn’t end up being as useful as we’d hoped. We also found that the oven had trouble getting above 800℉ even on full power (although Ooni says it can reach 950℉). This didn’t affect pie quality, but it’s worth noting. Our pies came out evenly cooked with tender crusts, crispy bottoms, and bubbly cheese. This is absolutely a great pizza oven, but we enjoyed the Arc XL’s cooking experience, heat retention, and build quality a bit more. Ooni Koda 16 The Ooni Koda 16 was previously our top pick, but Ooni has since come out with a second-generation option, the Koda 2 Pro, which we tested for this review. We still like the first-generation Ooni Koda 16 for its size, price, and overall performance. The L-shaped burner ignites easily and heats the stone to 950 degrees in less than 20 minutes. From there, the oven can crank out a perfectly charred Neapolitan pizza in just 90 seconds. Like any pizza oven, there’s a learning curve to heat management, though this task was easy with the Koda 16. The 16-inch surface also offers plenty of space for maneuvering or using with a cast-iron skillet to sear and roast steak, chicken, fish, and vegetables. As mentioned, the upgraded Koda has a Bluetooth digital thermometer, which is a nice-to-have, but not essential, so if you're okay with using an infrared thermometer, the Koda 16 is still a great option. Gozney Tread The Gozney Tread makes a convincing case for taking your pizza oven on the road. At 30 pounds, it’s technically portable, though adding the carrying bag, stand, propane tank, and other accessories makes it more of a car-camping situation than a spontaneous beach-day accessory. Still, tester Jeff Akin found that the Tread heats quickly, holds its temperature well, and turns out beautifully charred, leopard-spotted 12-inch pizzas. It also cools to the touch in under 30 minutes, making it easier to pack up after cooking. Even if you never take it farther than your backyard, it’s one of our favorite small outdoor ovens—albeit a pricey one, especially once you add the accessories. Gozney Dome Gozney’s top-of-the-line oven is an excellent performer. It heats up quickly, has a generous mouth to accommodate full-size pizzas, and features dual fuel capabilities that let you choose between the ease of gas or the hands-on flavorful option of wood. This is a heavy oven, though—nearly 130 pounds—and should be elevated for comfortable use. To that end, it’s a little disappointing that the stand is sold separately (and costs an extra $350), especially when the price tag of the oven itself is quite high. But if you’re in the market for a pro-quality home pizza oven, you’ll be happy with the Dome. Pizza ovens we don’t recommend This outdoor electric oven can get up to 700°F, which is pretty impressive for such a small appliance at an affordable price point; however, we found the cook to be uneven, with the crust burning more quickly than the bottom could crisp up and the cheese to melt. The first thing to know about the Breeo pizza oven is that it is not a stand-alone pizza oven. It’s an addition to either one of Breeo’s smokeless fire pits or to its newer live fire grill. In one way, that offers you some versatility, but the pizza oven is heavy to put on and take off all the time, 60-plus pounds, even without the two-piece stone. It’s particularly good atop the live fire grill because that puts it nearly four feet off the ground, a comfortable height to slide pizzas around. The Breeo reached temperature incredibly quickly: The temperature of the pizza stone was nearly 800°F in less than 25 minutes. But the temperature would drop rapidly if the fire wasn’t fed frequently. We did love the size of the Breeo, which can accommodate a pizza 14-inches in diameter. Once it’s set up, this is a good user-friendly choice for a wood-only oven. Can’t decide between the ease of gas and the smoky flavor of wood? The Ooni Karu 2 Pro gives you both, sort of. Like the other two multi-fuel ovens in Ooni’s lineup, the Karu 2 Pro (a larger version of the Karu 12) seems intended first as a wood-fired pizza oven, and it excels as such. As with any wood-burning oven, it takes some practice to master temperature control, though multiple dampers and a glass door on the front offer several levers for managing heat. However, we found the Karu 2 to be problematic when converted to propane or natural gas. Due to the overhead position of the burner, it was challenging to keep the toppings from getting scorched before the crust was done. With quite a bit of practice, we were able to find the balance, though it was far more challenging than with other ovens tested. If you want a well-made, easy-to-use wood-fired pizza oven, we highly recommend the Ooni Karu 2. If you think you’re more likely to use the gas functionality, there are far better pizza ovens for less money (specifically, the Ooni Koda 16). At first glance, the Halo Versa pizza oven is intriguing, featuring dual two-level burners and a rotating stone “allowing for hands-free pizza making.” However, upon closer inspection, it’s a bit of an over-engineered mess. Even at comparable temperatures, pizzas take twice as long to cook on the Versa, and at times, we couldn’t get the rotating stone to stop. (Yes, trying to slide raw dough onto a spinning stone is as perilous as you’d think.) To be fair, you can produce a fine pizza with the Halo Versa, though it’s well worth the extra $100 to upgrade to the Ooni Koda 16. This pizza oven was too powerful for its own good. It heated to 850°F in under 20 minutes and kept climbing from there, easily exceeding 1000°F. While impressive, it’s both unnecessary and somewhat dangerous. We got close to the front of the oven to check the thermometer and the sheer heat singed our hair. Maintaining a consistent temperature was incredibly difficult, and we alternated between making great pies and completely burning the next one. For the price, there are better options out there. FAQs Should you get a gas or wood-burning oven? Our top picks are all gas pizza ovens (except for the electric Current), and that’s because they’re just so much easier to use than wood-burning ovens. For versatility’s sake and the likelihood you’ll actually use them on a regular basis, we think gas is the way to go. There are good wood-burning ovens like the Karu 2 Pro, but if you go that direction, know they’re much more of a commitment to cook with. How expensive are backyard pizza ovens? For a full-size oven, you should expect to spend between $800–$900. But in terms of cost, you need to budget quite a bit more than just the cost of the oven itself. At the very least, you’re going to need a table or stand capable of supporting the considerable weight. And a cover to protect your new outdoor pizza oven from the elements. And a pizza peel, turning peel, serving peel, oven brush...you get the idea. To fully equip your new oven, plan on spending about 50% of the price of the actual oven on related accessories. Meet your reviewer Olivia Tarantino: I've been making pizza at home for four years and have tested 20 ovens, indoor and outdoor, across gas, wood, and electric.

item.title: Meta memo reveals what its new 'Hatch' AI agent can do, from booking a restaurant to finding a dog sitter
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 6.42
It can DJ. It can order food. It can book you a table at a restaurant. And of course, it can access your Instagram. These are some things Meta says its coming AI agent can do, according to an internal memo seen by Business Insider. Known internally as "Project Hatch," the new agent is Meta's answer to OpenClaw, the autonomous AI assistant that went viral earlier this year as companies increasingly bet on AI capable of performing tasks rather than just answering queries. A product manager told staff in an internal channel last month that Hatch was being made available to employees outside its Meta Superintelligence Labs group for testing. The memo described Hatch as "a personal agent that's always working on your behalf to help achieve your goals and improve your life, your health, your relationships, your personal finances and more." The memo to staff included a list of things Hatch could do. "It has its own computer so it can do anything you can do online, like filling out forms, buying something, or performing deep research," it said, in a section titled "What makes Project Hatch different from an AI assistant?" Meta is positioning Hatch as a general consumer product capable of performing a range of computer-based tasks, at a time when generalist agents are taking off. Google launched a similar tool, Gemini Spark, earlier this year, while OpenAI and Anthropic also have agents capable of controlling users' computers. A new AI assistant from the startup Instinct, which users can call or text, has also generated buzz in recent weeks. Hatch could become a new way for Meta to make money from its AI investments. While the company has been working to catch rivals with new models and a new coding agent, its AI revenue has mostly come from improvements to its advertising products. It could not be learned what Meta plans to charge for Hatch or an exact launch timeline. The Information previously reported that Meta plans to launch Hatch in the next few weeks and that it has considered charging up to $200 a month for it. A Meta spokesperson declined to comment. Meta wants to crack the AI agent market The memo said Hatch can connect directly to apps such as email and calendar, and gave Spotify, Instagram, and OpenTable as examples. "It has great memory and can remember more than most AIs," the memo read, adding that users can "approve any sensitive actions" before they happen. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has previously touted his vision of a future in which everyone has their own personal AI assistants capable of performing tasks. "Meta is the company primarily focused on building personal superintelligence for everyone," he said in a manifesto earlier this month. The memo said that Hatch would be highly personal to the user. "You design your agent, so no two are alike. You name it, shape how it talks and decide what it pays attention to. If it gets something wrong, tell it and it adjusts," the memo said. The product manager who posted the note said they had built a Hatch agent named Veda that had helped them find a new dog sitter, purchase a Father's Day gift, and change their sleep habits. Hatch also works in the background "even when the app is closed," the memo added. Have something to share? Contact this reporter via email at hlangley@businessinsider.com or Signal at 628-228-1836. item.title: OpenAI issues call for 'collective action' on cyber defense: 'We have a limited window'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.82
OpenAI says there's a "limited window to strengthen cyber defenses." More than 100 organizations joined OpenAI in an open letter calling for companies and governments to strengthen cybersecurity defenses before it's too late. Of particular note, rival Anthropic is one of the signatories, a sign that even the two biggest AI companies can find common ground. "In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable," the company wrote in an open letter. "The companies and public services our communities depend on—from hospitals to water treatment plants to the infrastructure that powers the internet—are at risk." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said, "There is not much time to act." "this is a critically important moment for cyber defense with AI; there is not much time to act," Altman wrote on X. "we are happy if you want to work with us or any of our competitors or partners, but please take this moment seriously. only an urgent and intense collective response will work." The letter comes as OpenAI continues to disclose information about how rogue agents broke out of what was presumed to be a secure testing environment before hacking into Hugging Face in search of answers to cheat on internal testing. Altman had portrayed the breach as a watershed moment. "This is the first security incident that I have felt very viscerally," Altman said during a recent interview. The letter lays out suggestions for organizations, cybersecurity companies, governments, and frontier AI companies. The recommendations include calling on governments to better fund cyber defense, asking cybersecurity companies to share "threat intelligence and tested playbooks," and urging AI labs to "share tools, playbooks, and credible threat assessments" with those who need it the most. "We call on leaders across industry and government to bring the full weight of their technology, resources, and expertise to this effort," the letter reads. "Put cyber-capable AI in the hands of defenders, starting with the teams protecting essential services." Other notable tech signatories include Microsoft, Google, Amazon Web Services, Oracle, Cisco, IBM, and CrowdStrike. Hugging Face, the victim of OpenAI's breach, also signed. A number of notable companies are also part of the group, including Citi, General Motors, Visa, Capitol One, Mastercard, and Citadel. You can read the full open letter here.

item.title: Google employees are already testing the next Gemini Flash AI model
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.55
Google just released a new AI model this month. Its employees are already testing the next one. Some staff have begun using a preview version of Gemini 3.8 Flash, highlighting the breakneck pace of the AI race as Google pushes out new models just weeks apart to keep up with OpenAI and Anthropic. The new model — dubbed "Gemini 3.8 Flash Preview" — was made available to staff on Google's internal coding platform, Jetski, according to images Business Insider obtained. One employee testing the new model said it already felt noticeably better than 3.7 Flash, but emphasized it was too early for a full review. Google declined to comment. With 3.5 Pro still missing and Anthropic and OpenAI sprinting ahead in the AI race, Google no longer has a frontier model. Instead, it has doubled down on its "Flash" models, which offer greater speed and lower costs for users, at a time when customers are keeping a closer eye on their AI bill. Google refers to these models as its "workhorse models" for coding and running agents, which often consume tokens faster than chatbots. Agentic assistants designed to help with everyday tasks are proving to be the next hot thing among the AI companies. Google launched its Gemini Spark agent earlier this year, and Meta is testing its "Hatch" agent internally. Google has been improving its Flash models at a rapid clip. Gemini 3.6 Flash rolled out in July, and 3.7 Flash followed just three weeks later. During the company's Q2 earnings call, CEO Sundar Pichai said the company would aim for an almost monthly release cadence. The employee preview suggests a public rollout of Gemini 3.8 Flash may not be far away, but it's not a guarantee. Some keen-eyed AI sleuthers are convinced they have spotted Gemini 3.8 Flash on Arena AI, a website for benchmarking models that Google has previously used to test upcoming releases. item.title: Dollar General is adding more $1 items. It's stealing a page from supermarkets' playbook
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.53
Dollar General is doubling down on the $1 price point. A selection of 600 items priced at $1 each, which the chain calls "Value Valley," had comparable sales growth of 16% during the company's second quarter — a much faster clip than broader same-store sales growth of 3.5%, it said on Thursday. In total, Dollar General stocks about 2,000 items that cost $1 each. It expects to grow that number by 40% in the second half of 2026 in time for the holiday shopping season, COO Emily Taylor said on the retailer's earnings call. Expect that selection to grow "even more so into 2027," CEO Todd Vasos said. "We have got real plans to expand that $1 price point to offer even more value for the consumer," he added. Dollar stores used to be true to their name, with everything on their shelves priced at $1. Inflation has changed that, though: In 2021, Dollar Tree raised prices on most items to $1.25 and has since experimented with items priced at several dollars each. That's a different direction than Dollar General appears to be taking, said Arielle Feger, a senior analyst at EMARKETER, Business Insider's sister company. While Dollar General has long sold items that cost well over $1 each, many of those items are food and other consumables that draw people into the store, Feger said. The chain began adding freezers stocked with food items priced at $1 each to its stores earlier this year, Vasos said on the company's last earnings call in June. Dollar Tree's $1 item selection, by contrast, skews more toward discretionary items, such as home decor and toys. Dollar General's strategy is similar to the classic grocery store strategy of selling eggs and milk as cheaply as possible — even at a loss, potentially — to boost overall sales, Feger said. "It gets people in the door, and it gets them to continue to come back," she said. That strategy is particularly meaningful to customers who are trying to save money, Vasos said on Thursday's earnings call. Dollar General's average customer is "still gainfully employed" and "is seeing some gains in her income levels," the CEO said. But inflation and rising gas prices this year have offset that income gain, Vasos said, leading many customers to visit its stores more often and buy less each trip. By expanding its selection of $1 items, Dollar General will likely continue to attract customers, Feger said. "Consumers are habitual," she said. "We go to the same places, we expect the same things." Do you have a story idea about Dollar General or Dollar Tree? item.title: The US Air Force is working on its drone defenses, starting with AI and ending with shotguns
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.35
US Air Force personnel recently trained on a layered approach to countering drones, using artificial intelligence to spot them, electronic warfare to disrupt them, and shotguns as a last line of defense. The recent exercise highlights the US military's growing focus on having a variety of kinetic and non-kinetic systems to defend against uncrewed aerial systems. It's a work in progress as the different services figure out which capabilities best fit their missions and what lessons can be shared across the force. Earlier this month, the Air Force's 31st Air Task Force tested drone defense tactics against small uncrewed aerial systems, connecting different technologies to form a layered defense. "Through a crawl, walk, run approach, airmen gained practical knowledge of a full spectrum of layered counter-sUAS capabilities," the 31st Air Task Force's force protection superintendent said in a news release. "The ATF is posturing to provide tiered defense through detection, electronic warfare defeat, and physical interception of hostile drones." During the defensive training, airmen learned how to use AI systems to scan the skies. Those systems helped identify drones while filtering out non-threats like birds and planes. Personnel also trained on other weapons for defending against drones and electronic warfare threats. As part of the exercise, small high-speed drones mimicked hostile flight patterns, giving airmen the chance to gain experience detecting and tracking realistic targets. According to the press release, the exercise concluded with a live-fire element in which personnel used kinetic weapons like shotguns as final line of defense against drones. "The team successfully executed a capstone event that validated new tactics, techniques, and procedures across force protection and distributed communications," Col. Brad Dvorak, the 31st ATF commander, said in the news release. "Our mission is to enable airpower operations, anytime, anywhere. By establishing a sUAS instructor cadre, we trained our personnel on counter-sUAS architecture and employed unique solutions for airmen to track, jam, and kinetically defeat sUAS threats." The Air Force said it will review the lessons learned from the exercise. Recent counter-drone training across the US military has pursued a similar layered defense approach, as troops practice detecting, tracking, disrupting, and ultimately defeating drones. Even the exercises not focused specifically on countering drones have sometimes still seen troops carry shotguns or other weapons for close-range defense. In Ukraine, where drones dominate the battlefield, both sides have fielded a range of drone detection devices and electronic warfare systems for disrupting the radio frequencies used to connect operators and certain first-person-view drones. Some drones, such as fiber-optic drones, are immune to jamming, and in those cases, troops say the best defensive option available may just be a shotgun. Many Western militaries are still working through best practices for confronting these challenges. To make counter-UAS capabilities easier to acquire for US operations and give units greater flexibility to choose systems suited to the threat they expect to face, the Pentagon-led counter-drone task force has introduced a new online catalog that military, federal government, and law enforcement personnel can use to assess validated systems — from kinetic weapons to jammers — and submit requests to buy them.

item.title: 540 foreign tourists from more than 30 countries are missing in Nepal's flash floods
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.92
Nearly 600 foreign nationals are missing after deadly floods hit the Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday. The flooding began on the morning of August 26, when a surge of water, mud, and debris entered Nepal from the autonomous Chinese region of Tibet via the Bhote Koshi River, Nepal's Tourism Board said. About 390 bodies have been recovered, per an update by the Nepal police at 9 p.m. local time Thursday.
