Nepal's foreign ministry said in an update at 8 p.m. that 596 foreign nationals were missing in the country. The list includes 66 Americans and 25 Canadians, as well as travelers from the UK, Australia, Malaysia, and Ukraine. 167 of the missing foreigners are from neighboring India, authorities said. In total, people from more than 30 countries are missing. The US State Department said in a press release that it was deploying a disaster response adviser and providing $500,000 through Catholic Relief Services for shelter, supplies, clean water, and sanitation. It also said the US Embassy in the capital Kathmandu is working with local authorities to locate and assist Americans. Global Affairs Canada said it was aware that Canadians had been affected and was ready to provide consular assistance. It said power outages were making communications difficult. The floods hit communities along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers, north of Kathmandu. The US Geological Survey initially recorded a magnitude 4.4 earthquake about 40 miles north of the capital. It later updated its event page to say that no earthquake occurred and that the signal came from a glacier collapse and debris flow that released energy equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. What triggered the glacier collapse is still being investigated. CCTV footage shared online showed walls of water, mud, and debris hitting Gyirong port, the border crossing between the two countries, while other footage showed widespread damage in nearby towns. Nepal's disaster management authority said 27 foreign tourists had been rescued from Rasuwa by Thursday afternoon. Two army helicopters were deployed to support rescue efforts. The Tourism Board said other parts of Nepal were unaffected. It advised travelers to avoid rivers, bridges, and damaged roads, and to postpone trips to flood-hit areas until officials say conditions are safe.

item.title: 18 states that have never won Miss USA
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.27
Miss USA held its first pageant in 1952, but not every state has taken home the crown. While Texas, California, and Hawaii have repeatedly won the prestigious title, other states — including Arizona, Florida, and New Jersey — have struggled. Here are the 18 states that have never won Miss USA. Alaska The closest Alaska has come to the Miss USA crown was in 1964, when Patricia Marlin placed second runner-up. Alaska has placed four additional times in the pageant's history, most recently with Alyssa London, who made the top 10 in 2017. Four of the state's queens have won the Miss Congeniality prize, including in 2022 and 2023. Arizona While Arizona has never won Miss USA, it assumed the title in 1980 when Jineane Ford, who originally placed first runner-up, inherited the crown after Shawn Weatherly won Miss Universe. Arizona has frequently appeared in the Miss USA semifinals, with three second runners-up and two third runners-up. But it has not placed at Miss USA since 2016, when Chelsea Myers made the top 15. Colorado Colorado was closest to the Miss USA crown in 1963 and 2010, when Rhea Looney and Jessica Hartman placed third runner-up. The state most recently placed at the Miss USA 2024 pageant, when titleholder Jessi Kalambayi reached the top 10. It was the first time Colorado had placed at Miss USA since 2012. Delaware Delaware has only placed once at Miss USA, becoming the last state to ever place in the pageant's history. Renee Bull broke the streak in 2015 when she made it to the top 11. She also tied for the Miss Congeniality title with Miss Alaska Kimberly Agron. Miss Delaware 2025 Tetra Shockley made history as the oldest woman to compete at Miss USA. The 44-year-old also won the Miss Congeniality title that year. Florida While Florida has never won Miss USA, it assumed the title in 1967. Cheryl Patton, who placed second runner-up, inherited the crown after Sylvia Hitchcock won Miss Universe and the first runner-up, Susan Ellen Bradley, declined to take the title. Florida has also had two first runners-up, and more than a dozen contestants have made it to the semifinals. The state last placed at Miss USA in 2025 with titleholder Lou Schieffelin, who made it to the top 10. Georgia The closest Georgia has come to the Miss USA crown was in 1993, when Erin Nance was named first runner-up. Contestants from Georgia have also won second runner-up six times — in 1986, 1988, 2001, 2006, 2014, and 2016. Georgia last placed at Miss USA in 2025, when Savannah Miles reached the top 10. Indiana Holli Rene Dennis almost nabbed the Miss USA crown for Indiana in 1981, when she won first runner-up. Indiana contestants also won second runner-up in 1966 and 2002. Indiana last placed in 2020 when Alexis Nicole Lete was third runner-up. Maine The closest Maine has come to the Miss USA crown was in 2010, when Katie Whittier placed fourth runner-up. Maine last placed during the Miss USA 2025 competition, when Shelby Howell made the top 20. She also won Miss Photogenic. Miss Maine 2023 Juliana Morehouse made history as the first married woman to compete at Miss USA. Maryland Miss Maryland Mary Leona Gage won Miss USA in 1957, but she was dethroned after it was discovered that she was married and had two children. Married women and mothers were not allowed to compete at Miss USA or Miss Universe until 2023. Maryland assumed the title of Miss USA in 2012 after Nana Meriwether inherited the crown from Olivia Culpo, who won Miss Universe that year. Maryland last placed at Miss USA in 2023, when Savena Mushinge reached the top 20. Montana Montana has placed three times at Miss USA, all before 1960. Montana last placed in the Miss USA competition in 1958, when Sharon Tietjen made it to the top 15. New Hampshire The closest New Hampshire has gotten to the Miss USA crown was in 2000, when Bridget Vezina was named first runner-up. The state has placed six times at Miss USA, most recently in 2025 when Mona Lesa Brackett made the top 20. Brackett made history as the first woman to compete in Miss USA wearing a hijab and a burkini. New Jersey New Jersey nearly nabbed the Miss USA crown in 2025 when Ivy Harrington placed first runner-up. Contestants from the Garden State also placed first runner-up at Miss USA in 2017 and 1991, and took the second runner-up spot three times — in 1989, 1990, and 2008. North Dakota North Dakota has come close to the Miss USA crown twice. Audra Mari placed first runner-up in 2014, as did Caitlyn Vogel in 2021. Vogel was the last Miss North Dakota titleholder to place at Miss USA. Oregon Oregon came closest to winning the Miss USA crown in 2025, when Chantéa McIntyre was named second runner-up. McIntyre, a mother of four, became the first married woman and the first mother to ever reach the top five at Miss USA. Oregon also won second runner-up in 1976. South Dakota Miss South Dakota Madison Nipe landed the state's best placement at Miss USA in 2018 when she made the top five. South Dakota most recently placed at Miss USA in 2021, when Caroline Pettey made the top 16. West Virginia West Virginia has almost won the Miss USA crown twice. Ruth Parr won first runner-up in 1957, as did Kelly Anderson in 1984. The state last placed at Miss USA in 2022, when Krystian Leonard made it to the top 16. Wisconsin Wisconsin nearly won the Miss USA crown in 1974 and 2023, when Mary Lynn Cook and Alexis Loomans placed second runner-up. The last Miss Wisconsin titleholder to place at Miss USA was Aneisha Cox, who made it to the top 20 during the 2025 pageant. Wyoming Wyoming's closest attempt at the Miss USA crown was in 1986, when Beth King placed in the top 10. The state has only placed twice in the Miss USA competition, most recently with Claire Schreiner, who made the top 15 in 2010.

item.title: Jensen Huang says AI data centers can fix the very grid they’re straining
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.84
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says the AI industry needs to do "better" when it comes to data centers. "The technology industry, the builders, and, have to do a much better job working with the communities to get prepared for this AI infrastructure build-out," Huang told CNBC's Jim Cramer on Wednesday when asked about how Nvidia's customers could show communities they are serious about data center concerns. Huang is the latest voice in tech, and arguably the biggest so far, to acknowledge that the industry has to do a better job of selling communities on building data centers. Polling shows that Americans have become deeply skeptical of the massive facilities that house the advanced chips that train and serve AI demand. Huang said the industry needs to sell the idea that data center construction can help reindustrialize the nation. Addressing a frequent concern, Huang said data centers could actually lower energy costs. "It is also the case this is the first time in probably the last century that we're able to invest in sustainable energy, invest in improving our energy grid, securing our energy supply, reducing the cost of energy across the country," he said. "This is the first time in history that we're able to do that because of the enormous market dynamics, the market forces that are able to invest in the energy ecosystem." Business Insider has previously reported that rapid data center expansion could increase electricity costs. A recent study by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found that data centers could reduce consumer costs by adjusting their power consumption. The MIT researchers found that data centers that shift their power consumption to off-peak hours could lower average energy costs by up to 4% in the Mid-Atlantic, 5% in Texas, and 2% in 11 western states compared to facilities that didn't change their consumption patterns. The researchers studied power grids in each of those three areas due to the prevalence of data centers there. There is a big caveat to their findings. The researchers said that under some scenarios, data centers would need to shift nearly 50% of their energy consumption to non-peak hours, such as the afternoon. On Wednesday, Nvidia reported that data center revenue totaled $89 billion in the second quarter of FY 26, up 117% from a year ago. The figure also surpassed Wall Street's estimates, illustrating just how lucrative the broader AI buildout is for the world's largest company by market cap. Like President Donald Trump, Huang warned of the costs to the US if data centers aren't built out. "We have to make sure that our communities, our society, all of our companies, all of our people in the United States embrace this technology so that we can take advantage of what this technology could do for all of our ecosystems, all of our economy, and all of our societies," Huang said. He added, "Otherwise, we're going to get left behind." At the same time, the vibes in the US look increasingly dour. Governors have moved to pump the brakes on data center construction amid a growing public backlash. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who is seeking reelection, imposed an effective moratorium on new data center construction until state agencies complete a comprehensive audit. Abbott was rather blunt about how he went from declaring Texas the "epicenter of AI development" to imposing a moratorium in less than a year. "They basically dug their own grave for the problem that's been caused for them, and that's why they got the backlash they deserve," Abbott said during an interview on ABC's "This Week."

item.title: Ukraine says Russia used its upgraded, longer-range 'Iskander-1000' missile in a bombardment of Kyiv
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.57
Russia fired an upgraded version of its Iskander short-range ballistic missile for the first time in a summer strike on the Ukrainian capital city, the country's military intelligence agency shared this week. Russian forces have significantly ramped up their ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine this year. These strikes come as Russia upgrades its arsenal and Ukraine struggles to procure sufficient numbers of critical air-defense interceptors. On Thursday, Ukraine's GUR, the country's military and defense intelligence agency, said that Russia had used an upgraded ballistic missile, the 9M723-2 or "Iskander-1000," against Ukraine for the first time during a complex bombardment of Kyiv this summer. The Iskander-1000 is an upgraded variant of the 9M723-1, a ballistic missile fired by Russia's Iskander system, with a larger engine and launcher that extend its range. Ukraine has assessed that these modifications have increased its maximum range to about 340 miles, about 100 miles farther than its predecessor. It added that most other components remain the same. The first combat use of the Iskander-1000 highlights Russia's ongoing investments in expanding and improving its ballistic missile arsenal. Ukrainian officials have said such weapons are becoming an increasingly prominent part of Moscow's strike campaign. The additional range on the upgraded 9M723-2 missile allows Russian Iskander launchers to operate from farther back while still threatening Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. Ukraine has tracked evolutions in Russian ballistic missile technology, including changes in maneuverability that make the weapons more difficult to intercept. These developments have at times challenged Ukrainian air defenses, such as the US-made MIM-104 Patriot surface-to-air missile system. Last fall, for instance, a US defense intelligence assessment found that Ukraine's Patriots struggled to consistently intercept Russian ballistic missiles due to certain recent "tactical improvements" Moscow had made to the weapons. The Patriot is a top-tier air defense platform in Ukraine and is considered its best defense against Russian ballistic missiles like the Iskander and the air-launched Kh-47M2 Kinzhal, but it's not infallible. Right now, though, Ukraine is running low on interceptor missiles. Some nights, Ukraine hasn't been able to intercept a single missile. Russia has also expanded its arsenal with assistance from North Korea. Earlier this month, the Ukrainian Air Force said North Korea's KN-23 missile, which is a rough copy of Russia's Iskander missile, had been used in two strikes. Ukrainian and Western officials have assessed that ongoing military cooperation between North Korea and Russia has allowed both countries to improve their weapons and technologies.

item.title: The rise of sleep tourism
item.description:
Source: CNN Travel Score: 6.01
Editor’s Note: Sign up for CNN’s Sleep, But Better newsletter series. Our seven-part guide has helpful hints to achieve better sleep. Going on a vacation might seem like a rather unconventional way to try to improve your sleep habits. But sleep tourism has been growing in popularity for a number of years, with an increasing amount of sleep-focused stays popping up in hotels and resorts across the world. Interest has skyrocketed since the pandemic, with a number of high profile establishments focusing their attention on those suffering from sleep-deprivation. Over the past 12 months, Park Hyatt New York has opened the Bryte Restorative Sleep Suite, a 900-square-foot suite filled with sleep-enhancing amenities, while Rosewood Hotels & Resorts recently launched a collection of retreats called the Alchemy of Sleep, which are designed to “promote rest.” Zedwell, London’s first sleep-centric hotel, which features rooms equipped with innovative soundproofing, opened in early 2020, and Swedish bed manufacturer Hastens established the world’s first Hästens Sleep Spa Hotel, a 15-room boutique hotel, in the Portuguese city of Coimbra a year later. Pandemic impact So why has sleep suddenly become such a big focus for the travel industry? Dr. Rebecca Robbins, a sleep researcher and co-author of the book “Sleep for Success!” believes this shift has been a long time coming, particularly with regards to hotels. “When it comes down to it, travelers book hotels for a place to sleep,” she tells CNN Travel, before pointing out that the hotel industry has primarily been focused on things that actually detract from sleep in the past. “People often associate travel with decadent meals, extending their bed times, the attractions and the things you do while you’re traveling, really almost at the cost of sleep,” she adds. “Now, I think there’s just been a huge seismic shift in our collective awareness and prioritization on wellness and well being.” The global pandemic appears to have played a huge part in this. A study published in the Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine found that 40% of the over 2,500 adults who took part reported a reduction in their sleep quality since the start of the pandemic. “There has been heightened attention to sleep in the Covid-19 era, and likely, because so many people have struggled with this [sleep],” says Dr. Robbins. Prioritizing sleep Hypnotherapist, meditation and holistic coach Malminder Gill has also noticed a change in attitudes towards sleep. “Everything seems to be moving towards longevity, and I think that has really fueled things,” Gill tells CNN Travel. “Because it’s no great surprise that sleep is an important aspect of our lives. Lack of sleep can cause lots of different issues in the body, and for your mental health. “So, anxiety, depression, low mood, mood swings – all sorts of things, on top of the tiredness.” Gill has partnered with the Cadogan, a Belmond Hotel in London, to create a special service catered to guests with sleep issues called the Sleep Concierge. The service includes a sleep-inducing meditation recording, a pillow menu with options that cater to guests who may prefer to sleep on their back or side, the option of a weighted blanket, a bedtime tea developed specifically for the service, and a scented pillow mist. “Different things work for different people at different stages of their life,” Gill says of the different items offered within the service. Sleep-inducing practices “We’ve tried to stack the odds in our favor. If you combine all of those things, I would say there’s a higher chance of a better quality sleep. But I don’t think there’s a one size fits all.” The types of sleep-focused programs and/or retreats offered by hotels and resorts also tend to vary, with different establishments approaching the concept in different ways. Luxury hotel brand Six Senses offers a variety of full sleep programs, ranging from three to seven days or more, at a number of its properties, while Brown’s Hotel, a Rocco Forte hotel in Mayfair, London, recently launched, ‘Forte Winks’ a two-night experience especially created to help aid guests “into a serene sleep.” “Sleep is so important and we noticed there was a trend in sleep tourism happening, and wellness in general, after lockdowns and Covid,” explains Daniela Moore, senior group PR manager for Rocco Forte Hotels. “So we wanted to take the opportunity to showcase Brown’s as a hotel that cares about you getting the best night’s sleep.” For Gill, the emergence of more and more of these types of experiences is a sign that the “narrative of staying up to get things done,” is being challenged, and people are beginning to have a deeper understanding of just how important sleep is. Quick fix? But can short term sleep-focused travel experiences actually have a long term impact on a person’s overall sleep? According to Dr. Robbins, travel experiences centered around “healthy sleep strategies” that aim to supply guests with the tools they need to improve their sleep can be hugely beneficial, provided a reputable medical or scientific expert is involved in some way to help to determine whether there may be something else at play. “If someone comes to one of these retreats, and isn’t seeing any progress, it could be because they have an untreated sleep disorder,” she explains, pointing to conditions such as sleep apnea, restless leg syndrome, or insomnia as potential examples. “That’s why it’s vitally important to make sure that hotels are partnering with scientists and medical professionals that can impart these strategies carefully.” Mandarin Oriental, Geneva has taken things a step further by teaming up with CENAS, a private medical sleeping clinic in Switzerland, to curate a three-day program that studies guests’ sleeping patterns in order to identify potential sleeping disorders. Although the majority of sleep-focused establishments and experiences tend to fall within the luxury travel sector, Dr. Robbins believes that all hotels and resorts should be making this a priority. “There are ways to make it meaningful for each level,” she adds, pointing out that “it doesn’t cost much at all to leave a pair of earplugs next to the nightstand.” As sleep tourism continues to grow, Dr. Robbins says she’s looking forward to seeing “who really continues to pioneer and think creatively about this space,” stressing that there are countless avenues that haven’t been fully explored yet when it comes to travel and the science of sleep. “The notion of travel actually rejuvenating you and allowing you to return home refreshed and restored is a really exciting proposition,” she adds. Top image credit: Rocco Forte Hotels

item.title: Asia Pacific set to lose title as the world's largest travel region
item.description:
Source: CNN Travel Score: 5.97
Editor’s Note: Sign up for Unlocking the World, CNN Travel’s weekly newsletter. Get news about destinations opening, inspiration for future adventures, plus the latest in aviation, food and drink, where to stay and other travel developments. Asia Pacific is home to some of the world’s most beloved travel destinations, from the natural beauty of Bali to the urban buzz of Singapore. These dreamy vacation hotspots – teamed with the region’s business power – secured Asia Pacific the title of world’s largest travel region for much of the past decade. But with destinations like China and Japan comparatively slow to drop Covid entry restrictions, air travel in Asia Pacific remains low compared to the region’s pre-pandemic levels. And a new report from international travel industry analysts the Centre for Aviation (CAPA) predicts Asia Pacific will no longer be the world’s largest travel region by the end of 2022, ceding the title to Europe. Where once Asian Pacific air traffic accounted for more than a third of all global passenger journeys, aviation in the region remains down by 45% compared to pre-pandemic levels, according to CAPA. Meanwhile, CAPA suggests European air travel has recovered to roughly 85% of pre-pandemic levels, even accounting for the continued impact of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Slow recovery In 2019, 3.38 billion passengers transited through Asia Pacific airports. In contrast, CAPA reports that current predictions from ACI Asia-Pacific – an industry organization that represents airports in the region – suggest 1.84 billion passengers will have passed through Asia Pacific travel hubs by the end of 2022. A key factor in this slow recovery is China’s “zero-Covid” border policy and Japan’s slow relaxation of travel restrictions, at least according to ACI Asia-Pacific and CAPA. Japan is set to officially reopen to tourists on October 11. “What happens there has an outsized impact on the rest of the region,” says CAPA of China and Japan, pointing out they’re two of the region’s top travel markets. CAPA reports that most travel in Asia Pacific destinations remains at 50% or more below 2019 levels, with only a couple of exceptions, such as India, which is only 11% below its 2019 figure. Domestic travel in Asia Pacific is recovering faster than international travel, notes CAPA – domestic travel within China, for example, is only down 5.4% compared to 2019 levels. All in all, CAPA predicts Asia Pacific won’t see a full return to pre-pandemic travel figures until the end of 2023 or early 2024. “Even then, recovery is dependent on countries opening their borders and ending lingering travel restrictions, as well as the wider economic and epidemiological situations,” reads the report. CAPA is arguing for “harmonization of international travel rules” and “political commitments towards openness and freedom of movement” as well as a continued vaccination drive, to aid travel recovery. Top photo of the Great Wall of China courtesy Powerstock/Adobe Stock

item.title: Hong Kong is opening up to tourism -- but is it too late?
item.description:
Source: CNN Travel Score: 2.28
Market vendor Mr. Chan gestures around what used to be one of Hong Kong’s busiest streets. “There are no tourists now, whatsoever,” he says. Mr. Chan sells silver earrings, necklaces and scarves on Tung Choi Street in Kowloon, which is famous for its robust night market. The past three years have been harsh on him. He kept his stall open until 10 p.m. before the pandemic, but these days he closes at 7 p.m. He hopes for swift change with the end of quarantine, which had a devastating effect on businesses that relied on tourism. Hong Kong has taken steps in recent days to reopen itself to the world, by first lifting its mandatory three-day hotel quarantine, then announcing a global banking summit in November. The city is also planning to give away 500,000 million airline tickets, worth around $254.8 million, to global visitors, along with residents, as part of a “market recovery campaign.” Officials hope these moves will revive Hong Kong’s status as an international business and travel hub, but some locals feel the changes may be too late. A long winter The lifting of the quarantine was received with elation by the city’s residents, who have endured more than two years of crushing pandemic measures. At its most strict, Hong Kong’s quarantine rules required incoming travelers to spend 21 days in a hotel room paid at their own expense. Only Hong Kong residents were permitted entry. Those unlucky enough to come from certain regions or countries with high numbers of coronavirus cases could find themselves in a government-run facility. As a result, travel in and out of the financial hub was at record lows. Once news of the end of quarantine was announced on Friday, September 30, travel-starved Hong Kongers flocked to book flights online. The city’s flag carrier Cathay Pacific set up a virtual “waiting room” to get onto its website, where hold times could easily stretch to 30 minutes. The online travel booking service Expedia said its website also saw a 9-fold surge in search for flights from Hong Kong to Tokyo and 11-fold for flights from Hong Kong to Osaka. However, the interest in flights to Hong Kong remained unchanged, Lavinia Rajaram, Expedia’s Asia head of public relations, said. An uneven success Though hotel quarantine may be gone, the city still imposes a 3-day period during which visitors are barred from dining in restaurants or going to bars. That and the complicated visiting requirements, which include a pre-flight vaccination certificate and negative tests, may deter potential visitors. In November, Hong Kong plans to host the International Rugby Sevens tournament, which has been held every year since 1976 except for the past two years. A popular spectacle that drew fans from abroad before the pandemic, it is doubtful how many will brave the border restrictions. While drinking is allowed, food will be banned at the event. Fans will also be required to wear their mask at all times except when drinking, according to the city’s government. Hong Kong’s Asian neighbors including Japan, Taiwan and South Korea took steps in past weeks to remove the last remaining barriers on travel, making them more attractive destinations for international travelers. Another cloud hanging over the forecast is the continuing zero-Covid regime in mainland China. In 2019, the last year before travel became heavily restricted, 78% of the city’s visitors came from the mainland. Too late for some The government’s effort to reopen and promote the city came too late for Maxence Traverse, a restaurant owner who had to shut his business, Honi Honi Tiki Bar, last year. He says the nine-year-old bar could not survive the 2019 protests and the pandemic. After a six-month hiatus, he opened a restaurant in the city’s Tai Hang neighborhood but he is fighting to keep it going, he said. Traverse’s business is one of many in the food and beverage industry that shut down permanently during the pandemic. Some of the city’s iconic Cantonese restaurants – including Mido Cafe, Jimmy’s Kitchen and Lin Heung Tea House – have also closed their doors. Traverse was greatly upset when he saw an interview with Hong Kong Health Secretary Lo Chung-mau, in which Lo said Hong Kong will continue to open up unless a new Covid variant emerges. “I cried. Depression. Really hard, that hard feeling. I said, ‘Not again.’ Nearly third year in a row. You know, it’s been tough,” Traverse said. He believes simply reopening the city will not be enough to restore what drew him there 12 years ago. “We need to be providing excitement for Hong Kong, because right now we lost so many things,” he said. CNN’s Jan Camenzind Broomby and Jadyn Sham contributed reporting.

item.title: The Answer to 'Where Is the International Date Line?' Depends on How Much Time You Have
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 6.75
Traveling across the International Date Line (IDL) can get weird—seriously weird. Let’s say you’re looking for a change in scenery from the Edenic climes of Auckland and fall smitten with the whale-filled waters of Vancouver. As far as long-haul flights go, this one doesn’t seem too out of the ordinary—if you fly from New Zealand on a Tuesday, you’ll land in Canada the Monday before since you crossed the IDL from the left. But that’s assuming you’ve crossed the line just once. Because of its jigsaw shape, your journey across the Pacific would more so resemble a game of time-travel hopscotch. All this to say, asking yourself where the International Date Line is, is only natural. And as it turns out, the origin story of this Parasaurolophus-headed imaginary line is more complicated than you’d think. How the International Date Line came to be Portuguese navigator Ferdinand Magellan’s surviving crew on the Victoria first documented the time-skipping phenomenon of global travel on Thursday July 10, 1522, whilst stopped at Cabo Verde. On track to become the first expedition to circumnavigate the world, the Magellan sailing came across a strange error in their log books on the home stretch of their nearly three-year journey: despite their fastidious record-keeping, they had somehow fallen back a day compared to the local calendar. As it turns out, while they kept sailing westward, they continually encountered local noon later than they would have from their point of departure, as every 15 degrees of westward travel approximately corresponds with one hour of later local time. As they traveled a full 360 degrees around the world, their record-keeping ultimately fell a full 24-hours behind by the time they returned to Portugal. Successive travels, observations, and a beloved Jules Verne novel all about the hijinks and perils of hot air balloon flight would later make common knowledge of the fact that circumnavigation results in the gain (if traveling westward) or the loss (if traveling eastward) of a day, and the idea that this difference in time would require its own place on our maps gradually came into fruition. Mapping out time took further root in October 1884 during the International Meridian Conference held in Washington, DC, which convened 25 different nations to create a global standard for keeping track of time. The existing status quo was to measure time from a destination’s local meridian, its longitudinal position on Earth. At the precise moment the sun passes a destination's meridian, which derives from the Latin word “meridies” meaning “midday,” that locale experiences its solar noon. But this subjective practice made for a logistical nightmare when it came to coordinating trade routes, communicating using the newfangled telegraph, and scheduling train times. To create this global standard, the conference sought to establish a “universal day,” a 24-hour date scale synchronized to the beginning and end of a day measured from a designated prime meridian, a zero-degree longitudinal line from which all time zones would be defined relative to. As the late 19th century was the height of British sea power and the majority of countries present defaulted to using British maps for navigation anyway, Greenwich, England, was elected the location of the prime meridian, though not everyone left a fan—France did not adopt Greenwich Mean Time until 1911, and on the whole, the global adoption of a Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) would prove slow, taking several more decades to fully realize. But the International Meridian Conference still provided a crucial basis for determining where the calendar turns on the globe, even if it did not formally set it. Theoretically, the same calendar day that Greenwich, England, experiences would end halfway across the globe where the 180th meridian lies, and thus the drawing of the prime meridian also implied the existence of its hypothetical twin, the International Date Line, though its actual plotting would prove to be neither straight nor straightforward. More a boundary than a border Even prior to 1884 when an approximate meridian was established for the IDL, individual nations decided which day on the calendar they would observe primarily based on trade interests, and these preferences still impact the shape of the IDL to this day. For instance, when Spain claimed the Philippines as a colony, the new territory's closest tie to its mother country lay in Acapulco, Mexico, which observes the prior calendar date to the rest of Asia. As a result, the Philippines fell back a day to synchronize with the Western hemisphere, dragging a proverbial “date line” way out west. And after Mexico gained independence in 1821, the Philippines later switched back to observing the same date as its Asian neighbors in 1844 to align with new trade interests in China and the Dutch East Indies. Another prominent change to the global observance of dates came in 1867 when Alaska was purchased as a US territory. Following the purchase, Alaska began abiding by the same calendar date as the United States rather than Russia, which at the time observed the Julian calendar, falling 12 days behind the US's Gregorian calendar. The official date of the transfer took place on Saturday, October 7, 1867, on the Julian calendar, which was Saturday, October 19, 1867 on the Gregorian calendar to the west of the IDL. But because Alaska moved to the east of the line, the date also shifted to Friday, October 18, 1867, a date now celebrated as the state holiday Alaska Day. That the Philippines sits on the same side of the date line as the rest of Asia and that Alaska observes the same date as the contiguous US are preferences the current iteration of the IDL still abides to. While the date line starts at the 180th meridian in the North Pole, it quickly curves to the east to slip between Russia and Alaska before course correcting west past the 180th meridian to make sure all the Aleutian islands fall west of the line. While most map projections depict the part of the world the 180th meridian cuts through as open ocean, this region of Pacific is peppered with Oceanian island nations—each with their own preferences on the calendar date they’d like to observe. And these preferences continue to change to this day. Recent shifts to where the IDL is drawn include when it was pulled eastward to accommodate Kiribati, which wanted the entirety of the country under the same date. On the eve of 1995, the eastern half of the country, which was a day behind its western half skipped Friday, December 31, 1994, and went straight into Sunday, January 1, 1995, to join its other half in being the first country to ring in the new year. The latest change to the IDL came in 2011 when Samoa and neighboring New Zealand territory Tokelau skipped to the west of the line by omitting Friday, December 30, 2011, altogether. Because the IDL doesn’t function as a border that delineates the boundaries of a nation’s territory, its resources, or other formal sovereign limits, where it’s drawn is still left up to “to each, their own” rules as the line is imaginary—and therefore flexible. Meaning, countries don’t have to ask permission or confer with any international law if they choose to change where they fall along in the line. So long as they pass a national law shifting time zones, reset their clocks accordingly, and publicize the change so mapmakers and other relevant parties can keep up, countries effectively dictate where the IDL is drawn through… just vibes.

item.title: The Simple Exercises We Should All Be Doing on a Long-Haul Flight, According to Pilates Instructors
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.82
Ah, the long-haul flight. The one that brings the promise of far-flung destinations and, if you’re anything like me, a stiff back and sore neck. Indeed, even for the most intrepid travelers, sitting in one place for over nine hours is far from optimal for the body—no matter which class your ticket is. But a little movement can go a long way, and there are some simple steps we can all take to improve our chances of arriving at our destination in one (malleable) piece. Through a series of gentle exercises—simple enough to perform from the comfort of the plane seat—our muscles can get just enough movement to prevent pain upon landing. But which moves should you be practicing that won't disturb the people next to you? We spoke to Pilates instructors to find out… Why Pilates? Pilates is a low-impact conditioning method that was invented in the 1920s by Joseph Pilates to help World War I soldiers recover physically. The conscious movements, which build strength and improve flexibility, can be done in small spaces and even seated, making them ideal for long-haul travel. Making a few targeted movements during a flight can help “reduce stiffness, make you feel more comfortable when you arrive, and combat puffiness by helping with overall circulation,” says Jessie Seleio, Stott Pilates instructor at Real Pilates. Though you don’t have to be a seasoned practitioner to try any of the below, if you’re a frequent traveler, consider taking regular classes so your body has a “stronger foundation and is better equipped to deal with long periods of sitting and traveling”, advises Lisa Sayers, Co-owner of House of Burn. Why movement is key This is not about doing a full Pilates routine in the aisle. Firstly, that would potentially be quite annoying for your fellow passengers and the crew. But secondly, you don’t actually need to make extreme movements in order to feel the benefits in your body. Having worked as cabin crew before opening her own Pilates studio, Sayers confirms, “You feel the effects of a long-haul flight far more in your body as a passenger than you do as a crew member. One of the biggest differences is simply movement.” While passengers often remain seated for hours at a time, crew spend the majority of the flight on their feet, which decreases their chances of stiffness. Adding in some timed walks or stretches is key to arriving feeling fresh. “Simply changing position, moving your joints and getting up whenever it’s safe to do so can make a massive difference,” says Sayers. Pilates stretches to do on a long-haul flight Deep diaphragmatic breathing Sitting in one place for hours can “compress the diaphragm and restrict your circulation,” explains Seleio. You can combat this by practicing deep diaphragmatic breathing, which will help to “maintain oxygen flow, reduce muscle tension, and keep your nervous system calm”. To do this, “place yourself towards the front of your seat with your spine lengthened. Inhale deeply through your nose for a count of four, allowing your rib cage to expand sideways. Exhale slowly through your mouth for a count of four, gently drawing your navel toward your spine and allowing your ribs to soften inward," instructs Seleio. “Repeat five times.” Shoulder rolls To help release tension in your shoulders and upper back, which can so easily become tense when sitting in a rigid seat, you need to make sure your movements go beyond just adjusting your neck pillow. To do this, Seleio says, “Sit upright with your arms relaxed by your sides. Slowly roll your shoulders up toward your ears, then back and down, encouraging your shoulder blades to glide smoothly across your ribcage." Perform five to eight repetitions, then reverse the direction. Pelvic tilts When instructed to stay in one place, our pelvis, seeking comfort, can tilt itself into an anterior (towards the front of your body) or posterior (towards the back of your body) position. If you allow this and don't consciously maintain a neutral posture, it can cause an achy lower back and, over time, a deformed posture. To help find your even position, do some pelvic tilts between over- and under-extension. Not only will this give your lower back some movement and release, but it will also help you to find your healthy neutral sitting position. “Take a deep breath in and gently arch your lower back, tilting your pelvis backwards,” says Sayers. “As you exhale, round through your lower back and tilt the front of your pelvis up towards your body. Slowly alternate between the two positions to add movement.” Seated knee lifts with ankle movement Simply lifting your knees while in your plane seat can improve your blood circulation and activate your hip flexors and core. Start by “sitting tall with your core gently engaged,” says Seleio. Then, “slowly lift one knee a few inches off the floor without leaning backwards. While keeping the knee lifted, point your toes away from you, then pull them back toward your shin three to five times. Lower the foot in a controlled manner and repeat on the other side. Continue alternating sides for 10 to 20 repetitions.” Isometric palm press We can all be guilty of slumping into our seats or rounding our shoulders as we get lost in a classic film on the in-flight entertainment system. Adding some isometric palm presses can help bring an awareness back to your posture, activate your chest muscles, and release tension in your shoulders. “Bring your palms together in front of your chest with your elbows relaxed,” says Seleio. Then, “press your palms firmly into one another while maintaining an upright posture and engaged core. Hold the contraction for five to 10 seconds, then release. Repeat the movement five to eight times”. Spinal rotations When sitting for over an hour, our spine can become impacted as pressure builds on the discs in our lumbar spine. To keep your thoracic spine (the mid-back) more mobile, you can release tension through gentle twisting movements. “Sit up nice and tall, keeping your shoulders relaxed and away from your ears,” says Sayers. Then “gently rotate your upper body from side to side. You can gradually move a little further into the rotation each time, but keep the movement controlled and never force a deep twist”. Toe taps Regardless of whether you’re wearing compression socks or not, your legs and ankles can often become swollen when sitting for long periods. One of the best things you can do to alleviate this is to “get up and walk around when possible,” explains Sayers. But if the seatbelt sign is firmly switched on, you can make a difference by moving your feet. To keep the blood moving and to give your core a mid-flight activation, toe taps are simple but effective. “Sit tall with your spine lengthened and core gently engaged,” starts Seleio. Next, “Lift one foot a few inches off the floor while reaching the opposite hand to tap the toes. Return to the starting position with control and alternate sides. Continue for 10 to 20 repetitions”. Throughout this exercise, you should maintain an upright posture and “avoid collapsing through the chest as you reach for your foot”. With thanks to Sabrina Aparicio Bellesa, Pilates instructor at Real Pilates. A version of this story originally appeared on Condé Nast Traveller Middle East.

item.title: 13 Stopover Flights to Help You Get the Most Out of International Airfare
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.13
Adding an airline stopover to your next flight itinerary is one of the best ways to maximize your airfare and stretch your vacation time. Many international carriers offer these free mini-visits as a way to entice travelers to visit their home country or city. Stopover programs are often booked as an extended layover and can offer stays from 24 hours all the way up to 15 days. Plus, they’re completely free to add during the flight booking process. Even with airfares getting more expensive across the industry, there’s still no extra charge for adding a stopover to your itinerary. A handful of airlines even include complimentary stays at five-star hotels, discounted sightseeing tours, savings at local restaurants, and more. The free perks are usually coordinated with the destination’s tourism board, which wants to impress travelers and garner repeat visits. Whether your carrier offers numerous free amenities or just allows you to add time to your connection, the stopover program is likely still worth taking advantage of, if only for the opportunity to explore an intriguing destination for the night. Here, we’ve rounded up 13 airline stopover programs that are worth booking and will allow travelers to explore Paris, Madrid, Dubai, Istanbul, Reykjavik, Lisbon, Panama City, Munich, Doha, Abu Dhabi, Helsinki, Osaka, and more—all for no additional charge in airfare. This story has been updated with new information since its original publication date. Air France Just launched in July 2026, Air France’s new Paris Stopover program allows passengers connecting through Charles de Gaulle International Airport (CDG) to add up to a four-night stay in the City of Light. Stays can be added on either outbound or return legs, and fliers can also add travel packages curated by Extime Travel. As part of the travel deal, visitors get a stay in a four-star or five-star hotel located in Central Paris (or near Disneyland Paris), transfers, and “hand-picked local experiences,” all starting at about €400 per person. The “Paris Must-See” package includes access to some of the city’s most famous sites, like the Eiffel Tower, Louvre Museum, and a cruise on the Seine, while the “Disneyland Paris” travel package includes entry to the Disneyland and Adventure World Parks. When booking a flight with a connection through Paris, travelers will see a box that says “Paris Stopover” above the search results. After you book your airfare, you can then choose from among the Extime Travel packages available on the Air France site under “My Bookings.” Packages are tailored to the length of each stopover and are available to book until 48 hours before departure. Lufthansa Travelers can spend up to seven days among the fairytale castles, historic beer halls, and Gothic architecture in Munich at no extra cost, thanks to Lufthansa’s new stopover program in the Bavarian capital. An option to add a stopover on the outbound or return journey will be displayed automatically during the flight booking process if one is available on the itinerary. When booking is complete, travelers can opt into receiving information on activities, benefits, and special offers from Lufthansa’s travel partners, including discounted hotel stays and tours of iconic landmarks in the region. Among the offers are 20% off the flex room rate at the Rosewood Munich, 25% off tours of Neuschwanstein Castle and Linderhof Palace, 25% off a hop-on, hop-off bus tour of Munich, and more. Fiji Airways If you’re traveling to Australia, New Zealand, or another destination in the Pacific, why not add a free 48-hour pitstop in the tropical paradise of Fiji to your itinerary? Fiji Airways allows passengers transiting through its hub in Nadi the option to explore the islands for a couple of days before continuing with their journey. Take time to enjoy some of the world’s best snorkeling, surfing, and coral sand beaches. To book, travelers can visit the carrier’s dedicated Fiji Stopover page and purchase their airfares with the “Multi-City / Fiji Stopover” toggle on. (Fiji Airways operates four gateway cities in the US: Los Angeles, San Francisco, Honolulu, and Dallas.) Once your airfare is locked down, choose from one of the airline’s stopover accommodation packages, which include two-night stays at top-notch local resorts like the Shangri-La Yanuca Island or VOMO island, plus perks like return airport transfers, daily breakfast, spa discounts, and late checkout, starting at about $225 per night. You’ll also get access to affordable excursions like sailing tours and ziplining, starting at about $100 per person. TAP Air Portugal Offering free stopovers in two cities—Porto and Lisbon—TAP Air Portugal has one of the most flexible programs out there. Plus, it allows travelers to stay in either city for up to 10 days. The stopover booking process is super simple, as TAP has integrated it into its standard booking field. All you need to do is choose your travel dates, departure city, and destination as usual, then click the “Add Stopover” button. This will open a pop-up window where you can input the details of your stopover, including whether you'd like to visit Porto or Lisbon and for how long. When your flights are squared away, you can book a discounted hotel stay by browsing TAP's list of hotel partners. The list offers booking codes with average savings of 10-20% off your stay. You'll also have access to discounts for restaurants, museums, and walking tours. Browse the airline's stopover offers page to see the full list. And once you wrap up your stopover, you also get a 25% discount on airfare to a second destination in Portugal, like the Azores archipelago. Turkish Airlines Travelers on Turkish Airlines on any itinerary from the US with at least a 20-hour connection in Istanbul qualify for the carrier's Stopover in Istanbul offering. The program is one of the most generous when it comes to accommodations, giving all fliers a free hotel stay: Passengers flying from the US in economy class can stay two nights in a four-star hotel free of charge, and business class passengers get three free nights in a five-star hotel. There's also an option book additional nights at contracted hotels offering discounted stays starting at $49 USD per night. Turkish Airlines has recently simplified its stopover booking process, making it easier than ever to take advantage of the program. There is now a “Stopover in Istanbul” button right on the airline's booking page. Iberia With its Stopover Hola Madrid program, Iberia allows travelers to stay in the Spanish capital for as little as 24 hours, all the way up to seven days and six nights at no extra cost in airfare. Passengers can add a stopover to either their outbound or return flight and select the length of their stay on the airline's booking page. Stopover customers are also afforded a host of discounts, including 20% off tickets to the Prado museum, a free public transportation card valid for two days that can be picked up at the airport, and reduced hotel stays through the airline's partners. IcelandAir If you're interested in adding a few days in Reykjavik to your next vacation, book with IcelandAir, which offers free Reykjavik stopovers from one to seven days for its transatlantic passengers. When booking your flights, simply click the “Stopover in Iceland” button and choose how many days you'd like to stay. While there's no additional airfare involved, IcelandAir's program does not include a free or discounted hotel stay, so passengers will need to factor that in as an extra cost. However, the airline's stopover page does offer suggestions for a wide range of affordable sightseeing tours, like an abbreviated tour of the Golden Circle (from $112), a Northern Lights small group tour (from $126), and a whale watching tour (from $150). Qatar Airways One of the best airline stopover programs is Qatar Airways', which offers a valuable hotel bundle. The carrier offers stays of up to four days in Doha, with bundle rates for four-star hotels starting at just $14 USD per person per night. If you want to upgrade to a luxury five-star hotel, the fee starts at $23 USD per person per night, which is still a deep discount. And of course, the stopover will cost you nothing in terms of extra airfare fees. To score the bundle, book your stopover through Qatar Airways' dedicated page, which allows you to select the leg of the journey you'd like to stop in Doha and for how many days. Once your flights are booked, visit the airline's stopover hotel booking page to browse options for your stay. Choose your hotel and input your flight information during the booking process to receive the discount. Also available during your time in Doha are discounted tour packages that range from activities like kitesurfing lessons, a private Bedouin dinner in the desert, souq tours, and many more. The carrier has also added a special F1 experience to its stopover lineup for 2026. Travelers who book a Doha stopover between November 27 and 29 include a 3-day T16 Grandstand ticket to the F1 Qatar Airways Qatar Grand Prix for each person traveling on the stopover. Etihad With its “Stopover on Us” package, Etihad is offering free stopovers in Abu Dhabi. The one- or two-night packages include a free stay at a three-star hotel in the city, plus perks like 24-hour check-in and free in-room Wi-Fi. Among the hotel partners are the Grand Hyatt Abu Dhabi, the Yas Plaza Marina by IHG, the Millennium Downtown Abu Dhabi, and the Intercontinental Abu Dhabi. To add the stopover, you need to first book a flight connecting through Abu Dhabi in any cabin class. Then, select your stopover package and check hotel availability on the airline's stopover page. It's important to note that a flight reservation is required to check the program's hotel availability (which is not guaranteed) and bookings must be made at least 72 hours before travel. Copa Airlines Travelers can take up to 15 days to explore Panama City with Copa Airlines’ stopover program. Copa passengers can add a stopover in the capital city—one of the best places to go in South America in 2024—on either the outgoing or return leg of their journey. Travelers can stay in Panama for as little as 24 hours all the way up to two weeks without needing to pay extra airfare. (Copa also offers the option to add a second stopover to your flight itinerary for $250 USD.) To book the stopover, simply go to the booking page on Copa’s website and toggle to the “Multi-city/Stopover” tab. The program now includes discounted hotel stays, including up to 48% off stays at boutique properties like Central Hotel Panama Casco Viejo or 30% off oceanfront hotels like Bambuda Santa Catalina. The savings also extend to tours, activities, restaurants, and car rentals. Emirates With its Dubai Connect program, Emirates offers travelers with extended layovers in Dubai an array of complimentary perks, including a one-night hotel stay, visa, meals, and transfers to and from the airport. Passengers in economy through first class are eligible for these perks. To qualify for the program, your layover must be between eight to 26 hours for economy and premium economy tickets or six and 26 hours for business and first class tickets. Your connection time must be the shortest available—meaning you have to depart Dubai on the next available flight to your destination or your itinerary won’t be eligible. When passengers arrive in Dubai, they can head to the Dubai Connect desk in the arrivals terminal for their free car transfer to their hotel. The airline usually puts Dubai Connect passengers in the Copthorne Hotel Dubai, the Le Méridien Airport Hotel Dubai, or the JW Marriott Marquis, but it’s possible travelers will be booked at a different property at the carrier’s discretion. While at the hotel, all applicable meals will be included as part of the service. You can book Dubai Connect online at least 24 hours before your layover. For a longer stopover experience, travelers can book a multi-city itinerary on the airline’s booking page. Toggle the “advanced search” feature and input Dubai International airport as an additional destination between your city of origin and final destination. When your flights are booked, you can add on Dubai hotels and experiences through Emirates’ Dubai stopover page, which offers discounts and extra perks like 24-hour hotel check-in. Japan Airlines Billing itself as one of the most “stopover friendly” airlines in the industry, Japan Airlines offers extended layovers in cities like Osaka and Kyoto. Essentially, JAL’s program allows fliers to book multi-city itineraries with stays in stopover destinations of at least 24 hours. Although the airline doesn’t offer free perks once you arrive in your stopover city, it’s definitely still worth taking advantage of the feature to see more stunning destinations throughout Japan. Plus, booking is easy. Simply use JAL’s “multi-city/stopover” search tool to find options for your free pit stops in some of the nation’s most popular destinations. Finnair Spend up to five days in Helsinki soaking up Nordic culture with Finnair’s stopover program. The airline offers extended stays in Finland’s capital city at no extra cost to fliers—the itineraries can be booked as a multi-city trip. (Just select the “multi-city” option under the trip type drop down menu when booking.) Although Finnair doesn’t offer any deals on activities or accommodations in Helsinki, the carrier has curated layover guides to the city that offer recommendations on what to see and do—perhaps a spin through the Helsinki Design Museum, followed by a French-Finnish meal at Restaurant Savoy?—plus logistics on the fastest ways to get to and from the airport.

item.title: The Triumphant Return of the Airline Seatback Screen
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.09
Airline passengers are all too familiar with onboard perks disappearing from planes, whether it’s free seat selection or in-flight snacks, complimentary checked bags, or simply the ability to recline your seat. Now, however, some of the largest US airlines are bringing back one passenger-beloved amenity: seatback entertainment screens. Thanks to a rising demand for more premium products, airlines are reversing course on the steady elimination of individual entertainment screens and are now adding them back to their fleets across all cabin classes. Just several years ago, the demise of the seatback screen had seemed all but certain as part of airlines’ never-ending quest to cut costs and maximize profits. “These systems are expensive to purchase, expensive to install, and have ongoing costs including repair and programming updates,” says Mike Taylor, senior managing director of travel, hospitality, retail, and customer service at JD Power. Plus, airlines figured that 80% of passengers were flying with their own smartphones, laptops, or tablets, so it would be simpler to nix the screens and offer content for travelers to access on their personal devices, according to Taylor. “But difficulties in connecting, the quality of in-flight Wi-Fi, and the variability of streaming bandwidth among various types of aircraft account for the deficit between seatback and streaming experiences,” he says. One of the most notable about-faces on screens is a new initiative from American Airlines. The Fort Worth-based carrier said it will be adding seatback screens back to every seat in its narrow-body fleet of aircraft, including onboard new planes set to be delivered in 2028 as well as retrofitting its existing jets with screens. “In the race for premium traffic, American felt like they couldn’t compete with Delta and United—which have leaned into screens—without their own,” says Gary Leff, an airline expert and travel advisor. United, for one, has been on a mission since 2022 to add seatback screens to every seat in its fleet as part of its Good Leads the Way campaign to improve its onboard experience. As part of that plan, the carrier unveiled 13-inch TVs in economy, which rank among the largest coach screens in the world, aboard its new Dreamliner 787-9 planes. Likewise, Alaska Airlines has been adding its first-ever seatback screens in the carrier's history to its new Dreamliner fleet that debuted in late 2025 and now flies their long-haul international routes from Seattle. Although Delta never reduced the seatback screens in its fleet, the carrier has been heavily investing in its in-flight entertainment system since 2023 with the launch of Delta Sync, which offers a personalized, smart TV-like experience with benefits like the ability to pause a movie on one flight and resume it on the next one. Experts say that aside from the race to provide premium products, there are a few additional factors pushing airlines to reinstate their own TVs at every seat. For one, screen technology has advanced by leaps and bounds compared to a decade ago, when the elimination strategy became popular. Now, the screens are “far less expensive to install than they used to be, since it no longer requires running wires to each seat to feed content,” Leff explains. “The screens can receive their content wirelessly from a server on the plane.” Not only that, but the latest screens offer perks like 4K display, Bluetooth connectivity for wireless headphones, USB-C charging ports, and personalized content. That last feature could even help carriers actually make money off of the systems, too. “The screens also offer a revenue opportunity to monetize the time and attention of the passenger, a desirable demographic to advertise to, with personalized content. They know who is seated at each seat,” says Leff. At the end of the day, passengers simply prefer a seatback screen as a way to get lost in a movie or show while on a long flight. According to JD Power’s airline satisfaction survey data, seatback screens add between 60 and 90 points of customer satisfaction to an airline’s overall score, which is based on a 1,000 point scale. “That is a significant difference in satisfaction in airline experience,” Taylor says.

item.title: This Fall, Leaf Peep from a Gondola, Helicopter, or Tree House
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.96
Americans call it “leaf peeping,” while the Japanese call it “momijigari.” Whatever the culture, there’s a term for witnessing the changing colors of leaves, a universal act that spurs awe and wonder and makes one reflect on the passage of time. Fall foliage is worth booking a trip around, but you need not limit yourself to the standard hike or road trip. While we’ll always have these classic leaf-peeping excursions, there’s excitement in reinventing a ritual. Once you start to experience the first chills of the season, consider getting a little whimsical: Mush your way through the Alaskan forest, float away on a hot air balloon in the Finger Lakes, or zipline past the Rockies. You could rent a run-of-the-mill cabin somewhere in the Hudson Valley, or you could go big with a tree house, complete with floor-to-ceiling windows. Ditch that standard New England inn and opt instead for a houseboat in coastal Maine, perfect for riverside scenery. The possibilities are endless, and the experiences on this list will ensure you see the changing colors of fall from all kinds of perspectives. Below, seven alternative ideas for leaf peeping across the US. Hop on a gondola While mountain resorts are best known for skiing in the winter, many keep off-season tourists happy with scenic sky rides. Take the Gondola SkyRide at Stowe Mountain Resort, for instance, which carries visitors up to Mount Mansfield, Vermont’s highest peak. Running until mid-October, the ride is an excellent way to bask in New England’s autumnal glory and drops passengers off right at the resort’s Cliff House Restaurant for a scenic meal. Similarly, the Gondola at Telluride Mountain Village in southwest Colorado allows visitors to take in golden aspens from 10,800 feet above and can be used to access various hiking trails. Over at Lutsen Mountains in Minnesota, leaf peepers can take the Summit Express to get some of the best views in the state, including sightings of the Sawtooth Mountains and Lake Superior. Embark on a scenic train ride Nothing says cozy fall trip quite like an old-fashioned choo choo train, and luckily, the country is teeming with locomotives for every kind of traveler. Wine lovers will enjoy the Napa Valley Wine Train, especially between September and November, when harvest season is in full swing, and the vineyards and trees turn shades of gold, orange, and red (temperatures at this time also hover in the 80s—glorious). Prefer something a bit more outdoorsy? Amtrak’s Pacific Northwest Fall Foliage train takes passengers on sightseeing tours of Mount Rainier and Olympic National Park, which boast vibrant maples (and thinner crowds) from mid-September through October, while the Blue Ridge Railway offers dedicated fall foliage tours for those who’d like to experience the beauty of the Toccoa River. For something even more adventurous, Rail Explorers offers an unconventional approach to the train track with pedal-powered bikes you can use to ride the rails, with scenic locations in New York’s Catskills and West Virginia’s Elk River region. Mush your way through the forest In Fairbanks, Alaska, the leaves start changing as early as mid-to-late August, and you don’t have to wait until the snow falls to have an authentic dog sledding experience. On Last Frontier’s unique mushing ride, you’ll have a four-legged team guiding you through the Alaskan forest on UTVs, “learning all about dog mushing, racing, and Alaskan off-grid living along the way,” the website says. The host, Chase, is a former Yukon Quest racer, and he’ll introduce you to his team of dogs, who will be very excited to run after their long summer hiatus. (Because Last Frontier is a co-op, different mushers run their own dogs and make sure their animals are well taken care of). Glide past the trees on a cruise The foliage surrounding the banks of New York’s Hudson River is so striking, it makes sense why it’s served as the subject for a history of landscape paintings. Circle Line offers two cruises for Hudson Valley leaf peeping—an eight-hour journey up to Bear Mountain State Park past the Palisades, or a shorter four-hour run toward Hook Mountain—each with beer, pretzels, and all kinds of other Oktoberfest fare. Adventurers looking for more of a day trip will enjoy the dock at Bear Mountain State Park, where they’ll have about three hours on land to hike, while those opting for the shorter trip will still get to sail past the George Washington and Mario Cuomo Bridges, looking out for hawks, ospreys, and bald eagles along the way. Each departing from Midtown Manhattan, these cruises offer ideal day trips for New Yorkers itching to explore nature beyond Central Park. Zipline through the mountains Adrenaline seekers, this one’s for you—see the trees in a flash on a zipline tour through the mountains. From mid-September to late October, Idaho Springs, Colorado, becomes flush with golden aspens, and you can spend half a day taking in the beautiful scenery from six different aerial lines along the treetops with Arkansas Valley Adventures. Or, if you’d rather get your views from down south, Saluda, North Carolina, is a sight to behold from mid-October through early November, and this Gorge Zipline Canopy Tour will suspend adventurers above the Green River Gorge for unforgettable views of changing maples and alders. Book a unique, foliage-friendly stay Sometimes, autumnal scenery can be so arresting, you can’t help but spend hours soaking in the views. There’s no shortage of fall-foliage-friendly Airbnbs and vacation rentals across the country, so make the most of your autumnal getaway with an unforgettable stay. Commerce director Madison Flager is a big fan of this tree house in Phoenicia, New York, with its soaring windows and proximity to cult-classic Phoenicia Diner. If you’d rather hole up in coastal Maine, White Barn Inn in Kennebunkport (a consistent Reader’s Choice winner) offers a collection of houseboat stays plopped on the Kennebunk River, where you can enjoy your morning coffee from a private rooftop deck, gazing at the golden landscape. - Check availability for the Treehouse in Phoenicia, New York - Check availability for the White Barn Inn & Spa Get a true bird's-eye view There are gondolas, and then there are more extreme ways to soar above the trees. If you fancy floating away on a hot air balloon, head to New York’s Finger Lakes region for a ride above Letchworth State Park, known as the “Grand Canyon of the East,” for a one-hour journey with Liberty Balloon Company. You’ll see vibrant trees framing a 600-foot gorge and three different waterfalls, all from the comfort of your balloon. Or, go big with a private helicopter tour of the Hudson Valley with Wings Air Helicopters, departing from Midtown Manhattan. In just one hour, you’ll soar over the Sleepy Hollow Lighthouse, Bear Mountain, Lyndhurst Mansion, and Kykuit, the Rockefeller Estate, all while enjoying the patches of color.

item.title: 9 Affordable Miami Hotels That Prove You Can Do Luxury for Less
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.92
Miami has never exactly been shy about excess. Between the pastel Art Deco façades, palm-lined streets, glittering pools, and top-notch restaurants where lunch can easily turn into an all-afternoon affair, this is a city that makes it tempting to spend. But after enough trips here, I’ve learned that you don’t necessarily need to splurge on your hotel to get the tried-and-true Miami experience. Some of the city’s best affordable hotels are characterful little boutiques, historic beach hotels, and design-minded stays where the location does more of the heavy lifting than the room rate. At these value-forward bases, you can wake up a few blocks from the sand, wander down Ocean Drive for a cafecito, or retreat to the pool after a day in the sun—all without handing over your entire vacation budget at check-in. From South Beach to Brickell and beyond, these are the affordable Miami hotels—all with average nightly rates under $250—that I’d recommend booking for a stunning stay that won't break the bank. FAQ: What part of Miami is best to stay in? The best area to stay in Miami, of course, depends on your preferences. South Beach is ideal for beach lovers and nightlife seekers, offering a lively atmosphere with easy access to Little Havana, the beach, and buzzy restaurants. For a more cultural experience, consider Wynwood or the Design District, known for art galleries and trendy spots. Downtown Miami provides a central location, great for business travelers and those who want proximity to museums and shopping. Coconut Grove offers a more relaxed vibe. Where should I stay in Miami for the first time? For first-time visitors, South Beach is often the top choice due to its iconic beaches, vibrant nightlife, and easy access to popular attractions. Staying here puts you close to Ocean Drive, the Art Deco Historic District, and numerous shops and restaurants. It’s perfect for a mix of relaxation and exploration. If you prefer a quieter area, consider Coconut Grove or Brickell, which both offer a more laid-back atmosphere but are still centrally located for sightseeing. What is the average price of a hotel in Miami? The average price of a hotel in Miami varies depending on the season, location, and hotel type. On average, expect to pay between $150 and $350 per night for mid-range accommodations. Prices can spike during peak seasons, such as winter or major events like Art Basel, when rates can exceed $500 per night. Budget options may start around $75 to $100 per night, while luxury hotels can range from $400 to over $1,000 per night. How we choose the best affordable hotels in Miami: Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. More Miami travel recommendations Read our complete Miami travel guide here, which includes: - The Best Things to Do in Miami - The Best Restaurants in Miami - The Best Bars in Miami - The Best Miami Airbnbs This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: Designer Thebe Magugu on Where He Shops and Dances in Cape Town
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.67
“The fashion in Cape Town is so inimitable because it takes from our own culture and heritage,” says South African fashion designer Thebe Magugu. Though he's based in Johannesburg, work frequently brings him to the capital—including for a suite he designed at Mount Nelson, a Belmond Hotel, Cape Town, which he filled with works by local artists. For Magugu, whose current collection “looks at the changing face of African spirituality,” it's the people wearing his clothes who help preserve his vision. Here, the spots he never misses. Art institutions, big and small “The Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa is one of the most beautiful buildings in Cape Town. Inside is the largest collection of contemporary art by Africans and the continent's diaspora. I also love Southern Guild gallery around the corner, and my friend Anelisa Mangcu's space, Under the Aegis.” Trawling for inspiration “I like introducing compelling objects from Longmarket Street into my look books. It's lined with people selling African masks, straw mats, and wood carvings of various animals, both realistic and mythological. I always go without a plan, but I know that someday I'll need the items I find.” Get into the groove “Music is a big part of my life in Cape Town—I associate it with being out in the community. I shop at Roastin' Records and dance with friends at Souk. Gqom Therapy is [dedicated to] a new genre of South African dance music and a must-do party with the best sound system.” Shop and rub shoulders “I always recommend concept shop AKJP Studio, which was started by my friends Keith Henning and Jody Paulsen. It stocks some of the greatest South African fashion designers and, from 6 p.m., turns into a bar frequented by local creatives.” This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: The Best Airbnbs on the Greek Island of Sifnos, From a Converted Windmill to a Modern Apartment
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.65
The Greek island of Sifnos is petite but perfectly formed. The smaller size means you can get a good sense of the place over a long weekend, but you’ll likely still want to return. Its expanse of sandy white stretches is divine, and a scattering of villages sewn throughout unspoiled landscapes hum with activity during the summer months. Most importantly, the food scene is excellent. Thankfully, there’s no shortage of wonderful Airbnbs in Sifnos to book on every corner of the island. Below, we’ve picked our favorite Sifnos Airbnbs for 2026. We've vetted these listings based on Superhost or Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. Our top picks: - Best for couples: Converted windmill, Artemonas - Best for families: Sleepy seaside home, Hersonissos - Best for big groups: Elevated Cycladic rental, Platýs Gialós - Best for interior design fans: Traditional stone apartment, Kamares - Best for a room with a view: Cozy cottage, Artemonas - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: Proximity to the beach, panoramic sea views, outdoor spaceThe views here are unmatched—sitting and watching as the space catches the golden afternoon light over Kamares Bay is exactly the reason so many make the pilgrimage to Greece year after year. A stay here ensures a front-row seat to the island’s buzzy marine hub, where all rooms are bright and spacious, opening onto their own balconies showcasing incredible panoramic sea views over glistening waters. Plus, you’re just a three-minute stroll from the soft sands of Sifnos’s popular main beach. This makes for the best of both worlds: easy access to tavernas and sunset-dappled paths to amble down, along with good proximity to the scenic Agia Ekaterini trail, which leads to a secluded turquoise cove perfect for rock diving and snorkeling away from the main summer crowds. Location: Kamares Things to do nearby: Agia Ekaterini, beach, Kamares Bay - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Spacious terrace, coastal views, direct sea accessHistory buffs, here’s one for you: Steeped in local artisan history, this is a local type of stay for truly getting under the skin of the island. Once a heritage pottery, this converted shop offers immediate access to the glittering sea in the sleepy fishing hamlet of Hersonissos—a little-known northern haven largely sheltered from the summer winds that are characteristic of this region. The renovation was carried out with families in mind, with a spacious terrace where children can play and adults can read on a lounger against a sumptuous backdrop of wide, uninterrupted coastal vistas. In a fun twist, you can step right off the lower courtyard into the clear sea via a built-in ladder, and it’s just a few wandering steps to a selection of quiet local tavernas. Location: Hersonissos Things to do nearby: Local tavernas, water access - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Olive trees, original stone walls, pergola, terraceSettled within a vibrant garden bursting with olive trees and a blur of purple bougainvillea, this lovingly restored cottage is yet another pretty Greek Cycladic home, this time just outside the labyrinthine village of Artemonas. There’s plenty of character imbued within the original stone walls—you’ll love the built-in masonry beds—and there’s a sprinkling of ceramic accents throughout that honor Sifnos’ rich pottery heritage. A new modern kitchen and naturally cooling design keep your stay easy and comfortable. Each room opens directly onto a stone-paved courtyard shaded by a pergola, for effortless indoor-outdoor living that flows from morning until night. The showstopper is the sun-warmed terrace—the best spot in the house to enjoy breakfasts as the sun rises and evening drinks while gazing across the glittering Aegean. Look closely and you might spot sister Greek islands Mykonos, Syros, and Antiparos. Location: Artemonas Things to do nearby: Artemonas, Apollonia - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 3 baths Why we love it: Shared veranda, private balcony off the primary bedroom, shared swimming poolDappled light spills across the gardens where this particularly aesthetic home, surrounded by silver-leafed trees, awaits. The space has all that Greek traditional whitewashed calm outside, matched with sleek contemporary living once you head through the door. It’s a larger home than average for the area, with room for the whole family, incorporating breezy open-plan interiors, three bathrooms, and two airy bedrooms.
