This is for sleepy, relaxed weekends, with a layout naturally encouraging a relaxed lifestyle. There’s a shared shaded veranda on the ground floor, and the primary bedroom has a private balcony with incredible sweeping views of the glittering Aegean Sea. Cool off in the shared swimming pool after exploring the island; for a sociable bolthole for families seeking an authentic Sifnian escape, this is a great option just slightly away from the main bustle. Location: Platýs Gialós Things to do nearby: Beaches, restaurants, mini-markets, cafés - Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Windmill, historic building, air conditioningSifnos has around 60 windmills scattered across its rolling landscapes, and here's the chance to take over one as your own. The hosts have worked hard to ensure the renovations pay homage to the mill’s 157-year history—it was built in 1864 and continued to function until 1965—while squeezing in everything you’ll need. There’s a comfy double bed, TV, air conditioning, a fully-equipped kitchen, and even a separate bathroom. One note: Try to pack light, as there are quite a few steps up a hill to reach the mill, and nobody wants to tackle that while lugging heavy luggage. Location: Artemonas Things to do nearby: Artemonas Square - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Proximity to the beach, shared courtyard, outdoor dining tableNow, this is the epitome of beachy Greek bliss—a huge, one-level, airy apartment right on the sands, with plenty of comfy sun loungers, a chef’s kitchen, convivial dining space, and super-smart interiors tying everything together. With two double bedrooms and a third with two single beds, it’s a good choice for family breaks or, really, anyone who wants to stay as close as possible to the waves and salty sea air. Location: Platis Gialos Things to do nearby: Platis Gialos Beach, hiking trails - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Balcony, mountain views, booksBuilt in the 13th century to form part of a castle’s tower, this little Sifnian house is now better placed to serve as your home away from home in the peaceful village of Kastro, which has some of the prettiest pedestrian streets on the island. A minimal palette of grays, whites, and neutral woods is pepped up with bold flashes of blue on the doors and window frames; peer out for gorgeous views over the mountains beyond. Location: Kastro Things to do nearby: Kastro, Seralia Beach - Number of guests: 5 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Pet-friendly, sound system, outdoor dining areaIt’s impossible not to feel cheery inside this airy apartment. It’s dopamine-dressed to perfection with zippy yellow window frames, a powder blue Smeg fridge, smidges of green on the ceiling beams, and a checkered marble floor. The external space is even better, with a positively idyllic courtyard ripe for sundowners against a backdrop of Greece’s famous blazing sunsets. You’re right by the sights of vibrant Apollonia and just steps away from the start of the traditional paved path to Ano Petali. Take a walk one day before stopping in at one of the clutch of nearby tavernas for a pick-me-up en route home. Location: Apollonia Things to do nearby: Apollonia, Ano Petali, tavernas - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bath Why we love it: Air conditioning, hammock, dedicated workspacePerched on a hilltop just on the cusp of buzzy Appollonia, this newly renovated apartment sits waiting for you to check in. Sandy hues and natural materials give way to sparkly seascapes, hugged by distant mountains, from the courtyard—sit out with a morning coffee and enjoy. Previous guests have raved about this Airbnb; it’s spotlessly clean, tranquil, and the views across the town are unbeatable. If you’re lucky, you might even return home to a complimentary bottle of wine or cake one day, too. Location: Ano Petali Things to do nearby: Apollonia, Artemonas

item.title: These Best Museums in Tokyo Showcase the Japanese Capital's Unparalleled Arts Scene
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.51
As anyone who has ever dined, partied, or simply wandered around Tokyo will attest, the Japanese capital marches to its own, singular beat. So it makes sense that the best museums in Tokyo are a far cry from the stodgy mausoleums of yesteryear. In lieu of squat buildings full of dusty dioramas, picture cutting-edge modernist structures by some of the country's top architects. Many of the premier art spaces forgo a permanent collection entirely in favor of a constantly rotating roster of high-profile shows by big names, local and international. Even the smaller collections strive to present their subject matter in clever, often wildly creative ways. Not sure where to go first? Here are our picks for 12 of the best museums in Tokyo. Read our complete Tokyo travel guide here, which includes: How we choose the best museums in Tokyo Every review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that museum. When choosing museums, our editors consider institutions that offer an insider’s view of a destination, keeping authenticity, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. - Read Full ReviewPrince Asaka Yasuhiko, uncle to Emperor Hirohito, came home from Paris smitten, and the residence he and his wife Princess Nobuko completed in 1933, built by a team led by Yokichi Gondo, is the result: a marvelous blend of Deco and Japanese design set in a meticulously sculpted garden planted with dozens of flowering species. It feels like an Agatha Christie novel set in 1930s Tokyo. A contemporary annex, supervised by Hiroshi Sugimoto, added gallery space and a café. While there’s no permanent collection, the museum’s holdings comprise more than 250 works, most of which are incorporated into the design of the house itself . Henri Rapin's interiors conjure the glamour of the age in dark wood and brass, geometric ornament and sumptuous surfaces. René Lalique supplied the crystal chandeliers and glass front doors (fun fact: his first proposal featured nude female figures; the Japanese side asked him to reconsider), and there's a marble relief by Ivan-Léon Alexandre Blanchot. Outside, modern work is scattered across the grounds, including Kan Yasuda's striking white marble Wind. - Read Full ReviewA quirky little art museum hiding in plain sight, just outside the Marunouchi North ticket gates of the busiest commuter hub on earth. It opened in 1988 and, in 2006, closed for six years while Tokyo Station underwent restoration. The museum was relocated to the North Dome and reopened in 2012. The second-floor galleries put you inside Tatsuno Kingo's 1914 original station—a symbol of Western-style modernization, with brickwork and white-framed windows in the Queen Anne style. From the corridor, you can watch the commuter traffic flowing through the station below while getting an up-close view of the ornate carvings beneath the domed ceiling. The range runs from traditional Japanese painters like Kobayashi Tokusaburo to Léonard Tsuguharu Foujita, the midcentury artist whose wartime work still divides opinion. Past exhibitions have also covered the Finnish designer Tapio Wirkkala and the textile artist Miyawaki Ayako. If there's a throughline, it's a penchant for niche creators over marquee names. - Read Full ReviewIt bills itself as an immersive experience and delivers: Shohei Shigematsu supervised a spatial redesign that begins with a striking approach of 24 torii-like structures and projected imagery easing you backward in time. A delight, spread across the fifth and sixth floors in two halves, the Edo Zone and the Tokyo Zone. A full-scale recreation of Nihonbashi Bridge anchors it; the Nakamura-za kabuki theatre, once admired from outside, can now be entered. New life-size reconstructions include the Hattori Clock Shop, which leads visitors from Edo into modern Tokyo, and a faithful reproduction of the interior from the Dojunkai Daikanyama Apartments from 1927. Tempura and sushi stalls have joined the Edo streets, stocked with fabulously realistic plastic food, and screens project changing skies over the rooftops. Much of the collection is hands-on, too: you can climb into a palanquin or a cycle buggy, or shoulder the pole-and-bucket rig once used to haul fish through the streets. - Read Full ReviewA sumptuous, surreal, camera-baiting museum devoted to multi-sensory digital art. Borderless 2.0 reopened in February 2024 in a purpose-built basement space at the Azabudai Hills complex in central Tokyo. There are no walls between works and no map to follow. Installations of constantly morphing patterns and designs flow seamlessly from room to room across a maze-like space, so a school of digital fish or a cascade of blossoms will simply wander off and reappear somewhere else. Getting lost is the intended experience. Alongside updated versions of Odaiba classics, the Azabudai Hills location debuts several major new installations: Bubble Universe, an interactive infinity room filled with glass spheres that ripple with light as you approach them; Microcosmoses, where glowing spheres run along complex overhead tracks; and an expanded series of atmospheric Light Sculptures that project dynamic 3D geometry using light beams and fog. - Read Full ReviewBy outward appearance, Tokyo's Ōta Memorial Museum of Art is unassuming. Even the inside is relatively small. Still, it never fails to provide an inspiring and edifying experience. The museum focuses solely on ukiyo-e, Japanese woodblock prints and paintings, primarily from the Edo Era (1603-1868). For most of his life, the former president of the Toho Life Insurance Mutual Company Seizo Ota collected such works, and three years after his death at age 83, the Ota Memorial Museum of Art was opened in 1980 to showcase his collection. Today, the museum’s collection numbers around 15,000 works. In order to best represent this collection, the museum puts together thoughtfully curated exhibitions, with works changing frequently and many exhibitions divided into separate rotations. Topics ranging from the prosaic to the fantastic are paired with meticulously researched, Japanese- and English-language explanations that provide fascinating rabbit holes into Japanese history and the so-called "floating world" that ukiyo-e depict. - Read Full ReviewA glass, steel, and concrete behemoth at the north end of Kiba Park, and one of Japan's largest museums devoted to contemporary art. Takahiko Yanagisawa's 1995 building announces itself before you're through the gate: a long steel approach of triangular frames punched through with circles, more industrial than inviting, which turns out to be the right register for what's inside. MOT closed for a three-year renovation and reopened in March 2019, and marks its 14th year in 2026. The collection is around 6,100 works, weighted toward postwar art and shown on rotation as the MOT Collection. Warhol and Lichtenstein are among the international names, with Japanese artists like Atsuko Tanaka and Yoshitomo Nara. The temporary program is the reason to keep checking the calendar. Big solo shows—Kohei Nawa, Ryuichi Sakamoto, David Hockney, Olafur Eliasson—sit alongside well-curated group shows of younger multimedia artists, plus regular forays into fashion, design, and architecture. - Read Full ReviewA small but thoughtful tribute to the works of Japan’s most beloved animation studio, the Ghibli Museum's design is as quirky as its collection. Director Hayao Miyazaki lent his personal touch to the building, which loosely echoes a grand Italian villa. A dense layer of greenery covers the exterior of the mansion and a 16-foot-tall robot soldier from the classic film Castle in the Sky peers morosely down from the rooftop garden. More than a museum, this feels like an immersive world. From the walk-through recreation of a Ghibli artist’s workshop to original sketches, the museum uses all sorts of methods to bring Miyazaki’s vision to life. It would be an Instagram dream, if photos weren’t forbidden inside. Anyone who grew up watching these films will love the details, like the ceiling fresco populated by Nausicaa, Kiki, and other familiar faces. Even the tickets are made of original 35mm film prints, and faucet handles resemble tiny creatures. - Read Full ReviewAt first, the somewhat austere, gray facade of the National Museum of Modern Art feels at odds with the surrounding greenery of Kitanomaru Park. Inside, however, is one of the finest collections of modern Japanese art in the world. Walking through the galleries on the fourth through second floors allows you to see some of the most turbulent periods in the nation’s past through the eyes of its most influential artists. The museum’s former film division is now the independent National Film Archive of Japan, located in Kyobashi. More than 13,000 paintings, prints, drawings, video installations, and sculptures reside within the museum’s vaults and exhibition halls. Although there are a number of significant international works, the permanent collection’s strength lies in Japanese masters from the Meiji Period onward. English-language signs provide crucial historical context for each artist. - Read Full ReviewThe institution itself is a national treasure—it's Japan's oldest museum. It also happens to be in one of Tokyo's oldest public parks, Ueno, which wanders a hundred or so acres and bursts with attractions like ancient shrines, temples, ponds, and over a thousand cherry blossom trees. Housing the world's most comprehensive collection of Japanese art, it only displays the tip of the iceberg, rotating its 110,000 artifacts regularly throughout five distinct exhibition buildings. Items spark curiosity, like samurai swords and fabulous kimonos, while ancient sculptures of Buddha and woodblock prints complete the array. Special exhibitions are frequent, and usually last two months. Two separate exhibitions often open simultaneously, and in the past ranged from delightful meditations on the arts of tea ceremony (ancient tea bowls and such) to surveys of prolific Buddhist sculptors. - Read Full ReviewThe Mori Art Museum, the flashiest member of the Roppongi Art Triangle, sits atop the 53rd floor of the Roppongi Hills Mori Tower. Still, past exhibitions have featured works by the likes of Ai Weiwei and Dinh Q. Lê. Curators here do an exceptional job of creating exhibitions that are as thought-provoking as they are Instagrammable. Exhibitions in both the Mori Art Museum and the Mori Art Center Gallery rotate throughout the year. Anything from all corners of the contemporary art world is fair game here, from intricate paintings by the local avant-garde to large-scale international multimedia installations. Nothing feels haphazard here and each individual work has the space it needs to shine. The museum’s location in a glitzy commercial complex means that it draws a mix of dedicated insiders and casual gawkers. Especially on a clear day, the spectacular view attracts at least as many visitors as the art. - Read Full ReviewDating back to the 1870s, the National Museum of Nature and Science, in Ueno Park, is a boon for parents with curious kids. Butterflies, a fallen meteorite, and all manner of marvels pertaining to the broad field of natural science make this sprawling museum feel like an extended field trip. There’s a special emphasis on the anthropological history, biodiversity, geology, and technological contributions of Japan here. With a modest entry fee for adults and free entry for children under 18, the museum offers hours of family-friendly entertainment without breaking the bank. The breadth of the museum’s permanent collection is staggering. Everything from dinosaur skeletons and in-depth exhibits on space travel to a lifesize model of a blue whale outside makes this place feel like a sprawling Wunderkammer. A few of the highlights include a World War II fighter plane, a Futabasaurus plesiosaur unearthed in Fukushima, and—more disturbingly—the taxidermied body of Hachiko, a famous Japanese dog who waited patiently for his master for years. - Read Full ReviewThis serene museum in Tokyo's Aoyama district, rebuilt by architect Kengo Kuma, is a contemporary temple for traditional art. A long, covered outdoor path alongside bamboo-clad walls serves as a minimalist entrance, but once inside, double-height interiors and glass walls stretch over 40,000 square feet while keeping the experience intimate. And while the museum mixes contemporary design and traditional art on the inside, the outside counts, too: The property is home to a stunning private garden that’s worth the visit all on its own. The bulk of the museum’s art was once the private collection of Nezu Kaichirō, the president of Japan’s Tobu Railway. After his death, the collection—pre-modern Japanese and East Asian art, from calligraphy to sculptures to ceramics—was preserved, and his son (and heir) established the museum on the site of the Nezu family residence to display the many works. Since the midcentury, the collection has grown and now comprises over 7,600 pieces. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: For Starry Waters and Tiny Glowing Squids, Head to These Best Places to See Bioluminescence
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.28
The best places to see bioluminescence around the world sit atop many travelers’ bucket lists. Whether it's through the pages of glossy magazines like ours, glittering on social media feeds, or told through the tales our jet-setting loved ones share on their return from their latest adventure, this natural phenomenon is undeniably captivating. Perhaps it's jellyfish that twinkle at the harbor’s edge or plankton that creates scenes akin to starry skies as toes paddle in the ocean. Either way, bioluminescence is a fascinating natural phenomenon that, once witnessed, is impossible to forget. However, it’s unlikely that you’ll see glittering, rippling waters by chance. Here, from the shores of Oaxaca in Mexico to Maldivian atolls via the British Isles, we reveal the best places to see bioluminescence in all its dazzling forms. It is generally safe to touch and swim in bioluminescent waters, especially in destinations where the sparkling waters are featured as tourist attractions with boat trips and excursions. However, some bioluminescence results from harmful algal blooms that can cause skin rashes and severe illness if ingested. When in doubt, research the area you’re visiting thoroughly and speak to guides on organized trips. 1. The Maldives The picture-perfect islands of the Maldives are some of the best places to see bioluminescence around the world, thanks to an abundance of plankton that illuminates the waves after sunset. While it’s possible to see the phenomenon on islands across the archipelago, one of the most famous spots of them all is on the quietest side of Vaadhoo Island, a minuscule island of the Raa Atoll known for its beachy corner nicknamed the sea of stars. When to go: Between June and October How to get there: Domestic flight and boat transfer from Velana International Airport in Malé Where to stay: Vaadhoo Island lacks the honeymoon-esque stays you may associate with the Maldives—check into InterContinental Maldives Maamunagau Resort and appreciate the glowing waters footsteps away from your beachside abode. 2. Mosquito Bay, Vieques, Puerto Rico You may not have heard of the picturesque island of Vieques. However, you’ve likely seen the spectacle that occurs after sundown, when Mosquito Bay becomes a glossy blue portal thanks to the bioluminescent dinoflagellate Pyrodinium bahamense, which glows blue when agitated. Glide through the waters on a clear-bottomed kayak with a local tour operator for a truly mesmerizing experience. When to go: December to April (dry season) How to get there: Direct flight from San Juan (SJU) followed by a ferry to Vieques Where to stay: Go back to nature—albeit with the luxury trimmings—at the cozy Finca Victoria. 3. Luminous Lagoon, Jamaica Home to dinoflagellates aplenty, Jamaica’s Luminous Lagoon is one of the most incredible excursions on the island, and a memorable way to shake up the evening itinerary. Hop on a tour boat at sunset, and, soon enough, the water’s epipelagic zone will come alive with a vibrant blue light. Watch as sea life darts under the boat’s hull, leaving phantasmagoric lines of light in its wake. Should you choose, some tours allow you to hop into the (surprisingly shallow) water and watch as splashes create incredible displays of light. When to go: December to April (dry season) How to get there: Drive from Sangster International Airport (MBJ) Where to stay: Kick back a 30-minute drive away from the spectacle with an indulgent all-inclusive stay at Sandals Jamaica Caribbean Cay. 4. Jervis Bay, New South Wales, Australia Considering the length of its coastline and the abundance of wildlife that lies offshore, there are surprisingly few places to spot notable displays of bioluminescence around Australia. That said, places do exist, with Jervis Bay in New South Wales being one of the most famous. As the noctiluca scintillans dinoflagellate species washes ashore, settle into the powdery sand and watch the water’s ripples create an effect akin to the Northern Lights on the shore. When to go: Summer; September to February How to get there: About a 2.5-hour drive south of Sydney Airport Where to stay: Escape the hustle and bustle of everyday life with a glamping trip like no other at Paperbark Camp. 5. Krabi, Thailand There are a few bays and coves in this popular region of Thailand that promise a watery light display on clear nights. Ao Nang Beach is one of the most famous and most accessible, with beachside hostels, restaurants and bars a stone’s throw from the shoreline offering places to hide out in ahead of nightfall. While no less famous, perhaps, Phra Nang Beach is another spot a little further along the coast for a peaceful, intimate bioluminescent session reachable by boat transfers from Ao Nang Beach. When to go: November to May How to get there: 20-minute drive from Krabi International Airport Where to stay: Phulay Bay, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve is just a 40-minute drive from the glistening waters. Expect villas, pavilions, sprawling pools, and access to dazzling beaches through the lush landscape. 6. Toyama Bay, Japan While many of the best places to see bioluminescence around the world are so due to an abundance of glowing plankton and algae, the story is a little quirkier in Japan’s Toyama Bay come spring. Here, the bioluminescent performance atop the otherwise pitch-black Japanese waters is caused by a considerably larger creature—the firefly squid. Join a fishing trip and watch as the organisms emit blue light from photophores, creating a wet and wild firework display as they are pulled from the icy depths. When to go: April - May How to get there: Hokuriku Shinkansen bullet train from Tokyo Where to stay: The DoubleTree by Hilton Toyama is a perfectly plush spot to rest in between city exploration and bay visits. 7. Oaxaca, Mexico One of the most popular places to visit for bioluminescence in Mexico is the Laguna de Manialtepec, a coastal lagoon about west of Puerto Escondido. As fish (and people braving the water for a dip) dart through the waters, the twinkling algae that call the lagoon home make the water turn fantastically phosphorescent. A little farther on, similar experiences are available at Lagunas de Chacahua. When to go: July to October (rainy season) How to get there: Fly to Oaxaca Xoxocotlan International Airport (OAX), typically via Mexico City. Where to stay: You’re spoiled for choice along this stretch of Mexican coastline—consider earthen Hotel Escondido Oaxaca or eclectic Grana B&B. 8. Koh Rong, Cambodia By day, the Cambodian island of Koh Rong is a natural playground for families and couples who take to the water armed with snorkeling gear, looking down at the vibrant sea life below. By night, the waters beyond the powder-soft sands take on a life of their own, akin to a starry sky beyond the resorts and lush vegetation. While the bioluminescent plankton isn’t unique to Koh Rong—you can spot it on other Cambodian isles—the lack of light pollution around these shores makes nighttime beach strolls and boat excursions under the new moon unforgettable. When to go: November to May How to get there: Fly to Phnom Penh, then catch a bus to Sihanoukville port and catch a boat transfer to the island Where to stay: The Royal Sands Koh Rong is the plushest address on this gorgeous island. 9. Cornwall, England The waters that surround the British Isles aren’t the first that come to mind when you think of the best places to see bioluminescence. However, come summer, the English Channel throws a few surprises upon Cornwall’s shores. Some of the most notable places to spot starry shores in this corner of the world include Grebe Beach, a hidden gem at the end of the Helford River. On balmy nights, the water can turn a luminescent blue with a splash. Elsewhere, in Penzance, the bioluminescent action is best observed at Pedn Vounder, where, a few times a year, the Channel puts on a display under the constellations. When to go: July and August How to get there: A five or six hour drive from London's Heathrow Airport Where to stay: In Falmouth, The Greenbank Hotel, a charming waterside retreat, gets our vote. In Penzance, hang out with the cool crowd at Artist Residence Cornwall, where unique bedrooms are set within a storied 17th-century property. 10. Cat Ba Island, Vietnam The region around Vietnam’s Halong Bay has long been a hotspot for those seeking glowing waters. However, being one of the stops on most travelers’ bucket lists, crowds and light pollution from boats and cruise ships mean the starry displays are notably more striking in the quieter coves and bays. Enter Cat Ba Island’s beaches, where splashes at sea equate to dazzling scenes. The natural wonder is best experienced on an overnight boat tour, as captains typically anchor in quiet spots under sparkling skies. When to go: June to October How to get there: Bus transfers from Noi Bai International Airport (HAN) in Hanoi Where to stay: Why not take over your own incredible villa while soaking up the island’s tranquil vibe from Valía Villa Cat Ba? 11. Waitomo Glowworm Caves, New Zealand Instead of a swimsuit, pair of flippers, or a kayak, the bioluminescence hiding in one of New Zealand’s most recognizable natural wonders requires visitors to wear comfortable shoes and a warm jacket. The Waitomo Glowworm Caves have been a tourist attraction for more than 130 years, with travelers passing through the awe-inspiring caves in silence, watching as the Arachnocampa luminosa glowworm species—only found in this part of the world—show off their captivating colors. When to go: Year-round How to get there: About 120 miles south of Auckland Airport (AKL) Where to stay: Assuming you’re based in Hamilton, about an hour’s drive north of the caves, for a few days, check into The Narrows Landing Hotel. A version of this story originally appeared in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: The Whimsical British Country-House Fantasy Is Taking Over Upstate New York
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.82
“Britain is a country of great eccentrics,” muses interior designer Adam Greco, whose own view of ‘British whimsy’ manifests in charming chintz and heirloom curios, filtered through the lens of cultural treasures like Sherlock Holmes and Mary Poppins. It's a highly romanticized spin, something the New York City–based designer, who's worked on properties like London's The Ned and Oslo's Sommerro, felt wanting in the hospitality space, even across many landmark British hotels. “As a foreigner I remember walking into a grand hotel on London’s Regent’s Street and thinking it looked like a function room in Cincinnati inside,” he says. “It was disappointing.” Recently, though, a wave of UK properties have started to embrace the kinds of cultural eccentricities that Greco saw as lacking in those hotels. This updated approach to the whimsical British aesthetic, all vintage bric-a-brac set alongside some serious art collections and sumptuous fabrics, is best expressed in the UK at properties like the Three Horseshoes in Batcombe, about 20 miles south of Bath, and the Fort Road Hotel in Margate along the southeast coast. Lately, the design aesthetic has captured America’s attention, and found a home in upstate New York: Soho Farmhouse is due to open its outpost in Rhinebeck, New York, next year. The team behind the Cotswolds’ Estelle Manor is said to be searching for a property in a similar patch close to the Hudson Valley and the Catskills. These new builds are a bid to lure affluent New Yorkers who have outgrown the Hamptons, and, as former magazine editor turned hotelier Dorian Grinspan puts it, “provide something wilder, that feels genuinely rural rather than relocated.” Grinspan’s own property, Maison Monna, is two and a half hours from the city in Old Chatham, a charming hamlet he discovered when vacationing in the area with his partner. With Monna, he wanted to speak to this new breed of luxury traveler, someone who wants to feel “comfortable, cared-for, but not smothered,”—a natural companion to British whimsy's lived-in, been-here-for-decades sensibility. Maison Monna was a perfect canvas for the expression of this trend, largely because it had sat untouched on the market for so many years. The style of the three-bedroom house is Greek Revival, though records show its bones date back to the Quakers (it makes sense, then, that scenes for Mona Fastvold’s award-winning The Testament of Ann Lee were shot close by). To populate it, Grinspan looked to his personal archive of antiques, yet by the time it all arrived, he explains, the effect was “a bit too monastic.” The fix? “To add a little British whimsy.” That translated into custom upholstery; fabrics sourced from textile sellers Merchant & Mills and Notting Hill’s Cloth Shop; DeVol sconces; and cheery ruffled skirting in the kitchen. It also meant being open to quirks and imperfections—Grinspan wanted the creak in the floorboards. He was even okay with gaps, “so long as no one falls through.” With Maison Monna, the style softens the property’s Shaker roots (it was built in 1796), but at the Six Bells in Hudson Valley’s Rosendale, British whimsy is interwoven with pure American nostalgia. Greco, who designed the three-story 1850s property for entrepreneur Audrey Gelman, explains the distinction is key: “It’s Audrey’s love of late 20th century catalogue Americana, the Vermont Country Store and Lillian Vernon,” with its bold ginghams, Laura Ashley florals, and ruffled baskets, trussed up in a design vernacular that feels unmistakably English. When guests step onto the property, Greco’s aim was to create a sense of “déjà vu, or something uncanny—like, have I been here before? Did I imagine this? Is this where my grandmother had her first kiss?” Of the property’s 11 rooms, it is the Innkeeper’s Suite that is his favorite, with a built-in, hand-painted box bed, a hallmark of so many English country homes. Forty minutes further into the Catskills in Hensonville, 2025 Hot List winner The Henson is a marked example of a softer interpretation. At this 16-room inn, living spaces are flooded with natural light, and touches of bouclé and natural woods create a serene, homey feel. The family portraits that hang in the hotel’s ‘living room’ aren’t purely decorative, either—they are hand-me-downs from co-owner Ely Franko's grandparents, who once hung them in their home in Turkey (Ely and his wife Danielle co-own the property alongside chefs Jeremiah Stone and Fabian von Hauske Valtierra). Ditsy floral quilt toppers add a sentimental anchor to bedrooms, while vintage pieces threaded throughout the rest of the property have been lovingly sourced by the experts at New York’s The Somerset House. It’s the same unfussy, lived-in register that both Grinspan and Greco have also created in their respective projects, but here it is without direct reference to Britain at all. And perhaps that is the point. It’s not that a handful of hoteliers and designers are taking a cut-and-paste approach to decorating these properties but rather that they’re paying homage to the instincts behind it: a resistance to newness, artful curation of clutter, and a veneration of the past through beautiful antiques. It is a design language that’s developed enough that American hotels now speak fluently.

item.title: The Best Places to Travel in December Before the Holiday Rush
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.65
The best places to go this December are a mix of old, easy-to-reach standbys and out-of-the-way destinations that are sure to reward you with one-of-a-kind experiences once you get there. If you’re the type who gets on flights for food, pop over to San Francisco for 48 hours or sneak away to Seville for a long weekend, where enticing restaurants and long-anticipated hotel openings make for compelling city breaks. For those who love to get off the beaten path, try a winter escape in Finland’s Oulu, a European Capital of Culture; or a desert dream in Abu Dhabi’s Saadiyat Island, where the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is finally cutting its ribbon. And if you’re chasing a summer vibe, head to the Southern Hemisphere’s adventure capital Queenstown, New Zealand. Sure, you might have holiday obligations, as you do every December, but why not travel right after Thanksgiving? Or make a stop at one of the best places to travel in December, all featured on our annual list of the Best Places to Go, on the way to the places where you have to go. (For more ideas, find our full list of the best places to go in 2026 here.) This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: How to Party Like a Local in Mykonos, According to a Seasoned Veteran
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.63
My first Mykonos trip ran on family time: pool swims at my uncle’s sugar-cube villa, a nap mandated by my mother, then dinner at 10 p.m., which, in our Greek family, qualified as an early-bird booking. At 15, I discovered what those naps had been preparing me for at Sea Satin, the late-night dining room for models and designers beneath the windmills, where one half of Dolce & Gabbana was celebrating a birthday a few tables away. White napkins began circling overhead, and people climbed onto the tables one by one until we were up too, a bottle of vodka sweating in its bucket below. My aunts and uncles had no children of their own and therefore a generous idea of my limits, so my glass kept finding its way back to full. On the switchbacks home, I asked my uncle to pull over and spent several minutes bent over the roadside scrub. When I climbed back in, he handed me a napkin, turned the radio back up, and apparently decided the incident did not merit a report to my mother. An island that had spent decades pairing glamour with license was perhaps the wrong place to entrust an adolescent to unusually permissive relatives. Le Corbusier and Albert Camus came when Mykonos was still a rough stop on the way to Delos. Jacqueline Kennedy’s 1961 visit brought the cameras, and that era’s guest list went on to include Grace Kelly, Brigitte Bardot, Sophia Loren and Maria Callas. Celebrities made the island visible, while gay travelers gave its nights their freedom and much of their character. Pierro’s opened in 1972, when Pierro Aversa and Andreas Koutsoukos began fitting drag queens, fishermen, aristocrats, and designers into 540 square feet. Gaultier and Valentino passed through town, while Grace Jones danced at Remezzo. Now craft beer is brewed on the island, and casual Chora bars pour proper cocktails into paper cups and send revelers off into the night. Greek musicians share the calendar with international DJs, periodically reminding Mykonos of which country it belongs to. The familiar bottle-service caricature leaves out the drag stages of the old port and the smaller rooms where a night can change direction without a reservation. Prices remain high and the roads maddening, but few Mediterranean islands offer so many convincing ways to reach sunrise. After enough summers on both sides of the nap, I have settled on seven rules that every visitor needs to know. 1. Make two plans: one for the day, and one for the night Mykonos operates in two shifts, the day party and the night, punctuated by a return to the hotel to shower and change. Choose one beach club for the day and stay until sunset, a pivotal moment on the Mykonos agenda that everyone does differently. As for your day plans? There are plenty of options. At Nammos, where you'll find polished excess, the sunny days move from beach beds at Psarou into a long fish lunch and dancing. Scorpios gathers force more gradually, reaching its peak around the sunset ritual. Jackie O’ Beach carries a poolside lunch into early-evening drag, while Alemagou justifies the drive north to get their when its calendar promises an open-air set. Afterward, return to the hotel and begin again, before choosing a dinner that can carry you into drinks or dancing and, eventually, after-hours. Just avoid crossing the island during the dinner era—it'll turn your night into one marked by traffic. 2. Confirm what, exactly, it is that you booked A booking confirmation can name the right venue while committing you to the wrong part of it. Scorpios splits its reservations four ways: Restaurant, Beach, Sunset Beach, and the Terrace Music Rituals. A proud dinner booking can seat you at a communal table while the ritual you came for happens two zones over. On the sand, an Oasis cabana comes with only a partial sea view, with “Private Beach” being the waterline category. At Cavo Paradiso, the cliffside open-air club above Paradise Beach that has booked international DJs since 1993, VIP does not mean a table. A ticket admits you to VIP Area 100, an elevated first-come standing section with its own bar and no assigned seats. An actual table requires a separate reservation and a 50 percent deposit two days ahead, then gets released 30 minutes after your slot. Have any concierge forward the venue's own confirmation rather than a summary. Before paying, get the zone and seating type in writing, plus whether the booking extends into the late-night program. 3. Choose your sunset venue by its volume Sunset can be a lowkey drink before dinner or it can be the evening’s main event, so decide which vibe you want before reserving a table—and by vibe, we mean volume. The Garden, on the hillside property that Yehudi Menuhin acquired after visiting in 1962, keeps the music low enough for conversation. Scarpa in Little Venice draws a standing crowd and raises the house music as the light drops. Scorpios is the full commitment, with a terrace program that begins in late afternoon and can carry the night toward dinner. Check the artist calendar before booking, since your friend’s triumphant TikTok posted on Sunday says very little about Wednesday’s fete. 4. Dinner can be your final destination, but it doesn't have to be In Mykonos Town, dinner can likewise contain your whole evening, complete with entertainment, or merely set things into motion. Lío is the full-night choice, building an à la carte meal around modern cabaret before becoming a club at 12:30 a.m. If you intend to move afterward, finish dinner first and keep the rest of the night on foot. A sealed to-go cocktail from TYCO buys time while the group settles on a mood. From there, Skandinavian means a loud courtyard and familiar summer hits. Astra offers a more polished dance floor beneath its ceiling of fiber-optic stars, while Lola keeps jazz and chanson at conversational volume. For drag, Jackie O’ carries the island’s queer nightlife tradition into the early morning. 5. Drink locally, then follow the Greek chorus Though Mykonos imports most of what appears in its ice buckets, the island makes its own wine and beer and it's easy to find time to enjoy both. Mykonos Vioma pours organic estate wines at its farm near Ano Mera, while Mikònu moved its taproom in 2026 to Mathios Taverna in Tourlos, where prickly-pear ale comes with dinner and a sea view. After dark, look for a room that has a Greek accent. Nōema’s Sounds of the Avli brings Greek-rooted live and electronic performance to a reservation crowd. On its Greek-music nights, Thalami offers the less polished version after midnight, when regulars and seasonal staff take over the choruses. If a panigiri is taking place in Ano Mera, ask a local when to arrive and attend as a guest rather than a customer. 6. Make your plans based on the artist, not the venue The venue supplies the setting, but the musical art determines the crowd and the shape of the night. In other words, check the calendar before making reservations anywhere. Scorpios suits melodic sets that gather slowly through sunset, while SantAnna books larger house names for pool-scale productions. Alemagou requires a dedicated trip north, so the lineup should justify the drive. Cavo Paradiso belongs to another hour entirely: It opens at 11 p.m., brings on international headliners around 1:45 a.m., and can continue until dawn. Give Cavo its own night and absolutely leave the following morning, maybe even the afternoon. 7. Book the ride home before the first drink Plotting your ride home is a daytime errand. Before dinner, open a WhatsApp thread with a private-transfer dispatcher and tell them where you're staying and how many seats you need, plus a guess at where the evening ends. There are two dispatcher numbers to save: Transfers in Mykonos covers point-to-point and on-call service, while SZS accepts a live location with 30 minutes' notice and replies with an arrival time and a plate number; whomever you book with, make sure to reference a landmark that a car can actually reach and get the fare in writing, then pad everything by an hour in July and August. An evening that begins with dinner in Chora and finishes at a late club is better served by a driver on demand, though Cavo Paradiso's reception will arrange the ride back with an hour's warning. Uber summons the same taxis everyone else is calling, and the last KTEL bus helps only when its timetable agrees with yours. Obviously, the rental car stays where it is once the drinking starts, and Vespas and quads belong to the sober daylight.

item.title: The Best Airbnbs in Denver Whether You’re After Winter Snow or Summer Sun
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.44
Denver, Colorado, is full of adventure in every season—from winter skiing and summer hiking to rainy-day wanderings through an impressive array of arts and culture offerings. One of my favorite things about living in Denver is the neighborhood diversity: Whether you’re looking for a walkable spot that feels like a welcoming local community, a trendy district with buzzy energy and round-the-clock entertainment, or a quiet, pet-friendly greenspace with a lake path, we’ve got it all. Lucky for visitors, there’s also a wealth of vacation rentals to pick from once you do decide which neighborhood to bunker down in. Whether you prefer a charming and historic house dating back to the Victorian era, a sleek artist's loft, or a modern architectural marvel, there’s no shortage of unique places to stay in the Mile High City. Read on for some of the most iconic home bases for an unforgettable trip. No matter what you're in town to see or do, these Denver Airbnbs deliver. —Molly O'Brien We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, editor stays, ratings, amenities, location, decor, and previous guest reviews. Our top picks: - Best for views: Groovy studio with skyline views - Best for pets: Pet-friendly historic home with a hot tub - Best for couples: Unique tiny home in a shipping container - Best for groups: Magnificent (and massive) South Denver art house FAQ: What are the best neighborhoods in Denver? The best neighborhood to stay in Denver depends on what type of trip you’re looking for. Those who prioritize walkability, buzzy energy, and plenty of trendy bars and restaurants will love LoHi (Lower Highlands). If artsy vibes with fun breweries and dining outposts is what you crave, RiNo (River North) is a great place to set up camp. Those seeking something a bit more upscale and refined with the hottest spots for dining, drinking, and arts and culture will love Cherry Creek (which I affectionately call The Beverly Hills of Denver, due to its wealthy—but still welcoming—atmosphere). LoDo is where Union Station, Coors Field, and Ball Arena live, making it a fantastic entertainment hub. Don’t miss Five Points if you seek authentic soul food, City Park for some of the best urban outdoor spaces, and Washington Park for some of the most historic architecture and a down-to-earth feel. When is the best time to visit Denver? As a Denverite, I’ve found every season offers an abundance of activities. Since the sun is so strong here at 5,280 feet of elevation, the air doesn’t feel as chilly, even on the most brisk winter day. Summertime brings sunny days perfect for strolling around an urban lake or biking along a flowing river. Fall is a fantastic time for leaf peeping and enjoying some of the local seasonal produce in the crisp Mile High air. Wintertime is for snow sports—it’s a season most Denverites actually look forward to due to the breadth of different ski resorts nearby. Spring is when the ground starts to thaw, and barring the occasional random snowstorm (we’re told not to plant anything in our gardens until after Mother’s Day), most days feel mild and pleasant enough for a city stroll. What are the best things to do in Denver? Arts and culture lovers can’t miss a stop in the Arts District on Santa Fe, a show at the Denver Performing Arts Complex, or an experience at Red Rocks Park and Amphitheater—which is free and open to the public to explore, outside ticketed showtimes. Those seeking an educational day out will enjoy the Denver Botanic Gardens (for the flora nerds), the Wings Over the Rockies Air & Space Museum (for the aviation enthusiasts), or the Museum of Contemporary Art with its rotating exhibits and beautiful open-air rooftop space. Refueling is easy, because there’s always somewhere new and interesting to eat between one of the many casual food halls like Denver Central Market or Avanti F&B and the more upscale eateries, including Michelin-rated outposts like Alma Fonda Fina or Margot. Shop till you drop along the 16th Street Mall, which features hundreds of storefronts lining a pedestrian-only promenade, capped by Larimer Square, which was the city’s first block, commercial district, and first designated historic district. And since Denverites work hard and play hard, planning for proper relaxation and recovery is essential, which is easily doable at one of the many local wellness institutions like Sway Wellness Spa, unique spots like the Oakwell Beer Spa, and classics like The Spa at Four Seasons Hotel Denver.

item.title: 10% Off Priceline Promo Code for August 2026 | Condé Nast Traveler
item.description:

Booking travel often means navigating fixed prices on flights, hotels, and car rentals—but Priceline has been finding ways around that since 1999. Originally known for its experimental “Name Your Own Price” feature, the platform has evolved into a go-to booking site with access to 28 million properties across 220 countries and territories, plus discounts of up to 60% off hotels, rental cars, cruises, and flights. I'm always looking for ways to stretch my travel budget a little further, whether I'm booking a spontaneous weekend escape or mapping out a longer trip itinerary. Priceline is one of the first places I check for deals, especially when I can stack on a promo code. From up to 60% off Hotel Express Deals to up to 20% off rental cars and 50% off flights, these Priceline coupons can leave a little more room in the budget for the parts of the trip I'll actually remember. Use our Priceline coupon code for 10% off outdoor travel Whether you're planning a romantic escape or a beach trip with friends this summer, you can take 10% off on popular outdoor favorite destinations with code TAKEITOUTSIDE, from select national parks, and coastal cities to mountain towns. Looking for even bigger savings on adventures? If you’re in the market of planning a road trip, take advantage of Priceline’s Great American Road Trip sale. Here, you can score up to $650 off of hotel and flight packages in classic Route 66 cities, destinations with big personalities (from Las Vegas to Austin), desert and southwest hot spots, and more. Additionally, you can take $20 off of hotels and rental cars when you spend $250 with coupon code ROADTRIP. Save 25% on hotels with Priceline in the End of Summer sale What better way to celebrate the end of the season than a good travel deal? If you book by August 30, you can take advantage of the site's 25% off deal on select hotel bookings for stays all the way through December 28. While there's not one page for all of these hotels, you can look for the End of Summer badge (on the right side of each hotel listing) when searching for hotels in your region of choice, from New York City to Miami and beyond. Save up to 55% on Priceline Deals without a promo code You don't necessarily need a promo code to save on Priceline. Rather its general Deals page rounds up various ways to spend less, including vacation bundles that can save you up to 55% when you combine flights, hotels, and rental cars in one single booking. You can also find deals on popular destinations and up to 20% off featured rental car brands, making it always worth checking the page before you book. Take up to 60% off on on mystery trips with Priceline Express Deals For an even bigger discount—and a little more mystery—try Priceline's Express Deals. These offers let you choose your travel dates, destination, preferred star rating, amenities, and price range, but keep the hotel name and exact location hidden until after you book. In exchange for that element of surprise, Priceline offers some pretty significant discounted rates, with savings of up to 60%. That said, these fun Express Deals are best for flexible travelers who aren't set on a specific hotel and would rather save than know every detail upfront. The same concept can apply to flights and other travel bookings featured through Priceline's Express Deals offerings, though the exact discounts and availability vary. One important catch: Express Deals are non-refundable, so take note of that prior to booking. Priceline also offers VIP Deals, which are exclusive offers and benefits for rewards members. Simply sign up and in to your Priceline account to see which exact VIP savings are available to you. Sign up for a 10% off Priceline coupon code and VIP discounts If you book through Priceline regularly, it's worth signing up for the free Priceline VIP rewards program. Unlike traditional hotel loyalty programs, Priceline VIP rewards your overall booking activity across hotels, rental cars, and more, with each tier unlocking deeper discounts and extra perks. - VIP Member: With a free sign up, join with one simple email that gets you instant access to member pricing, including up to 10% off Express Deals with an eligible promo code for hotel and rental car bookings. It's an easy way to save without committing to a paid membership. - VIP Blue: Once you've completed two eligible trips, you'll unlock VIP Blue status, which includes savings of up to 50% off at more than 15,000 hotels, up to 15% off rental cars when added to an existing trip, and access to additional member-only offers. - VIP Platinum: Frequent Priceline users can reach Platinum status after 25 completed trips. Fun benefits include a fresh 10% off Express Deals coupon after every completed trip, savings of up to 50% at more than 45,000 hotels, enhanced rental car discounts of up to 20%, and additional exclusive member offers. Compared with other online travel booking rewards programs—such as those from Hotels.com, Vrbo, and Booking.com—Priceline's VIP program stands out for rewarding bookings across multiple travel categories rather than focusing primarily on accommodations, making it a useful option if you regularly bundle different parts of your trip. (Trust me, it's worth it.) What to expect when you book Priceline Express Deals Express Deals and VIP Deals offer great savings, but they work a bit differently: Express Deals offer up to a 60% discount automatically on rental car companies, hotels, and flight carriers—but the catch is that you won't know the hotel name until after you book. It's a bit of a mystery with a surprise element attached: travelers select ideal travel dates, location, and general preferences such as star rating, amenities, or price range, but the hotel name and exact location remain hidden until after you book. This allows Priceline to offer you a discounted rate, as hotels can fill their rooms without publicly lowering their prices. On that note, Express Deals are ideal for travelers who are flexible and open to a bit of mystery in exchange for significant savings. It's a great option if you're not set on a specific hotel and are willing to take a chance on where you'll stay, and for those who value savings over knowing every detail upfront. Though do note, Express Deals are non-refundable. VIP Deals, on the other hand, are exclusive offers available to rewards members, with some discounts and benefits that aren't available to regular users. To view these deals, make sure you're signed into your Priceline account. Get 50% off your stay with Priceline military discounts Priceline has partnered with the American Forces Travel (AFT) to offer up to an extra 50% off travel with pre-negotiated rates on flights and hotels. The AFT, supported by Priceline, is the US Department of Defense's official online leisure travel site for active military, Guard or Reserve, US Coast Guard, retired military, and all eligible MWR patrons. Check if you're eligible and complete their authentication process to save on your next trip. What to know about Priceline coupon codes if you want to max out your discount For your easy reference, there are a few things you’ll want to know before you check out. Priceline promo codes usually have capped discount values, but the brand frequently offers discounts of around $50 or $75 off for hotels, as well as up to $625 off flight and hotel coupons for bundle deals. The most frequent promo codes are for the site’s hotel Express Deals, and new offers are typically released around two to three times per month. The majority of Priceline promo codes are exclusive to VIP rewards members—and lucky for you, the program is quick and free to join with email sign up. (From there, you'll receive a single-use, unique promo code when you join.) More member perks look like: Saving up to 50% off hotels, rental cars discounts, and early access to sale promos. Do note that the durations of promos vary—sometimes, only lasting 24 hours, and others lasting up to a month. As Priceline promo codes are often first released to email subscribers and mobile app users, you'll want to download the app and turn on notifications so you don't miss a beat. Time your booking right by following along on Condé Nast Traveler for exclusive discounts. For more information, most terms and conditions can be found on their website. What to do if your Priceline promo code isn’t working If your Priceline promo code isn't working, don't assume it's invalid and give up—most codes come with a handful of restrictions. Double-check that the code hasn't expired, that it's valid for the type of booking you're making, and that you've met any minimum spend or eligibility requirements. Some discounts apply only to Express Deals, while others are limited to hotels, rental cars, or select flights, and many can't be combined with another promotion or automatically discounted rate. It's also worth quickly confirming that you're signed in to the correct Priceline account, especially if you're trying to redeem a VIP-exclusive offer, as many member discounts are tied to your account rather than available at checkout for everyone. If everything looks right and the code still won't apply, removing and re-adding your booking or trying a different browser or device can sometimes resolve the temporary issue. And if all else fails, Priceline's customer support can confirm whether the promotion is still active or help identify why it isn't applying to your reservation.

Non-runners love ’em, too: Commerce editor Meaghan Kenny swears by the Hoka Cliftons for long travel days, walks, and workout classes—“I wear them everywhere,” she says. Whether you’re new to the brand or a repeat shopper looking to save on your next order, here are the best Hoka coupons, promotions, and discount codes available right now. It’s free to join, and once you do, you’ll receive a unique discount code to apply to your next purchase. This is an easy way to save on a higher-ticket item you've been waffling over.
