item.title: The Most Comfortable Joggers to Travel In
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.25
Joggers are one of the first things I reach for when getting dressed for a travel day—and they’ve also become a permanent part of my postpartum wardrobe. More polished than traditional sweatpants but far more comfortable than jeans, my favorite joggers have gotten me through long flights and train rides, hours spent walking around Manhattan, and vacations everywhere from Florida to Paris. Sure, wide-leg pants may have stolen the spotlight as of late, but in my humble opinion, versatile joggers still deserve a place in your suitcase, whether you need a lightweight pair for sightseeing in the heat, cozy fleece for a chilly flight, or something elevated enough for dinner and drinks. Fabric and fit can make all the difference, with options ranging from breathable linen and cotton gauze to performance materials like nylon, as well as cozy fleece and cashmere. Ahead, 13 pairs that are prime for travel—with comfort, versatility, style, and practicality top of mind. Top picks: Vuori’s aptly named Performance jogger is an easy choice for long road trips, whether you’re cruising California’s coast or spending a weekend exploring New England. The brand’s ultra-soft, moisture-wicking DreamKnit fabric@e offers four-way stretch, so you can comfortably spend hours in the car without feeling restricted. (Commerce director Madison Flager calls these some of the softest travel pants she's ever worn; she recommends a darker pair, as the lighter colors aren't totally opaque.) An elastic waistband and two stash pockets add to their road-trip appeal, and they come in regular and long lengths, plus a slew of colors. Material: Polyester and elastane These high-waisted Lululemon joggers are the pair to pack for warm-weather destinations like Miami or Tulum, thanks in part to their sweat-wicking fabric. Their buttery-soft, light-as-air construction and relaxed fit offer plenty of breathability and unrestricted movement without extra bulk, whether you’re heading to a morning Pilates class, exploring the city on foot, or squeezing in a quick workout between plans. Discreet hand pockets, including one with an interior card sleeve, add a functional touch for days on the go. Material: Nylon and lycra Sightseeing in Rome or heading to dinner in the South of France calls for something cool and comfortable, and L’Agence’s Mariko joggers fit the bill. Made from 100% linen, the breathable pants are well-suited to rising temperatures, while the mid-weight fabric and tailored silhouette keep them from reading as beachwear. A drawstring waist and pull-on design make them comfortable enough for hours of exploring, while adjustable zippered cuffs lend a more polished finish. Think of them as a chic, comfortable alternative to jeans or trousers for warm-weather trips. Material: Linen I’m a longtime fan of Rag & Bone’s viral sweatpant jeans, and this jogger version might be even more convincing: The denim print is practically undetectable, right down to the faux button and distressed accents. Despite looking like jeans, they pull on easily and have a comfortable elasticized waistband, which I especially appreciated postpartum, plus functional side pockets. The pure cotton construction is comfortable enough to wear for hours on a plane, yet polished enough to head straight out in after landing in cities like New York or Paris. I also love that they work across seasons without leaving me overheating in summer or too chilly in winter. Material: Cotton Quince is known for its high-quality, wallet-friendly capsule wardrobe staples, and these SuperSoft Fleece joggers are no exception. Their cozy, stretchy fleece makes them an especially smart choice for staying warm on notoriously chilly long-haul flights, while two front pockets and a drawstring waistband add practicality for travel days. Choose from six colors ranging from petal pink to navy, and pair them with the matching hoodie for an extra-cozy in-flight set. Material: Tencel, modal, polyester, and spandex These lightweight joggers are a great pick for jam-packed trips when you need one pair of pants to keep on from morning to night—say, a national-park getaway that mixes hiking with sightseeing and plenty of time on the road. Quick-dry material makes them versatile enough for a morning hike, an impromptu yoga class, or hours spent exploring, while a thick waistband keeps things comfortable on the go. Five pockets offer plenty of room for small essentials like AirPods and keys, making them especially practical for days when you’d rather leave the bag behind. Material: Nylon and spandex Another pair recommended by Flager, Cozy Earth’s bamboo joggers are exceptionally soft thanks to a blend of bamboo and viscose, making them the pair to reach for when comfort is the top priority—think overnight flights to Europe, long layovers, or lazy mornings spent ordering room service at your hotel. Pair them with a T-shirt and matching pullover for an easy athleisure set that’s comfortable enough to sleep in on the plane but not so relaxed that you look like you're wearing pajamas. Material: Bamboo viscose, acrylic, spandex Beach trips and coastal escapes to places like Newport or Charleston call for something light and breezy, and Gap’s Cotton Gauze Easy Joggers fit the bill. Made from airy, breathable 100% cotton gauze, the relaxed, ankle-length pants are light enough to throw on over a swimsuit for an afternoon by the water but polished enough for drinks afterward—just add the matching oversized gauze shirt, et voilà. An elasticized drawstring waist and cuffs keep things comfortable, while side pockets add practicality. Shoppers have plenty of choice here: The pants come in standard, petite, and tall sizes and in eight colors ranging from hot pink to classic black and navy. Material: Cotton Skims is known for its comfy loungewear, and the brand’s cotton fleece joggers are just the thing for cozy cabin weekends in the Catskills. Made from a soft cotton-polyester blend, the loose-fitting pants feature an interior drawcord for an adjustable fit—ideal for slow mornings over coffee, curling up by the fire, or making a quick run into town. They’re available in sizes up to 4X and can be paired with your favorite tee or tank, or the matching hoodie or zip-up for head-to-toe comfort. Material: Cotton and polyester Active beach days, outdoor hikes, and hours spent under the sun call for more than just lightweight clothing—sun protection matters too. Enter Marmot’s AirExchange UPF 40 joggers, a smart pick whether you’re hiking volcanic trails in Hawaii or exploring Costa Rica’s national parks. Breathable, quick-drying performance fabric offers added sun protection without weighing you down, while a tapered silhouette and adjustable drawstring waistband keep the fit comfortable. Material: Polyester Cold-weather travel doesn’t have to mean sacrificing style. Quince’s cashmere joggers are hard to beat for the price, especially for a winter weekend in Aspen. Made from 100 % Mongolian cashmere, the medium-weight knit delivers serious warmth without feeling bulky; according to the brand, its cashmere is three times as warm as wool and is ethically sourced. The tapered, tailored fit feels more put-together than your average sweatpants, whether you’re wearing them on a flight or lounging après-ski. Pair them with the matching cashmere hoodie for an elevated travel set, or wear them separately once you arrive. Material: Cashmere Alo’s Polar fleece joggers are made for active winter trips to places like Park City, Utah, or Stowe, Vermont, when staying warm between outdoor adventures is key. The soft, insulating fleece comes in handy whether you’re grabbing lunch after a morning on the slopes, exploring a ski town, or heading to a workout. The roomy, relaxed cut leaves plenty of room to move, while cuffed hems streamline the silhouette and zippered pockets keep small essentials secure. Pair them with the matching Polar Fleece Retreat cover up for an easy après-ski set or add a statement coat before heading out. Material: Polyester When bar-hopping or nice dinners are on the itinerary, these satin joggers make it easy to dress up without settling for an uncomfortable outfit—especially on a weekend in Nashville or New Orleans. The silky, high-shine fabric feels decidedly more night-out-ready than your typical joggers, while an elasticized drawstring waist and pull-on design make them easy to wear for hours on the town. Cargo and side pockets add a practical touch, and elasticized ankle cuffs offer the legs some shape. Material: Polyester This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: A Fall Capsule Wardrobe Helps You Pack Less and Wear More
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.20
It seems that as soon as summer temperatures start to dip, my urge to book a trip goes up—and that's when I start thinking about my fall capsule wardrobe. Sometimes it’s the Cotswolds, with its charming limestone cottages covered in ivy, calling me, the same way a long weekend of antiquing and sipping cider in the Hudson Valley or climbing rocky Atlantic coastlines in Maine does when chillier mornings appear. Summer travel may get all the hype, but seasoned travelers know that autumn is one of the most magical times of year to experience the world, no matter where you’re headed. They also know the challenges that come with trying to dress—and pack—for chillier months. (It’s true: Packing for fluctuating temperatures can feel almost as restrictive as carry-on requirements.) The good news is that building a fall capsule wardrobe works just as well on the road as it does in your closet at home. From thermal layers to trenches, each of these staples in our shoppable list makes for an easy throw-and-go uniform, so you spend less time on outfits and more time wandering through charming small towns, strolling local festivals, or settling in for an aperitivo. Below, 13 staples to build out your travel capsule wardrobe this fall. The perfect tee Possibly the essential of all essentials, the white tee. I start here because I believe every outfit should do so for ease. Have a funky trouser that needs a match? A wool skirt that feels impossible to pair otherwise? This is the basic you can pair with nearly everything you own–jeans, trousers, skirts, leggings, you name it. Best of all, these super-soft tees from Madewell, Everlane, Buck Mason, and Vuori have that lived-in feeling right from the start. The long-sleeve for layering A long-sleeve shirt is a perfect base layer for most fall outfits. Make sure yours is lightweight, breathable, and packable. I love tossing a long-sleeve in my carry-on for casual daytime outfits and cool mornings. Gap, Intimissimi, and Banana Republic make a few of my favorites. The cozy cardigan There’s a reason Taylor Swift wrote an entire song about one—and why it always finds its way into our suitcases once the weather cools. Even if you’re headed to a warm-weather destination like Nantucket, there’s something effortlessly chic about draping a cardigan over your shoulders. And it’s a classic for a reason: slung over your shoulders, buttoned up, paired with denim or a slip skirt, on the plane, and long after you’ve arrived. The versatile dress A packable dress needs to check three boxes, in my opinion: It should come in a versatile, neutral color, resist wrinkles, and be easy to layer. Bonus points if it's machine washable, which some of these picks are, including Quince's washable silk long-sleeve dress. From a sporty Uniqlo style that can be dressed up or down to an earth-toned, fingertip-length dress from Reformation, these staples are worth their suitcase space. I’m especially loving this minimalist slip from Diish that works as well with sneakers during the day as it does with kitten heels for a night out. The wool coat Skeptics will scoff at the thought of packing a wool coat. But there’s a reason you see so many people wearing them over their sweatsuits in the airport security lines. When you arrive at a destination during peak autumn—think London, New York, Vermont—you’ll realize the coat is not only necessary, it’s the whole outfit. Pro tip: Wear yours on the plane to avoid packing it in your already-full suitcase. Not just a work-appropriate icon, the button-down is a tried-and-true layering piece for travel, especially in autumn. It can be tied around the waist, slouched over the shoulders, or worn open over a tank when temperatures fluctuate throughout the day. Plus, it's lightweight, meaning you can pack one or two in your suitcase without ending up in dreaded almost-zipped luggage territory. The trouser My recommendation when packing a trouser? Opt for a sweatpant-like option rather than a heavy, sturdy, business-professional version. You’ll get the look—refined, polished—without sacrificing comfort during your travels. I especially love athletic brands for maximum comfort, but Abercrombie & Fitch, Aritzia, and Bonobos also make trend-forward options that don’t skimp on soft materials and relaxed silhouettes. The trench coat A slightly oversized trench deserves every bit of the praise it gets. Not only is it a forever classic, but it's lightweight, water-resistant, and ideal for unpredictable weather. It's the perfect in-between layer for crisp afternoons everywhere from Scotland to New York City. The straight-leg jean A fall wardrobe roundup feels incomplete without a mention of the straight-leg jean, just as it would without the inclusion of a white tee. And they pair beautifully together no matter where you are or what time of year. It’s the outfit you’ll reach for when you’re not quite sure what’s on the itinerary yet. The slip-on shoe Whether on a business trip or checking your step count in a new city, you’ll need a reliable shoe to get you to and from. Luckily, I have quite a few for you to choose from—whether that means a sneaker-flat hybrid or a polished loafer. The comfortable slip-ons below were selected for their functionality just as much as their fashion. The comfortable sneaker No packing list is complete without a comfortable sneaker. Just imagine tackling connecting flights or heading out on a city walking tour without a pair. (Shuddering at the thought? Me too.) That’s why a sneaker is essential for every traveler in every destination. These neutral-colored options from OnCloud, Vivaia, and New Balance stand out for their all-day comfort and support. Wear them with quite literally everything—jeans, trousers, dresses, and more—to cut down your packing list and save your feet. The fall boot Again, a boot is a commitment while packing, but one with incredible payoff. Smaller ankle boots don’t take up as much space if you’re packing light. If you’re not hopping on a flight and are in a car instead, en route to a harvest festival or an orchard, you can get away with bringing a pair of tall riding boots. Pair these from Jenni Kayne with a flannel or barn jacket for all your cozy outdoor adventures this season. The everyday handbag The best travel bags can transition from day to night and, of course, hold a couple of souvenirs while you're at it. I love bigger bags that can double as under-the-seat personal items during flights, like those from Free People and Leatherology, or smaller crossbody totes. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Meaghan Kenny.

item.title: These are the quietest islands in the world right now – and 3 British gems have made the top 20
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.90
There are times when all we desire is a bit of peace and quiet. Life can be a noisy, overstimulating affair as we juggle multiple plates at once, and aside from a stint in a sleek spa hotel, a little bit of serenity is enough R&R to send us back on our way. Overtourism is a greater issue than ever, as millions of travellers flock to the same cities and coastal hideouts. Crowds equal noise, and it’s easy to return from an adventure feeling more burnt out than before. For those of us seeking a more tranquil holiday destination, BookRetreats.com new index has uncovered the quietest islands in the world – perfect for the ultimate reset. According to the leading retreat booking site, searches for "quiet destinations" are up 1,268 per cent year on year globally, while the site’s latest survey found that 56 per cent of those asked now want to retreat for quiet in nature. With insight from silence researcher and psychology professor Olga V. Lehmann, BookRetreats.com analysed several islands against six criteria: road density, untouched nature, air traffic, uncrowded space, dark skies and natural coastal spots. Islands were then ranked according to the UN Environment Programme's definition of a quiet soundscape. "Islands have always been where we go to get away from it all, but very few are still as quiet as they once were," says Sean Kelly, co-founder of BookRetreats.com. "Our Unspoilt Index maps where the last genuinely quiet ones are, and what's clear from the data is that they're peaceful because people chose to protect their quiet." So, where should we be heading to escape the noise? Not some of our favourite European hideouts, it seems. Malta ranks last on the list of 100 islands with a meagre score of just 5.3 out of 100. Santorini ranks 99th thanks to 64km of major roads packed into 76 square kilometres of land, while Tenerife ranks 93rd and Ibiza 85th. Other destinations that didn’t fare too well include the Thai isle of Phuket in 95th place, Martinique in 90th and the Isle of Wight in 81st. However, Brits needn’t travel too far to find peace. St Martin’s, the third-largest of the Isles of Scilly, ranks fifth in the index. The quietest island in the United Kingdom has no main roads, no airport and just 135 residents. Reachable by ferry or via a short flight from Cornwall to St Mary’s, then a boat, this dreamy isle with its 12 beaches is the ultimate day trip for a reset. It’s not the only British gem in the top 20, either. Scotland’s Isle of Skye ranks 11th, where more than 1,600 square kilometres of moor and mountain is shared by just 10,000 people. There’s one hub and several smaller villages and hamlets scattered along the coast, with an otherworldly landscape popular among nature lovers and hikers during the summer months. However, it’s New Zealand’s third-largest and lesser-known island, Stewart Island, that claims the title of the quietest island in the world. The world’s southernmost International Dark Sky Sanctuary is almost entirely untouched and virtually free of artificial light. The Greek island of Anafi is second, with a tiny population and no airports or main roads. Here, we’ve rounded up the 20 quietest islands in the world right now, so you can plot your next adventure and relax like never before. The quietest islands in the world 2026 20. Palawan, Philippines 19. Vis, Croatia 18. La Digue, Seychelles 17. Mljet, Croatia 16. Salt Spring Island, Canada 15. Boa Vista, Cape Verde 14. Herm, Channel Islands 13. Magnetic Island, Australia 12. Isla Holbox, Mexico 11. Isle of Skye, UK 10. Santa Catalina Island, USA 9. Havelock Island, India 8. Koh Rong, Cambodia 7. Koh Chang, Thailand 6. Tioman Island, Malaysia 5. St Martin's, Isles of Scilly, UK 4. Lord Howe Island, Australia 3. Ilha Grande, Brazil 2. Anafi, Greece 1. Stewart Island, New Zealand

item.title: The latest travel advice after flash floods on Nepal-Tibet border
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.77
This is an evolving news story – the information below is up-to-date as of 5pm BST on Thursday 27 August 2026. For the latest updates in the UK, visit BBC News and Gov.uk. On 26 August, a flash flood swept through Nepal’s Rasuwa district near the Tibet border, killing at least 389 people and leaving hundreds of travellers missing, as per reports. These include visitors from countries including the United Kingdom, the United States, South Africa, Malaysia and India. At least 573 people were rescued on Thursday 27 August. While the exact cause is still being investigated, Nepal's Foreign Affairs Minister Shishir Khanal initially told parliament an earthquake in the Himalayan region at 8.37am local time had triggered an avalanche, which may have blocked a river and unleashed devastating flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border. The US Geological Survey has since said that “glacial collapse and debris flow” triggered the deluge. Domestic security forces are leading large-scale search, rescue, and relief operations, and the country is also receiving backing from neighbouring and international authorities. China is mounting a parallel response on the other side of the border, where the Gyirong area in Tibet has also been hit. President Xi Jinping has called for all-out efforts to find those missing and strengthen monitoring against further disasters. India has offered humanitarian assistance, with emergency supplies and NDRF personnel being prepared for potential deployment. South Korea, meanwhile, is sending a joint rapid-response team. The International Red Cross and Red Crescent network has also activated emergency teams and relief supplies. Which areas in and around Nepal are impacted by the floods? In Nepal, Syapru Besi and Timure in Rasuwa district remain the worst affected areas, while damage has also been reported along the Trishuli River in Nuwakot. On the other side of the border, the Gyirong area of Tibet also recorded fatalities. “At approximately 10:30am, due to a mudslide occurring on the Nepalese side, major casualties and missing persons were caused at the Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Shigatse City, Tibet,” Xinhua reported. Regions lying around and below the Bhote Koshi river, which flows from Tibet to Nepal, remain on high alert, with local authorities confirming the main road to Kathmandu – which is an important commercial and passenger corridor connecting the capital city to western Nepal, the southern plains (Terai), and the border with India – is closed. The effects are also being monitored downstream in India, where authorities in Bihar have put six districts along the Kosi, Gandak and Ganga systems on alert for rising river levels as floodwaters move south. Travel disruptions Travellers flying to Nepal should distinguish between Kathmandu airport operations and access to the flood-hit north. Passengers with flights to or from Kathmandu should check their individual flight status with the airline before leaving for the airport. The main disruption is on the ground, with roads and bridges leading towards Rasuwa, Syabrubesi and the Tibet border damaged by the floods. Authorities have advised against travelling into affected areas while rescue operations continue. Travellers with onward road transfers, trekking itineraries or Kailash Mansarovar plans should contact their operator before setting out and should not assume that a previously arranged vehicle or route remains operational. Those already stranded in affected areas should follow instructions from local authorities rather than attempting to cross damaged roads or river corridors. What are governments advising travellers? The Nepal Tourism Board has issued an urgent advisory asking tourists to avoid flood-affected areas and postpone non-essential travel. It has specifically flagged Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan, as well as the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors, and urged travellers to check road conditions before setting out. The Board has also shared emergency contact numbers on X. Visitors can call the Board’s helpline at 1234 (toll-free) or 1144 (emergency hotline), or contact the Tourist Police at (+977) 9851289445. The UK government's Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) handle on X is advising travellers in the region to follow local guidance and stay alert. UK citizens requiring assistance can call (+977) (0)14237100 from Nepal or +44 (0) 207 008 5000 from the UK. The US Embassy in Kathmandu has triggered a security alert, urging American citizens in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Chitwan and Tanahun to avoid riverbanks and low-lying areas, seek higher ground and stay away from flood-affected areas. For urgent assistance, US citizens can call (+977) 1-423-4000 or email KathmanduACS@state.gov. Malaysia’s Foreign Ministry, through its embassy in Kathmandu, issued a note saying they are actively monitoring the situation after losing contact with 11 Malaysian nationals believed to be in Rasuwa. Malaysians in Nepal have been urged to remain vigilant, follow instructions from local authorities and contact the embassy if they need assistance. The Embassy of India in Kathmandu has issued emergency contact numbers for Indian nationals affected by the floods: (+977) 9851316807 and (+977) 9709107500. This article was first published by Condé Nast Traveller India.

item.title: Thinking about golden years adventures? These are officially the best holiday destinations for retired travellers in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.52
On the whole, we’re living longer than ever. Advances in medicine, technology and education mean life expectancies are continuously rising, with record numbers of healthy octogenarians and nonagenarians around the world. Consequently, fewer of us are viewing retirement as a time to slow down. The retirement gap year is very much on the rise and, timed with children flying the nest and starting their own families as parents’ careers come to a well-deserved end, curious baby boomers and those of the silent generation are setting their sights on a host of jetsetting adventures. But which destinations are best suited to these travellers? While tastes and interests vary greatly, octogenarians seek different experiences on their travels than those of globetrotters before starting university. To uncover the best destinations in the world for retired travellers in 2026, the travel specialists at Firebird Tours have pitted some of the world’s most popular holiday destinations against each other across several metrics. The study considers scores for walkability, healthcare, peace and safety, while factoring in museum discounts, the number of Michelin-recognised restaurants and a score for the number of UNESCO Heritage Sites. Japan has been named the best destination in the world for retired travellers right now, trumping other destinations by an impressive margin. While it proves an increasingly popular option for younger travellers, Japan is home to the largest proportion of over-65s (29.5 per cent), its cities are deemed extremely walkable, and there are myriad Michelin options for touring gourmands. Germany is second, with a notable safety score and plenty of UNESCO World Heritage Sites – but it’s let down by measly discounts for seniors on public transport and in cultural venues. Such discounts are considerably better in Spain, which ranks third, while fourth-place Slovenia’s score is bolstered by a large senior population and its walkable landscape. Below, see the destinations retirees are travelling to in their droves – and see the full study at firebirdtours.com. The best countries in the world for retired travellers 10. Canada =8. Netherlands =8. Finland 7. Denmark 6. Austria 5. Switzerland 4. Slovenia 3. Spain 2. Germany 1. Japan

item.title: A new V&A display will celebrate Freddie Mercury with 8 of his most legendary looks this autumn
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.24
The V&A South Kensington is honouring Freddie Mercury, one of the most-loved figures in rock music, with a new exhibit this autumn, as a trail celebrates the 80th birthday of Queen frontman. Freddie Mercury | Splendid Things runs from 24 October 2026 to 17 January 2027, and showcases eight legendary looks from the rockstar’s career across six stops curated by award-winning designer Tom Piper. The looks span the 1970s and ’80s, with highlights including a striking monochrome ensemble Freddie wore for an early Queen gig at Imperial College that featured on the cover of Queen’s debut album in 1973, and Wendy de Smet’s ‘Mercury Wing’ catsuit worn on stage for the Night at the Opera tour. Other exhibits include the crown and cloak designed by Diana Moseley worn on the Magic Tour, including for Freddie’s last stage appearance with Queen at Knebworth in 1986, alongside accessories and items from Mercury’s personal wardrobe that offer a glimpse of the man behind the rockstar persona. The trail has been curated in collaboration with Freddie’s former fiancée, close friend and confidante of 20 years, Mary Austin, who lends seven looks for the three-month display. Kate Bailey, senior curator of theatre and performance at the V&A, said: “We are thrilled to display Freddie’s most iconic costumes at the V&A, celebrating one of the greatest performers and songwriters of all time. Reflecting his love of ‘splendid things’ and his passion for art, design and fashion, Freddie will be very at home in the V&A galleries.” The trail comes alongside several exciting exhibitions across the V&A’s museums. Schiaparelli: Fashion Becomes Art continues its spellbinding run across The Sainsbury Gallery until early November, before Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires opens its doors to culture vultures across galleries 38 and 39 the same week.

item.title: How Lima's creative crowd are drawing on the country’s heritage to dream up contemporary objects
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.91
Shopping in Lima has long been a vibrant multisensory experience. This mesmerising coastal metropolis, home to some 10 million people, oozes a creative spirit shaped by a fusion of today's high-rise dwellers and centuries-old traditions from Peru's Indigenous peoples. Whether it's chic ceramic from independent studios, accessories from forward-thinking designers who collaborate with artisans or contemporary homeware that'll have you searching for an extra suitcase before the journey home, this is the ultimate shopaholic's guide to the Peruvian capital. Herbario Verónica Castillo was moved to make her own natural creations as she became increasingly aware of the toxins in the products we use on our bodies and around our houses. This grew into Herbario, developed with her friend Mariana Otero and Yerko Zlatar of Puna homeware – the brands have adjoining retail spaces in the same multipurpose building in the artsy Barranco district, which also houses an art gallery. Five scents created using a palette of essential oils such as lemongrass, jasmine and ylang-ylang define a range that includes body oils, room sprays, perfumes and soy wax candles. Address: Jr. Colina 128, B, Barranco, Lima Website: herbario.pe Polen Barranco is home to several independent ceramics studios, which, between them, make tableware for some of the city’s top restaurants: Central, Mayta, Maido and Mérito. There’s no sign outside, yet it’s impossible to miss Polen, with its cheery pink and orange exterior. Inside, potters including founder Elizabeth Vásquez create their own glazes and clay recipes. Test fragments dangle on strings in the corridor like wind chimes. One room is a curation of prototypes from past commissions; another is a shop full of milk jugs, goblets and candle holders. Address: Delucchi 205, Barranco 15063, Peru Website: polenceramicstudio.com Altamar Ceramic Studio It’s a similar set-up to Polen at Altamar Ceramic Studio, where Nagib Zariquiey and a small team (including his mother, Diana Morcos) showcase their wares. Inspired by the landscapes of Peru, pieces include sea creatures, coral-like vessels, sculptural vases in interesting textures, pink marbled coffee cups and earthy plates. Elsewhere, Sergio Murga Rossel of Null Lab sells the extras he makes by appointment at his studio. Address: Calle Libertad 255, Barranco 15063, Peru Website: altamarceramics.com; @null.lab La Zapateria Handmade Right next to Mérito restaurant in Barranco is La Zapateria Handmade, a tiny space with a workshop upstairs and blue foot moulds hanging from the ceiling. Cowboy boots, lace-ups, trainers and loafers are crafted using leather from Peru and beyond. Shoes can be customised with quirky elements such as a mint-green accent on a pair of smart slip-ons or a square-toe sole on block-heeled boots. There’s also a small selection of school satchels and tote handbags. Address: Calle Melgar 216, Barranco, Lima, Peru Website: cooperativehandmade.com Escvdo At Escvdo, Chiara Macchiavello’s womenswear spotlights crochet in bestsellers such as a co-ord set inspired by ancient geometric patterns from the Libertad region. Address: Jirón Comandante Juan Fanning 108, Barranco, Lima 15063, Peru Website: escvdo.com Alessandra Petersen Lima’s most forward-facing fashion labels collaborate with artisans to showcase heritage craft techniques in modern ways. Hand-knitting is a focus at Alessandra Petersen’s 1920s townhouse boutique, where shaggy alpaca jackets take centre stage alongside green jumpsuits and silk ombre skirts. Address: C. Atahualpa 479 -A, Miraflores LIMA 18, Peru Website: @alessandrapetersen Ayni In an unassuming apartment block near the Inka Market, B Corp-certified Ayni uses baby alpaca wool, Pima cotton and plant-based dyes for pastel sweaters with crochet cuff detailing, hand-knit skirts and cardigans with heart-shaped embroidery. The company also runs a training programme for the artisans it works with. Address: Jr. González Prada 355, Of. 204, Miraflores, Peru Website: ayni.com.pe Estrafalario Estrafalario employs female former prisoners, many of them survivors of gender-based violence, to make clothes – white cotton waistcoats embroidered with birds and flowers, neon pink knitted jumpers with decorative candy-striped yarn – from recovered materials. Address: Jr. Colina 128, Barranco, 2nd Floor Website: estrafalario.pe El Cacaotal After US-born Amanda Jo Wildey moved to Peru to write a thesis on cacao and the chocolate value chain, it was a case of right place, right time. The country’s craft chocolate boom was just beginning, but there were very few places to buy what was being produced. So in 2017 she opened her chocolate shop, El Cacaotal, now located above Ciclos Café and roastery run by her husband, coffee expert Felipe Aliaga. Wildey works directly with about 20 ethical producers and farmers, including Kuyay and Scrap & Chocolates, recognisable by the alpaca motif on its brown paper packaging. The aim is to encourage customers to think of chocolate like wine: the taste changes depending on where it has come from. Flavour wheels give a reference to the hallmarks of each region’s cacao (fruity, nutty and sweet for the bars made in Ayacucho, for instance). Wildey also offers bookable tastings. Address: Jr. Colina 111, Barranco 15063, Peru Website: elcacaotal.com Lorena Pestana From wing ear cuffs in her Mythologies collection to puma necklaces and delicate dragonfly and hummingbird pendants, jeweller Lorena Pestana is influenced by the ancient civilisations of the Amazon and Peru, such as the pre-Inca Moche. At the front of her small shop, contemporary pieces are laid out in glass boxes and on wooden plinths, and her workshop is at the back. She mainly works in 18-carat gold, silver and bronze, but also uses glass beads and stones including aquamarine and sapphire. Address: Ca. Gral. Borgoño 756, Miraflores 15074, Peru Website: lorenapestana.pe Dédalo A local institution, labyrinth-like Dédalo has been a Lima shopping staple for more than 30 years. The central room feels like an art and design gallery specialising in wood and pottery (leaf-shaped chopping boards, earthy espresso cups), while each side nook reveals something new: alpaca scarves and jumpers by Mia Peru; linen and organic cotton womenswear by Melisa Serna and Nathalie Shapiama; and fringed knitted cardigans by AwA Peru. One space is dedicated to jewellery, another to table runners, and at the back there’s a leafy courtyard café for coffee or cocktails. Address: Jirón Sáenz Peña 295, Barranco 15063, Peru Website: dedalo.pe Ka Concept Store A 10-minute walk away from Dédalo, Ka Concept Store, founded by art director and stylist Angela Kusen, stocks Peruvian labels including painterly Mozhdeh Matin, DNI, known for its T-shirts with tongue-in-cheek slogans, and bold Balkanica, whose colourful designs reference pre-Columbian symbols. Address: Cajamarca 404, Barranco 15063, Peru Website: @ka_______conceptstore Puna Multidisciplinary contemporary homeware studio Puna sells geometric motif wall hangings, terracotta vessels, embroidered tablecloths and abstract hand-dyed cushions by weavers in San Pedro de Cajas, a central Andes town known for its tapestries. Address: Jr. Colina 128, Barranco 15063, Peru Website: puna.com.pe Yunuik Yunuik is the only store in Lima to specialise in objects made by Indigenous peoples in the Peruvian Amazon Basin. Highlights include Shipibo throws, bowls from the Awajún culture and painted wooden birds. Anthropologist founder Josefa Nolte worked for the Ministry of Culture before opening her shop nearly three years ago, and her knowledge of some of the Peruvian Amazon’s 51 ethnic groups (including the Achuar and Yanesha) is exceptional. Gentle birdsong plays while visitors browse, and the name of each maker and community is written on every piece. Address: C. Bellavista 590, Miraflores, Lima 18, Peru Website: @yunuik.artisans

item.title: Ibiza’s best Airbnbs for families, complete with shallow-entry pools and sunset terraces

Ibiza has it all. Flying the flag for the Balaeriac for decades, the island is well-known for its storied nightlife scene, sparkling celebrity hangouts and full-blown luxury.
