item.title: “Our earth is only one polka dot among a million stars in the cosmos”: remembering Yayoi Kusama, the girl who covered the world in polka dots
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.58
In 2016, a day before she was to enrol as a student at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, Sunaina Rajan made a pit stop in Los Angeles for a single day. Word had gone round that one of Yayoi Kusama’s Infinity Mirror Rooms was on view at The Broad, the museum that had opened downtown the year before. She joined the line, and waited in it for seven hours till it was her turn to enter the room, albeit for under a minute, strictly timed by a staff member standing outside, who’d briskly open the door once the seconds ran out. “You really get just a very short glimpse of it,” recalls Rajan, who opened Gallery Maxima in Mumbai’s Fort district earlier this year. “But the physical experience is so unforgettable from the moment you enter, the way you experience it…you’re immersed in it completely.” The legendary Japanese contemporary artist passed away earlier this month on 14 August at a hospital in Tokyo, aged 97. Her studio and her gallery, David Zwirner, announced her death on 26 August. The cause was multiple organ failure. Few artists have altered the physical act of looking at art as completely as she did, and she got there first, in 1965, with Infinity Mirror Room – Phalli’s Field, where hundreds of hand-sewn phallic forms, spotted in red, carpeted the floor of a mirrored room that repeated them into the horizon. “Traditionally, museum-going has been about standing in front of one masterpiece and really taking it in,” Rajan shares. “She inverts that completely. Instead of stepping into the museum to see a work, you’re now stepping into the work.” When Yayoi Kusama: Infinity Mirrors opened at the Hirshhorn in Washington, DC, in 2017, it drew nearly 160,000 people, and the museum recorded its highest spring attendance since opening in 1974. The show went on to Seattle, back to The Broad, then to Toronto, Cleveland and Atlanta. In 2023 her work arrived in India for the first time as an Infinity Mirrored Room at the Nita Mukesh Ambani Cultural Centre (NMACC) in Mumbai, now part of its permanent collection. Two years ago, Rajan made a longer pilgrimage to Naoshima, the island in Japan’s Seto Inland Sea given over almost entirely to contemporary art. “You need three modes of transportation to get there – first by bus, then train, then ferry; and you can walk the whole island in under an hour,” describes Rajan, At the end of a pier sits her yellow Pumpkin, which was installed there in 1994, swept into the sea by a typhoon in August 2021, and remade and returned to the same spot on 4 October 2022. What struck Rajan was that the reverence held there too, with nobody enforcing it. “In contrast, there’s no one attending to it, no security timing you. There’s just this sort of decorum around her work, because there’s so much respect for it.” Elsewhere on the island, Kusama’s mirrored spheres sit in a body of water, near buildings by Tadao Ando. “What’s fascinating to see is how the architecture, the art and nature interact with each other,” Rajan points out. The life and art of Yayoi Kusama Kusama was born in Matsumoto, in Nagano prefecture, on 22 March 1929, into a family who ran a seed nursery: fields of flowers on one side, a violent and unhappy household on the other. In her lifetime, she recalled being a child when the hallucinations started. Sometimes it was benign, the millions of white pebbles in the riverbed at Matsumoto, which she would lie and stare at; and sometimes it was not. The episode she returned to for the rest of her life involved a tablecloth: she looked at its red flower pattern, looked up, and found the same pattern across the ceiling, the windows, the walls, and finally over her own body and the universe beyond it. She described the sensation as beginning to self-obliterate, to dissolve into endless time and space. So, she started drawing them to record each vision, which took some of the terror out of them. She found the dot along the way, smaller and stranger than decoration, and compared the single dot to her own life: one particle among billions. The dots were the symptom; making them, over and over, was the treatment, and nearly 70 years of work came out of that single loop. Her pumpkins came from the same fields. As a schoolgirl, she visited a seed-harvesting ground with her grandfather, where she saw her first pumpkin. What she loved about them, she said later, was their “generous unpretentiousness”. Rejecting her dreams of becoming an artist, her mother wanted her to be a housewife and repeatedly tore up her drawings. Kusama, instead, went on to train in traditional Nihonga painting in Kyoto, and on 15 November 1955 she wrote to American painter Georgia O’Keeffe (a stranger to her, whose work she had found in a second-hand book) to ask how a Japanese girl might make a life as an artist in the United States. O’Keeffe wrote back within three weeks. She told her to get to a city, asked what she wanted for the watercolours, offered to show them to a dealer, and advised her to put her work in front of anyone who would look at it. In 1957 Kusama destroyed most of her work and left, first for Seattle, then New York in the summer of 1958, where she spent the rest of her 20s and 30s, creating her vast, obsessive Infinity Net paintings, which were showcased at the Brata Gallery 1959; the Accumulations, ordinary furniture swallowed by soft phallic forms, which debuted at the Green Gallery in late 1962 alongside the Pop artists Claes Oldenburg and Andy Warhol; and, in November 1965 at the Richard Castellane Gallery, Infinity Mirror Room – Phalli’s Field, the first of the mirrored environments that would eventually take over the internet decades later. In 1966 she turned up at the Venice Biennale without an invitation, laid 1,500 mirrored balls on the grass outside the Italian pavilion and sold them for two dollars each beneath a sign reading “Your Narcissism for Sale”. By the end of that decade she was staging anti-war happenings in Manhattan, painting polka dots onto naked bodies. She went home to Japan in 1973 and, in 1977, voluntarily checked herself into Seiwa Hospital in Tokyo, where she lived for the rest of her life, walking each day to a studio across the road. The entire second half of her career was made from that arrangement. In 1993 she became the first artist given a solo presentation in Japan’s pavilion at Venice; then came two major artistic collaborations with Louis Vuitton in 2012 and 2023, her own museum in Shinjuku in 2017, and a scale of fame that very few living artists have known. “Our earth is only one polka dot among a million stars in the cosmos,” Kusama once mused. For Rajan, that is the inheritance: “She took something as simple as the polka dot or the pumpkin, which is so ordinary to us, and made it a portrait of her… showing us that art can be an environment that you’re entering into, and created that incredible legacy for so many artists to come.” How to follow the dots The best place to discover and take in Kusama’s work is on Naoshima, Japan, where her infamous yellow Pumpkin sits at the end of a pier below Benesse House and a red one waits at Miyanoura Port, free and open at all hours (though much of the island closes for maintenance through stretches of January and February). In Tokyo, the Yayoi Kusama Museum spans five narrow floors in Shinjuku; tickets go on sale online on the first of each month for dates two months ahead. And in Matsumoto, where she was born, the city’s museum of art holds a year-round display, with her Great Gigantic Pumpkin outside. Beyond Japan, the touring shows have wound down, so what’s left is permanent: two rooms at The Broad in Los Angeles, Gleaming Lights of the Souls at Louisiana outside Copenhagen, and (closest to home) the Infinity Mirrored Room at NMACC in Mumbai, acquired after her India debut in 2023. This article was first published by Condé Nast Traveller India.

item.title: 19 best hotels in the Dolomites, from boutque stays to superb ski spots and wellness pioneers, 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.45
In winter, a dramatic, snowglobe scene of jagged, rocky spines protruding from snowy coats, dusted pine forests and frozen lakes surround the best hotels in the Dolomites. And it all thaws for summer’s ‘hills-are-alive’ buttercup meadows and lush valleys. Glassy lakes and church spires piercing the crisp, blue skies. The Dolomites mountain range are maddeningly beautiful – a cinematic landscape dotted with storybook chalet towns and villages, the Brothers Grimm sort that wind up on a panettone tin and genuinely, truly exist. Along with Ortisei, Brixen and Santa Magdalena, Cortina d’Ampezio is one of these – a now world famous Italian ski resort following its moment in the spotlight during 2026’s Winter Olympics. It’s the Narnia-like wonders such as the Tre Cime di Lavaredo, Lago di Braies, Alpe di Siusi and the Marmolada Glacier that have afforded the Dolomites their UNESCO World Heritage label. And where French and Swiss Alpine towns have chipped their identity amid the jet set glitz and Oligarch glam, the Dolomites remain deeply rooted in Ladin culture and traditions, with Roman and Milanese weekenders setting a palpably Italian (not touristy) tone, and history, notably in South Tyrol region, expressed through unique dishes and local rhythms. Dolomiti winters are stewing in a thermal pool or admiring the enrosidira (the pink hue cast on the jagged peaks at sunset) with a glass of Lagrein, having whooshed down the slopes or trudged through silent pine forests that day. Summers are following trails scribbled across the peaks, skirting glacial lakes and wallowing in outdoor pools with valley views. And from restrained, foodie eco-boutiques to spa stalwarts with steaming outdoor pools tipping over pastoral valleys and easy access to the slopes, the best hotels in the Dolomites are well aware of their year-round appeal. Editor's picks of the best hotels in the Dolomites - For ski: COMO Alpina Dolomites - For a view: Forestis Dolomites - For families: San Sonnea Family Dolomites - For a boutique stay: My Arbor How we choose the best hotels in the Dolomites Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels.

item.title: Could this pretty little Georgian market town be North Yorkshire’s answer to the Cotswolds?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.04
Is Helmsley the Cotswolds in microcosm? The small market town in North Yorkshire might be small, but it has some of the characteristics: it has biscuit-toned, chocolate-box cottages, a star-studded culinary scene, an ancient castle with walled gardens, a notable Cistercian abbey and beautiful country and coastal walks nearby. The town is perfectly placed to explore the rugged Yorkshire coastline, as the starting point for The Cleveland Way National Trail and sits at the edge of the North York Moors National Park – it’s a bucolic base for a wild and wonderful weekend in the countryside. In 2024, The Good Food Guide named Helmsley and the Howardian Hills the “most exciting food destination” and the title has been retained in 2026. My mother is from Helmsley and I know how passionate locals are about high-quality homegrown produce – there are some incredible places to eat, some that still feel under-the-radar. There’s no direct train to Helmsley and I would advise travelling by car anyway, because there’s so much to see in the area: Castle Howard and the Howardian Hills are within easy reach (a 20-minute drive), the Kilburn White Horse and its high-up countryscape (a 15-minute drive), Goathland and the purple heather of the moors and the sleepy shores of Sandsend or the higgledy-piggledy streets of Robin Hood’s Bay (both around a 50-minute drive). And if you just want to relax with no big plans, do local walks, eat well and sleep well, you’re onto a winner; I always feel restored after a visit. Here are my tips for Helmsley and beyond. Our favourite things to do in Helmsley See Helmsley Castle and Helmsley Walled Garden Small but mighty Helmsley Castle and Helmsley Walled Garden are a must. Historically, it has been a medieval fortress, an Elizabethan mansion and a Georgian ruin. My tip: make a pit stop at the lovely walled garden, which was once a filming location for The Secret Garden. Grab a table at indie Vine House Café, where seasonal plates from the garden like asparagus and mint frittata are served with love – the formidable homemade cakes and freshly baked scones are things of beauty. Address: Castlegate, Helmsley, York YO62 5AB Website: english-heritage.org.uk; helmsleywalledgarden.org.uk Visit the weekly market and browse the boutiques I’d recommend wandering Helmsley’s pretty cream-stone boutiques set around the market square – do venture into the little side streets as there are some hidden gems. There’s The Helmsley Bookshop to browse, Twig & Twine, a florist and vintage homeware shop, pop into Ryeburn of Helmsley ice-cream parlour or Hunters of Helmsley delicatessen has amazing Yorkshire fare: meats, cheeses, chutneys (and pies). Go to Helmsley Market (every Friday; 8am-4pm), it’s a great place for antique finds, handcrafted gifts, flowers and local farm produce – including Yorkshire cheeses. It’s slap-bang in the centre of town and is served with a side of Yorkshire banter. Address: Market Place, Helmsley Website: yorkshire.com Explore gorgeous countryside and coastal spots Rievaulx Abbey, Kilburn White Horse and The Cleveland Way National Trail are all nearby – I’d recommend the decent (7-mile circular) walk from Helmsley to Rievaulx, especially when the woodlands are carpeted in bluebells. The Cistercian abbey (circa 1132) was the first Cistercian abbey in the north of England. Kilburn White Horse is an iconic stop, a 318ft long mare set into Sutton Bank – with inspiring patchwork views of the countryside – you can actually walk the 10 miles from Helmsley, as it is the start of The Cleveland Way National Trail, a spectacular 109-mile route cusping the coastline and moors. Stargazing in the North York Moors National Park is dreamy. Where to eat and drink in Helmsley Book ahead for a table at The Star Inn at Harome. It’s just a skip-and-a-hop from Helmsley in serene Harome, but my top recommendation for a splash-out meal. Harome is worth a look at any time as it’s an endearing place – all mushroom-topped cottages, duck ponds and country idyll but Andrew Pern’s original Star is a classic, a special place to dine. The menu pays homage to the region's natural larder with an excellent balance of seafood and meat – try the pan-roasted skri cod or herb-roasted pork tenderloin; split the date cake ice cream with salted caramel. Spy the Kilburn Mouseman furniture in the restaurant; it’s a nod to British craftsmanship. These are star-studded parts and Michelin-starred or recommended restaurants nearby include The Black Swan at Oldstead and Mýse for whip-smart tasting menus, plus a plethora of excellent country pubs such as The Abbey Inn and restaurants like Pignut & The Hare that rank highly. You will always eat well here. Where to stay in Helmsley I’d recommend visiting Helmsley for a long weekend or as part of a longer tour of the countryside or coastline – you won’t want to dash through it all. For an iconic sleepover, I would book dinner and stay at The Star at Harome (a five-minute drive), or in Hovingham (a 10-minute drive); my pick is Mýse for a two-person stay – with its cosy-cool, cream-on-cream interiors, original beams and Chapter Organics lotions and potions. For a coastal stay, I love Saltmoore in Sandsend; the hotel has a brilliant brasserie, a glossy spa and is set just near the beach – it caters so well to families. For longer stays and larger groups, Beautiful Escapes has some stylish spaces.

item.title: I fly 77,000+ miles a year – this is my non-negotiable long-haul travel uniform in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.82
As a professional travel writer, I cover a lot of ground. This year, I’m hopping on several flights per month ranging from long-hauls to Vietnam, Cape Town, and Hawaii, to slightly shorter jaunts to Paris, Rome, and Greenland – a whopping 77,000+ miles so far and counting. One thing that’s hugely important on any trip? Staying comfortable in transit. With all that time in the air, I've perfected my travel uniform, aka the comfortable airport outfit I always wear for long travel days, no matter where I’m headed. My trusty formula almost never veers from the relaxed clothing staples below, from supportive shoes to the perfect tee and a sleek bomber jacket. Read on for my tried-and-true picks that always keep me looking and feeling my best on every journey. A light jacket Cabin temperatures are notoriously cold, but then you’ll step off the plane and into the Med and overheat immediately. As such, layering on a flight is key, and a lightweight jacket is the cornerstone of the look. Rather than reaching for an oversized hoodie that can quickly look scruffy in a lounge, a cropped or smart bomber style adds a little polish to an otherwise casual outfit. They can also be folded and used as an impromptu pillow in a pinch. Look for crease-resistant fabrics and deep pockets that can house a passport, lip balm, and boarding pass for frictionless airport security screening. The perfect tee A good T-shirt is the unsung hero of long-haul travel. When you’re sitting in the same seat for nine hours, the texture against your skin matters immensely. My golden rule is to completely avoid synthetic blends that trap heat and opt instead for 100 per cent organic cotton or ultra-soft jersey t-shirts with a dense weight. A great travel tee needs to hold its shape after hours of reclining, have a non-restrictive crew neckline, and not sheer out or cling after a few washes. Neutral, versatile shades like creamy oat, charcoal, or classic white makes it easy to style whatever you’re wearing, giving you a breathable base layer that should stay fresh through multiple time zones. Put-together trousers Gone are the days when being comfy in the airport meant sacrificing style for baggy grey tracksuit bottoms. Modern travel trousers offer the stretch and ease of loungewear, with crisp tailored finishes. Wide-leg cuts in soft, flexible fabrics and those with tailored pull-on waistbands are my go-to choice for long travel days. They allow complete freedom of movement – whether you’re folding your legs up on a long-haul flight or sprinting through terminals to catch a tight connection – without digging into your waist. The beauty is in their incredible versatility; paired with trainers and a clean tee, you achieve an effortless look that feels like wearing loungewear while looking entirely intentional. Plus, if you’re headed straight to a meeting upon landing, they can be immediately dressed up by swapping your trainers and jacket for boots and a blazer. Compression socks After a 13-plus-hour flight from Ho Chi Minh City to London left one of my legs swollen and uncomfortable this year, I vowed to always wear compression socks on long flights. High-altitude cabin pressure combined with hours of sitting can severely hamper circulation, leading to fatigued legs and fluid retention. Integrating a dedicated pair of graduated compression socks into my travel routine has been a total game-changer. Designed to gently encourage blood flow back up towards the heart, they significantly cut down on in-flight aches and post-flight ankle swelling. My favourites are those made from breathable bamboo fibres – and aesthetically, there are plenty out there these days that look just like regular crew or knee socks, sliding under trainers without sacrificing comfort or style. Comfortable shoes Navigating huge airport terminals, endless security queues, and European cobblestones all in one day means one thing: your footwear needs to prioritise comfort and support above all else. For long-haul travel days, I find a good pair of trainers to be a complete non-negotiable. I rotate between a few different styles, but no matter the pair, they’re always trainers I can rush around the airport in and wear socks with in case I need to take my shoes off in a security line. Seamless luggage set No travel uniform is complete without the luggage to bring all your gear along with. Navigating terminals with multiple bags quickly turns chaotic if your luggage strategy relies on mismatched totes and awkwardly sliding straps. A clever luggage set allows for effortless mobility and proper integrated organisation, so your essential items remain within arm’s reach while your hands stay free for your coffee. My go-to setup is a smooth-rolling carry-on paired with a dedicated travel tote as an under-seat cabin bag, finished with a sleek sling bag where I keep my cards and passport. Look for luggage with trolley sleeves that slide over case handles, polycarbonate or aluminium exteriors that will withstand turbulence, and bags with internal compartments to reduce stress and keep tech, travel documents, and flight essentials sorted throughout your trip. More editor-approved shopping guides to shop now

item.title: 17 of the best hotels in the Cotswolds our editors love for a UK staycation with character for 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.67
The Cotswolds is a British favourite for a reason. Nowhere does stylish country pubs, grand manor houses and hip boutique hotels quite like it. Choosing the best hotels in the Cotswolds, then, is a tricky ask. From the quintessential to the contemporary, the foodie-focused to the spa-centric, each has the temptation to move here long-term. There's also the ever-welcome fact that it's equally beautiful in the depths of winter as in fair weather. Here, wellies are part of the uniform, trudging through muddy fields and stepping over stiles are par for the course and hunkering down by an open fire to thaw out somehow feels more romantic in winter, anyway. Bookmark the best things to do, add a visit to a farm shop to your list and swoon over Sunday roast menus to plan the ultimate escape-from-the-city weekend. Editor's Picks of the best hotels in the Cotswolds Best for foodies: Bull, Burford Best for wellness: Dormy House Hotel & Spa Best boutique stay: The Pig, Gloucestershire Best for couples: Cowley Manor Best for families: The Fish Best dog-friendly stay: Lygon Arms - Read Full ReviewDown a suitably grand wide driveway where grazing sheep stretch out in the sprawling grounds near Winchcombe, you’ll find the newly renovated Dumbleton Hall. This 19th-century Cotswold stone estate has entered an ambitious new chapter following a major restoration inside and out. Built on a historic wool fortune – the Cotswolds area is well loved for its wool products, as well as its lavender – the manor house has long been a literary and cultural hub, having hosted the likes of Charles Dickens, Elizabeth Gaskell, and John Betjeman, among others. Now, within the old stone exterior, it’s a thoroughly refreshed take on country living, with maximalist Belle Époque-inspired interiors (they’ve somehow made leopard-print rugs work in an olde-worlde country manor) and far-reaching bucolic views across the hotel’s peaceful grounds and lake. It’s a true taste of the good life, made a little more elevated – settle in by a roaring hearth, tuck into a seasonal British plate, then sip slowly on something in the Library Bar, which is lined wall to wall with books. It stands out against neighbouring Cotswolds heavyweights by deftly combining the grandeur and scale of an old estate with an intimate ease that evokes staying at a stylish friend’s country seat over a stuffy old hotel. Charley Ward Address: Dumbleton, Evesham WR11 7TS Prices: From about £300 per night. - Read Full ReviewFrom the front, Dormy House Hotel & Spa is every inch the classic honey-hued manor house, but behind the doors lies a carefully curated world of food, fireside lounging and standout wellness that far exceeds expectations. Step through the reception rooms, where roaring fires, leather armchairs, muddy boots and a refreshingly informal ‘no-front-desk’ welcome set the tone. The House Spa is the undeniable star. Its thermal suite invites hours of gentle drifting between steam rooms, saunas and hot-and-cold experiences, including a bracing snow shower and a forest-mist drench shower infused with essential oils. Outside, a bubbling hot tub awaits, best enjoyed as mist rises into the often-blustery British air. Dining at The Back Garden, the hotel’s fine-dining restaurant, delivers exactly what you’d hope for from a refined country hotel: modern British cooking rooted in superb local produce, with estate-grown vegetables and locally reared meat taking centre stage. After long walks across the surrounding hills and a few blissful hours in the spa, the bedrooms are a welcome reprive. Bright, calm and quietly luxurious with roll-top baths, thick robes make the idea of check-out hard to come to terms with. Breakfast is indulgent, with generous spreads of cheeses, compotes, overnight oats, granola and fresh fruit, alongside classic à la carte favourites like eggs royale and hearty house specials, including the aptly named ‘Fully Dormy’ for those with an appetite for the day ahead. Chloe Laws Address: Willersey Hill, Broadway, Worcestershire, WR12 7LF Prices: From about £350 per night. - Read Full ReviewA 16th-century coaching inn turned boutique hideaway – so far, so classic Cotswolds. But as soon as we clamber from the (branded) Defender and slip into reception, it's clear that Bull Burford is about to challenge our expectations. The first clue? There's a Dalí over the fireplace, and a Basquiat hanging over the chess table. Media mogul Matthew Freud bought this 1536-built inn a few years ago. From the outside, it retains a rather wonky charm, looking every bit the quintessential coaching house. Inside, however, Freud has filled every blank wall and disused corner with such an astonishing array of art from his personal collection that you gaze upon works from more world-famous artists during a stroll about the hotel than you might at many a major gallery or museum. The 18 bedrooms are deeply cossetting, carvenous spaces to tap out from reality for a while – we stayed in the Honeymooner, which had plump armchairs next to an exposed-brick fireplace for sinking into with a book (there was a stash of Penguin Classics on a shelf for forgetful types), a freestanding bath, and a separate dressing room for gussying up for supper. Plus, Freud and his team have added restaurants and drinking dens that are as good as anything you'll find in the UK's bigger cities right now – Wild, an open-fire restaurant under canvas in the hotel's courtyard, is the jewel in the foodie crown. Add to the mix personable staff, a treatment suite for facials or massages, and a plum position on the sloping high street of the cute Cotswolds village of Burford, and you've got a country weekender which swaggers rather than simpers. Sarah James Address: 105 High Street, Burford, Oxfordshire, OX18 4QR Prices: From about £270 per night. - Read Full ReviewThe Fish is a playful, woodland hideaway just a stone’s throw from Farncombe Estate’s other properties – Dormy House Hotel & Spa and Foxhill Manor – yet it feels like an entirely different offering. Tucked into the trees above the Vale of Evesham and a brisk stomp from the postcard-pretty village of Broadway, it’s made for weekend escapes that balance fresh air with frivolity. While more affordable and better suited to families and groups than its refined siblings, The Fish still delivers its own brand of luxury. Think sheepskin-draped lounge chairs, crackling open fires, cool Scandinavian-inspired interiors and tongue-in-cheek touches, from Hideaway huts named after A Midsummer Night’s Dream characters to treehouses designed for late-night drinks. What really makes it special is the staff and their “nothing’s too much” approach. Food is a highlight, with seafood taking centre stage in the fine-dining Hook restaurant, alongside relaxed crowd-pleasers served in buzzy communal spaces, perfect after long days spent roaming woodland trails, partaking in one of the many activities on-site (like archery) or sinking into an outdoor hot tub beneath the trees. Accommodation ranges from stylish hotel rooms to sprawling tree-lined Hideaway huts with private terraces, making it easy to tailor your stay, whether you’re planning a romantic retreat or a full-blown girls' getaway. It’s informal, fun and refreshingly unfussy, the kind of place that I could see myself returning to again and again. Chloe Laws Address: Farncombe, Broadway, Worcestershire, WR12 7LH Prices: From about £225 per night. - Read Full ReviewWaking up in Cowley Manor feels like you’ve tumbled down the rabbit hole and into a world of comfort, indulgence and serenity, even if just for a night. It’s owned by the Experimental* and – as expected – it’s designed in the brand’s signature contemporary-cool way. Prepare to start planning how best to replicate its interiors at home. Curious, considering its heritage house shell and historical ties to Lewis Caroll’s Alice In Wonderland inspiration. There are subtle nods to the story throughout: gilded gold door embellishments take the form of the rabbit head, and keys are marked on the hallway carpets. It’s not outlandish, though – this is a hotel that’s all about its guests. The spa and pool are simply heavenly, and many while away the day in the glass box that surrounds the water, glancing up from a book only to spot a bunny hip-hopping along outside. Others choose to set up camp in the bar, which is all roaring fire and chairs you can sink into while sipping on one of the mixologist’s most creative concoctions. Wander the grounds before dinner and discover hidden pathways through the surrounding woods before heading to the deep red dining room, where romance comes as a byproduct of any meal. Sarah Leigh Bannerman Address: Cowley, Cheltenham GL53 9NL Prices: From about £350 per night. - Read Full ReviewAn artist's impression of the Cotswolds would probably look a little something like this: a quaint high street, imposing historical buildings made of classic Cotswold stone, and snow falling gently as you cosy up alongside a crackling fire. If you managed to picture that in your head, you’ve probably accurately imagined The Lygon Arms. Standing proudly on Broadway high street – regularly named one of the prettiest high streets in the UK – The Lygon Arms offers that rare experience of a country getaway with plenty of things to do within walking distance, leaving guests to lean into slow weekends spent strolling or sipping as they wish. A former coaching inn dating back to the 1300s, guests soak up the history of the property from the minute they step inside – from the not-quite-straight stairs leading up to the rooms to the many framed maps and trinkets that point to fascinating anecdotes from the building’s many years of service, the charm of the past is inescapable. The hotel offers a surprising 86 rooms – surprising because the many winding corridors and hidden rooms hide the space of the place incredibly well. Rooms themselves vary, depending on whether you’re in the historical rooms (The King Charles I suite, for example, is where the King and his supporters once assembled, and offers a four-poster bed and coat of arms above the original fireplace, plus original paintings) or Courtyard Suites, which overlook individually landscaped gardens. Guests have plenty to indulge in during their stay – whether it’s a treatment in the spa or a dinner at the Grill hotel, with a menu from James Martin consisting of classic British fare done incredibly well. All this to say: when it comes to check-out, you might find it difficult to leave… Abigail Malbon Address: High Street, Broadway WR12 7DU Prices: From around £150 per night. - Read Full ReviewCows amble by The Pig on the way to the milking parlour, glancing over the wall at the vine-covered facade and crenellated porch of this Georgian rectory; later in the day, guests amble into their own parlours, finding an armchair that suits and peering through mullion windows at the scenes outside. In the cocktail bar – a bucolic space with green stools like grassy knolls and a flower-strewn panel taking up most of one wall – daylight streams in, illuminating the coloured glassware like a stained-glass window while a moustachioed bartender shakes the first of the day’s Martinis. In the garden outside, lovingly shaped box trees line the pathway like oversized berets, moss-coated branches twist towards the sky and Adirondack chairs recline on the lawn – even in winter, this is a garden full of interest and colour. Not all the rooms look out over Rosemary Verey’s garden but, in a sense, all are garden rooms – designed to complement the planting outside with intense floral prints that spread across wallpapers, lamp shades, cushions and bed-end benches, with hazy, green-painted walls that seem to give a burst of chlorophyll and vintage Murano flower chandeliers. This is the 10th in The Pig ‘litter’, and established principles apply: food and drink are central to its concept. In the restaurant, comfort food of the best kind – not trying to be clever but with some original flourishes and strong flavours, from the fallow pithivier and ceviche-like monkfish tail paired with white mooli to a Jerusalem artichoke risotto. The wine list has plenty to like, including several English fizzes and The Pig’s own Tuscan wines. Rick Jordan Address: Barnsley, Cirencester GL7 5EE Price: From about £220 per night - Read Full ReviewWindy country lanes, lined with chocolate-box sandstone houses, lead to teeny-tiny Clanfield – a village in the heart of the Cotswolds and home to The Double Red Duke. It’s a 17th-century coaching inn turned pub/restaurant with rooms. We arrive on a typically soggy Saturday in the midst of the English winter. Luckily, wellies and umbrellas await our arrival, but stepping through the door, it’s obvious why guests are using the weather as an excuse to stay indoors. Families cluster around the log fire wearing jumpers and muddy boots and kids play board games while sipping hot chocolate. Parents, on the other hand, have (rightly, in my opinion) chosen local pints and espresso martinis to fuel their afternoon. In summer, it’s a different story. Green vines cover the exterior, and bright purple lavender trails along the edge of the beer garden, which is filled with wooden tables and cheery, candy-striped parasols. There’s a bunch of different sized rooms to choose from depending on your crew and your (or their) preferences. All come with a deep standalone bath and a selection of deliciously smelling 100 Acres bath salts. In ours, the Marshall radio is playing classical music when we arrive. Next to it sits a jar of fresh cookies that we consume immediately. Lunch and dinner are served in one of three rooms and each has its own character. Steak cuts are scribbled on the chalkboards early doors and crossed out throughout dinner service as hotel guests and outsiders fill claim their own. We enjoyed a T-bone fireside with a bone marrow gravy mash and chunky chips. After, we don the hotel’s walking boots and amble the nearby fields, asking staff for advice on the best local walking routes. Sophie Knight Address: Bourton Rd, Clanfield, Bampton OX18 2RB Prices: From around £150 per night. - Read Full ReviewThe Rectory sits in Crudwell, one of the most charming small villages in the Cotswolds. The Grade-I listed All Saints' Church is visible from the hotel’s gardens and well worth a visit, whether for religious reflection or a nose at 12th-century features. Alex Payne purchased this Georgian manor house in 2016, and the country folk and burnt-out Londoners soon cottoned on. 18 bedrooms split between the main property and a separate cottage offer all the trappings of a cosy Cotswolds hideout – the latter is favoured by families and groups, with direct access to the manicured gardens. Bocca di Lupo alumni Jake Simpson is in charge of the kitchens, which serve up brunch classics and continental spreads by morning and European-inspired a la carte dishes come evening. Guests who aren’t too exhausted after long days navigating the surrounding walking routes stick around a while in the bar and lounge spaces, sipping espresso margaritas beside a crackling fire and chatting – or playing Scrabble – until it’s time to sink into their goose-down bedding. This is the spot for a charming escape in one of England’s most naturally stunning settings – with a fantastic in-house restaurant and a destination pub on your doorstep. Connor Sturges Address: Crudwell, Malmesbury SN16 9EP Price: From about £170 per night. - Read Full ReviewEngland isn’t short of vast, sumptuous country estates and perfectly fetching manor houses. But Lucknam Park, Emblems Collection peeps over the rest from lofty heights. This Grade II-listed pile – creamy stone dressed with creepers tangling down its tower like Rapunzel’s hair, best glimpsed from the melodramatic beech-lined driveway – has been around since the late 17th century, and operated as a hotel under its current ownership since the end of the 1990s. Staying here is a deeply reassuring reminder that, sometimes, the classics endure for a reason. Plump four-poster beds are covered in rich floral fabrics or set against wallpaper patterned like humbugs. Original sash windows welcome in West Country sunshine that glints off chandeliers; in the cosy bar, martinis are whipped up cheerfully by informal but expert staff; and the bikes and golf carts lined up at the entrance can whizz you around the estate at the drop of a hat. These are just some of the smart touches that elevate Lucknam Park, Emblems Collection from reliably traditional to top-of-its-game. Many come here – and repeatedly – for the restaurant (executive chef Hywel Jones’s team have worked to keep the kitchen’s Michelin star for 20 years and counting). But then there’s the 111Skin facials, the gloriously steamy indoor-outdoor pools, the horse riding, clay pigeon shooting and archery. Whatever their poison, guests all appear at breakfast with the unfakeable air of those who are truly rested. There’s no other weekender in the country that does it quite like this. Sarah James Address: Lucknam Park, Chippenham SN14 8AZ Prices: From about £312 per night. - Read Full ReviewThe Painswick opened to great fanfare in 2016 under the Calcot Collection banner – it’s big sister, Calcot Hotel & Spa, is about a half hour drive away in Tetbury – and soon after plaudits followed, making it one of the hottest stays in the south of England. A decade later, it has kept all the stuff that originally attracted rave reviews, and also moved with the times. Not too much though: that gorgeous, 18th-century Cotswold-stone building is still the star, sitting proudly atop a bucolic hill. A dander around the local area will pass an hour, and there are short walks to the nearby Painswick Beacon hilltop, and further along on The Cotswold Way. It is the ideal place to spend a weekend, and many, many people do: we can confirm The Painswick thrums on Saturdays, even in the depths of a dark, wet January. The hotel’s common areas are welcoming but unfussy – there's a sense that you could sit around on the sofas, saying hello to fellow guests and snacking on unctuous Scotch eggs, for an entire, unhurried day, despite the fact you’re likely only there for 48 hours. The George’s Suite is a stunner – bigger than my most recent London flat, it has a fireplace, deliciously gigantic bed, rolltop bath; all the good stuff. At sunrise, golden light pours in from the balcony which looks out onto loungers on the West Country-meets-Tuscany-style lawn. There are cookies to nibble on and a copy of Cotswolds classic Cider with Rosie to dip into while stretched out on the gigantic, comfortable sofa. The other rooms in the hotel, of which there are 16, are no less well-thought-through (even the smallest ‘Cosy’ options feature a kingsize). Radios in each provide ambient company and give the whole affair an unhurried feel. A three-bedroom cottage is also available for family stays, and pets are welcome for a small fee. Suzie McCracken Address: Kemps Lane, Painswick, Gloucestershire, GL6 6YB Price: From about £210 per night. - Read Full ReviewOriginally the village bakery, this 17th-century, red-brick pub reopened in spring 2026 after a complete renovation, as the latest addition to The Potted Goose Group. Now, four rooms and a handful of cabins are ready for booking, too – making this a great option for bedding down on a weekend away in the Cotswolds. There are just four rooms: three above the pub and one at the back, accessed via outside stairs. All are similar in style, featuring leather headboards, patterned wallpapers, velvet cushions on the bed, and blue-and-white ceramic lamps topped with Ikat-pleated shades. I stayed in room one, which has wallpaper on the vaulted ceiling (it really works) and a huge bathroom with a roll-top bath. It’s near the pub’s smaller dining room where I sat at one of the outside tables with a pot of tea and ate the homemade cookie that was waiting for me on arrival. There are also five air-conditioned cabins (including a shepherd’s hut) in a wildflower garden, each with individual outdoor seating areas and a shared firepit. Inside, the aesthetic is more neutral, from the rustic wood and white walls to the terracotta tiles in the bathrooms. For anyone interested in craft, Whichford Pottery, a two-minute walk away, is a must. The family-run company hand-throws terracotta pots for everyone from Daylesford to Kew Gardens, and an open workshop policy means you’re free to wander round and watch the makers at work. Once you're done crafting, head back to and order the bar's twist on a Paloma – it has honey at the bottom while the Eastern Standard No.2 – a take on Soho Farmhouse director Tom Kerr’s original – swaps gin for tequila and mezcal. Emma Love Address: Ascott Road, Whichford, Shipston-on-Stour, Warwickshire, CV36 5PE, England Prices: From about £195 per night. - Read Full ReviewWhen Estelle Manor stomped onto the scene in 2023, there hadn't been a Cotswolds hotel opening like it for a while. A Grade II-listed manor, it's lived many lives over the last three centuries: as a hunting lodge, a World War II maternity ward, a police training academy. In 2018, Sharan Pasricha (founder of Ennismore and the man behind hotels such as the slick Hoxton group and the recent makeover of Scottish grand dame Gleneagles) purchased the hall and set about a five-year renovation that got local tongues wagging. A tip-to-toe renovation draped layers of texture across the manor's excellent bones; 108 bedrooms and suites were dressed in sumptuous fabrics; a smattering of larger cottages and houses were added for those seeking privacy. There's also a gym, a heated-year-round outdoor swimming pool (especially magical during the festive season, when a Christmas tree sparkles at one end), and a 3,000-square-metre Roman-inspired bathhouse and spa. Estelle is part country-house hotel that anyone can book, part members club for clued-up, well-heeled country darlings. At any given time, the public spaces – wood-panelled drawing rooms, a richly textured bar with a roaring fireplace – are humming with activity from weekend-ing families or couples as well as members grabbing lunch or tapping away on laptops. There are a few member-only spaces, but most of the main house is accessible for hotel guests. The restaurants are a major draw: my sister and I grabbed small plates and Champagne in the Brasserie on arrival during our stay, although, it being a Sunday, the staff tried their hardest to suggest a roast. We restrained as we had supper booked that evening in the swish Billiards Room – and thank goodness, as the sheer amount of dim sum, bao and roast duck we consumed left us waddling back to our room. Rooms are supremely comfortable, so we fell into a sleep so deep that I felt fully rested for the first time in my 30s. This is the smart set's favourite Cotswolds hotel for a reason. Sarah James Address: Estelle Manor, Eynsham, North Leigh, Park OX29 6PN Price: From about £850 per night. - Read Full ReviewWith its tangle of honey-dipped farmhouses and tithe barns, gravel paths edged with blousy lavender and olive trees and couples playing pétanque on the immaculate lawns, Thyme – in the chocolate-box pretty, chichi Cotswolds village of Southrop – smacks of Provence. When owners Caryn and Jerry Hibbert moved to Southrop from London over two decades ago, their original plan had been to open a small cookery school with a clutch of rooms. But bit by bit, as the risk of local redevelopment loomed, they snapped up more and more buildings in the village. Today, Thyme is not just a hotel but a perfect little Cotswolds hamlet, with sustainability, a deep-seated love of the land and the idea of nature as one of life’s greatest healers right at its heart. Thyme’s 31 bedrooms are dotted around the estate, with none more than a five-minute walk away from the hotel’s main hub. Individually styled by Caryn, each one is joyously different from the next. In high summer, Thyme’s black slate spring-water swimming pool is a lovely spot to while away an afternoon. Tucked away in the gardens behind the main farmhouse, Thyme’s sage-shuttered, green-and-white-tiled Meadow Spa has been a firm fixture and major draw for some time. Lately the thing everyone’s talking about is the brand-new Botanical Bothy, an exclusive-use, deeply luxurious Hamman-like standalone space, a few footsteps away from the seven main treatment rooms. There’s also a tennis court and yoga studio, and the land around here cries out to be explored: pack your wellies and carve out time for an amble through the kitchen garden or the picturesque Cotswolds countryside. Teddy Wolstenholme Address: Thyme, Southrop, Lechlade GL7 3NX Prices: From about £390 per night. - Read Full ReviewIn the pretty little village of Charlbury, where honey-hued homes radiate a level of quaintness only the Cotswolds can achieve, sits The Bull. Phil Winser and James Gummer, the pair behind The Pelican in Notting Hill, oversaw the restoration here. The result is an impeccable interior ambience; fires are roaring, candles are burning, and plush leather chairs are ready to envelop you for a cosy afternoon. The team have kept things minimalistic and focused on bringing the history of British pubs to life with wooden-beamed ceilings, winding staircases, and perfectly preserved stone floors flowing into the bedrooms, where subtle textures and colours create a cossetting vibe. Room 6 was our home for the weekend. It's a show-stopper. A canopy bed frame with a sloped ceiling gives way to my favourite feature, the freestanding bathtub, which comes equipped with a log fire and a view of Charlbury High Street. If by some miracle you can pull yourself away from your room, I’d recommend heading downstairs for what is destined to be a delicious meal conjured up by head chef George Williams. Take the server’s advice, as everything is local, seasonal and a celebration of British produce. Top off your evening with a tipple by the fireplace for the perfect night cap to your day and weekend getaway. Amber Port Address: Sheep Street, Charlbury, Chipping Norton OX7 3RR Prices: From about £170 per night. - Read Full ReviewThis is the kind of place you check in to and simply don't want to leave. For a weekend reset and a true escape to the countryside, it's perfect, and it puts a signature Soho House spin on Cotswolds country life. The restaurant in the Main Barn is where those familiar with the other properties will feel most at home, but the accommodation here is unique its surroundings, and includes huts, cabins and even an 8-bed cottage for larger groups. The wellness offering is front and centre, and it's been amplified tenfold for 2026. Alongside the cold plunge, heated outdoor pool, Reformer Pilates classes and seriously snazzy TechnoGym, it's also home to two new fitness studios and specialist recovery treatments like Red Light Therapy and Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy. But if your idea of wellness is simply being away from the city, getting from A to by by push-bike and sinking into an armchair with a spicy margarita, there's plenty of opportunity for that, too. Sarah Leigh Bannerman Address: Great Tew, Chipping Norton OX7 4JS Prices: From about £350 per night. - Read Full ReviewThis is one of those ‘if you know, you know’ boltholes with a loyal following of sleep-deprived parents. Calcot Manor & Spa has all the countryside charm and honey-hued good looks of a Cotswolds farmhouse, along with a sprinkling of clever details that makes it magic for families with little ones. Sitting on the bucolic fringes of antiques-heavy Tetbury, the country house hotel includes a wisteria covered farmhouse surrounded by a cluster of tastefully renovated barns and cottages. Further afield is 220 acres of idyllic rewilded countryside, home to orchid meadows, sweet little bunny rabbits and roe deer. Rooms are spread across the manor house, the surrounding cottages and the barn, with all manner of higgeldy piggeldy set ups and design – from snug cosy rooms to sprawling split-level family suites. All overflow with character-filled Cotswold loveliness – original beams, twee floral wallpaper, plush headboards and freestanding tubs. New for 2026 are The Hides – two treehouses with cosy living rooms, private decks and additional loft bedrooms ideal for children. While tinies explore the big, shiny multi-story Playbarn an Ofsted-approved crèche, weary parents make their way to the outdoor fireside hot tub at the spa. All gather together at supper, where children can enjoy a dedicated 5pm teatime before heading off to bed – the hotel's baby-monitors reach the lavender-lined and light-filled Brasserie. The chance to tuck in to elegantly plated, fresh-from-the-farm fare while off-the-clock is worth the trip in itself. Lauren Burvill Address: Calcot Manor, Gloucestershire, Tetbury GL8 8YJ Prices: From about £350 per night. How we choose the best hotels in the Cotswolds Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels. This is our edit of the best hotels in the Cotswolds.

item.title: We threw our own phones into the sea to find the best waterproof phone pouches in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.61
There are so many adventures where a waterproof phone pouch is a must: paddleboarding over a Scottish loch, dipping into a hot spring in Iceland, kayaking on one of the many lakes in Montenegro, or just lolling by the beach or pool at a resort. Above and beyond the protection your average phone case offers, a waterproof phone pouch creates a full-on barrier around your device, which (depending on the pouch) can be enough for you to even take underwater photos, let alone withstand the odd splash. Plus, a waterproof phone case will often come with additional design features to make your life easier, like a lanyard or strap so you can go hand-free (and pockets empty). Some can even float. With something like this, which needs to keep expensive equipment safe, it’s important to know that you’re getting a product that really stands up to the task. To save you from having to find out the hard way, Traveller editors have tried out a slew of waterproof phone bags and pouches to find out which will really keep your phone dry. As usual, we have been thorough with our testing. On our first run, we trialled pouches with a tissue inside, to ensure there was no immediate water damage, followed by an old (and small) Apple phone. Finally, we braved it with our current, expensive phones inside to see if they survived. We didn’t tiptoe around this testing – with each round, all of the pouches were tossed into a pool or ocean. Luckily, all phones and tissues came out unscathed, which bodes well for waterproof phone pouches in general, but some pouches outshone others in various ways. These are the ones that have made our list. Below you’ll find the best waterproof phone pouches to bring on your next beach trip, cruise, or rainy-day hike. The best waterproof phone pouches at-a-glance The best waterproof phone pouches, tried-and-tested by our editors Other good options: How we test the best waterproof phone pouches To find the cases truly worthy of protecting expensive tech, our editors put a batch of top-rated universal waterproof pouches through a rigorous multi-stage test. We began in the bathroom sink, submerging each pouch filled with dry tissue paper to check for immediate leaks, before advancing to an old iPhone 6. Once proven watertight, we braved the ultimate test: locking in our current, everyday mobile phones – one Pixel and one iPhone – and plunging them directly into the open sea – evaluating seal strength, touch sensitivity, floating capabilities, and photo clarity along the way. Can you swim with a waterproof phone pouch? If your chosen waterproof bag is high quality (read: one from our list above) yes, you can usually swim with it, but it’s important to check that it has been designed for swimming conditions first. The IP rating will indicate how waterproof or water-resistant the pouch is (IP68 or higher means it has been designed to be safely submerged in water). You should also check the recommendation for how deep it can go, ensuring it’s at least one to two metres. Can you take photos through the best waterproof phone cases? Touchscreen can be used through some waterproof pouches, but not all. And the sensitivity is likely to be impacted if the pouch is in water or wet. The plastic of the pouch can cause some image distortion or glare, but some of the best waterproof phone pouches have dedicated camera lens windows to help avoid this. Can you still use your phone in a waterproof pouch? You can still use your phone in most waterproof pouches to some extent, but the touchscreen may be less responsive, face/touch ID might not work, side buttons are likely to be harder to press and audio will be muffled. How deep can a waterproof phone pouch go? The depth a phone can be safely submerged in a waterproof pouch varies depending on the material and design, so it’s best to check with each product. Some waterproof phone pouches can only go as deep as one metre, while others can reach 10 metres. But remember, the deeper you go, the greater the water pressure and the greater the risk of leakage.

item.title: My favourite Greek island villa: a clifftop fortress with an infinity pool and unbeatable sunset views
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.35
Where in the world graces the top of passionate sunset seekers’ bucket lists more than Santorini? There are few places on the planet where time stops as our star makes its descent into the distant azure, voices hush as brows furrow and cameras silently capture the moment. The jiving and jostling atop the homes, hotels and restaurants of Fira, Santorini’s capital, ahead of this performance have become as iconic as the show itself. It's a ritual I've longed to be involved in for years, and booking a villa escape to the island felt like the right way to do it. As it turned out, the villa itself was perhaps more spectacular than the skies. Beyond Santorini’s northernmost town, past the telegenic tumble of pristine white properties crowned in royal blue that climb up Oia’s cliffside, a Bond-esque lair awaited me and a group of friends. This is where we'd call home for the next few nights and it's fair to say we were wowed. On entering the property, faced with the well-equipped kitchen and a table adorned with sparkling wine and savoury and sweet welcome treats, we felt at home but after a full inspection, we realised only jetsetters who primarily reside in a clifftop fortress could use the term so freely. But we do feel at home. After our first afternoon arriving in intervals, we’re soon curled up in our preferred shaded or sun-drenched corners like the heat-exhausted felines that roam the harbours beyond, clutching glasses of fizz or orange sodas. From this moment on, just as much of our stay is spent sprawled across the villa’s outdoor spaces as its sleek interiors, if not more. Each of the villa's four king-size bedrooms has direct access to the shared terrace spaces and the interior living areas. Days begin with bouncy exits onto the terrace, iced coffees in hand (coffee pods are among the complimentary cupboard fillers). Mornings fly by into breezy afternoons, SPF liberally reapplied as fruit juices are swapped for local beers sourced from nearby stores as someone’s nominated to put on a spread. As for the spreads, it’s recommended to hire a car for a full fridge-stocking excursion. With breakfast in the nearby hotel included and all but one dinner and a few lunches planned in Oia and Fira, we made do (as a gaggle of exhausted type B travellers) by stocking up from stores nearby – Oia Mini Market is the closest, with slightly larger ones along the main road. The lush villa’s exterior space of 316 square metres includes two Jacuzzis where late-night bubbles are enjoyed once the sweltering afternoon becomes a distant memory, while the fire pit can crackle under the night sky with a little help from the concierge team. The infinity swimming pool becomes the central hub of the sun-soaked action for much of the morning and afternoon, with swimwear drying off before the collective upteenth plunge is taken and a new disc jockey sets the waterside mood for an hour via Bluetooth speakers (portable ones not provided). There’s no fear of disturbing neighbours, and the mood can be set by Spotify playlists or the distant crash of waves. Once the salty residue from the island breeze is scrubbed off in en-suite showers, plates are laid and the outdoor kitchen comes to life as we sizzle meats on the outdoor gas hob. Salads are tossed and side dishes cook in the ovens indoors as we steal moments in the golden hour light, camera timers set to capture moments in front of one of the world’s most iconic sunsets. We clink mismatched shot glasses filled to the brim with ouzo with cries of “Yamas!” into the constellations glittering above us, and commit ourselves to an investigation of Oia’s nightlife. We settle nicely into Hassapiko, sipping cocktails into the small hours while befriending the yacht crews, locals and nocturnal tourists that surround us in the moonlit courtyard. It feels sacrilegious not to take to the water beyond our infinity pool, so we secure coveted spots on one of Sunset Oia’s shared catamaran cruises one afternoon. We’re escorted to and from the boat in plush cars, but the departure from Ammoudi Port – famed for its waterside seafood restaurants – means a journey of mere minutes. Hours drift by plunging into hot springs beside the volcano, snorkelling above glistening sealife just off Red Beach and feasting on Greek specialities before we anchor, securing a new sunset vista before repeating the nights before. In addition to the complimentary return transfers, daily breakfast at Santo Pure for all guests and direct villa check-in, the attentive team are able to tailor and itinerise trips as much, or as little, as you desire. Whether it’s a knock at the door from a sommelier for private wine tastings (the island’s volcanic soil produces some impeccable tipples), yoga sessions on the terrace or in-villa spa treatments, there’d be little reason to leave the property if the island’s secrets weren’t so enticing. Our knock at the door comes not from a sommelier, but from the team as they ready us for our transfer, insisting no one lift a finger as our luggage is loaded into the back of a plush transfer car. As we wind through Santorini’s roads past vineyards and storied properties, we yearn for one more dose of the sunset view from that terrace, after an island initiation none of us will forget in a hurry.
