item.title: Where the Chefs Eat: Tamar Adler's favourite restaurants in Madrid
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.06
Where the Chefs Eat asks your favourite chefs for their top restaurants in cities across the world. For this edition, we sit down for coffee with Tamar Adler. Tamar Adler is a woman of many great achievements. She is a James Beard Award-winning author, a mother, and a Vogue contributing editor. Yet, as she opens her latest publication Feast on Your Life, it is evident her battle with depression has been utterly crippling. She describes how the autumn of 2023 left her on the floor, both mentally and physically; “I’d recently taken inventory of my life,” she says. “What I’d turned up felt meagre. Somehow, my mistakes and missed chances dwarfed my accomplishments, haunting and hunting me.” This wasn’t the first time Adler had faced the demon that is depression – she has suffered it her whole life – but, from it, her latest book was born, and the result is a stunning diary of food, day-to-day life and the beauty found in the smallest of things. Feast on Your Life began as a gratitude list of sorts, suggested by her husband as part of his efforts to help her. The list was “predictable,” as she says. “Husband, son; warm bed – that sort of stuff.” And, yet, what grew was a gratitude for everything around her – the smell of coffee, “clouds of challah bread” and the “abrasive tang” of pineapples. The repetition of certain things in the kitchen, the stunning description of food – all become entries in a diary for Adler that helped her to rebuild. They bind together into a stunning book that celebrates life, and food, of course, in the most beautiful of ways. When I speak with Adler from her new home in Madrid, I ask her what it is about food that she feels really pulled her out of the grip of such a dark place. “I think it's a few things,” she muses. “I think obviously the immediacy of it is really important: it's right there, and it's unavoidable. So many of your senses are engaged in cooking and eating. You have to be completely present in it. And I think that amount of presence really does kind of remap your brain, even in tiny ways in the moment, because it sort of changes your attention, moving you from the terrible abstract to the sensory present.” And, for those who have suffered depression, even getting out of bed in the morning can feel like climbing a mountain, so the physical closeness of one’s kitchen itself also helps. “When you finish really being present,” she continues, “you actually do think a little bit differently. And, so, I think it does a really amazing job of diverting you towards a way of experiencing the world that is positive and non-abstract, and that is really grounded in the present moment. And it does it through your senses. I think because food demands so much of our senses, it's almost the perfect tool.” Adler’s book is a beautiful tribute to the smallest of acts – stirring a spoon in a cup of coffee, peeling a juicy, fresh grapefruit – and serves as a reminder that joy can be found in all things great and small. But it isn’t just for those suffering. It is a vessel for anyone seeking respite from their day, and it can be read from front to back or enjoyed in small sections. She explains that it is not only “for people in the midst of a major depression, but for those who want a kind of primer that they could turn to every day for a little bit of a reminder that there is something good and that it's right in the kitchen; that it's super close. It's not like you even have to leave your house for it. You can find it right where you are.” Today, her kitchen is in the Las Letras neighbourhood of Madrid. With her husband and nine-year-old son, Adler moved to the Spanish capital city in August 2025. “We really wanted to spend some time abroad, and my husband and I speak Spanish, so we knew we wanted it to be a Spanish-speaking country,” she tells me. “The city is so beautiful and vibrant, so it was a pretty easy decision.” She continues, “I have felt, since moving here, that my daily experience is sort of like a bath in beauty. And that's really incredible. I can't think of another place that I've been to that has so many fountains. There are fountains all over Madrid, and that is just an incredible thing, to always be in the presence of moving water; to always be hearing and seeing moving water is pretty fantastic.” Adler’s ability to appreciate beauty in all its forms, coupled with her profound knowledge of food, makes her a very reliable source for local Madrileño restaurants, and she shares with us her current five favourites. Dolores Dolores is right on the corner near my house, and we go there for one specific thing: the matrimonio (a tapas dish combining anchovies and a boqueron, which is a white pickled anchovy). The right time to do that is just before dinner. So, we tend to go at about 7pm. It’s always packed. We always get this dish wherever we go, but the best that we’ve ever had is at Dolores. What makes theirs so amazing is they make their own boquerones, so they buy their own anchovies, and then they cure them in vinegar in-house, and then when they give them to you it’s like a big beautiful fillet of the anchovy and a house-made white anchovy. They do it with parsley and, I think, garlic and you eat it on potato chips. I don’t think anyone has come to see us in town and not been taken there for that and not totally loved it. Address: Pl. de Jesús, 4, Centro, 28012 Madrid, Spain Farah A Palestinian woman called Heba Kharouf runs Farah, and she is always there. I love to get the lubina (sea bass), which comes with a tahini sauce, and another sauce – they won’t tell you what’s in that one, though it tastes a bit like mustard. It’s served as a whole fish. It’s just amazing. They also have a salad that is truly great. It’s like a chopped Middle Eastern salad with date syrup and pink peppercorns. Address: C. de los Mancebos, 2, Centro, 28005 Madrid, Spain Website: restaurantefarah.com Restaurant Sasha Enter my favourite restaurant in Madrid. The restaurant reservations open up either six or seven days in advance, but you have to book to go because it’s so popular. It’s small and it’s entirely generous. It is the most seasonal, menu-changing restaurant I have encountered in Madrid. It really is different every time. They only put a price on the menu next to the things that they have at that time. It changes dramatically based on what the kitchen sees and loves and gets in. I love the tortilla there. I think it’s called a ‘lazy’ tortilla, a tortilla vaga. Sometimes it will be made with potato chips, morcilla and pickled peppers or it might be served with a fillet of fish. The last time I got it, it was made with shrimp, finally sliced zucchini and some spring vegetables; it’s super simple but just perfectly done. The fried artichokes are also amazing. Address: Zona ajardinada, C. de Juan Hurtado de Mendoza, 11, Posterior, Chamartín, 28036 Madrid, Spain Website: restaurantesacha.com Ton Ton Ton Ton is super delicious and super chic. It’s dark and romantic and small, but it’s just very special. I love the artichoke and the beef tartare. You share lots of very small things, and it’s the perfect date restaurant or intimate diner spot. Address: Calle de Jordán, 7, Chamberí, 28010 Madrid, Spain Website: tonton.rest O’Pazo The same people who ran the renowned restaurant Desde 1911 are behind O'Pazo. It’s unreal. They cook absolutely perfect seafood; perfect in every way. I ordered everything when I visited. We had percebes (barnacles) – the kids tried that, which was really fun. We also had the pink shrimp from Palamos, which I love, along with oysters and tiny little clams. Oh, and I loved that for the main course they served a bowl of potato chips and a bowl of sprouts as the vegetable sides. You can look at all the fish behind you and just pick out what you want. Address: C. de la Reina Mercedes, 20, Tetuán, 28020 Madrid, Spain Website: opazo.es/movil Feast on Your Life by Tamar Adler (Swift Books); £18.99

item.title: “I hope they feel good, hope they feel happy, I hope they feel safe”: remembering Dolly Parton, hotelier, traveller and Dreamer-in-Chief
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.06
Dolly Rebecca Parton was born on 19 January 1946 in Tennessee to parents Avie Lee Caroline and Robert Lee Parton Sr. Dolly credited her mother with her musical abilities, which saw her sell more than 100 million records worldwide across a roster of 49 studio albums through seven decades, as Avie would keep Dolly and her many siblings entertained with stories and ballads. Dolly’s earliest public performances were in the church, and her Christian faith played a major role in her life, undoubtedly trickling into her countless philanthropic efforts over the decades. By the age of eight, she owned her own guitar, and it seems her record-breaking career was written in the stars very early on. At the time of her death this week, Dolly Parton had composed more than 3,000 songs, had 25 chart-toppers on the Billboard Country Music Charts and 44 country albums in the top 10 – a record for any country artist. Dolly put the business acumen she credited her father for into the creation of Dollywood Parks & Resorts, which Regan Stephens discussed with the icon in the interview below in 2023. A statement on the Dollywood Parks & Resorts website reads: “With heavy hearts, the Dollywood family mourns the death of our beloved Dreamer-in-Chief, Dolly Parton. Everyone at Dollywood shares the sorrow of countless people around the world touched by Dolly's warmth, wisdom and generous spirit. Dolly's heartfelt wish was that Dollywood always remain a place of joy, hope and togetherness – a space where families and friends could honour her memory, not with silence, but with laughter, music and shared dreams. “The greatest privilege of my life has been helping Dolly bring her dreams to life at Dollywood,” said Eugene Naughton, Dollywood Parks & Resorts President. “Dolly's heart was as vast as the mountains she cherished, and her compassion knew no bounds. She inspired generations to dream boldly and love deeply. While we grieve her loss, we are honoured and committed to carry her light forward. Her legacy will continue to shine in every melody sung, every smile shared and every dream kindled within these gates.” In a video announcement posted on 25 August 2026, Dolly Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver announced her death, which was later understood to have followed a brief battle with cancer. In the video, he said: “By her example, we believed that anything was possible. She never saw a door she couldn't open, and the doors she opened made and changed history. My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you. She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD, and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family, whether you liked it or not… May God bless Dolly Parton, and may God bless you all. She will always love you.” Below is an interview originally published in November 2023, where Dolly Parton spoke with Regan Stephens about her vision for Dollywood's HeartSong Lodge & Resort, her deep connection to the Smoky Mountains, and the simple pleasures of life on the road. Dolly Parton opened HeartSong Lodge & Resort in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, a glittering rhinestone in the Dollywood Parks & Resorts empire. Set in the rolling foothills of the Great Smoky Mountains, HeartSong Lodge is an homage to the region where Parton spent her childhood – a place that continued to inspire her throughout her 50-plus-year career. The hotel is the second Dollywood resort, joining nearby DreamMore Resort & Spa, which opened in 2015. “Some people are calling me a hotelier now,” she told a crowd gathered to watch the dedication of the hotel that day. HeartSong’s design weaves in its natural surroundings in both striking and subtle ways. In the heart of the 302-room lodge, a four-story stone fireplace (made with local stones, some still covered in moss) anchors an airy atrium, which faces sweeping floor-to-ceiling windows. Fauna and flora of the region pop up throughout the common areas, too: colourful monarch butterfly-shaped trusses are built into the ceiling beams, and inside the elevators, backlit photos show scenes of the Smokies throughout the seasons. Guest rooms also draw inspiration from the Great Smoky Mountains, from the fireflies that trim the lighted bathroom mirrors and murals of bears, owls, and other woodland creatures in nature splashed on the bedroom walls to the sound machines that play a custom mix of soothing sounds – like a campfire crackling or birds singing. Many rooms have balconies that look out over the outdoor pool complex and the surrounding wooded hills. But while HeartSong is a celebration of the Smokies, guests can find plenty of nods to Parton herself, including her larger-than-life portrait hanging in the entryway, and an array of her guitars, her handwritten songs, and other personal treasures on display inside Acoustic Lobby, a private dining room on the resort’s first floor. Like DreamMore, the lodge is designed to facilitate families spending time together, with activities like Parton’s Imagination Library story time and the outdoor campfire where, each evening, guests can gather around to toast marshmallows for “roasties” (think s’mores, but with a more creative and rotating array of ingredients.) Ahead, read Parton's 2023 interview with Condé Nast Traveller about HeartSong, her go-to room service order, and more. Can you tell us about the concept behind HeartSong, and what was most important to you when it came to the hotel’s design? Well, we're proud of everything we do at Dollywood. And every year, we have huge dreams. And, of course, we were so proud when we opened our DreamMore Resort eight years ago. And people just love that and it stays booked all the time. We thought, well, we need another hotel. So what will it be? It needs to be a lodge right here in the Smoky Mountains, as deep in the hills as we can get it. And it needs to have some balconies where people can step out on the balconies and feel like they're part of nature. In the mornings, they can hear the birds and the squirrels and just go out and have their coffee or a little snack. But we felt like it would be good since I grew up in a cabin in the mountains, and kind of just more deep woods than what the DreamMore resort is. And so we just thought that would be a perfect thing, it fit my personality, it fit my childhood. And so sure enough, we are open now and we're so proud of it. What role does your own life or personal connection to the Great Smoky Mountains play in the hotel? You can see the mountains from the hotel, of course. I grew up at the foothills of the Smokies. But we wanted people to feel like they were part of the Smokies, because we know that the national park is the most beautiful and the most popular in the United States. So I've always been really proud of the fact that I was born and raised up here. And so of course I always try, when we do anything at Dollywood, to keep things close to home, things that I understand, things that are part of my childhood, part of my life. These things come natural to us when we start dreaming: What would be good next for us to do? So we're going to build more hotels. I'm not sure what all the themes will be, but this one will always be really special. Because it's more of a country life, although it's bigger. It has a huge convention center, people are going to be able to come to have conventions and even family reunions. You’ve been everywhere – how have your own travels inspired the hotel? Was there any amenity or design element you had to include? I've been all over the country, I've been all over the world, but there are those great places – like when you go to a lot of the ski resorts, places up in the mountains where they have a lot of lodges. When I would go to those places, I always felt so at home, because it reminded me of my own home in the Great Smoky Mountains, whether it be in Aspen, or any of those great places. I’ve seen similar places to our HeartSong lodge, with big hearths, where you really feel like you're really in a big country home. I'm influenced by everything, I'm like a sponge. I just soak up everything, every memory made. I can usually apply that to something else, when the occasion arises. What are your favourite hotel amenities? I think it's really important that you have a really good, comfortable bed, because I sleep so well, when I come up here, even to the DreamMore resort. And it’s real important to have a great bathroom where you have your shampoos and conditioners, and all those comforts of home. I think feeling that you have the comforts of home in a great hotel – we work real hard for that. We cater to our families as well, our bunk beds, and things for the children. Families love that. And the kids certainly do. And we incorporated that into the HeartSong lodge as well, because it was such a big hit at our DreamMore resort. So I just think, having a place that feels like home. And also, the lighting on the bathroom mirrors is so good here. Yeah, well, it is important to have good lighting and good mirrors. That's a big deal, especially to women. Do you have a go-to room service order? I am so simple. Although they have the best foods ever at all of our restaurants – we are so proud of our chefs – but I'm still one of those burger and fries kind of people. You know, when all else fails, get a cheeseburger, some French fries and a cola, and you can't go wrong. What's one memorable experience you hope guests will have during their stay at your hotel? What do you want guests to take away from a stay? I hope they feel good, hope they feel happy, I hope they feel safe. And I'm pretty sure they're going to feel petted and spoiled just a little bit- stuff they might not get when they're home. Especially a mama who's always having to do everything at home, this way, she can get to be pampered just a little bit too. So I think that it's important that they go away thinking, that was such a great vacation, and I felt special. And I know it's so important for you to have families spend time together, and there seem to be plenty of ways you can do that here at the resort. I'm big on family, you know, I grew up in a big one. And we've always tried at Dollywood to make it a family destination, from the rooms [at the resorts] to the foods, to the outside activities like the marshmallows and the campfire sings. All the things that you can have fun with your friends and family, where it really feels like you're in a safe environment, but you really feel like it could be way out somewhere in the wilderness. There's so much to see and do at the lodge here. You can just stay at the hotel and have a great time. I would love to hear about the new Dolly Parton Experience coming in 2024 – which aspect of the museum are you excited for your fans to see? I am so excited about the new museum. I had my own little museum here for many, many years, and we outgrew the space. So we had to expand. Dollywood has been growing at such a fast rate of speed over the last several years, and the museum was no different. In this new day and age, there are so many wonderful things you can do from the technical end, making things bigger and more colourful, more radiant, and really just having more of an experience for people, more of an adventure, so to speak. So we're really proud of that. They're gonna get to see and know everything that I've done since I started, even before I started: my childhood, my people, my faith, my dreams, and seeing them all come true. So they're gonna get to walk through my whole life.

item.title: Trees are vital for cooler cities, but they need help too
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.95
Walking beneath the trees this historically hot summer, sometimes felt like autumn had already arrived: dry, dead leaves crunching underfoot, and crowns tinged yellow or completely bare. That's a problem because large leafy trees help make our cities more livable. They block sunlight, reduce pollution, store carbon, provide habitats for biodiversity to thrive, soak up otherwise harmful stormwater runoff and even boost the mental and physical health of residents. "When trees go away, those things go away as well," Nina Bassuk, who runs the Urban Horticulture Institute at the US-based Cornell University, told DW. That's why cities and scientists are racing to figure out how to save trees and choose smarter ones for the future. Why cities need trees As humans have burned fossil fuels to power industry and heat homes, the planet has become hotter, making the role of urban trees ever more vital. Why? Because they essentially act like giant air conditioners, which makes a big difference in hot cities. Inside a tree's canopy, temperatures can be up to three degrees cooler than the surrounding area. This is down to evapotranspiration, the process of trees absorbing water and releasing water vapor through their leaves. In addition, trees cast shade, which keeps their surroundings from heating up in the first place. "When we stand under a tree, the temperature we perceive can be 10 to 12 degrees Celsius (18 to 22 degrees Fahrenheit) lower than right next to it," said Matthias Beyer, a hydrologist at the Institute of Geoecology at TU Braunschweig. And it's not just cooling. There have been numerous studies correlating all sorts of other positive effects of robust trees. One showed that cities with more tree canopy had lower rates of cardiovascular disease. Another concluded that greener school surroundings were associated with better grades in high schools. And further research suggested that more greenspace exposure during pregnancy can lead to healthier outcomes for newborns. How much water do trees need to survive drought? Though a warmer climate makes trees more necessary, it also makes it harder for them to thrive. Healthy trees need a minimum of 10 to 15 liters of water a day, but mature ones with full foliage require up to four times that. While there may be a temptation for cities to focus on planting new, less water-hungry trees, experts agree that the priority should be protecting older, struggling ones. Research shows it would take around 400 saplings to replace the benefits of an old tree with a crown circumference of 20 meters. Once trees reach maturation, their benefits can be exponential, but this takes time and lots of maintenance. "A lot of trees can't deliver the full function until 40, 50 years from the day they were planted," said Henrik Sjoman, a researcher at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences. The best way to water trees It's better to give trees a large amount of water over a short period so it can soak down deep, rather than letting it stay in the upper soil layers, where much of it evaporates. For newly planted trees, a ring of metal or sturdy plastic is often fixed into the ground around the trunk. Where that's not available, a shallow depression around the tree can be created, allowing the water to pool. What matters is not damaging any surface roots in the process. When the soil is extremely hardened, so-called irrigation bags or cushions can help. Water drips slowly but steadily into the soil through small holes on their underside. The water mustn't sit on the surface for long periods, since that can cause rot, which damages the tree. But sometimes the soil has been heavily compacted to support sidewalks above, meaning water can't get through at all. Thirty years ago, Bassuk helped pioneer a method that mixes specially sized gravel in with the soil. It lets the stones bear the load of the sidewalk, while leaving more space for roots to stretch across dense urban ground. "As long as you get the soil and the stone proportions right, you can compact it and yet trees can access that and grow for long distances," Bassuk said. How to choose the right trees for cities When it comes to climate adaptation, there's also the question of which trees to plant in the first place. Historically, Sjoman says urban tree selection was often driven by aesthetics and design, which led to the over-planting of single species that were vulnerable to threats like pests or disease. Horror stories of Dutch elm disease wiping out entire populations in the 20th century helped to transform urban forestry planning, placing the focus far more on diversity and climate adaptation. The 10-20-30 rule of thumb was coined in 1990 by the late Frank Santamour, who worked as a research geneticist at the US National Arboretum. It states that urban forest populations should include no more than 10% of any one species, 20% of a single genus or 30% of any family. In Germany, there are several tools and databases that offer planting guidance, and several cities are taking part in an official street tree test. The idea is that 45 species are tested at more than 220 locations to gather knowledge of how they thrive. Another resource is the CITREE database, which categorizes almost 400 species of woody plants, sortable by more than 50 different features, including leaf density, fruit color, allergy potential, limb breakage and more. The key feature cities need to select is drought tolerance — considering the immense biological strain urban trees are facing in an ever-warming world. But knowing the benefits trees offer a city means that is not the only factor. "The demands of trees today — it's so much bigger, so much deeper than it was just a couple of decades ago," Sjoman said. This article was adapted from German, with additional reporting. Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: Why Germany's Volkswagen could cut 100,000 jobs
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.10
1. Why is Volkswagen holding crunch talks with workers? Volkswagen's management is holding extraordinary meetings with workers this week amid an unprecedented cost-cutting drive, including reports of up to 100,000 job losses and the possible closure of several German car factories. Germany's auto industry faces a deep structural crisis due to intense pressure from Chinese rivals, the transition to electric vehicles (EVs), higher production costs and other challenges. As Europe's biggest carmaker by volume, VW has the heaviest exposure to overcapacity in its German plants, high fixed costs and its reliance on China. Workers have been particularly concerned by how the restructuring was communicated so far, which representatives have described as "disastrous." Nine separate meetings will be held, starting on Tuesday at VW's headquarters in Wolfsburg, with talks at other sites including Emden, Zwickau, Braunschweig and Hanover before the end of the week. Workers had already agreed to around 50,000 job cuts, mainly through voluntary redundancy schemes. But management now thinks a further 50,000 jobs will have to be lost. 2. Why does Volkswagen need to make such drastic cuts? CEO Oliver Blume has stressed that VW is in a "more than critical state" and that the measures adopted so far are not enough to restore competitiveness. "We are oversized. That often makes us too slow and too complicated," he told staff in an interview on the company's intranet last week. With nearly 630,000 workers, VW has grown more bloated than its peers over decades after choosing to control more stages of production — including components and software — while mopping up rivals such as Skoda, Porsche, SEAT and Bugatti. The automaker was also slow to transition to EVs just as Chinese competitors gained ground, causing a large sales drop in its former number one market — China. Blume warned that VW is currently over-producing around half a million vehicles in Europe every year. While closing German factories would be a last resort, Blume said management "cannot currently see any way of them remaining profitable in the 2030s." Other automakers have criticized Germany's high operating costs, including Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Källenius, who last month spoke of a 70% cost gap between the firm's Hungarian and German operations. 3. What reaction is expected from workers? Blume is expected to face an angry reaction from VW employees, who rank as some of the best-paid auto workers in the world thanks to the power and influence of unions and the works council. After already accepting VW's earlier restructuring plans, Christiane Benner, the head of the IG Metall union, said workers "are getting another slap in the face." During the meeting with workers in Wolfsburg on Tuesday, VW works council chair Daniela Cavallo said "trust" in Blume and the executive board "has been damaged," but "not yet beyond repair." Last month, VW's supervisory board — which includes shareholders and worker representatives — rejected the second round of cost-cutting proposals. The move is further complicated as VW is part-owned by the state of Lower Saxony, which holds 20% of the voting rights. The state has refused to sign off on the plans, according to German media reports. "Lower Saxony is automotive country ... and this must remain so," said Olaf Lies, the state's premier on Monday. "Now it is important to me that we find joint solutions." 4. How is Volkswagen planning on getting back on track? Blume told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper last weekend that he had drawn up "the largest transformation plan in the history of the Volkswagen Group." His Target Vision 2030 plan aims to cut VW's model lineup by half and lower overheads, particularly in Germany. The automaker will also reduce its global production target, which peaked at about 11 million vehicles in 2018, to 9 million a year in the future. Faced with rising competition from China, along with US tariffs, geopolitics and red tape, Blume warned that VW management has to "assume the risks will get worse, worldwide." Most global automakers are struggling to react to Chinese EVs flooding global markets, increasingly unpredictable markets and the mounting pressure of EU net-zero rules, which include fines for not hitting emissions targets. Blume told the newspaper that the next few years would be "decisive" in determining which carmakers remain viable. He said although VW achieved a solid 3.8% operating margin, the profits are not enough to invest in new technologies, products and maintain the company's sites. Edited by: Tim Rooks

item.title: India news: Modi, Putin to hold bilateral talks in SCO summit
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.99
What you need to know - India's Prime Minister Modi is visiting Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan - He is due to hold talks with Modi - India's Foreign Ministry says 300 Indians are missing in Nepal and 200 are stranded in Tibet - Most were pilgrims on Mansarovar Yatra - India sends 10 metric tons of disaster-relief supplies to Nepal - US panel on religious freedom urges government to place sanctions on RSS members This blog has now closed. Read below for the biggest headlines coming out of India on Thursday, August 27: Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed. Thank you for reading! We're closing shop now. Thank you so much for following along! Make sure you catch us again tomorrow for another daily wrap of all things India! WATCH: Why Ladakh's ghost villages could have a future again Abandoned homes, shrinking glaciers, water shortages and empty fields tell one story. But two educational initiatives tell another: Change is possible, the future can look different. India's Modi to hold bilateral talks with Putin Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is set to hold bilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the upcoming Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in the Kyrgyz Republic, India's Foreign Ministry confirmed. "A meeting is scheduled between both the leaders of India and Russia on the sidelines of the summit," Foreign Ministry official Sibi George said in a special briefing. "Both sides are expected to review the entire gamut of bilateral relationship during the meeting between the leaders on the sidelines of the SCO in Bishkek," he said. Modi is set to visit Uzbekistan from August 29-30 on a bilateral visit, after which he will visit the Kyrgyz Republic for the 26th SCO Summit from August 31 to September 1. Russia and India are both permanent members of the SCO, along with China, Pakistan, Kyrgyzstan and Iran. The confirmation of Modi and Putin's upcoming meeting comes just days after Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar met the Russian leader in Moscow for a meeting of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation. "I hope to see him soon," Putin had said then speaking of Modi, adding that he was expecting to meet the Indian prime minister at the SCO summit. India and Russia have had long-standing bilateral ties despite Russia's growing closeness with China and Western pressure on India to distance itself from Moscow economically amid the war in Ukraine. IN DEPTH: India: Assam tea industry faces climate-driven labor crisis The problems facing upper Assam's tea gardens are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore for workers like Bidesh Kamar and Sumitra Tanti. Recent floods disrupted work for weeks in the northeast Indian state, adding even more uncertainty to their already precarious livelihood. More than 50 tea gardens were damaged following a devastating storm that swept across parts of Assam. "Life has become unpredictable," Tanti told DW. "The weather can disrupt work, while wages remain low and work is not as dependable as it once was," she added. Kamar said the economics of tea have changed. Their experience points to a growing problem for Assam's tea industry. With the business becoming less profitable and working conditions more uncertain, the industry is struggling to retain the experienced workforce which forms the backbone of the state's tea production. Read thefull story here. Modi wants India to boost participation in Olympic sports India's performance at the Olympics can only improve if the nation increases its participation in events it previously didn't take part in, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said on Thursday. "In the Olympics, there are so many different sports... Indian teams don't even participate in half of them. Meaning, we don't even compete for a huge chunk of the medal tally," he said in a virtual address to hundreds of athletes, students and volunteers who had gathered at multiple Locations for the Khelo India Dialogue. "Other countries of the world win medals in those sports, and we don't even participate in them. To increase our medal tally, we will have to master these sports as well," he said. India participated in only 16 of the 32 sports at the 2024 Paris Olympic Games. The Khelo India Dialogue, which translates to "Play India Dialogue," came ahead of India's National Sports Day on 29th August. Nearly 300 Indians missing in Nepal, 200 stranded in China: India's foreign ministry At least 488 Indian nationals were "uncontactable" or "stranded" in Nepal and China as of Thursday afternoon, India's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in a briefing. "There are 288 Indian nationals who remain uncontactable. These include 73 Indian nationals working on Trishuli 1 power project. Our embassy in Kathmandu is in touch with the project head," Jaiswal told reporters, adding that the missing Indians come from several states, including Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Kerala. As of 1 p.m. local time, 21 Indian nationals from Tamil Nadu had been rescued in Nepal, Jaiswal said. "Our ambassador has spoken to the people in the group and has assured all possible help," he said. Hundreds of Indian nationals were also stranded on the Chinese side of the disaster. "A number of Indian nationals who had gone on the Kailash Mansorovar Yatra are stranded on the Chinese side. There are approximately 200 Indian nationals there who have sought our assistance for evacuation," the spokesperson said, adding that the Indian embassy in Beijing was coordinating with local authorities for their safe return to India. Jaiswal warned that the flash floods had put authorities in a "dynamic situation," with the numbers of those missing, stranded or rescued likely to change in the upcoming hours. US religious freedom panel urges sanctions against India's RSS chief ahead of NYC visit A bipartisan US panel on religious freedom urged the US government to impose targeted sanctions on Mohan Bhagwat — the chief of a controversial Hindu nationalist group in India which is closely associated with India's current ruling party. Bhagwat is currently on a visit to the US and is scheduled to speak at an event in New York City's Madison Square Garden on Saturday. "We urge the US government to consider targeted sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials complicit in religious freedom violations, including revoking the visa issued to Mohan Bhagwat," Asif Mahmood, chair of the US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), said in a statement. The USCIRF is a bipartisan body of the US government which monitors religious freedom around the world and accordingly makes policy recommendations. Those recommendations are not binding. India's Foreign Ministry has dismissed the panel's assertions and accused it of being biased against India. About the RSS Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS, is often referred to as the Sangh. The group describes itself as a "Hindu-centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus and disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance. The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization. In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities. Meanwhile, rights groups say that the RSS promotes majoritarian ideology fueling intolerance towards minorities, especially muslims, in India. Read more about the controversy surrounding Bhagwat's upcoming event in NYC. NDRF says no adverse impact from Nepal floods in UP, Bihar so far Indian states on Nepal's southern border have faced "no adverse impact so far," India's disaster response officials told Indian media on Thursday, a day after Uttar Pradesh and Bihar were put on high alert. "The situation is being monitored for potential future impacts. We have reserve teams available; if the need arises, the state government will be informed, and they can be deployed immediately," National Disaster Response Force's IG Narendra Singh Bundela told news agency ANI. The Central Water Commission was keeping an eye on water levels which may impact Indian territories in the future, India's Home Ministry had said on Wednesday. India sends more aid to Nepal while disaster personnel on standby India has dispatched a second tranche of relief supplies to flood-affected Nepal on Thursday, External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said. "A second flight has just taken off, carrying 37.5 tonnes of HADR (Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief) material, medicines and food packets for Nepal," he said in a post on X, accompanied by a video which showed the material being loaded onto a military aircraft. On Wednesday, India had sent 10 tonnes of aid material, including essential medicines. However, no disaster relief team has been sent to sites so far, India's National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) IG Narendra Singh Bundela said in a press conference on Thursday morning. "At present, no NDRF team has been sent to Nepal. Teams have been kept on standby. If a request is received from the Nepal government and the Government of India decides accordingly, an NDRF team will be sent," several media outlets reported him saying. Indian Embassies in Nepal and China said they had set up helplines for information on Indian nationals impacted by the floods. Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with his Nepali counterpart Balendra Shah on Wednesday to express condolences on the lives lost. "India is prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance. Our teams are closely coordinating on rescue and relief efforts," he had said in a post on X. Over 170 Indians missing in Nepal-Tibet floods More than 170 Indians were unaccounted for in the Nepal-Tibet flash floods, Nepal's tourism officials said on Thursday, as Indian authorities coordinated with their Nepalese counterparts on rescue and relief efforts. Nepal's police and tourism officials said that of the 800 tourists missing in the country, 177 were from India. Meanwhile, Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal on Thursday said that over 300 Indian tourists were missing. He was speaking to journalists from Indian news channel NDTV World at the Anviksha Summit in Kathmandu. "Foreign nationals, including Indians, take the route in the affected area to the Mansarovar Yatra. Close to 300 Indians have been reported missing and the government is trying to establish contact with them," Khanal said. Kailash Mansarovar is a high-altitude site in China's Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists. At least 165 people have died in the flash floods which occurred at the Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday. Over 1,300 were missing in both Nepal and Tibet. Nepal's police authorities have said they expect the death toll to rise. Several Indian states have reported that dozens of their residents were among those missing in Nepal, as per local media reports. Verified videos of the disaster showed massive masses of debris-laden water sweeping away dozens of people at various locations. The disaster has washed away homes and villages. Welcome to our coverage Hello! This is Mahima Kapoor from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the latest from across India. More than 130 Indians are among the hundreds missing in Nepal's flash floods in what is being described as the country's worst disaster in years. The flood was triggered on Wednesday when an Avalanche reportedly blocked the flow of a tributary of the Bhotekoshi river. The river water swept away locals, pilgrims, proterties and whole villages in minutes. India's central and state governments have sprung into action to account for their missing, coordinate information and send aid to the affected areas. Meanwhile in the national capital, a student-led protest over an alleged suicide at the country's premier technology institute has entered its fourth day. In other news, a US panel on religious freedom has urged the US government to consider targeted sanctions against the chief of a right-wing Hindu nationalist group closely associated with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The panel's recommendation came days before the said chief is scheduled to speak at a private event in New York City's Madison Square Garden, which NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he opposes. Stay tuned for all of this and more!

item.title: Remembering Dolly Parton: 8 facts about the icon
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.71
More than 100 million records sold, 25 No. 1 hits on the US country charts, 11 Grammys and three Emmys — country star Dolly Parton was one of the most successful singers in the world. On Tuesday, her nephew Bryan Seaver announced in a video shared on Parton's social media channgels that his aunt had passed away. "Dolly... opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent," Seaver said in the video. "She never saw a door she couldn't open, and the doors she opened made and changed history." Here are eight facts from eight decades of Dolly Parton. 1. Cornmeal for the doctor Dolly Parton came from humble beginnings, growing up with 11 siblings in Sevier County, Tennessee. Born on January 19, 1946, her parents paid the doctor who assisted at her birth with a sack of cornmeal — though some sources claim it was oats. Parton was born into a musical family and learned to play the guitar when she was 7. She gave her first performance on television at age of 10. 2. No 'Dumb Blonde' Multiple sources have reported Parton's IQ to be at least 140. Her first song, which entered the US country charts on January 21, 1967, was "Dumb Blonde." In it, she sings "this dumb blonde ain't nobody's fool." It was a bold start for her entry into 1960s show business, at the time dominated by men. "I'm not offended by all the dumb blonde jokes because I know I'm not dumb… and I also know that I'm not blonde," she said of the stereotype. 3. Impressive parade of wigs Across her seven-decade career, Parton loved following fashion trends — especially when it comes to hairstyles. Her trademark platinum blonde hair, though — as mentioned above — was never truly her own. Rather than spoil her hair with bleaching, she began wearing wigs from early on. It's said her collection numbered over 350 different wigs. Parton never made a secret of her cosmetic surgeries. Over time, she used it to change her face and figure — but she always remained the friendly superstar with a big heart. In 2025, Forbes magazine valued Parton's fortune at around $450 million (€387 million). She shared her wealth with people in need for decades — in particular in her home state of Tennessee, but also around the globe. 4. Promoting reading for kids Since 1995, Parton's The Dollywood Foundation has been sponsoring books for children as part of her Imagination Library program. From the day a child is born, parents can apply to receive a book every month up until the age of 5. More than 300 million books have already been distributed in five English-speaking countries: the US, Canada, Australia, UK and Ireland. The program is funded by the foundation itself, government support and private donors. Recently, however, some Republican-governed states in the US have announced plans to scrap financial support for the Imagination Library. Parton, who didn't have children of her own, founded the library program in honor of her father Robert Lee Parton — who was unable to read. Each year, the foundation also awards five university scholarships to high school graduates from Sevier County. The Dolly Parton Scholarships of $15,000 are aimed at "students who have a dream they wish to pursue and who can successfully communicate their plan and commitment to realize their dreams," as stated on the foundation's website. 5. A million dollars during COVID In 2020, Parton donated $1 million to the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, Tennessee, where the biotechnology company Moderna was working on a COVID-19 vaccine. On the BBC's "The One Show" in November 2020, she said of her donation: "I'm a very proud girl today to know I had anything at all to do with something that's going to help us through this crazy pandemic." A few months later, she received the vaccine on camera and rewrote her hit-song "Jolene" to "Vaccine" for the occasion. 6. Hundreds of 'Jolene' covers "Jolene" is one of the most frequently covered songs in pop music history. The web portal cover.info notes over 80 official cover versions — from famous artists to indie musicians. Countless other versions can be heard on YouTube and other platforms. One of the most popular covers was the raw and gritty 2004 interpretation by US duo The White Stripes. Parton herself has recorded several versions of her famous hit — accompanied by a cappella group Pentatonix, for instance, or alongside her famous godchild, pop star Miley Cyrus. In 2016, all of them got together to perform it live together on The Voice. 7. Two world hits in one day Parton wrote both "Jolene" and "I Will Always Love You" on the same day in 1972. When Whitney Houston covered the latter two decades later, it became an instant global hit. You might be surprised to know that "I Will Always Love You" was never meant to be a romantic song. In fact, it was about Parton ending her professional collaboration with her mentor, country star Porter Wagoner. Speaking with radio host Howard Stern in 2023, Parton recalled the conflicted emotions she felt when writing the song. "How am I going to make him understand how much I appreciate everything, but that I have to go? I thought, well, what do you do best? You write songs. So I sat down and I wrote this song." Houston's '90s cover version earned Parton another $10 million in royalties. Speaking in 2021 on "Watch What Happens Live," she revealed that she invested the money into an office complex in a Black neighborhood in Nashville, Tennessee. "I just thought, 'This was great. I'm going to be down here with her people, who are my people as well… I think, 'This is the house that Whitney built,'" she said. 8. Not the best doppelganger Last but not least: Parton said that she once took part in a Dolly Parton drag queen lookalike contest — and lost. On "The Ellen DeGeneres Show," Parton revealed that she had overdone her styling to avoid being recognized: She made her beauty mark bigger, her breasts larger and her hair bigger. All the contestants had to walk across the stage at a gay bar, and whoever received the most applause was declared the winner. In the end, it wasn't Parton who won. This article was originally written in German. It was first published on January 18, 2026 and was updated upon news of her death on August 25, 2026.

item.title: Ex-Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic dead at 84
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.42
Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladic, who was serving a life sentence for war crimes committed during Bosnia and Herzegovina's 1992-95 war has died, a United Nations official said. Serbian state broadcaster RTS reported on Thursday that he died in a prison hospital in the Hague, after suffering several strokes. A family member of Mladic, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the situation, confirmed the reports to the Associated Press and said Mladic's son, Darko Mladic, was on the way to the Hague. The International Criminal Court for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) convicted Mladic of charges including crimes against humanity and genocide in 2017, handing him a life sentence. The verdict was confirmed on appeal in 2021. Commenting on Mladic's death on Thursday, United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres expressed his support for the war criminal's victims. "The secretary-general stands in solidarity with the victims, survivors and their families who suffered the crimes for which Mr Mladic was found guilty," spokesman Stephane Dujarric told reporters.
'The butcher of Bosnia' Mladic was held responsible for his role in the 1992 to 1995 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including July 1995 massacre of some 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica. The slaughter, the worst single atrocity in Europe since World War II, saw him named the "Butcher of Bosnia." Under Mladic's command, Bosnian Serb forces besieged Sarajevo and other towns, operated detention camps for non-Serbs and enemy soldiers, and systematically killed prisoners. Former UN rights chief Zeid Ra'ad al Hussein described him as "the epitome of evil" after his conviction. "This is all lies, you are all liars," he shouted when he was sentenced to life in prison in 2017. On Monday, Serbia's justice minister, Nenad Vujic, asked for Mladic to be transferred to a Belgrade military hospital, warning that his death "could come at any time." Srebrenica massacre discredited international community Born in Bosnia in 1942, Mladic was a former Yugoslav army officer who rose to command the Bosnian Serb army during the 1992-95 war. A hardline nationalist, he portrayed the conflict as a historic struggle against Ottoman rule and celebrated the 1995 capture of Srebrenica. After the capture of the city, Mladic ordered the evacuation of women, children and the elderly but said all men of fighting age are taken prisoner. In the following days more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys are systematically butchered by the Bosnian Serb forces and their bodies dumped in mass graves. In 2022 The Netherlands apologized for the Dutch peacekeepers' failure to prevent the killings. Mladic himself have never repented. Edited by: Rana Taha Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: Trial date set for alleged 9/11 mastermind
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.35
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the alleged mastermind behind the terror attacks in the United States on September 11, 2001, has been given a trial date. Mohammed was captured in 2003 and has spent nearly 20 years in detention at Guantanamo Bay prison in Cuba. A US Air Force Judge late on Wednesday ordered that Mohammed and three co-defendants go before a military tribunal in June 2028. The long-delayed procedure has been hampered by legal wrangling over confessions made after torture, finding a location where he could be tried, and intense emotions regarding the man widely regarded as the main planner of the 9/11 terror attacks . An earlier plea deal in which Mohammed agreed to admit guilt in exchange for avoiding the death penalty was thrown out last year. The new trial will see Mohammed, as well as Walid Muhammad Salih Mubarak bin 'Atash, Mustafa Ahmed Adam al Hawsawi, and Ali Abdul Aziz Ali stand trial in a US military court with service members acting as jury. Who is Khalid Sheikh Mohammed? Born in Kuwait in 1965, he is alleged to have been sympathetic to anti-Soviet Islamist causes before getting a degree in mechanical engineering from a US university in 1986. He worked for a time as an engineer for the Qatari government. According to US intelligence agents, in the early 1990s he participated in a plot to bomb airliners traveling between the US and Asia that was never realized. He is believed to have met al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden shortly after that. As the group's head of propaganda, he is accused of having helped plan the 1993 World Trade Center bombings, the 2002 Bali bombings in Indonesia, and the murder of US journalist Daniel Pearl as well as 9/11. What is Mohammed charged with? As the suspected mastermind of the September 11 attacks, he is charged with 2,977 counts of murder, terrorism, hijacking aircraft, and attacking civilians. Because his charges are classified as war crimes, he will be tried by a military tribunal. It is possible that he could be given the death penalty, but judges may seek to avoid that outcome because it can lead to a lengthy appeals process. Edited by: Karl Sexton If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Could new US sanctions tear China and Iran apart?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.35
China has pushed back on what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions" after the US announced new measures earlier this week to cut off all potential sources of revenue to Iran. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday described the sanctions package as an "economic D-Day" against Tehran, and warned any economic engagement with the regime would "expose those responsible to the full reach" of US power. China is Iran's top trade partner and provides a lifeline to Tehran mainly through oil purchases, but also with banking, technology and dual-use goods, which can be used both for civilian and military purposes. When asked whether Chinese banks would be included in the new measures, Bessent warned that "no one was above the reach of US sanctions." But with US President Donald Trump due to meet his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in September, Washington will need to be careful with any moves affecting China-Iran trade ties. China's big banks still safe The initial US sanctions package stops short of targeting major Chinese banks. Instead, it focuses on 60 smaller entities, individuals, and vessels, both in mainland China and Hong Kong, that are part of the ecosystem supporting "illicit nuclear and missile technology procurement, cyber operations, and oil‑revenue generation networks." China purchases up to 90% of Iranian oil exports, some of it through independent "teapot" refineries which end up rebranding the oil or using intermediaries to bypass US sanctions. In May, China's Commerce Ministry ordered domestic businesses and teapot refineries to ignore US restrictions targeting several of these refineries. At the time, Bessent said China's Iran oil purchases amounted to "funding the largest state sponsor of terrorism." Beijing balances between Iran and its rivals On Tuesday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said cooperation between China and Iran "has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted." China maintains a transactional relationship while framing instability in the Middle East as a failure of US policy. At the same time, Beijing also projects the image of a stable, responsible superpower, and avoids being lumped together with rogue states the US accuses it of supporting. Beijing also values its trade ties with Saudi Arabia and the UAE, prompting it to carefully balance its relationships to avoid alienating Iran's regional rivals. The ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the US sanctions package are likely to be on the agenda when Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian attends the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Kyrgyzstan, scheduled for August 31 to September 1. The SCO focuses on Eurasian security and is part of China's strategy of creating a "multipolar" world order to counter the global influence of the US. China has been "trying to deepen its engagement and expand the scope of its relations with Gulf countries. From this perspective, Iran remains a useful and important partner for China, but it is not irreplaceable," William Yang, senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group, told DW. "In some ways, China benefits from Washington's continued involvement in regional security and defense and is not seeking to replace the US in that regard," Yang added. Is US power waning in the Middle East? However, US military setbacks during the Iran war have called this security umbrella into question and have changed the strategic landscape in the Middle East, Gu Xuewu, political scientist and director of the Center for Global Studies at Germany's University of Bonn, told DW. "Against this backdrop, Beijing will not yield to US pressure to sever economic and trade ties with Iran or to help the US maintain its presence in the Middle East," Gu said. Since the Iran war was launched in late February, Beijing has consistently called for a diplomatic solution to the conflict. This week, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Jian said that Washington's strategy of "economic asphyxiation" will fail to resolve the crisis and will only further intensify Middle Eastern tensions. "China disapproves of the US' assertive behavior in this region, and is even less willing to accept the US using every means at its disposal to hinder cooperation between Arab states and China in the areas of energy, the military, science, technology, and trade," said Gu. He added that Beijing has no interest in fighting a "decisive battle" with the US in the Middle East. "It is enough to provoke the US into making mistakes in the Middle East and to allow it to continue making further mistakes without interfering," he added. Trump-Xi summit looms large In 2025, when the US tried to pressure China with massive tariffs, Beijing hit back by threatening to cut off the supply of rare earth minerals, forcing the Trump administration to retreat. Since then, Trump has tried to stabilize the US-China relationship, including with a high profile summit in Beijingthis May. Now, Chinese leader Xi is due to visit Washington in September. "Since Beijing and Washington are both focused on paving the way for the highly anticipated summit on September 24, I don't think either country will take drastic action on Iran to jeopardize the summit," Yang said. However, he added that China will "maintain its baseline engagement with Iran and will be prepared to defend its economic interests if the US government begins to target Chinese businesses with secondary sanctions." If the US hits large Chinese companies and banks with sanctions, then it is foreseeable that China will respond with equivalent retaliatory measures while maintaining its ties to Iran, says Professor Gu. However, he added that Beijing will not "abandon the painstakingly negotiated plans for a summit." "We will see China and the US on a collision course over the Iran issue, even as they engage in friendly discussions during the summit between Xi Jinping and Trump," Gu said. Edited by: Darko Janjevic

item.title: Tech giants urge global response to AI cybersecurity threats
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.25
More than 100 companies, including AI giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Perplexity, have signed an open letter calling for a global effort to strengthen AI-powered cybersecurity threats. "We have a limited window to strengthen cyber defenses," the letter read. "In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable." Other signatories to the open letter include Adobe, AMD, Cisco, Dell, Oracle, IBM and German tech giant SAP as well as Deutsche Telekom. Letter urges more funding, resources for cybersecurity The companies called for a broad response, ranging from end-user companies strengthening their own security protocols to "frontier AI companies" building new observability and security tools to cope with AI-powered threats. In particular, they also called on governments to pay for local and international responses to new threats to cybersecurity. "Fund cyber defense, starting with essential services that lack the staff or budget to act," the letter read. In the United States, the Trump administration has imposed deep cuts to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) last year, cutting staff by around a third. The letter also urged governments to "expedite the expansion of trusted access programs, especially for critical infrastructure supply chains, and broaden access to defensive capabilities for other defenders." AI agents reportedly go rogue Last month, OpenAI said two of its models escaped their test environment, gained access to the internet and attacked Hugging Face, a site that AI developers use to store and share code. The incident prompted Anthropic to check if its own models had also carried out similar attacks. It found three incidents in which a Claude model broke out of its testing environment and breached the systems of three organizations. In June, the "Five Eyes" intelligence community — consisting of the US, the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand — issued a rare joint statement warning that new AI models were "fundamentally transforming both offensive and defensive cyber capabilities." "The timeline is not years, it is months," the statement said. Edited by: Sean Sinico If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Was the heat of this summer really 'normal?'
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.13
As a summer of European extreme heat draws to a close, politicians are looking back at the toll. Germany recordedaround 14,000 heat-related deaths, almost two-thirds in one scorching week of June alone. A Dutch bank estimated summer heat will cost the EU €180 billion ($209 billion) in lost GDP. And in June, European farmers lost approximately 9 million tons in grain crops. Climate change, long a politically charged topic, has become a daily reality for people around the world. These effects and more are making it increasingly difficult to challenge what people are seeing with their own eyes. Yet that hasn't stopped the global populist right from trying. Richard Tice, deputy leader of the UK's far-right Reform Party said "climate change has always happened, it always will," adding that it was arrogant to try to stop it. He encouraged the British public to enjoy the heat. In the United States, Harriet Hageman, a Republican politician and potentially Wyoming's next senator, told far-right channel Real America's Voice that Europe’s heatwave was business as usual. "It's called summer. Some years are hotter than others and some years are colder than others," she said. "But that's just the cyclical nature of weather." And Tino Chrupalla, co-leader of Germany’s far-right AfD party told a journalist in recent days that it's been a "completely normal summer." He dismissed climate change as "hype."
But claims like these don't stand up to scientific scrutiny. As NASA statesplainly: "Scientific evidence continues to show that human activities (primarily the human burning of fossil fuels) have warmed Earth's surface and its ocean basins, which in turn have continued to impact Earth’s climate." This was not 'a completely normal summer' This summer has been historically hot. Independent climate monitoring bodies, including the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) in the US, the Copernicus Climate Change Service in the European Union and the Japan Meterological Agency, all called last month either the joint-warmest or joint-second warmest month on record. The conditions have led energy plants to halt production, outdated concrete motorways blowing up, and older buildings overheating during the day and barely cooling down at night — threatening inhabitants with exposure to heat stress. The extreme heat was felt almost everywhere on the globe. According to NOAA's data, it was the warmest July ever for North America, Africa and Asia. The continental United States just surpassedits warmest July records. They were previously set in 1936, during the infamous Dust Bowl that scorched the US Great Plains with extreme temperatures, and in 2012, when North America suffered an extreme heatwave. And the daily average sea surface temperature hitits highest level since records began in 1979 — reaching 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 degrees Fahrenheit) this month. That's a result of both human-driven warming as well as El Nino, a climate cycle that weakens trade winds and warms tropical Pacific surface temperatures. How climate change supercharged this summer's fires In Spain, the far-right Vox party saidfires — which burned more than 254,000 hectares of land across the country this season — were not connected to climate change. Yet experts agree rising global temperatures played a major role in the intense wildfire season that also scorched large parts of France and Canada. That's because extreme heat creates ideal conditions for wildfires to start and spread. A field of climate research called attribution science explores the extent to which climate change exacerbates extreme weather events like this summer's wildfires. Using models, researchers compare the likelihood and intensity of an event in today's climate with a simulated world in which there is no human-caused warming. Analyses done this summer showthat hotter global temperatures created conditions that made the wildfires in Spain 20 times more likely to happen, and twice as probable in France. This is due to a phenomenon known as weather whiplash, where ecosystems swing dramatically between wet and dry conditions. When the planet warms, the atmosphere holds more moisture, rainfall is intensified, and plants grow. Then, in summer, that same warm atmosphere draws water from soil and plants, worsening drought and drying out vegetation, turning it into the perfect fuel for fires. "We know — and this is mathematically proven — that the probability of having fire weather that can sustain and create this kind of event has been altered by climate change," Francesca Di Giuseppe, a fire forecast project coordinator at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, told DW about this summer's fires in Spain and France. Climate change's ripple effects Overall, this summer has left its mark in numerous ways that are impossible to ignore. Bodies of water across Europe are drying out under the intense heat. Parts of the Rhine, Danube and Po rivers have fallen to historically low levels, making it impossible for ships to pass through in some spots. This has a number of knock-on effects. Drinking water costs could rise dramatically as much of Germany's clean water first passes through reed-filled riverbanks that are crucial for filtration. Supply chains are also be disrupted, as vessels can't carry as much cargo when water levels are lower, increasing prices across the economy in products like steel or petroleum. In America, drought conditions are wreaking havoc on crops and livestock. In June, the US Department of Agriculture said the 10-month stretch from August 2025 to May 2026 was the nation's driest period since 1976-77. Now, 59% of the country's sorghum is being grown in areas experiencing drought. More than half the nation's cattle production and almost two-thirds of spring wheat production is happening under water scarcity. Such conditions can put direct strain on the country's food supply, increase prices and threaten rural livelihoods. By any measurement — thermometers, drought maps, or death tolls — and in much of the world, this summer has been historically extreme. Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: Can Germany defend itself against drone attacks?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.05
On August 25, German media reported on a third drone allegedly found near Leipzig/Halle Airport in August. A drone and a substance — which initial assessments suggest could be around 50 grams of Hexogen, a highly explosive military-grade explosive — were reportedly discovered in a field outside the airport grounds. Consequently, public broadcasters NDR and WDR, and the daily broadsheet Süddeutsche Zeitung are speculating about a plot that may be far more extensive than what has been publicly disclosed so far. Speaking on the sidelines of a federal government retreat in the state of Brandenburg, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) stated: "Germany has increasingly come into the crosshairs of hybrid attackers." Merz also pointed to measures aimed at better protecting the public. Just a few days ago, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) inaugurated a drone security research center in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, not far from Leipzig and Halle in Saxony. How could drones laden with explosives fly unhindered near or into Leipzig/Halle airport and remain unnoticed for at least several hours? Interior Minister Dobrindt had immediately spoken of a "hybrid attack scenario" which he suspected came from "foreign powers." Suspicion has been directed at Russia, also because one drone was said to have been located near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. The Federal Prosecutor's Office has taken over the investigation. However, drone sightings over airports and ports, industrial sites and military properties have been increasing in Germany. In 2025, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) recorded more than 1,000 suspicious drone flights. Last October, drones disrupted air traffic in Munich for several hours, stranding numerous passengers. There is not sufficient drone protection at German airports, security expert Nico Lange warned. "We do not possess the sensor networks and sensor beams needed to spot all types of drones, especially low-flying, slow drones," he told DW. The European Association for Unmanned Aviation has also long pointed out weak points in Germany's drone defense. "That a drone could apparently reach the airport tarmac and be discovered rather by chance, shows where the core of the problem is," said chairperson Gerald Wissel in relation to the latest incident. The association suggests "the establishment of real-time monitoring of the lower airspace as well as the mandatory tracking of all airspace participants via ADS-L" — a radio communications system that makes drones in an airspace electronically visible. Why coordinating Germany's drone defense is difficult Interior Minister Dobrindt wants to remedy this by setting up new institutions. In December, he launched the Joint Counter Drone Center (GDAZ) in Berlin. There, information from the federal police, state police, secret service and armed forces is collated around the clock. But the incident at Leipzig airport shows that even a new hub is of little use if a dangerous drone at a large airport cannot be discovered and intercepted. Drones move quickly, and any response must be decided within minutes. Doing so is made more difficult by Germany's system of divided responsibilities. If a suspicious drone takes off somewhere in the country, it's initially a matter for the state police. Germany has 16 police authorities, one for each of its 16 states. Only when the drone moves over a large airport or railway facility are the federal police allowed to step in. Will Germany's federal police lead on drone defense? Security experts and opposition politicians in Germany's Bundestag federal parliament have called for clear regulation and consolidation of responsibilities. "The muddle over responsibilities in drone defense is a substantial danger to our domestic security," said Irene Mihalic, lawmaker with the opposition Green Party and herself a former police officer. Many, including the Greens, suggest the federal police should take the lead when it comes to drone defense. The federal police set up a new special unit for drone defense in December, and Dobrindt now wants to expand the unit following the incident at Leipzig airport. Originally, 130 staff positions across four locations were planned. In the future, there will be 300 personnel across eight locations, to "be on site quickly and flexibly when needed," according to the Interior Ministry. Who is allowed to shoot down a drone in Germany? As so often happens following dramatic incidents, there have also been calls to deploy the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, to take care of drone defense efforts at airports. However, current German law maintains that police are responsible for upholding security in the country. A Defense Ministry spokesperson warned that protecting its own facilities, with their "tens of thousands of kilometers of fencing," is already a challenge for the Bundeswehr. Adding 24/7 protection of civilian infrastructure "would proclaim a false sense of security that we could never achieve," he added. In an emergency, the police are allowed to ask the army for assistance. To achieve legal clarity in this regard, Germany amended its air security law in March. For the first time, it allows the Bundeswehr to shoot down drones outside their own premises to prevent "a particularly serious disaster." Why German airports and train stations still lack protection There is also a lot of catching up to do when it comes to the technical equipment used to defend against drones. "There were big announcements at airports about positioning drone defense systems. They are more like detection systems," Manuel Atug, a spokesperson for the independent Critical Infrastructure Working Group (Arbeitsgruppe Kritische Infrastruktur) told DW. "So far, they have not intercepted a single drone, and at some airports they have still not yet been put in place." The German Police Union (GdP) has also lamented the lack of resources for drone defense. "Unsafe train stations, unsafe airports and a police force which has to beg for money, law changes and the latest defense technology are really disconcerting," criticized GdP federal chairman Jochen Kopelke. An Interior Ministry spokesperson said large airports were steadily being equipped with drone defense technology. "The federal police have already procured a considerable amount of equipment. The eight large airports are prioritized: Frankfurt (Main), Munich, Berlin, Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Cologne/Bonn, Stuttgart and Leipzig/Halle," she said. The plan is for all of these airports to be equipped with mobile drone defense technology by the end of the year. This article was originally written in German. It was first published on August 14, 2026, and updated on August 25 to reflect news developments.

item.title: Nepal flooding: 'We are disconnected from Kathmandu'
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.85
With the death toll in Nepal well into the hundreds and rising following a massive flash flood on Wednesday, the full scope of destruction remains unclear. People from the affected areas told DW that many villages remain both physically and electronically cut off from the capital, Kathmandu. Bidhya Rajput, a journalist based in the capital, said her home in the Sole village in Nepal's Nuwakot District was swept away by the Trisuli River. "As far as we know, only four or five people from Sole village could save their lives by fleeing towards the hills. Others couldn't make their way as the floods came up suddenly," she told DW. The government has declared Nuwakot, along with Rasuwa and Dhading districts, to be the most affected by the deadly floods. Rajput told DW her husband's parents remain missing. Her father-in-law, a teacher, may have been caught in the flood while returning home after work, according to the school principal. Rajput's husband has left for the village in search for news on his family members, despite the roads being damaged and swept away in many places. Rajput said that there are no further updates from the village as there has been no electricity or mobile communication since early morning on Thursday. "The state's rescue and relief efforts have been centered mostly on bigger cities," she said, adding that "state assistance is yet to reach Sole." Villagers said the same area was affected by flooding last year, but many villagers managed to get to higher ground and the water did not reach as high as on Tuesday. "Had the villagers received early warning information, [and] could have presumed that this time floods would be so massive, they could have fled to safe locations like last year," Rajput said. "This time, they couldn't get even that chance." 'Two of my close relatives are missing' But Usha Kiran Timsena, an opposition politician from Nuwakot, said police and local officials did issue a warning that a massive flood was coming. However, many people in the area simply didn't account for the scale and speed of the mass of water. "Many those who were a bit far from riversides took it lightly and couldn't flee once the flood reaches to their places," she told DW. "Two of my close relatives have been missing since yesterday morning. There has been no further update or contact since then." Authorities said that more than three dozen bridges, including vehicular and suspension bridges, as well as a dozen hydropower dams, have been destroyed by the floods. Sujan Lohani from Dhading told DW that he never imagined that the flooding and destruction caused by the Trishuli River could be so massive and widespread.
