It features the latest and brightest OLED display technology available, a 5K resolution that's incredibly sharp and an expansive screen that fills your entire field of view. It also has the ability to jump between 5K 165Hz and 1080p+ 330Hz modes at the touch of a button, which can be useful for shooters. Put it all together, and you've got a true sweet spot of ultrawide features. Now you might think Alienware is lagging behind the likes of LG and Samsung, both of which offer 49-inch ultrawide screens, but that number doesn't tell the entire story. Whereas most of those screens are very wide but not very tall with 1,440 vertical pixels, the Alienware 5K has the useful height of a 32-inch 4K screen (2,160 pixels). Couple that with 5,120 ultrawide horizontal pixels, and you've got a screen that can fill your entire field of view, making it far more immersive for both gaming and diving into massive media editing timelines. While the Alienware 39-inch 5K monitor is certainly pricey at $1,100, it's significantly cheaper than LG's 5K2K ultrawide UltraGear, which currently sells for $1,600. I'd also bet the two monitors share the same LG panel, as they both offer the same features, right down to dual 5K and 1080p modes. That makes Alienware's offering a bit of a deal — at least that's how my screen-obsessed brain would justify it. It does so many things well, I wouldn't mind shelling out for this screen. What's notable about the Alienware 39 5K? Similar to Alienware's new 34-inch ultrawide, the 39 5K isn't big on design flourishes. Its plastic case is simple, yet functional, and the only trace of decorative lighting is along the small Alienware logo on the rear. Crucially, it offers both height and tilt adjustment, something that's sorely lacking on Apple's $1,600 27-inch 5K Studio Display. Alienware was likely able to keep costs down by going with a relatively simple case (that could be a reason LG's comparable ultrawide is $500 more), and you can always throw the display on a monitor arm if you don't like the case's aesthetic on your desk. The display is what really makes the Alienware 39 5K special. It's powered by LG's latest four-stack tandem OLED panel (essentially four OLED panels on top of each other) with a three-subpixel RGB stripe. That's meant to deliver sharper text than earlier WOLED (white OLED) panels, which often display purple fringing around letters. Its new OLED technology helps it deliver between 500 and 1,300 nits of HDR brightness, and it also supports Dolby Vision. The monitor also covers 99 percent of the DCI-P3 color gamut, making it accurate enough for professional video and photo work. OLED screens are already known for their deep black levels, since they don't rely on traditional backlighting technology like LEDs. The Alienware 39 5K takes things a step further with a polarizer layer on its panel, which rejects ambient light from reflecting off of the screen itself. That makes for darker black levels across all lighting environments, even very bright rooms. The Alienware 39 5K's native 165Hz refresh rate is slower than most monitors we see today — the company's 32-inch and and 34-inch OLEDs hit 240Hz and 280Hz, respectively — but I'd argue it's more than enough for most games. As I mentioned, the monitor can also switch to a 2,560 by 1,080 pixel mode to achieve a far faster 330Hz refresh rate. You can also scale it to standard 4K at 165Hz, or 24.5-inch (1,520 by 855) and 27-inch (1,680 by 945) at 330Hz. Obviously, those modes sacrifice resolution for increased speed, but they could be useful features if you need to hop into the occasional competitive Overwatch match, where a faster refresh rate could give you the edge when it comes to landing a headshot. As with every OLED screen, burn-in, or the imprinting of static ghost images directly on the screen, is a potential concern. But Alienware claims the 39 5K has several features to avoid that fate. Its tandem OLED panel can get brighter than previous OLEDs with less electrical stress on every layer of the screen. The screen also has a "personalized algorithm" that uses machine learning to predict your usage over time and optimize energy levels for every pixel. "The algorithm improves upon the 'OLED Pixel Dimming' technology, which controls light for each of the 33 million pixels individually in 8K resolution, ensuring accurate color reproduction in both light and dark scenes," Alienware said in its review documentation. The Alienware 39 5K also features pixel refresh and pixel shift routines to keep screen uniformity, which are common among OLED screens. The company offers a three-year panel exchange warranty, which includes coverage for burn-in. It's hard to predict how long the hardware will actually last, but this OLED monitor has a better chance than many to reach my hypothetical 10-year milestone. As for connectivity, the Alienware 39 5K sports two HDMI 2.1 ports: one with eARC and ARC, for connecting soundbars and receivers, and the other with HDMI 2.1 FRL to support its 5K2K resolution and high refresh rate. There's also a DisplayPort 2.1 connection and a USB-C with DisplayPort (and 90W power). A USB-B connection is used to pipe data back to your computer, and there are also two USB-A and one USB-C port for connecting accessories. In-use: Ultrawide nirvana I've begun to feel a bit like Goldilocks when it comes to gaming monitors. I love the Alienware 32, a standard 16:9 widescreen, but I wish it were a bit wider. The Alienware 34 ultrawide impressed me, but I wish it were as tall as the 32's 4K screen. And while larger ultrawide screens like the LG UltraGear 49 looked absolutely insane on my desk, they were typically unwieldy. I couldn't comfortably see the sides of those screens, and they also felt a bit too short. The Alienware 39 5K gets everything just right. I knew I was going to love this monitor the minute I placed it on my desk and I realized it perfectly eclipsed the Alienware 32 OLED that was sitting right behind it. The inner portion of the Alienware 39 5K was an exact match for the 32's entire display, while the ultrawide sides filled out my peripheral vision. Finally, this is a monitor I can immerse myself in completely without rearranging my desk, or fretting about not having enough vertical screen space. While the Alienware 39 5K isn't a QD-OLED screen like the 34-inch ultrawide I just reviewed (which uses a Samsung panel), it still felt like a next-generation OLED, with none of the dimness I've encountered on older screens. Its 300 nits of SDR brightness was more than enough for browsing the web and general computer work, while its 500 nits of HDR performance made games like Control, 007: First Light and Overwatch 2 practically leap off the screen. And in those peak moments of 1,300-nit HDR brightness, like sunlight bouncing off the windshield of an impeccably polished British Racing Green Jaguar, my eyes almost always teared up. PC gaming has never looked this good. Control felt like an entirely new game when I replayed it on the Alienware 39 5K. I originally experienced it on an older 32-inch Dell ultrawide screen without HDR, but that was nothing like playing it on an ultrawide display that covered my entire desk. Outside of playing Control on a virtual reality headset, where I could scale up a virtual display to the size of a theater, I've never been so immersed in the game. Having the extra horizontal display area made it easier to keep track of enemies trying to flank me, and the Alienware 39 5K's excellent HDR performance made the gleaming floors and office clutter of the FBC seem far more realistic. I also spent several hours playing Overwatch in the screen's native 5K2K resolution and 165Hz refresh rate, as well as its 2,560 by 1,080 and 330Hz mode. They're both impressive for different reasons. Overwatch 2 looked ludicrously sharp and detailed in the higher resolution, naturally. It's such a low-impact game that many modern video cards should have no trouble reaching 120 fps at that resolution. (I was playing on an RTX 5090, and as you'd imagine, it was just fine.) Not surprisingly, Overwatch was far less detailed in the lower resolution — with a 39-inch screen, it's hard to ignore blurry textures and text. But it was noticeably smoother as I hopped around the map, hoping to score a headshot with Hanzo and learning how to handle D.Mon's sick mech-suit. There wasn't any noticeable tearing as I rushed around the map and frantically tried to prove my worth, thanks to the monitor's G-SYNC and Freesync support. The one downside of the Alienware 39 5K's high resolution is that you'll need a decent amount of power to see the screen's full potential. I was testing it on a desktop powered by a Ryzen 9 9950X3D and an NVIDIA RTX 5090, which is far beyond what regular gamers have access to. You'll need a video card that offers decent 4K performance, at the very least, and you'll likely have to lean on frame generation and upscaling to play games in 5K. Lower-resolution ultrawide screens, meanwhile, are far more forgiving when it comes to GPU power. When I was able to peel myself away from games, I also loved using the Alienware 39 5K to browse the web, take notes and write a large chunk of this review. Text looks absolutely crisp, though I'll admit I was never truly bothered by the purple text fringing on older OLEDs. The screen's ultrawide resolution also makes it perfect for watching anamorphic widescreen movies and videos, which fill the entirety of the display. Just be aware that standard 16:9 widescreen content will have black bars along the sides of the screen (at which point, this is effectively just a 32-inch 4K monitor). The Alienware 39 5K features the same basic on-screen controls as Alienware's other monitors, except now its control joystick is along the bottom rear of the monitor, instead of right on the bottom edge. I found it easy to navigate, though it's certainly a bit more archaic than the smart display controls I've seen on Samsung's monitors. You'll also need to deal with its menus every time you want to switch display modes. Should you buy the Alienware 39 5K? If you're in the market for a large gaming monitor, the $1,100 Alienware 39 5K is definitely one to consider. It offers more vertical screen space than most other ultrawides, it has the latest and greatest OLED screen technology and it's cheaper than LG's 39-inch 5K2K monitor. Consider it an investment in your gaming future. And given that monitor prices haven't exploded like other components, it's probably smarter to invest in a good screen now, instead of a RAM or GPU upgrade. Wrap-up I can't think of what else I'd want in a gaming monitor, honestly. The Alienware 39 5K is large enough to immerse me in all of my favorite games, it's one of the brightest OLEDs I've ever seen and it can also transform into a faster esports screen on a dime. Just put me in a room with this screen for the next decade, and I'll be happy.

item.title: The UK has legalized plug-in solar (but don't rush to buy a kit)
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 3.16
The UK has legalized plug-in solar (but don't rush to buy a kit) Experts say it's worth getting your home's electrical systems checked first. In March, the UK announced it would end its longstanding ban on the sale and use of plug-in solar panels. And today, August 27, is the date that the various laws and regulations have changed, making it legal to buy and install a small solar setup yourself. The move has been in the works for a while as part of a raft of initiatives to reduce the nation's dependence on fossil fuels. It's a big move, and one that could help countless households reduce the cost of their power bills. Here's what you need to understand and, crucially, a note not to rush into this too soon for plenty of sensible reasons. What is plug-in solar? Unlike professionally installed systems, plug-in solar gear can be plugged into a standard wall socket. Rather than generating vast amounts of power, the idea is to use one or two panels, connected to your home via microinverter, for a trickle of extra juice. You won't be able to live off-grid with them, but might be able to cut some of the costs of your power bill. The modest cost of the hardware and the fact you don't need to pay a professional to install it should encourage adoption. Given how expensive energy is in the UK, even a small cost saving should be meaningful over time. And it may be the first chance many of the 5.4 million people living in apartments in the UK get to embrace the solar revolution. Is it used anywhere else? Plug-in solar is widely used in other European nations, but the most obvious example is Germany. Around half the German population rent their homes, a barrier to the widespread adoption of solar power. In 2019, Germany implemented Balkonkraftwerk (literally "balcony power plant") to allow renters to hang plug-in panels from their balconies. It added legal protections to this right in 2024, preventing landlords from objecting to their use. According to Germany's plug-in solar association, more than 1.2 million people have already installed systems. What are the specs? A legally-compliant plug-in solar system comes in two parts: solar panels and a microinverter. The former is like any other solar panel, but they'll be easier to install on balconies and other DIY-able areas. The latter, if you're unaware, is a unit converting DC electricity to AC, making it suitable to be connected to your home's electrical system. The UK is aping Germany's example, limiting the size of these plug-in solar systems to avoid overwhelming its power grid. Inverter output is capped at 800 watts, which is the maximum amount of power that can be pushed into a home's electrical system. Depending on if you get one or two panels, there will be a higher upper limit on generation, but 800W is all you'll be able to use at one time. And it's worth knowing that even if a panel promises to generate 450W, you may not actually get that much depending on a number of factors. When did things start to change? When the Labour government won the 2024 election, it promised to supercharge domestic clean energy production. With the rationale of creating "energy independence from dictators like Putin," it committed to tripling solar generation by 2030. In June 2025, it outlined its solar roadmap, where it pledged to "explore [the] potential" of plug-in solar installations. One month later, it commissioned a safety study to look into the feasibility of widespread use. Then, on March 24, 2026, the government said it would make plug-in solar available to buy "within months." The government said it would work with regulators and infrastructure providers to update the relevant rules. Why did the UK resist plug-in for so long? The UK's rules around solar power are so strict that only professionally installed systems are legal. But successive administrations have held back on even looking at changing the rules for plug-in systems. When asked by Engadget earlier this year, a government spokesperson refused to answer the question directly but it appears the concern was around safety. A report from electrical industry website efixx suggests it's the way the UK's system was set up that there were more risks than for European plugs. Wait, are our homes unsafe? The Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET) is the body which is the authority on electrical installation. In partnership with the British Standards Institute (BSI), it maintains and publishes the British Standard focusing on electrical installations. Earlier this year, it carried out research into the electrical safety of British homes and how confident homeowners were. The results were concerning, with fewer than a third running the required annual check to ensure their systems were safe. More importantly, it revealed a number of bad habits which are commonly the cause of major electrical fires in homes. This included a cavalier attitude to leaving chargers running for extended periods of time and using visibly-damaged sockets. Alarmingly, almost 20 percent of respondents said they daisy-chained extension cords, a serious fire risk. It pointed to data from charity Electrical Safety First, which said more than half of all house fires are caused by misused or faulty electrical equipment. Are there any other technical hurdles? According to the IET's Mark Coles, there aren't just hurdles to overcome, but issues so vast as to potentially derail the entire concept of plug-in solar in the UK. Coles is the IET's head of technical regulations who has been developing standards for more than two decades. He said it "was a surprise to hear the announcement from the government," and shared grave misgivings about the implementation of the program. In fact, the same day the government announced its plan to open up plug-in solar, the IET issued a warning. As well as reminding consumers that the systems aren't yet legal, it urged people to get their home's wiring checked out by a professional. "What may be safe in one home may pose a significant risk in another," it said, "professional verification is the only way to be sure." For instance, the UK standards around Residual Current Devices (RCDs) were designed for one-way electrical traffic. "Think about your circuit breaker, your fusebox, you've got an electrical supply coming in, and cables going out to feed your appliances," he said. When you put electricity on the final circuit, traveling in the opposite direction, you "can burn out the device because it's not designed to take an electrical supply on that side." It was only a few years ago that the UK opened up to bi-directional RCDs which can take two-way traffic, but even now, the older hardware is still "for sale now, still being installed now." This isn't just about an inconvenience to your wiring, either, since if an RCD fails, it could be fatal. Coles added that, as much as Germany's system has been lauded, it was able to launch on the basis of decisions made several decades prior. The wiring, plugs and consumer units in Germany are two-pole which is overall less safe than the British version, but much easier to accept power in from both ends. By comparison, "the plugs and sockets in the UK are not suitable for plugging an electrical source in," said Coles. He added the rules covering British plugs "very clearly says you shall not plug in a low-voltage generating set [which is what a plug-in solar system is]." He also expressed concerns that as there was no universal standard for plug-in solar units, it would be impossible to offer certainty to regulators and consumers. And, as an additional risk, insurers may not pay out in the event of a fire given using such a system would break the rules around safe plug use. If someone is still interested in getting a plug-in system, Coles advises them to get their wiring checked out by a qualified electrician. And, crucially, to brace themselves for the potential that they won't be able to use it unless they have some or all of their home's electrical systems re-wired at significant cost. "It isn't just as simple as going to buy this unit and plugging it in," he said. Luke Osborne, technical director at Electrical Safety First, added his concerns around the issue of new technology coming into contact with older wiring. "Plug-in solar panels may negatively impact protective devices such as RCDs, which protect against electric shock," he said. He also called for the government to "give clarity on how it will address these concerns," to ensure "the UK boasts the best and safest solar panel roll out in Europe." Hang on, what about this website I've found... In the months between the initial announcement and the implementation date, there has been a lot of uncertainty. And some people have done their best to take advantage of that ambiguity. For instance, there were retailers already using phrases like "Plug in Solar" in their product descriptions. In some instances, the detail that those systems cannot actually be installed yourself is nestled in a separate tab. On reseller platforms like Facebook Marketplace, Engadget found a listing for kits on sale claiming that these systems were legal before today's changeover. This listing dangerously suggests that all a user does not need to use a qualified electrician if they know how to wire in a cable to a plug socket. On eBay, there are listings with product renders of microinverters plugged into power sockets, with the claim "No electrician needed from July 2026" in the description. So, what do I do? I wanted to do my bit and save some money! Fortunately, the government has teamed up with major UK retailers who will be selling legally compliant kits. That includes Argos, Currys and Wickes, and we'll likely see systems emerging from major manufacturers like EcoFlow and Anker Solix in the coming months. Given the data from the IET, it's likely your home's electrical systems haven't been checked in a while anyway. So it would make sense to get someone to check your wiring to make sure you're safe, and then to wait for these legitimate systems to become available. Being patient now may save you an expensive call with your home insurers should you choose to sprint ahead.

item.title: Speedo launches its own smart swim wearable
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 2.95
Speedo launches its own smart swim wearable SpeedoIQ is a tiny tracker that sits inside a pair of Vanguard goggles. There are a handful of swim-tracking goggles on the market, but none can lay a finger on market leader Form. Speedo, arguably the biggest name in swimming, is gunning for the king with the launch of SpeedoIQ, its new "swim intelligence" platform. The company promises SpeedoIQ will offer "real-time insights" on pace, distance, breathing, head position and turn performance. It's also been approved to wear in competition by World Aquatics, which alone might make it essential for athletes to take a look at. SpeedoIQ is a removable module which will sit inside the latest version of the company's standard Vanquisher swim goggles. When the user is out of the pool, they can sync it to their app to see how they did, including getting a sense of their head placement. Speedo adds that its new system is the "only" one of its kind that can analyze all your types of swimming stroke. Users will likely get coaching information to help them improve, no matter if they're an olympian or a neophyte. Speedo's clearly throwing an elbow or two toward its competitors, saying that its post-swim data will not "distract the user." I'd argue, from experience, that having a little transparent heads-up display relaying your stats is far more useful. Speaking as someone who hadn't clocked I was slowing down on a lap, seeing my split times get longer motivated me to pick up the pace. One benefit is that the system does not require any form of subscription, although the company has yet to say how much SpeedoIQ will cost, or when you'll be able to get your hands on one.

item.title: Meta is closing a loophole that allowed people to record with their smart glasses' light covered
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 2.77
Meta is closing a loophole that allowed people to record with their smart glasses' light covered It's the second update in less than two months to address privacy concerns. Meta is making yet another change to its smart glasses to try to prevent people from covertly recording others. The company is rolling out a software update that closes one loophole that allowed people to bypass the LED by covering it up while a recording was in progress, according to Alex Himel, Meta's VP of AR. The seemingly simple loophole is one that has been repeatedly highlighted online in tutorials about how to bypass the light. "The camera won't start recording if the LED is blocked, but some people try to bypass this by starting a recording and then covering it up," Himel wrote in a post on Threads. "A fix for this is starting to roll out – the camera will now stop working if the light is covered during a recording." The change is the second time in less than two months that Meta has issued a software update to address privacy concerns and unwanted recording. The company announced last month that it would disable the cameras on glasses if it detected that people had physically damaged the recording light. Meta has been trying to get ahead of a growing backlash against the product that has been fueled, in part, by people using the devices to covertly film and harass others in public. Instagram has also banned the accounts of some of the people behind these videos. But the company has yet to stop all of the tactics people have found to surreptitiously record others. There's also a thriving market for cheap accessories that can bypass the recording light without detection, as Engadget recently reported. Elsewhere, Meta is starting an "education and awareness campaign" meant to explain how the glasses' LED works, according to a spokesperson. The company has already put up a billboard in Los Angeles as part of the campaign. The billboard, pictured above, says that the Meta Glasses are "designed for everyone" and "not just the people wearing them." The recording light is illuminated in the accompanying photo. There's also a URL that links to a privacy-focused section on the product's website. Meta is planning to roll out similar ads and videos in other cities where it has sold a lot of glasses. Himel suggested that Meta is still working on additional privacy features for its glasses, too. "We're going to keep rolling out updates like this to make sure the capture LED can reliably alert bystanders when photos or videos are being captured for someone's gallery," he wrote. "Only a tiny minority of people try to get around these protections, and the fact they have to go to these lengths shows our efforts are working." Update, August 27, 2026, 1:40PM PT: Added additional information about Meta's ad campaign.

item.title: Sony's Reon wearable air conditioner saved my sanity through multiple heatwaves
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 2.01
Sony's Reon wearable air conditioner saved my sanity through multiple heatwaves It looks like an alien is attached to your spine, but it works. Earlier this month, temperatures where I live in London hit 100.6 Fahrenheit. It was the country's hottest day of the year, and part of the third heatwave of an oppressive summer. I am not built for this. The UK is not built for this. Air conditioning remains a rarity outside shops and offices: Research from the University of Reading estimated that there's A/C in just 4.3 percent of English homes – compared with 90 percent of US homes. The trains I commute on don't have it either, nor do many bars, restaurants and other places I visit often. As the second heatwave struck, I was willing to do anything for some relief. Sony has experimented with wearable air-conditioning tech for years, but for most of that time the Reon Pocket series was a curiosity. They were difficult to find, and performance was middling. The company kept improving how much cooling the device can deliver, while making it more comfortable, less obtrusive and more power efficient. The $260 Reon Pocket Pro Plus is the series' latest model. The main thing is that it's surprisingly effective at cooling your body down. The device uses the Peltier effect: A long, electrically cooled metal plate sits against the back of your neck and the top of your spine. That positioning is the whole trick. So much of your circulatory system passes through that area that the Reon effectively becomes a cooling station for your blood flow. With the Pro Plus, Sony says it can drop the plate an additional two degrees Celsius (3.6 Fahrenheit) over the previous model — a 20 percent jump in cooling performance in a single generation. Hot air is propelled up and outward through an exhaust that peeks over the neckline of your clothing. The Pro Plus ships with an attachment that extends the exhaust further and lets you adjust its angle, which was essential for me with anything that had a collar or a thick hem — shirts, jackets and structured necklines. If you're just wearing a tee, you can use the shorter vent. While you can hear the fans whir in a quiet room, the device is remarkably quiet, especially compared to many handheld electric fans. Sony's built-in algorithms monitor temperature changes on the device and in the surrounding area. The Pro Plus includes a smart tag you can clip to your bag that adds another data point by tracking ambient temperature and humidity. In practice, the tag was useful at times but unreliable at others. It unpaired easily, the reconnect button is finicky and it's only as effective as you are at remembering to take it with you; I regularly grabbed a different bag (or no bag at all) and left the tag at home. Honestly, I couldn't detect a tangible difference in cooling when it was around. The Reon Pro Plus performed just as efficiently without it. Outside of these summer months, the Pro Plus also has a four-level warm mode for winter, but I haven't tested those yet. Obviously. Sony says the Pro Plus can cool for up to 10 hours on its second-highest manual setting, or up to 15 hours in Smart Cool mode, where it adjusts output based on its sensors. As with any cooling product, mileage will vary widely depending on context and environment. During peak heatwave days — and World Cup matches in pubs without air conditioning — I got closer to four or five hours. I'd assumed I wouldn't be able to charge it while wearing it, but you can, if you're willing to have a USB-C cable billowing out of the bottom of your clothes. A real upgrade is the physical buttons on the device itself. You can do almost everything the companion app offers without your phone: power, switching between manual and smart modes and adjusting the cooling up or down. Sony says the Y-frame neckband that holds it in place has 40 percent more securing force compared to older models. I haven't used the immediately previous iteration — I tried a very early version of this tech years ago — but it stays put surprisingly well. However, it could be subtler. Under a jacket or blazer, or anything more structured, the silhouette smooths out. But I mostly wear slouchier shirts and tees, and in those it looks like a robot bug has been glued to your neck. People will notice. People noticed. A few assumed it was a medical device — and it certainly looks like one. The combination of a cold surface and a hot body also generates a fair amount of condensation underneath your top, although I'd still take that over sweating. Thankfully, the Pro Plus is splash- and sweat-resistant. Wrap-up Nothing else really does what Sony's Reon devices do, effectively. Shark's $150 ChillPill is the closest thing, and it's a smarter take on the handheld fan than most, bundling a cooling plate and a Dry Touch mister alongside the fan mechanism. But misting fans are fussy and largely futile on a packed commuter train, and can be completely ineffective during high humidity. You also have to hold the thing, or prop it up somehow. That's one benefit of the Reon I didn't appreciate until weeks in: it's entirely hands-free.

item.title: Samsung's wild new Odyssey lineup includes a 1,100Hz gaming monitor
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 2.00
Samsung's wild new Odyssey lineup includes a 1,100Hz gaming monitor Also shown off was the 49-inch Odyssey OLED G9. Samsung has been showing off a quartet of gaming monitors at Gamescom, and they're equipped with frankly ridiculous technology that we puny humans are arguably not even capable of truly appreciating. But hey, they sure are fun to write about. There's glorious overkill wherever you look with this lot, but let's start with the 27-inch Odyssey G6, which Samsung has proudly dubbed the world's first 1,100Hz gaming monitor. The final refresh rate makes the finished G6 (somewhat hilariously) an extra 60Hz smoother than the 1,040Hz prototype Samsung unveiled ahead of CES last year. In either case, we are firmly in the territory of talking about refresh rates that are way beyond what the human eye is even able to perceive, but this monitor is clearly intended for the most hardcore esports edge cases only. Response time is 1ms, and to take advantage of the maximum 1,100Hz refresh rate you'll need to settle for 1080p. Knock it down to 600Hz and you can play at 1440p through Dual Mode. This one has an IPS display, and will be available in the second half of 2026, though Samsung is yet to reveal pricing details. Next, and only slightly less bonkers, is the Odyssey OLED G8, a 32-inch 4K monitor that can switch between three different refresh rates. The lowest of these is 4K at 360Hz (already faster than most mere mortals could ever need), then you move up to 520Hz at 1440p and 680Hz at 1080p. You get support for FreeSync Premium Pro and G-Sync, while Samsung's Glare Free anti-reflection coating should prevent unsightly reflections during daytime play. Again, no prices have been announced yet. Samsung also revealed the 49-inch Odyssey OLED G9, a 360Hz DQHD (5,120 x 1,440) monitor which is also a world-first at that size. It's a QD-OLED Penta Tandem panel with a peak brightness of 1,300 nits. Switch to the 2,560 x 720 Dual HD mode and you can crank the refresh rate up to 720Hz. It's another case of total excess, then, from the display's humongous dimensions right through to its display tech. Rounding off the 2027 Odyssey lineup is the Odyssey OLED G7, a (you guessed it) world-first 42-inch curved OLED monitor with a taller 16:9 aspect ratio than the entire desk-spanning G9. It rocks a 165Hz refresh rate, 1000R curvature and max 4K resolution. We don't know exactly when this one is coming either, or how much it will cost.

item.title: Why pissaladière is the perfect taste of late summer
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 3.06
Why pissaladière is the perfect taste of late summer Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. A savoury tart of caramelised onions beneath a latticework of salted anchovies and black olives, pissaladière may be the perfect late-summer dish. “Have it with a glass of rosé and you’re instantly in the south of France,” says food writer Sudi Pigott. “You’ve got sweetness from the onions, saltiness from anchovies, acidity from olives and fat from pastry. The perfect harmony,” says chef Adam Byatt of Michelin-starred Trinity in Clapham, where the dish has been on the menu every summer for 20 years. “Once you’ve got the ingredients, all you’re doing is constructing and letting the oven do its work.” Though the dish originates from Genoa and is often called “French pizza”, pissaladière’s name derives from peis salat, the Old Provençal name for salted fish. This was mixed with olive oil, herbs and spices to produce a sauce called pissalat, which was spread over bread, before adding onions, then baked. A pastry base is now more common. In his forthcoming book Trinity: The Cookbook, Byatt suggests using rough puff pastry “as it doesn’t rise as much”. In the south of France you also find the dish made with fougasse (similar to Italian focaccia) or other yeasted doughs. “Lighter puff pastry works better if you’re having pissaladière as a snack,” says French Classics author and chef Matthew Ryle. “For lunch or dinner, I prefer a more substantial bread.” Pissalat may be the traditional topping, but good luck finding any. Or making it yourself. In Consider the Anchovy, Pigott recounts tracking down a jar in a Nice market, where a stallholder explained the laborious process of macerating, sieving and pounding it requires. When asked how she uses the condiment, she answered: “As you anglais might use ketchup. In everything.” Pissalat adds “oomph, though it can be a bit much”, says Pigott, who compensates for the lack of it in her recipe by cooking the onions with garlic, rosemary, thyme and bay leaves. She uses red onions with shallots. Byatt prefers Italian white onions for their sweetness, cooked “low and slow” until they turn dark and jammy. To finish, top the pastry with the onions, decorate with Niçoise black olives and Ortiz or Consorcio anchovies, then bake for 20 minutes. Serve it just above room temperature. “If not as an appetiser, offer a crisp green salad alongside for a supremely pleasing supper,” says Pigott. “It adds a Riviera riff to picnic food too – if it survives late-night fridge raids.” Comments

item.title: Look For These New Nonstop Flights Taking Off In 2027
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 6.90
Planning for your next trip can never start soon enough, especially if you are hoping to score a good deal or redeem frequent flyer miles on your flight. That’s why staying on top of the newest airline route launches can be helpful. After all, that’s often when mileage redemption seats can be easier to find. And there are quite a few to consider now for the year ahead. This week, United unveiled a slew of new and innovative routes. The carrier has made headlines in recent years for adding dots to its map that no other U.S. airline offers, like Greenland, Madeira in Portugal and Mongolia. And the delivery of its new Airbus A321-XLRs allows it to serve smaller cities that would otherwise not see flights using widebody aircraft capacity. These are some of the latest airline route announcements to keep in mind as you plan travel for the year ahead. United If you belong to United MileagePlus, your miles just got a whole lot more interesting. United is adding flights in the coming year with fervor. Expect nonstop flights from its Newark hub to Luxembourg; Ljublana, Slovenia; Olbia and Catania in Italy; Ibiza and Valencia in Spain; Marseille, France; and Terceira, Portugal in the Azores. For many of these cities, United’s arrival will be the only long-haul flight from the U.S. fueling tourism, business and cargo demand. It will also connect the dots from Washington Dulles to Toulouse, France and Milan Malpensa, Italy. To Japan, new flights from San Francisco to Okinawa and Los Angeles to Osaka are also planned. A Denver-Paris link connects its Rocky Mountains hub to the French capital. All of these flights are scheduled to start in the spring of 2027. Bermudair Bermudair is adding the first-ever link between the New York area (via Newark airport) and South Caicos in the Turks and Caicos. Previously, travelers would have to take a boat or small plane from Providenciales instead. The route will start Dec. 20, just in time for the holiday season, and operate twice weekly. The growing airline coordinates with smaller destinations that don’t have nonstop airlift from the U.S., to fill a gap that larger airlines are not filling. This route, for example, began in a partnership with Salterra, A Luxury Collection Resort & Spa on the island. The 85-acre Marriott Bonvoy property is just a 10-minute drive from South Caicos airport. Alaska Airlines Alaska Airlines is extending its transoceanic footprint even farther for the next summer season, announcing new seasonal, nonstop service from its Seattle/Tacoma hub to both Athens and Paris starting next May. These destinations join its existing long-haul service across the Atlantic to London Heathrow, Reykjavik and Rome. The flights will operate with the carrier’s new Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft, which were added in the recent merger with Hawaiian Airlines. The carrier now has seven long-haul destinations with plans to almost double that from its Seattle hub by 2030. Delta Delta Air Lines has new routes of its own, including one set to start this fall and offering huge cash and SkyMiles discounts. Nonstop service between Atlanta and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia will connect the two SkyTeam hubs and help with the growing push for tourism by kingdom officials. Those not staying in Riyadh can also make connections to Saudia and Riyadh Air flights to other points across the Middle East and Asia. This is in addition to recently announced nonstop flights from Austin to Paris CDG (the first nonstop between the French and Texan capitals) and Los Angeles to Manila, both starting next March. The announcement also comes on the heels of Delta opening its second business class Delta One Lounge at LAX. On the island vacation front, it will fly from Detroit to Aruba and New York JFK to Liberia, Costa Rica starting this December. It is also moving its JFK to Bermuda flight to depart from New York LaGuardia instead. And for those looking to expedite their Medallion earnings, all of these routes are available to book via Delta Vacations. In doing so, your spending on flights and hotels all count toward Medallion Qualification Dollars, inching you closer to elite status for next year. American American made a splash earlier this year by returning to Venezuela, the first U.S. carrier to do so in years. Nonstop flights between Miami and Maracaibo began earlier this year in addition to its Caracas flights (although these are on hold due to recent earthquake damage). On the long-haul front, American is adding service between Chicago and Kahului, Maui in December. This is in addition to American’s new flights to two airports in south Florida that were previously reserved for private flights. Both Vero Beach and Naples, Florida will be connected to the airline’s global hubs. Naples gets double daily service to Charlotte while Vero Beach gets a weekly flight to Philadelphia in addition to its regular flights to Charlotte. Vero Beach also has new service on Breeze and JetBlue. Like United, American will also use its new Airbus A321-XLR to connect Philadelphia with Porto, Portugal, its second destination there. Other Airlines In May, JetBlue launched new service between Boston and Milan Malpensa. Star Alliance member Avianca will begin flights between Fort Lauderdale and both Barranquilla and Cali, Colombia. This brings the airline’s Colombian route map from the airport to four cities. Maverick air carrier JSX is adding a new flight between Santa Monica and Oakland, California starting in September, with all passengers enjoying a business class experience. And if you have a United Explorer Card, it comes with $100 each card anniversary year to use on JSX flights (refunded in the form of a statement credit). MORE FROM FORBES

item.title: 6 Essential Stops On Your Own Odyssey Across The Mediterranean
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.50
The critical and box office success of The Odyssey has aroused a lot of interest in the places where director Christopher Nolan filmed one of the most gorgeous movies of recent times. Tourist boards and travel agencies are already churning out itineraries that include places (in six different countries) where the epic film was shot on location. But here’s a different angle: How about undertaking an island-hopping Mediterranean odyssey to the places that might have been the real-life locations of Homer’s fictional tale? Other than Ithaca and Troy (and possibly the Strait of Messina) there’s no proof that any of the other places ever existed. But that’s half the fun: Visiting the spots mentioned in the book and imagining the extraordinary things that might have taken place. Ithaca (Greece) This is the easy one. It’s an actual island in the Ionian archipelago of western Greece. There’s no archaeological evidence to suggest the island was ever ruled by anyone named Odysseus (or his wife Penelope). Ancient coins bearing his image have been discovered in Ithaca, but these were minted several hundred years after Homer wrote the epic and were likely based on his story rather than a real person. Having said as much, the island does boast a Palace of Odysseus, a hilltop complex overlooking the sea that’s been dated to around the 13th century BC, so it would have existed during the Late Bronze Age when the story was and centuries later during Homer’s time. Nowadays Ithaca is far more famed for its excellent beaches, turquoise coves, hiking trails through olive groves, and picturesque villages like Frikes and Vathy. Troy (Türkiye) Discovered in the 1870s by amateur archeologists Heinrich Schliemann and Frank Calvert — who then plundered the ruins of many buried treasures — Troy is definitely a real place. There is evidence that battles took place on the site, although nothing has yet been uncovered that conclusively proves the Trojan War or its legendary horse. The modern archaeological park contains ruins dating back around 5,000 years, with Bronze Age walls and Roman structures among the best preserved. Opened in 2018, a new museum houses artifacts from Troy and other nearby ancient sites. And you can climb inside a full-scale replica of the Trojan Horse. Djerba (Tunisia) Odysseus made several eventful landfalls on what is believed to have been the coast of North Africa including a brief encounter with the Lotophages (“Lotus-Eaters”). His men tripped out on the abundant lotus fruit, a narcotic ecstasy that had them refusing to reboard their ship until forced by Odysseus. Nowadays Djerba offers a different kind of bliss — the sun, sand and sea of a Mediterranean beach holiday. The coast boasts a number of large, five-star, all-inclusive beach resorts, as well as Arabian palace-style spa hotels. Djerba also offers an array of water sports and four-by-four trips into the desert on the nearby Tunisian mainland. But no more lotus fruit. Sardinia (Italy) Depicted as both mermaids and women with birdlike bodies, the Sirens of Greek mythology lured sailors into the rocks (and their deaths). Odysseus told his men to stuff beeswax in their ears to avoid their enticing songs and had himself lashed to the ships mast so he could listen without being able to react as they sailed past a rocky coast. As to where that transpired, some historians point to Sardinia as a possible location. Two different spots on the island have embraced the legend. The Golfo Aranci, a scenic bay on the northeast coast, is graced by Il Canto della Sirena, a bronze statue by Pietro Longu that mechanically rises from the sea as alluring music plays from loudspeakers on shore. On the southwest coast, Sirena Sardinia Diving School offers guided dives to the Pinnacle of Salidu and a bas-relief of a mermaid hugging a dolphin at the entrance to an underwater cave. Strait of Messina (Italy) Two of the most dangerous challenges faced by Odysseus and his crew transpired in the Strait of Messina, the waterway that divides Sicily and mainland Italy. First, they had to navigate around Charybdis, a massive whirlpool that threatened to suck them underwater. Second, they had to avoid the six-headed Scylla, a carnivorous she-monster that lived among cliffs on the mainland side. While either would make a terrific tourist attraction today, they are both products of Greek mythology and Homer’s imagination. What modern Messina does flaunt is an unspoiled Sicilian ambience of ancient churches, flamboyant fountains and superb seafood restaurants set around a busy little harbor protected by a golden statue of the Virgin Mary. Crowning a mountaintop on the outskirts of Messina, the Sanctuary of Dinnammare provides a panoramic view of the entire strait. Gozo (Malta) Some scholars point to Gozo as a possible location of Ogygia, the island where Odysseus was shipwrecked (after his boat was destroyed by Zeus) and where he was mesmerized for seven years by the seductive sea nymph Calypso. Gozo was already well known in the Greek world when Homer penned the epic poem. And Calypso (if she existed) certainly wasn’t the only person living there. But that’s beside the point. Modern Gozo is one of the most enchanting islands in the entire Mediterranean, a mosaic of baroque churches and citadels, towering sea cliffs and rocky swimming holes, coastal hiking trails and Ramla Bay with its red-sand beach. A 25-minute ferry ride from “mainland” Malta, Gozo offers fresh-off-the-boat seafood (try the aljotta fish soup) and a range of accommodation from posh beach resorts and modern boutique hotels to charming old harborside hotels.

item.title: The Safest Cities In The U.S. For 2026, According To A MoneyGeek Report
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.25
Looking for the safest cities in the U.S.? MoneyGeek has released its annual report on the safest cities in America. The report analyzes the latest FBI city-level crime data alongside the economic costs associated with crime to rank 315 cities across the country, including a look at the safest big cities in the U.S. I’ve been covering MoneyGeek’s annual safety report since 2022, and its approach is different from many other reports of the safest cities in the U.S. Rather than focusing solely on crime rates, MoneyGeek attempts to quantify the broader impact of crime by translating violent and property crimes into an estimated societal cost. The result offers another way to compare safety across cities of different sizes. You can see how the results have changed in my coverage from 2023, 2024 and 2025. To determine the 2026 results, MoneyGeek evaluated 315 cities with populations over 100,000, using the latest available FBI city-level crime data, which covers crimes reported in 2024. The analysis considered violent crimes including murder, rape, robbery and aggravated assault, as well as property crimes such as burglary, larceny and motor vehicle theft. MoneyGeek then combined those figures with published research assigning an estimated societal cost to different types of crime. Those costs include direct expenses such as medical care, property loss, criminal justice and lost productivity, as well as harder-to-quantify impacts such as pain, suffering and reduced quality of life. The estimates have been adjusted to 2026 dollars. The result is a crime cost per capita that accounts not only for how frequently crimes occur, but also for their severity. According to the research MoneyGeek uses, one murder carries the same estimated societal cost as 84 aggravated assaults. According to Nathan Paulus, senior director of content and SEO at MoneyGeek, that distinction can produce some surprising results. “Most crime is property crime. Most of the cost of crime isn’t, and that’s why some of the safest cities on this list have property crime rates you’d expect from a much rougher place,” Paulus told me in an interview. Bellevue, Washington, is a good example. It ranks No. 29 out of 315 cities on the list, despite having a higher property crime rate than 223 cities that rank below it, including New York, Miami, Las Vegas, Phoenix and Los Angeles. For travelers, the findings offer another data point when researching a destination, and Paulus says it’s worth looking beyond a city’s overall ranking. “A murder and a stolen bicycle both count as one crime in a crime rate, which is why cost tells you more than the rate alone,” he says. “If you’re traveling, skip the ranking and read the property crime column instead: that’s the crime you’re most likely to meet, and it moves independently of a city’s overall rank.” For people considering where to live, the report can also help put the broader financial implications of crime into context, since crime can affect everything from property values and insurance costs to local government spending. The Safest City In The U.S. For 2026, Carmel, Indiana, leads the list as the safest city in America. Located just north of Indianapolis, Carmel has an estimated crime cost of just $186 per resident, the lowest of all 315 cities analyzed in the report. What puts Carmel at the top is its exceptionally low level of violent crime. “Carmel has the lowest violent crime rate of any city in the ranking, and violent crime is what this method weights most heavily. It didn’t need the lowest property crime rate to finish first, and it doesn’t have one,” says Paulus. Carmel has a violent crime rate of 66 incidents per 100,000 residents, the lowest in the study. Its property crime rate is 813 per 100,000 residents, demonstrating the distinction between simply counting crimes and MoneyGeek’s approach of factoring in their estimated societal costs. Carmel is followed by Allen, Texas, which ranks second with an estimated crime cost of $277 per resident. Ramapo Town, New York—last year’s safest city in America—comes in third at $285 per resident, followed by Fishers, Indiana ($310) and Amherst Town, New York ($324). Carmel isn’t entirely new to the top of MoneyGeek’s rankings. It ranked fourth in the 2023 edition of the report. But there’s also an important caveat when comparing results from year to year: The universe of cities included in the analysis can change depending on the availability of FBI crime data. “Some of the movement between editions is the field changing rather than the cities changing. We added cities that couldn’t be ranked before because their crime reporting was incomplete,” says Paulus. This year, MoneyGeek evaluated 315 cities, compared with 292 in last year’s report. The Safest Large Cities In The U.S. MoneyGeek’s report also ranks the safest large cities in the U.S., looking specifically at cities with populations over 300,000. This part of the report is particularly interesting because it allows for a more apples-to-apples comparison among major American cities. For the third year in a row, Irvine, California, ranks as the safest large city in America. With an estimated crime cost of $447 per resident, Irvine also ranks No. 19 among all 315 cities in the study. “Irvine has been the safest large city three editions running now, not just this one. It gets there on violent crime: No city its size in the ranking has a lower rate,” says Paulus. Irvine has a violent crime rate of just 84 incidents per 100,000 residents. Coming in No. 2 on the large cities list is Virginia Beach, Virginia, with an estimated crime cost of $645 per resident. Honolulu, Hawaii ($664), Henderson, Nevada ($924) and El Paso, Texas ($951) round out the five safest large cities in the U.S. Honolulu is also notable for another reason: With more than 900,000 residents, it is one of the largest cities in the analysis, yet its estimated crime cost per capita remains among the lowest in the country. Another interesting comparison is Henderson and nearby Las Vegas. Henderson ranks No. 95 overall, with an estimated crime cost of $924 per resident, while Las Vegas ranks No. 179, at $1,819 per resident. Safety: Why Crime Costs Matter One of the most revealing aspects of MoneyGeek’s report is what happens at the other end of the rankings. Because the methodology weighs crimes according to their estimated societal costs, a city doesn’t necessarily need to have the highest overall crime rate to have one of the highest costs of crime. Birmingham, Alabama—the lowest ranking city in the report—illustrates this point. It has the highest estimated crime cost in this year’s analysis, at $10,152 per resident, followed closely by Memphis, Tennessee, at $10,074. “Birmingham doesn’t have the most crime in this ranking. It has the deadliest crime, and at the bottom of a list like this, that’s what decides the order,” says Paulus. The numbers help explain why. Memphis reported 6.3 times as many violent offenses and 5.4 times as many property offenses as Birmingham. But Birmingham reported 115 murders compared with 249 in Memphis, despite having roughly one-third of Memphis’s population. That gives Birmingham a homicide rate about 45% higher than Memphis. And because homicide carries such a high estimated societal cost in MoneyGeek’s methodology, it has an outsized effect on Birmingham’s results. Homicide accounts for about 79% of Birmingham’s estimated crime cost, roughly $8,000 of its $10,152 per-resident total. In Memphis, homicide accounts for about 56% of the estimated cost. The report also shows why total crime cost can be misleading when comparing cities of dramatically different sizes. New York City has the highest overall annual cost of crime in the country at approximately $13.9 billion, but on a per-capita basis, it’s not the most dangerous: New York City ranks No. 166 out of 315 cities. That distinction gets back to the premise behind MoneyGeek’s methodology: The number of crimes alone doesn’t necessarily capture their impact. Looking at cost per resident makes it possible to compare cities of different sizes while also accounting for the severity of the crimes taking place. Read on for the 15 safest cities in the U.S. and the 10 safest big cities in the U.S. In MoneyGeek’s original report, “Safest and Most Dangerous Cities in America by Cost of Crime,” you can see the ranking of all 315 cities, including the lowest-ranking cities in the U.S. Ranked: The 15 Safest Cities in the U.S. for 2026 - Carmel, Indiana - Allen, Texas - Ramapo Town, New York - Fishers, Indiana - Amherst Town, New York - Naperville, Illinois - Sugar Land, Texas - Temecula, California - Gilbert, Arizona - Centennial, Colorado - Chandler, Arizona - Cary, North Carolina - Goodyear, Arizona - Meridian, Idaho - Carrollton, Texas Ranked: The 10 Safest Big Cities in the U.S. for 2026 - Irvine, California - Virginia Beach, Virginia - Honolulu, Hawaii - Henderson, Nevada - El Paso, Texas - San Diego, California - Lexington, Kentucky - Mesa, Arizona - Omaha, Nebraska - Boston, Massachusetts MORE FROM FORBES:

item.title: Navigating 6 Of Europe’s Most Popular Cruise Departure Ports
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.20
Barcelona, Marseille, Rome and Southampton are familiar names on European cruise itineraries, but busy ports do not all perform the same role. Some welcome thousands of passengers for a few hours of sightseeing. Others are turnaround ports, where one group leaves the ship and another checks in to begin a vacation. For travelers choosing a European cruise, a major departure port generally means more ships, more sailing dates and a wider choice of itineraries. A definitive ranking is difficult because European ports report statistics differently. Some publish total traffic, including day visitors, while others separate passengers embarking and disembarking from those making transit calls. British statistics, for example, exclude transit passengers but count round-trip passengers at both departure and arrival. Even so, the latest data reveals a clear group of leading departure hubs. Southampton, England Few European ports are as closely associated with beginning a cruise as Southampton. British government statistics recorded 2.6 million international cruise passenger movements through the port in 2025, excluding passengers visiting during a port call. Southampton is especially important to P&O Cruises and Cunard, while its five cruise terminals also serve international operators including Royal Caribbean, Princess Cruises, MSC Cruises and Norwegian Cruise Line. Its greatest strength is the sheer choice of sailings. For overseas passengers, however, the transfer from the major London airports makes a pre-cruise hotel stay sensible, even though Southampton has its own smaller airport. Barcelona, Spain Barcelona combines a major cruise hub with one of Europe’s most popular urban destinations. In 2025, passengers embarking or disembarking accounted for 58% of its cruise traffic, demonstrating that Barcelona is far more than a day-call destination. The port is a key starting point for Western Mediterranean itineraries, often combining Spanish, French and Italian ports. Extensive international air connections also make it relatively straightforward for North American travelers to reach. However, cruise tourism has become politically contentious. The city and port have agreed to reduce the number of cruise terminals from seven to five by 2030 as part of a broader attempt to manage visitor numbers and port traffic, along with implementing a hike in cruise passenger tax earlier than planned. Civitavecchia, Italy Cruise lines commonly market Civitavecchia as Rome, although the port is a separate coastal city requiring a transfer from the Italian capital and its airports. Despite that complication, Civitavecchia is one of Europe’s cruise giants. It handled a record 3.56 million cruise passenger movements in 2025, including 1.73 million embarkation and disembarkation movements. Its appeal is straightforward: passengers can combine time in Rome with a voyage through the Western or Eastern Mediterranean. Arriving at least one night before departure allows time for sightseeing and reduces the risk of flight or transfer delays resulting in a missed sailing. Hamburg, Germany Hamburg’s scale can be overlooked outside the German-speaking cruise market. More than 1.4 million cruise passengers embarked from the city during 2025, an increase from approximately 1.3 million the previous year. AIDA Cruises has a substantial presence, but ships from MSC Cruises and several international lines also use Hamburg. Its location makes the city a natural starting point for voyages to Norway, Northern European cities, the British Isles and destinations farther into the North Atlantic. The port operates several terminals, so travelers must check exactly where their ship is docked. The newer HafenCity terminal is integrated into a major waterfront development with subway and bus connections, while Steinwerder generally requires more planning. Also popular with the German market, Kiel is particularly well positioned for cruises into the Baltic and Scandinavia. The port handled 1.11 million cruise passengers from 187 ship calls in 2025, its busiest season to date by passenger numbers. Piraeus, Greece Piraeus serves as the cruise gateway to Athens and a natural launch point for voyages through the Greek islands and Eastern Mediterranean. The port handled 1.86 million cruise passenger movements in 2025, an all-time high. Approximately 1.09 million were homeport passengers, continuing rapid growth from just over one million in 2024. Piraeus offers access to island-focused itineraries featuring destinations such as Mykonos, Santorini, Rhodes and Crete, often alongside Turkish ports. A pre-cruise stay in Athens is worthwhile, although passengers should remember that the terminals are in the separate port city of Piraeus. Copenhagen, Denmark Copenhagen is not Europe’s largest cruise departure port, but it is one of the most useful for international travelers planning a cruise around Scandinavia or the Baltic region. The Danish capital welcomed almost 866,500 cruise passengers across 316 calls in 2025. Of those calls, 111 were turnarounds, meaning the ship began or ended an itinerary and changed passengers in Copenhagen. Copenhagen’s strongest advantage is the destination itself. The city offers enough museums, architecture, food and waterfront neighborhoods to justify arriving several days before departure rather than treating it simply as a place to board the ship. Choosing A European Cruise Departure Port An embarkation port should be seen as more than simply the place where passengers board the ship. For North American travelers flying to Europe, cities such as Barcelona, Rome and Copenhagen can add another destination to the vacation, making a pre-cruise stay feel like an extra port of call. Southampton offers exceptional itinerary choice, while Hamburg and Kiel provide access to a cruise market that can be less visible to English-speaking travelers. Piraeus is hard to beat for island-focused Eastern Mediterranean routes. The best departure port is ultimately the one combining the right itinerary with manageable flights and a city worth visiting before the ship leaves. MORE FROM FORBES

item.title: New Mexico Tourism Board And Chex Mix BOLD Rev Up For Route 66’s 100th Year
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.08
With Route 66 turning 100 this year, the U.S. state that’s home to the longest continuous stretch of the Mother Road is offering a snack that’s tied to a special sweepstakes. The New Mexico Tourism Department has partnered with General Mills to create a limited-edition Chex Mix BOLD bag commemorating the state and its association with this iconic road. According to Nicole Barker, the department’s media relations manager, the tourism board has been planning how to honor New Mexico’s role in Route 66’s centennial for the past few years. “We saw an opportunity to bring that story to life through a brand that feels quintessentially American and synonymous with road trips,” explained Barker. “Chex Mix BOLD was a natural fit. It’s a nostalgic, family-friendly snack that has long been a staple for travelers hitting the road.” This special edition Chex Mix BOLD incorporates packaging inspired by New Mexico and Route 66. It’s marketed as having a garlic and herb flavor. The front side of this Chex Mix BOLD bag sports illustrations of hot air balloons, desert scenery, a classic car and a “Welcome to New Mexico” road sign. This special snack run started when the staff at New Mexico Tourism Board connected with General Mills’ Salty Snacks team through Instagram. “From there, the collaboration came together as a fun and unexpected way to introduce travelers to New Mexico’s legendary stretch of Route 66,” added Barker. Barker noted that this New Mexico-themed Chex Mix BOLD packaging has been rolled out at participating convenience stores across the United States. If you don’t come across this special bag in your travels, here’s another way to potentially connect with the Mother Road and the Land of Enchantment (New Mexico’s state nickname). A “Chex Mix™ Hits the Road in New Mexico” sweepstakes offer a chance to engage with the collaboration and for contest entrants to experience New Mexico’s iconic stretch of Route 66 for themselves. New Mexico Magazine is partnering on this sweepstakes, which offers the chance for travelers to win a curated Route 66 adventure for two. The grand prize includes five nights of hotel accommodations across Gallup, Albuquerque, Santa Fe and Tucumcari; a VIP experience at Acoma Pueblo Sky City; passes from the Museum Foundation of New Mexico; a $1,000 airline gift card; and a mid-size rental car to use for the duration of the trip. The deadline for entering the sweepstakes is August 31, 2026 at 11:59:59 p.m. ET. “Route 66 is one of the most celebrated road trips in the country, so offering a curated New Mexico adventure was a natural extension of the campaign and an exciting way to inspire people to start planning their own journey along the Mother Road,” said Barker. Along with the Chex Mix BOLD collaboration, the New Mexico Tourism Department has been implementing various special events, storytelling measures and marketing efforts throughout 2026 to spotlight the communities, businesses, people, culture and experiences linked to New Mexico’s stretch of Route 66. In addition to major cities, other stops in New Mexico along Route 66 extend to Pecos, Santa Rosa, Moriarty, Grants and Laguna Pueblo.

item.title: Up To 90 American Tourists Thought Missing In Nepal Floods—Here’s Why Accurate Numbers Are Hard To Come By
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.62
Topline More than four dozen Americans are missing in Nepal’s flash floods, Nepal’s tourism organization estimates—but with no real-time registry of Americans traveling abroad, the State Department has struggled to provide accurate numbers in similar crises. Key Facts At least 389 people have been killed in catastrophic flash floods that swept through the border region between Nepal and Tibet, according to Nepalese authorities. At least 667 people, including 65 Americans, are missing, according to the latest update from the Nepal Tourism Board. As of 8 a.m. EDT, the State Department was “aware of approximately 90 Americans who may be impacted by the floods in Nepal/China cross-border region” and “not aware of any U.S. citizen deaths,” an agency spokesperson told Forbes. Officials in Nepal said the disaster appeared to be "triggered by a landslide associated with a glacial event in the Himalayan region, sending a sudden and destructive surge of water downstream." The State Department said Wednesday the agency was “closely monitoring the situation and is deploying a disaster response advisor to the region” and will provide $500,000 in assistance through its global award with Catholic Relief Services.” Crucial Quote “We’ve called Nepal and we’ve offered any help that they need. You know, we have a very good relationship with Nepal and that was brutal,” President Donald Trump said Thursday in the Oval Office. “Nobody’s ever seen anything quite like that where very powerful, strong, well-built buildings were wiped out like they were toothpicks.” The Rescue Operation Is Ongoing Early Thursday morning, the Nepal Tourism Board released a list of 27 individuals rescued in the Rasuwa area, including two U.S. citizens: 52-year-old Anjana Raja and 55-year-old Pattabiraman Venkatesan. They have been released and are in good health, NBC News reported. The State Department told Forbes it is aware of a third American who was “safely rescued in Nepal.” U.S. Government’s Difficulty In Accounting For Missing Citizens Americans are not required to tell an embassy when they enter or leave a country and the State Department does not have a real-time registry of Americans traveling abroad. During an international disaster, the department has to build numbers based on calls from families, data from local authorities, and information from airlines, hotels and tour operators—and then eliminate duplicates and fact-check whether the people in question were actually in the affected area. The State Department strongly encourages travelers to enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP), a free and voluntary service where U.S. citizens and nationals can share travel plans abroad so they can be quickly contacted in case of emergency. But since relatively few travelers enroll, State Department officials cannot rely on STEP to produce an accurate, real-time count of Americans in a country. During the 2024 Haiti crisis, for example, State Department spokesman Matthew Miller said “it’s impossible for us to know for sure” how many Americans were in Haiti because most U.S. citizens don’t register with the government when they travel abroad. Twenty years earlier, the State Department received more than 30,000 inquiries about Americans who might have been affected in the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. Officials had to painstakingly work through the cases individually, using families, airlines, hotels, tour operators, foreign governments and people on the ground to determine who was actually in the disaster area. Ultimately, the State Department determined that 33 U.S. citizens died in the tsunami. Key Background A flash flood entered Nepal through the Bhote Koshi River in Rasuwa at 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday, sending a torrent of water through Himalayan villages. “A group of scientists believe a glacier may have broken off and fallen into the valley below, which triggered or at least compounded the effect of the landslide,” CNN reported. A sizable number of the foreign tourists and travelers missing or stranded in the northern border region were thought to be on a pilgrimage to 21,000-foot Mount Kailash, a sacred Himalayan peak in southwestern Tibet, near China’s borders with Nepal and India. It holds significance for Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and the Tibetan Bon tradition. Chinese authorities warned on Thursday that a barrier lake on the Nepal-Tibet border could breach in the coming days, further complicating rescue efforts. The U.S. mission in China, which includes the embassy in Beijing, has warned Americans in China that “continued rainfall and unstable slopes sustain the risk of secondary landslides and additional outburst floods.” Further Reading A Looming Flood Disaster Question — How Fast Is Nepal Warming? (Forbes)

item.title: This Buzzy City Has Been Ranked Europe’s Most Affordable Fall Escape
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.17
Shoulder season vacations are booming as travelers opt to schedule trips during cooler weather and when there are fewer crowds, with the result that a once more affordable travel period is becoming more expensive. But you can still find wallet-friendly prices in Europe if you know where to go. Research by the UK travel agency Thomas Cook analyzed a range of cost factors and shows there are 13 cities offering a full day of sightseeing, food and refreshments, local transit and accommodation in a mid-range hotel for €100 ($116) a day or less, per person. Albania’s Capital City Is The Most Affordable Fall Destinations Of all the city trips that offer exceptional value, Tirana comes up top, with an average daily cost of just €59 ($68) this September. Albania’s capital city boasts beautiful architecture, a lively cafe culture and easy access to beaches, national parks and lakes. While Albania has become one of Europe’s fastest-growing tourism markets, it’s still under the radar compared to destinations like Italy or Spain, so tourists can enjoy much quieter sightseeing and all-around great value. There is an abundance of three-star accommodation options (116) with an average cost of €32 ($37) per person, per night in early September, offering travelers great value on what is typically the most expensive part of the trip. Foodies will be delighted by the low cost of eating out, too. The average price of dinner at an inexpensive restaurant is €8.50 ($9.86), while a coffee (€1.99 / $2.30) and a local beer (€1.50 / $1.74) are also very affordable. You can also explore Tirana’s history and culture at wallet-friendly prices, with the average cost of paid attractions coming in at €4.50 ($5.22). The city’s Blloku district, once reserved exclusively for Communist Party elites, is now Tirana's trendiest quarter, packed with cafe terraces, bars and independent boutiques. Romania’s Capital Is A Budget-Friendly City Bucharest, the capital of Romania, comes in as the second most affordable European vacation. It earned the nickname Little Paris when prominent French and European architects were hired to redesign the city’s center. Bucharest now has an eclectic architectural mix, from the Palace of the Parliament, one of the world's largest administrative buildings, to the neoclassical Romanian Athenaeum. A getaway here comes in at an average daily cost of just €66 ($77) per person. Average accommodation prices are around €32 ($37) per person per night and there are 176 three-star options to choose from. Eating out is also very affordable, with dinner costing just over €12 (under $14) on average and lunch at a fast-food restaurant costing under €7 ($8). Paid-for tourist attractions are slightly more expensive than in Tirana, but still cost under €9 ($10) on average. A daily bus pass (around €1.50 / $1.74) is also inexpensive, offering tourists hassle-free travel around the city. Affordable Vacation Spots In Europe For Fall Antalya, a city on Turkey’s coastline, offers tourists great value too (€78 / $90 a day). This includes affordable accommodation (€36 / $42), and the cost of eating out is among the lowest in the study. Both dinner and fast-food lunches can cost under €9 ($10) per person. However, the average cost of tourist attractions is slightly higher than that of other affordable destinations on the list, at €19 ($22). But budget-conscious visitors can also explore attractions such as Kaleiçi, Antalya’s Old Town, and Hadrian’s Gate for free. Antalya was also recently ranked the best destination to catch some fall sunshine. Poland’s capital, Warsaw, offers great value for tourists too, with an average daily cost of €78 ($90). The city’s Old Town is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site after it was meticulously rebuilt after WWII. Aside from its historical significance, it boasts a vibrant nightlife and cultural scene. For smart spenders, the city’s top museums and galleries also offer free admission on set days. Accommodation costs an average of €41 ($48) per person per night, while the average cost of tourist attractions is under €8 ($9). Eating out is also affordable, with an average dinner costing under €11 ($12), while lunch at a fast-food restaurant is under €10 ($11). Rounding up the top five most affordable European city trips is Istanbul, Turkey. Turkey’s largest city boasts incredible architecture, history, and a bustling cultural scene. It’ll cost travelers around €82 ($95) a day to enjoy a full day out in the city. Hotels in Istanbul are among the most affordable in the study, costing €28 ($32) per person, per night at a three-star hotel on average. Eating out is also affordable, with dinners and lunches costing a roughly €9 ($10) and €8 ($9), respectively. Getting around the city is also hassle-free thanks to an extensive public transit system; a daily bus pass will cost travelers under €4 ($4.60).

item.title: Inside The Nuclear Bunker Becoming Canada’s Strangest Luxury Hotel
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 3.91
Most luxury hotels sell the view, but The Diefenbaker has no windows. Hidden beneath a grassy hill in Debert, Nova Scotia, the two-story, 64,000-square-foot complex was built in 1964 to withstand nuclear attack. Its thick concrete walls and blast doors are being converted into 50 privately owned suites that operate as a boutique hotel when their owners are away. The concept blends a hotel, a private members club, and a doomsday shelter. Guests can book an underground stay with access to a spa, fitness center, gourmet dining, a coffee shop, and a cigar lounge. Owners buy a more permanent asset: a secure suite they can reclaim if an emergency closes the hotel and the bunker returns to its original purpose. Renovations started in 2025, and project co-owner Paul Mansfield reports that about $8 million has been invested so far. The plan is to finish the first 15 suites in 2027, with the rest ready by the end of 2028. Since the transformation is ongoing, the hotel experience, security, and long-term survival systems are still in the planning stage and have not yet been tested. The hotel program stands out as the most unique part of the business model. When owners are away, their suites are available for booking, and the revenue is shared between the owner and the developer. If there is a real emergency, hotel guests have to leave so owners can come back. Most of the time, it operates like a luxury vacation rental, but the main reason to buy a suite only becomes clear if an emergency actually happens. There are 50 suites, split into two types. Palisade Suites are about 300 square feet and work well for one or two people. They have 14-foot ceilings, a private loft, and their own climate controls. Martello Suites are larger at about 600 square feet and can sleep up to four people. These also include lofted storage and extra room for custom interiors. Buyers can combine neighboring units and pick their own layouts, finishes, and furniture. Prices are not shown publicly, and interested buyers need to go through a vetting process first. According to sales materials, a Palisade Suite costs about $1.25 million, while a Martello Suite is about $2.5 million. Instead of a standard condominium deed, buyers get what the developers call a registered ownership stake in the complex. The annual membership fee is significant: $100,000 for a Palisade Suite and $200,000 for a Martello Suite. The developers say this fee includes security, dining, medical support, and wellness services. By September 2025, the project team reported that 11 suites had sold during the early sales period.
