The main challenge is turning a former government shelter into a place people would actually want to visit. The shared spaces are designed to give the bunker a resort-like feel, with a full-service spa, sauna, relaxation rooms, yoga and fitness areas, a coffee shop, cigar lounge, and restaurant-style dining. The plan also includes on-site medical care and mental health counseling, which could be especially important if residents need to stay underground for weeks or months. To make up for the lack of natural light, OLED lighting is set to mimic the pattern of a typical day. The suites have 14-foot ceilings and lofted areas to help reduce the sense of being underground. Owners can also customize their interiors, which would otherwise look like identical concrete spaces. Matthias Fitzthum from Bespoke Home & Yacht Security, who is consulting on the project's security, explained in our interview that the design also considers the psychological effects of long stays underground. He suggested adding large digital screens in places like the spa to show outdoor scenes. “I would open walls, virtually,” he said. The goal is to give the feeling of ocean views, movement, and daylight in rooms without real windows. The developers expect the completed property to require about 40 staff members, plus specialists for its expanded data center. That gives the project the scale of a small resort, although the service operation must work around security procedures that are unusual for any conventional hotel. The security plan includes biometric entry, round-the-clock surveillance, and thermal radar. The developers brought in Bespoke Home & Yacht Security, a German company known for working with wealthy clients. Their services include close protection, international extraction, armored transport, anti-drone technology, and reinforced safe rooms. Fitzthum explains that security goes far beyond the bunker doors, starting at the property’s edge and including drones, underground sensors, and airspace monitoring. “If we turn the switch and we go for code red, then all the systems are up and running, and then nobody will be able to get in there,” he said. During normal hotel operations, some systems stay on standby. In an emergency, Fitzthum says the hotel would close to regular guests and only owners would be allowed in. “No hotel guests will be allowed, because we will bring in the owners, and we need all the capacities for the owners.” The bunker is built to protect both people and valuables. There will be climate-controlled vaults for art, wine, jewelry, and precious metals. Fitzthum adds that secure storage will also be available for rent to those who do not own a suite. The 15,000-square-foot data center will have backup power and protection against cyber attacks and signal interception. Fitzthum also wants owners to have the option to rent secure data storage inside the bunker for highly sensitive information. “I would keep this data inside the Diefenbaker bunker,” he said. The project now goes beyond the original building. Fitzthum explains that server operations will move to a second secure building nearby, which will eventually be connected by an underground tunnel. This change will open up more space in the main bunker for hotel rooms and residences. He adds that they are also considering another secure building for collector cars, motorcycles, and other valuable vehicles. With these features, The Diefenbaker is designed to serve as a private base for people, data, and valuables, as well as a hotel or residence. Debert Airport is less than half a mile away, so residents with private planes can easily reach the property. For others, Halifax Stanfield International Airport is about a 50-minute drive. The location offers privacy but is still accessible from cities like Boston, New York, Toronto, and Montreal without complicated travel. The nearby former military airstrip is also important for emergency planning. Fitzthum says Bespoke is creating a subscription-based extraction service for owners and their families, using former military staff and private planes if regular travel becomes difficult. “We have standby time for less than 24 hours, and then we can go wherever they want,” he said. This service could also include private medical evacuation to a suitable hospital if a client becomes seriously ill while traveling. According to the developers, the completed complex will be able to provide its own energy, water, and food for six to nine months. The plans feature a private solar grid, water purification on site, and underground food production. There will also be a second secure building to help with food production, so the kitchen can keep running even if deliveries are interrupted. Fitzthum explains that staff and security will have their own living spaces inside the bunker, which means the property could keep operating during a long lockdown. The plan also includes medical facilities on site and areas where residents can have privacy if being confined becomes too stressful. These features are key selling points, but none have been fully tested yet. The bunker also has a spa and cigar lounge, giving it a hotel-like feel. Still, its success as a shelter will come down to the basics: steady power, clean water, good ventilation, and enough food. In 1959, Prime Minister John Diefenbaker ordered the construction of emergency shelters as the risk of nuclear war grew. The Camp Debert bunker, finished in 1964, was one of six regional shelters built to protect government and military leaders. Its walls, a meter thick, could withstand a five-megaton nuclear blast from about two kilometers away. Filtration systems were installed to block chemical, biological, and radioactive contamination. The building stored enough food and water for about 350 officials to live underground for up to 90 days. Their families were not allowed inside. The shelter’s purpose was to keep enough leaders safe so the government could keep running after an attack, rather than to protect the local community. The bunker was taken out of service in the 1990s and later opened for tours before it became a secure data storage site. The current owner, Jonathan Baha'i, also used it for laser tag, esports events, and a Cold War-themed escape room. These activities stopped during the pandemic, and most of the property sat unused until plans for a hotel and residences came together. The shelter has already proven helpful in a real emergency. When Hurricane Fiona hit Nova Scotia in 2022, Baha’i opened the shelter to coworkers and their families, offering heat, food, and power. While this situation was not the disaster the bunker was designed for, it showed how the building could help during a regional crisis. Mansfield says more people are interested in fortified properties as buyers worry about extreme weather, international conflict, and other disruptions. Fitzthum adds that the potential buyers are more diverse than the developers expected. At first, they thought only wealthy people near Halifax, Boston, New York, Toronto, and Montreal would be interested. But now, inquiries have come from Europe and the Middle East, including families looking to buy several suites. “I spoke to several clients of mine globally, and a lot of them are super interested,” he told me. He says the market is unusually mixed, with buyers ranging from young people with crypto wealth and inheritors to older families with established money. For many, the main draw is not about expecting a certain disaster, but about having a safe, staffed place to go if normal systems break down. The project offers this peace of mind to a small group of buyers who can afford both the suite and the high annual fee. The Diefenbaker is designed to serve three purposes at once: it’s real estate, a boutique five-star hotel, and a fully functional survival shelter. When owners are away, the hotel keeps the suites in use. The residences generate capital and ongoing fees. The original bunker adds a unique history that sets this project apart from any new resort. Most hotel guests rarely notice the walls around them. At The Diefenbaker, those strong, secure walls are the main feature. The spa, dining room, and custom suites help make the concept appealing. Still, what buyers truly get is the chance to stay safe during a crisis, behind doors that lock tight. MORE FROM FORBES underground bunker hotel

item.title: These Are The Most Annoying Airplane Passenger Habits, Per TPG Data
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 3.75
Airplane etiquette can feel like an unwritten rulebook for certain kinds of travelers, but for others, that rulebook can have a completely different set of rules. Weirdly enough, new survey data commissioned by TPG (The Points Guy) and conducted by YouGov suggests that the frustrations travelers feel among one another when traveling is growing. The survey suggests that most travelers call for being more mindful of the people sitting around you, with certain habits proving to be more annoying than others. Here are the ones that stood out the most based on the survey: Playing music without headphones and loud conversations The biggest gripe among travelers is when other travelers play music without headphones or have loud conversations. 27% of survey respondents noted that these types of disturbances were the most annoying in-flight behavior with 40% saying that airlines should ban phone or video calls during flights. Reclining your seat without asking first 51% of respondents said that reclining your seat in economy is only acceptable if you check behind you first, 21% said that it’s fine to recline at any point during takeoff, and just 10% said that passengers should never recline in economy. Taking your shoes off or going barefoot onboard The survey showed that 8% of respondents said that passengers taking their shoes off or going barefoot was the absolute most annoying behavior they’ve encountered on airplanes. The middle seat armrest debate The middle seat tends to be the objectively worst seat on the airplane… like, when was the last time someone told you they were a middle seat person over being a window or an aisle person? So it’s generally considered good etiquette to give the person in the middle both armrests. However, only 11% of respondents said the middle seat passenger should automatically get both armrests. On the other hand, 31% of respondents said everyone should share the armrests equally, while 20% said the middle seat passenger should receive priority. Rushing ahead to exit the airplane first According to the survey, 65% of Americans believe that passengers should exit the airplane row by row, from the front of the plane to the back. A mere 10% said that passengers should push forward when they see an opening, and 9% said it was acceptable to cut ahead if they’re trying to make a connecting flight.

item.title: ‘Everybody Digs Bill Evans’ Is A New Film About Jazz, Grief And Genius
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 3.57
The first notes you hear on Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue, widely regarded as the best-selling jazz album of all time, are by Bill Evans at the piano. It is a fitting introduction to a musician whose influence extended far beyond his own recordings. The new film Everybody Digs Bill Evans takes an intimate look at a pivotal period in the life of the jazz pianist, focusing on 1961, two years after Kind of Blue. This isn’t a standard music biopic: rather than racing through his childhood and career highlights, it concentrates on a few months of personal upheaval, offering an intimate portrait of the man behind the music. The film’s director Grant Gee was a worthy winner of the Silver Bear award for Best Director at the 2026 Berlin International Film Festival, one of the most prestigious prizes in international cinema. The story starts in New York in 1961, as Bill Evans and his trio are reaching a creative peak at the famous jazz club, the Village Vanguard. The performances result in two live recordings that became two landmark albums, Sunday at the Village Vanguard and Waltz for Debby, albums that are still widely available today. Their success is shattered when bassist Scott LaFaro dies in a car accident shortly after the recordings, leaving Evans so devastated from the loss of his musical soulmate that he is unable to return to the piano. The film follows the difficult months that follow, as he retreats from performing and battles grief and heroin addiction, while family members try to draw him back into everyday life. Everybody Digs Bill Evans is a biographical drama about the celebrated jazz pianist and composer, written by Mark O’Halloran and adapted from Owen Martell’s novel Intermission. Rather than telling Evans’ story chronologically, director Grant Gee uses a distinctive visual structure: the black-and-white sequences follow the central events of Evans’ life, while bursts of saturated color act as flash-forwards, offering glimpses of what lies ahead. The approach gives the film a dreamlike quality, suggesting how Evans’ past continues to shape his future. It also marks Gee’s fiction feature debut, following acclaimed documentaries including The Gold Machine, Patience (After Sebald) and Innocence of Memories. He is also known for music documentaries such as Joy Division and Radiohead’s Meeting People Is Easy. One of the film’s greatest pleasures is its exceptional ensemble cast. The performances feel natural and emotionally precise, giving the story warmth and depth. Anders Danielsen Lie, a classically trained pianist himself, plays Evans in a career-defining performance. The Norwegian actor is best known internationally for Joachim Trier’s Oslo, August 31st, The Worst Person in the World and Thelma, as well as roles in Bergman Island and The Night Manager. He brings both intensity and restraint to Evans, capturing the pianist’s extraordinary talent alongside his vulnerability. This is a young actor to watch, one clearly on the rise. Bill Pullman and Laurie Metcalf are equally impressive as Evans’ parents, with Pullman bringing warmth and concern while Metcalf conveys a mother’s mixture of fierce love, frustration and helplessness. Barry Ward as Evans’ older brother Harry and Valene Kane as his complicated on-and-off girlfriend Ellaine also give remarkable performances. Release dates There will be previews of Everybody Digs Bill Evans before its 11 September 2026 UK release date, including on September 1st at Curzon Soho in London, featuring a Q&A with Bill Pullman and director Grant Gee. The film will be released in the United States later this fall.

item.title: How To Spend Two Days In Naples
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 3.32
Long celebrated as the crown jewel of Florida’s Gulf Coast, Naples combines white-sand beaches, multimillion-dollar estates and enough golf courses to fill several vacations. But look beyond the palm-lined avenues, and you will discover an evolving destination with a lot more to offer. Peek a little closer, and you will find one of the nation’s great automotive collections, a 170-acre tropical garden, cool independent restaurants, a waterfront food-truck park and a pickleball complex with a staggering 65 courts. Even Naples’ late-night scene has grown, with cocktail rooms now keeping glasses raised into the wee hours. The easiest way to arrive is through Southwest Florida International Airport in Fort Myers, approximately 35 to 45 minutes away by car. With no convenient passenger rail service into Naples, renting a vehicle or arranging a transfer remains the smartest move. Make Naples Beach Club, A Four Seasons Resort your headquarters. The 220-room beachfront resort sits within easy reach of Old Naples and is loaded with reasons to lounge on-property. Guests can request one of its complimentary electric Mokes on a first-come, first-served basis — it makes a spin around town an open-air joyride, if you’ve never tried one. Onsite, the tri-level Sanctuary Spa at Naples Beach Club holds a 3,200-square-foot thermal circuit with steam rooms, a Finnish sauna, a heated whirlpool, cooling elements, an ice lounge and experiential showers. Dining spans from seafood beside the sand at HB’s to Latin-inspired bites at Sunset Bar. And check out the latter’s lavish $100 Gulf Shore Margarita, made with Patrón El Alto, Grand Marnier Cuvée Louis Alexandre and lime that’s presented with a keepsake Yeti shaker. When you pull yourself away from the property, here is how to give Naples a proper 48-hour spin. Day One Start at Wolfmoon, a bakery and coffee bar nestled inside Naples’ greenery-filled Kaleidoscope Garden Club. Croissants are essential here, with options ranging from classic almond to ones oozing with vanilla custard. Your next stop is Naples Botanical Garden, a utopia of tropical flora from Florida, Brazil, Southeast Asia and the Caribbean. Hop on a guided tram tour if you’re looking to save those steps for later. A few minutes down Bayshore Drive, Celebration Park is a waterfront gathering place built around a rotating fleet of food trucks. Grab lunch and claim a table overlooking Haldeman Creek. It’s now time for a tough choice between horsepower and history. Automotive devotees should reserve tickets well ahead for Revs Institute, which opens Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays. Its collection explores the automobile as a feat of engineering, a competitive machine and an agent of social change. Porsches, Ferraris, Ford GT40s and more are regularly in rotation. For a look at the area’s past, there’s Historic Palm Cottage. Built in 1895 from tabby mortar — a mixture of sand, shells and water — the 3,500-square-foot structure is Naples’ oldest house. From Palm Cottage, you are already near Third Street South and only a short ride from Fifth Avenue South — consider these Naples’ main drags. Spend the remaining daylight exploring both districts. Third Street South, regarded as Naples’ birthplace, sits two blocks from the Gulf and is lined with boutiques, galleries, courtyards and restaurants. Fifth Avenue South is a livelier counterpart with additional shops, art galleries and cultural venues lining the strip. For dinner, snag a courtyard table at Campiello, housed in the historic Naples Mercantile Building on Third Street South. Its rustic Italian menu centers on meats cooked over an open flame and regionally inspired morsels. Naples does not shut down immediately after dessert. Sidebar pours cocktails in a stylish Fifth Avenue-adjacent room and, nearby, The Vine Room serves wine and cocktails overlooking Fifth Avenue South. Day Two Head north for breakfast at Three Sixteen, a specialty coffee shop and bakery near Wiggins Pass. A slate of breakfast fare fuels the morning, and then it’s over to one of Southwest Florida’s finest stretches of coastline. Delnor-Wiggins Pass State Park occupies a barrier island where the Cocohatchee River meets the Gulf. Its beach is primed for swimmers and shell seekers. After rinsing off the sand, choose an afternoon destination based on your retail appetite. Waterside Shops is Naples’ luxury option, with 60-plus retailers and restaurants, including Dior, Gucci and Hermès. For shopping with a broader entertainment roster, head to Mercato. The open-air complex has an Alamo Drafthouse Cinema, live music and seasonal happenings. If two days of pastries, beach time and cocktails have you craving competition, drive south to the US Open Pickleball Championship’s home, the USOP National Pickleball Center. The center contains 65 outdoor courts, a pro shop, clinics, leagues and open-play sessions. Finish at Nat Nat, an intimate natural-wine bar and kitchen along Tamiami Trail. Chef Ming Yee changes the menu weekly according to what local farms and fishermen supply. The restaurant recommends ordering the entire compact menu and letting the team match each dish with wine. Sure, it is a bold ask — but after a couple of days of doing Naples properly, why hold back now? MORE FROM FORBES

item.title: 3 Major Moves Silversea Cruises Is Making Right Now—From A New Hotel To Culinary Sailings
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 2.65
It’s full speed ahead for Silversea. The luxury expedition cruise line continually pushes the boundaries of adventure, with a globe-spanning portfolio of more than 900 destinations across all seven continents. Silversea’s fleet of 12—eight classic ships and four expedition vessels, including the Forbes Travel Guide Four-Star Silver Endeavour—has never sacrificed comfort for adventure. And like any passionate explorer, Silversea refuses to stand still. This season, the company leans further into the idea that a voyage should be shaped by the place itself—not just pass through it. New itineraries spotlight a destination’s most vivid traditions, the cruise line finds fresh ways to taste a region through its harvest and a soon-to-open, first-of-its-kind hotel extends the journey before the ship even sets sail. Here are three things we’re most excited to see on Silversea’s horizon. S.A.L.T. Comes Ashore S.A.L.T. (which stands for “Sea And Land Taste”), the experiential dining program built around each region’s distinct culinary traditions, has done much to earn Silversea its reputation as a foodie-approved cruise line. Now, with the launch of S.A.L.T. Culinary Voyages, the brand has prepared something even more special. On August 27, Silver Spirit launches the first of the Grape Harvest voyages, a series of seven sailings timed to Europe’s autumn harvest season across Portugal, Spain, France and the United Kingdom. Each stop brings its own flavor to the journey. In Portugal, passengers cook alongside a countess at her historic estate. In Sainte-Croix-du-Mont, France, they join a black truffle hunt, followed by a tour of the château and a leisurely, three-course lunch revolving around the day’s forage. Onboard programming bridges land and sea just as seamlessly. Guests can savor a chef-led, nine-course tasting menu at La Dame spotlighting Portugal and northern Spain’s seasonal bites, participate in a Bordeaux wine tasting hosted by the ship’s sommelier or take part in a live seafood masterclass, starring the Atlantic coast’s catch, with the executive chef. Although each itinerary charts its own course, certain signature moments carry through all sailings, among them a caviar presentation to welcome guests aboard and a harvest brunch featuring the season’s bounty. All voyages are further united by four themes: gather, craft, celebrate and indulge. With “gather,” passengers share a meal together. “Craft” centers on hands-on techniques, from blending your own port in the Douro Valley to crafting cocktails at the S.A.L.T. Bar mixology class. “Celebrate” ties each stop to a local custom, perhaps a champagne toast after a successful truffle hunt. And “indulge” covers the collection’s more decadent highlights such as cognac tastings, caviar offerings and multi-course lunches. Silversea’s Summer in Japan Japan has long been a mainstay of Silversea’s Asian cruise routes, but passengers can now experience it in a new way: the line’s first full summer season in the country. Next summer, Silversea will have six sailings designed around Japan’s most important festivals. Kyoto’s Gion Matsuri—a monthlong celebration featuring ornate, multi-ton floats—dates back to the ninth century. Two July sailings place passengers at the heart of the festival, widely considered Japan’s most famous. Passengers on the earlier journey get the vibrant pre-parade evenings, with paper lanterns, crowds and food stalls taking over the streets. Meanwhile, those on the later sailing catch the pinnacle procession of intricately decorated wooden floats on July 17 and 24. Another option is a two-week, round-trip cruise departing Tokyo on July 27, with a port of call at Osaka and visits to Hokkaido and Busan in South Korea as the festival season shifts north. The voyage features the Aomori prefecture’s lauded Nebuta Matsuri, where gigantic, colorful washi paper floats illuminate the night sky. Finally, an August sailing from Tokyo to Seoul gives passengers a front-row seat for the Awa Odori dance festival in Tokushima, which attracts more than a million people each year. From reserved seating, guests will take in Japanese folk dance during the more than 400-year-old tradition. An Elevated Basecamp As a luxury cruise line, Silversea aims to make the journey as memorable as the destination, so the debut of the brand’s first hotel feels like a natural evolution. The Cormorant at 55 South will open October 19 in Puerto Williams, Chile, the world’s southernmost city. The property gives passengers on the line’s Antarctica Fly Cruise a place to stay while skipping the demanding four-day crossing of the Drake Passage. Instead, the journey begins and ends at The Cormorant at 55 South, with a chartered flight of just under two hours carrying passengers to and from the King George Island research station, where the ship departs. The 150-room lodge shares the cruise line’s essential design principles: spacious, soaring ceilings; windows that overlook stunning views of the Patagonian landscape; abundant natural light; and local materials like wood sourced from Andean forests to ground a sense of place. Expect culinary programming on par with Silversea’s ships. Guests can start with Chilean cacao and pastries, then return in the evening to swap stories over meals and cocktails starring native ingredients. Latitude 55 takes a warm, family-style approach to dining, with a menu focused on the region’s distinctive flavors. Bar Sur serves as the property’s social hub. As at sea, S.A.L.T.’s immersive culinary experiences provide a deeper taste of the region. The days saved by skipping the Drake Passage crossing opens the trip to travelers who once had to wait to make the logistics work, since the old route demanded two full weeks away. Above all, the new Antarctica Fly Cruise amenity brings a sense of ease, offering comfort and more flexibility if the weather turns. MORE FROM FORBES

item.title: 10 Exotic Marathons—The World’s Most Surprising Running Races
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 2.12
Active travel and interest in outdoor sports has been booming since before the pandemic, and running is no exception. All of the biggest marathons, London, New York, Berlin, Boston, Chicago and so on, have been selling out in record time with record fields for the past few years. Even though London recently switched to a 2-day format with twice as many entries, over 90% of the more than 1.3 million applicants were rejected for 2027, and getting into any of the largest races—all of which are in major cities—has become a nightmare for recreational athletes. The good news is that there are plenty of races that are still easy to get into, especially if you look at growing number of unique events in far flung and singular locations around the globe, like these 10 exotic marathons. These unconventional events make for great stories, great memories, and are perfect options for those seeking to run a 26.2 mile race away from home and double up on the trip as a fun vacation. Known as “runcations,” “racecations” or “destination marathons,” this is a hot travel and fitness trend I wrote about recently here at Forbes. Since most people spend between three and five hours completing the event, the rest of your trip should be a great and memorable vacation, and these fit the bill. I also just wrote about big changes in one of the most desirable tourism locations here in the U.S., for anyone interested in running the “new” Las Vegas marathon. 10 Exotic Marathons Lewa Safari Marathon, Kenya You might be surprised to find that there are several marathons run amidst lions, leopards and giraffes through the unfenced wilds of African safari reserves and National Parks, and the Lewa is just one of the most prominent examples. Magical Kenya, the brand name for the nation’s tourist board, has been investing in, developing and supporting an entire series of mountain and trail races throughout the country, and this one offers both a full and half marathon on dirt roads through a UNESCO World Heritage designated wildlife conservancy in northern Kenya. Armed rangers are on the course alongside guests, since the route runs through rhino, elephant and big cat territory. Runner’s World Magazine put it on their Top 10 "must do" marathons list. About 1,200 runners from 30+ countries enter and it’s easy, no lottery, no ballot (late June 2027). Christmas Island Marathon, Australia Where? This is physically one of the more challenging races on this list, but by far the hardest part for most readers will be getting there. Where is Christmas Island, you might ask? No, it’s not at Santa’s North Pole workshop, but rather in the Indian Ocean, approximately 900-miles from the coast of Western Australia, and while it is governed by Australia it is much closer to Indonesia’s Jakarta. Qantas flies there twice a week from Perth, so plan on an extended “runcation.” The course for this race is mostly dirt trails, and Christmas Island has seaside cliffs and a high central plateau, rising sharply from sea level to almost 1200-feet, and almost two thirds of the island is National Park. Run coastal cliffs, tropical landscapes and rainforest, possibly viewing abundant wildlife and the Island’s famous red crabs along the way—then tell all your friends and check out their puzzled expressions (August 2027). St. Helena Island, British Overseas Territory Located 1,200 miles west of the coast of Africa and1,800 miles east of South America, in the middle of the South Atlantic, St. Helena bills itself as the World's Most Remote Marathon, and it’s hard to get more exotic than that. It’s the size of San Francisco but with a population of around 4,000 people. Considering its location, it is a recognizable name chiefly due to the fact that it is where Napoleon was exiled and imprisoned from 1815 until his death here in 1821. For most of its tourism history the only way to get to St. Helena here was a 5-day boat trip from Cape Town, South Africa, but in 2017 one flight a week was launched from Johannesburg, so while it’s much easier, there’s still no way to visit for less than seven days. The marathon anchors the island’s official “Adventure Week,” and you can add in some rugged guided hiking, diving with sharks, snorkeling, kayaking and exploring the island’s history. There’s even a single golf course, and St. Helena produces some of the rarest coffee on the planet. Like the Christmas Island race, it is rugged, largely off-road and has substantial elevation changes, with cliffs, mountain paths and green forest (February 28, 2027). The Dead Sea Marathon, Israel Run at 1,300 feet below sea level, this is the lowest elevation marathon in the world—enough said. Much of it is run on pier-like dikes and salt and dirt embankments normally closed to the public as well as the desert, with very little pavement. There are also 5, 10, 15 and 50K options, plus a half-marathon (Feb. 5, 2027). Haulin’ Aspen, Bend, OR There are plenty of off-road trail running races, and this dominates the “ultra” category of races longer than standard marathon, such as 50K (31 miles), 50-miles, 100K (62-miles) and 100-miles. But surprisingly, there are very few classic marathons entirely on dirt trails at the standard 26.2 miles distance, and this is one of those (there’s also a regular half marathon). The good news is that dirt is less punishing and easier on the joints and muscles, the bad news is the rolling terrain makes it challenging, especially with a big 700-foot climb in the final stage. But the great news is that is it in Bend, a wonderful outdoorsy town with a fun, craft beer-driven aesthetic (August 2027). Laguna Phuket Marathon, Thailand If you suffer from jet lag, this might be the foreign race for you. It is the largest annual sporting event on Thailand’s tourism epicenter of Phuket and features a unique “Sunset-Sunrise” concept, with a 3AM start time so most of the race is run in the dark, with the sun coming up for the finish, well suited for long haul international travelers and beating the heat. Then recover on the island’s beautiful beaches for the rest of the day (June 13, 2027). EVA Air Run, Taipei, Taiwan OK, so Taipei isn’t quite as exotic as Christmas Island or a Kenyan safari park, but it’s one of the most overlooked great cities of the world for American tourists and went up in my book after the Chinese takeover of Hong Kong. Taipei is safe, modern, has some standout attractions (Taipei 101, National Palace Museum, etc.) and an amazing, world-class food (and whisky) scene. It’s also very easy to get to in style as Taiwanese airline EVA is one of the best and most luxurious carriers on the planet, with excellent business (and coach) class and lounges, and flies non-stop from eight major U.S. cities including New York, Chicago, Dallas, Houston, Los Angeles and Washington, D.C. Because EVA is the main race sponsor, they offer some great travel packages including air, something almost no other marathon can match, and the full-marathon is capped at very leisurely 4,000 runners. After about the first four miles, almost the entire race runs up and down both sides of the central Tamsui River, much of it through parks and urban greenspace. It’s a great way to take in the sights of the city and there is also do a Half Marathon, 10k and 3k (October 2027). Chubb Bermuda Triangle Challenge, Bermuda “Run? We thought you said rum,” is a tagline for this marathon, which claims to be the only one in the world dedicated “Rum Stops” along the route, sponsored by Bermuda’s Goslings. That’s the story-telling hook, but it also offers great scenery, frequent ocean views, a mild climate, and the marathon begins with a free ferry ride from Hamilton to the start at the Royal Navy Dockyard. A unique three-day race weekend includes a festive Friday night one miler through Hamilton, a Saturday 10K and Sunday half or full marathon, giving travelers the option to do all three and complete the iconic “Bermuda Triangle Challenge” (or half Triangle, January 17, 2027). Kentucky Derby Festival Marathon, Louisville, KY The Kentucky Derby is known as the “most exciting two minutes in sports,” but the month long festival lead up has about 70 other events in Louisville, including the Kentucky Derby Festival Mini Marathon & Marathon. The big moment comes around Mile 8 when runners enter the nation’s most famous racetrack, run through the track’s infield and then out past the iconic Twin Spires where champions are crowned, a one of a kind opportunity (April 24, 2027). Juneau Marathon/Half Marathon, Alaska No list of 10 exotic marathons would be complete without Alaska, a Bucket List travel destination for many. Summer is short and sweet in “The Last Frontier,” and this race, a Boston Marathon qualifier, is held In late July. Juneau is located in the world's largest temperate rainforest, the 17.1-million-acre Tongass National Forest, surrounded by water on one side and icefields on the other. The city has just one main road and can only be reached by air or boat (Alaska Airlines and Delta, just two hours from Seattle). The race route is flat and sea-level, with just 75-feet elevation change, along the shores of Douglas Island, with views of mountains, glaciers, and potentially humpback whales, orcas, sea lions, seals, bald eagles, black bears, porcupines and marmots. Before or after the marathon, you can explore Juneau’s 250-miles of hiking trails, a tram to the top of Mount Roberts, 38 area glaciers that can be visited by foot, paddling, helicopter or floatplane, and the city boasts some of Alaska's best whale watching (July 31, 2027).

item.title: India Is Sticking With America—for Now
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 6.17
President Donald Trump, in his second term, has severely tested the U.S.-Indian relationship. He has slapped tariffs on India, threatened to impose secondary sanctions, gotten considerably closer to Pakistan, and enthusiastically engaged with China—the country India considers its biggest long-term military threat. Yet these strains have not led to the rupture that some observers had predicted. Nor have they forced a fundamental reorientation of Indian foreign policy. Instead, New Delhi has adopted what might be called an “America plus” strategy, in which it seeks to sustain partnership with the United States while widening its engagement with other powers, namely U.S. allies. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has responded with unusual restraint to Trump’s provocations and has resisted demands to pull away from Washington. With the United States, India has continued trade negotiations, increased defense cooperation, and expanded technological and commercial ties. In addition, he has sustained the Quad, a regional security organization that also includes Australia, Japan, and the United States; drawn closer to U.S. allies; preserved relations with Russia; and sought to lower tensions with China. These efforts do not represent a retreat from the United States or a strategy of multialignment. India is trying to reduce its exposure to American volatility, but it still recognizes that Washington is its most important partner. After all, when it comes to cultivating a great-power patron, India doesn’t have better options. China and Russia will never buy Indian goods and services on the scale that the United States does, nor can Russia help India balance China. These realities have protected the U.S.-Indian relationship so far. But if Trump continues to bully India, public opinion could force Modi to abandon his restrained approach. GROWING APART? Through 2024, Modi and his ruling Bharatiya Janata Party were excited at the prospect of Trump’s return to power. Modi had established an unusually warm personal relationship with the president during the latter’s first term. In 2019 and 2020, they headlined rallies together in Houston and Ahmadabad, expanded bilateral cooperation on defense, and developed a common approach to Asian security. At the start of Trump’s second term, it seemed the friendly personal relationship between the two leaders would continue. At a White House meeting in February 2025, they announced an ambitious agenda for trade, defense, energy, and technology. To signal goodwill, the Indian prime minister accommodated Trump by slashing some of India’s tariffs on U.S. products and accepting a planeload of deported immigrants. But the relationship soon soured. Trump took credit in May 2025 for ending a brief military conflict between India and Pakistan. While the Pakistanis hailed Trump’s intervention, the Indians refused to acknowledge that the president had done anything of the sort, sticking to New Delhi’s standard position that its disputes with Islamabad are purely bilateral and do not require outside mediation. Trump then took a shine to Pakistan’s army chief, Syed Asim Munir, and elevated Pakistan in the White House’s diplomatic priorities by using Islamabad as a mediator in negotiations with Iran and blessing the trilateral security pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey. Modi has largely avoided confrontations with Trump. Trump also became friendlier with China, another Indian rival. In his first term, he sought to build stronger partnerships with Australia, India, Indonesia, and Japan to construct a new regional architecture in Asia to balance China. But in his second term, he has spent a significant amount of time engaging with Chinese leader Xi Jinping—even talking loosely of establishing a “G-2,” under which China and the United States would meet regularly to hash out global problems. Trump has also failed to hold the annual summits of the Quad, raising doubts that the United States is committed to that security partnership and to preventing Chinese dominance across Asia. Trade tensions have also inflamed U.S.-Indian relations. When Trump punished India with high tariffs for its protectionism and for buying Russian oil, many Indians felt that their country was being unduly singled out. Washington had carved out exceptions for itself and some European countries to buy Russian oil, and the Biden administration had even encouraged India to buy Russian oil under a price cap as part of a plan to stabilize the global oil market. By late 2025, India faced some of the highest tariffs of any U.S. partner. It is for these reasons that Indian public opinion started to turn against Trump in 2025. The opposition leader Rahul Gandhi accused Modi of surrendering to American pressure. Long-standing skeptics of the United States argued that Washington had proved itself unreliable. Critics of Modi started mobilizing farmers against a U.S.-Indian trade deal by characterizing the careful opening of India’s agricultural market to U.S. goods as an overly large concession. Sections of the political class have suggested that India would be better off forging closer ties with China and Russia. Modi has mostly ignored these calls and largely avoided confrontations with Trump. Last year, India finalized a new ten-year defense framework with the United States that deepens bilateral and regional security cooperation. When the annual summit of Quad leaders failed to materialize in 2025 because Trump refused to participate, New Delhi worked to preserve the forum by hosting a meeting of Quad foreign ministers instead. Modi also persisted with difficult trade negotiations and invested considerable political capital in overcoming the resistance of India’s traditionally protectionist trade bureaucracy. The United States, for its part, has made modest efforts to repair the relationship. In August, for example, the U.S. ambassador in New Delhi called the contested region of Kashmir “an important part of India,” signaling that Washington remains sensitive to India on this issue. ROUGH START Modi’s restraint comes, in part, from that fact that it took India years to build a solid relationship with the United States. For decades after India’s independence, suspicion of the United States permeated the Indian political class, defense establishment, bureaucracy, and scientific community. It was reinforced by Washington’s alliance with Pakistan and its engagement with China during the Cold War, India’s socialist leanings in the decades after its independence, in 1947, and New Delhi’s close relationship with the Soviet Union. The end of the Cold War created an opportunity to repair the U.S.-Indian relationship, but progress was slow. Prime Minister Manmohan Singh’s 2005 civil nuclear agreement with President George W. Bush was a decisive breakthrough. It ended India’s nuclear isolation and opened the way for a broader strategic partnership. Yet the agreement encountered intense resistance from the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, the communist left, and critical sections of Singh’s own Congress Party. When Modi became prime minister, in 2014, he was determined to strengthen ties with Washington. He developed productive relationships with three successive American presidents: Barack Obama, Trump, and Joe Biden. He pressed the Indian bureaucracy, armed forces, and scientific establishment to work with their American counterparts. His government concluded long-delayed foundational defense agreements, widened intelligence and military cooperation, revived the Quad, and promoted deeper engagement with the United States in the realm of critical and emerging technologies. Modi’s political dominance at home allowed him to contain any backlash to growing ties to Washington. By the time Trump returned to office, Indian engagement with the United States was undergirded by expanding connections with American businesses, universities, and the Indian diaspora. In a speech to the U.S. Congress in 2016, Modi declared that India had overcome its historical hesitation to partner with the United States. Today, the U.S.-Indian relationship has acquired a resilience that neither Trump’s volatility nor India’s long-standing anti-American tendencies can easily undo. India’s economic ambitions, military planning, and technological aspirations all, to some degree, now revolve around the United States. A WANDERING EYE To be sure, Modi has also strengthened ties with other great powers since he became prime minister. In 2023, for example, Russia became India’s top supplier of oil. And although its share of India’s arms imports has fallen over the past two decades, Russia remains an important supplier of weapons to the Indian military. Modi’s outreach also extends to China. When he came to power, he hoped that rapprochement with China was possible, but a series of military crises in 2014, 2017, and 2020 delayed those plans. Today, New Delhi is eager to lower tensions with Beijing, with the goals of reducing the risk of conflict, of seeking a boundary settlement, and of hedging against potential improvement in U.S.-Chinese relations. Since 2024, India has made it easier for Chinese professionals to get visas, resumed direct flights between the two countries, and lifted some restrictions on Chinese investments. In September, Xi will make his first visit to India since 2019. Many analysts argue that these overtures to Beijing and Moscow constitute a strategy of multialignment—the act of balancing many partners without committing to any one bloc or country. But that is not quite right. A more apt description for this strategy would be “America plus.” India, a country that has historically hedged its relationships, now has quite a few eggs in the U.S. basket. And when it has diversified its ties, it has mostly done so with U.S. allies, such as Australia, Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom, and European countries. India’s growth strategy is linked to these partners more than ever before. India recognizes that neither China nor Russia can replace the United States as similarly valuable economic partners. The United States is India’s largest market for goods and services and a critical source of capital and technology. U.S.-Indian trade, in goods and services, reached $240 billion in 2025, with a surplus in India’s favor. China is one of India’s largest trading partners, but the relationship is severely lopsided. In 2025, India ran a goods deficit of well over $110 billion with China. Beijing is an important supplier of manufactured products, but it cannot offer India a market as big as that of the United States, nor can it provide India access to the range of advanced technology that the United States does. Russia likewise imports few Indian goods and is not a source of today’s advanced technologies, such as artificial intelligence. India’s ambitions, to some degree, now revolve around the United States. India’s recent trade diplomacy reflects its “America plus” strategy. Having refused to join the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership in 2019, a group dominated by China, New Delhi has signed free trade agreements with New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the European Union. It has also expanded economic cooperation with Australia and renewed trade talks with Canada. The United States and India finalized a consequential trade deal in February, the first of its kind between the two countries, which promises to increase bilateral trade to $500 billion by 2030. But Trump has yet to sign off on it and continues to look for new ways to impose tariffs on India. India also relies on the United States and its partners for security. Tensions along the disputed Chinese-Indian border cooled after deadly clashes in 2020, but China remains India’s principal long-term adversary. The conventional military balance along the border favors Beijing. China spends four times more on defense than India does, has developed a massive military presence in the Tibet region across the Himalayas, continues to expand its naval presence in the Indian Ocean, and is deepening its defense relationship with Pakistan. Washington provides New Delhi with access to intelligence, advanced military technology, joint exercises, and a wider network of security partnerships. The Quad continues to show potential as the regional maritime coalition that could limit Chinese domination of Asian waters. India has also expanded cooperation with U.S. allies on defense production, technology, resilient supply chains, and maritime security. India couldn’t turn to China or Russia for these needs, even if it wanted to. India still relies on Russia for some weapons and spare parts, but Moscow’s capacity to balance China has diminished. Since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russia is too reliant on China to be able to meaningfully curb Beijing. Nor can the BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, two groups dominated by China and backed by Russia, serve as sources of that balancing. India understands that Washington has its own economic and political reasons to stabilize relations with Beijing. New Delhi is also convinced that the underlying competition between the United States and China—over technology, maritime power, alliances, and the regional order—will not disappear. Even if Trump softens Washington’s stance toward Beijing, the structural basis for U.S.-Indian cooperation is likely to endure. BREAKING POINT Modi has so far managed to contain the damage caused by Trump. But there are limits to his capacity to do so. A growing section of India’s political class is itching to see New Delhi confront Washington, even if such a move hurts their country. The most immediate danger to the U.S.-Indian relationship comes from proposed U.S. legislation that would authorize tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries that buy Russian energy. If the bill becomes law—and Trump does not grant India a waiver—it would damage the Indian economy and contribute to a sense among Indians that the United States is no longer a natural partner. If the United States targets India while making allowances for other countries, a dormant anti-Americanism in India will reawaken. Until recently, Modi’s domestic political dominance shielded his approach to the United States from domestic criticism. But recent youth protests, which began over leaked examination papers, have pierced Modi’s aura of invulnerability. If his authority at home continues to erode, he could face more backlash from both the right and the left over his perceived deference to Trump, and he may eventually find defying Washington to be politically useful. Such anti-American sentiment may not produce a formal rupture in the relations with the United States. But it could slow defense and technological cooperation and provide more impetus to hedge. In the worst case, Modi might come under pressure to make concessions to China to stabilize the border and bring in more Chinese investment and technology. New Delhi would also have less reason to buy U.S. weapons. And India could stop playing a moderating role in the BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization—for example, by no longer diluting efforts to dethrone the U.S. dollar as the world’s dominant currency. India has not yet reached that point. Critics of Modi’s prudent management of Washington have not come up with a convincing alternative strategy for how India should handle the growing power imbalance with China. It is easy to call for more productive ties with Beijing, but China’s terms for lasting peace with India—which include a territorial settlement that favors Beijing and reducing security ties with the United States—would be too costly to bear. Nor has China helped any other country rise economically or technologically. Put simply, India’s path to economic growth and technological modernization would be much harder without the United States. Strengthening ties with U.S. allies and working with Trump, for now, remains India’s best bet. item.title: The Impossible Middle East
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.23
The Middle East is no stranger to conflict. But even by its standards, the last six months have been extraordinarily chaotic. Ever since the United States and Israel went to war against Iran on February 28, countries in the region have faced cycles of drone and missile strikes against their military bases, energy infrastructure, and water desalination plants. Their airports and oil refineries have repeatedly needed to pause operations. And their regular ports have at times sat idle, thanks to Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Despite months of negotiations, Tehran and Washington seem poised to keep fighting on and off in an effort to wear down the other’s materiel and willpower. In fact, the war has expanded. More members of Iran’s regional proxy network, including the Yemen-based Houthis and Iranian-aligned Iraqi militias, joined the fray, and a port in Egypt was hit by drones. (No country has claimed responsibility for that attack, but the United States blamed Iran.) As the conflict drags on, damage to the Middle East will extend far beyond infrastructure. It will deepen the Middle East’s fault lines. Some economies will be affected more than others, which could upend even the Gulf states’ traditionally stable politics. Institutions central to the region, such as OPEC+, could further come under extreme stress. There are measures that Middle Eastern governments can take to address these challenges, but none are straightforward, and all have their own set of consequences. To survive an era of increased disorder, then, the region’s countries will have to rethink how they relate to the wider world—and, most important, to each other. A HOUSE DIVIDED Middle Eastern states have long had their differences. They have feuded, for example, about Israel, political Islam, and oil policy. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have contrasting visions for the region and beyond, including Libya, Sudan, and Yemen. But the war is deepening all these rifts and creating new ones. The UAE has resented the muted nature of the condemnations that Oman, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia have made of Iran’s attacks on Emirati infrastructure. The countries have differences on how to handle the war itself and an unpredictable Trump administration. These disagreements have piled onto existing disputes, feeding resentment and making the region’s differences harder to manage. They are frustrating efforts to adapt to the evolving war. The conflict has also begun to divide the Gulf from the United States, its main security guarantor. When U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House, many Gulf governments believed that their relationship with Washington would improve after a turbulent four years under the Biden administration. After all, Trump had a friendly and transactional political approach toward the region during his first term. Middle Eastern officials made ostentatious efforts to win him over, including by pledging to spend trillions of dollars in the United States, raising oil output, funneling investment deals to the president’s own family, and, in the case of Qatar, gifting him a private jet. But then Trump launched not one but two wars against Iran, prioritizing Israel’s desire to debilitate the Islamic Republic over the Arab states’ desire for stability. This showed the region that Washington cannot be trusted. The Middle East has long worried about its dependence on the United States and has thus been diversifying its partnerships since the Arab Spring, in 2011. But in the past, these efforts were largely aimed at threatening or coercing Washington to act in their favor. Now they are more serious. This month, for example, Saudi Arabia forged a mutual defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey. Regional governments are buying more weapons from suppliers in Europe, South Korea, Turkey, and even Ukraine. Finally, they continue to look to China and Russia for political and economic partnerships. They are especially interested in forging more economic ties with China, which already trades hundreds of billions of dollars worth of goods with the region. China is currently the top destination for crude from the region. Any pivot away from the United States will be limited. There is no alternative security partner, at least right now: China is loath to use its economic might to offer military assistance, Russia is bogged down in its own war, and Europe struggles to coordinate on defense issues. (From the Gulf’s perspective, Europe is also too focused on Gulf domestic issues.) These governments are also unhappy with Chinese and Russian efforts to assist Iran in the war by, respectively, offering Tehran material that it can use to rebuild its defense industrial base and helping it improve its targeting. And although American bases can make host states targets, regional governments still want a U.S. military presence and American protection. But unlike past efforts to diversify, this limited shift away from Washington will be more meaningful. It will focus on fulfilling Gulf needs more than hedging against U.S. policies it dislikes, and that may be enough to lessen the United States’ influence over the Middle East. In fact, some regional actors might engage more with Iran, offering it a stake in the Middle East’s security in exchange for less threatening behavior. After all, if Washington cannot keep them safe—and may even add to their insecurity through its aggressive actions, from their perspective—then they may need to talk with Tehran, particularly given that years of containment have failed. The war, and in particular Iran’s direct targeting of the Gulf, makes this approach a tough pill to swallow. But it also makes it all the more necessary. As Tehran digs in its heels on fighting Washington, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and even the UAE will need to speak more with Iranian officials to get themselves out of the crossfire. THE BEST OF BAD OPTIONS The Middle East, of course, cannot rely solely on foreign powers to shield itself from long-term disruption. Its states will also need to strengthen their own defenses, starting with better air and missile interceptors and counter-drone capabilities. These countries’ domestic industries are not yet mature enough to meet the region’s needs in the near future, and they still rely heavily on partnerships with foreign manufacturers. But the sector is growing, and the war may last long enough for these firms to produce more of the weapons that the Middle East needs. Yet the growing political fractures could make it hard for regional states to collaborate on defensive measures. The Middle East, for example, might be reticent to further integrate its air and missile defense networks or to improve early warnings for potential attacks, given that it requires sharing intelligence and sensitive information. Its countries could struggle to remain interoperable as they start deploying increasingly diverse military equipment. And if each state is jockeying for scarce military resources, such as in-demand air defense interceptors, defense could even become a new area of competition. This could prove particularly devastating to the region’s less wealthy states, such as Bahrain and Jordan, which do not have the money to substantially increase their defense budgets and will need help from their neighbors. Furthermore, no matter how much the region spends on defense, it will not be able to intercept every future Iranian attack. No protective system is impenetrable when it needs to cover millions of square miles and shoot down an onslaught of drones and missiles, particularly given that Iran continues to improve its capabilities. Political and security fractures will further reduce the efficacy of air defense networks. That bodes ill for the region’s economic future. Most of the Middle East depends on oil and gas exports for revenue, and Iran has proved more than capable of slowing this trade by threatening to strike its infrastructure. Tehran, for example, can indefinitely disrupt the Strait of Hormuz, through which most of the region’s oil and gas passes, simply by firing on vessels that pass through it—or even merely threatening to do so. Some Middle Eastern countries can instead export via the Red Sea, which is bookended by the Suez Canal and the Bab el Mandeb Strait. But these waterways are still vulnerable to attacks from Yemen’s Houthi military group, which is aligned with Iran and has periodically disrupted the waterway over the last three years. Even the few countries directly connected to the wider ocean, such as Oman and the UAE, must worry about Iranian strikes on their ports. Middle Eastern actors have figured out how to improvise under pressure. Should the Middle East keep struggling to export oil and gas, it could experience domestic political trouble. This is most obviously true for more oil-dependent states, such as Iraq, which will struggle to pay its substantial public wage bill without hydrocarbon earnings. It is also true for Bahrain, which runs one of the highest debt burdens in the world. But richer countries could run into trouble, too. Over the last two and a half decades, the Gulf has used the proceeds from oil and gas sales to build up some of the world’s largest sovereign wealth funds. (Three, one in Kuwait, one in Saudi Arabia, and one in the UAE, have assets close to $1 trillion.) Oil has long funded the Gulf’s expensive social contract, in which governments provide citizens with cushy jobs and high-quality services in return for political acquiescence. If the closure of the region’s waterways and the drying up of hydrocarbon exports become a lasting norm, that deal may come under strain. Arab countries are certainly aware of these risks, and they are taking steps to avoid facing them. Some, for instance, will invest in pipelines that can bypass the region’s chokepoints. But regional pipeline politics have proved tricky in the past, complicating relations between, among other states, Iraq and Turkey, and Qatar and Saudi Arabia. This infrastructure also remains vulnerable to attacks or sabotage. As a result, Middle Eastern governments will likely converge on one solution: building oil storage abroad. The mechanism is simple. Whenever the Strait of Hormuz is open, countries can rush out supplies and fill up overseas tanks. Importing states can then draw these supplies down when the waterway closes. Such a system will work for everyone, not just the countries that have unfettered access to the Strait of Hormuz thanks to geography. Overseas oil storage also has the benefit of distance, making it much harder for Iran to attack, although this process will not be immune from other disruptions. Some Middle Eastern states are, in fact, already taking steps to increase their overseas storage. Kuwait, for example, is looking to expand its oil-storage network, potentially in South Korea and Japan. The UAE is weighing plans to increase crude storage in India, and several Middle Eastern producers in addition to Kuwait have indicated that they are interested in storing their oil and gas inside South Korea. But the solution is only partial: storage facilities are, after all, finite. And by partially solving one problem, they will create another one. The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its ten affiliated states (known as OPEC+) has contentious quotas around oil production. Increasing overseas storage could worsen these disputes. It could also lead more countries to produce above the agreed limit, as states use overseas storage to justify excess production, furthering various OPEC+ divisions. ENDURANCE CONTEST Despite all these challenges, history offers signs that the region can make it through the U.S.-Iranian conflict, and perhaps even avoid serious lasting scars. It is not the first war that the region has had to muddle through in tough circumstances. It bounced back from the eight-year Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s. It withstood Iraq’s 1990 invasion of Kuwait and the United States’s 2003 invasion of Iraq. In several of these instances, many Middle Eastern actors figured out how to improvise under pressure. Egypt managed to write off half of its public debt and escape a crisis by siding with the United States against Iraq in 1990. Qatar overcame the restrictions of pipeline geopolitics in the same decade by making a debt-funded bet on a new technology: turning natural gas into a liquid to export it on ships. When that gamble paid off, Qatar became one of the richest states in the world. The Middle East today has some thinking to do. It will need to draw up new ways to preserve its wealth, to pursue greater self-sufficiency, and to diversify—and even own—its security. It needs a new mechanism that can help local countries manage their differences and unify against common threats. Doing so is the only way the region can survive this conflict and withstand the next one.
