item.title: The Future of Ukraine’s Drone Democracy
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.58
On August 19, the Ukrainian parliament voted overwhelmingly to confirm Ukraine’s new defense minister, ending weeks of uncertainty at a crucial phase of the war. For more than a month, Ukrainians had taken to the streets of Kyiv and other cities to protest President Volodymyr Zelensky’s firing of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. His successor, Yevhenii Khmara, is a special operations officer, best known for leading Operation Spider’s Web, the successful attack on Russian strategic bombers deep inside Russia. But the political fallout from this summer’s upheaval is not over. The removal of Fedorov, whom many Ukrainians considered highly effective, set off a series of decisions by Zelensky to reshuffle the cabinet, and more consequentially, the heads of military and law enforcement agencies. Shortly after dismissing his defense minister, Zelensky sought to quell the public backlash by also firing Oleksandr Syrsky, the unpopular commander of the armed forces. As a result, the president was simultaneously replacing the two figures—the defense minister and the head of the military—officially responsible for Ukraine’s defense against Russia. That this was happening at the very moment Ukraine was gaining the advantage on the battlefield has made the changes all the more fraught. For one thing, the large-scale protests themselves mark a new stage in Zelensky’s relationship to the electorate. Unlike any previous protests since the full-scale invasion, Ukrainians directly challenged the president’s handling of the war, introducing a dynamic that is unlikely to go away. Perhaps even more consequential, on the eve of the parliament’s vote on Fedorov’s successor, Fedorov released a controversial video address in which he declared that Ukraine needed a “system reboot” and called for wartime elections—the first time that not merely a prominent Ukrainian figure but a member of Zelensky’s inner circle and one of his former closest allies had done so. Until now, most Ukrainians have dismissed the prospect, since elections cannot be held while the country is under martial law. Amid these developments, something else has become increasingly clear: one of the unforeseen consequences of Ukraine’s transition to drone-centered warfare has been the expansion of civil society in new ways. The embrace of a decentralized, technology-driven defense strategy has required new forms of cooperation between military and civilians, giving far more people a stake in matters of national security and military strategy. And that has created a new reality for the country’s leadership. A DIFFERENT WAR A crucial factor driving the events of this summer is the evolution of the military confrontation with Russia into a drone war. This reality, which began to take hold in 2024, has accelerated Ukraine’s transition from foreign-supplied to domestically produced weapons: some 95 percent of drones are now assembled inside the country. Moreover, although Ukraine remains heavily reliant on its scarce supply of American interceptors to defend against ballistic missile attacks, it is far less dependent on foreign systems and intelligence than it was at the start of the war. The shift to a drone-centered battle space has fundamentally altered combat tactics, the expertise required of soldiers, and the way arms are purchased. It has also rendered some kinds of legacy systems, such as armored vehicles and short-range artillery, increasingly obsolete. Yet it is not the drones themselves that have made the shift so dramatic. To exploit the full potential of unmanned warfare, Ukraine has adopted an integrated digital architecture linking unmanned platforms with situational inputs and intelligence. It has also pursued an unprecedented level of digital coordination, as well as decentralized production and procurement of weapons and of digital technologies themselves. Fedorov was one of the key architects behind the deployment of this drone infrastructure. Unlike many other officials or military leaders, he not only possessed an acute understanding of the battlefield, the weapons deployed in it, and the data streaming from it, but he also had the ability to build, coordinate, and continually upgrade a comprehensive digital system to manage it. Although he served as defense minister for only six months, Fedorov had driven this shift as the head of the Ministry of Digital Transformation, a government agency he created in 2019 and ran until 2026. Drawing on a team of specialists, the agency had set out to replace traditional bureaucratic procedures across government with more efficient digital platforms; a secondary goal was reducing corruption. After Russia’s full-scale invasion, Fedorov’s team became a driving force within the government for Ukraine’s drone program. Since the acquisition of drones initially fell outside formal procurement, the agency was able to largely run the process through its own “Drone Line” initiative. At the same time, it began building a new digital infrastructure to manage drone warfare. Some of these capabilities, such as Delta—a cloud-based system for managing the entire battlefield—had been designed earlier by volunteer-led civic initiatives. But the Ministry of Digital Transformation gave them crucial government support. It also introduced rewards for army units that successfully deployed drones and, later, for those operating unmanned maritime systems and ground robots, as well. Some military analysts worry that these kinds of incentives risk “gamifying” the war or that they oversimplify operational realities. Yet by providing continuous feedback, the programs provide valuable real-time battlefield intelligence, as well as sophisticated data sets for assessing the performance of weapons and units. Fedorov’s team, relying for a time on Zelensky’s backing, pushed for new policies and funding mechanisms to accelerate the military’s digital transformation. It also set out to streamline the military bureaucracy and bring greater transparency to wartime procurement, which has been highly vulnerable to corruption. Over 900 Ukrainian companies now produce thousands of drone models and components. To manage this huge and fragmented sector, the ministry introduced new systems to coordinate logistics, certification, and deployment. Overall, these changes have been significant. Step by step, drones have allowed Ukraine’s armed forces to acquire or sustain capabilities that have traditionally come from missiles and airpower. In 2025, Ukraine had reached parity in the air domain with Russia along the frontline; by 2026, Ukrainian drones and missiles were also able to reach Russian command-and-control centers, cut off logistics, and prevent some Russian assaults. Although Moscow can still outcompete on resources, using oil revenues and vast state spending to finance its aggression, Ukraine’s new digital architecture has enabled it to do more with less, multiplying the effect of particular weapons by connecting sensors, operators, and strike platforms into a unified system. NEW WEAPONS, OLD WAYS Despite their undeniable value, these innovations have often come from outside Ukraine’s military establishment, and sometimes in opposition to it. Overshadowed by the large number of civilian recruits after 2022 is the fact that the Ukrainian army began the war staffed by professional soldiers, with inherited doctrines and lines of command. Although the military established the Unmanned Systems Forces as a separate branch in 2024, its traditional mechanized, infantry, and armored brigades still bore the brunt of the fighting while integrating drones at their own pace. And as with any large national armed forces, the existing hierarchy has resisted wholesale change. Many commanders have embraced drones as weapons—just as they would tanks or guns—yet without fully understanding the structural changes needed to make them effective. Similarly, Ukraine’s established defense industry, which has long counted on existing relationships and contracts, has also resisted the overhaul. Until recently, drone contracting has remained a comparatively small sector. Even though it involves hundreds of millions of dollars, expensive traditional capabilities such as artillery and other conventional weapons systems continue to consume most of Ukraine’s defense budget. Over the past year, however, the balance has shifted: the military’s procurement priorities and the financial interests surrounding them have begun to adjust to drone-centered warfare. And that has created new forms of pushback. Almost from the beginning of his tenure as defense minister, Fedorov and his team were targeted by smear campaigns on anonymous Telegram channels. These have linked him to various military scandals and alleged corruption in the drone industry. Fedorov blames the attacks on entrenched interests—defense contractors and powerful insiders—who were threatened by the shift in war priorities. As one example, he has cited his successful efforts to reduce the price of a procurement deal for short-range artillery that was becoming obsolete, given the expanding kill zones. He also said that Zelensky had received persistent complaints that the digital reformers were breaking a functioning system and disrupting the delivery of essential equipment to frontline troops. At the same time, as large amounts of funding, especially from Ukraine’s international partners, have been directed at drone technology, established defense contractors and well-connected political actors have sought to gain a piece of the pie. They are now moving aggressively to compete with drone startups on drone contracts. Taken together, these tensions brought pressure on Zelensky to move more slowly on the military transformation—which Fedorov had been pushing to accelerate. But the president had failed to understand just how much the public had become invested in Ukraine’s new way of war, and the remarkable results it had begun to achieve. PRESSURE FROM BELOW By the spring of 2026, if defense contractors had misgivings about Fedorov, the Ukrainian public had become increasingly dissatisfied with Syrsky, Ukraine’s commander in chief. Syrsky had notched several strategic victories, including the battle for Kyiv and the liberation of the Kharkiv region during the first year of the all-out war. He had also embraced drone warfare, expanding drone procurement and battlefield integration, although that was part of the army’s broader evolution. Yet many soldiers saw him as a commander who emphasized discipline and was prepared to sacrifice lives when he considered it necessary to achieve a military objective. Within the military, Syrsky had long taken pride in staying close to the frontlines, sometimes to the point of micromanaging the battlefield. But there was also a growing sense among officers and soldiers that he was beginning to value personal loyalty within the command structure above military effectiveness. He had a tendency to sideline talented younger officers and to use his control over promotions and resources to consolidate his own influence. According to some soldiers and officers, these habits risked undermining battlefield readiness, including on the most critical sectors of the front. Then, in June, Ukrainian journalists published a bombshell investigation uncovering horrific allegations of abuse in an assault regiment—a unit that had been given privileged support by Syrsky. The revelations included evidence of violence and unlawful killings within the unit. Although a formal military investigation followed, public criticism remained intense and serving military personnel spoke out. Many laid the blame on Syrsky personally for allowing this to happen. It was after this scandal that Zelensky made the ill-timed decision to fire Fedorov. In the eyes of many Ukrainians, the president was siding with those who opposed reforms. Almost immediately, thousands of people took to the streets of Kyiv and other cities. To contain the public outcry, Zelensky then moved quickly to fire Syrsky and install Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi as his replacement, a choice that was broadly welcomed. Drapatyi, 43, had entered the military in 2014 as a battalion commander and risen through the ranks, while taking part in many defining battles. He is known for embracing new approaches, including the digital battlefield promoted by Fedorov, supporting promising officers, challenging army leaders when necessary, and championing operations that minimize casualties—a priority that Ukrainians value. Meanwhile, Zelensky named Khmara to replace Fedorov. Since 2011, Khmara—in his late 30s or early 40s—had served in Alpha, the Security Service of Ukraine’s special forces unit, and was considered to have an unblemished record. (He had to leave active military service and formally become a civilian before assuming the post, which by law must be held by a civilian.) Yet Zelensky’s moves failed to resolve the underlying tension between the Defense Ministry and the military’s general staff. By law, the defense minister is supposed to nominate the commander in chief to the president. But this time, Zelensky once again effectively selected the commander himself, creating a situation in which the general staff continues to see that it answers to the president, not to the defense minister. LOST MOMENTUM? A larger question is how this political upheaval will affect the war. Fedorov was fired just as the reforms he had been advocating for were helping Ukraine turn the tide against Russia. By spring 2026, Ukrainian long-range drone strikes were beginning to erode one of Russia’s greatest strategic advantages: its oil sector. Kyiv also continued to disrupt Russian logistics in the south, particularly in Crimea, while also attacking oil refineries across the European part of Russia, including Moscow and St. Petersburg. But many wonder whether Fedorov’s dismissal will slow that progress. In Russia, pro-war commentators openly celebrated Zelensky’s decision, viewing it as a rejection of one of the main architects of Ukraine’s military modernization. Hours after his dismissal, representatives of several foreign governments and international technology firms, including the Italian minister of defense and Palantir’s CEO, Alex Karp, offered him positions, which he declined. Zelensky has also offered him several alternative roles in Kyiv, but Fedorov has refused them all because they came with limited decision-making power. Still, he seems almost certain to gain an important place within the government or defense sector sooner or later. Despite Zelensky’s appointment of innovation-minded leaders to replace Fedorov and Syrsky, the future of Ukraine’s digital war ecosystem remains uncertain. Unlike Khmara, who takes office without an established cadre, Fedorov brought to the defense ministry the team he had already built at the Ministry of Digital Transformation. Although only a few of the digitization specialists Fedorov brought to the Defense Ministry have left so far, many more may be pushed out. By calling for elections, Fedorov signaled a move into opposition, raising questions about whether his relationship with Zelensky would deteriorate—and what this would mean for close associates still holding official posts. By design, Ukraine’s digital battlefield infrastructure has the capacity to rapidly evolve in response to changing combat demands. The system can function without Fedorov or his team, but it remains unclear whether it can maintain the pace of evolution needed to stay ahead of Russia. The immediate risk is lost momentum. DEMOCRACY IN THE BALANCE The democratic culture that took hold in Ukraine in 2014 and drove the protests this summer continues to be one of the country’s greatest military strengths. Many of Ukraine’s most important military adaptations have come from below—from individual soldiers and commanders but also from civilian entrepreneurs. Hundreds of private initiatives have advanced technologies, software, manufacturing, and logistics in ways that have dramatically improved the way Ukraine fights. Too many military units, entrepreneurs, engineers, and civic activists are now invested in this ecosystem for a single political decision to dismantle it. But the disruption could affect Ukraine’s ability to iterate new advances on the battlefield—at a moment when the overall dynamic of the war hangs in the balance. For Zelensky, the political damage of his decisions this summer cannot be undone. Ukrainians have largely remained united behind the president in the face of external pressure, including after Donald Trump’s return to the White House in 2025. Nonetheless, he has shown more than once that he is out of step with ordinary Ukrainians. Already a year ago, his effort to restrict the role of Ukraine’s anticorruption authorities provoked major protests and significantly diminished confidence in his leadership. Now, his decision to fire Fedorov has only reinforced that perception. Until this summer, Fedorov had avoided attention, presenting himself as a manager, not a politician. Yet Zelensky’s abrupt decision to dismiss him—for reasons the public still does not understand—made Fedorov one of Ukraine’s most popular figures almost overnight. Now, Fedorov’s call for elections has significantly raised the stakes. In his video address, Fedorov—without mentioning names—again spoke about powerful vested interests that have meddled in government and defense and resisted the changes Ukraine needs to maintain its military advantage. He also asserted that, with no end to the war in sight, Ukraine needs a broader debate about political accountability and decision-making. Clarifying his initially vague but surprising address, the former minister pledged to outline the technical and security logistics of wartime voting—specifically for soldiers, refugees, and frontline residents—to enable a realistic debate on holding elections. Under martial law, elections are barred. Until now, only external powers—Russia or the United States—had questioned Ukraine’s political legitimacy without elections. Most Ukrainians deemed wartime voting dangerous and impractical, fearing that staging elections would simply divert attention, funds, and effort from the front. But Zelensky is in his seventh year as president, under a constitution that permits two consecutive five-year terms. Having made consequential, unpopular decisions, he has increasingly given the sense that he has stopped reading the country’s mood. Fedorov’s announcement may not precipitate an immediate change, but it has started a debate that could play out in the coming months and years. Until now, when it came to the question of holding elections, it had seemed that Ukraine would know when the moment arrived: at some point, in an active, outspoken society, even during war, Ukrainians themselves would demand democratic accountability. This does not mean that Fedorov will automatically gain popularity if he decides to run. His call for wartime voting has alienated some public figures and politicians who backed him as defense minister. They see his intervention now as less a push for accountability than an open political challenge to Zelensky—one that risks draining attention from the reforms that Fedorov had previously championed. With the war likely to continue for the foreseeable future, the urgent question facing the country now is to what degree the people should be given a direct say in the war’s course: how it fights, by what means, according to what strategy, and with what broader vision for its defense. The rise of drone warfare has made military strategy more inclusive, giving a wider range of people—from civil society representatives and tech innovators to members of frontline military units—the expertise and leverage to shape it. That means, on a popular level, more engagement in the war than ever. But for the country’s leaders, it has also created a powerful new set of voices to be reckoned with and be held accountable to—ones that, in the future, may well demand an even greater say. item.title: The ‘Stability-Instability Paradox’ Comes for Markets
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.52
The ‘Stability-Instability Paradox’ Comes for Markets This is not yet an economic catastrophe, but it could very easily become one. The impasse in U.S. President Donald Trump’s war against Iran has now lasted for so long that even jokes about Groundhog Day have grown stale. Recent months have seen rounds of punishing airstrikes, followed by announcements that peace talks are resuming. None of this has moved the needle. Now the administration has returned to another dated strategy: maximum economic pressure, or as U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has put it, an “economic D-Day” against which Iran cannot hope to stand. The administration seems to believe time is on its side, and that the ongoing blockade and sanctions on Iran’s trading partners will succeed where bombing has not. The impasse in U.S. President Donald Trump’s war against Iran has now lasted for so long that even jokes about Groundhog Day have grown stale. Recent months have seen rounds of punishing airstrikes, followed by announcements that peace talks are resuming. None of this has moved the needle. Now the administration has returned to another dated strategy: maximum economic pressure, or as U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has put it, an “economic D-Day” against which Iran cannot hope to stand. The administration seems to believe time is on its side, and that the ongoing blockade and sanctions on Iran’s trading partners will succeed where bombing has not. But this is a dangerous game. And the fact that escalation and dire global consequences have been largely managed up to now makes that danger greater, not smaller. The war has dragged on in part because its economic consequences have remained manageable, yielding misplaced confidence that they will stay that way. During the Cold War, strategists identified what became known as the “stability-instability paradox.” Once the United States and Soviet Union possessed the ability to destroy each other with nuclear weapons, direct superpower war became almost unthinkable. Yet the ironic result was not a stable and predictable peace. Confidence that neither side would deliberately start a nuclear war actually created more room for competition below the nuclear threshold: proxy wars, covert operations, military interventions, and regional crises. Yet conflict below the nuclear threshold could and did escalate. Proxy wars drew direct superpower involvement. Conventional confrontations triggered nuclear alerts. The very confidence that catastrophe was too irrational for either side to permit encouraged the risk-taking that made catastrophe more likely. We are seeing something similar right now. Markets have absorbed an extraordinary disruption since the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began in February. The overnight loss of as much as 20 percent of global oil production did not cause a worldwide economic meltdown. Prices rose, supply chains shifted, and governments released reserves. That’s largely thanks to mitigation measures put in place since the first major oil shock in 1973. Bypass pipelines, releases from strategic petroleum reserves, and the growth of new, greener technology all contributed. Some poorer countries experienced shortages and rationing, but there was no global collapse. The relatively mild impact also relied a lot on luck. The market was oversupplied prior to January, and drawing down so-called floating storage, a euphemism for sanctioned Russian and Iranian oil tankers trapped at sea, in effect added to global reserves. Chinese policy choices were pivotal: Beijing had been aggressively buying excess oil to fill its own reserves before the war, allowing it to cut imports by as much as 5.5 million barrels per day. Through this combination of planning, adaptation, and luck, oil traders have remained mostly sanguine. The milder-than-expected shock in oil prices has reinforced a broader assumption that somehow the war will end before a genuine crisis hits. Even the collapse of the cease-fire into an untidy tit-for-tat of airstrikes and the administration’s apparent commitment to long-term economic pressure have done little to dent that confidence. But surviving one stage of a crisis does not tell us where the next stage will lead. That is where the lesson of the stability-instability paradox comes in. In Cold War crises, no one could predict with confidence which might cross the nuclear threshold, which is what made them so dangerous. The same uncertainty hangs over the current energy crisis. We do not know how long the war will continue, whether traffic through the Strait of Hormuz will improve or deteriorate, whether additional infrastructure will be struck, or whether some new political or military development will suddenly change the calculus for Washington, Tehran, or other actors. What we do know is that the economic damage so far is substantial. Oil prices today are hovering around $90 a barrel. With energy embedded in every part of the global economy—from fertilizers to manufacturing, refrigeration, and food processing—higher oil prices travel quickly into consumer prices. Inflation over the past half-year in the United States averaged almost 3.5 percent, above the Fed’s target and historical average consumer price index growth, while inflation globally is also rising. Meanwhile, most buffers that made the initial shock manageable are depleted. U.S. strategic petroleum reserves are now at their lowest level since the 1980s. Some traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz, but today’s oil volumes compare unfavorably with the cease-fire period, and even more so with the prewar period. Gulf energy production remains partially closed, while threats from Yemen’s Houthis could endanger oil traveling via bypass pipeline. Normally, scarcity would draw capital toward new supply and alternatives. But investors betting on sustained higher prices have repeatedly been burned, in part because Trump’s repeated claims that the war is nearly over keep pulling prices back down, weakening the very market signal that might build resilience. In short, we are not out of the woods yet, and we have no functional market mechanism for knowing how far from the edge we actually are. Markets are not states. But the underlying logic is reminiscent of the Cold War paradox: Belief in the existence of an ultimate ceiling on escalation can make behavior below that ceiling more aggressive. An oil crisis cascading into global economic catastrophe created by this war therefore remains entirely possible. Despite U.S. military efforts to increase oil shipments through the strait, world markets remain millions of barrels short of their prewar production levels. Inflation is creeping back up, while refinery attacks in the Russia-Ukraine war are adding further pressure to the price of oil and gas products from jet fuel to propane. The administration is betting that its economic pressure on Tehran will bear fruit before its own pigeons come home to roost. It may be right. But no one really knows. That uncertainty should also shape how we think about future conflicts. In a globalized world, economics and war are increasingly inseparable. The most likely flash point for a future conflict between the United States and China, a war over Taiwan, would also be an economic war that could cost the global economy $10 trillion by some estimates. The old stability-instability paradox was dangerous because confidence about avoiding catastrophe could itself encourage the behavior that made catastrophe possible. We may now be watching a new version develop in real time. Global energy markets’ resilience so far has prevented this war from becoming an economic catastrophe, but that success is no guarantee the threshold won’t be crossed. It may instead bring us much closer to the brink. Emma Ashford is a columnist at Foreign Policy and senior fellow with the Stimson Center’s Reimagining U.S. Grand Strategy Program. She is also an adjunct assistant professor at Georgetown University and the author of Oil, the State, and War. X: @EmmaMAshford Matthew Rojansky is president and CEO of the U.S. Russia Foundation. item.title: Why Even a Cornered Putin Won’t Press the Red Button
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.05
Why Even a Cornered Putin Won’t Press the Red Button Great powers have been humbled many times without escalating to nuclear war. In Western debates about how to aid Ukraine—and how the war might end—there is a widespread view that Ukraine cannot and should not defeat Russia outright or fully expel it from its territory. Indeed, few Western politicians openly support Ukraine’s “victory,” instead using vague phrases like helping Kyiv “as long as it takes.” Since Moscow has nuclear weapons, so this line of thinking goes, it losing the war is not only impossible but, in fact, undesirable. To avert a humiliating defeat, Russia might risk Armageddon and use its nuclear arms, and surely Ukrainian territory and sovereignty are not worth that. Having given up its nuclear weapons in 1994, Ukraine is doomed, in this narration, to accept at least some of Russia’s demands. Many prominent Western voices have promoted some version of this narrative. University of Chicago academic John Mearsheimer, who was adamant before February 2022 that Russia would not attack Ukraine and predicted a Russian victory multiple times since, warned the West not to push “a great power to the brink” because Russian President Vladimir Putin “might then turn to nuclear weapons.” In Western debates about how to aid Ukraine—and how the war might end—there is a widespread view that Ukraine cannot and should not defeat Russia outright or fully expel it from its territory. Indeed, few Western politicians openly support Ukraine’s “victory,” instead using vague phrases like helping Kyiv “as long as it takes.” Since Moscow has nuclear weapons, so this line of thinking goes, it losing the war is not only impossible but, in fact, undesirable. To avert a humiliating defeat, Russia might risk Armageddon and use its nuclear arms, and surely Ukrainian territory and sovereignty are not worth that. Having given up its nuclear weapons in 1994, Ukraine is doomed, in this narration, to accept at least some of Russia’s demands. Many prominent Western voices have promoted some version of this narrative. University of Chicago academic John Mearsheimer, who was adamant before February 2022 that Russia would not attack Ukraine and predicted a Russian victory multiple times since, warned the West not to push “a great power to the brink” because Russian President Vladimir Putin “might then turn to nuclear weapons.” Similarly, Harvard University’s Stephen Walt has warned various times that Russia might resort to nuclear escalation. “There is the possibility it could escalate, particularly if Russia thinks it’s losing and believes that it would be a catastrophic defeat,” he said in 2023. “And that’s something that should worry all of us.” Indeed, the Biden administration slow-walked military deliveries to Ukraine—especially advanced weapons and anything that could be used to strike Russia—because it believed in the threat of nuclear escalation. However, at no point did Kyiv or its Western partners remotely plan to impose a catastrophic defeat on Russia in the sense of Ukrainian troops marching into Moscow. Ukraine merely aims to liberate its own territory and restore the internationally recognized borders that Russia itself accepted in multiple treaties and agreements before 2014, when it began to invade, occupy, and illegally annex around one-fifth of Ukraine. What’s more, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky does not even aim for complete liberation anytime soon. In 2025, Kyiv announced (and has since repeated) that it would accept a cease-fire agreement establishing the current front line as a future line of contact. In other words, Ukraine would accept a partial victory by Russia in order to achieve peace. A brief history of war shows that apocalyptic thinking about a cornered great power resorting to nuclear escalation is misplaced. In the 1960s, nuclear-armed France lost a brutal colonial war in Algeria, which was not just any overseas colony but a fully annexed part of metropolitan France and home to 1.6 million European settlers. The United States lost in Vietnam, and the Soviet Union lost in Afghanistan—in each case, it was a humiliating defeat that neither superpower tried to prevent with nuclear escalation. China, too, lost a war against Vietnam that it did not choose to escalate, and neither did the United States when it, like the Soviets, lost in Afghanistan. Each time, a nuclear power faced an astounding defeat by a much smaller, non-nuclear enemy and did not press the red button. Today, nine countries possess atomic arms, and most of them are fighting or have fought wars against non-nuclear states. Yet since the United States bombed Hiroshima and Nagasaki in Japan in 1945, why have these nuclear-armed states never again used weapons of mass destruction to achieve their war aims? Why have they not even credibly threatened to use them—if one discounts, as one should, Russia’s propagandistic saber-rattling since 2014? In parallel to the technological advancement and proliferation of nuclear weapons since 1945, the world’s thinking about these weapons has evolved, too. As a result of intense international deliberation about the global consequences of atomic war and nuclear winter, an informal worldwide taboo on using these weapons has emerged. To be sure, nuclear arms continue to play a prominent role in national security planning and discourse—as instruments of deterrence and ultimate tools of national defense in case of truly existential, all-out war. At the same time, the strategic futility and moral irresponsibility of using nuclear weapons in the context of limited foreign interventions has become widely acknowledged. The widespread belief in the strength of this taboo has even allowed non-nuclear states to attack nuclear-armed nations. In 1973, for instance, Egypt and Syria—neither of which possessed atomic weapons back then or possesses them today—attacked Israel, even though the latter was known to have an unofficial but fully developed nuclear arsenal by that point. In 1982, non-nuclear Argentina began a war with nuclear-armed Britain over the Falkland Islands. The story of Ukraine’s disregard for Russia’s nuclear arsenal is both similar and different in some ways. Since the start of Moscow’s long war against Ukraine, which began with the invasion of Crimea in 2014, Russian officials have—in thinly disguised form—repeatedly threatened to use nuclear weapons. Not only have these intimidation attempts become shriller and more frequent since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, but Russia also demonstratively changed its nuclear doctrine in 2024 to lower the official threshold for nuclear escalation in a conventional war. Moscow’s apocalyptic rhetoric since 2014 has been very effective in Europe and the United States. Among other factors determining Western hesitation in backing Ukraine, the Kremlin’s coded yet well-understood nuclear threats have led Western governments to provide weapons to Kyiv with much restraint, significant delay, numerical limits, and restrictions on their use. In Ukraine itself, by contrast, the direct effects of Russia’s yearslong nuclear signaling have remained close to zero. Kyiv has continuously violated Moscow’s putative red lines, including the first ground invasion of Russian territory since World War II, drone bombing runs against Moscow and St. Petersburg, and the systematic destruction of strategic targets deep inside Russia. Some of the attacks on Russian territory were conducted with Western weaponry such as British Storm Shadow missiles. These attacks negate even the new, lower-threshold nuclear doctrine. In 2024, Putin said , “We will consider such a possibility [of nuclear retaliation] when we receive reliable information about a massive launch of air and space attack assets and them crossing our state border.” Kyiv has been conducting increasingly massive drone and missile operations inside Russia with little attention to the Kremlin’s doctrinal specifications and its propagandists’ dark warnings. There is no need to view Ukraine’s actions as hazardous. They are based on more rational calculations than reflexive Western fear of Russian nuclear escalation. To be sure, Kyiv is under no illusions that Moscow would be constrained in breaking the nuclear taboo by ethical considerations, given the Kremlin’s virulent Ukrainophobia. Rather, there are high practical risks if Moscow were to use nuclear strikes to defend illegitimately captured foreign territory rather than its own legitimate homeland. The full range of aftereffects of such an unprecedented violation of international law, rules, norms, and customs is difficult to foresee—including for Putin and his entourage. These risks are magnified by reputational vagaries: Escalation could be seen as a sign of weakness, of a great power incapable of prevailing against a non-nuclear middle power with conventional means. (In their reluctance to capitulate after losing a conventional war to Iran, U.S. President Donald Trump and his inner circle now face a similar risk calculus that makes nuclear escalation by the United States unlikely.) The net sum of strategic gains and losses for Moscow from the explosion of one or more atomic warheads in or over Ukraine is unpredictable. Unless Kyiv fully capitulates, Moscow is likely to lose more—perhaps far more—than it would gain from escalation. Given Ukrainian societal resilience and will to fight thus far, it is unlikely to simply back down in reaction to a nuclear hit. The rest of the world, including many non-Western countries like India, is not going to take a Russian break of the nuclear taboo lightly. In contrast, Moscow has had much success by merely threatening to use nuclear weapons in Ukraine. Although the Ukrainians have ignored such threats, Moscow’s nuclear signaling greatly hurt Kyiv by way of nervous Western governments limiting their aid in reaction to Russian rhetoric. It was no coincidence that nuclear saber-rattling often peaked during Western debates about sending weapons to Ukraine—in the early days of the war, when it was about sending any weapons at all, and later, when it concerned battle tanks, fighter jets, or long-range missiles. Oddly, the one residual likelihood of a potential nuclear escalation in the Russia-Ukraine war could emerge in the opposite scenario from what many Westerners fear. Mariana Budjeryn, a nuclear historian at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, argued in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists that the Kremlin may feel encouraged to use atomic arms not to prevent some sort of humiliation but when it is already close to winning. Similar to how the United States decided to use atomic bombs to hasten its impending victory over a prostrate Japan in 1945, Moscow could go nuclear to transform an already advantageous military situation into a quicker success. Russia would still incur global political costs from breaking the nuclear taboo, “but these costs could be better mitigated by a winning Russia than a losing Russia,” Budjeryn argued. Western countries, she wrote, might be disinclined to impose severe military costs on Russia in response if Ukraine looks like a lost cause. “Opprobrium from China will matter less to a Russia that won its war in Europe,” she continued. Finally, “Russia’s nuclear use is bound to make an impression in NATO capitals and allow Russia to shape the broader post-war settlement in Europe to its advantage.” Both Western awe of Russia as an atomic superpower and fear of a Russian nuclear reaction to losing in Ukraine are misinformed. During the past eight decades, nuclear-armed states have repeatedly lost interventionist wars and even been attacked by non-nuclear countries. If nuclear escalation was indeed likely or even inevitable should Russia begin to lose in Ukraine, then a similar scenario should long have happened in a previous case where an interventionist power was militarily cornered by the victim of its invasion. According to this logic, Russia should have already gone up the ladder of nuclear escalation since 2022, rather than merely talking about it. Decisions about the degree, kind, and duration of support for Ukraine should not be guided by angst and strategic myopia. They should be informed by a concern for the victims of criminal aggression, solidarity among democratic nations, and a basic self-interest in the preservation of elementary international order. Moscow may not have any moral qualms about exploding a nuclear warhead in Ukraine. Yet history shows that such an escalation is unlikely, unless the mass of the Ukrainian army starts to advance deeply into Russia’s legitimate state territory. As long as the Kremlin believes that the world’s reaction to a Russian nuclear adventure will be resolute and have devastating consequences for Russia itself, it will continue to refrain from entering such an uncertain path. Andreas Umland is a policy fellow at the European Policy Institute in Kyiv, an analyst at the Swedish Institute of International Affairs’ Stockholm Centre for Eastern European Studies, and an associate professor of political science at the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy. item.title: Don’t Freak Out Over the Pentagon’s Europe Plans
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.85
Don’t Freak Out Over the Pentagon’s Europe Plans Congress, European nations, and Trump himself stand in the way of major changes. The U.S. military is considering what units to cut and what to keep in Europe as part of the Trump administration’s rethink of force posture on the continent. But competing priorities could stymie the Defense Department’s ability to make the major drawdowns that some officials are pushing for. On July 27, Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby announced the start of a six-month review of U.S. forces in Europe, meant to move “fast and irreversibly toward Europe taking primary responsibility for its conventional defense.” The U.S. military is considering what units to cut and what to keep in Europe as part of the Trump administration’s rethink of force posture on the continent. But competing priorities could stymie the Defense Department’s ability to make the major drawdowns that some officials are pushing for. On July 27, Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby announced the start of a six-month review of U.S. forces in Europe, meant to move “fast and irreversibly toward Europe taking primary responsibility for its conventional defense.” And this week, he traveled to Europe for meetings with NATO leaders and U.S. military personnel to discuss the plan, which he has dubbed “NATO 3.0.” The United States keeps around 80,000 military personnel in Europe, nearly half of whom are stationed in Germany. Other countries hosting U.S. military personnel include the United Kingdom, Spain, Italy, Poland, Romania, Greece, and Estonia, among others. That military presence is there to help protect the host countries, but it has also long served as a means for Washington to project power into Africa and the Middle East, via airfields, naval bases, or medical facilities that take care of wounded military personnel. The United Kingdom and Germany are particularly important for U.S. airpower, while Spain, where multiple U.S. naval destroyers are based, is important for sea power. However, Colby has long urged the U.S. military to focus on Asia over Europe and the Middle East in order to confront what he views as the rising threat of China. And with U.S. President Donald Trump’s perennial distaste for NATO now exacerbated by his anger over European allies’ refusal to join the war in Iran, Colby may see his chance. Some early indications suggest that Colby’s team could propose substantial cuts to U.S. forces in Europe. In October 2025, the Defense Department withdrew a rotational unit of around 3,000 troops that had been based primarily in Romania. In December, the United States reportedly told European nations that they should be ready to take over most of their conventional defense as soon as 2027. In May of this year, the Pentagon abruptly canceled a planned deployment of troops to Poland, though Trump appeared to reverse course just days later, announcing instead that Washington would be sending 5,000 troops to the country; however, so far, no troops have been sent. And in June, the United States announced significant reductions in the number of forces, aircraft, and warships that it would provide to Europe if NATO were attacked. Colby’s team is likely under the gun to move quickly, said Katherine Thompson, who formerly worked for Colby at the Pentagon and is now a senior fellow at the Cato Institute think tank. “You may have a different political party assuming the presidency in 2028, so you want to cement as many gains as you can to make it very difficult to undo,” she said. Colby’s team is preparing four possible options, Reuters reported Thursday. Those options will be ready for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s review by Nov. 6. As for which countries could potentially see a U.S. troop drawdown, that may be driven more by professions of loyalty to the Trump administration than pure military considerations. The United States recently sent a questionnaire to NATO member nations asking if the country has been “publicly supportive” of U.S. foreign policy, if the country is buying U.S. weapons, and what “restrictions,” countries have placed on U.S. bases. The document also asked countries if they’d be willing to speak out against efforts to buy European weapons. Under this logic, Spain and Italy are perhaps the most at risk for some form of politically motivated punishment, given their respective leaders’ declining relations with Trump over the Iran war. Spain is important to NATO defense due to its hosting of U.S. destroyers at Rota, while key U.S. forces in Italy include spy aircraft and an Army brigade. Germany has already suffered from this type of policymaking, when Trump announced that the United States would withdraw 5,000 troops from the country after German Chancellor Friedrich Merz criticized the Iran war. The United States has said this process will take “years,” though, suggesting that the withdrawal could be countermanded by future administrations. The Department of Defense did not respond to a request for comment. But Colby’s ambitions may be complicated by politics outside the Pentagon’s control. For one, the Trump administration’s ongoing war on Iran depends in part on access to U.S. air and naval bases in Europe, meaning that those assets are less likely to be moved out of Europe. “I think in the naval domain, you’re unlikely to see any major changes,” said Jennifer Kavanagh, the director of military analysis at Defense Priorities, a Washington think tank. She cited the high demand for naval forces based in the Mediterranean for projecting U.S. power regionally. Even when it comes to other types of forces, “I think the scope of things that are likely to change in the near term, realistically, is probably pretty small,” said Kavanagh, who has advocated for reducing the U.S. military presence in Europe. Past efforts led by the Pentagon to reduce forces stationed in Europe have also not gone down smoothly with Congress. The October withdrawal of troops from Romania prompted a rebuke from the U.S. Sen. Roger Wicker and Rep. Mike Rogers, respectively the top voices on the U.S. military in the Senate and House of Representatives. The move “undermines deterrence and risks inviting further Russian aggression,” the two wrote. Congress subsequently inserted language in the bill authorizing 2026 defense funding that would set a floor of 76,000 military personnel in Europe. The number of military personnel can decline, but only following the Pentagon proving to Congress that it has consulted with European allies, among other measures. Other points of tension between Congress and Colby have included a pause on aid to Ukraine and a move to cut security funding for the Baltic states. Since then, Congress has appeared to signal its displeasure with the Pentagon’s troop moves in Europe by not yet confirming two key Colby aides: Alexander Velez-Green, for deputy undersecretary of defense; and Austin Dahmer, for assistant secretary of defense. The two had confirmation hearings in November of last year. European nations, too, have their traditional means to lobby—through Congress—as well as by talking up their support for Trump, such as through the questionnaire sent out by the Pentagon. That means that countries that buy a significant share of U.S. weapons, such as Poland, or that have provided support for the war in Iran, such as Romania, may be able to preserve a U.S. presence, even if Pentagon policy planners don’t see the need. Some Eastern European nations are also reportedly offering to cut the cost of basing troops in their countries. Meanwhile, Secretary of State Marco Rubio has indicated that he wants the United States to remain a stronger force in Europe and was reportedly involved in a decision to slow roll removing U.S. troops. That’s not to say that Colby doesn’t have cards to play. In accordance with the new provisions requiring the Pentagon to consult with allies before cutting troop numbers below 76,000, Colby has made a point of publicly showing that he has held meetings with key European allies. Colby’s job may also be made easier by the forced retirement of Gen. Christopher Donahue, the commander of U.S. Army forces in Europe. Meanwhile, the Army, the service with the largest footprint on the continent, is without a confirmed chief of staff and is reportedly set to lose its top civilian leader, Dan Driscoll. Two generals most aware of the threat from Russia have also left in recent months: the top coordinator of allied support efforts for Ukraine, Gen. Curtis Buzzard, and Lt. Gen. Charles Costanza, head of the Poland-based V Corps. But no matter what the Pentagon plans, it will still have to face the greatest wild card of all: Trump’s mercurial tendencies. Trump’s reversal of the Pentagon’s decision to withdraw troops from Poland came after outreach from Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, with whom Trump is close. Other European leaders—notably NATO chief Mark Rutte—have proved to be similarly adept at wooing Trump. “These reviews are always a lot of hype, and then the changes are always less than what we expect,” Kavanagh said. item.title: Is Europe Ready for a New Era of Russian Dirty Tricks?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.80
Is Europe Ready for a New Era of Russian Dirty Tricks? After the Kremlin’s failure in Ukraine, Putin’s new plan aims westward. Europeans are rattled. A bomb-laden drone attacked a Ukrainian cargo plane in the eastern German city of Leipzig, but it failed to go off. In another incident, German authorities revealed that they had thwarted an assassination plot targeting the CEO of one of the country’s leading drone-manufacturing companies. Outside Rome, a titanic blast destroyed an ammunition factory whose products are used by Ukrainian forces—just a few days after another explosion hit a plant in Bulgaria whose owner was previously reported to have been targeted by Russian security services. And a Spanish fighter jet on a NATO air-policing mission shot down a drone that crossed into Romanian airspace. A NATO spokesperson said that the drone was probably of Russian origin. And that was just the first half of August. Europeans are rattled. A bomb-laden drone attacked a Ukrainian cargo plane in the eastern German city of Leipzig, but it failed to go off. In another incident, German authorities revealed that they had thwarted an assassination plot targeting the CEO of one of the country’s leading drone-manufacturing companies. Outside Rome, a titanic blast destroyed an ammunition factory whose products are used by Ukrainian forces—just a few days after another explosion hit a plant in Bulgaria whose owner was previously reported to have been targeted by Russian security services. And a Spanish fighter jet on a NATO air-policing mission shot down a drone that crossed into Romanian airspace. A NATO spokesperson said that the drone was probably of Russian origin. And that was just the first half of August. None of this is completely unprecedented. For many months now, Europeans have been assailed by a series of hostile actions, some clearly traced back to Russia, that have aimed to undermine Europe’s efforts to support Ukraine. Russia has cut undersea cables, jammed GPS signals, and staged sabotage using disaffected locals recruited through the internet. Some observers have taken to describing this campaign as gray-zone warfare, referring to aggressive measures that fall below the threshold of outright war. Right now, though, the “gray-zone” modifier looks euphemistic and increasingly obsolete—especially given the growing brazenness of Russian threats. On Aug. 12, Russian President Vladimir Putin pledged unspecified retaliation against any countries daring to interfere with Russia’s so-called shadow fleet of oil tankers—a clear reference to a recent decision by the European Union that would allow the confiscation of Russian oil from sanctioned vessels. In an interview two days later, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov extended the threat to include any countries that dare to support Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invaders. “We will adopt much harsher methods to destroy everything that enables the West to fuel Kyiv’s war machine,” he declared. “We are already doing this, and [the Europeans] are already moaning.” Yet Europe continues to dither. German officials seem to be awaiting proof that Russia was behind the Leipzig attack before responding—a good example of why Moscow always goes to great lengths to make its involvement deniable. But if Europeans think that observing the diplomatic niceties will save them, then they have another thing coming. Putin and his minions have every reason to up the ante. For well over four years now, the men in the Kremlin have tried to defeat the Ukrainians through direct combat. Far from succeeding, they’ve now had to look on as Kyiv’s drones and missiles pound oil refineries and military targets deep inside Russia. Putin’s next-best option—getting his friend U.S. President Donald Trump to strong-arm Ukraine into accepting Russian war aims through U.S.-led negotiations—has also petered out. That leaves plan C: an intensified effort to undercut European support for Ukraine, whether through subversion, intimidation, or influence operations that are aimed at elevating pro-Moscow parties and politicians. Putin’s most effective minion, former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, fulfilled this function for years. Now, the Russian president is betting that his allies in Germany or France may soon be able to do even more. For Putin, targeting Europe is the most obvious choice on a limited escalation menu. There’s little reason to believe that Russia isn’t already throwing everything it has at Ukraine short of nuclear weapons—and there is ample reason to conclude that the Kremlin won’t go that far. (And even if Putin did break the taboo and deploy a tactical nuclear weapon, it would be unlikely to stop the Ukrainians from fighting.) Europe, on the other hand, is vulnerable and divided. The only question at this point is how creative Putin will get. Unlike his European counterparts, the Russian president has professional grounding in the fine art of dirty tricks. The Soviet KGB, where Putin served for 16 years, placed particular emphasis covert operations, including sabotage, subversion, and targeted killings. Putin’s colleagues proved especially adept in their sponsorship of terrorism, supporting everyone from the Palestine Liberation Organization to the Official Irish Republican Army, both of which received training and weapons shipments from the Soviets. KGB agents directly supplied rocket-propelled grenades, machine guns, and silenced pistols to the radical Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, the same group that killed three and took more than 60 hostages at the OPEC summit in 1975 under the leadership of terrorist mercenary Carlos the Jackal. The Soviet-allied East German secret police, the Stasi, supported the Red Army Faction’s terrorist attacks in West Germany; Putin served as a KGB liaison to the Stasi during his stint in East Germany in the 1980s. The campaigns of violence staged by all these proxies proved highly destabilizing for European democracies throughout the last three decades of the Cold War. Back then, many of the groups supported by the Kremlin were left-wing in orientation. Putin’s Russia is less strictly bound by ideology, which might make it a more flexible partner. Some groups are clearly out of bounds, such as the Afghan branch of the Islamic State, which killed 149 people in an attack on a Moscow concert hall in 2024. Yet the Kremlin is also closely allied with Iran, has extended official recognition to the Taliban, and maintains good diplomatic relations with Hamas. In 2020, U.S. intelligence services concluded that Russia had offered bounties to Taliban insurgents for killing U.S. and allied troops fighting there. Russia could easily leverage such contacts to find candidates for attacks on European targets—perhaps with the FSB supplying state-of-the-art fake documents and identities for the perpetrators. Potential attackers don’t even have to breach the EU border; a bloody assault on European tourists in a vulnerable overseas vacation spot could have the same effect. The Russians wouldn’t need to advertise their involvement (just as they didn’t during the Cold War). But they could then amplify the effect with their vast disinformation apparatus, perhaps touting fears of migrants and highlighting the fecklessness of current governments. Aside from instilling fear in the minds of European voters, such an attack could also have the effect of enhancing the popularity of anti-establishment parties such as the Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the French National Rally (RN) of Marine Le Pen. The recent attack on the Berlin Pride parade, which killed one person and injured 29, appears to have given the already-surging AfD a boost in the polls just weeks before critical state elections next month that could see it take real power for the first time. Both the AfD and the RN have a history of receiving Russian support; both are deeply skeptical of aid to Ukraine. Putin will be happy to make mischief that will help them win more votes, especially now that he seems to be getting bolder. Weaponizing migration offers similar benefits. In 2015-2016, Russia orchestrated a campaign to push migrants across its borders into Norway and Finland. In retrospect, that effort looks like a dress rehearsal for a subsequent move in 2021, when Moscow-allied Belarus, likely collaborating with Russia, triggered a brief but intense crisis in the EU when it started sending large numbers of undocumented migrants across its borders with Poland and Lithuania. True, those borders have since been beefed up—but that’s hardly cause for complacency, as the recent discovery of tunnels under the Belarus-EU border shows. Another promising candidate for such an operation is Libya, where Russia has built up a strong military presence as part of its efforts to support would-be dictator Khalifa Haftar. Libya is also a major transit route for migrants to Europe. If it chose to put pressure on Europe that way, it probably wouldn’t be much of a lift for the Kremlin to organize a full-scale boat people crisis. According to the Europeans themselves, critical infrastructure across the continent remains vulnerable. In 2022, cyberattacks on oil refineries in Belgium, the Netherlands, and Germany sent shockwaves through the European energy industry. Just imagine what hacking tools assisted by artificial intelligence might accomplish today in determined hands. The EU is in the process of implementing a wide-ranging program for improved cybersecurity, but one is inclined to wonder if Brussels bureaucrats are au courant with the latest innovations. Just a few days ago, hackers successfully attacked Ceva, one of Europe’s biggest logistics and shipping firms, causing delays for deliveries across the continent. Perhaps it was just a coincidence that the hack took place at the same moment that Ukraine is staging long-distance raids on logistics facilities run by Wildberries, the Russian equivalent of Amazon. Until now, Russian attempts at physical sabotage have been hampered by Moscow’s reliance on freelance operatives recruited through the internet. If Putin wants to get more serious on this front, whether by using trained saboteurs or better-controlled drones, he will have plenty of targets to choose from. European infrastructure still has plenty of vulnerabilities—from critical undersea cables and pipelines to liquefied natural gas terminals. Poland and the Baltic states have let it be known that they’re stepping up security around power plants, dams, and other sensitive installations, specifically citing “false-flag” provocations that Russia might try to pin on Ukraine. Germany’s top general has warned that Moscow is using drone incursions to probe NATO air defenses. His comments in the Wall Street Journal came just a few days after the same paper reported that U.S. intelligence agencies are worried that the Kremlin could be preparing to stage a provocation to throw the Western alliance off balance. That could take the form of a Russian military incursion into some hard-to-defend bit of NATO territory, such as the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard in the Arctic Ocean, where Moscow already has a nearly century-old presence. The aim would be to widen rifts within the alliance and sow doubts about the credibility of its security guarantee to a member under attack. Yet any attack on NATO territory would entail considerable risk. The alliance might respond by triggering Article 5, its collective security clause—and then Russia could find itself at war not just with Ukraine. The problem is that NATO so far has done little to suggest that it can marshal such resolve. Trump is distracted by his disastrous war of choice in Iran, and the Europeans themselves are still riven by differences over Ukraine and how best to help it. As Putin’s prospects of victory on the battlefield diminish, he may decide that he has even less to lose by intensifying his European plan C. Correction, Aug. 27, 2026: A previous version of this article misstated the name of the Official Irish Republican Army. Christian Caryl is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a former Moscow bureau chief for Newsweek and U.S. News & World Report, and the author of Strange Rebels: 1979 and the Birth of the 21st Century. item.title: Why Iran Might Escalate
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.67
Why Iran Might Escalate As Trump’s economic warfare takes its toll, Tehran will be tempted to go on the offensive in search of greater leverage On Aug. 19, Iranian Central Bank Gov. Abdolnaser Hemmati offered one of the most candid accounts yet of the state of Iran’s economy, stating that Iran’s oil exports had almost stopped owing to the U.S. naval blockade. He added that Iranian industries had access to 30 percent less foreign currency than a year earlier. As a result, Hemmati said, the economic situation was even worse than in 2018 through 2020, when U.S. President Donald Trump unveiled his maximum pressure campaign against Tehran. That same day, Trump announced a new campaign of “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale” against Iran, warning that countries providing Tehran with “any type of lifeline” would face “TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences.” On Aug. 19, Iranian Central Bank Gov. Abdolnaser Hemmati offered one of the most candid accounts yet of the state of Iran’s economy, stating that Iran’s oil exports had almost stopped owing to the U.S. naval blockade. He added that Iranian industries had access to 30 percent less foreign currency than a year earlier. As a result, Hemmati said, the economic situation was even worse than in 2018 through 2020, when U.S. President Donald Trump unveiled his maximum pressure campaign against Tehran. That same day, Trump announced a new campaign of “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale” against Iran, warning that countries providing Tehran with “any type of lifeline” would face “TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences.” Hours later, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared that the blockade would be combined with the toughest sanctions that the U.S. had ever imposed. Bessent added that the increased economic pressure could make another large-scale military operation unnecessary. It now appears that instead of continuing bombing campaigns, the United States is relying on economic warfare and a naval blockade to secure Tehran’s capitulation. For Washington, this would minimize the risk to its forces and the pressure on its munitions stockpiles. For Tehran, in turn, this disparity of costs represents a challenge. As a result, Iranian political and military figures have called for Iran to respond with a more offensive military doctrine. They argue that Iran should now take steps to change the situation and make the United States pay much more for keeping the blockade in place. For years, Iran relied on an approach known as “strategic patience” when facing pressure from Israel and the United States. Under this approach, Tehran responded to direct attacks but tried to limit the scale of its response. The goal was to impose costs without starting a wider war that could become an existential threat to the Islamic Republic. Iran also used the so-called “axis of resistance,” a regional network of armed groups, as part of its strategy. These groups helped Tehran keep its conflict with Israel and the United States in the gray zone and much of the fighting away from Iranian territory. In January 2020, Qassem Suleimani, Iran’s Quds Force commander, was killed in a U.S. airstrike near Baghdad International Airport. In response, Iran fired ballistic missiles at bases hosting U.S. forces in Iraq, but it gave Iraq advance warning before the strikes, allowing the U.S troops to take shelter. Trump then decided not to retaliate. In April 2024, an Israeli airstrike on the Iranian Embassy complex in Damascus killed seven Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) members. Twelve days later, Iran responded by launching more than 300 missiles and drones at Israel. Most were intercepted, and no one was killed. Iran followed the same pattern later, particularly after the U.S. bombing of its nuclear sites in 2025. All of these limited responses were designed to prevent a full-scale war with the United States, but in the end, they failed to do so. The limitations of this approach became even clearer on Feb. 28 as U.S. and Israeli strikes targeted and killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei as well as top military commanders and political figures. At this point, with nothing left to lose, Tehran reassessed its strategy. Seeing the stakes as existential, the regime hit back, attacking U.S. bases and infrastructure across the region and closing the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. naval blockade and economic pressure on Iran now pose a new threat that Iranian officials may consider to be “existential.” On Aug. 13, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the U.S. Navy could continue the naval blockade indefinitely. For Iran, each day that this situation continues means less oil revenue, less access to foreign currency, and more damage to an economy that is already in serious trouble. Strategic patience was useful for the Islamic Republic as long as it could tolerate the pressure. But with the naval blockade, time is running out as Tehran loses leverage. The result has been a steady drumbeat of comments from Iranian officials threatening escalation. If Iran decides to take a more offensive approach, that doesn’t mean that Tehran wants a long war. The primary goal would be to make the blockade so costly that Washington would ease it or negotiate an end to it. When Iran’s supreme leader appointed Ahmad Vahidi as the commander of the IRGC on Aug. 9, his appointment letter called for called for “maximum deterrence” and readiness to conduct “powerful offensive operations against the enemy.” Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior advisor to the IRGC, made a similar point on Aug. 12, saying the appointment decree required the IRGC to develop the capabilities needed for an offensive doctrine. “The Guards should be able to carry out military operations in enemy territory when ordered,” Naqdi said. Days later, Yadollah Javani, the IRGC’s deputy commander for political affairs, made the same point, saying Iran’s actions remained defensive but could take on an offensive character. On Aug. 17, a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran would move toward a “fully offensive” posture as diplomacy reached a deadlock. The official also said that Tehran was ready to launch a “timely and precise” attack to break the U.S. naval blockade if talks failed. On Aug. 22, roughly two weeks after becoming secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, a former IRGC commander, said in an interview with Iranian state broadcaster IRIB that the country’s defense strategy had changed. “Our defense strategy has evolved. Iran today will not be the Iran it was before the war,” he said, adding that there would also be changes in how the country conducts war and diplomacy. Earlier in August, economist Majid Shakeri—an advisor to Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the parliamentary speaker—argued that Iran should manage a long period of neither war nor peace. However, just 10 days later, after Washington announced its new economic pressure campaign, his language changed. “A military response by Iran to America’s economic attack is necessary, reasonable, and timely,” he wrote. “Now is the best possible time for military escalation by Iran.” Shakeri was not alone in calling for a tougher response. Hours after Trump announced his new economic pressure campaign, Alireza Salimi, a member of parliament’s presiding board, warned that “if Iran cannot export its oil, no country will be able to export oil.” Subsequent statements have hinted at what kind of escalation Tehran might envision. Earlier this summer, the hard-line newspaper Kayhan proposed attacks on important commercial centers and oil facilities in countries hosting U.S. forces. On Aug. 18, it called on the Supreme National Security Council to authorize “powerful offensive operations” to break the blockade. On Aug. 19, Iranian Armed Forces Chief of Staff Ali Abdollahi warned Persian Gulf states that helping U.S. military operations would mean joining the war against Iran. The next day, the IRGC-affiliated newspaper Javan published comments by Mehdi Mohammadi, an advisor to Ghalibaf, who said that Iran would tolerate the blockade only for a “reasonable period” before possibly resuming preemptive operations. He pointed to Yemen and the role that the Houthis could play around Bab el-Mandeb. Later in the same Aug. 22 interview, Rezaei warned neighboring countries not to join the U.S. economic campaign. He said Iran would first ask them to stay out, but if they took part, Tehran would consider them enemies and target their interests. Iran would then prevent “a single drop of oil” from passing through the Persian Gulf, he said. Rezaei also noted that Iran had attacked U.S. bases but had not yet targeted American economic interests in the region. The Financial Times, citing two unnamed Iranian sources, reported separately that Iran was considering attacks on subsea fiber-optic cables in the Strait of Hormuz if Washington resumed military operations. These statements do not represent a specific plan nor official target list, but they nonetheless suggest that debate over a change in strategy has become more serious. Disrupting shipping or regional energy infrastructure would push oil and gasoline prices higher and add political pressure on Trump ahead of the November midterms. On Aug. 20, Bessent said, “It is going to work in Iran, and we are going to collapse this regime.” Officials in Tehran are unlikely to see that statement as an offer to negotiate. Their response after Khamenei was killed showed that they make different calculations when they believe the Islamic Republic faces an existential threat. Closing the Strait of Hormuz was intended to shift more of the economic burden of the conflict onto the United States and global energy markets. But Iranian leaders may now believe that closing the strait alone has not put enough pressure on Washington to change its position. If Iran decides to follow this path, it could open a Pandora’s box, because the United States may respond on a larger scale and the two sides could end up in another full-scale war. But Iranian leaders may also believe that continuing under the current conditions is no longer an option. Unless mediators bring Tehran and Washington back to talks and the two sides begin implementing their memorandum of understanding, Iran may decide to act before its economy becomes even weaker and it loses more leverage.
