item.title: Americans Aren’t as Skeptical of Foreign Aid as Washington Thinks
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.65
Americans Aren’t as Skeptical of Foreign Aid as Washington Thinks Today’s political debate rests on a faulty assumption. Much of the debate over the future of foreign aid rests on a core assumption: that Americans have lost their appetite for it. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio put it plainly last year when he told officials at the U.S. Embassy in Guatemala that foreign aid is “the least popular thing government spends money on.” This perception of unpopularity is shaping the debate over foreign aid’s future in Washington. The prevailing assumption is that any successor to the now-shuttered U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) must be smaller, more transactional, and more narrowly tied to U.S. interests to survive politically. But that assumption rests on a misreading of what Americans actually want. The stakes extend well beyond U.S. policy. When the United States dismantled USAID at the start of the second Trump administration, other leading donors pulled back in step. Analysts found that the sudden retraction of U.S. aid contributed to the political conditions driving aid budget cuts in the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and elsewhere. This produced the largest single-year decline in foreign aid ever recorded: Official development assistance from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development’s (OECD) Development Assistance Committee fell by 23.1 percent in 2025. Much of the debate over the future of foreign aid rests on a core assumption: that Americans have lost their appetite for it. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio put it plainly last year when he told officials at the U.S. Embassy in Guatemala that foreign aid is “the least popular thing government spends money on.” This perception of unpopularity is shaping the debate over foreign aid’s future in Washington. The prevailing assumption is that any successor to the now-shuttered U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) must be smaller, more transactional, and more narrowly tied to U.S. interests to survive politically. But that assumption rests on a misreading of what Americans actually want. The stakes extend well beyond U.S. policy. When the United States dismantled USAID at the start of the second Trump administration, other leading donors pulled back in step. Analysts found that the sudden retraction of U.S. aid contributed to the political conditions driving aid budget cuts in the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and elsewhere. This produced the largest single-year decline in foreign aid ever recorded: Official development assistance from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development’s (OECD) Development Assistance Committee fell by 23.1 percent in 2025. National polling consistently finds that while “foreign aid” is an unpopular label, Americans widely support many of the programs that it has long funded: humanitarian relief, global health, food security, and disaster response, among others. While Democrats and Republicans differ on detail, bipartisan majorities support maintaining current aid spending levels and giving medicine and food aid to developing countries. For years, polls found that while Americans often overestimate how much the United States spends on foreign aid, their support for aid rises substantially when they learn that it accounts for roughly 1 percent of the federal budget. In 2025, in the wake of USAID’s dismantling, the Pew Research Center found that around eight in 10 Americans supported providing medicine and food aid to developing countries. Roughly one year later, a Rockefeller Foundation-commissioned survey by Echelon Insights found broad bipartisan support for foreign aid. Nearly 90 percent of Americans supported aid aimed at preventing disease, while 80 percent favored reforming and strengthening foreign assistance rather than eliminating it. Americans’ support for aid is strongest when framed around humanitarian need. Pew’s 2025 survey found that while most Americans supported medicine and food aid (80 percent), lower numbers (63 percent) supported economic development aid, and even fewer (39 percent) supported military aid. Among those most skeptical of aid, Echelon Insights’ 2026 survey found that voters most aligned with U.S. President Donald Trump specifically want aid that is accountable, tied to U.S. interests, and focused on concrete humanitarian outcomes. Their priorities for a redesigned aid system include independent audits of aid spending (49 percent), evidence of impact on threats to the United States (47 percent), and clear program end dates (41 percent). Overall, Americans’ views on aid spending are more positive in some areas than their European peers, suggesting that U.S. influence on aid cutbacks in Europe is in spite of, rather than because of, levels of support from the American public. The Development Engagement Lab—a research collaboration between University College London and the University of Birmingham that tracks public attitudes toward aid spending in the United States, U.K., France, and Germany—found in 2025 that 55 percent of Americans favored maintaining or increasing the current aid budget, compared with 54 percent of Germans and 45 percent of Britons, while French support was highest at 59 percent. So, while U.S. politics may be emboldening some European governments, particularly the U.K., to deprioritize aid, it is doing so despite American support for aid outpacing some of its major European peers. In this sense, the United States is not the public-opinion outlier that today’s political debate assumes. If anything, it is the U.K., a country with a long history in delivering consequential aid budgets worldwide, that shows the weaker public mandate when it comes to aid spending. To be sure, American views on foreign aid are mixed. The program where I conduct research at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace—Carnegie California—surveys Californians in an annual survey about their views on the role of diplomacy, humanitarian aid, and development support to U.S. security and prosperity. The share answering that these levers matter “a great deal” for U.S. interests rose through the disruption, from 46 percent in 2023 to 48 percent in 2024 to half of respondents in 2025. And their overall views on whether the United States should play a leading role in promoting human rights and democracy around the world grew on the survey from 47 percent in favor in 2023 to 57 percent in favor in 2025. Whatever is driving Washington’s aid retrenchment, it is not a straightforward reflection of eroding public appetite. Not every aid program enjoys equal public support. Health and humanitarian aid draw the most durable, cross-partisan, and cross-national support of any category tested, in the United States and in the comparison countries alike. Economic development aid and democracy promotion draw majority but softer support, more sensitive to how the program is described and who is describing it. Military and strategic aid remain the most politically contested category by a wide margin, both in the United States and internationally. The American public’s continued support for U.S. aid systems matters because Washington is in middle of redesigning its development architecture. Americans also appear to recognize the consequences of dismantling it: A February 2025 survey by KFF found that two-thirds believed eliminating USAID would lead to more illness and death in low-income countries, and 62 percent expected more humanitarian crises worldwide. A year after USAID’s closure and the merging of the vestiges of aid into the country’s foreign affairs system, the U.S. State Department has yet to articulate what a coherent successor looks like. The Modernizing Foreign Assistance Network found that the department has eliminated the functions that once handled strategic planning, but details on how funding pipelines are managed remain elusive. While the United States has announced notable ad hoc investments in aid to faith-based organizations and global health systems, such as the global vaccine alliance Gavi, questions remain as to what a coherent investment in aid’s future will look like. Some analysts continue to warn that the fragmentation that has long plagued U.S. aid has only worsened since USAID’s absorption by the State Department and that any durable successor will need to rebuild the bipartisan coalition that sustained the aid system’s most successful innovations, from PEPFAR to the Millennium Challenge Corporation. What’s largely missing from that conversation is the public’s position. If policymakers assume that voters have rejected development assistance as a core feature of U.S. policy, they risk building a successor to USAID around a political constraint that the public itself does not actually impose. The point isn’t that Americans want the old USAID restored unchanged. It’s that policymakers have overstated the political constraints that they face in redesigning it. Polling suggests a more nuanced reality: Many Americans continue to back the goals that foreign assistance has long pursued, even if they are open to reforming how those goals are achieved. The risk is that misreading what Americans want could drive a narrower, less effective development strategy during a rare window to redesign the aid system. There is also a message for capitals beyond Washington, where the United States’ retreat has already shaped debates. Even before the 2025 cuts, the United States spent roughly 1 percent of its federal budget on foreign aid, a share that most Americans wildly overestimate. By the standard international measure—aid as a share of gross national income—the United States gave just 0.09 percent in 2025, after cutting aid spending 56.9 percent in real terms that year. Despite its own retrenchment the U.K. still gave more than four times that share (0.43 percent) in 2025, even as it falls further from its legislated target of 0.7 percent, a target that it hasn’t hit since 2021. Only four countries—Denmark, Luxembourg, Norway, and Sweden—currently meet that benchmark. If allies are reading the United States’ retrenchment as evidence that the American public has soured on international engagement, then the polling suggests that they are drawing the wrong conclusion: American support for aid remains at least as strong, and in some cases stronger, than support in Europe. A U.S. retreat cannot rest on the presumption that traditionally generous European states will pick up the slack, when their own citizens are, on this measure, less convinced of aid’s value than Americans are. Decisions about what replaces USAID will shape not only the United States’ development strategy but expectations about the future of international cooperation more broadly. Those choices should be guided by what Americans believe, not by assumptions that have hardened into conventional wisdom. Rachel A. George is a lecturer in the International Relations Program at Stanford University. She is also a research fellow at the Georgetown Institute for Women, Peace, and Security, and previously worked at the Council on Foreign Relations. She holds a bachelor’s in political science from Princeton University, a master’s in Middle East studies from Harvard University, and a doctorate in international relations from the London School of Economics and Political Science. item.title: What an Extradition Trial Reveals About Moscow’s Influence in Africa
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.64
What an Extradition Trial Reveals About Moscow’s Influence in Africa New details have emerged about a network of pro-Russian actors in the Sahel and beyond. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief. The highlights this week: Benin’s failed coup highlights a network of pro-Russian actors across the continent, the dispute over Zambia’s fraught election continues, and the Tanzanian government suspends an independent newspaper. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief. The highlights this week: Benin’s failed coup highlights a network of pro-Russian actors across the continent, the dispute over Zambia’s fraught election continues, and the Tanzanian government suspends an independent newspaper. Africa Brief will take a break for the next two weeks. Our regular programming will return on Wednesday, Sept. 16. Moscow’s Expanding Network A coup thwarted in Benin last year has highlighted a network of pro-Russian actors in Africa, according to new details that have emerged from an ongoing extradition trial in South Africa. The December mutiny, which was led by Lt. Col. Pascal Tigri and included the temporary seizure of the national broadcaster, collapsed within hours following military intervention from neighboring Nigeria. However, subsequent legal proceedings have shed light on how local pro-Russian influencers and movements work to achieve shared aims across African borders. In its bid to prosecute those involved in the failed coup, Benin filed extradition requests for individuals in a number of African countries. This included Tigri, who fled to Togo—though his exact whereabouts remain unknown—and pro-Russian social media influencer Kemi Seba, who escaped to South Africa. In April, South African police arrested Seba (whose real name is Stellio Gilles Robert Capo Chichi), who is wanted by Benin for “inciting” the coup. South African prosecutors allege that Russia funded and orchestrated an illegal escape plan for the 45-year-old Seba. According to South African police, Seba was arrested with more than $18,000. Pretoria’s intelligence has suggested that the cash originated from Russia and was to be paid to Francois van der Merwe, a leader within the Afrikaner white nationalist group Bittereinders, to facilitate cross-border transport of Seba and his 18-year-old son from South Africa into Zimbabwe and on to Europe to carry out terror attacks, according to court documents revealed earlier this month. Seba and his legal team reject the accusations. All three individuals—Seba, his son, and Merwe—were arrested together. Merwe had previously attended a September gathering of neofascists in St. Petersburg, Russia. Despite growing up in France, Seba, who has about 1.5 million Facebook followers, has been a highly vocal critic of French neocolonialism in Francophone Africa on social media. He was stripped of his French nationality in July 2024 after he had previously been arrested for allegedly inciting anti-French and antisemitic sentiment. A month later, Niger appointed Seba as a special advisor to Nigerien President Abdourahamane Tchiani and gave him a diplomatic passport. In December, on the day of the Benin coup attempt, Seba posted a video that he later deleted, which hailed the mutiny as a “day of liberation” and praised the fall of “a clan of predators preying on the economy and freedoms.” He has also widely praised Russia on social media. Russia has fostered close ties with Benin’s neighboring junta-led nations of Niger, Burkina Faso, and Mali. Analysts have suggested that Seba’s pro-coup posts were part of a highly coordinated network of African diaspora influencers that worked to amplify the putschists’ messaging to create a false impression of popular support for the coup. This appears to be a trend not just in the Sahel, but also across Africa. In 2022, the U.S. State Department accused Russia’s defunct paramilitary Wagner Group of using Seba and other influencers to spread pro-Kremlin narratives. In some cases, fake journalists wrote hundreds of pro-Russian articles in more than a dozen African countries, from Senegal to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. While it may be tempting to dismiss Benin’s coup plot and other destabilizing events in Africa as simply Russian orchestrated, Moscow seeds its influence by tapping into systemic problems with democratic backsliding. Benin’s mutineers cited then-President Patrice Talon’s cuts to health care, the cancellation of state-funded kidney dialysis, and crackdowns on political activities as reasons for their insurrection. Last year’s failed putsch was the second coup attempt against Talon, who had been widely accused of dismantling one of West Africa’s once-vibrant democracies and jailing political opponents. Talon stepped down this April after completing his two-term limit—but not before changing the constitution to extend presidential and legislative terms from five to seven years and creating a new Senate. Since his term ended, Talon has occupied the Senate presidency, Benin’s third-highest-ranking office. Measures to suppress public dissent have expanded considerably in the eight months since the coup. Talon’s successor, President Romuald Wadagni, faced just one challenger after many opponents failed to secure enough of the required endorsements from lawmakers to run. For now, Seba’s lawyers have filed for asylum for him in South Africa, saying that he fears for his life if sent to Benin. The extradition trial will continue on Sept. 23. The Week Ahead Friday, Aug. 28: The ratings agency Moody’s reviews its credit rating for Tanzania. Sunday, Aug. 30: Guinea-Bissau holds a constitutional referendum that would increase presidential power. Wednesday, Sept. 2: The Council of the European Union’s Africa Working Party holds a meeting in Brussels. What We’re Watching Zambia’s disputed election. Nearly two weeks after the country’s Aug. 13 presidential elections, Zambians are still contesting incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema’s victory against opposition leader Brian Mundubile. On Monday, Zambian authorities closed the country’s courts, a day before the deadline for Mundubile to file a petition against the election outcome. Critics argued that this was a calculated move by the government to prevent Mundubile, who is in hiding due to alleged threats against him, from formally challenging the vote. According to the official tally, Hichilema secured a second five-year term with 61 percent of the vote. The Christian Churches Monitoring Group found inflated turnouts in 30 constituencies, though election observers whom I spoke with said that despite the apparent ballot rigging, Hichilema would likely still have won. Regardless, the optics of the vote—as well as the arrest of opposition politicians and the fatal shooting of Mutotwe Kafwaya, an opposition member and former cabinet minister, during an election night raid on Mundubile’s home—has damaged Hichilema’s legitimacy in what was one of Africa’s most resilient democracies. Zambian authorities claimed they acted on intelligence about a potential insurrection and that they recovered high-grade weapons during the operation. “The securitization of Zambia has been something that’s been ongoing for a very long time—and the use of security apparatus and also the narrowing of the political space,” Menzi Ndhlovu, a lead analyst at Signal Risk, told Foreign Policy. Expect any pressure from the international community to be limited as this plays out due to Zambia’s strategic importance in a fierce race between China and Western nations for critical minerals. Tanzanian repression. The Tanzanian government suspended independent newspaper Mwanahalisi’s operations for six months starting last week after it reported that Vice President Emmanuel Nchimbi had rejected calls to resign following a falling out with President Samia Suluhu Hassan. (Nchimbi later resigned on Tuesday.) Authorities claimed that the story lacked balance and care in editing, including an error in a photograph caption, which incorrectly identified the information minister as Nchimbi. The move is the latest crackdown on civic space in Tanzania. Last month, security forces arrested 130 people for allegedly “inciting criminal acts” around the time of a planned July 7 protest, which the government banned. This follows last October’s demonstrations against Hassan’s reelection, when more than 500 Tanzanians were killed. Despite the political climate, U.S.-backed Orion Critical Mineral Consortium is negotiating a deal to invest more than $500 million in a large nickel project in Tanzania. Zimbabwe’s new senators. Last week, Zimbabwean lawmakers approved 10 new senators appointed by President Emmerson Mnangagwa, following a new constitutional amendment that expanded the country’s upper chamber from 80 to 90 members. Most of the appointees are loyalists or political financiers for Mnangagwa’s ruling party, the Zimbabwe African National Union-Patriotic Front, including oil and mining tycoon Kudakwashe Tagwirei, who has long been linked to allegations of corruption and cronyism in Zimbabwean politics. Some analysts believe that Tagwirei is likely to become Mnangagwa’s handpicked successor. The constitutional amendment, which was passed in June, also replaced direct elections of the president with parliamentary appointment and allows Mnangagwa to stay in office until 2030 by extending presidential terms from five to seven years. Last year, leaders in Cameroon, Chad, Ivory Coast, Djibouti, and Guinea-Bissau also changed laws to extend their terms or remove barriers to future reelection, according to a new Freedom House report. FP’s Most Read This Week - Realism Is Unrealistic by Matthew Kroenig - The U.S. Is Learning the Wrong Lessons in Iran by Bret Devereaux - The Top 10 Ways Trump Has Made America Weaker by Stephen M. Walt What We’re Reading Uganda’s succession plan. In Foreign Policy, Maurice Oniang’o details how Yoweri Museveni, Uganda’s 81-year-old president, who has ruled the country since 1986, is maneuvering to transfer power to his son, Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who has increasingly used the military to suppress political opposition. “While Museveni has generally exercised coercion through institutions, bending democratic structures to his will, his son seems to make no effort to retain legal or constitutional cover,” Oniang’o writes. Why Africa backs Infantino. FIFA President Gianni Infantino has engaged in a flurry of diplomacy in response to demands that he resign after he pushed to privatize the World Cup. Importantly, he has secured backing from the Confederation of African Football (CAF), which represents 54 FIFA member associations. In New Lines Magazine, Kwangu Liwewe Agyei argues that the CAF serves as a vital lifeline for Infantino, despite its institutional leverage being weakened by financial dependency on FIFA. “The continent has the numbers to influence who runs world soccer,” Agyei writes. “The bigger question is whether it can use that power to shape how world soccer is run, or whether its financial dependence on FIFA will continue to limit how far its leaders are willing to push back.” Nosmot Gbadamosi is a multimedia journalist and the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Africa Brief. She has reported on human rights, the environment, and sustainable development from across the African continent. item.title: The U.S.-Canada Trade War Is Full Steam Ahead
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.27
The U.S.-Canada Trade War Is Full Steam Ahead Ottawa issues retaliatory tariffs to go “dollar for dollar” with U.S. duties. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at tit-for-tat tariffs between Canada and the United States, Iran and China’s response to Operation Economic Outcast, and the spread of Ebola across Central Africa. ‘Everyone’s in for an Economic War’ Canada announced retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday, the latest salvo in the ongoing North American trade war. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at tit-for-tat tariffs between Canada and the United States, Iran and China’s response to Operation Economic Outcast, and the spread of Ebola across Central Africa. ‘Everyone’s in for an Economic War’ Canada announced retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday, the latest salvo in the ongoing North American trade war. Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump abruptly postponed planned 50 percent tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods for a 72-hour period, citing progress in ongoing talks. Both Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney expressed initial optimism about a potential deal; however, negotiations collapsed on Friday, with Ottawa accusing Washington of trying to destroy key Canadian industries. The next day, the 50 percent U.S. tariffs went into effect. Trump also warned on Monday that the United States will raise tariffs on cars, trucks, and auto parts to 50 percent starting Jan. 1, 2027. “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time, calling the relationship “not sustainable.” Canada is one of the United States’ largest trading partners, accounting for around $872.3 billion in bilateral trade in 2025. In response, Ottawa vowed on Tuesday to impose tariffs as high as 50 percent on roughly 700 U.S. products—including clothing, electronics, and foodstuffs—beginning Sept. 8. Most notably, Ottawa revealed that it will be doubling duties on U.S. aluminum and steel to 50 percent in an effort to go “dollar for dollar” with sweeping U.S. tariffs. The new Canadian levies will cover around $20 billion of U.S. imports annually—the same value as Canadian exports affected by U.S. levies. “Ultimately, the terms proposed by the U.S. administration were uneconomic, unfair, and ultimately unacceptable,” Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said on Tuesday, referring to last week’s talks. “They asked too much of Canada and offered too little in return.” The trade war has been accompanied by a war of words between Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford, with the two men trading personal insults. Discussing the U.S. tariff threat, Ford told a Toronto radio station on Monday that Trump can “kiss my ass,” and during a press conference later that same day, he described Trump as a “dictator” and a schoolyard bully. “He’s the type of guy in school that would take your lunch money one day, take your toque off your head the next day, and then steal your running shoes,” Ford said. Trump lashed out on Truth Social in response, accusing the Ontario premier of being Carney’s “Flunky” and calling Ford “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford.” On Tuesday, Trump posted that “The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer.” In another post, Trump called Canada “easily the most difficult and unreasonable” country that the United States deals with. Analysts suspect that tit-for-tat tariffs are far from over. If the United States goes through with its auto duties or if it chooses to escalate in other ways, Canada could look to impose duties on more vital goods. On Monday, Ford said that Canada should consider harsher measures and warned that Ontario could cut off electricity to the United States; Ontario supplies electricity for Michigan, Minnesota, and New York. “We’re all in,” Ford said. “Up here, we’re at a fever pitch; everyone’s in for an economic war. They know they’re going to have to sacrifice.” Today’s Most Read - Washington Is Creating Forever Enemies by Adam Weinstein - Ditching Chinese Rare Earths Is Hard. Just Ask Japan. by Christina Lu - The U.S. Is Learning the Wrong Lessons in Iran by Bret Devereaux What We’re Following Promising retaliation. Iran vowed on Tuesday to resist the United States’ latest sanctions scheme against the regime, which includes threats of so-called secondary sanctions against any country that chooses to maintain business ties with Tehran. “When a bully declares that every bank, company, port, and government must choose between obeying Washington’s whims or facing American vengeance, this is no longer just about Iran,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei wrote on X. Tehran is not alone in its ire. China similarly pushed back against the campaign, which the White House has dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast,” pledging on Tuesday to defend its interests while accusing the Trump administration of disrupting the global financial order. Although U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent refused on Monday to specify which countries might be targeted by these sanctions, China remains Iran’s top trading partner. However, Bessent said that the White House is “giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior” before sanctions are applied, noting that “the president is making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime.” The U.S. sanctions threat risks undermining a summit between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington next month. That meeting is expected to prioritize ways to stabilize volatile bilateral relations. Ebola’s spread. African health ministers convened in Ethiopia on Tuesday for a three-day World Health Organization (WHO) regional summit. The conference aims to address emerging health challenges and brainstorm best strategies to counter them, including bolstering local healthcare systems, strengthening health financing, and retaining more healthcare workers. “Africa’s next health chapter must be defined by ownership over dependency, integration over fragmentation, and practical action over words,” Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie said on Tuesday. The rapid spread of Ebola throughout the Democratic Republic of the Congo is likely to overshadow much of this week’s conversations. Monday marked 100 days since Kinshasa first declared its 17th Ebola outbreak. In that time, the Bundibugyo virus has become the deadliest, fastest-spreading strand on record, with health experts estimating at least 2,600 fatalities, including more than 300 people in just the past week. Around 5,600 cases of Ebola have been detected, almost entirely in Congo and neighboring Uganda. A key challenge of the outbreak has been the lack of approved treatments. Clinical trials are underway to test the Ervebo vaccine, which was used during past Ebola outbreaks. However, it is unclear if Ervebo will be effective against the rare Bundibugyo strand responsible for this outbreak, which has devastated rural communities and front-line workers. Secret trip to Russia. CIA director John Ratcliffe reportedly flew to Moscow on Tuesday for talks with Russian officials, marking the highest-level visit by a Trump administration official to the country since January. Neither Washington nor Moscow has commented on the purpose of Ratcliffe’s trip, but it occurs as U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine have largely stalled. The unannounced trip is believed to be Ratcliffe’s first visit to Moscow since he became CIA chief. The Financial Times reported that ahead of the flight, the White House asked Ukraine to suspend long-range strikes on several major Russian cities, which have proved detrimental to the country’s critical infrastructure, during Ratcliffe’s trip. On Monday, Russian President Vladimir Putin declared that the Kremlin can temporarily seize control of such facilities if private owners fail to adequately protect them against Ukrainian strikes or do not rebuild them after. Ratcliffe’s visit comes the same day that Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican’s foreign minister, met with his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov, in Moscow. Gallagher pushed for an end to the Russia-Ukraine war and said that he and Lavrov agreed to cooperate on humanitarian issues, such as the care of children impacted by the conflict. Tuesday’s meeting was the first in-person talks between Russia and the Vatican in five years. Odds and Ends For nearly 20 years, the title of fastest human on Earth has gone to Jamaican sprinter Usain Bolt, who ran the 100-meter dash in 9.58 seconds. But on Saturday, a Chinese-made humanoid robot beat that time by 0.19 seconds. Electronic athleticism was on full display during Beijing’s World Humanoid Robot Games over the weekend, when advanced automatons competed in tennis, boxing, soccer, and other sports. However, experts are hesitant to hand over Bolt’s title to a human-looking machine, especially since the winning robot finished its race by slamming full speed into a padded wall, requiring actual humans to pick up its pieces. item.title: Myanmar Shows War Doesn’t Stop Mining
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.11
Myanmar Shows War Doesn’t Stop Mining Critical minerals are still flowing out of conflict zones, but accountability is harder than ever. Rare earths help make the world cleaner, smarter, and more connected. But in Myanmar, their extraction leaves behind poisoned rivers, scarred hillsides, dispossessed communities, and rising health risks. Supply chains centered around China are pulling heavy rare earths from Myanmar’s conflict zones, revealing a larger shift: Extraction of strategic resources no longer necessarily depends on stable governments or consolidated state authority. In some places, supply chains can adapt to the fragmented political order that war produces. The Kachin Independence Army, one of many groups fighting Myanmar’s central government, seized Pangwa, the hub of Kachin state’s rare-earth industry, in 2024. But instead of severing the supply chain, it simply put control of a critical point in new hands. Production has continued almost unimpeded. Rare earths help make the world cleaner, smarter, and more connected. But in Myanmar, their extraction leaves behind poisoned rivers, scarred hillsides, dispossessed communities, and rising health risks. Supply chains centered around China are pulling heavy rare earths from Myanmar’s conflict zones, revealing a larger shift: Extraction of strategic resources no longer necessarily depends on stable governments or consolidated state authority. In some places, supply chains can adapt to the fragmented political order that war produces. The Kachin Independence Army, one of many groups fighting Myanmar’s central government, seized Pangwa, the hub of Kachin state’s rare-earth industry, in 2024. But instead of severing the supply chain, it simply put control of a critical point in new hands. Production has continued almost unimpeded. Myanmar accounts for an estimated 16 percent of global rare-earth mining output, and it may supplies nearly half of global production of heavy rare earths, which are critical for the defense industry and green energy. Most are extracted in Kachin and shipped across the border for processing in China, which dominates downstream refining and manufacturing. Political instability is generally perceived as a risk to mineral supply. Yet cases such as the conflict-torn eastern Congo show that strategically important minerals continue reaching international markets even during wartime. Myanmar extends this logic to rare earths, confirming that supply chains can adapt to conflict and, in some cases, even take advantage of the fragmented authority it produces. Beijing does not rely solely on Myanmar’s central government. Chinese actors also engage with military authorities, ethnic armed organizations, local militias, borderland elites, provincial officials, and business intermediaries. Conflict does not stop extraction; it changes who controls it, who profits from it, and who bears its costs. Heavy rare earths are both strategically indispensable and environmentally destructive to extract. As China tightened environmental regulation at home from the 2010s onward, some of the most damaging mining activity shifted into northern Myanmar, where weak oversight, armed conflict, and proximity to the Chinese border made extraction easier. Once mined, the minerals are mixed with material from other sources during transport, processing, and refining, making it extremely difficult for governments, manufacturers, or consumers to determine the origin of the components used in technologies that are marketed as part of the green transition. Neither the 2021 military coup nor the ensuing civil war in Myanmar has shifted China’s strategic interests there. Beijing has continued to prioritize access and project security regardless of which actor controls a particular area. Operations at the Letpadaung copper mine and the oil and gas pipelines, for example, resumed or continued under greater military protection after the coup. These projects have generated resentment over land confiscation, environmental damage, militarization, and unequal benefits, but they also demonstrate the resilience of Chinese-linked infrastructure and extraction, which has proved highly adaptable. That adaptation is most visible in northern Myanmar, where overlapping systems of authority involving ethnic armed organizations, military-linked actors, militias, brokers, local business elites, and Chinese intermediaries oversee the extraction of rare earths. Different groups control mining areas, checkpoints, taxation systems, and transport corridors. Satellite investigations have identified roughly 400 rare-earth mining sites in Kachin state, concentrated particularly in Chipwi and Momauk townships, while reporting from areas controlled by the Kachin Independence Organization (KIO) points to continued expansion. The KIO now controls Kachin state’s rare-earth industry after its armed wing captured Pangwa from military-affiliated militia and border guard forces. Mining revenues finance both military operations and public services in areas under the organization’s de facto administration, while the KIO also provides support to the broader Spring Revolution. As a result, production costs have increased; Chinese investors are cutting labor costs or moving to other locations in Shan state, including regions controlled by ethnic armed groups like the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), United Wa State Army (UWSA), and National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA), as well as areas near the Thai border and Laos. But mining is still continuing. This creates a difficult trade-off: The extraction that sustains resistance and local governance also causes environmental damage that may undermine the KIO’s claims of responsible rule. Although the organization said that it has introduced mining, environmental, labor, and occupational-safety regulations, miners have reported that enforcement remains weak. Rare-earth mining has also expanded into parts of Shan state controlled by the UWSA and NDAA, raising concerns about cross-border pollution in northern Thailand. The threat to rivers, public health, and local livelihoods has prompted growing criticism from Thai communities, civil society groups, and academics, including a recent protest outside the Chinese Consulate in Chiang Mai that Thai police dispersed, which left two protesters injured. The most common extraction method, in-situ leaching—injecting chemicals directly into the ground to dissolve minerals bearing rare earths—is relatively cheap but carries major environmental risks. Pollution from mining areas has entered tributaries feeding the Mekong, Irrawaddy, and Salween rivers. In northern Thailand, for example, the Kok River was found to contain extremely high levels of arsenic, and communities downstream have reported discolored water, declining fish stocks, sick elephants, and restrictions on using river water for drinking or agriculture. Communities living near mining areas bear the brunt. They face exposure to contaminated water, polluted soil, and unsafe working conditions. Workers frequently perform hazardous tasks involving toxic chemicals for low wages and with little or no protective equipment, and cases of sexual exploitation involving women workers have also been widely reported. Accountability mechanisms are weak or entirely absent. Local communities bear the long-term environmental costs while Chinese investors capture most of the profits. These consequences are not unique to rare earths. The Letpadaung copper mine, for example, became associated with violent crackdowns on protesters, forced evictions, and allegations that local communities bore the environmental and social costs while military-linked and foreign actors captured most of the economic gains. However, conflict and fragmented authority can deepen these risks by dispersing the responsibility among multiple actors, making it unclear who is responsible for enforcing standards and compensating affected local communities. Myanmar exposes one of the central contradictions of the global energy transition. The technologies meant to power a greener and more sustainable future are frequently built on extraction systems embedded within civil war, fragmented governance, environmental destruction, and coercive political economies. This may represent an emerging model for how strategic extraction increasingly functions in parts of the 21st-century global economy. A similar dynamic is visible in eastern Congo, where M23’s capture of the Rubaya mining area in 2024 did not halt the coltan trade. U.N. experts documented the group monopolizing exports from the area through Rwanda. As in Myanmar, territorial control changed without severing the commodity chain. Together, Myanmar and eastern Congo illustrate a broader pattern: Conflict does not always interrupt strategic supply chains. In some cases, they adapt to conflict, move through it, and even depend on the forms of fragmented authority that war produces. Western governments increasingly demand “clean” supply chains while remaining structurally dependent on extraction systems that they have little ability, or willingness, to regulate. Myanmar shows why conflict itself must be treated as part of supply chain governance rather than merely as an external disruption to it. Otherwise, the world risks building a cleaner future on poisoned rivers, militarized borderlands, and communities that are left to absorb the costs of someone else’s sustainability. Kristina Kironska is an assistant professor at Palacký University, Olomouc, where she heads the Myanmar Studies Center, and co-director of the Central European Institute of Asian Studies (CEIAS). Jan-Sha is a Myanmarese academic, writing under a pseudonym due to the sensitivity of the topic. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: China’s Success Is Forcing a U.S. AI Rethink
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.78
China’s Success Is Forcing a U.S. AI Rethink Silicon Valley obsessions may have led Washington down a dead end. The United States has bet the farm on artificial intelligence across the board, from industry to finance to government policy. But the combination of a China shock and multiple cases of AIs gone rogue, set against the backdrop of a growing populist backlash, have forced a moment of truth that calls into question the foundational assumptions guiding U.S. development and regulation of AI. The July release of Chinese start-up Moonshot’s Kimi K3 open-weight model, which proved nearly as capable as closed U.S. frontier models, stunned the American AI industry, which has largely ignored open models in favor of closed ones. Open-weight models provide users with free access to the “weights,” or the parameters that shape a model’s outputs, enabling easier customization and lower-cost access than closed models. The United States has bet the farm on artificial intelligence across the board, from industry to finance to government policy. But the combination of a China shock and multiple cases of AIs gone rogue, set against the backdrop of a growing populist backlash, have forced a moment of truth that calls into question the foundational assumptions guiding U.S. development and regulation of AI. The July release of Chinese start-up Moonshot’s Kimi K3 open-weight model, which proved nearly as capable as closed U.S. frontier models, stunned the American AI industry, which has largely ignored open models in favor of closed ones. Open-weight models provide users with free access to the “weights,” or the parameters that shape a model’s outputs, enabling easier customization and lower-cost access than closed models. Until Kimi K3, many presumed that this ease of customization—and sharing of intellectual property in the form of open weights—meant sacrificing advanced AI capability. U.S. policymakers and developers prioritizing the pursuit of AI superintelligence were shocked when Kimi achieved both openness and frontier capability at once. Kimi K3’ s success raised the serious possibility that while the United States has been pursuing closed frontier capability, China has been running a different race—and winning. So how did the United States go down what may be entirely the wrong path? Just what artificial general intelligence (AGI) would mean is widely disputed, but it’s a concept that’s used widely in American AI strategy. The most basic interpretation of AGI is that it means AI that matches or surpasses human intelligence—but this definition struggles to encompass the broad set of ideas that people hold when they talk about human intelligence itself. Practically speaking, “AGI” is often used in the United States as a catch-all for the end goal of AI development, with little measurable or testable dimension to it. So, when and how did such an ambiguous, even eschatological, goal such as AGI become the endgame for American AI policy? Much of the answer lies in Silicon Valley’s sci-fi-inspired, techno-utopian/techno-dystopian culture. An almost religious movement has arisen from the work of sci-fi authors such as Vernor Vinge and Ray Kurzweil, conceiving the idea of AI superintelligence merging with or superseding human control of the planet. This belief in the future omnipotence of AI is evident in industry leaders’ approaches to Washington earlier in the 2020s, when tech CEOs such as Sam Altman begged Congress to regulate AI and control its risks, in a move that only served to reinforce policymakers’ idea that AI could be unprecedentedly powerful. After all, what kind of CEO would ask to be regulated, unless they thought their product was dangerous? The assumptions behind the rationale for continuing to develop AI despite its potential danger were that its supposed omnipotence could be equally consequential for economic growth and the greater good. Any discussion of the danger of AI only served to reinforce the reason to develop it. However, this dual nature had an important implication—if another country secured advanced AI, it would have great power to do harm. The idea of “recursive self-improvement” (RSI) in AI compounded this worry about foreign leadership in the technology. In an RSI scenario, superintelligent AI becomes able to modify itself, conducting autonomous research in which the AI continuously improves its own intelligence. Assuming that AGI comes with RSI capacity means that the first AI developer to reach AGI will forever be one step ahead of the competition, since the AGI will continuously improve itself. This idea may seem far-fetched, and it carries the weight of significant assumptions that are still hotly contested between AI technologists and national security experts, but it has taken root deeply in policy spaces. The assumptions have been that if AGI is as powerful as figures such as Altman have claimed, then the first country to reach AGI will have a permanent lead in the technology. Accepting those premises means that there is a clear imperative for the United States to get there ahead of China and do so in a closed, secretive way that ensures that competitors stay behind. This assumption has driven American AI policy to prioritize competition with China above all else, anchoring U.S. policies such as export controls, deregulation and state AI law moratoriums, and proposed open-source AI bans. But China’s success demonstrates that U.S. assumptions are flawed. The sanctions, export controls, and bans mostly incentivized China to seek end-runs around tech curbs and accelerate its efforts toward autonomy—and toward pursuing a pragmatic approach to AI that is more focused on results than teleological end points. While the United States was running the frontier AI race, China has had a wholly different approach, focused on diffusion; deployment; and building on its “Digital Silk Road,” which made China-friendly 5G standards the norm and installed its digital infrastructure in much of the world. China was developing “good-enough” open models that could be deployed cheaply and at scale, appealing enormously to markets in the rest of the world that wanted to access cheap AI and didn’t have a need for frontier performance. Beijing’s strategy of applying and diffusing its cheap, easily customizable and freely available open-weight AI has led to wide global use, including in the United States. Chinese AI accounts for about 30 percent of AI apps used globally, especially in the global south, and Alibaba’s Qwen AI app has been downloaded more than 3 billion times. China’s approach has also emphasized utility for low-resourced users, producing significant advantages in small, modular language models that may perform worse on advanced capabilities but are easy to run locally. China’s widespread diffusion of AI has positioned Beijing to lead in setting global standards, while at the same time managing to nearly match the United States in frontier AI capabilities. In a measure of how these shocks flummoxed the Trump administration, its reaction to Kimi K3 was to consider banning Chinese open models. Less predictably, this response helped trigger a remarkable development, portending an 180-degree shift in AI strategy. In response to fears that the government would ban open models, Silicon Valley launched a bold statement making the case for open-weight AI as key to U.S. leadership, signed by virtually all major tech actors save Anthropic, including the most avid supporters of President Donald Trump in Silicon Valley, such as Palantir and Andreessen Horowitz. A new consensus is thus beginning to take shape in Washington, this time in favor of open models and closed frontier models such as Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s flagship offerings. A few days after the letter was published, Nvidia announced its own “Open Secure AI Alliance for AI Safety and Security.” The letter’s argument for openness is closely tied to the other foundational shock in Washington—the concrete demonstration of AI’s cyber risks. Particularly alarming is a recent series of episodes of AI agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and more going rogue during testing. In a classic sci-fi nightmare, the AIs escaped their sandboxes, accessing the open internet and even colluding with each other to hack external companies. AI doomers have been warning for years of this kind of “AI misalignment” risk, in which the technology defies human instructions and pursues goals using methods outside of its mandates. As cyber and misalignment concerns have mounted, the Trump administration has moved away from its total laissez-faire anti-regulation posture and in June, it unveiled an executive order to begin to address AI safety and cybersecurity. Though it is reportedly being revised, the order, drafted in consultation with major tech firms, calls for voluntary screening of new AI models for safety concerns. This will almost certainly prove to be inadequate in what will be an evolving, zigzag path to regulation and standards, likely to be driven by future calamities rather than foresight. After all, we don’t know what we don’t know about AI’s capacity for improvisation, and the technology is becoming more capable at an exponential pace, faster than initially anticipated. Thus, more than 1,300 worried AI developers from leading AI firms issued a call to the U.S. government: There is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control. … We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development. Taken together, recent developments should prompt a rethinking of U.S. assumptions about AGI, innovation, and more broadly the zero-sum competition with China. Is there a finish line for technology? Given China’s different strategy, how much is a six month first-mover advantage worth? And what are the costs of letting China take the lead in global diffusion? Two completely separate sets of systems, standards, and regulations would portend a catastrophic trajectory for AI. Yet the stakes of AI for the industry and the U.S. economy of multitrillion-dollar investments, increasingly circular, make for a powerful force limiting introspection. If the U.S. bet on closed AI is in question, then the implications for the American economy and for geopolitics writ large could be immense. The top seven publicly traded U.S. companies by market cap are all AI leaders and collectively comprise 32 percent of the stock market’s value. Overall, 45 percent of the S&P 500 is supported by AI-related stocks. Amid the Kimi news, many pundits are already worrying about high-capability open models reducing the market share for American closed AI leaders such as OpenAI and Anthropic, which are propping up the U.S. economy. But openness and closedness don’t have to be a zero-sum game; industry experts state that there will be use cases for both closed and open models in the global economy. Economic incentives aside, the emerging industry consensus on open source is a promising sign of adjusting AI strategy. Easing the pace of AI development (as developers themselves have suggested) and creating government safety and transparency standards might slow innovation but could reassure markets and the public. Better insight into why AIs go rogue could mean a bubble deflating instead of bursting. This doesn’t necessarily mean abandoning AGI or the frontier—in fact, as Kimi K3 has shown, maybe we can have both. The biggest challenge is attaining global safety and regulatory standards, and the accompanying requirement that the United States and China reach some level of cooperation on AI governance. However self-serving the strategy may be, China’s recent global AI conference demonstrated its commitment to multilateral controls and standards, and AI discussion is on the agenda for the Sept. 24 summit between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. This can be a key opportunity to work toward global institutions and agreements—perhaps the International Atomic Energy Agency, which governs nuclear cooperation, can be a model—that monitor, evaluate, and enforce safe AI that is trustworthy and human-aligned, whether open or closed. Robert A. Manning is a distinguished fellow with the Strategic Foresight Hub at the Stimson Center, where he works on its global foresight and China programs. X: @Rmanning4 Giulia Neaher is a research analyst at the Stimson Center’s Strategic Foresight Hub, focusing on AI governance. item.title: Iran, Oman Agree to Temporary Strait of Hormuz Deal
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.64
Iran, Oman Agree to Temporary Strait of Hormuz Deal Tehran vows to keep the waterway closed if Washington does not accept its terms. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at an Iranian-Omani proposal for the Strait of Hormuz, deadly flash flooding in Nepal and Tibet, and rising Israeli extremist violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. Tehran’s Demands for Hormuz Iran and Oman reached a revenue-sharing agreement on the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, with Muscat saying it is “hopeful” that the deal will be formalized soon. Meanwhile, Tehran warned that the critical waterway will remain closed if the United States fails to accept the proposal’s terms. “The U.S. is obstructing this process, causing progress to be delayed,” said Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at an Iranian-Omani proposal for the Strait of Hormuz, deadly flash flooding in Nepal and Tibet, and rising Israeli extremist violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. Tehran’s Demands for Hormuz Iran and Oman reached a revenue-sharing agreement on the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, with Muscat saying it is “hopeful” that the deal will be formalized soon. Meanwhile, Tehran warned that the critical waterway will remain closed if the United States fails to accept the proposal’s terms. “The U.S. is obstructing this process, causing progress to be delayed,” said Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The announcement goes further than the joint Iranian-Omani statement issued Tuesday that spoke of a “phased framework” for resuming shipping transits through the thoroughfare. Although the initial declaration had proposed a “joint temporary navigational corridor” and bilateral efforts to clear sea mines in the strait, it stopped short of unveiling any formal deal or mentioning the possibility of charging tolls—a key demand of Tehran’s. Global oil prices dipped on Wednesday in response to the news. Both Brent crude and West Texas Intermediate dropped more than $2 per barrel from Tuesday’s highs of roughly $88 and $82, respectively. But U.S. President Donald Trump does not appear eager to accept the Iran-Oman proposal. In an interview with conservative radio host Glenn Beck on Wednesday, Trump insisted that the strait was already open, undermining Tehran’s threat that it will keep the waterway blocked if Washington does not concede. “We take a lot of ships through the strait now. We’re taking them in,” Trump said. “Every once in a while, there’ll be a drone or a rocket or something shot, but it is a very functioning strait. A lot of oil is pouring out.” Only 14 vessels were in the Strait of Hormuz at time of writing on Wednesday, according to TankerMap, which tracks oil and natural gas tanker traffic. Before the war began, an average of roughly 130 ships passed through the waterway daily to transport roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas supplies. Part of the reduction is due to fears about the continued presence of sea mines in the area, which “no one except Iran knows the location of,” Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi maintained on Wednesday. He went on to dismiss Trump’s claims that all the mines have been cleared. The Iran-Oman proposal comes just two days after the Trump administration unveiled Operation Economic Outcast, which threatens to impose so-called secondary sanctions on all countries that continue to do business with Tehran. At the time, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent insisted that the White House is “giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior” before these sanctions take effect. However, Iran and its top trading partner, China, have already vowed to resist Trump’s economic warfare. “When a bully declares that every bank, company, port, and government must choose between obeying Washington’s whims or facing American vengeance, this is no longer just about Iran,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei wrote on X on Tuesday. Today’s Most Read - Washington Is Creating Forever Enemies by Adam Weinstein - Everything You Always Wanted to Know About IR Grad School by Stephen M. Walt - What Donald Duck Can Teach Trump About Going to War by Julian E. Zelizer What We’re Following Rising death toll. Flash flooding in Nepal and the Chinese territory of Tibet killed at least 157 people on Wednesday and left hundreds of others missing, including more than 340 foreign tourists. The exact number of potential casualties and the total cost of damages remain unclear, but authorities expect the death toll to rise. Thousands of people live in villages downstream of the flooding, and officials have already documented the destruction of key bridges, schools, and hydropower facilities. Scientists studying the disaster believe that a large chunk of ice broke off from a glacier and fell into Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River, triggering the flooding. “There was no rain in Nepal, so we were not expecting anything like this,” said Narendra Pariyar, the chief district officer of one of the country’s affected areas. The force of the ice avalanche was so strong that seismologists initially recorded it as an earthquake. It is too early to determine why the landslide occurred, but scientists have not ruled out global warming, which may have accelerated the glacier’s collapse. Wednesday’s disaster is expected to test the government of newly elected Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah, whose victory in March was driven by a youth-led anti-government protest movement. “Please be patient,” Shah said in a statement on social media. “The government takes full responsibility for your rescue, treatment, food, and shelter. In times of such a disaster, we all need to stand together.” Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered local authorities in Tibet to “make every effort” to rescue missing civilians, and he reiterated a need for better flood prevention measures. West Bank violence. A far-right Israeli lawmaker severely damaged a monument in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday amid a rise in extremist violence against Palestinians. According to video footage shared on social media that was verified by the New York Times, 35-year-old Zvi Sukkot as well as several of his aides used a sledgehammer to smash a limestone statue in the Palestinian village of Madama. The monument featured an outline of all territory between the Jordan River and Mediterranean Sea with the word “Palestine” written in Arabic in the middle, as well as names of Palestinians who have been killed in the conflict with Israel over the years. Sukkot defended his actions, saying that the monument included the names of Palestinians who had attacked Israelis, including Yamen Faraj, a militant commander who was allegedly involved in a 2003 suicide bombing. The leader of Sukkot’s party, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, similarly justified Sukkot’s behavior. Israel “should have long ago dismantled the terror monument,” Smotrich said, adding that dozens of other statues across the West Bank should also be destroyed. However, in a rare show of disagreement, the office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the assault. “Taking the law into one’s own hands, particularly by public figures, is unacceptable,” the office said in a statement. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) confirmed that Sukkot and his aides had been visiting the city of Madama as part of a guided tour of Palestinian communities and that the tour was conducted “under the security of IDF troops.” However, the military said that in attacking the monument, Sukkot and his aides had “acted deceptively and manipulatively, without authorization, departing entirely from the approved framework.” Rami Nassar, the head of the Madama village council, accused the Israeli military of failing to immediately intervene, and no soldiers are seen trying to stop Sukkot and his aides in the video. “They provided a shield for this criminal act,” Nassar said. The IDF said that when troops saw what was happening, they notified their commanders, who then instructed the forces to halt the tour and take Sukkot and his aides out of the village. Deadly nursery fire. A fire at a hospital nursery in Islamabad killed at least 14 newborn babies on Wednesday. According to local authorities, only one infant in the nursery at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences’ facility was rescued. An initial investigation suggests that an exploding air conditioner in the maternity ward triggered the blaze, which remained confined to the nursery. No other injuries or outside damages were reported. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ordered Health Secretary Aslam Ghauri, the country’s highest-ranking health civil servant, to be removed from office over the incident and convened a high-level meeting to discuss next steps. “A tragedy involving children is an irreparable loss,” Sharif said. Wednesday’s fire marked one of Pakistan’s deadliest calamities involving minors in recent years. Opposition leaders condemned Sharif’s administration on Wednesday for failing to provide basic safety measures at public hospitals. According to the World Bank, Pakistan’s healthcare expenditure in relation to its GDP is among the lowest in South Asia. “Administrative failure and regulatory oversight lapses have turned these institutions into danger zones,” said Abdul Ghafoor Shoro, the secretary-general of Pakistan’s leading doctors’ association. Odds and Ends Turn up the music! The Air Guitar World Championships kicked off in Finland on Wednesday, with more than 50 musicians from 13 countries vying for the No. 1 spot. This year’s theme, “Rockin’ in the Free World,” marks the 30th anniversary of the international competition. According to the event’s website, its mission is to promote world peace, including the end of all wars and the reversal of climate change. “You can’t hold a gun while you play the air guitar,” the competition states. item.title: Germany’s Rhine River Is Drying Up
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.59
Germany’s Rhine River Is Drying Up The economic damage is just one of the consequences. The Rhine River recently reached a depth of only 21 centimeters in the German town of Kaub—the lowest reading since Germany started keeping records at that gauge in 1880. The significance of those low water levels is vast. Culturally, the Rhine has long been central to German national identity—the border that has been fought over for centuries and memorialized in famous poetry and operas. Economically, the Rhine is connected to the planet’s largest chemical complexes. These days, the barges that go down the Rhine are moving at just a fifth of their full capacity. Why is the Rhine administered by one of the world’s oldest international organizations? Is the Rhine drought of global economic significance? And what aspects of human history are being revealed by the Rhine’s receding waters? The Rhine River recently reached a depth of only 21 centimeters in the German town of Kaub—the lowest reading since Germany started keeping records at that gauge in 1880. The significance of those low water levels is vast. Culturally, the Rhine has long been central to German national identity—the border that has been fought over for centuries and memorialized in famous poetry and operas. Economically, the Rhine is connected to the planet’s largest chemical complexes. These days, the barges that go down the Rhine are moving at just a fifth of their full capacity. Why is the Rhine administered by one of the world’s oldest international organizations? Is the Rhine drought of global economic significance? And what aspects of human history are being revealed by the Rhine’s receding waters? Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter. Cameron Abadi: The Mannheim Act of 1868 first internationalized the navigation of the Rhine; it also established the Central Commission for the Navigation of the Rhine, which is the organization still responsible for governing shipping today on the river today. Is this the oldest continuously operating international organization in the world? Adam Tooze: Some people claim that it is. It certainly goes back a long way. It was a product of the Congress of Vienna of 1815. That’s what set this in motion. This was the great peace conference after the Napoleonic Wars, perhaps the classic demonstration of the kind of logic, not to say wisdom, of post-revolutionary conservative geopolitics: the idea that you could organize the world in a concerted way, a kind of concert of powers that would manage the world, the dream of Henry Kissinger and everyone that came afterward in the 20th century. This had a technological side. And that was—in this case, before the advent of railways—the management of waterways. And out of that came a convention signed at Mainz in 1831 that began to remove those river tolls that were so pesky and that Kaub was all about. And it’s out of that that the Mannheim Act was signed in 1868. The timing is not altogether accidental. The mid-19th century is the moment of the emergence of modern internationalism. I mean, I immediately thought, “Well, what about the international Red Cross, which is also a product of that same moment?” It comes into existence in 1863. The first big scientific congresses began to meet internationally in the 1850s. The great exhibition of 1851 was the biggest trade fair in history. So, this mid-19th century moment is precisely where you would expect this kind of institution to emerge from. I think you would say it’s a powerful confirmation of the basic logic of what in international relations theory is called functionalism. In other words, that there is great-power politics, which produces the tragedy of international politics, which is the security dilemma. My security is your insecurity, and the more security I search, the more insecure you become. And so, there is this problem, this tragedy of international relations. But there is another liberal functionalist view that says, “Hold your horses, that’s all very well. Yes, states do conflict, but we also have all these common interests.” And so, it’s not surprising that we see institutions and innovations emerging to take care of those common interests along functional lines. This was a theory that really took off in the early 20th century and is commonly invoked to explain things like European integration. Because in the end, on this same border bisected by the Rhine, there are Germans, French, Belgians, and Dutch. And it all turns out that they actually all have profoundly similar and identical economic interests, which lead to things like the coal and steel community and the European common market in the 1950s. And this, a hundred years earlier, would be the kind of seed of that logic, which is, “Hey, we may fight wars, but in the end, this is a waterway and we’ve got to figure out how to manage it, and so let’s do some internationalism.’ And then there’s only so many times you can sit down with your counterparts from the other side of the Rhine and agree on technical management logics without constituting some kind of community that transcends pure national interest and security logic. And so, I think you could invoke this as a rather striking example of that kind of functionalist logic in international relations. CA: There has been a lot of discussion in Germany about the economic impact of the drought in the Rhine. But is this drought also of global significance? AT: Well, I mean, I think we probably shouldn’t overrate it. Only about 5 percent of German logistical traffic goes on waterways at all, and 80 percent of that is the Rhine. But when the Rhine is disrupted, it does have a big impact. So, when there were the big floods in 2018, the flooding took, I think, 0.3 to 0.4 percent off German GDP, which is roughly what Germany is expected to grow at this time. So, I mean, part of the attraction of this story at the current moment is that the German economy’s pulse rate is so goddamn low that anything that disrupts it threatens to upheave, obstruct .and violate any further prospect of economic growth. And then there’s the other thing about this, which is that it sits at the nexus of one of the most symbolic elements of German capitalism, which is the chemicals industry. And BASF, which sits in Ludwigshafen and is a Rhine-based heavy chemicals business. And if you think of the three big, iconic names of German industrialism in the 20th century, one would probably be Krupp making steel, and another one might be Mercedes-Benz making cars. And the one in the middle is Rhenish chemical capitalism. And that’s IG Farben. And IG Farben’s core component, the heavy chemicals component of IG Farben, the people that won the Nobel prize for the Fritz Haber-Carl Bosch process is BSF in Ludwigshafen, their business is centered on this axis. They also were the driving force in the huge debate in 2022 during the early phase of the war in Ukraine over the question of whether Germany could do without Russian gas. Again, in the end, it was BASF that was at the core of that conversation, because they take a lot of Russian gas as their feedstock. So here, when we start tweaking these elements of the German system, we see not just really huge pieces of GDP so much as highly symbolic elements of the German industrial and economic system showing their vulnerabilities. BASF is a rich company; they’ll find ways of accessing the raw materials they need. But to find themselves at the mercy of weather, heat, temperature, and rock formations in the Rhine and medieval castles just makes for a kind of configuration of history that is that is truly, truly peculiar. And it’s one, I think, that we have to start getting used to. And when you look at the numbers, it’s kind of bonkers. When you especially look at the Kaub bottleneck, there’s a rock formation there that costs a couple of million euros, probably, to shave off. And they just haven’t gotten around to doing it. And all of a sudden, you’ve got a fraction of 1 percent of GDP on the line that might be disrupted here. And the ecologists will say, ‘Well, just digging the ditch deeper, the channel deeper won’t add water to the Rhine.’ That is absolutely true, it won’t fundamentally change the ecological challenge here. But Germany right now is like an aged, arthritic economic system that is facing a series of combined pressures on it. And so, I think it just does rather vindicate that kind of story that this notionally highly sophisticated powerhouse industrial economy could find itself at the mercy of the question of whether the water level is one or two inches too high or too low. It’s extraordinary. CA: As the water recedes, World War II munitions and sunken vessels are being revealed, and so are hunger stones, carved warning markers from other historic droughts. What is the significance of this archeology of human history that we’re now encountering? AT: The hunger stones are these extraordinary objects that literally have on them the inscription, “If you see this line, weep.” In other words, you’re going to have a terrible harvest and there’s going to be famine. It’s quite the message. Yes, this is part of the story of these places, which takes us right back to your wonderful question at the opening: What do these rivers do? Because they’re both channels of communication and zones of conflict. And right now, it’s not just the Rhine that’s affected by very low water, but the entire European river system. And this has been most dramatic in the Danube, where there’s extremely low water levels, as well. And what’s come to the surface is an entire fleet of, I think, 200 vessels that the Wehrmacht, the retreating German army, sunk deliberately into the Danube River to block presumably Soviet maritime forces coming up from the Black Sea, I guess. And so, then Serbia and other countries are having to sort out how they deal with this detritus that’s emerged from the late war stage. And so, this is another one of these extraordinary effects of what we used to call the anthropocene, this collective massive transformation of the ecological system that we are sited within it. All of a sudden, the effects of the ensuing crisis are that they expose things that we thought were buried forever and that were out of reach. And no, they’re coming back now. Skeletons of forgotten battles are coming back to view. Adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription.
