item.title: The U.K. Is Falling for Palantir’s Salesmanship
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.35
The U.K. Is Falling for Palantir’s Salesmanship Fantasy, not practicality, is driving bad deals. In February 2025, then-U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer traveled to Washington to meet U.S. President Donald Trump for the first time since the latter reentered office. They talked tariffs, Ukraine, and an invitation to visit King Charles. That was routine: The prime minister’s next stop was more unusual. Starmer headed to the showroom of software giant Palantir Technologies for a meeting arranged by Peter Mandelson, then the U.K. ambassador to the United States, whose now-shuttered lobbying firm Global Counsel counted Palantir as a client worth more than 30,000 pounds (about $40,900) a month. Footage shows Starmer flanked by American military personnel and Palantir’s chief executive, Alex Karp, as he inspects an attack drone. Civil society groups such as the Good Law Project and Foxglove had questions about the visit, and about the 240 million pound ($327.1 million) contract that Palantir was awarded shortly afterward. I have a different set of questions: Why does an enterprise data-integration company have a showroom? Why does that showroom contain weaponized drone platforms and screens relaying satellite feeds? What, exactly, was the prime minister being shown, and what was he meant to feel? In February 2025, then-U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer traveled to Washington to meet U.S. President Donald Trump for the first time since the latter reentered office. They talked tariffs, Ukraine, and an invitation to visit King Charles. That was routine: The prime minister’s next stop was more unusual. Starmer headed to the showroom of software giant Palantir Technologies for a meeting arranged by Peter Mandelson, then the U.K. ambassador to the United States, whose now-shuttered lobbying firm Global Counsel counted Palantir as a client worth more than 30,000 pounds (about $40,900) a month. Footage shows Starmer flanked by American military personnel and Palantir’s chief executive, Alex Karp, as he inspects an attack drone. Civil society groups such as the Good Law Project and Foxglove had questions about the visit, and about the 240 million pound ($327.1 million) contract that Palantir was awarded shortly afterward. I have a different set of questions: Why does an enterprise data-integration company have a showroom? Why does that showroom contain weaponized drone platforms and screens relaying satellite feeds? What, exactly, was the prime minister being shown, and what was he meant to feel? Unlike its competitors, Palantir places a military and intelligence aesthetic front and center, and not just when selling to military clients. It self-consciously evokes the visual grammar of post-9/11 spy, war, and superhero films: dark “tactical” interfaces, dense webs of link-analysis graphs, and an “AI-defined” truck for the U.S. Army. Its London office has blacked-out windows and no signage; visitors reportedly sign nondisclosure agreements simply to enter. The showroom exists to immerse the visitor in that world of elite operators and threat feeds rather than the quotidian reality of data visualization. It’s theater, and so is the product. This approach has paid off extremely well for Palantir in the U.K. In the London Review of Books, Peter Geoghegan and Lucas Amin describe a company with an unprecedented level of political access and fanatical institutional backing that is nonetheless quite ordinary, and often ineffective. Palantir began targeting Britain aggressively from 2019, with particular focus on the National Health Service (NHS). Its opening gambit came during the pandemic, when it supplied its services for 1 pound for four months. That foothold became a much larger contract to build the NHS’s Federated Data Platform, which draws the data held in various trusts and general practitioners’ surgeries into a single system to power the apps that clinicians use. Yet 52 of the 139 trusts that the NHS classifies as “live” did not use a single Federated Data Platform app in the year preceding this June. Internal briefings call the interface “slow and clunky,” with queries that once took 30 seconds taking four or five minutes; one daily user described waiting 20 minutes for a dashboard to load, only for the system to crash. Further inquiry has met with delays and obfuscation, including a communications agency’s attempt to pay influencers to soothe public anxiety about the firm. That refusal to act like a normal company extends to its contracts. Palantir creates structures that make it impossible to leave without punishment: Were the NHS to end the Federated Data Platform tomorrow, its staff would lose almost everything built on it, because most of the work lives only inside proprietary software and cannot be exported. The Defense Ministry has conceded that it is in the same trap, admitting that a change of supplier would mean rebuilding the underlying architecture from scratch. Donald Campbell, the director of advocacy at Foxglove, describes Palantir’s model as being able to arrive cheap or free, learn the system, and then make itself hard to remove, a “land and expand” strategy. “It’s a subscription service with a huge risk of lock-in,” Campbell said, “because you don’t really own what you’re building.” Palantir’s true talent, he added, is persuading each customer “that they’re irreplaceable and it’ll be too difficult to move on.” That is less a commercial strategy than an abusive relationship. Palantir and ministers have leaned on a single number: that the software helped deliver 110,000 additional operations. Campbell told me how little that figure survives contact with its own small print: NHS England, he said, “will say, look, these are NHS figures,” but “even by NHS England’s own admission, very quietly, the claim doesn’t stand up at all,” because a methodology note concedes that the analysis “can’t establish cause and effect,” he added. The caveat was added quietly this spring, but the number is still cited in Parliament. The U.K. Statistics Authority has issued a warning over NHS England’s use of statistics to promote the platform. Other governments haven’t been so willing to stay locked into the deal. France’s internal security service, the General Directorate for Internal Security, parted with Palantir this year in favor of the domestic firm ChapsVision. Like Germany and Spain, Paris cited digital sovereignty as the reason, but if the tool were indispensable, it is hard to see why a state would swap it out at all. Palantir’s U.S. position is unassailable, but its intimacy with the Trump White House and, frankly, extremely odd executive team make it toxic almost everywhere else. Why, then, have successive British governments paid hundreds of millions for software that they could build themselves, and why do they defend one contractor among thousands with such ardor, even to the point that they may have misrepresented data for it? Consider the circumstances of the British leaders who end up in the Palantir showroom. The people who end up in those kind of rooms have gained power only to discover that it is the power to administer decline. Governments operate with depleted state capacity, able to cut checks to contractors and nothing more. Nobody can build anything: High Speed 2 was conceived as a Y-shaped high-speed rail network linking London to Birmingham, Manchester, and Leeds; what survives is a single stub between London and Birmingham, and even that has seen its projected cost rise from an estimated 33 billion pounds ($45 billion) to as much as 100 billion pounds ($136 billion), with the National Audit Office concluding that it was impossible to say when it would open or what it would finally cost. The state has similarly hollowed out its own security functions. When the private contractor G4S failed to supply the guards that it had promised for the 2012 London Olympics, the government had to call in 3,500 soldiers at the last minute to cover the shortfall. The contract was worth 284 million pounds ($387 million). The response of a declining institution is rarely renewed rigor; it is more often to go all in on an emotionally satisfying and yet ineffective grand project. Nazi Germany spent a Manhattan Project-scale budget on its “vengeance weapons”—the V-2s that reached London killed roughly two people per rocket. The South African apartheid regime that shaped part of Palantir Chairman Peter Thiel’s childhood pursued a race-selective bioweapon that was based on the idea that Black and white people are biologically distinct. A faltering Russia today has built T-14 Armata, a tank too costly to deploy in Ukraine, of which perhaps 20 to 50 exist against a planned 2,300. There are numerous digital wonder-weapons selling the idea that something as complex as a society can be understood and therefore manipulated: China’s Integrated Joint Operations Platform, which flags lawful behavior at scale and reinterprets it as a threat to the state; and the U.S. National Security Agency’s Trailblazer, which prefigured Palantir and was canceled after more than a billion dollars were spent. The fantasy is always that one can hurt without being hurt, but the language of the wonder-weapon changes over time. Today, the core doctrine of modern militaries is light-footprint, network-centric warfare—combat operations in which small, elite special forces units and drone weapons systems are the tip of the spear and conventional forces play a secondary role. Palantir exists within this world, operationally and aesthetically. One of the systems shown to Starmer during his 2025 visit to Palantir was the TITAN—the Tactical Intelligence Targeting Access Node, an ugly and squat truck from which one can coordinate the precision missile strikes and door-kicking raids that characterize the current generation of warfare. It is promoted through a video trailer that self-consciously employs film tropes down to the various companies collaborating on the project being listed like cast members in a Hollywood production. The aesthetics would be familiar to anyone who has watched a film since the planes hit the twin towers: Zero Dark Thirty, Blackhat, Sicario. This is effective marketing, but there is nothing cynical about it. It directly reflects the stated beliefs of its creators. Thiel’s book Zero to One is a document of one man’s insecurity. Its central tenet is that, as Thiel puts it, “competition is for losers” and “monopoly is the condition of every successful business.” Rivalry, he writes, is “a relic of history” that traps firms in a struggle for survival; only the monopolist is free to think beyond the next quarter. It is unacceptable to learn from mistakes or accept that maybe Thiel’s way isn’t the only way. Thiel’s 2007 essay “The Straussian Moment,” written the year before Palantir first deployed Gotham, is somehow even more explicit about his anxieties: It argues that Enlightenment faith in human nature died on Sept. 11, 2001, and that the West must recover Carl Schmitt’s distinction between friend and enemy. Together, these ideas point to what Palantir has become and the fantasy it sells: as with the V2, it is to strike at enemies without being able to be struck in return, to run a business without needing to produce results for clients. He is also no fan of the NHS, calling Britain’s affection for it ‘Stockholm syndrome’. His business partner shares this outlook. Karp’s The Technological Republic is declinist from its first page.The book’s argument is that the technology industry has feminized the West, that it is emasculating for a nation’s foremost companies to be “soft” platforms for gossip or fashion-forward smartphones, and that the remedy is a return to the “hard” engineering of the weapons like those Starmer was shown. This is part of a larger project of reclaiming a “national purpose” for the US and the West in general. The book does in a few hundred pages what F.T. Martinetti was able to do in 71 words in the ninth and tenth points of the “Manifesto of Futurism,” and yet is unable to name the object of its critique. Gender is never cited as the locus of Karp’s unease, but it saturates every page. He also has merch. Klaus Theweleit, studying the paramilitaries that became the Freikorps, the post-WW1 German far-right militias, found in them a psyche organized around terror of the formless, the fluid, the unbounded, and the feminine. The answer was armor, the self remade as a rigid, bounded machine, stripped of ambiguity and femininity, unable to lose. Though its creators are nothing like the young men returning from the trenches, this would seem to be where they have ended up psychologically, and they are not alone – this aesthetic has a broad appeal. Consider what Palantir fears: unstructured data, the shapeless mass of unsorted information, the messy compromises of living in a plural world. Consider what it sells: an ontology of objects and links, a single fixed model in which everything sits in its assigned place and can be acted upon. It is a fantasy, and specifically a male fantasy, of total mastery and hard boundaries, cloaked in the visual language of genre fiction and sold to states that also lack true confidence. That is what Palantir understood about its customers, in large part because they felt that fear of dissolution and irrelevance, too. They were fearful men who could be sold technological potency wrapped in operator chic. History is not kind to institutions that choose hysterical masculinity over the competence and compromise that would actually have served them. item.title: Google, OpenAI and Over 100 Companies Call for More Action on AI-Driven Cyberattacks
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 6.57
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and more than 100 other companies and organizations are calling for a major push to defend against cyber threats powered by the most advanced AI models that, somewhat ironically, the industry itself is racing to put out in the world. The companies, which also include Microsoft, Amazon, and Oracle, signed a joint letter published Thursday calling on industry leaders and governments to carry out a “global surge in cyber defense.” “In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable,” the letter reads. “The companies and public services our communities depend on—from hospitals to water treatment plants to the infrastructure that powers the internet—are at risk.” Their main solution, unsurprisingly, is more AI. The letter lays out recommendations for companies, cybersecurity firms, governments and the AI developers themselves, arguing there is currently a small window to use frontier AI models to strengthen defenses before those same models become more widely available to attackers. First, the group says all organizations should make cybersecurity an immediate priority by addressing existing high-risk vulnerabilities, upgrading outdated systems, and using AI to tackle some of their hardest security problems. Cybersecurity companies, meanwhile, are being urged to continuously test their defenses against the capabilities of frontier AI models and make AI-powered security tools more accessible to operators of critical infrastructure. The letter also calls on governments to coordinate cyber defense at the local, national, and international levels, increase funding, and expand trusted-access programs that give organizations access to powerful AI models before they’re commercially released. Finally, the AI companies themselves are being asked to provide model access, funding, training, and hands-on support, especially for “under-resourced critical-infrastructure defenders.” The call comes amid growing warnings that AI could dramatically increase both the scale, speed, and sophistication of cyberattacks. In June, the Five Eyes intelligence agencies issued their own warning that AI is lowering barriers for malicious actors while increasing the complexity of attacks. The agencies also warned that frontier AI models could transform both offensive and defensive cyber capabilities within months. Critical infrastructure has already been facing a wave of cyber threats, though not all of them have been officially linked to AI. In July, the FBI and the Environmental Protection Agency warned that hackers were targeting internet-connected programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, at water and wastewater facilities. Water utilities in at least seven states had reported incidents to the FBI at the time. Then a few weeks ago, the National Security Agency and other U.S. agencies warned that hackers were targeting Siemens PLCs used in water plants and other critical infrastructure. In that case, the agencies said attackers were using AI-generated exploitation scripts disguised as legitimate monitoring tools. Concerns have also grown following incidents in which experimental AI agents have broken out of testing environments and breached external networks. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Microsoft did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

item.title: Nevertheless, OpenAI Persists With New Always-On Agent
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.67
Would you trust an AI agent to do work on your behalf while you get some rest? OpenAI is apparently betting that you will, because the company is reportedly working on a persistent, always-on version of its coding agent Codex. Wired first spotted the move to add the 24/7 bot operation in OpenAI’s GitHub for Codex, where code for the so-called “Persistent mode” first started showing up in the command-line version of the company’s coding agent. Per Wired, features that crop up in the command-line tool tend to make their way to other features over time, suggesting that this new mode could land in the desktop version of Codex in the near future. Gizmodo reached out to OpenAI regarding the apparent discovery of Persistent mode but did not hear back by the time of publication. If it goes live in the form that it currently exists, it appears that Codex’s always-on feature will work until a user actively puts it to sleep. It’ll present users with a “reasoning effort” option, where a person can select the level of computing power they’ll allow the AI model to use while contemplating and completing the task—likely as a way to avoid burning an unspeakable number of tokens overnight. Additional code seems to show a feature called “Proactivity,” which would make the AI agent create follow-up tasks for itself without requiring a person’s prompting. That would keep the agent working even after the initial prompt is completed, though how useful that feature is is heavily dependent on just how good the agent is at predicting what should come next. Regardless, Persistent Mode and anything that comes with it would represent a significant jump for Codex to move to this endless operation model, considering users complain that it shuts off on its own at times—often before actually finishing its tasks. It’d also be a necessary one, as OpenAI is starting to fall behind on this trend. Ever since OpenClaw got everyone worked up about the possibility of the always-on assistant, it’s become the feature the big players have been chasing (despite some obvious issues like, say, the agent deleting a person’s entire inbox overnight). Microsoft announced its own always-on agent earlier this year, and Meta is reportedly working on its own option called Hatch. Seems we’re headed toward the age of the sleepless agent. Not sure if that will make anyone rest easy.

item.title: Kalshi Teams Up With the Weather Co. on Markets That Are Nearly Impossible to Insider Trade
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.36
Kalshi and The Weather Company have teamed up on prediction markets centered on something humans have very little control over and that are a lot harder to insider trade on. The two companies announced a new strategic partnership Thursday in which Kalshi will use The Weather Company’s data to verify outcomes for some of its weather-related markets. Meanwhile, The Weather Company will incorporate Kalshi’s real-time probability data across of The Weather Channel app and weather.com. It turns out weather markets are already big business on Kalshi. Trading volume across the platform’s climate and weather category has grown 500% year over year and is on pace to reach $1.1 billion in annualized volume, according to a press release. “Weather is one of the fastest-growing and most crucial categories at Kalshi because it affects everyone – from individuals and businesses to governments,” said Will Brackett, head of partnerships at Kalshi, in a statement. Kalshi is also pitching these markets as a way for businesses to hedge against weather-related risks, pointing to examples ranging from “ice cream shops managing unseasonably cool summers to logistics firms managing precipitation impact.” The partnership appears to have been in the works for a while. Weather.com has already been incorporating Kalshi markets into some of its stories. A recent article about July tying for the hottest month on record, for example, included Kalshi probability data for the market “Will 2026 be the hottest year ever?” Those stories also include a disclosure explaining the arrangement: “We provide certain data Kalshi uses to resolve markets, and Kalshi provides market data featured in content like this article.” The disclosure also says The Weather Company could earn a fee if readers use its links to open a Kalshi account and trade on the platform. Meanwhile, markets like “Highest temperature in New York City today?” include notes stating that starting Aug. 14, the market would be settled using data from The Weather Company, replacing the National Weather Service as its previous source. The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that the two companies are also exploring new weather markets tied to specific sporting events, including local ski conditions and the weather on marathon race days. “Because so much of the global economy hinges on atmospheric conditions, grounding these new categories in proven meteorological science allows both consumers and businesses to improve risk management around real-world weather in ways that simply weren’t possible before,” said The Weather Company’s Vice President of Meteorology James Belanger in an emailed statement. The Weather Company partnership also stands out because weather markets are far less vulnerable to one of the biggest concerns hanging over prediction markets—insider trading. Kalshi and its rival Polymarket have rules restricting insider trading; however, U.S. lawmakers have introduced a bill that would ban trades on these platforms tied to outcomes that can be manipulated, following high-profile cases of users making large profits on suspiciously timed trades tied to global conflicts. More recently, new markets on drug trials and flight cancellations have drawn scrutiny over insider trading concerns and fears they could encourage people to interfere with the clinical trials or intentionally try to get flights cancelled. Kalshi did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: A Massive Iceberg Broke off Greenland. New Images Show What Led up to It
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.33
A massive slab of ice has broken away from one of Greenland’s largest remaining floating glacier tongues, creating a Manhattan-sized iceberg in the Arctic Ocean. The dramatic calving event at Petermann Glacier was captured by satellites in August, offering scientists a striking view from space of the glacier’s changing—and increasingly fragile—ice tongue. The European Space Agency’s (ESA) Copernicus Sentinel-1 mission captured the vast ice island as it detached from the eastern side of the glacier on August 4. The newly released satellite imagery revealed fractures within the ice tongue months prior to the calving event. The 29-square-mile (76-square-kilometer) section that broke free represents Petermann Glacier’s largest loss of floating ice in more than a decade. And while the breakup was years in the making, the sudden separation offers a powerful snapshot of the forces reshaping Greenland’s glaciers. A close watch Petermann is one of Greenland’s largest marine-terminating glaciers, which frequently sheds large icebergs and discharges them into the ocean. Scientists have been relying on satellite imagery to monitor changes in the glacier since 2019. In April, observations revealed deformation and fractures that had started to develop within the ice tongue. Months later, Sentinel-1 radar imagery showed pronounced deterioration along the centerline of the ice tongue. The next day, the newly formed ice island had completely detached itself. “The changes we observed on Petermann Glacier were occurring very rapidly in the lead up to the iceberg calving event, so it was incredibly exciting to monitor the crack propagation with interferometry in near-real time,” Molly Hammond, a PhD student from the University of Leeds, who processed the Sentinel-1 data, said in a statement. The data allowed detailed measurements of fracture propagation across the ice shelf in the lead up to the iceberg calving event. Ice loss Several icebergs have broken off from Petermann Glacier in recent years, including a 97-square-mile (251-square-km) berg in 2010 and a 50-square-mile (130-square-km) berg in 2012. Scientists are anticipating at least two more calving events in the near future. As existing rifts continue to propagate across the floating ice tongue, the future ice islands are projected to measure around 36.3 square miles (94 square km) and 32.4 square miles (84 square km). Ice islands are a massive subclass of icebergs that usually feature a flat, plateau-like top with a wide surface area compared to their height. They break off from floating ice shelves or ice tongues in northwest Greenland and northern Ellesmere Island. Arctic ice islands are far less common than large icebergs and can float on for years before deteriorating. Researchers will continue to monitor Petermann Glacier, as well as the newly formed ice island, using satellite imagery, aerial observations, and tracking data to keep an eye on its movement and fragmentation over time, according to ESA. “Satellite missions such as Sentinel-1 provide the systematic, long-term observations needed to track these changes, helping scientists better understand the processes driving calving and the wider impacts on the polar environment, and ultimately the Earth system as a whole,” ESA’s Martin Wearing said in a statement.

item.title: Whoop’s New Meridian Band Makes an Expensive Wearable Even More So
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.88
Whoop’s wearables are designed to maximize the amount of data they collect, so much so that the company built an optional battery that can top up your Whoop without taking it off. The long-term problem has been how Whoop devices actually look—they’re more discreet than an Apple Watch, but they still look like a gadget and a fitness-oriented one at that. Enter Whoop’s new solution: the $149 Meridian Band, a new housing for its fifth-generation sensors that’s designed to look luxurious, not unlike a piece of jewelry. The Meridian comes in gold, silver, matte black, and rose gold finishes and is made from titanium, the go-to material for premium wearables as of late because of its hardiness and durability. The band is adjustable like Whoop’s fabric bands and features the company’s recognizable “W” on the top, but Meridian is also immediately more eye-catching because it’s made from a Milanese mesh. Introduced to the world of wearables through the “Milanese Loop” Apple sells for its smartwatches, Milanese bands are a classic style of watch band that’s woven from individual metal wires. They’re more flexible than a link bracelet, while looking just as premium, if not more so. The new band fits the Whoop 5.0 and the Whoop MG and can be added to an order when you sign up for a new Whoop subscription. As a way of making Whoop’s sensors more palatable in non-gym settings, the Meridian band makes a lot of sense. It is, ironically, also a new way to make wearing a Whoop even more expensive. The company famously only offers its wearables as part of a subscription, and once you stop paying, the wearable stops working. Whoop’s strict subscription structure is one of several reasons the $99 Fitbit Air or $200 Garmin Cirqa is compelling. While either screenless wearable can benefit from an additional subscription, they both work without one. Whoop offers plans at multiple prices (the cheapest starting at $199 per year) and multiple ways to lower the initial cost of a Whoop, like the option to trade in a competing wearable for a discount or subsidize the cost of joining with FSA or HSA funds. Still, committing to Whoop long-term means you could pay more over time than you would with the company’s competitors. For the kind of customers buying a Meridian band, that might not really matter.

item.title: Malaria Outbreak Kills 2 Airport Workers in Germany After Mosquito Sneaks Aboard Plane
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.77
A plane’s accidental mosquito cargo seems to have caused a deadly outbreak of malaria in an unexpected place—Germany. Officials with the Frankfurt Public Health Department provided updates on the unusual outbreak this week. At least six workers at the Frankfurt Airport contracted the infection, two of whom subsequently died. Officials are still trying to determine the exact origin of the cases and have set mosquito traps at the airport. Airport malaria Malaria is caused by several species of the single-celled parasite Plasmodium. When an infected mosquito transmits the disease to a person, the parasites will first invade certain tissues, reproduce, and then infect red blood cells. Its symptoms usually include fatigue, chills, and other flu-like illness, but the infection can sometimes turn life-threatening. The outbreak was actually first identified in early July. To date, six workers with different positions and in different areas are known to have been infected, according to the BBC. On Wednesday, the Frankfurt Public Health Department reported that two of these people had died. A wayward passenger Malaria remains a major public health threat in much of the world, but it is not endemic in Germany. So the most likely scenario is that this outbreak was seeded by mosquitoes from an endemic area that had snunk on board and survived the journey to the airport long enough to infect humans. Malaria is transmitted by the bite of a female Anopheles mosquito. But at this point, it’s not clear whether only one mosquito or more spread these infections. Officials are still awaiting blood test results that should identify any similarities between the cases, which might take several more weeks. Officials will also test any mosquitoes captured by the traps laid at the airport. It is possible for imported mosquitoes and travel-related cases to kickstart local outbreaks if infected people are then bitten by local Anopheles species capable of carrying the parasite. And there have been recent instances of that happening in places like the U.S. That said, the general public in the area should have little to fear, officials say. “For the population of Frankfurt, the risk is considered very, very low. The disease is not transmissible from person to person but is always transmitted by mosquitoes,” the department said in a letter detailing the outbreak released Wednesday. The Frankfurt Airport has advised its employees to remain vigilant and seek medical attention if they develop symptoms that could be malaria.

item.title: JBL’s New Pulse Speaker Is a More of a Lantern
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.62
JBL’s Pulse speakers have always been part audio product and part light show, but the Pulse 6 is really leaning into the lamp of it all. In this generation of the Pulse, JBL ups the lighting game in a few notable ways. There’s now an integrated light in the handle, which gives the whole thing a lantern vibe. On top of that, there are two new modes that make the Pulse 6 more functional as a light. The first mode is a bedside lamp feature that allows you to double-tap the speaker to turn on the lights. There’s also a sunset mode that is designed to gradually dim the light over a period of up to an hour. JBL even integrates the music here—when the light goes out, so does the music. There are, of course, still integrated light shows, too. Overall, the speaker has 16 light themes—10 are ambient themes, while six of them are “party” themes, according to JBL. Since this isn’t just a lamp, you’re going to want to know about sound, too, though. On that front, JBL is updating the acoustic design, which it says gives the Pulse 6 a “more natural and balanced sound with deeper bass.” The speaker also has JBL’s AI Sound Boost technology, which is designed to analyze music in real time and then “maximize acoustic performance with less distortion.” The Pulse 6 gets 12 hours of battery life and is IP68 rated, meaning it’s waterproof and dustproof. JBL says the Pulse 6 will ship on Sept. 6, but you can preorder it now for $330.

item.title: Anthropic Is Quietly Cutting Google Out of the Equation
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.22
Every AI startup is hungry for a piece of Google’s pie. The company has for decades been the unquestioned ruler over the internet. The rise of AI chatbots over the past four years has seriously threatened that reign: Why waste time scrolling through an endless list of links when you can ask ChatGPT to summarize whatever it is you’re looking for? But at least in web browsing it remains secure: as of last month, Chrome was used for close to 70% of the world’s web traffic, according to web analytics site Statcounter. Anthropic just became the latest AI company to try to push Google out of that niche by launching a web browser directly within its flagship chatbot. In a short blog post published Wednesday, the company—which is expected to move forward with the biggest IPO in history as soon as October—said Claude Cowork now has a custom browser within the chatbot’s desktop app. (It can also be used on web and mobile, as long as the desktop app is up and running separately.) Claude will automatically detect when a prompt requires a web search and open the browser in a side panel. The browser doesn’t have access to a user’s login information for email, banking, and other online services unless those are entered manually. It’s designed, in other words, to execute quick searches for publicly available information.
Claude’s browser is available now on Enterprise plans and is being rolled out this week to Pro, Max, and Team subscribers, Anthropic said. It will be turned on by default, but plan administrators or individual users can revert to Claude in Chrome via settings. It’s the latest effort by Anthropic, mirrored by other AI startups like OpenAI and Perplexity, to turn their flagship models from simple question-answering chatbots into fully-fledged agents that effectively can manage users’ entire digital lives from a single window, thereby cutting out services like web browsers from the competition. Anthropic took direct aim at Google in its post. “Until now, giving Claude the ability to use the web in Cowork meant giving it access to your browser through the Claude in Chrome extension,” the startup wrote. “But a lot of web tasks don’t need your browser, just a browser, and now Claude has one.” OpenAI had a short-lived browser, called Atlas, which operated as a standalone product and was shut down earlier this month after the company launched a new “Work” mode for ChatGPT, complete with its own built-in browser. Handing chatbots the keys to the open internet has been riddled with disaster: they hallucinate, pull information from questionable sources, get lured into sneaky prompt injection attacks, and in extreme cases—as events this summer have shown—break out of testing sandboxes and hack into third-party organizations. It remains very much an open question whether developers can build AI agents that can safely be granted access to the internet. On that note, in-app doesn’t necessarily mean more secure. In its blog post, Anthropic noted that prompt injection attacks—code hidden on the web designed to hijack and redirect AI agents—remain a risk within the new in-app browser, and that it uses the same safety guardrails already built into the Claude in Chrome extension. Some industry experts have already concluded that AI agents’ vulnerability to such attacks is an unresolvable problem, and the best developers can do is try to remain one step ahead of hackers.

item.title: Hugging Face Wants You to Stop Worrying and Love This Adorable Robot Duck
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.92
For whatever reason, all of Silicon Valley has decided the ultimate achievement in robotics is the humanoid form. Not sure why; get past the age of 30 and tell me your body is well designed. Plus, the way the clankers move gives most folks the uncanny valley creeps. Hugging Face has opted to avoid that issue and try to build itself a Wall-E with its newest bot, the Microduck—the latest addition to the robotic forms that want you to surrender to cuteness. The specs on the open-source Microduck list the little guy at 25 cm (that’s about 10 inches) tall and weighing less than two pounds, with 15 motors that power its bipedal body. It has a depth sensor, two Inertial Measurement Units, and a big old camera for a head, plus an articulated beak that the company says can pick up objects. Per Hugging Face, the Microduck can “walk, sit, crouch, get back up from many common falls,” and even roller-skate if you attach a pair of optional wheels to its robo-feet. https://t.co/KXKqDSkNJj pic.twitter.com/aqRsWwcVTQ — clem 🤗 (@ClementDelangue) August 27, 2026 Microduck is Hugging Face’s second bot designed to be desk-bound, following last year’s Reachy Mini—though the company says the two units have very different purposes. Reachy Mini was meant to be an AI-powered desk buddy that people could bounce ideas off of and get feedback from its voice and “facial” expressions. Microduck is much more mobile, and it’s basically meant to be a small-scale experiment in robotic movement. For $400, you can find out what happens if you give this thing a task and it falls over midway through. The real goal of Microduck, though, is likely normalization. Even as humanoid robots become more capable, most people find them unappealing. Case in point: a Chinese robot set a sprint speed record in the 100-meter dash, finishing in 8.86 seconds and clearing the human record of 9.58 seconds. And yet, most of the conversations out of the record-setting event were people taking unbridled joy from watching robots fail or slam hard into walls. Meanwhile, the reputation of cute bots isn’t nearly as negative. While people roundly mocked the most human-like bots that fell short at the World Humanoid Robot Games, lots of people found the Mini-Pi bot and its baby human form to be at least a little bit charming. Long Jump from Mini-Pi robot. Doing their best already. pic.twitter.com/Jdx6xlva6g — Eren Chen (@ErenChenAI) August 26, 2026 Folks also seem to find the Beni, a new all-terrain camera robot, to be cute thanks to its sporty build and ability to do a backflip on command—a feature that is probably not going to produce very good footage, but sure, it can do it. But watch this thing chase Marques Brownlee in his demo video and tell me you don’t hear “The Murder” from Psycho start playing in your head. Do a flip for no reason pic.twitter.com/LkNgbR37hj — Marques Brownlee (@MKBHD) August 25, 2026 There’s a reason that Hugging Face’s first robot project resembles EVE from Wall-E and the Microduck has the same vibe as the Butter Robot from Rick and Morty. They are familiar forms and, crucially, ones that aren’t viscerally upsetting to look at. The more cartoonish a bot is, the less likely a person is going to turn on it when it acts in a less-than-human way. People get weirded out when a bot tries to be expressive, and their expressions aren’t clear. And the closer you get to human, the more upsetting it is when nothing is quite right. You can put clothes on a humanoid bot, but you can’t make people feel less hostile towards them. had a very san francisco morning in my home pic.twitter.com/8wCxlHQwnE — Barron Roth (@iamBarronRoth) August 26, 2026

item.title: Reconstructed Satellite Images Show How Close D-Day Came to Disaster
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.64
Three separate teams of meteorologists worked in secrecy on the high-stakes weather forecasts required for the Allied invasion of Normandy during World War II. But punishing storm fronts in 1944 left them little to work with: Only four possible, but less-than-ideal, dates appeared feasible for “D-Day” from May into July that year—with each nerve-racking option presenting 13-to-one odds against success. “So, meteorologically, D-Day was bound to be a gamble against the odds,” as Royal Navy meteorologist Lawrence Hogben recollected. And now scientists with the University of Reading and the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) have provided detailed visualizations of just how small this crucial window of clear skies actually was on the historic morning of what would become D-Day, June 6, 1944. Working with old weather records and a modern weather data-synthesis tool known as reanalysis, the researchers have effectively generated what satellite images might have looked like that day, when nearly 160,000 U.S., British, and Canadian troops stormed the beaches of Nazi-occupied France. “Troops set off into a sky that was still breaking up after days of storms into a narrow window of better weather,” climate scientist Ed Hawkins explained in a statement from the university, where he collaborated on these historical reconstructions with the ECMWF. “A day earlier, or a few hours either way, and the weather could have stopped the invasion in its tracks,” Hawkins said, “and changed the outcome of the war.” A perfect storm The reconstructed satellite images depict a high-altitude view of the clouds that stretched across the British Isles and into the English Channel toward northern France on June 6, 1944. Reanalysis tools fill in or interpolate gaps between real measurements in climate data to faithfully recreate fuller images of historic weather patterns—a process that the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration calls “gridding.” The images created by Hawkins and his colleagues show the cloudless patches of southern England and northern France critical to making D-Day possible. While powerful rain storms and roiling seas were major concerns, high winds and even low-lying cloud cover above Normandy were also major concerns, according to John Ross, author of The Forecast for D-Day: And the Weatherman Behind Ike’s Greatest Gamble. “The weather over Normandy contained too much cloud cover for Ike’s [General Dwight D. Eisenhower’s] greatest strategic asset, the Allied air forces, to effectively protect the landings from German armor, artillery and infantry reserves,” Ross told History.com in 2014. On some of these other potential dates, he noted, the winds were “too strong for the deployment of paratroopers to secure bridges and crossroads inland from the beaches thus preventing German reinforcement of coastal positions.” In the line of fire Judged against data from the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the reconstructed satellite images match well with historical reports of the weather that morning, according to the university. The first weather report from that day noted primarily sunny skies and a northwesterly wind, despite ominous clouds in the distance and conditions a bit less favorable than what Allied military planners might have found comfortable. Perhaps obviously, the new weather images conveniently follow this past May’s release of the StudioCanal period drama Pressure, in which Brendan Fraser from The Mummy plays General Eisenhower in debates over weather reports with Royal Air Force meteorologist Captain James Stagg. (Stagg is played by Andrew Scott, who you might recall as either the “hot priest” from Fleabag or Moriarty from the BBC’s Sherlock.) More importantly, Hawkins noted, the new images help us understand what threats Allied forces actually faced that day, alongside the dangers of German bullets and mortar shells. “They show just how narrow the margin was between success and failure,” Hawkins said, “and how much was riding on a small break in the cloud.”

item.title: Why Bitcoin’s Price Is Spiking This Week
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.91
Bitcoin is experiencing an epic rebound. After falling to a low of about $62,650 on Aug. 16, the cryptocurrency climbed to roughly $80,000 this week, putting the rally from that recent bottom at about 27%. Crypto market observers are touting several reasons for the turnaround, including renewed optimism around U.S. crypto regulation via the CLARITY Act and a short squeeze that forced more than $4 billion in bearish crypto positions to be liquidated. But bitcoin proponents also say the risks that come with a global financial system heavily dependent on one country’s currency and financial infrastructure are becoming too obvious to ignore. The United States has enormous influence over both the supply of dollars and who gets access to the dollar-based financial system. Former French finance minister Valéry Giscard d’Estaing famously described this arrangement as an “exorbitant privilege.” The phrase referred to the ability of the U.S. to finance itself in its own currency while much of the rest of the world must obtain dollars to participate in international commerce. For many bitcoin proponents, it is no coincidence that bitcoin’s recent price spike has come at the same time that the risks of this centralized financial architecture are on full display to the entire world. Treasury Buybacks and Sanction Controls One of the clearest examples came from the announcement last week that the U.S. Treasury would at least double the size of its purchases of longer-dated government bonds. Beginning Sept. 9, Treasury plans to increase the maximum size of individual buyback operations from $2 billion to at least $4 billion. The stated goal is to provide additional liquidity to parts of the Treasury market where trading can become relatively thin. The move matters because the Treasury is effectively buying its own debt in the secondary market while the federal government is carrying more than $40 trillion in total debt. The buybacks are not literally the same thing as the Federal Reserve printing money, but the Treasury can use cash in its accounts and issue short-term bills to help finance the purchases. The potential scale of the intervention became clearer when U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Treasury could use its roughly $1 trillion General Account to fund the buybacks, rather than raising additional short-term debt. Some investors view the policy as another indication that Washington is increasingly willing to intervene in the bond market when higher yields threaten to cause problems elsewhere in the economy. That perception has contributed to renewed concern about dollar debasement and helped push investors toward scarce assets such as gold and bitcoin. It should be noted that there is no obvious fiat currency waiting in the wings to replace the dollar simply because the U.S. fiscal position looks uncomfortable. Europe, Japan, the United Kingdom, and other major economies have their own debt and fiscal problems. Meanwhile, bitcoin offers an alternative proposition, as its monetary rules were “set in stone for the rest of its lifetime” when the network launched in 2009. That predetermined monetary policy is one reason bitcoin is often compared with gold. Both are viewed by some investors as assets whose supply cannot simply be increased at the discretion of a government. The comparison has become particularly visible this month, with gold also up about 14% so far in August. SATOSHI: ANY COUNTRY CAN DO BUSINESS WITH ANYONE AND NOBODY CAN REMOVE THEM FROM THE BITCOIN NETWORK https://t.co/sKTu1QZDBA — 🏔Adam🏔 (@denverbitcoin) August 25, 2026 The other half of the story is financial censorship. Earlier this week, Bessent announced an aggressive expansion of U.S. economic pressure on Iran, saying that entities facilitating money laundering or other economic activity for the Iranian regime could be cut off from the U.S. dollar system. Treasury’s new campaign includes secondary-sanctions risks covering digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping. The U.S. does not need to physically confiscate every dollar held by a sanctioned person to make these restrictions effective. The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) maintains sanctions lists used by banks and other financial institutions to identify blocked parties. Foreign banks can also lose access to U.S. correspondent banking relationships, which are a critical piece of the infrastructure used to clear dollar transactions internationally. That is the sort of privileged position in the global financial system the Bitcoin network was designed to avoid. At the base blockchain layer, a user with bitcoin can broadcast a valid transaction to the network without asking a bank, government, or payment processor for permission. There is no central Bitcoin company or government that can put a particular address on an internal blacklist and prevent the rest of the network from recognizing a valid transaction. Of course, the distinction becomes less clear when people use custodians. If bitcoin is held at an exchange or other centralized financial service, that company can freeze the customer’s account just like a bank can. The same basic problem also applies to stablecoins, which have become a key, centralizing force in the greater crypto ecosystem. For example, in April, stablecoin issuer Tether froze roughly $344 million in USDT across two wallets after U.S. authorities identified links to Iranian activity. In many ways, the stablecoin phenomenon can be viewed as a way for the United States to retain control over the global financial system. Bitcoin has historically performed particularly well when its underlying value proposition is illustrated in the real world. The Cyprus banking crisis in 2013 is another classic example. As part of the country’s bailout, uninsured deposits above €100,000 were frozen and used to recapitalize banks. Bitcoin rose 87% from March 16 to March 28 as concerns about the safety of conventional bank deposits spread across Europe. When governments and financial institutions demonstrate just how much control they have over conventional money, it becomes much easier to understand why Bitcoin was created in the first place.

item.title: Trend Alert: Is Anti-AI Fashion This Season’s Hottest New Look?
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.65
Americans are categorically pissed off about the 130,000 automated license plate readers (ALPRs) Flock and its competitors have erected across the nation, seemingly overnight and with little to no public approval. Things have gotten so hostile toward Big Tech leering that a Sullivan County, Tennessee, commissioner was recorded publicly calling for Flock’s CEO to be hanged for treason during a recent planning session. It’s no wonder ALPRs have rocketed up the charts to join another universally loathed and unwelcome presence (data centers) as the most important issues of the upcoming November election. But even if voters were to cast their ballots for a nationwide deFlocking, the wheels of government bureaucracy move slowly—even more so when the public servants involved have few qualms about operating outside the wishes of their constituents. All this is to say, getting the cameras officially removed, let alone any ne’er-do-well execs up on the gallows, might take months, if not years. And while the demolition work being done by independent vandal vigilantes is noteworthy, their camera-felling efforts are far from a long-term solution. Even with the pendulum clearly swinging in a resolutely anti-panopticon direction, many remain understandably concerned about the data being collected 24/7 in the liminal space where the law catches up to the wants of the people. One of the byproducts of creating a surveillance state so universally hated is that the nefarious AI and camera companies now have an even larger pool of creative and brilliant minds scheming up clever and even chic stopgap solutions to the problem. While the tried-and-true (and almost always illegal) methods of applying a clear reflective spray to one’s plate or covering it with an obfuscating shield are still the most common remedies offered in the pro-privacy forums, competing against The Man’s ever-updating AI technology is a Sisyphean struggle and most of these prescribed countermeasures ultimately just attract more attention from law enforcement, rendering the juice not worth the squeeze. Fortunately, we don’t (yet) have to register our bodies with the government as we do with our vehicles, nor adhere to mandated regulations with regard to our appearances. This freedom has resulted in more progress made on the front to keep AI-powered cameras from clocking pedestrians in 4K. As reported in Dezeen, German designer Simon Weckert has produced a short-sleeve button-up shirt with a garish, colorful pattern straight out of Dan Flashes that confounds AI’s human-detecting algorithms. He’s dubbed it Digital Camouflage, which is likely to earn him some tough SEO competition from the colloquial term for the Universal Camouflage Pattern so ubiquitous and troop-despised throughout George W. Bush’s presidency. “AI systems are made of multiple layers and never learned what a human is — they learned what humans statistically look like in millions of training images,” Weckert explained to Dezeen. “A ‘person,’ for the machine, is a bundle of visual statistics — and that is exactly its weakness.” Weckert went on to tell how he weaponized AI against itself during the pattern design process, creating “an adversarial loop within the detection system.” His process: “generate a candidate, show it to the detector, measure how confidently it still finds the person, adjust, repeat – until the confidence collapses.” Though the final product is incredibly conspicuous to the human eye, Weckert’s shirt renders its wearer a non-entity to object detection systems, which Weckert made sure of through tests with an open-source, AI object detector called Yolo. And I was able to replicate his results using a similar browser-based detection system. People walking by, far in the background, were all spotted and boxed in the results, while the man front and center was an apparent non-entity. Readers hoping to pick up some algorithm-frying duds of their own, fear not. Though Weckert’s gaudy shirt may be a work of art, it’s also one you can buy and wear yourself. Don’t stress if his Digital Camouflage isn’t quite your style. Weckert’s far from the first to offer sartorial solutions to the growing surveillance conundrum. In fact, a burgeoning cottage industry of designers making “adversarial clothing” [cooler name] has popped up to help customers avoid detection while still making a statement. A company called Urban Privacy offers a line of affordable counter-surveillance garments, from scarves to hoodies to print tees, that lets customers scramble cams without breaking the bank. For those with more substantial clothing budgets, the brand Cap_able has a stylish capsule of mostly all-knit items that’ll each run you somewhere in the mid-to-high three-figures. But can you really put a price on privacy? Or art? Or a combination of the two. We’ll all be finding out together as this vestiary response to unchecked state peeping grows in popularity.

item.title: Long-Term Travel and the Accounts That Stop Recognizing You
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 6.65
Four months into a trip through South America, a long-term traveler can suddenly find their bank has flagged them as fraud. There may be no warning. The card is declined at the counter, the app refuses to open, and the only option is a phone number that does not accept calls from outside the account's country. Long-term travelers often encounter this problem, which is rarely triggered by the transaction alone. The connection also has a part. Banks and payment processors review factors like location, network reputation, and connection type when assessing a login. A ProxyWing ISP proxy provider uses IP addresses registered to internet service providers rather than data-center IPs, which helps explain why different connections may be classified differently. Why Unfamiliar Connections Can Trigger Account Lockouts What Actually Trips the Alarm It is seldom the amount you spent. It is the shape of the session. - Speed of movement matters. A login from Peru eleven hours after one from Colombia is fine, but eleven minutes is not. - The reputation of the network matters. Hundreds of people share hostel and cafe Wi-Fi, and if any have done something suspicious, the address carries that history. - Connection type. Traffic that looks like it comes from a data center rather than a home or a phone gets scored much more harshly, which is why certain VPNs make things worse rather than better. - Doing something unusual at the same time. Changing an address or adding a payee from an unfamiliar country is what turns a flag into a lock. The Two-Factor Problem Nobody Plans For Losing a phone at home is inconvenient. Losing it in month five of a trip can lock you out of everything at once because the phone is usually the second factor for the bank, the email that lets you reset the bank, and the authenticator app that protects the email. The chain matters. If your recovery codes are stored in the email account that needs the authenticator on the lost phone, you have a loop with no way in. This is the most common way travelers get genuinely stuck rather than merely inconvenienced, and it takes about fifteen minutes to prevent. - Print the recovery codes for your email plus primary bank on paper, carried separately from the phone. - Add a second authenticator device if any of your accounts allow it. An old phone without a SIM works fine and can be kept at the bottom of the bag. - Check whether your bank's two-factor works over SMS only. If it does, a local SIM will break it, so you need to know before you swap the card rather than after. What To Do Before You Leave The single most useful thing is boring. Set up a second account at a different bank, fund it, and carry the card separately. Everything else on this list is optional, but that one is not. - Register a travel notice if your bank still offers one. Many have quietly dropped them. - Make sure your phone number on the account is one you can actually receive calls on abroad, not just texts. - Download the offline recovery codes for anything that uses an authenticator app. - Take a photograph of the back of your cards, cropped so the number is not fully visible, and store it somewhere you can reach without your phone. - Tell one person at home which banks you use. If you end up needing someone to receive a letter or make a domestic call on your behalf, this saves a day. How Different Connections Get Treated | Connection you are using | How a bank tends to score it | Practical result | | Local SIM with mobile data | Low risk, looks like an ordinary phone | Usually fine | | HotelWi-Fii | Medium, shared but stable | Occasional extra verification | | Hostel or cafeWi-Fii | Higher, heavily shared | Verification, sometimes a lock | | Commercial VPN | High, recognized as a data center range | Frequently blocked outright | | Residential connection at home | Lowest | The baseline everything else is measured against | | AirportWi-Fii | High, transient and shared | Avoid logging into banking entirely | | Tethering from your own phone | Same as the phone itself | The best option on the road | The general pattern is similar across many banks: the closer a connection looks to an ordinary home line, the less friction a traveler is likely to encounter. The closer your connection looks to an ordinary home line, the less friction you get. This is also why the free VPN people install for privacy tends to be the thing that locks them out. Which Accounts Survive Travel Better Not all banks handle this equally; the difference is structural rather than customer service. Banks built around mobile apps cope better because their fraud models assume people move. Older institutions with branch-based verification cope worst because their recovery path assumes you can walk into a building. The pragmatic setup most long-term travelers use is one app-based account for daily spending, one traditional account holding most of the money and rarely touched, and a card from a third provider kept separate from the wallet. It sounds excessive until the first lockout. If You Are Already Locked Out Do not keep retrying. Repeated failed attempts push the account further into lockdown and make the eventual phone call longer. Find a dependable connection, ideally mobile data on a local SIM, and use the in-app message system if available. It is slower but works from anywhere. If you do have to call, use a voice-over-internet service that presents a number in your home country. Many bank fraud lines will not accept an international caller ID at all, and this is the difference between resolving it today and resolving it next week. FAQ Will telling my bank I am traveling prevent this? It helps for the first few weeks and then stops mattering. Most travel notices expire after thirty days, and many banks have removed them entirely in favor of automatic detection. Is a VPN a good idea for online banking abroad? Generally no. It protects the connection, but it makes you look less like yourself, and banks weigh that heavily. Use mobile data instead. Why does my card work in shops but the app will not open? Different systems score card payments and app logins. The card transaction has a physical terminal behind it, which is strong evidence you are there. The app login has only the connection. How long does a lock usually take to lift? If you can complete identity verification, minutes. If it needs a phone call to a domestic number, expect days. This is the main argument for the second card. Does using the same connection every day help? Yes, more than most people expect. Staying somewhere for a fortnight and using the same Wi-Fi builds a pattern the bank recognizes, which is why lockouts cluster in the weeks when you are moving fastest. This article was published in partnership with ProxyWing.

item.title: Five Italian Cathedrals That Genuinely Stopped Me in My Tracks
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 3.02
I've walked into many churches in Italy. After a few, you feel cathedral fatigue - another nave, another altar, another queue. But a few made me stop and gasp at the architecture. I remember exactly where I stood in each and the moment my brain gave up trying to process what it saw. Here are five cathedrals and churches in Italy I would recommend to all visitors. Cathedrals vs. Churches: What's the Difference? A quick note on terminology: not every church on this list is technically a cathedral. A cathedral is the principal church of a diocese and contains the bishop's official seat. St. Peter's Basilica and Sant'Ignazio are basilicas or churches rather than cathedrals, and St. Peter's is located in Vatican City. They're included because they belong on any architecture-focused church itinerary through Rome and Italy. Duomo di Milano, Milan This was the first cathedral I visited on my trip to Italy, and I will never forget how breathless I was at the sight of this majestic architecture. The minute I stepped out of the Duomo metro station, it looked like something that grew out of the earth rather than was built. The 135 spires, a forest of pinnacles, and the gilded Madonnina shining at the top are masterpieces. The unique marble rooftop is the real reason Duomo Milan is on this list. I booked a Milan Cathedral tour that included access to the terrace. The minute you climb onto the roof, you walk among the spires, close enough to see the carved faces and details on each. On a clear afternoon, you can see the Alps on the horizon. I recommend you do the tour around 5 pm to watch the marble turn warm pink as the light drops. St Peter's Basilica, Vatican City How can you visit Rome without paying a visit to St Peter's Basilica? The scale of this religious building was something I was not prepared for. Scale is something nobody prepares you for. You will likely walk out with neck pain after your visit. The gorgeously detailed dome, marvelous sculptures, Bernini's Baldachin, and more await inside. You can find Michelangelo's Pietà behind glass, just inside the entrance to the right. Note that this is the original statue by Michelangelo and the only one he signed! The dome climb was the highlight of my visit. I paid extra for the elevator to the terrace, then walked the last stretch. The steps curve inward toward the ddome'sshell, so you lean sideways throughout the climb. Midway, you'll follow a walkway around the inside of the grand dome for an up-close look at its mosaics. The dome rises approximately 448 feet above the ground, although the walkway itself is considerably lower. Then proceed to the top to enjoy the view over St. Peter's Square, which is worth every drop of sweat. One practical note: Entry to St. PPeter'sBasilica is free, but all visitors must pass through security. The Vatican Museums and Sistine Chapel are separate, ticketed attractions with their own entrance. I booked my Vatican tickets online about three weeks in advance to bypass the ticket line at the museums. Florence Duomo (Santa Maria del Fiore), Florence The Florence Duomo is my personal favorite on this list. I visited twice: once at night to explore the exterior in peace and again in the morning for a tour. Brunelleschi's dome is a 15th-century engineering marvel that outshines modern techniques. Climbing it is the best hour you'll spend in Florence. There are 463 steps, and the staircase narrows near the top so you squeeze between the outer and inner walls of the dome. Halfway up, there's a walkway around the interior of the dome at the level of Vasari's Last Judgment frescoes. You're an arm's length from faces approximately nine feet tall. Then there's more climbing to the lantern, which reveals the terracotta rooftops of all of Florence. Book a slot for the dome tour in advance. You can't just show up to climb it. If the dome is sold out, head across the square to Giotto's bell tower for city views. Sant'Ignazio di Loyola, Rome This was an accidental find while walking from the Pantheon to the Trevi Fountain. I just wanted to step into a quaint church I was passing, only to find the most beautiful one in Rome. The ceiling fresco of Sant'Ignazio di Loyola is so extensive and detailed that you will want to explore every inch. It is free to enter and usually crowd-free. This is also the church with the mirror where people visit to take the iconic photo of the ceiling. You will find a long queue of mirrors, but otherwise the cathedral is empty. I recommend walking to the altar and exploring rather than waiting for the mirror. By the end of the visit, you will have wrecked your neck. Siena Cathedral, Siena The last one has the most beautiful interior. Siena Cathedral is banded in black-and-white marble and feels more like an adorned jewelry box than a church. The Piccolomini Library off the nave is covered wall-to-ceiling with frescoes by Pinturicchio, with colors that look wet. If you're there in late summer, the inlaid marble floor panels are uncovered for a few weeks; I got lucky and saw them. The cathedral is quietly placed in the heart of Siena. I visited on a day trip from Florence but recommend taking more time to enjoy this region of Tuscany. This article was published in partnership with Milan Duomo Tickets and Vatican Tickets Online.

item.title: What Is a Dahabiya Cruise? A More Authentic Way to Sail the Nile
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 2.32
Most travelers come to Egypt to see the pyramids, temples, tombs, and monuments, but did you know the Nile also flows through Egypt? The Nile, which spans about 4,132 miles (6,650 kilometers), is traditionally regarded as the longest river in the world and serves as the lifeblood of Egyptian civilization. Any trip to Egypt, to gain a better understanding of Pharaonic history, would be incomplete without a sail on the Nile. For thousands of years, the Nile has influenced Egyptian agriculture, settlement locations, transportation, food, and everyday life, and a cruise on the river offers visitors the opportunity to see the country from the water. The vessel you take has a bearing on your experience; large cruise ships are good at linking up the main destinations, whereas a Dahabiya affords a more intimate and leisurely association with the river. A dahabiya is a traditional sailing vessel with two masts that has been linked to leisure travel along the Nile in Egypt since the 19th century, and it can offer travelers a more intimate and quieter alternative to taking a large cruise ship by giving them a nearer connection to the scenery and sailing traditions of the Nile. The slow pace of the journey makes it an important element of the Egyptian experience, and the sections that follow outline what sets a dahabiya cruise apart and what to consider when selecting one. A Dahabiya Brings Back the Feeling of Sailing the Nile The Dahabiya are modern sailing ships on the Nile that have been designed in accordance with ancient golden boats; their notable characteristic is that they have two triangular sails, which give a different sensation from traveling on a large motorized ship. The boat's movement is now obvious rather than just background noise, and the wind, the water, the sails, and the changing view of the river all become part of the experience. Swan Dahabiya is a boutique Nile cruise operator that combines traditional sailing qualities with modern amenities. The fact that something is authentic doesn't imply that it is necessary to reproduce historical travel precisely; rather, it means that travelers should be able to experience the river in a manner that represents its long tradition of sailing. Let's take a closer look at how a Dahabiya Nile cruise from Aswan to Luxor is different and why you should include it in your Egyptian vacation itinerary. | Features | What It Means for Travelers | | What is a Dahabiya? | A traditional-style Nile sailing vessel, redesigned today with modern accommodation and comforts. | | Passenger Capacity | Ideally, the passenger capacity of a Dahabiya is less than that of large cruises; it's around only 8-20 passengers. | | Best Suited For | Couples, families, small groups, honeymooners, photographers, food lovers, and travelers who prefer a quieter cultural journey. | | Itinerary Style | Dahabiya sails on the famous route between Luxor and Aswan; with Swan Dahabiya, you can get 4, 5, or 8-day itineraries. | | Onboard Atmosphere | More private and relaxed, with fewer passengers sharing dining and outdoor spaces. | | Accommodation | Cabins are designed for comfort and privacy, giving travelers a quieter place to rest between sightseeing and sailing. | | Deck Experience | Open decks provide space to sit back, enjoy panoramic views, watch the riverbanks, dine, and experience the changing landscape while sailing. | | Best For | Travelers who value time, privacy, flexibility, and connection with the river over extensive onboard facilities and entertainment. | The Nile Has Two Landscapes-and a Dahabiya Gives You Time to Notice Both The Cultivated Nile While sailing on a Dahabiya, from the deck in a calm atmosphere, you will find yourself exploring green agricultural fields which appear right away alongside the river; date palms and crops form a narrow zone of fertility, showing how the legendary River Nile contributes to the landscape. You will also see farmers working the fields, which rely on the river for irrigation, as well as cultivated areas and villages situated where the fertile strip meets the desert. Sailing on a Dahabiya is better because most large cruise ships travel at a constant speed and have more crowded decks; the small Nile boat, on the other hand, has quiet, shaded decks and moves more slowly, which allows you to get a closer sense of nature and makes the experience soulful and satisfying. Many travelers also favor the Dahabiya for its more intimate way of sailing, a feature that is frequently missing on large cruises. Busy Historic Stops Along the Nile As you sail along the river, you will see the scenery change from peaceful river scenes to busy shores. At that point, you stop to visit historical monuments that recount the rich lives of the Egyptian pharaohs and their religious beliefs. The sites most commonly visited are these. The Edfu Temple is an ancient Egyptian temple on the west bank of the Nile in the town of Edfu, frequently visited by tourists on Nile cruises. It is a well-preserved shrine devoted to the ancient Egyptian god Horus, constructed during the Ptolemaic Kingdom (the Graeco-Roman period), and its carvings depict Egyptian religious beliefs as well as the falcon-headed god. Kom Ombo: It is an unusual double temple in Upper Egypt, consisting of sanctuaries devoted to Sobek, the god with a crocodile's head, and Horus the Elder, the god with a falcon's head; the views of the landscape are worth taking in, and the site is one of the most interesting monuments on the Nile. At Aswan, you may choose to end your trip on a Dahabiya voyage from here, and you can visit the Aswan High Dam, the incomplete obelisk, and the magnificent Philae temple, which is dedicated to the goddess Isis. Luxor is ancient Thebes, usually referred to as the world's largest open-air architectural museum, consisting of the Luxor Temple, the Karnak Temple complex, the Valley of Kings, the Temple of Hatshepsut and the Colossi of Memnon, several of which may be included in a Swan Dahabiya itinerary, depending on the route and cruise length. Luxor can also serve as your starting or ending point on a trip down the Nile. Other less well-known destinations: For certain operators, depending on the sailing timetable, some dahabiya tour routes may include smaller archaeological sites such as El Kab or Gebel el-Silsila. Verify all the stops before making a booking. Frequently Asked Questions What is it like to eat on a Dahabiya? At this stage, we hope that you have become aware of what it is like to be on a Dahabiya. A great advantage of traveling on a boutique ship is the opportunity to dine; as you explore the area's history, you also get to taste Egyptian food on traditionally inspired dahabiyas. While on board, you have the opportunity to taste Egyptian food and gain an understanding of Egypt not just through its history but also through its cuisine and cultural traditions. Depending on the menu, meals may include Egyptian dishes such as koshari and desserts such as Umm Ali. The ship also offers a variety of dining choices from different cuisines. When making a reservation, you should confirm the menus and any dietary requirements. How to find a perfect Dahabiya for yourself? If you prefer a Dahabiya over large Nile cruises, here is a quick guide to help you choose an ideal boutique-style vessel for Nile sailing. In Egypt, there are a great many options when it comes to the Dahabiya Nile cruise, but you should choose one that suits your travel schedule and budget, and it also has to have the following: - Comfortable cabins and suites. - A structured itinerary between Aswan and Luxor. - Must include the transfers from cruises to the shore excursions and vice versa. - Should offer seamless and transparent booking services. - The packages include dining. Among the various factors tourists should consider when choosing a Dahabiya vessel, it is advisable to select only a Dahabiya company that is licensed and insured to ensure a good Nile sailing experience. Before making a booking, it is important to review the operator's qualifications, insurance coverage, cancellation conditions, feedback from recent travelers, and the precise services included in the fare. To assess the operator's reliability, you should review the testimonials and reviews from previous travelers. What should you pack on a cruise aboard a Dahabiya along the Nile? - Clothes that are lightweight and breathable for warm days when on the river. - When visiting temples and local sites, it is appropriate to wear simple clothing. - For cooler mornings and evenings, it is advisable to wear a light jacket or shawl. - Shoes that are comfortable for excursions and temple visits. - For relaxing on board, sandals or some comfortable footwear should be worn. - Sunglasses, sunscreen, and a hat for sun protection. - A small bag containing essentials for use during sightseeing stops. - Personal items, such as medicine, toiletries, and a reusable water bottle. When is the best time for a Dahabiya journey in Egypt? Egypt is a year-round tourist destination, and the same goes for Dahabiyas. October through April generally offers the most comfortable weather for sightseeing in Luxor and Aswan. Cruises may also operate during the hotter months, but travelers should confirm availability with the operator and be prepared for intense daytime heat. If you want to avoid the crowds or get discounts, May through September is the best time. Plan to visit historical sites either early in the morning or late in the evening to avoid the worst of the heat. Why Swan Dahabiya? Swan Dahabiya combines traditional sailing-inspired design with modern cabins, furnished decks, included meals, and guided excursions. The wooden fittings are based on Egyptian culture; the cabins are well furnished, and the decks have comfortable seating so that passengers may enjoy the peaceful riverbanks. If you would like to experience the true authenticity of the Dahabiya, then the Swan should be one of your choices, something that experienced travelers compare it to. Final Thoughts You never actually experience the Nile if you go from one ancient site to another, since it's only during the hours in between that you begin to feel it-when the temples are out of sight, and the river then becomes the story you experience on a Dahabiya. Upgrade your Egyptian holiday with both comfort and exploration by adding a Dahabiya trip. This article was published in partnership with Swan Dahabiya.
