item.title: How People Without Formal Power Gain Influence
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.85
Share Podcast How People Without Formal Power Gain Influence A conversation with author and entrepreneur Pamela Meyer on five ways executives can indirectly assert themselves. In today’s increasingly decentralized workplaces, leaders often need to get things done without having direct authority over the people they depend on. So how can you influence colleagues, clients, vendors, and even senior executives without simply telling them what to do? Pamela Meyer, founder and CEO of Calibrate, says the answer is learning to read the room—and understanding the informal networks, emotional dynamics, and hidden sources of power that shape decisions. She explains five paths to indirect influence: becoming an influence spotter, a backchanneler, a precision mover, a connector, and a pulse reader. Meyer also explains why the best influencers focus less on how they’re performing and more on what the people around them need. Meyer is the author of How to Read the Room: The Art and Science of Social Observation and the HBR article “Five Ways to Wield Influence When You Lack Authority.” ALISON BEARD: I’m Alison Beard. ADI IGNATIUS: I’m Adi Ignatius. This is the HBR IdeaCast. ALISON BEARD: Adi, I don’t know if you’ve noticed this, but because of the way we work today, a lot of us are often leading people we don’t have direct authority over. That’s true whether you’re working on a cross-functional team with clients or outside vendors when you’re trying to manage up. ADI IGNATIUS: When you’re trying to manage your podcast co-host. ALISON BEARD: Yeah, that too. It is very hard. And so today we’re going to talk about the rising importance of indirect influence to persuade people to buy into your ideas, marshal resources, succeed in your work, and advance in your career. Our guest argues that it’s one of the most important skills to develop. ADI IGNATIUS: All right. Consider me influenced. Tell me what to do. ALISON BEARD: Well, she argues that it starts with listening and observing. It’s about recognizing the informal networks, emotional dynamics, and hidden decision makers that exist inside every organization and among external stakeholders and knowing how to work with them rather than against them. And she’s going to share some of the best ways to go about that. Pamela Meyer is the founder and CEO of Calibrate. She wrote the book, How to Read the Room: The Art and Science of Social Observation, and the HBR article, Five Ways to Wield Influence When You Lack Authority. Here’s our conversation. So why is indirect influence so much more important now than it was in the past? PAMELA MEYER: Well, one of the reasons is that we don’t live in a hierarchical world anymore. In fact, in most organizations, authority is really distributed. And so we need to learn ways to work ourselves around an organization, have influence, but not at the same time cause what we call reactance. So what we find oftentimes is when someone tries to influence someone and they put pressure on them, it almost always threatens their autonomy. And when their autonomy is threatened, they pull back, they have reactance, and they’re not able to be influenced. And so now what we really need to do is teach people a sort of artful way to make their way through much more complicated organizations with much more complicated people with different ages and different generations at different levels of seniority and find ways to match their path to the person that they’re actually trying to influence. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. And we do hear so much about how important it is to be authentic and transparent, but what psychologically is going on that just telling someone what you would like them to do or what you think they should do doesn’t work when you’re not their boss? PAMELA MEYER: It actually goes back to social determination theory, which is a very stable theory of psychology developed in the ’80s. And it’s a theory of motivation. Human beings have three very profound needs that they express in the workplace. One of those needs is for competence. One of those needs is for relatedness. And one of those needs, which is really profound, is for autonomy. We really need to feel that we have agency. And what happens with influence and what happens with reactance is that it takes away our sense of autonomy. So what happens, people start distorting the way they express it in the room. Somebody, for example, who, you’ve probably seen this many times at an organization, you can’t get them to do what you want. You just keep asking them. Oftentimes those people are declared, oh, they have executive function issues. No, that’s not what’s happening usually. It’s usually a bid for autonomy. They just don’t want to be told what to do. And so oftentimes what we need to do is think through psychologically when we’re asking somebody to do something for us or we’re trying to get something done or we’re trying to steer a group. What are the needs that each of these people have? And how can I satisfy that so that I can actually provide them with a sense that they are actually making the decision themselves? ALISON BEARD: So you talk about five paths to indirect influence. And the first is figuring out who might not be at the top of the org chart, but still has hidden power. So how do you get better at spotting those people? PAMELA MEYER: I call these people the influence spotters. The bad influence spotter is the one who looks at job titles and says, “Okay, that person has influence.” The good influence spotter walks in the room. They pause. They look around. They’ve done a lot of research on who’s who ahead of time. And then to figure out who actually has influence, they particularly focus on decisions that are being made, who actually influences a hard decision. So when they can figure that out, who might be influencing the decision, where are the micro alliances, who’s looking at whom when there’s a disagreement. Once they start to spot who has influence, then they do what we call a chain analysis. They actually go back a few chains and they figure out who’s influencing that person. So influence spotters are analytic. There’s an art to it and there’s a science to it. They’re artful observers, but they’re also scientific thinkers. They think through who might be influencing the person who actually has the influence, who’s got their ear. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. So I think you’re beginning to answer my next question is sort of when you figure out those people, and I think we all know who they are, like, oh, that person really seems to have a lot of power. How do you bring them on your side? PAMELA MEYER: Well, you have to do it gently and carefully. You don’t just call up somebody and you don’t just… For example, let’s say you decide that the CEO’s long time confidant is the real power in the room. You’re not going to just call that person up and say, “Hey, let’s have coffee.” You’re probably going to really insult the person who really owns that decision. So you have to be very artful and very careful about it and kind of make it optional to open up a conversation with that person. Make it gentle, make it optional. Maybe just get to know them a little bit. You don’t necessarily want to call somebody up and have a direct conversation with them about the exact concern you might have in the moment. You’ve got to be artful about it and you’ve got to kind of work around it and get to know them and bring something to the table. If you think somebody’s the real influencer in the room and you need something from them, also think what are you going to bring to them that’s going to be helpful to them? ALISON BEARD: And I think one thing that really struck me in working with you on the article and in reading the book is that this advice isn’t just for sort of aspiring leaders who quite obviously don’t have any influence. It’s actually for really senior leaders too, who can’t seem to sort of move the needle in the direction that they want. And so they need to be finding these influence spotters within the C-suite or on the board, right? PAMELA MEYER: Yeah, absolutely. Part of what’s happened is our culture really rewards what we say and not what we see. It rewards speaking instead of watching. So a lot of people that are sitting on boards who have a lot to do and they’re flooded with noise and information and many, many more decisions and they’re distracted, they’re preoccupied, they have a lot of stuff going on in their working memory. They don’t have time to think thoughtfully about this at all. And so instead of sitting back and observing and trying to figure out who really has influence, they’ll blurt out exactly what needs to get done or they’ll miss the timing in the moment. And they’re backfiring completely when that happens. They really should not be doing that. They should be thinking it through much more slowly, much more thoughtfully. And usually if you do that and you have an eye towards when a room is shifting, you can get a sense of what caused that and where that influence might be. ALISON BEARD: So the next approach is becoming a backchanneler. What exactly do you mean by that? PAMELA MEYER: So the backchanneler is the one who takes a meeting that’s really frozen where two factions in a meeting just can’t figure it out and a decision can’t be made. And they pull one of those players or two of those players off to the side. Oftentimes today this happens virtually. It’s not necessarily happening at work. Although it does happen at TGI Fridays, it doesn’t always happen on the telephone. And they have a backchannel conversation. They have a private conversation. They open a backchannel. A backchannel has been a function of diplomatic influence for all of history. And it happens as well at the boardroom level and it happens at the junior level. And backchannelers can be unbelievably, unbelievably talented and they can get a lot done. But sometimes what we see is the wrong person tries to open up a backchannel. If you’re not trusted and you’re new to an organization and you all of a sudden start opening up a backchannel and kind of lurking in the corners and having private conversations with people, people are just going to consider you a political animal. If you want to be a backchanneler, ask yourself if you’ve earned the trust of people to do that before you open that backchannel because it’s not for everybody. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. I mean, again, in this age of transparency, great value placed on being upfront with people, this does seem like a tricky thing to get right. So what advice do you have for people who want to do it without being seen as a manipulative political person? PAMELA MEYER: So the most important piece of advice is to do it temporarily. Opening up permanent backchannels makes you look like a power grabber and it makes you look transactional. But if you have a particular item that you want done, you have a decision that needs to be made, you have a frozen conversation that needs to be unlocked, open the backchannel and then close it. Say thank you, that was great. Bring it back to the meeting and make it public that you all had that conversation or not. You don’t have to necessarily make it public, but bring the finalization, bring the final decision public so that people understand that the whole thing doesn’t happen in the backchannel. The best backchannelers, the ones who are the most talented at it that I’ve seen in organization after organization, are the chiefs of staff. They’re the ones that are, they’re pulling someone aside and they’re saying, “Hey, I noticed you were interrupted in that meeting. You didn’t get to talk. I’m putting the postmortem report together. What is it you wanted to say? Let me get that in.” They’re the ones that are observing the room really carefully and they serve usually a CEO or a COO or a CFO. And so people take them very seriously. Sometimes they’re not trusted because they have the ear of power. But the really talented chiefs of staff use the backchannel in a very flexible and a very talented way. And they’re the best backchannelers that I’ve seen. ALISON BEARD: And so the rest of us can learn from how they do it. PAMELA MEYER: I think so. ALISON BEARD: Okay. Another path is being a precision mover who knows sort of exactly the right time to exert influence. Why is timing so very important? PAMELA MEYER: First of all, I just want to say it’s really hard to be a good precision mover because most of us are not regulated enough. We’re not emotionally regulated enough, nor are we strategic thinkers enough to figure out what’s the right time to bring this decision. What’s the time to release this information? What’s the best time to have the labor negotiation? So the strategic thinker tends to be oftentimes the precision mover. It’s very, very hard to get right. One thing that precision movers do really well that most of us don’t even think to do is instead of thinking in moments, they think about time windows. So they’ll say, “Oh, the next quarter might be a good time. Let me just think about when in that quarter I can bring this information forth.” But precision movers often backfire all the time. It’s really hard to do it well. So let’s say, for example, you have really bad news that you need to release and you’re trying to be a precision mover and you’re being thoughtful about it and you’re like, “I’m just going to hold this back one more week.” Well, someone else is going to release that information. It’s going to completely backfire and you’re going to look evasive. So it’s really easy to be a bad precision mover and it’s really hard to do it well, but I will say that there are CEOs all over this country and all over the world who made their way from being an intern all the way up to the top of the organization by being thoughtful and by being precision movers. So it can deliver absolutely outsized influence, but there are very, very few people that do it extremely well. ALISON BEARD: So definitely approach with caution, but is there a way to build up those skills so you’re better at it? PAMELA MEYER: I think you could consider precision moving a micro skill. You could try it in small ways. Let’s say you have a hire you want to bring to your boss. Well, don’t bring the resume up until the perfect time. Let’s say you need to take an extra week off, or let’s say someone’s told you they want to change to a remote work. Or let’s say you’re about to make a hard decision on firing somebody. These are micro decisions. They aren’t major strategic decisions for an organization. Practice those skills. I think it’s a great idea. Go in and try to figure out the best way to time it. And if it backfires, it’s a little bit negative. It’s probably somewhat uncomfortable for you in terms of how you need to navigate next, but you haven’t lost the whole game. ALISON BEARD: Okay. Let’s move on to being a connector. How does that help the leader themselves gain influence, putting other people together? PAMELA MEYER: So connectors can give you unbelievable influence if you’re thoughtful about it. I mean, what connectors do is they find gaps and they provide something in the gap. Let’s say a form of expertise. Let’s say there’s a project that’s across many, many divisions. They allow a certain form of coordination. They can also just figure out that two people would really get along and work well together and they’re in two different places and put them together. So connectors can be incredibly influential and many of us can be connectors. You don’t need to be a leader to be a connector. Oftentimes you’ll see connectors are people at much lower levels in an organization and they found they have social skills, they love people. This is a way that they can actually get an on-ramp into an important conversation and have some influence in the room. But connectors also, again, you can be a good connector or a bad connector. And we’ve all been on the receiving end of that. I mean, when I was single, people would call me up and they’d be like, “Oh, I have a blind date for you to go on.” And so oftentimes I go on that date and I’m like, “That person wasn’t right for me at all.” Sometimes you’re a favor for the other person. It’s not actually mutually beneficial to both people. And so we see this oftentimes. Oftentimes the traditional advice is send somebody a news article, go for coffee, tell them you were just thinking about them. People sniff that out overnight. It is so easy to sniff out someone who’s transactional, who’s collecting people, who’s kind of a surface connector, who wants to have a huge Rolodex. That’s not going to work in this era because we’re in an era where anybody can call anybody. It’s not the way it used to be. You can use LinkedIn, you can use any other platform, and you can find your way through any connection to connecting with anybody you want. So I tell people, dial it back. Be much more thoughtful about it. If you want to be a valid connector, somebody that people really listen to and you don’t want to waste their time, only connect people when you know that both sides are going to benefit from it. Because if you don’t, they’re not going to take you seriously and they’re going to sense that you’re doing it for yourself rather than for them. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. I’m laughing because I just got an email from a college friend who said, “Oh, I have someone in Boston who you might want to interview.” And I’m like, “No, I don’t want to interview that person. Why would you think I want to interview that person?” PAMELA MEYER: I mean, informational interviews are out, sending around news articles that might be interesting, out. Would you meet my daughter’s friend? Out. Yeah. ALISON BEARD: Exactly. PAMELA MEYER: Don’t do favors. Only be someone who’s known for really thinking through what people need and you’ll have incredible influence from it. ALISON BEARD: The final path to influence is being a pulse reader. So explain a little bit more about what you mean by that. PAMELA MEYER: So the pulse reader is the person who reads the vibe of the room. They’re the person who understands what people need from a kind of heart perspective. Indra Nooyi, the former head of PepsiCo, she ran a $64 billion company, 260,000 employees. And she was famous for writing letters to 400 of her best employees’ parents every year to tell them in a paragraph what they accomplished as essentially sending a message, “You raised a successful person and I’ve noticed it.” She got at the heart of what mattered in that culture. And that’s incredibly, incredibly influential. And the pulse readers are able to do that. They’re able to kind of observe what the room needs, but the really good ones also have the ability to articulate what it needs. So if you’re someone who figures out, “Oh, everybody’s really stressed out because AI is coming in and it’s going to take everybody’s jobs. There’s ambient dread all over the organization. I need to really help with this.” It’s not going to work unless they can actually name in the moment in a way that people resonate with what’s actually happening. So that’s the art and science of it. Again, you can be a great pulse reader, but if you don’t have the ability to actually talk in an articulate way about what’s going on, nobody’s going to pay attention to you. ALISON BEARD: So again, how do you develop those skills if they don’t come naturally to you? PAMELA MEYER: So there are a couple ways that you can do that. As a pulse reader, the most important skill you can take on is pausing. Walking in the room, pausing, trying to think through what will make this room better. Getting out of your own self-monitoring, getting out of your own self-consciousness and thinking through who in this room needs something? What do they need? Do they need a sense of relatedness? Do they need to be given more agency? Are they somebody where they’re making bids for competence and they actually need me to acknowledge that they are competent? Start with pausing, observing the room, and trying to figure out what it is people need. And if that’s too complex for you and it’s a really busy day and it’s an incredibly busy meeting and you don’t have time to figure all that out, step back and ask yourself, you know what? As you look at each person in the room, are they a visionary or are they a detailed person? Just make it that binary. If you start to do that and you start to think about people that way, you’ll just get out of your own way and you’ll start to read the pulse. People do this with kids when they’re teaching them how to identify their emotions. You can make a list of all the possible emotions you might see in a room. You might actually ask, are people nervous? Are they anxious? Are they dreading something? Are they warm? What’s actually happening in the room? And use that vocabulary to start naming it. And you’d be amazed if you actually walk into a room with that list of vocabulary words and you start to throw them out there. You’ll know. It’s like a fishing expedition. You throw it out there, you’ll know, people will start nodding. They’ll start looking at you. You’ll get a sense when you throw out what you think is happening, they’ll give you the positive feedback that what you said is actually the real case. I’ve often had a situation where I’ll walk in a room and I’ll say, “You know what? I think the problem is we’ve got a trust issue here. We really don’t trust that this outside vendor that we’re working with is going to deliver. Let’s just be clear about it. Do we need to back up and re-license or do we need to confront them directly? What do we need to do?” The minute you say there’s a trust issue, the heads start nodding. All of a sudden you’ve kind of named what’s at the core of it. ALISON BEARD: And this seems like something that everyone can get better at because it really involves staying quiet, listening, looking. It doesn’t require those sort of timing skills or political skills. It’s much more about being empathetic. PAMELA MEYER: I think so, but I think it also involves understanding that there’s an element of timing to this as well. A pulse reader can read the pulse, run away and write the right memo, not necessarily name it in the moment. So if you’re in a room and the room is, this is going to sound a bit metaphysical, but you’ll be able to feel it if you actually walk in the room and you try to practice this. If you ask yourself, is this room expansive or is it contracting? Are people still frictionless? Are the jokes not landing? Are people blurting out kind of a bad laugh at a bad joke? Do you have a sense that people are kind of withdrawing? In that kind of contracted environment, you don’t necessarily, even if you know what the problem is and even if you know you could name exactly what’s at the pulse of that. It’s not necessarily the right time to do that because there’s already an incredible amount of tension in the room. Maybe you just wait. If you’ve got a room that’s expansive and there’s like a frothy, happy, almost like a, I wouldn’t say happy, but let’s say there’s a room that’s expansive and there’s a big argument going on, but there’s trust in the room and you kind of feel the friction and the room feels like people are willing to kind of get into the muddy middle of it. That’s a time when you really can be a pulse reader. You can have an incredible impact. ALISON BEARD: In the executives that you counsel and coach, are you trying to get them to build all of these skills in tandem or do you tend to encourage them to focus on particular ones? PAMELA MEYER: So I spend a lot of time coaching people not only to develop these skills, because you certainly need room reading skills and you certainly need to be able to walk into a room and understand and intuit where the power alliances are, who’s got influence, who’s withdrawn, who’s actually taking up too much space and shouldn’t be. All of that I can teach them to do. But I also spend an enormous amount of time with executives retraining them on how to prepare to walk into the room because there’s a lot you need to do before you even walk in the room to be effective. I teach them what I call the triple B method. We actually profile people. We look at their background, their behavior, their beliefs. We figure everything out we can about them before you walk in the room. For example, I know you and I went to high school right down the street from each other. ALISON BEARD: Oh, I didn’t realize that. PAMELA MEYER: Yes. I went to Sidwell, you went to Walt Whitman. ALISON BEARD: Yep. Okay. PAMELA MEYER: I know you were a star athlete in college. Still hold the record for best assists in volleyball. ALISON BEARD: Wow. You’ve done a deep dive. PAMELA MEYER: Yeah, of course. I know you care about your local community. I know a lot about you before I walk in the room. And we train executives to do that and to try to understand as much as they possibly can about somebody. Not just their background, but also what are their belief systems? What kind of behavioral, we call it behavioral residue, they may leave in the room. Really, who are they as a whole person? Why? Because if you want influence downstream, you’re going to need some way to connect with them. You need rapport. You need to understand them in a much more deep way. And certainly you can, I mean, you can use AI to kind of speed read somebody in the bathroom right before you meet them if you don’t have a chance to do that. But what we do is much deeper and it’s much more thoughtful. And we actually spend a lot of time retraining professionals on how to invest the time to do that well because that is where they get their edge. There are a lot of people that can walk in and kind of wing it in a meeting, but managers tell me over and over again when I consult to them, please tell my staff to prepare because I know who’s prepared and who’s not when they walk in the room. ALISON BEARD: And tell listeners about your own unique background that’s prepared you to teach executives on these skills, these reading the room skills? PAMELA MEYER: Well, so I spent over a decade teaching people how to detect deception and how to elicit information from people. We use this on inside threat detection and on figuring out when people might be deceptive and certainly in negotiation. And I did that for a very, very long time and I still do that. I still train people all the time on lie spotting and deception detection, but the environment’s changed. We’re in the middle of a trust epidemic now. And so what used to be kind of a quaint polarization, people are in different silos, it’s much more embittered. People really feel it. And the reason I wrote this book, How to Read the Room, is because I really want to get people back to a much more reasonable and thoughtful conversation into that middle ground and learning how to kind of be brokers of trust because we’ve got a real problem. Everybody, every single person, every single audience that I talk to, every single organization I work with will tell me, yes, people are way too polarized and we’ve got to do something about it because we’re all going to have to get along. The more positive the environment you’re in, the better work you’re going to get from people. If you push them down and you take autonomy and agency away from them, they’re going to withdraw and they’re going to become embittered and you’re not going to get their best work. So you can have a room full of absolutely brilliant people and if they can’t read each other, it’s very emotionally expensive for the organization and for them. So I teach people to read each other, to read the power dynamics, and also to really focus on how to develop trust in teams because that ends up being much, much more important downstream than just having a collection of geniuses in the room. ALISON BEARD: So is the idea that leaders can either do all of these things themselves or if they’re more senior in the organization, make sure that they have people on their teams to play each one of these indirect influencing roles? PAMELA MEYER: I think every leader needs a panoply of talented, diverse, skilled people around them. I don’t think it makes sense to say, “Okay, I need one backchanneler, one influencer, one precision timer.” What I do think you can do with leaders though is to attune them to these skills. So when they’re interviewing people and when they’re developing people to kind of note, does this person have the emotional intelligence to be a pulse reader? Does this person have the strategic long-term thinking skill to be a precision timer? Does this person have enough personal sway if they were an influence spotter to actually be able to have a conversation with the person who’s the most influential in the room? So I think it’s a matter of not finding somebody who can go on every path, but on thinking through a new set of skills that will help people read the room and be more influential long term. But I think it would be very dangerous to select just for somebody who’s good on these skills. The bottom line is that it’s a great idea to have diversity across your team, but you shouldn’t take every path literally. These are skills, they’re composite skills. So it’s worth understanding what the paths are so you can really select for those skills here and there. So if somebody walks in the door and they have emotional intelligence, that’s great, but you might want to ask yourself, do they have the ability to be kind of regulated enough to be a precision mover as well? Would they be able to withhold information for two weeks if you ask them to do that? Does somebody have the pulse reading skill? Well, you don’t necessarily want to ask yourself, do I need a pulse reader in the room? But you might want somebody who’s articulate enough about how they describe what happened in a room that the emotional resonance of it was able to be understood. So you don’t want to create a phantom cabinet of every single path taker, but you do want to focus on the skills and see if you can start to select for them a bit. ALISON BEARD: So let’s say our listeners have heard this podcast, they’re bought into the idea of exerting indirect influence more effectively. What is something or a few things that they should do in the next week or the next month to start building these muscles? PAMELA MEYER: The first thing you want to do is you want to just think of the room as not one audience. When you walk into the room, pause, get a sense of the vibe, look around, be prepared, know as much as you can before you walk in the room, but realize this is a collection of individuals with very different needs. So it’s not one audience. Do not focus on how you’re going to sound, what people are going to think about you, your performance. Focus on how you can make that room better. Once you do that, you’ll be able to pick a path to influence. The second thing I think is that you probably want to think through, like if you’re trying to figure out what’s happening with influence in the room, where are the influencers? Where can I make a difference? You probably want to watch the room and take particular note of when there’s a challenge to authority, when there’s an inflection point, when there’s a battle, when a joke lands badly, when something happens in the room that kind of shifts the energy. One thing that you can do that you probably didn’t do before, instead of watching the action and getting the popcorn out and saying, “Whoa, those two are really having a fight,” look around the room. Who’s glancing at who? Who’s already landed on a Slack channel? Who’s leaning towards someone else? Where are those micro alliances starting to form? Once you start to look past the action in the room and instead at the patterns that occur after something important has happened, after there’s been a major shift, once you start to focus on that and really build that muscle, you’ll start to see paths to influence everywhere. ALISON BEARD: Wonderful. Well, thank you for teaching me and our listeners how to build more influence in our organizations. Thanks so much for being on the show. PAMELA MEYER: Goodbye. It’s been great to be with you. Thanks for having me. ALISON BEARD: That’s Pamela Meyer, founder and CEO of Calibrate and author of the book, How to Read the Room: The Art and Science of Social Observation, and the HBR article, Five Ways to Wield Influence When You Lack Authority. Next week, Adi speaks with Jared Diamond about some of history’s great leaders and how much of what they accomplished was due to chance. If you found this episode helpful, please share it with a colleague and be sure to subscribe and rate IdeaCast in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. If you want to help leaders move the world forward, consider subscribing to Harvard Business Review. You’ll get access to the HBR mobile app, the weekly exclusive insider newsletter, and unlimited access to HBR online. Just head to hbr.org/subscribe. Thanks to our team, senior producer, Mary Dooe, and senior production editor, Kristin Murphy Romano. And thanks to you for listening to the HBR IdeaCast. We’ll be back with a new episode on Tuesday. I’m Alison Beard.

item.title: What Separates AI Agents That Ship to Production from Those That Don’t
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.63
The enterprise AI conversation has quietly shifted. Two years ago, executives asked whether their organization could build an AI agent. Today they are asking whether their organization can trust an AI agent. The question of trust runs on two fronts: the agents they have built that now run in production and the coding agents their developers rely on daily to build software. Most organizations can’t trust their agents in either case. Working demos of AI agents are common, but agents customers depend on day after day that improve over time and hold up to real-world edge cases are rare. Closing the gap is not a modeling problem. It is a verification problem. Organizations can build software at agent speed, but they cannot yet verify software at agent speed. Traditional software testing is a solved problem: Engineers write unit tests, continuous integration blocks regressions, and deployments are gated. But AI agents break every assumption behind that playbook. They are nondeterministic. The same input can produce different outputs. Small changes to a system prompt or tool description can cascade into failures that only appear in multi-step workflows. A model upgrade meant to improve performance can introduce silent regressions no one notices until customers report them. Five Components of the Feedback Loop Many engineering teams still operate their agents the way they first tested them: manually, in a spreadsheet, iterating on prompts, and hoping a fix does not quietly break three other workflows. The business consequences add up quickly. Projects that reach a working demo stall for months, sometimes indefinitely, because the team cannot demonstrate the agent is safe to release at scale. Engineering time drains into whack-a-mole debugging. Release cycles slow down. Anticipated return on investment (ROI) does not materialize because the agent never reaches the customer-facing scale the business case required. Cost visibility becomes its own problem, as fleets of agents, including the coding agents that developers are running on their laptops all day, can quietly drive up spend that no finance team can attribute. The gap between organizations that have institutionalized this discipline and those still improvising compounds every week. The teams closing the gap treat AI agents like a software product, with a real feedback loop built on observability. Five components define the foundation: - Production traces flow continuously into an observability layer using open standards, so every agent decision, model call, tool invocation, retrieval, and response is inspectable. - Evaluation moves from brittle string matching to layered evaluators, including large language model (LLM) judges scoped narrowly to specific behavioral checks and deterministic code-based tests where they apply. - Real production traces, including failures, become the golden data sets teams evaluate against, not synthetic happy-path examples. - Experiments compare prompt, model, and configuration changes against those data sets before anything ships. - Continuous integration pipelines gate merges on evaluation pass rates. Because the underlying instrumentation follows OpenTelemetry-based open standards, the same discipline works across cloud-native runtimes without locking teams into any single vendor’s stack. What is new, and where the industry is heading, is that the loop itself is starting to run without humans driving every step. Long-running agents now surface what to investigate, propose fixes as pull requests, and grade their own work with engineers supervising and approving rather than executing every task. An Advanced Testing Framework One AI-native engineering team has spent more than two years building and operating a production agent that helps developers debug and improve other agents. The team’s earliest testing framework was a spreadsheet. What changed everything was the shift to treating real production traces, measured in trillions of spans and evaluated across tens of millions of evaluation runs, as the foundation of engineering. Today the team runs continuous evaluations in production, gates every prompt and tool change behind continuous integration (CI-integrated) evaluation suites, and increasingly uses long-running agents to triage, categorize, and prioritize the team’s own production failures. What used to take hours of engineer debugging now takes minutes. The team ships faster, catches regressions before customers do, and continues to improve the agent even as usage scales. The durable advantage in agentic AI will not come from the underlying model. Foundation models will keep getting better and cheaper for everyone. Code is being commoditized by coding agents. Models are being commoditized by the menu of foundation models available on every hyperscaler. What is left and what compounds is context: the observability, the evaluations, the release discipline, and the feedback loop that makes every deployment safer than the last. Enterprises accelerating agentic AI on AWS are increasingly relying on partners that have already built this discipline into their own platforms. To see how AWS and Arize are helping teams operationalize agentic AI in production (agents running in your applications and the coding agents building them), visit Arize on AWS Marketplace or explore the resources at arize.com/partners/aws.

item.title: Do Your B2B Customers See the Value You Deliver?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 2.82
Summary. Many B2B companies suffer from a “value gap”: Customers benefit from their products but cannot clearly measure, articulate, or defend that value to stakeholders within their companies. Most B2B companies have long harbored a costly blind spot: a gap between the value they create for customers and the value those customers can see, measure, and defend. For many, early strong growth masks the problem until sales slow or competitive alternatives drag down margins. Closing that gap is an executive decision—and one most leadership teams have never explicitly made.

item.title: Hugging Face opens pre-orders for its trainable open-source duck robot
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.88
Hugging Face is best known as a community for open AI collaboration, but now it's venturing further into hardware. The company has released the Microduck, an open-source duck robot that you can buy and train yourself. The new bot is equipped with a camera, LiDAR, and inertia sensors that help it navigate and interact with its environment, including with its beak. It can already perform activities like grabbing objects and even roller-skating, but its main allure is learning new tricks. You can train it in simulations (either locally or on Hugging Face Jobs) and test the results in the real world. The development kit, simulation software, and training code are available on GitHub. In theory, this both offers greater transparency (as you know what the robot is doing) and the option to bring similar systems to other robots. Pollen Robotics, which Hugging Face acquired in 2025, is responsible for the robot. The two have already released Reachy Mini and Reachy Mini Lite desktop robots that are powered by either Raspberry Pi or your existing PC. Microduck is available to pre-order now for $399 and should ship before Christmas. It includes a battery, cable, and controller, but you can also buy a $39 Accessory Pack (including the rollerskates, a laser pointer, ball, and NFC materials), a $39 Charger Pack (two extra batteries), and a $119 Dev Pack that includes the batteries and NFC tags as well as spare motor parts and Hugging Face credit. Nvidia and OpenAI loom over the launch Right robot, wrong time? The Microduck debut comes at an awkward moment for Hugging Face. Nvidia is set to acquire Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, according to The Information. While the two companies have worked together for years and routinely advocate for open-source AI, it's not clear how this would affect Pollen Robotics' projects. There are no guarantees you'll see more devices like Microduck. It also follows a July 2026 incident where OpenAI models broke out of security sandboxes meant to keep them offline, compromising Hugging Face as well as some of OpenAI's own internal research systems. OpenAI has since identified causes, such as a lack of internal safeguards and even AI agents co-conspiring on "unauthorized" message boards. OpenAI has since toughened its security measures, and rivals like Anthropic have reported similar crises. However, the Microduck is still launching when the safety of Hugging Face's platform is facing close scrutiny. Even if a repeat incident is unlikely, the breakout is unlikely to inspire confidence in some would-be Microduck buyers.

item.title: Your Microsoft Excel file needs a hidden backend worksheet
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.20
Nearly every Microsoft Excel workbook I own—especially those I share with others—contains a hidden backend worksheet. It's essentially the engine room of my workbook and helps me keep my spreadsheets organized and functional. Here's why you should have one too. While hiding a worksheet is a good way to keep the inner workings of a workbook out of view, it's not a foolproof security measure, so it shouldn't be used for sensitive information or passwords. How to hide your backend worksheet Hiding a worksheet the well-known way All visible worksheets in an Excel workbook are displayed as tabs across the bottom of the Excel window. However, providing there is more than one worksheet in your workbook, you can hide certain sheets from view in just a couple of clicks. Simply right-click the backend worksheet tab at the bottom of the Excel window, and click "Hide." The sheet then instantly disappears from the worksheet menu. In case someone unhides your backend worksheet, it's worth adding a note at the very top to make it clear that they don't need to make any changes. Something like "This worksheet is for reference only" will do the trick. If you need to unhide it again, right-click any visible tab, and click "Unhide." Then, in the Unhide window, select the relevant worksheet (or more than one by holding Ctrl as you click them), and click "OK." Bear in mind, however, that many people know about hiding and unhiding worksheets in this way, so I'd only recommend you use this option if the workbook is for your eyes only. Making a worksheet very hidden If you plan to share your workbook with others, go one step further and make your backend worksheet very hidden through the VBA editor, as fewer people are aware of this extra level of invisibility. To do this, first, press F12 to save your workbook. Then, press Alt+F11 to open the VBA window. Before you make a worksheet very hidden, you need to activate the two panes that enable you to change a worksheet's visibility status. First, click "View" on the ribbon, and select "Project Explorer." Then, click "View" again, but this time, select "Properties Window." Now, in the Project Explorer pane, expand the options until you see a list of the worksheets in your workbook, and click the backend worksheet you want to hide. Then, in the Properties window, click "xlsSheetVeryHidden" in the Visible drop-down menu. Finally, click "Save" in the top-left corner of the VBA window, and click "X" in the top-right corner to close it. Now, even if someone unhides the hidden worksheets by right-clicking a sheet tab, the very hidden sheet won't reappear. To show the very hidden sheet again, head back to the VBA window (Alt+F11), select the backend worksheet in the Project Explorer pane, and change the Visible status to "xlSheetVisible" before saving and closing the VBA window. Keep your lookup tables out of the way Save space and avoid mistakes For me, the main reason I set up a hidden backend worksheet is so that I've got somewhere to store my lookup tables. This is because they often take up valuable real estate if stored in a visible worksheet. What's more, lookup tables usually contain important information that can be accidentally edited if they're not safely tucked away. In this example, I use the XLOOKUP function to generate student grades based on their scores. In fact, I have the same setup on each tab in my workbook. Storing the reference tables in a hidden backend worksheet—rather than in the same worksheet as the calculations themselves—saves room in each worksheet for information that needs to be seen. Also, if I share my workbook with others, keeping the lookup tables out of the way means they'll be able to focus on the information that matters. Hide the datasets that feed PivotTables Condense everything down Continuing the theme of maintaining worksheet tidiness, a hidden backend worksheet is particularly useful if you get your main data insights from PivotTables. After all, nobody needs to see large, clunky datasets if they've been tidily converted into a PivotTable on a visible worksheet. Here, the hidden backend workbook contains a dataset that is 700 rows down and 13 rows across. On the other hand, this corresponding PivotTable is more condensed, easier to manipulate, occupies fewer cells, and is easier to read. As a result, the visible version of the dataset is much easier to interpret and manipulate than the hidden version, and it leaves more room in the worksheet for extra data visualization, like a PivotChart, slicers, or a timeline. As with lookup tables, hiding the source dataset also protects it from unwanted modifications. Store values that drive calculation Crunch numbers invisibly If, like me, you prefer referencing cells in your formulas rather than hard-coding values, a hidden backend worksheet can be a great place to store values that fuel your calculations. What's more, you can name the precedent cells in the backend worksheet to make referencing them easier. Let's say you need to work out the total cost of each product after 20% tax is added. However, because the tax only changes every 12 months, you don't need constant access to the cell containing this variable. Instead, you can create a named precedent cell in your backend worksheet. First, select the cell where the calculation value will go, and use the name box in the top-left corner of the Excel window to name it. Then, type the value into the cell, and add text to an adjacent cell so that you know what the value represents. Now, you can reference this named cell in your formula, even if the worksheet is hidden or very hidden: =[@Cost]*Tax Then, when the tax value changes the following year, you can temporarily unhide the hidden backend worksheet to update the value. Create an end point for 3D references Keep your datasets from spilling into each other As an academic proofreader, I create a new worksheet each month to keep a tally of my monthly word count (cell D2). I then use those monthly values to keep a running total of the number of words I've read overall (cell H2). As a result, when I add a new worksheet for a subsequent month, I need Excel to include it in the running total. This is where my hidden backend worksheet comes in handy. In cell H2, I typed: =SUM('Feb 2023:Backend'!D2)
where - Feb 2023 references the first worksheet in my workbook, - Backend is the name of my hidden backend worksheet, which was the rightmost tab before it was hidden, and - D2 is the cell in each worksheet that contains the figure I want to sum. Because the backend worksheet was the rightmost tab in the workbook when I hid it, it stays in this position, even when I add new worksheets. This means that any monthly worksheets I add subsequently will be picked up in the 3D reference. Finally, to ensure I don't accidentally add a value to cell D2 in the hidden backend worksheet, I've filled it in red and added a note, "Leave red cell blank." Don't lose data that needs to be kept safe Lock down those numbers You can use a hidden backend worksheet to store data that needs to be preserved but doesn't currently need to be on show in the unhidden worksheets. Much like when you're clearing out your attic, there are some things you're sure you'll need in the future but don't need at the moment, so you'll stick them in a box for safekeeping. The hidden backend worksheet serves the same purpose. For example, here, I've kept the lookup tables from previous years, even though they're no longer referenced in any formulas. This means that I can refer back to this data at a later date if necessary, like if I want to analyze historical trends or re-use old figures. Store personal notes and reminders It's great for instructions, too A final purpose of a hidden backend worksheet is to store textual information that you can refer to if needed, such as instructions, contact details, reminders, or a list of deadlines. This saves having to create a separate workbook or Word document altogether, and keeping the details out of sight means your workbook stays well-organized. If you end up having too much information on your hidden backend workbook, simply add more! Just make sure you keep them all well-maintained so that you're not storing unnecessary data and, consequently, making your Excel file larger than it needs to be. You've built a backend, now set up a homepage As well as using a hidden backend worksheet, you should also add a homepage worksheet to your Excel file that welcomes collaborators, gives instructions on how to use the workbook, directs people to the best places for support, and contains key information like data snapshots and deadline dates.

item.title: Home Depot is handing out free Milwaukee battery packs for Labor Day
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.00
If you're like me, you have a slew of power tools and not enough battery packs. To make matters worse, the battery cells are usually more expensive than the tools themselves. Thankfully, Home Depot is running another of its popular buy-one-get-one deals ahead of Labor Day, and it's handing out free Milwaukee 5.0Ah extended-capacity batteries. Anyone who frequents the Home Depot website should be somewhat familiar with this popular promotion. The big box retailer is constantly offering free tools or battery deals as an incentive to sell more gear. And with the fall weather quickly approaching, now is the perfect time to stock up ahead of all those DIY projects. Here's what you need to know. How to get your free Milwaukee battery (or tool) Buy a tool and get a free battery worth $169 Many of you should know the drill by now, but if not, here's how it works. Either way, buy a Milwaukee tool at Home Depot between now and Labor Day, and you'll get a free battery or tool. Hit the link below and grab yours today. item.title: I built an Obsidian knowledge base without writing a single word in the Obsidian editor
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.10
Working with note-taking apps and Markdown has worked out well for me over the years. I've been doing it for a while now, and I can't say I miss using GUI word processors. Obsidian is the app I use the most, so I created a general knowledge vault in the app. And I did it without typing a single word in the Obsidian editor. Setting up a General Knowledge Obsidian Vault keeps me organized Building a comprehensive knowledge base for all my hobbies and interests I am interested in just about everything. I like to code, experiment with tech, run TTRPGs, play guitar, paint, build models, make websites, read comics, and, well, you get the point. The idea is to make something I can use for work, hobbies, and reference quickly and within a self-contained vault. I write almost everything in Markdown and rather than print everything out, I think keeping things organized in Obsidian is the best way to go. I want to have something that's easy to index, search, and interact with that I can access across the devices I use. I add photos of important documents to my vault Saving my schematics, pictures, reminders, and charts A surprisingly effective way to add information to my vault is by taking pictures (or scanning) documents I might need to find quickly. This can be something as simple as the schematics for a Raspberry Pi board to the instructions for a tower fan I bought from Walmart. Rather than save a bunch of manuals and papers in a box somewhere, I can keep them in my vault for quick access or reference. I usually put them in a folder labeled reference photos. This way, I can just take a quick peek at the folder itself, find the image I'm looking for, use it for whatever I'm working on, and get on with my day. It's a small thing, but it's very handy. Since I name all my photos descriptively, importing them into Obsidian automatically retains their naming conventions, so I don't have to touch the editor at all, aside from importing them into a single Untitled note. The Obsidian Web Clipper saves a ton of time A simple method for saving important information To start building my knowledge base, I installed the Obsidian Web Clipper extension. The plugin is available for many different browsers, including most of the ones I use. I chose to install it on Firefox since that's where I do most of my research and browsing. I use it on my phone and desktop, since Firefox on Android allows users to install extensions. Plus, having it available on mobile makes information gathering easier. I started my knowledge base by visiting a few reference sites and saving info I use often. Then I grabbed some chord charts and lyrics for some songs I want to learn. Hey, I'll arrange that acoustic single-guitar version of Radar Love one of these days. I spent some more time adding long-form articles (I like to read them and take handwritten notes). The web clipper came in handy for building the bulk of the knowledge base. But I also found using a few other methods to be worthwhile. I also use handwritten notes and outlines to expand my knowledge Pen and paper have tremendous value even in our tech-based world I like to take notes. My handwriting is atrocious, but that doesn't stop me from hideously scrawling anything of minor importance in one of my many, many notebooks. Obsidian happens to allow you to add images to your vaults. So, if there's something vital that I catch in passing or can't save the entire source for some reason, I can snap a quick photo and upload it to my vault. I set up a dedicated folder for each set of notes I take by hand. It helps keep me organized, and I can make better sense of my notes, which is very helpful when I'm studying for certifications or different courses. Adding Markdown notes from the Linux terminal Configuring a simple TUI app to integrate with my Vault I'm a big advocate for using and working within the terminal. Command lines are clean, organized, and give me more control over what I do on my system. I watch/stream video, listen to music, navigate around my file system, code, and launch software from the terminal whenever possible. It's just my preferred interface. Most of the time, I'd rather write Markdown inside a terminal app rather than launch the full Obsidian app. I use micro for most of my notes and initial drafts. The cool thing about micro is I can use it with Termux on my phone or through the terminal on my desktop. I write my drafts or scribble notes (typos and all), then just save or sync (with Syncthing) them into the Vault's folder. Building my Obsidian knowledge base has been one of the most useful projects I've worked on in a while A knowledge base can be as detailed and expansive as the user wants to get. Some people like to incorporate LLMs into their knowledge bases while others take advantage of various plugins. I'll pass on both of those, because what I'm doing works for me. It's something I'll continue to do, just to help keep my accumulated knowledge, references charts, chaotic thoughts, and half-baked ideas all in one place.

item.title: Why your broken Linux drivers aren't actually Linux's fault
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.17
While Linux teams can fail to handle drivers for some devices effectively (or wisely), it's not always their fault. Whether the discussion involves distributions like Ubuntu with GNOME on Wayland, openSUSE with KDE Plasma on X11, or even Manjaro with Xfce on X11, each OS can experience potential device or driver problems. Over time, Linux driver incompatibilities have improved, but they still carry some hiccups. My first installed Linux distribution was Ubuntu 18.04 LTS (used X11), and I had to learn quite a bit to understand how to format the drive in my dual-boot setup, install the OS, and deal with driver issues and configuration challenges. It took some time to figure it all out, but I eventually got my TP-Link Bluetooth adapter, ASUS Wi-Fi antenna, and my older NIC functioning decently, just not as well as it did on Windows 10. I blamed Ubuntu for not working with my hardware 100%. Sure, there's nothing more frustrating than installing a distribution like Arch Linux 2026.03.01 only to find that it won't boot, or a device does not work properly or efficiently, if at all. That's where consumers (especially former Windows users) think their Linux distribution doesn't work as it should. The misconception is that it is Linux's fault when their GPU, USB Bluetooth adapter, network card, or another device doesn't work, but it's usually the other way around. Linux doesn't always have access to official drivers to build into the kernel If manufacturers don't release open-source drivers, Linux distribution teams can't access essential code Whenever you experience device/driver issues, it is often because of a lack of driver code availability for Linux teams. Developers usually have to reverse-engineer the products and try to build kernel drivers that work, but the Linux kernel is also getting smarter, which helps significantly. The only exception is when the manufacturer releases a proprietary driver for a device. Dev teams can't touch the code, of course, but you can install it on your Linux system if the OS allows it. My TP-Link UB-400 USB Bluetooth adapter (as mentioned earlier) only had drivers for Windows, so Ubuntu had no source code to use to make one. Ubuntu may have had a custom driver that could make it work, but I ended up installing a driver for another device that was recommended for my particular setup. As for the Wi-Fi adapter and the old NIC, you guessed it, they also didn't have a Linux driver for Ubuntu—or any Linux flavor for that matter. Customers complain about installation problems because of driver issues Incompatibility is the biggest challenge When I tried to use my ASUS PCE-AC68 Wi-Fi antenna, it wasn't playing nice with my old ASUS Essentio CM-1630 desktop where I installed Ubuntu 18.04 LTS. ASUS only provided Windows drivers, and Ubuntu didn't have a driver that made it work after installation. The problem was that the device did not support Linux at all, so I had to find another driver that could substitute its functionality. I eventually got it working, but of course, not at its full potential because the product only had official drivers for Windows. I certainly complained about Wi-Fi not working, but understood the complexities of the device having no Linux open-source or proprietary drivers. Other times, you may find your network card, old (or new) GPU, motherboard, or other device may not function effectively, if at all, assuming your Linux OS cannot find a compatible driver/kernel. While these situations can be Linux's fault, it is not always the case because of proprietary driver limitations. If the Linux dev teams reverse-engineer the device, they might create a driver that functions, but not as well as a proprietary driver that optimizes performance and features. One clever thing device manufacturers do is build features into their proprietary drivers, limiting what Linux teams can do, such as having no access to a device's exclusive GUI power management controls and functions or, more specifically, NVIDIA's exclusive Deep Learning Super Sampling (DLSS) integration. On the other side of things, the Arch Linux dev team suffered from NVIDIA's discontinued support for GTX 1000‑series and older cards with Pascal and Maxwell GPUs. Yet users with legacy GPUs are often left to install unsupported packages like nvidia-470xx-dkms from the AUR or find alternative workarounds on their own—one reason some Arch Linux users switch to other distributions. Their decision breaks apps like Steam (meaning more steps) and often requires advanced processes to make your older GPU work. This incident surely raised numerous complaints. Device makers don't always budget for a Linux development team A manufacturer's allocated funding has its limits There are so many variations of Linux operating systems, based on several display server protocols (Wayland, X11, etc.) along with desktop environments like GNOME, KDE Plasma, and Xfce. Custom functionality and different repositories also play a role in the uniqueness of various systems, meaning that it's a challenge to find the right staffing for Linux support and development. It also requires an allocated budget for such departments and divisions, so the drive for Linux users must remain in demand for the company to justify the expense. If you think about it, Windows and macOS are common household names, but they are also operating systems with easier driver management and GUI-based functionality—yeah, we all know the headaches there, too. But Linux is more of a hands-on system focused on commands for everything, although GUI functionality and application management have become more of a focus for consumers. Today, there's a little more consumer and commercial drive to switch to Linux, especially since Microsoft is ending Windows 10 updates and support. Some companies have had Linux departments for a long time, while others don't have the staffing or funding to create such a department. Misplacing the blame While some dev teams' decisions lead to blame, such as the Arch Linux Nvidia driver support incident, most device issues are not a Linux distribution's fault. If they have open-source drivers to work with, that's great. If they don't, reverse engineering is their only solution, unless a manufacturer releases proprietary drivers that you can install in your Linux distro. But even when they do offer proprietary drivers, you and Linux can be stuck with whatever they provide as a driver, good or bad.

item.title: The Myspace Dilemma Facing ChatGPT
item.description:
Source: Ian Bogost | The Atlantic Score: 5.32
My colleague Perry was clutching a Ben & Jerry’s ice-cream bar. Our office, which made websites at the turn of the millennium, had decided to try Kozmo.com, a new site that promised to bring DVDs, books, and treats to your door within an hour. We paid a couple of dollars for the ice-cream bar—delivery was free. Yet Perry’s eyes opened wide, the way they did when something bad was about to happen. Kozmo.com collapsed a year later, in April 2001, along with much of the rest of the dot-com economy that employed us at the time. Today, of course, the Kozmo.com model is everywhere—DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, and other services allow you to order almost any foodstuff to your door. Kozmo.com wasn’t a bad idea so much as a badly timed one. The marketplace wasn’t mature, and the business model for delivery hadn’t been established. The technology industry believes in the gospel of original ideas and disruptive innovation. But Kozmo.com, just one of many examples, shows how likely the first mover in a sector is to founder or fail or fall out of favor: Friendster and Myspace were first in social networking, but Facebook eradicated them. Treo and BlackBerry owned the smartphone market until the iPhone stamped them out. Early winners seem obvious and enduring, until they do not. Will the AI market be any different? No and yes. A year ago, OpenAI’s ChatGPT was a generic name, the Coke or Kleenex of generative-AI chatbots. Today, its competitors, especially Anthropic’s Claude, are advancing quickly. OpenAI’s fall from favor looks inevitable. But AI appears to work nothing like delivery apps, smartphones, social networks, or even computer operating systems. If ChatGPT becomes outmoded, it won’t be the result of OpenAI losing ground or failing to innovate. Instead, the entire generative-AI sector will have become a commodity, like soft drinks or facial tissues. That process has already begun. The logic of first-mover advantage is essentially colonialist: a land grab across a newly discovered commercial wilderness. In the early days of American industry, some of that wilderness really was untamed. DuPont ushered in the modern synthetic-fiber industry with nylon; Bell Labs invented the transistor, the foundation of modern electronics. A more boring path to success, made from standards, licensing, and distribution instead of frontier-crossing invention, proliferated in the 20th century. In the early 1980s, Microsoft pushed MS-DOS (and then Windows) onto various PC manufacturers to get the software into as many machines as possible. JVC’s VHS cassette beat Sony’s (in many ways superior) Betamax format because JVC licensed its format faster and more broadly, meaning more VCRs used the format and more video stores stocked it. In the early days of cable television, channels such as CNN and MTV sought to be carried on as many cable systems as possible. Retailers such as Walmart started saturating regions with stores, helping solidify supplier and distribution networks while slowly eroding competition from local businesses. By the 1990s, lessons from Microsoft, JVC, CNN, and others suggested that network effects—increased value derived from the number of users of a product or service—were central to land-grab victories. At the same time, technology shifted economic growth toward immaterial goods, such as software and online services. If a platform could scale fast and first, it could own the market. This rationale drove venture-capital investment during the entire internet era, from the dot-coms through Web 2.0 and the smartphone. User growth, market share, ecosystem lock-in, and brand awareness became more important than profit or even revenue. But success didn’t always come from being first. In many cases, what we now consider the big winner became the most familiar only after the market was established. Google was not the first search engine—Lycos, AltaVista, Ask Jeeves, and others filled that role years earlier. Google invented a better way to catalog the web, and then it built a viable advertising model atop that success. Facebook did the same with social networking; Apple did the same with smartphones. Zimride, which later rebranded as Lyft, offered ride-share services first, but Uber became dominant by expanding aggressively. Reversals of early success turn out to be far more common than first-to-market entrenchment. Given that history, OpenAI might seem more likely to cede ground than to retain it. The company’s apparent advantage has turned out to be more fragile than expected. (The Atlantic entered into a corporate partnership with OpenAI in 2024.) But something else has changed too. Just as the online-services market differed from the electronics market that preceded it, so too does the market for AI services differ from what came just before. A single AI victor may never emerge. Different AI companies are proving to be good at different things. Anthropic’s Claude, for example, is particularly effective at coding and at analyzing long documents. Sophisticated AI end users are using multiple services for different tasks. The various models—ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and so on—tend to trade places rapidly on various metrics of performance. ChatGPT won over many ordinary consumers—college students, say, or your aging parents. But workplaces, schools, and organizations adopt technology as a part of interoperating software suites such as Microsoft Office and Google Workplace. And unlike Uber and Amazon, AI has quickly become embedded in those. The network effects that lock users into an AI service are situated inside these software packages, up the value chain from GPT, Gemini, Claude, and other AI models. The AI is a (supposedly!) thinking utility that powers old business services in new ways, but it isn’t the service—or won’t remain so, at least. At work, AI is not a choice but a tool—welcome or not—to which employers subscribe that becomes a default. Initially, ChatGPT did the hard work of educating users on what large language models are and how they can be used. Now many consumer and business users understand what AI is and what it can do, and they have moved on to trying to figure out how to use it. Which AI they use has become less important—and perhaps less of a choice, besides. The technology of LLMs feels disruptive and world-changing—more like nylon or iPhones than like Kozmo.com. But the big AI companies’ models have reached parity fairly quickly. Switching costs are fairly low in the AI marketplace, compared with those of videocassette recorders, smartphones, or even social networks. Whether or not AI is ethical, effective, or even fit for purpose, the act of using it appears to be naturally promiscuous. Microsoft, Google, Facebook, Uber, and other platform-centric companies relied on winning users and holding them hostage. AI doesn’t seem to work that way. Instead, it looks more like corporate infrastructure or commodities. Companies don’t really care which cloud-computing provider they use, so long as the service is reliable and competitively priced. Firms will procure whatever hard disks, printer paper, or lunchtime slop bowls are convenient, suitable, and priced right. They seem likely to end up doing the same with AI. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman made the provocative statement last week that in the future, intelligence will be “a utility, like electricity or water.” Instead of taking that claim as hubristic—as Altman claiming that smarts will be owned by OpenAI—consider a far more mundane and probable idea: AI could become, in just a few years, a commodity as invisible and anonymous as power or plumbing. Nobody cares what company makes the lights work or the toilets flush, so long as they do.

item.title: Los Angeles getting personnel in place for a week of very dangerous heat
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 5.19
Los Angeles getting personnel in place for a week of very dangerous heat - Click here to listen to this article - With scorching temperatures forecast this week across Southern California, L.A. city and county agencies are preparing for worst-case scenarios. The Los Angeles County Fire Department said in a statement Monday that the county was “augmenting staffing and pre-positioning personnel and resources” to ensure a rapid response to wildfires. The Los Angeles Fire Department also has “predeployed resources citywide,” according to a statement by Mayor Karen Bass. The mayor urged Angelenos to “take this extreme heat seriously” and highlighted city facilities residents could use to stay cool. Most of L.A. County is under an extreme heat warning, and the National Weather Service also has issued a red flag fire warning for many interior portions of southwest California, including the interior mountains and adjacent foothills of Los Angeles, Ventura, Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties and the Cuyama Valley. The combination of extreme heat, gusty winds and low humidity brings a “significant risk” of “large plume dominated fires with rapid fire spread and extreme fire behavior,” according to forecasters. The weather service is forecasting high temperatures of up to 108 degrees across the lower mountains and foothills and Cuyama Valley, according to the red flag warning, which goes into effect at 10 a.m. Tuesday and is in place through 3 p.m. Friday. “A Red Flag Warning means that critical fire weather conditions will occur shortly,” the warning said. “Use extreme caution with anything that can spark a wildfire. Residents near wildland interfaces should be prepared to evacuate if a wildfire breaks out.” As of Monday night, Southern California Edison was considering planned power outages due to heightened wildfire risk for about 5,700 customers, or less than 1% of its total customers. About 4,000 of those who may be affected are in Los Angeles County, according to the utility company’s website. Experts say this year’s summer heat has been particularly grueling since nighttime temperatures have remained high and coastal areas have been hotter than usual. The county Fire Department said it “strongly advises” residents to check on vulnerable neighbors, family members and pets during the heat wave and advised residents to stay hydrated, use sunscreen and other forms of sun protection, such as a hat or umbrella, and to shift outdoor activities away from the hours of 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Anyone seeking relief from the heat by heading to the beach should take note: Elevated surf and strong rip currents mean an increased risk of ocean drownings, according to the Fire Department, which urged beachgoers to “exercise extreme caution.” Mayor Bass’ office said Monday that L.A. has “hundreds of locations” for residents to stay cool, including Recreation and Parks facilities as well as local libraries. The city has also extended operating hours from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. for nine pet-friendly dedicated cooling centers from Tuesday through Friday: San Fernando Valley - Canoga Park Senior Citizens’ Center (7326 Jordan Ave.) - North Hollywood Senior Citizen Center (5301 Tujunga Ave.) - Sunland Senior Citizen Center (8640 Fenwick St.) Near Downtown L.A. - Pecan Recreation Center (145 S. Pecan St.) - Highland Park Adult Senior Citizen Center (6152 N. Figueroa St.) - Lafayette Multipurpose Community Center (625 S. Lafayette Park Place) South L.A. - Algin Sutton Recreation Center (8800 S. Hoover St.) Westside - Pan Pacific Senior Activity Center (141 S. Gardner Ave.) Harbor - East Wilmington Greenbelt Community Center (918 N. Sanford Ave., Wilmington)

item.title: USC and UCLA bet big on AI to meet soaring student, job market demands
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 4.99
USC and UCLA bet big on AI to meet soaring student, job market demands - Click here to listen to this article - - UCLA, USC and other universities are launching new majors to train students either to build AI systems or to use them in the humanities. - USC’s AI degree immerses students in model-building aimed at producing industry-ready graduates. - The digital humanities department at UCLA uses AI tools to examine disciplines including history, languages and arts. USC and UCLA are joining the rush to embed artificial intelligence and new digital technologies into college coursework as the academic year begins, announcing new AI majors and initiatives, betting that degrees built partly or entirely around AI will launch careers and pay off after graduation. At USC, the Viterbi School of Engineering is launching its inaugural undergraduate artificial intelligence degree. The major is housed in the Mark and Mary Stevens School of Computing and Artificial Intelligence inside the engineering school. Students will spend four years learning to build the technology and to apply it to fields as far apart as drug discovery, robotics and agriculture. In Westwood, UCLA is taking a different approach, opening what officials describe as the nation’s first freestanding Department of Digital Humanities. A new bachelor’s degree in digital humanities will teach students how to integrate AI and digital tools into disciplines including sociology, archaeology, history, and the study of race and gender. These powerhouse Los Angeles institutions join a growing cohort of universities in California and nationwide responding quickly to a technology most undergraduates first encountered in chat bots or social media feeds in middle and high school. Some campuses — including the new programs at USC and University of San Francisco — are teaching students to build the systems. Others are showing them how to study, and improve upon, what the technology can do for society. Nearly all are requiring ethics courses along the way — as educators continue to grapple with cheating and with fears that heavy AI use will erode critical thinking. As universities crack down on AI, extreme monitoring policies and false accusations are fueling a deep mistrust between professors and students. UC Santa Barbara is also launching an AI major this fall. San Diego State started a bachelor’s degree in artificial intelligence and human responsibility last year, the first of its kind in the California State University system, pairing computer science with courses on AI ethics and on technology and the body. Not every campus is creating a major. Neither Stanford nor UC Berkeley, the state’s two biggest computer science powers, has created an undergraduate AI degree. This month, Berkeley announced a new master of artificial intelligence and machine learning two-semester professional degree. Stanford offers artificial intelligence as one of 10 tracks inside its computer science major. Caltech is taking an integrated approach: Rather than create an AI major or minor, the university says it trains students to understand AI and machine learning at a fundamental level so they can apply the tools across many fields. Three of the nation’s most selective private schools also grant an undergraduate AI degree: Carnegie Mellon, MIT and the University of Pennsylvania. Northwestern’s degree begins in fall. Digital humanities is scarcer. No Ivy League school, and no flagship public such as the universities of Michigan or Virginia, grants a digital humanities degree or houses a department. The University of Pennsylvania offers a minor. Princeton and Johns Hopkins run digital humanities research centers. Delivering what students and employers want Michael Horn, a faculty member at the Harvard Graduate School of Education who studies education trends, said the campuses are trying to meet the changing demands of their students and future employers. “They’re meeting market demand,” Horn said.
