The rent on the studio was cheap — about $1,500 a month — and the leasing agent, he said, told him he’d probably pay only an additional $50 for utilities. But three years after Porter moved in, his monthly bill for trash, sewer and water had more than doubled, to $182 from $86. He couldn’t figure out why; water rates charged by the city utility had not increased at the same rate. When Porter and his neighbors asked to see the math behind what they owed, the property management sent them a general overview of how the charges are calculated, but did not provide copies of specific bills. Unlike traditional utility bills, Porter wasn’t being billed by the provider but by a third-party company — Conservice, in this case — that uses what’s called a ratio utility billing system. This means that the landlord does not charge each resident for their individual utility usage but sends them statements based on a formula applied to the building’s total usage. So Porter asked Conservice for a breakdown of his individual bill. “Can I please see the proof that this is money that I actually owe you and see how you got [to] it?” Porter recalled asking the company. According to an email shared with The Times, a representative directed him back to his property manager. Amid growing national scrutiny of how companies price what they sell and the services they offer, tenants in L.A. have described mounting frustration as their utility bills have climbed and they struggle to see the math behind what they owe. The Times spoke with renters at six apartment buildings in L.A. whose landlords use a formula to split up shared utilities. Some renters are now demanding that this kind of billing practice — often handled by outside companies, which add on their own fees — be banned outright. But representatives for landlords say doing so would leave them with few desirable options for recouping the cost of utilities and would hurt conservation efforts. Splitting the bill Olivia Wein, a senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center, first heard about ratio utility billing systems 20 years ago. Since then, she said, she’s fielded more and more complaints about the practice from tenants and advocates. “This practice just kept emerging,” Wein said. When utilities aren’t included in the monthly rent, landlords have two main options. If the building doesn’t already have them, submeters can be installed so that tenants receive bills for their individual usage of electricity or water. Or landlords can take master-metered utilities and split them up based on apartment size or number of occupants, as in Porter’s building, a practice called RUBS, short for ratio utility billing system. It’s hard to say how common it is for tenants to pay utilities through RUBS. Two of the largest organizations that represent landlords, the National Apartment Assn. and the National Multifamily Housing Council, said they don’t track these numbers. But they used to. Two decades ago, researchers working on behalf of the National Apartment Assn. and city governments surveyed roughly 8,000 properties in the U.S. and found that renters living in 1 out of every 4 apartments were billed using RUBS. A more recent report provides a picture of how landlords bill for utilities in L.A. In December, the Los Angeles Housing Department recommended that city officials outlaw RUBS in rent-stabilized homes, as West Hollywood and San José have done. The department estimated that 19% of homes subject to rent stabilization had master-metered utilities and were therefore likely to use RUBS; that amounts to roughly 123,000 apartments in the city. A department spokesperson said they didn’t have an estimate for RUBS usage across all rental units, but there are probably tens of thousands more apartments that use this kind of billing and are not subject to the city’s rent stabilization law. Wein said it’s common for these kinds of billing systems to show up in older apartment buildings, where individual meters were not installed during construction. In the last decade, states have started mandating individual meters in multifamily buildings; in 2018, California began requiring that water submeters be installed in newly constructed residences with two or more units. Hanna Yoseph, a hairstylist who runs her own business, lives in a two-bedroom unit in a towering glass building in downtown L.A. While her $3,400 rent is the same each month, her utility bill, which includes charges for shared utilities including water, wastewater, hot water and HVAC, fluctuates by hundreds of dollars. In March 2025, Yoseph owed $332.50 for the utilities split and billed to her from a third-party company, Yes Energy Management. Three months later, her bill rose to $417.99. By October of that year, she was being charged $541. “I don’t know how to budget for it,” Yoseph said. Yoseph said she called Yes Energy Management and asked to see a copy of the bills that led to her individual charges. She said she was told she needed permission from the property management company. According to emails shared with The Times, Yoseph and the tenants association emailed management multiple times before being told they could set up an in-person meeting to view the bills used to generate their individual charges. But tenants responded saying they wanted digital copies so they could have the time to do their own math; they have not received a response. Last week, Yoseph said she spoke with a representative from Yes Energy Management who told her she was going to try to get her copies of the master bill calculations. (Attempts by The Times to reach Yes Energy Management for comment were unsuccessful.) In 2022, attorneys in San Diego sued Conservice, a major third-party utility billing company. In a class-action lawsuit brought on behalf of California renters, lawyers alleged that Conservice’s policy was to deny tenants the right to view specific bills or formulas used to calculate their individual charges. In an email, a representative for Conservice said the company does not have a nondisclosure policy. “Our goal is to provide residents with clear, accessible information so they fully understand how their individual utility charges are calculated,” said Brett Kraus, senior counsel for utility services. But tenants represented in this lawsuit claimed the company “uniformly” failed to provide exact calculations. Lawyers alleged this practice was not only unfair but violated state law and a tenant’s common law right to review bills they were expected to pay. In a settlement agreement reached last year, Conservice agreed to provide any California tenant disputing their bill with copies of invoices and formulas used to determine their specific charges. (Porter’s communication with Conservice was in 2023, before the company was subject to the settlement agreement. Tenants who spoke to The Times said they still have been unable to get this information from Conservice.) This kind of bill transparency is something landlords and tenants say they agree on. In December, L.A.’s housing department recommended that city officials adopt rules making it clear that tenants have a right to review master utility bills and create a process for tenants to dispute charges. “If your customer is paying for it, they should know what they’re paying for,” said Daniel Yukelson, executive director of the Apartment Assn. of Greater Los Angeles. Going on strike After Porter’s failed attempts to see copies of the master bills at his apartment in Koreatown, he started talking to neighbors having the same issues. Last summer, roughly four dozen residents of Virgil Square Apartments sent a letter to the owner of the property, Equity Residential, saying that since they could not see the specific calculations used to determine their bills, they would refuse to pay them. Tenants also said it was unfair to be subject to a billing system that stripped them of control over their own utility costs. “None of us has control over how much water our neighbors use, or whether the pool stays open in the winter when no one uses it,” the letter read. Tenants have been threatened with eviction for hanging signs outside their balconies calling attention to the utility billing method. Equity Residential, which owns about 15,000 apartments in the L.A. metro area, did not respond to a list of questions. Tenants at other buildings across the city said that with little power over what they were being charged for shared utilities, they felt few incentives to conserve — in a state whose water sources are quickly drying up. Collectively, that inclination could lead to bills soaring ever higher. “If we’re going to be charged for people’s water and they’re not going to pay attention to what they’re doing, I’m going to do laundry more often during the week because you’re already overcharging me,” said Caitlin Moran, a tenant living with her partner in a studio apartment downtown. But people in the apartment industry say that, unlike charging utilities as part of the monthly rent, RUBS gives tenants some sense of the cost of taking long showers or leaving the lights on. Fred Sutton, senior vice president of public affairs for the California Apartment Assn., said tenants paying utilities via RUBS have some “skin in the game.” “In older, master-metered buildings where individual meters may be impractical or cost-prohibitive, RUBS can connect residents more closely to the cost of shared utility use and encourage conservation,” he said. In marketing videos, Conservice promises to increase landlords’ profits while also lowering utility costs. In emails, Marc Treitler, Conservice’s general counsel and president of sustainability, said the company helps all parties save on utilities by auditing the bills it receives directly from providers before passing charges on to renters. “We have found tens of millions of dollars in overcharges,” he said. “Correcting these bills usually lowers the charges for the tenants.” In 1999, researchers looked at 32 multifamily properties across Texas, Florida and California, in an attempt to determine the effects of different billing methods on water conservation. They found that renters at submetered properties, where tenants were charged individually for their water usage, used an average of 39% fewer gallons per year than those living in apartments where water was included in the monthly rent. Renters billed via RUBS used 20% less water. A 2004 study also found that submetering led renters to conserve more water. But this time researchers found no statistically significant difference between the amount of water used when a utility payment was included in a tenant’s monthly rent and when they were charged using RUBS. Peter Mayer, a Colorado-based water use consultant and one of the lead researchers on the 2004 study, said RUBS may in fact have an anti-conservation effect. “It becomes in your own economic self-interest to use as much water as you can,” he said. “You want to be the highest water user in that building because then you have maximized your investment.” As for Porter, who is refusing to pay his RUBS bills in Koreatown, he said he’s been setting aside the money owed so he’s ready to pay when he can see exactly how these bills are calculated. “I’m willing to pay it if someone will show me it’s legitimate,” he said. This article is part of The Times’ equity reporting initiative, funded by the James Irvine Foundation, exploring the challenges facing low-income workers and the efforts being made to address California’s economic divide.

item.title: Big oil and gas companies are partly responsible for California's water woes, study finds
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 2.03
- Click here to listen to this article - - Scientific research has revealed how climate change is placing added strain on water in California and the Western United States. - In a new study, scientists estimate the role of carbon dioxide emissions from more than 100 of the world’s largest fossil fuel companies. In the last few years, multiple studies have shown that global warming is intensifying drought and worsening water scarcity in California and the Western United States. Now, scientists have found that a group of polluters is responsible for a large share of this drying. In their study, published this week in the journal Communications Earth & Environment, the researchers estimated that climate change shrank the peak annual snowpack in 11 Western states by 36% between 2014 and 2024, and reduced the flow of rivers and streams in spring and summer by 13% compared to a world without human-caused warming. They found that nearly half of those declines were caused by the planet-heating gases released into the atmosphere by 122 of the world’s largest fossil fuel and cement companies. New research shows global warming has become the dominant driver of worsening drought in the western United States. This group, which researchers refer to as the “carbon majors,” includes big producers of oil, gas and coal, both private corporations and state-owned enterprises in countries such as Russia, China and Saudi Arabia. “Collectively, they constitute a really big source of human-caused climate change,” said Emily Williams, the lead author and a climate scientist at UC Merced. The researchers used climate models to examine the effects of the companies’ carbon dioxide emissions since 1950. They also found that global warming, by drying out soil and making crops soak up more water, has increased irrigation water demand by 4%, and that this group of companies is responsible for about half of that. With days left in the legislative session, California lawmakers are considering several high-stakes energy and environment bills. The remainder of planet-warming gases are released by smaller fossil fuel companies, livestock agriculture, deforestation, landfills and other activities, according to the study. Even without rising temperatures caused by the use of fossil fuels, heavy water use is putting major strain on the West’s rivers, streams and groundwater aquifers, Williams said. “Climate change is taking what has been a precarious situation already and turning it into a crisis,” she said. Agriculture uses much of the water throughout the West. In California’s Central Valley, chronic overpumping of water from wells has caused major declines in groundwater levels. The scientists estimated in the study that at least 20% of the groundwater loss can be attributed to global warming. A spokesperson for the American Petroleum Institute, the largest oil and gas trade association in the country, did not respond Wednesday to a request for comment about the study. The research is based on sound scientific principles and methods, said Rob Jackson, a climate scientist at Stanford University’s Doerr School of Sustainability, who was not involved in the study. “Climate change is making our water problems systematically more challenging,” Jackson said. “We can no longer manage our water resources without thinking about how the atmosphere is changing, and how snowpack is changing.” It’s also important to consider, he said, that “a relatively small number of companies and sources have been responsible for most of the pollution in the air, and that some of those companies are still fighting the consensus on climate change and fighting climate action.” At the federal level, there is a heated political debate over climate lawsuits against oil and gas companies. Republican members of Congress are proposing to grant the fossil fuel industry immunity from lawsuits based on studies like this one, while Democrats oppose such legislation. In recent years, a growing body of research has focused on analyzing the role of climate change in worsening droughts, floods, heat waves and wildfires. Some studies have also examined the role of large oil and gas companies. For example, a 2023 study estimated that nearly 40% of the forest area burned by wildfires in the Western U.S. and southwestern Canada in the last 40 years can be attributed to the carbon emissions of the world’s largest fossil fuel producers and cement makers. A 2025 study found that the carbon dioxide released by such companies and their products has substantially worsened heat waves since 2000. In other research, scientists found that the last quarter-century has probably been the driest in 1,200 years in Western North America, and that global warming is responsible for about 40% of the drought’s severity. Even after a year and a half of wet weather, research shows the American West has experienced the driest 25-year period in 1,200 years. When might the megadrought end? Researchers have estimated that climate change is linked to about half of the decline in the flow of the Colorado River, which provides water for seven states and Mexico. This year, the river’s largest reservoirs have fallen lower than ever before. Record-breaking heat this winter and spring left mountains across the West with very little snow, and scientists recently determined in other research that climate change made such a snow drought four times more likely than before the rise of industry started releasing more carbon dioxide and driving global warming. In the latest study, the researchers said they focused on emissions since the 1950s because during that decade some companies began to have access to research indicating the use of oil, gas and coal could lead to dangerous climatic changes. Carly Phillips, a co-author and senior scientist at the nonprofit Union of Concerned Scientists, said that’s why research focusing on the role these companies play in the climate crisis is important. “Despite recognizing this science internally, they poured resources into a campaign of deception and obstruction to protect their profits,” she said.

item.title: Nothing OS 5.0 drops with Android 17 and on-device app building
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.30
What you need to know - Nothing OS 5.0 is here and combines a redesigned interface, deeper customization, smoother performance, and upgraded Essential AI tools. - Transparent widgets, wallpaper-adaptive icon colors, the new Geist typeface, and refreshed system icons give Nothing OS a more cohesive look. - Nothing OS 5.0 Open Beta begins for the Phone (3), with a stable release expected in mid-October and more devices joining the beta later. Nothing is giving its software a substantial refresh with Nothing OS 5.0, a major update built on Android 17. The latest software zeroes in on everyday interactions, blending a redesigned visual system with more customization, smoother performance, and more powerful Essential AI tools. The update is all about giving you more control and a smoother experience. The home screen gets a brand new theme with transparent widgets and a search bar that adds some depth, while app icons can now pull subtle color tints from your wallpaper to match your vibe. There’s a new system typeface, Geist, which is cleaner and easier to scan, and refreshed icons across the status bar, Settings, Camera, and Gallery. The Gallery also includes new options for sorting and filtering to help you organize photos. You also get more ways to make the phone yours. The lock screen has two new clock faces: the whimsical “Gooey” and the hardware-inspired "Micrographics." Please note the Micrographics clockface and the new home screen theme are still in development and will not be available in the Open Beta yet — they will be part of the general release starting October. The Glyph Interface now comes in an app, so all the features and sounds are in one place. There is also a new Glyph Timer widget and the Away Time widget that helps you monitor your digital habits by telling you how long you've been away from your phone. Nothing is also doubling down on its Essential AI tools. Essential Voice is faster, real-time transcriptions are better, and with the Ear (3), you can record audio directly from the Super Mic on the case. Smart Collections can suggest and organize content for you automatically. And for a fun twist, you can now create Essential Apps right on your phone; just tell it what you want in plain language and it’ll build it for you. Since it runs on Android 17, you get the latest features of the platform as well. That includes the capability to split out the notifications and Quick Settings panels and an enhanced Quick Share that works across iOS and Android via QR code. The update also brings new privacy indicators, expanded dark theme support, and a redesigned Recents menu. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android The Nothing OS 5.0 Open Beta program starts today for the Phone (3), with a stable release expected in mid-October. Other devices will be included in the beta program later. Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. item.title: Google Pay and Apple Pay are finally coming to Walmart
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.22
What you need to know - Walmart is finally embracing contactless payments, as Apple Pay and Google Pay are coming to Walmart and Sam’s Club after years of resistance. - Tap to Pay will reach all U.S. Walmart stores and Sam’s Clubs by the end of 2026, with fuel stations following by mid-2027. - Cash, chip cards, Walmart Pay, and Sam’s Club Scan & Go will remain available alongside the new payment option. Walmart is finally throwing in the towel on its notorious resistance to contactless payments. After years of pushing shoppers to its proprietary Walmart Pay app, the retail giant is rolling out standard Tap to Pay, meaning both Google Pay and Apple Pay are on their way to checkout lines near you. Starting August 24, Walmart and Sam’s Club locations nationwide will begin to deploy Tap to Pay, the retailer announced today. The feature will be rolled out to all of its U.S. stores and clubs by the end of 2026 and to its fuel stations by the middle of 2027. This allows shoppers to tap an eligible contactless card, phone or smartwatch at the payment terminal instead of having to pull out a physical card or open Walmart’s app. Android users can add an eligible card to Google Wallet and tap to pay when the feature is available at your store, Google says. Walmart will also allow customers to add eligible Walmart, Sam’s Club, and OnePay cards to compatible digital wallets. That sounds like a basic checkout upgrade for 2026, but Walmart has resisted it for years. Instead, the retailer promoted Walmart Pay, which uses a QR code at the register, and Sam’s Club offered Scan & Go, which let shoppers skip checkout altogether. Walmart also supported CurrentC, a rival mobile-payment initiative that ultimately shuttered a few years ago. Customers, meanwhile, kept asking. And they weren't the only ones. With most U.S. retailers already accepting contactless payments, Walmart’s holdout was becoming more conspicuous. The company has effectively admitted defeat now, realizing that forcing shoppers into its own system was putting its own customers at a disadvantage. Existing checkout options like cash, physical chip cards, Walmart Pay, and Sam’s Club Scan & Go aren't going anywhere – this just gives shoppers the frictionless checkout flexibility they’ve been asking for for years. And there's a practical privacy benefit: when you pay with a digital wallet, the retailer generally doesn't get the physical card number that's stored on your account. item.title: Meta patent might solve privacy concerns on smart glasses with a 'hardware lock'
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.11
What you need to know - A report discovered a Meta patent for new "hardware-level" locking for AI glasses microphones and cameras. - It's been stated that this method removes software completely, meaning no nefarious actors could reactivate your mic or camera without your knowledge. - The idea is to return privacy to the people, as Meta's AI glasses have come under severe backlash due to others recording people against their will or knowledge. Having a pair of smart glasses is one thing. But to many, it's an entirely different topic when you factor in cameras and microphones that can record you. A report claims Meta's filed a patent that could help bring our privacy back. The team at Patentlyze highlighted a patent from Meta that could help alleviate privacy concerns surrounding smart glasses. The publication states Meta has filed a patent for a "privacy shield" that's operated in full by hardware components. Software plays no role in muting/unmuting the microphone or cutting off the camera. As Patentlyze notes, this would be a notable shift from how these functions are operated on a device like a phone, which relies on software. According to its discovery, this "hardware mute circuit" would lock the camera/micrpohone at "atomically." This reportedly leaves no room for hackers or other nefarious attackers to activate these sensitive areas without you knowing. More importantly, Patentlyze says, "no app, no operating system update, and no remote hack can flip it back on." Other details in the patent mention that the "trigger," the act of muting or cutting off the camera, would need to come from a "verified hardware source." Right now, we can think of this as a button that you can press or perhaps a switch you can slide into a locked state. This is a patent, and, as always, there's no telling if or when we could see this on the market. At present, we have something to hold us over. Meta has a real problem This patent discovery follows the same line as a recent mandatory patch Meta pushed to its AI glasses last month. This patch deserves context. It was reported that users with Meta's AI glasses were covering the LED indicator that illuminates when the camera is active. It would let people record others without their knowledge. It was creepy and unsettling. These same malicious users found other means of getting around the LED indicator, such as drilling holes and other modifications. Meta's patch solves this. The company states that any tampering with the LED recording light will disable the camera completely. If the privacy light is tampered with or covered, this safeguard will activate. There's been no shortage of backlash from people about Meta's "pervert glasses," or however you may describe them. This update was a step in bringing back user privacy. Now, with this recent patent, it seems Meta isn't done. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Android Central's Take People, right? It's like the one bad student in class that gets the teacher made, so now we all have extra homework for the weekend. Painful. Something like this gives a company's product a bad rep. But it's more than that. Put Meta aside and just think on a street level. No one wants to feel like they're being watched. No one wants to be recorded. For what? Why are you recording them? A person's privacy is nothing to scoff at, and it's definitely nothing to defile. Nickolas is always excited about tech and getting his hands on it. item.title: A pair from Shokz: OpenRun Air 2, OpenFit Air 2 debut looks like the right fit for the gym
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.73
What you need to know - Shokz debuted a pair of earbuds early this week: the OpenFit Air2 and the OpenRun Air 2. - The OpenFit Air 2 is the brand's latest open-ear model, featuring a lighter weight, smaller charging case, improved patented drivers and algorithm for strong audio. - The OpenRun Air 2 is lighter than previous models with comfortable ear hooks and a neckband for stability. - Shokz says consumers can find these earbuds on August 27, starting at $129. If you've been eager to get running or working out, but dreading the lack of appropriate earbuds, Shokz has a dual launch that could help. The company has unveiled two products: the OpenFit Air 2 and OpenRun Air 2. This morning (Aug 24), Shokz published a press release detailing the launch of the OpenFit Air 2 and the OpenRun Air 2. Each pair focuses on the brand's open-ear and bone conduction-style devices. To make working out comfortable, the OpenFit Air 2 is the company's "lightest OpenFit" product at 7.2g. What's more, Shokz says it's redesigned the charging case to make it ~10.5% smaller, while also making it lighter. If you're out, Shokz highlights the OpenFit Air 2's eight-hour battery life. If you have the case, it can provide up to 36 hours of charge. However, if you're short on time, a quick 10-minute charge is said to provide up to three hours of listening. The OpenFit Air 2 features Shokz's Bassphere driver and OpenBass 2.0 algorithm, which offer "more dynamic sound in a compact design." Technically speaking, Shokz's new buds feature a 30-degree angled speaker. Since this is an open-ear product, the OpenFit Air 2 will direct sound into your ear for a "natural listening experience." This works in tandem with DirectPitch tech to make sure your audio remains private to you, and there's no leakage. Grabbing your phone, Shokz says consumers can download its app (Shokz App) to personalize your earbuds' sound with custom EQ profiles and four preset EQ modes. Sweat and water resistance help make the OpenFit Air 2 hold its own while you're exercising. The OpenFit Air 2 starts at $129; available in black, white, and Ice Blue on August 27. OpenRun Air 2 The OpenRun Air 2 is the company's latest bone conduction entry this year. Similar to the OpenFit Air 2, this product is 9% smaller, with a weight of 26.4g. Shokz highlights the Run's lighter and lower-profile approach compared to past versions. Of course, being a pair of bone conduction earbuds, the OpenRun Air 2 features unibody ear hooks and a neckband. Shokz says these should help facilitate better stability. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android On the other hand, we have PremiumPitch 3.0 to help the OpenRun Air 2's bone conduction driver. According to the post, this upgraded driver is an "all-metal, dual-coil, dual-reed structure engineered to deliver richer bass, greater vocal detail, and a more balanced listening experience than OpenRun." Consumers will receive 10 hours of listening on a full charge with the OpenRun Air 2. A quick five-minute charge in its case is said to deliver up to two hours of listening. If you're missing physical buttons, the OpenRun Air 2 provides a few. Shokz says these buttons offer "precise" listening control, alongside a microphone with AI-powered noise reduction software for calls. Users can also download the Shokz App for the OpenRun Air 2 for similar custom EQ profiles and modes like the OpenFit Air 2. On August 27, consumers can find the OpenRun Air 2 for $129 in black and Ice Blue. Additionally, Shokz has made this product available in Standard and Mini sizes. item.title: Rakuten Kobo's major in-store e-reader expansion at Best Buy makes it so easy to shop
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.53
What you need to know - Rakuten Kobo is bringing its e-readers to stores for the first time, and it's doing so with 500 Best Buy shops across the U.S. - Consumers can shop the Kobo Clara Colour, Clara BW, Libra Colour, Kobo Stylus 2, and Kobo Remote. - Online availability for these Rakuten Kobo products remains on kobo.com, Staples, Target, and more. If you've ever wanted to physically shop Rakuten Kobo products, you're getting your wish. Today (Aug 27), Rakuten unveiled its newest partnership with a major retailer across the U.S. A press release states Rakuten Kobo e-reader products are heading to 500 Best Buy stores across the U.S. This will be the first time that consumers can shop in stores for Rakuten Kobo products. Previously, as the company highlights in its post, consumers could only shop online for these e-readers. To complement the retailer expansion, Rakuten Kobo's CEO, Michael Tamblyn, said, "Many readers want to be able to pick up a device, see the screen, and feel it in their hands before they commit. With Kobo eReaders now available at Best Buy, more American customers can do just that." Coming to Best Buy stores will be the Rakuten Kobo Clara Colour and Kobo Clara BW. Both devices are "compact and waterproof." What's more, consumers can shop the expansive Kobo Libra Colour. Rounding out Rakuten Kobo's retail expansion are the Kobo Stylus 2 and the Kobo Remote accessories. While it's nice to actually see and envision how these tablets would look in your hands in a cozy chair, Rakuten Kobo says there's more to experience. After purchasing, the post states each e-reader provides access to the Kobo Store and Kobo Plus. The former lets you shop for new books to read, while the latter is a subscription service. Kobo Plus offers a selection of packages with "support for a wide range of eBook formats, and an industry-leading experience for borrowing eBooks directly from local public libraries with Libby and OverDrive." More e-readers hit Best Buy I think I'll always enjoy reading a physical book the most, but e-readers have continued to grab my attention. The idea of buying a book and not having to wait for it to ship or get delivered is nice. I can hop right in, cozy up in a comfortable place, and enjoy myself. Rakuten Kobo understands that sometimes, you need to see (and feel) the device you're interested in. It helps takes the guesswork out an important purchase. We covered Rakuten Kobo's launch of the Libra Colour and Clara Colour. These tablets feature E Ink's Kaledio 3 module screens with stronger processing and improved battery capacities. The Libra Colour, which is what consumers can find in-store at Best Buy, features a 7-inch display, 32GB of storage, and full support for the Kobo Stylus 2. Another highlight of the Libra Colour is its ergonomic design. Rakuten Kobo worked on its form factor with comfort in mind for longer reading sessions. If you enjoy reading a physical book, the Libra Colour might give you those same vibes—it's just digital. item.title: The PocketBook Q wants to be the e-reader you carry everywhere
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.40
What you need to know - PocketBook is ditching its classic wider designs for a tall, 5.84-inch e-reader that fits in your pocket. - The PocketBook Q features a 5.84-inch E Ink Carta 1300 display with 788 × 1576 resolution and 300 DPI, packed into a 154 × 75.8 × 6.5mm body weighing just 130g. - It has physical page-turn buttons that pair with a Linux-based OS that skips notifications, feeds, and scrolling-focused apps. PocketBook is stepping away from the classic, wider reader designs that we typically see across its lineup. The Swiss brand is announcing the PocketBook Q, a small device that ditches traditional ebook proportions for a tall, phone-like shape. The PocketBook Q is set to debut at IFA 2026 in Berlin, shrinking everything down to a 5.84-inch E Ink Carta 1300 screen — that's 788 × 1576 resolution at a crisp 300 DPI — packed into a body measuring 154mm x 75.8mm x 6.5mm and weighing just 130g. For reference, that's lighter than the 131g PocketBook Mini of 2013 and thinner than just about any e-reader the company ever made. Inside is a RockChip RK3566 processor, 1GB of RAM, 32GB of internal storage, and a 1550mAh battery that PocketBook says will see you through well over a month of reading. The storage, in particular, is double what is on offer in the PocketBook Era, giving the tiny reader plenty of space for e-books, comics, and audio without making the device any bigger. So why the phone format? The company is actually pushing the one-handed use. There are actual page-turn buttons on the side, so it feels more like flipping a page than swiping a screen. The Linux-based OS is simple: no notifications, no feeds, and no apps to keep you scrolling. There are only books, audiobooks, and a text-to-speech feature that reads any text file aloud using natural-sounding voices. PocketBook says the e-reader’s adaptive SMARTlight adjusts brightness and color temperature throughout the day. The Q supports 25 ebook formats natively — EPUB, PDF, MOBI, AZW, CBR, you name it — and Adobe DRM and LCP for library borrowing via the pre-installed PocketBook x Libby app. It features dual-band Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.0 for headphones, and USB-C with OTG support. It has an IPX4 water resistance, so it’ll survive a splash, though you probably shouldn't take it swimming. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Do people want an e-reader in the shape of a phone? PocketBook is betting the answer is yes — enough to price it at €175/$235 and release it this fall. Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. item.title: First of its kind: a flagship Samsung phone topped Android in Q2 2026, Apple still leads overall
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.30
What you need to know - Counterpoint Research published its report concerning the top 10 best-selling phones globally for Q2, and the Galaxy S26 Ultra surprised the results. - The Galaxy S26 Ultra, a premium phone, topped the charts for Android, marking the first time such a device has done so. - While Samsung and Apple dominated the top 10 in Q2 2026, Apple's iPhone 17 was number one. Research data is taking a look back at individual phone performance for Q2 2026. The discovery? A premium phone topped Android's charts for the very first time. This week, Counterpoint Research published its research into the global best-selling phones for Q2 2026, and one device was a surprise (via 9to5Google). The Galaxy S26 Ultra turned heads this past quarter, as the device claimed the top spot in the best-selling Android phone sector. Counterpoint cites its senior analyst, Harshit Rastogi, who said the S26 Ultra's performance "marks the first time an ultra-premium Android device has led Android sales in a June quarter." Rastogi highlighted the Ultra phone's Q2 performance over Q1 2026. Considering Samsung's first Galaxy Unpacked this year, sales "shifted more into Q2." What's more, research shows that the S26 Ultra not only outperformed the S25 Ultra, but it also accounted for "more than half of the series' sales" this year. While this is a first for Android, Samsung isn't at the top of the global best-selling phone list in Q2. That belongs to Apple's iPhone 17. The iPhone 17 Pro Max followed up in second, then it's the 17 Pro. The Galaxy S26 Ultra sits in fourth place, with the more expected Android leader, the Galaxy A07 (a mid-range phone), in fifth. Compared to this time last year, Apple and Samsung dominate the top 10 best-selling phones. In Q2 2025, Xiaomi snuck into the eighth spot, but not this time. Counterpoint adds that Apple and Samsung total 26% of the global smartphone sales, a 2% increase YoY. A downward trend The Galaxy S26 Ultra really caught people's attention. The Privacy Display is its standout feature. What's even more surprising is that the S26 Ultra beat Samsung's Galaxy AI series phones. These mid-range phones are usually the ones sitting the highest for Android (right under Apple). Think about it: these phones are cheaper. Compared to an S Ultra, the Galaxy A series is anywhere from $200 to $500. Much cheaper. Samsung and Apple's positive Q2 2026 was highlighted in another research report published by Omdia in July. It noted a 2% and 4% increase, respectively, for the companies. Omdia reported that the global smartphone market dipped 4% in Q2, placing the blame on the memory crisis. The current outlook on the smartphone market isn't a pleasant one. According to Omdia's projections, the market may continue to drop into Q3, then Q4. This would be significant, considering the holiday season is when the market tends to rise. In its report, Runar Bjorhovde, principal analyst at Omdia, said the "sharpest volume decline" is expected in the two upcoming quarters. "Contrained memory chip" supply and the issues that accompany it could sour a time when there are multiple device launches, festivities, and sales. item.title: 2nm chips who? Reports say TSMC is racing toward 1.6nm production in Q4
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.17
What you need to know - Overseas reports claim TSMC has developed a new 1.6nm process intended for a new A16 chip. - At present, this chip isn't designed for phones, but rather for AI and "high-performance computing" devices. - TSMC could begin mass production of this chip in Q4 2026, which could help bring the 1.4nm process into reality for mobile devices. There are reports from overseas sources that claim TSMC is taking significant steps toward a 1.6nm chip. This report, highlighted by Chosun Biz, claims the Liberty Times' sources suggest TSMC has "completed" its development for a 1.6nm chip (via Android Headlines). Apparently, this 1.6nm process is intended to work with the company's new A16 chips. It's been stated that TSMC increased the A16's chip density by ~8% (or higher). Moreover, its performance could be ~10% better than its 2nm process and ~15% more power-efficient. While this new A16 chip running on the 1.6nm process switches how it manages its power (for efficiency and performance), the report claims TSMC isn't targeting the usual crowd. The publication purports that TSMC's A16 chips are designed for AI and "high-performance computing" devices as its "main market." With that, it looks like we shouldn't expect this 1.6nm process in a phone chip anytime soon. Which, if you consider the timing, would put us in 2027. Mass production of these A16 chips could begin in Q4 2026. However, TSMC is supposedly using what it's done with its A16 chips and the 1.6nm process to develop a 1.4nm process. This version is suspected to make its way into phones. Chips are getting better, stronger, faster It's almost that time of the year when Qualcomm's next chip comes out. Hearing about 1.6nm is funny (even 1.4nm) since we're just on the edge of 2nm with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6. Expectations say this chip should feature TSMC's 2nm process. What's more, the SD 8 Elite Gen 6 could feature a 2+3+3 CPU structure. Another 2nm process chip we're expecting is MediaTek's Dimensity 9600. That should also debut soon, as we push into the final four months. Rumors aside, Qualcomm started teasing its next Snapdragon chips for its Summit 2026 event in Maui, Hawaii. We've heard rumors about Qualcomm making two flagship chips, and the company says we can expect "Dual 8 Elites" this year. It hasn't said what the other chip will be called; however, earlier reports said it would be the "Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 Pro." item.title: Qualcomm just broke the 5GHz barrier with its next Snapdragon chip
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.06
What you need to know - Qualcomm's next-generation Oryon CPU will reach clock speeds of up to a whopping 5GHz. - The new Oryon CPU uses a fully custom design, giving Qualcomm greater control over performance and efficiency. - Qualcomm's new FlexCache lets CPU cores dynamically share cache, helping improve gaming and multitasking performance. - Qualcomm is expected to unveil two new Snapdragon 8 Elite chipsets at its Snapdragon Summit in September. Ahead of the Snapdragon Summit next month, Qualcomm has shared more details about its next-generation Oryon CPU, sharing that it will be capable of reaching a whopping 5GHz clock speed. Smartphone chipsets have become ridiculously powerful over the past few years. Apple continues to push its A-series chips forward, while Qualcomm's Snapdragon flagships have steadily brought desktop-level performance to Android phones. Of course, we can't say the same about everyone (looking at you, Tensor G6). Now, Qualcomm looks ready to push things even further with its next-generation Oryon CPU. Qualcomm hasn't revealed its full next-generation Snapdragon platform just yet, but says the new Oryon CPU uses a fully custom design, with the company controlling everything from the microarchitecture to the entire CPU subsystem. According to Qualcomm, that level of control is one of the reasons it can push clock speeds all the way up to 5GHz. But Qualcomm says higher clock speeds aren't the only reason for the performance gains. The company is also focusing heavily on IPC (instructions per clock), which determines how much work the CPU can complete per clock cycle. Improvements here should translate into better performance across everyday tasks, from opening apps and browsing the web to more demanding workloads. Qualcomm has also introduced Oryon FlexCache, a new cache architecture that allows different CPU cores to access the same dynamically allocated cache pool. Instead of assigning a fixed amount of cache to individual cores, FlexCache allows the Prime cores to access the entire available pool whenever a workload needs it. The company says this should particularly help with workloads that constantly move between different CPU cores. In gaming, for example, better access to local cache could help stabilize frame rates and reduce stutters, while the same architecture should also help with heavier multitasking. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Qualcomm still hasn't revealed the complete details of its next Snapdragon flagship platform. The company has already teased that we'll see two Snapdragon 8 Elite chips at Snapdragon Summit 2026, though, so we should learn much more about both chipsets soon. Snapdragon Summit 2026 is scheduled to take place from September 22 through September 24 in Hawaii. Sanuj is a tech writer who loves exploring smartphones, tablets, and wearables. He began his journey with a Nokia Lumia and later dived deep into Android and iPhone. He's been writing about tech since 2018, with bylines at Pocketnow, Android Police, Pocket-Lint, and MakeUseOf. When he's not testing gadgets, he's either sipping chai, watching football, or playing cricket. item.title: The 'excellent' Garmin Venu 3 just crashed to a record low price — but is the 2023 smartwatch still worth it?
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.34
TL;DR: Amazon is slashing 34% off the Garmin Venu 3 (45mm), knocking the popular fitness watch down to its lowest price ever recorded. Garmin has been producing industry-leading fitness smartwatches for years, but major discounts on the wearables can be difficult to find outside of major sale events. This is particularly true if you're looking at the brand's popular Venu and Forerunner series of watches, which is why I was pleasantly surprised to see Amazon carve a record-smashing 34% off the price of the Garmin Venu 3 this week. This iconic fitness watch once topped our list of the best Garmin watches money can buy, but three years after launch, is the Venu 3 still worth it? It largely depends on what you're looking for in a wearable. Let's break it down. Garmin Venu 3 45mm: $449.99 $294.99 at Amazon Despite its slightly-advanced age, the Garmin Venu 3 still impresses with great battery life, comprehensive health tracking, and a vibrant AMOLED display. Grab the Venu 3 from Amazon today and you'll score 34% off your purchase. That's the biggest discount that the fitness watch has ever received. The Venu 3 is the predecessor to Garmin's Venu 4, which is currently sitting at the top spot in our guide to the best fitness watches of 2026. Shockingly, the last gen model actually surpasses the Venu 4 in a few areas, with better battery life (up to 14 days) and a lighter polymer casing. You also get the same accurate health sensors with both models, stainless steel bezels, and nearly-identical designs. Furthermore, the Garmin Venu 3 boasts a ton of comprehensive health and fitness monitoring features (including ECG), NFC and GLONASS GPS tracking, and a built-in microphone for calls. All good stuff, so what's the catch? Well, if you're accustomed to a newer fitness watch, the Venu 3 can feel a bit lacking in the software department. You get all of the Garmin basics, such as Body Battery, VO2 Max, and 30 pre-installed sports modes, but you miss out on newer additions like Fitness Coach, Health Status, and Sleep Alignment. The Garmin Venu 3 also doesn't have the built-in flashlight or dual-band GPS. That being said, with the current Amazon discount, the Garmin Venu 3 is a whopping $205 cheaper than the Venu 4. If you're a self-guided athlete who doesn't need all of the latest software features, the Venu 3 is a reliable fitness watch at an exceptional price. It'd also make an excellent entry-level watch for someone who's just now getting into tracking their fitness. For folks who want the latest and greatest in fitness-tracking technology, however, you may want to wait. After all, the Garmin Venu 4 is sure to get a hefty discount of its own one of these days, right? item.title: The Fitbit Air just got a seriously cute sleep upgrade
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.16
What you need to know - The Fitbit Air now comes in a Pokémon Sleep Special Edition with a Sleeping Pikachu strap. - The special edition tracker keeps its lightweight design, week-long battery, 50-meter water resistance, optical heart-rate sensor, and skin-temperature monitoring. - Overnight sleep and naps sync automatically with Pokémon Sleep through Health Connect on Android or Apple Health on iOS. - Sleep Score boosts Snorlax’s Strength to create “Drowsy Power,” with higher scores unlocking rarer Pokémon sleep styles. The Fitbit Air made its quiet debut earlier this year as Google's lightest wearable yet, but today it’s getting a colorful makeover that will make it much harder to ignore. Google has announced the Fitbit Air Special Edition Pokémon Sleep that turns your morning grogginess into in-game gains. If you’ve been MIA since the Air landed in early 2026, here’s the TL;DR: It's the screen-free tracker that weighs just 12 grams total. As Derrek Lee put it in his review for Android Central, this thing is forgettable in the best way. You put it on and forget it’s there, which is the whole point if you’re trying to get some quality sleep. The week-long battery is a lovely touch as well. The Pokémon Sleep edition retains all the things that make the Air so good — the 50-meter water resistance, the optical heart rate sensor, and the skin temperature monitoring — but swaps out the strap for one with a sleeping Pikachu. What’s interesting about this slight makeover is what happens when you plug your Fitbit Air into the Pokémon Sleep app. Your overnight sleep and daytime naps are auto-synced through Health Connect on Android or Apple Health on iOS, importing your sleep duration stats straight into the game. When you wake up, Pokémon with sleep types similar to yours gather around Snorlax, and your Sleep Score multiplies Snorlax's Strength to generate "Drowsy Power." The higher that number, the rarer the sleep styles you'll discover. Under the hood is Google Health’s sleep tracking, which now uses machine learning algorithms that are 15% more accurate at picking up sleep stages, naps, and those pesky overnight interruptions. With every purchase, you get a three-month trial to Google Health Premium, which gives you access to the AI-powered Health Coach that analyzes your trends and offers personalized tips. Preorders for the Fitbit Air Special Edition Pokémon Sleep start today at the Google Store and Target, with shipping beginning September 15. It's limited to the U.S. and Japan, so if you’ve been waiting for a reason to finally track your sleep, your Pikachu-themed excuse just arrived. item.title: The Garmin Fenix 9 raises the bar with faster maps and smarter training
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 2.91
What you need to know - The Garmin Fenix 9's AMOLED screen is twice as bright as the Fenix 8, with sapphire glass, leakproof buttons, and 40-meter dive resistance. - The Fenix 9 Pro features Garmin’s first titanium Fenix case, which uses nano-molding to combine metal and plastic, reducing thickness while keeping the watch lightweight. - Navigation is noticeably faster: 50% more RAM and a new map engine make map panning up to 30% faster, while 64GB storage doubles map capacity and holds up to 7,000 songs. Garmin is giving its flagship adventure watch a serious refresh with the Fenix 9 and Fenix 9 Pro, building on the Fenix 8 with brighter displays, faster maps, new training insights, and a more capable phone-free experience. The Fenix 9's AMOLED panel is twice as bright as its predecessor, and Garmin has included a scratch-resistant sapphire lens, leakproof buttons, and 40-meter dive resistance. The bigger technical jump comes from what Garmin changed underneath. The Fenix 9 has 50% more RAM than the Fenix 8 and a new map engine that makes panning up to 30% faster. A new perspective view adds more map detail at different distances, and 64GB of storage gives you double the map capacity and room for up to 7,000 songs. Garmin is also expanding its rucking tools, with support for changing pack weight mid-activity, GORUCK workouts, and targets based on up to 100kg of carried weight. When it comes to training, the new stamina zones and a stamina curve allow you to track how endurance improves with fitness and training history, providing more information on pacing for athletes. With compatible equipment, indoor rowers also get VO2 Max and power-curve insights. And then there’s the Fenix 9 Pro. The watch is the first to feature Garmin’s titanium Fenix case, made using nano-molding technology that combines metal and plastic at the molecular scale. Garmin says the approach keeps the watch lightweight while reducing its overall thickness. On the software side, both watches introduce Garmin Epic to group multi-day workouts into single shareable stories. The Pro’s AMOLED models go up to 3,000 nits, and the 51mm model uses a 1.5-inch display without a bigger case. Selected models also have solar charging like most fan-favorite Garmin watches, a green flashlight mode, and inReach connectivity for calls, messaging, LiveTrack, location sharing, weather updates, and SOS assistance. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android The Fenix 9 starts at $1,000 and the Fenix 9 Pro at $1,100. Both are available in 43mm, 47mm, and 51mm sizes, with battery life up to 29 days for the Fenix 9 and 31 days for the largest AMOLED Pro. Solar versions can last 57 days. What you need to know - RayNeo unveiled three new AR glasses: the iO smart glasses and the GT and GT Max. - The RayNeo iO puts its focus on productivity with a transparent HUD for information, four microphones for transcription, and Android/iOS compatibility. - The RayNeo GT series is more about entertainment, with three viewing modes and Dolby Vision support. - These AR glasses see retail availability begin on September 4; pricing will likely be revealed closer to that date. RayNeo unveiled a handful of new AR smart glasses for consumers early this morning (Aug 21) that aim to lead productivity and entertainment. The company had a lot to discuss this morning, and what kicked things off was the reveal of the RayNeo iO smart glasses. In its press release, RayNeo says the iO is "designed for professionals, executives, and multi-screen operators." For this product, consumers should think of productivity with glanceable "ambient intelligence." To achieve this, the RayNeo iO features a HUD (heads-up display) with 97% optical transparency that will consistently feed the user information. RayNeo says that at 1,300nits of peak brightness, the transparent HUD remains invisible to others, but clear to you. Since the iO is meant to be worn comfortably, RayNeo says the glasses weigh 33 grams. Ambient Intelligence is assisted by RayNeo's Ambient AI Productivity Suite. The RayNeo iO features the Ambient AI Life Log, which "operates in a low-power background tier to capture schedules and conversation contexts." If you were in an important meeting, the iO smart glasses can pick out dates and other details for you. The user can confirm what the glasses have picked out with a head nod to save them. Live Translation and the Auto-Teleprompter might also aid users in meetings and presentations. While the former is self-explanatory, the latter can provide the user with their script and scroll at their speaking pace. Multiple LLMs, such as Google's Gemini, OpenAI's ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek, are available. The RayNeo iO smart glasses take a different approach: they have no speakers. Everything you'd need for the day will appear on that transparent HUD. However, it does include a four-microphone array for transcription. RayNeo adds that this device features a 240mAh battery that can last up to two days with "typical use." Hardware-wise, the iO features a Smart Crown rotary dial above the right temple. These glasses will launch with Android and iOS compatibility. Additionally, as we've come to appreciate, the iO will debut with a "hardwired LED status light" that shines when you're recording or transcribing. RayNeo reveals that the iO will debut on September 4 in Polar Night and Dune. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Pricing will likely be revealed closer to this date. RayNeo GT series is pure cinema If we were to flip the script on AR smart glasses, what would we get? RayNeo says we'd get the GT and GT Max smart glasses with a strong focus on entertainment. As a duo, the GT series shares a few important features. According to its press release, the GT series features full Dolby Vision support. With this, and alongside the RayNeo Pocket TV Pro, the GT glasses natively support Dolby Vision with "real-time" AI SDR-to-HDR conversion. The other side of this is the GT series' quad-speaker setup, head-tracked spatial audio, and Whisper Mode directional transmission. Users can watch their favorite shows and movies with the RayNeo GT series, but your sofa might not always be available. To solve this, RayNeo includes three viewing modes: Steady (traveling bumps), Pinned (anchors screen, works with 3D experience), and Follow. The RayNeo GT Max takes its experience a little further. These lenses come with the Peacock Optical Engine 3.0 Max and a 5.5th-gen Tandem MicroOLED display. As a result, RayNeo states the GT Max delivers a 59-degree FOV and gives users the ability to scale their virtual screen between three sizes: 227 inches, 267 inches, and 307 inches. The GT series will join the iO smart glasses on September 4 for a retail release. Samsung's placed more focus on its in-house chip brand, Exynos, over the past couple of years. A rumor surfaced online this week, claiming the next chip could top Qualcomm's flagships. What's incredibly interesting is what these tests have allegedly shown regarding GPU performance. In a test, Samsung's SoC outperformed Qualcomm by 5% in a peak performance scenario. What's more, the Exynos 2700 also recorded "24% higher performance" over the 8 Elite Gen 6 and "22% higher" than the (rumored) 8 Elite Gen 6 Pro. In a multi-core CPU performance test, the Exynos 2700's scores were roughly 9% better than the Gen 6 Pro. AI, especially Galaxy AI, has been a focal point for Samsung in developing its next-gen phones. The company reportedly tested Qualcomm's chips and its in-house brand for AI performance and prompt understanding. In another test, Exynos 2700 generated responses and understood prompts faster than Qualcomm's chips. If this report is accurate, Samsung's chips could be in a better position compared to recent years. A brighter future for Exynos? In a bit of house cleaning, it's worth mentioning that Samsung created a "task force" to spearhead its Exynos chip creation. Samsung got serious about its in-house chip in 2025 in an "urgent" push for the Exynos 2600. What we received was an Exynos 2600 that was a major step in the right direction for Samsung. Exynos chips haven't always been the greatest, grappling with various performance and overheating issues. It's the latter point that Samsung is reportedly looking to solve with the Exynos 2700. Rumors in March said Exynos 2700 development was progressing with upgraded HPB (Heat Path Block) tech. This upgrade would help phones disperse heat better. Elsewhere, we heard speculation about the chip's performance in April. It was alleged that the chip could sport a 10-core structure with its fastest cores clocking in at ~2.88GHz. A ~12% performance boost could make the difference for the 2700 over the 2600. Android Central's Take Now this is interesting. I want to reserve my thoughts for when the Exynos 2700 gets announced, and we see its performance for real. To think that Samsung's chip could outperform Qualcomm's in graphics is interesting, but I'm going to be skeptical. Would I like for this to be true? Absolutely. Imagine the competition there. Imagine both sides pushing to improve their gaming graphics, pushing to improve CPU performance. Exynos has always been behind the crowd. If it's trying to step up, let it. item.title: Will plug-in solar panels affect your home insurance? An expert explains what you should know before fitting them
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.45
Plug-in solar panels are now legal in the UK, and they could have a real impact on your energy bills, but before you install them, you should know what impact they're likely to have on your home insurance. The panels themselves are very easy to fit (see our complete guide to plug-in solar for more details), but it's worth taking the time to research all the effects on your home before buying your own. To find out more, I spoke to Nathan Blackler, home insurance and utilities expert at Go.Compare. He explained that plug-in solar is new technology that insurers don't really have enough claims data on to price against, but says his main advice is to disclose any products and installations to your insurer, and check the policy documents to ensure there are no exclusions for your planned setup. Will your insurance premium rise? Blackler says that you might see a slight rise in your insurance premium after fitting plug-in solar panels, but it isn't guaranteed. "Because plug-in solar panels add to the total value of your property’s assets, your coverage limits may need to be adjusted," he says. "However, some insurers may simply note the addition of the system on your file without charging you extra. "The most important thing is keeping the insurer informed and ensuring there's nothing in your policy docs with your existing insurer excluding the use or installation of such systems." Will your plug-in solar panels be covered? Plug-in solar panels are a big investment (you can expect them to pay for themselves in three to five years), so you'll want to be sure that they're covered by your insurance. "Yes, they are generally covered, but typically under your contents insurance rather than buildings insurance, as they are classified as portable equipment rather than permanent fixtures," says Blackler. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. "However, coverage is strictly dependent on disclosure. Because plug-in panels feed energy directly into your home's electrical circuit, you are fundamentally adding a mini power station to your property. If you fail to tell your insurer about the installation and later suffer an electrical fire or fault, your policy could be invalidated." How do they differ from traditional roof-mounted panels? According to Blackler, from an insurer's perspective, the risk profiles for conventional roof-mounted solar panels and plug-in panels are completely different. "Traditional roof-mounted solar panels are permanent structural fixtures (covered under buildings insurance) that require installation and sign-off by MCS-accredited electricians," he says. "These setups can also be complicated with different ownership models like leasing and subscriptions, meaning customers do not own the panels, but they may still create an additional structural risk that some insurers increase premiums for. "Plug-in panels, on the other hand, are self-installed and exempt from mandatory electrician sign-offs. This introduces a new element of 'unmanaged electrical risk', especially in flats and leasehold properties where a poorly connected panel plugged into outdated wiring could push electrical fault and fire risks into communal parts of the building. Because installation quality is harder to verify with plug-and-play systems, insurers view them as a distinct and evolving category. "All this becomes increasingly complex when you also start to consider a battery or power cell installation along with solar panels. This adds a high-value electrical item, and as most home batteries are lithium-ion, they carry a small but significant fire risk. Again, this technology is relatively new to the mass market, and insurers are still gathering the data necessary to effectively price against it." Want to know more about plug-in solar panels and batteries? Find out why plug-in panels are now legal, but plug-in batteries are not — yet. item.title: Want to own a .slop domain? You could soon be in luck, along with .therapy, and .hype
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 4.62
- ICANN's 2026 application round saw over 1,600 new submissions - The last round was in 2012, when the internet was a very different place - 2026's submissions will likely include a lot of AI-related terms, including .slop ICANN, the nonprofit responsible for coordinating the internet's domain name system, is now combing through more than 1,600 applications for new generic top-level domains (gTLDs), following the closure of its latest round. The application round, which closed on August 12 2026, could eventually end up adding hundreds of new internet domains into the mix, spanning everything from novelty terms to AI-related keywords. Naturally, not all 1,600 will be approved, but the ICANN is yet to reveal what they are. According to the organization, the 'Reveal Day' will come no later than nine weeks after the August 12 closing date, subject to administrative checks. ICANN is now reviewing 1,600+ TLD applications That hasn't stopped some applicants from disclosing their submissions early. Link Freedom Group, one of the applications involved in the round, says it applied for 316 different TLDs including .slop, .token, .agentic and .agi. Other terms coined by various applicants include .hype, .therapy, .tea and .itiswhatitis. These latest TLD applications mark a major shift from the internet's early days, when simple .com, .org and .net domains dominated the web. 2012 marked a major shift, though, with around 1,200 TLDs being approved from the pool of 1,900, including corporate domains (.microsoft), geographic domains (.africa), sector domains (.bank) and more. Importantly, these rounds don't come around every day. In fact, 2012 was the last time applicants were invited to submit requests, so this year's round is a big deal against a backdrop of major AI investments. But they don't come cheaply, with ICANN charging an evaluation fee of $227,000 per application (or more for risky or complicated ones). ICANN also noted that, despite offering a 15-week application round, most submissions were actually sent in the final days. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! Besides adding new TLDs for the open internet, ICANN also announced in early 2024 that it wanted to introduce a new .internal domain to replace 192.168.x.x domains for enterprises and device vendors. That domain is now available for use away from the public internet. As for what comes next following this round, we'll have to wait around two more months to find out what's been submitted, and many more months before they eventually become available. item.title: Forget Disney’s BDX Droid — the $399 Hugging Face Microduck robot is even more adorable and versatile thanks to Lidar, NFC and, yes, roller skates
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 3.49
- Microduck is Pollen Robotics' new programmable robot - It looks like a cute robo-duck, and has some adorable, pre-baked interactions - It's up for pre-order priced at $399, and it should ship in time for Christmas If the measure of a successful robot is cuteness, Microduck could be the most successful bot in ages. Unveiled this week by Pollen Robotics (a division of AI company Hugging Face — yes, that Hugging Face), Microduck is a 25-centimeter-tall educational robot that appears to arrive with surprising mobility, balance, and personality. Pre-orders, which kicked off today (August 27) promise a $399 (that's the introductory price), roughly 1.7lb pre-built duck-like robot complete with a mouth that doubles as a gripper, a voice —duck calls, it seems — 15 degrees of freedom (basically a measure of the number of ways all the motors let it move), and motors that let it walk, waddle, move its head and, thanks to a pair of IMUs (inertial movement unit), stay upright even when pushed around. There's a single-eye camera paired with a Lidar system for navigating its environment and, perhaps, recognizing its owner. Pollen Robotics has yet to specify the camera's megapixels. There are also speakers for voice, and microphones for it to hear. The robot runs on a relatively low-power Rockchip RK3566 ARM chip that's backed by 1GB of RAM and 32GB of on-board storage. There's on-board Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, and a smallish 2,600mAh battery that promises roughly one hour of operation. These are not killer specs, but the teaser videos show a highly engaged and undeniably adorable little bot. I was particularly taken with how it can recover and stand back up after a fall (or being pushed over). Microduck will arrive with a lot of pre-programmed interactions, but much of the cuteness may come via its open-source platform and your programming skills. The Microduck kit will ship with an SDK that includes virtual training environments, along with training scripts and tools, and "a tested sim-to-real workflow." The idea, obviously, is that while you might grow to love Microducks' baked-in personality, it's what you can build with your kids that will really matter. This is an educational robot, after all. It's almost familiar It's also worth mentioning Microduck's obvious resemblance to another extremely cute, though entirely unattainable robot: Disney's and Star Wars' BDX Droid. Both robots are bipedal with a somewhat squat posture and cute, oversized heads, and as with the BDX-Droid, it's hard to believe the Microsoduck can stay upright. But that's where the similarities end. That semi-autonomous/remote-controlled BDX Droid is much larger, probably far more expensive, and is currently only wandering around Disney World. Plus, there are currently no plans to bring it to consumers. The $399 Microduck is just the base package, and Pollen Robotics also plans to ship an optional charger pack for $39, a dev pack that includes spare motors, cables, and batteries for $119, and an accessory pack that includes a laser pointer (perhaps for Microduck to chase), roller skates(!) that Microduck can wear and ride, and 10 NFC tags. One wonders if those tags might be used to trigger certain Microduck actions. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. Microduck is Pollen Robotics' second edu-robot, the first being the Reach Mini, an almost equally cute but more or less stationary desk companion robot. Pollen Robotics claims it sold 10,000 units. Microduck's success will likely depend on just how many of those endearing qualities are on display out of the box, and how much we have to code ourselves. Initially, you can fake some of it, since Microduck can be remote-controlled with a gaming controller; but the real fun happens when it starts to respond in unexpected ways. The other X factor is how many people are willing to pay almost $400 for a plastic and semi-autonomous robot duck. I know I'm intrigued, and wouldn't mind trying to program it to create the duck-bot of my dreams. Microduck is expected to ship by Christmas, and is available in Cream, Graphite. Lavender, and Sky.
