Search and rescue personnel saved two brothers on the morning of August 25 after they became lost in Wyoming’s Thorofare Valley, one of the most remote wilderness areas in the Lower 48. The two men, both in their 30s, stumbled into a wilderness camp, disoriented and low on food, a Teton County Search and Rescue (TCSAR) spokesperson told Outside. Authorities have not released the name of the men, but did say neither was injured. “They were kind of disheveled and dehydrated,” Anthony Stevens, TCSAR chief adviser, said. “They were obviously scared by this encounter. And I think they were really worried about the fact they didn’t have any food.” The Thorofare Valley is considered the furthest point from any road in the contiguous United States. Given their remote location, the two men were lucky to find help. “I think the closest road is 20 miles as the crow flies,” Stevens said. The valley sits about three miles from Yellowstone National Park‘s southern border, and roughly 20 miles east of Grand Teton National Park. The two men walked into the remote Hawk’s Rest Wilderness Camp in Teton Wilderness, located in Wyoming’s Bridger-Teton National Forest. Personnel at the camp contacted TCSAR, the group wrote in a statement. The hikers said they came into contact with a bear, though Stevens says it’s unclear whether the bear attacked. During their encounter, the men deployed one of their two cans of bear spray, and one tore his rain pants, though Stevens said it was unclear what caused the tears. Neither man showed signs of bear-related injuries, he added. Camp staff gave the men food and water and directed them to a nearby ranger cabin to wait for rescuers. Rescuers initially feared “a full-blown bear mauling,” Stevens said. But once TCSAR determined the men were safe and not in immediate danger, it opted to wait until the following day to send a helicopter to avoid flying into remote terrain at night. Responders flew the men to the TCSAR headquarters in Wyoming. Neither required additional medical attention. The encounter is one of a few in a series of bear-related incidents around the region this summer, including an August 10 black bear incident near Teton Pass and a May grizzly encounter near Old Faithful in Yellowstone National Park that left two men in serious condition.

item.title: A Hiker Tried to Free Solo a Cliff in Georgia While Wearing Sneakers. Rescuers Saved Him.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.31
A screengrab from the drone footage of a rescue on Mount Yonah (Photo: White County Public Safety) Outside features editor Frederick Dreier called rescuers in Georgia who recently saved a hiker on Mount Yonah. Will Roper of the local fire department talked us through the mission to bring the hiker down alive. A hiker in Georgia is lucky to be alive after he attempted to scramble up a well-known climbing route with little more than sneakers, a backpack, and his cell phone. On Tuesday, August 25, rescuers from the White County Public Safety (WCPS) division received an SOS call at 7 P.M. According to a WCPS Facebook post, a hiker was stranded on the side of Mount Yonah, a 3,166-foot granite dome located 90 miles northeast of Atlanta. Crews arrived on the scene and then flew a rescue drone up the mountain to locate the stricken hiker, whose name has not been released. They saw him approximately 260 feet up the mountain’s face on a steep slab of granite. He was standing on a 20-inch by 20-inch ledge and was unable to ascend or downclimb, the report said. “He was about 40 or 50 feet below the top of the mountain,” Will Roper, a firefighter and EMT who participated in the rescue, told Outside. “The rock face isn’t totally vertical, but there are spots that have some bigger hand holds that are almost vertical. It’s a really exposed face, and there are points at which there’s not a whole lot to grab onto.” Overhead video shows the hiker clinging to the side of the cliff, his low-top running shoes angled into the ledge to prevent him from falling. Mount Yonah rises 1,500 vertical feet from the northeastern corner of Cleveland, Georgia, and is a popular destination for local hikers and rock climbers. The eastern flank of the mountain is gradual and wooded, and it’s western face is a 300-foot wall of exposed granite. Mount Yonah’s granite face is the training site for the U.S. Army Rangers, which operates courses in rappelling and mountaineering on the peak’s steep granite face. Mountain Project, a website that catalogs rock climbing areas, lists 246 different routes, including 49 on the main face. Roper said that the top of the crag has numerous bolts and anchors that rock climbers use to ascend sport routes. Roper said hikers do occasionally ascend the peak’s rock face via a technical scramble, but reaching the top by foot requires detailed knowledge of the route, as well as proper gear. “You need to get beta from people or have a guidebook to know where you’re going,” he said. “A lot of people think Mount Yonah is an easy hike. We pluck people off of it all the time.” At the top of the peak, Roper and his team fixed webbing and ropes to natural anchors, and he then climbed into a safety harness. He rappelled down to the hiker just as the sun was dipping below the horizon. “He was very apologetic when I reached him,” Roper said. “He said he’d gotten on the wrong line and just got over his head. I appreciated his attitude.” Roper affixed a harness to the hiker, and then the two of them rappelled down 250 vertical feet to the nearest flat terrain. “He was really easy to coach back down once I got the harness on him,” Roper added. The hiker told Roper that he planned to follow the scrambling route up the peak, but lost his way and quickly found himself unable to ascend or descend. Rather than chance it, he decided to call for rescue. Roper praised the man’s decision to call for help. “It was a series of unfortunate decisions that got him into that hairy predicament,” Roper said. “I’m glad he decided to swallow his pride and give us a call. Had he attempted to downclimb or push to the top, there was a low probability of him getting out of the situation without a catastrophic injury, or worse.” The hiker, Roper said, was not properly equipped for such a strenuous climb, because he was wearing sneaker and he carried a massive and heavy backpack. “Most people I see on Yonah are in boots,” Roper said. “He seemed to be the least equipped of anyone I’ve seen.” Roper frequently climbs and trains at Mount Yonah, and said that when he sees hikers scrambling the rock face, they usually have helmets, day packs, and either hard-soled hiking boots or approach shoes. That’s because one wrong move, Roper said, can quickly lead a hiker into terrain that’s suited for rock climbers.

item.title: Rachel Entrekin Is Pushing the Limits of Human Endurance. She Also Pets Every Dog She Sees.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.86
Entrekin at the 2026 Cocodona 250 (Photo: Scott Rokis) This story contains mentions of disordered eating and suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide or self-harm, call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline toll-free from anywhere in the U.S. at 1-800-273-8255. Rachel Entrekin sat in a chair under a white Precision Fuel and Hydration-branded tent that was speckled with graphics of running gels, electrolytes, and water bottles. A giant tapestry of a ballroom that looked onto a desert with mesas and cacti at sunset adorned the back wall of the tent. Just outside, an inflatable red and green baby pool filled with pink flamingos and watermelon pool toys served as a cooling station for exhausted runners. Sunscreen was streaked across Rachel’s face as she hurriedly slurped noodles from a paper bowl. Her blonde hair was pulled back into a bun and big white sunglasses covered her eyes. Half a dozen team members worked on and around her. One rubbed her calves and thighs, another put ice in a white bandana and tied it around her neck, and a third got her hydration pack ready for the next section of the course. They all wore matching white button-up party shirts that Rachel helped design, with cacti, crowns, keyboards, and talk bubbles that read “Can I pet your dog?” A swarm of people hovered around the tent in a half circle with cameras and iPhones, clamoring to get a glimpse of the phenom. Seemingly unfazed, Rachel looked into the crowd, “Oh hey, there’s my parents!” The whole scene could have been mistaken for a bizarre pop-up carnival, but this was mile 159.6 of the Cocodona 250, at the Sedona Posse Grounds Aid Station. It was noon in early May, the second day of the 253-mile footrace from Black Canyon City to Flagstaff, Arizona. Rachel had run almost 160 miles and been on her feet for nearly 31 hours. She was leading the race overall. The next-quickest runner was a man, Kilian Korth, who won three 200-milers last year, setting the record for the Triple Crowns of 200s. He was about 30 minutes behind. Other than a slight grimace when a sore spot was rubbed on her leg, Rachel looked completely composed and not at all daunted by the 94 miles that still lay ahead. That’s why I was surprised when Addie Bracy, a professional ultrarunner who had paced Rachel for the last 35 miles, told me she was at a low. Everything hurt and Rachel was beating herself up for slowing down. Of course, slowing down is relative. The 35-year-old had held a head-spinning 10:46-per-mile pace across rocky mountain terrain, with tens of thousands of feet of elevation gain for the first 100 miles of the race. She was now running at a little over 13 minutes per mile. Addie told Rachel that it was OK to feel bad but that it wasn’t going to help. They needed to keep moving and make a plan for the next aid station. It was advice that had become a motto for Rachel: “bad times don’t last.” She needed to eat, drink, take an Advil and would surely feel better in 20 minutes. After a five-minute rest and refuel, she took off to a roar of applause with another pace runner and disappeared down a singletrack trail into the red rock canyons. If Rachel could hold on, she was on track to shatter the overall course record and become the first woman to ever win the race outright. I’d come to Cocodona to conduct research for a book I was writing on the evolution of female ultrarunners and was following another competitor, Megan Eckert. She’s best known for running 603 miles in six days and completing 383 miles at Big’s Backyard Ultra, a race of attrition where participants run around a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour, until there is one person left standing. I expected that Cocodona would have a competitive women’s field with Megan, ultra-running legend Courtney Dauwalter, 200-mile connoisseur Mika Thewes, and Heather Jackson, an Ironman champion and long-distance gravel bike racer turned ultra-runner. But I knew little about Rachel. I saw her for the first time the day before the race at runner check-in. It was sweltering. I’d squeezed under a tent overhang to find shade for myself and my two young sons who I brought on the reporting trip with me. Rachel, who had been mingling in the crowd, bounded onto the stage. She dropped onto the couch, kicked her tanned legs up on the coffee table, waved a red foam #1 finger, and with her hair in a waist-length side braid, beamed a megawatt smile. “This race is my Christmas,” she grinned. “I’m having the best day!” If it’s her Christmas, she’s certainly been the hardworking elf. There are athletes who spend more than a decade in the sport before anyone knows their name, an interviewer on the stage remarked. Rachel is one of them. “My life is a dream, dude. I get to be outside and get paid for it.” In 2013, at 21, she started running ultramarathons. By 2017, she had placed first overall at the Plain 100K in Washington State. Over the next five years, she took more than 20 first-place finishes on terrain that varied from technical 100-mile mountain races to 48-hour runs on flat dirt loops to fast 50Ks and setting Fastest-Known-Times (FKTs). From July 2022 to March 2026, she was undefeated in every race she ran. That streak came to an end when Courtney Dauwalter and Yngvild Kaspersen of Norway finished just minutes ahead of her at the Chianti 120K in Italy. Despite her success, Rachel got little traction from sponsors and scrambled to scrape together the gear and financial support she needed for her races. When she placed first for women at Cocodona in 2024 and set a women’s course record, she didn’t have a watch, wore gas station sunglasses, and sported a duct-taped hydration pack. With no nutrition plan, she spent much of the race throwing up. “Basically, all my shit was broken,” she joked in a phone interview. That did not stop the five-foot-three powerhouse from relentlessly pursuing the races she thought were “cool,” even when it meant defending her victories to would-be sponsors. For years, potential sponsors pushed Rachel to run more high-profile races like Western States 100 and Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB). They did not think the lesser-known local races and 200-mile-plus ultras like Cocodona that she chose to run were competitive enough or would garner the media attention they desired. But Rachel stuck to the races she loved, telling sponsors that even if it did not land her a professional contract, “a good run is a good run.” “Don’t let other people tell you what you should be interested in,” Rachel told me in an interview the day after she finished Cocodona this year. “Worst-case scenario, you get to spend your life doing things that you enjoy. Best-case scenario, other people start to enjoy those things too.” The next year, at the 2025 Cocodona, she finally got the break she had been working toward. With the help of Precision Fuel and Hydration, a UK-based sports nutrition company, Rachel was given her own nutrition coach, Emily Arrell. For the first time, Rachel had the expertise she needed to dial in her calorie intake. She dropped her course record from 73:31:25 to 63:50:55, placing first for women and fourth overall. The company signed her on as an athlete and more sponsorship followed. With that came an arsenal of gear, including her first running watch, and media attention. She quit her job as a physical therapist, where she often worked 50-hour weeks and had to squeeze her runs in at 4 A.M., and started running full-time. Her weekly mileage soared from about 70 miles to back-to-back weeks of 120 miles or more. Coming into the 2026 race, Rachel, who was nicknamed “The Queen of Cocodona” after her prior wins, said she had been able to offload her usual logistics and planning because she had a “literal drill sergeant” as her crew chief, a lineup of professional ultrarunners to pace her, and Emily, her nutritionist, telling her what to eat and drink along the way. The opportunity was not lost on her. “My life is a dream, dude,” exclaimed Rachel from the stage. “I get to be outside and get paid for it.” At mile 75.7, the buzz around Whiskey Row, a lively historic block in downtown Prescott, was electric. It was early evening and Rachel had taken the lead at mile 61. People murmured that with 177 miles to go it was still far too early to know who the winner would be—and yet the excitement was palpable. Spectators who were out for a drink, crew members, and media gathered several people deep in front of the 19th-century saloons and bars with glowing neon signs. Rachel zoomed past with remarkable efficiency. Overwhelmed by the size of the crowd, Maggie Guterl, who placed first for women in the inaugural Cocodona in 2021, and I moved to the grassy, tree-lined plaza next to the courthouse to wait for Courtney Dauwalter. She and Heather Jackson were in second and third place, about an hour behind Rachel. Five years ago, Courtney had paced Maggie out of this aid station to a much smaller crowd that, at the time, Maggie sheepishly remarked, felt like being a celebrity at UTMB, the Super Bowl of running races. Now, she said, she wouldn’t even mention her winning time—85:30:38. Rachel had already eclipsed it by nearly a day, and given how fast she was moving, it was likely to fall further. For the last four years, Maggie, 45, has been sidelined by injury, but in 2019 she was the first woman to win Big’s Backyard Ultra outright. She ran 250 miles. At the time, that number seemed impossible. Now, Megan Eckert, who was about three hours behind Rachel at Whiskey Row, planned to run more than 400 miles at Big’s Backyard in October. It’s hard to quantify how much the sport of ultrarunning, particularly women’s ultrarunning, has transformed over the last decade, John Medinger—a former 29-year Western States 100 board trustee—told me. The level of competition has risen so dramatically in the last few years that the fourth- or fifth-ranked female UltraRunning Magazine Ultrarunner of the Year in 2025 would have been first any other year. “It’s like you gaslight yourself into having a good time and eventually you do.” One of the aspects of the competition that has changed, though still controversial, is the extremely long distance of the races. While some people in the running community still argue that multi-day races like Cocodona are more thru-hiking events than actual runs, Rachel’s speed was making that theory feel archaic. She ran the first 100 miles of Cocodona under 18 hours and the next 100 in 23—both commendable times in a 100-mile event. She found her feet in ultrarunning as the 200-mile phenomenon was born. When race director Candice Burt put on the inaugural Tahoe 200 in 2014, it was the first time a single-loop race of that distance had been held in the United States. I was one of the 90 runners who toed the line that year. In many ways, we felt like guinea pigs. Following the race’s success, Candice, who had a cougar tattooed on her leg after she spotted one’s glowing eyes watching her on a solo night run, quickly created more 200-mile races, including the Moab 240. In 2018, I was once again at the Tahoe 200, this time writing about Courtney Dauwalter for the New York Times as she annihilated the course. Jamil Coury, the CEO of Aravaipa Running, one of the most influential companies in American trail running, was also running the race. Three years later, Coury would become the visionary behind the Cocodona 250. In 2026, Cocodona was broadcast on a 24/7 livestream to millions of viewers around the world. When Courtney blasted onto the scene, Rachel had just moved from Alabama to Seattle, Washington, and discovered the kind of big mountain trail running Courtney was dominating. She remembers when Courtney won the Moab 240 outright in 2017, went viral online, appeared on Joe Rogan’s podcast, and became a household name. That’s when she saw what she wanted to be: a professional trail runner. Rachel was born in Birmingham, Alabama. When she was a toddler and in early elementary school, her family moved from Alabama to Texas to South Carolina for her dad’s corporate job. Wherever they were, her mom, Karen, would enroll Rachel and her older brother in the sports programs kids in those areas were participating in—whether it was swimming, gymnastics, or soccer. The summer she turned eight, the family moved to Huntsville, Alabama. There she attended a small, private, Christian school. She thrived socially, played the flute and oboe in the band, taught herself Beatles and Coldplay songs on the piano by ear, and made the cross-country and soccer teams her freshman year. But Rachel, whose best friend went to the much larger public school, felt the private academy was too small and lacked opportunity. In tenth grade, despite her mom’s reservations, she transferred. Though the foreign language and advanced placement opportunities suited her, she did not make the soccer or cross-country teams her sophomore year and struggled to fit in. “I could do a lot of stuff, but I wasn’t the best at anything,” said Rachel, who referred to herself as fat in high school. “I felt the only thing I could do was be the funny one, and I was really good at not eating, so that’s what I did.” By her junior year, Karen, who shares her daughter’s blonde hair, intense blue eyes, and candor—and speaks with a distinct Southern accent unlike her daughter—sensed Rachel’s self-esteem was low. She said most of Rachel’s girlfriends were tall, blonde and super thin, and Rachel, who had a shorter, stouter build, did not have their body type. Then her senior year, she noticed Rachel was losing weight, going to the gym at odd hours, and often skipping meals. Karen took Rachel, then 17, to their primary care doctor, who initially thought she was fine. But two weeks later, when Rachel came back for her blood work follow-up, she had lost eight pounds. It was clear there was a problem. They tried outpatient therapy for anorexia, but it was not enough. In May of 2009, Rachel was down to 82 pounds. Karen, who is a nurse, wondered if her daughter would survive. She remembered sitting on the floor of Rachel’s room and watching her sleep in the middle of the day. “All I could see was her face, and it was pitiful,” she told me. “She was skin and bones, and she looked so old.” Rachel’s health had deteriorated so rapidly that she was experiencing fainting episodes. Her parents took the car keys, and Rachel’s plans to attend the University of Alabama at Birmingham, where she had a full scholarship, were postponed. What Karen did not know until I mentioned it in my Zoom call with her in July was a story Rachel told me in an interview after this year’s Cocodona. At 17, she attempted to take her life by overdosing on over-the-counter pain pills. Fortunately, the pills had expired and were not potent. A few days after graduation, which Rachel still managed to do with honors, the family dropped her off at an inpatient facility in North Carolina. She stayed for several months and, within days of returning home, told her mom she needed to go back. “I didn’t eat, fought with my parents, and used ineffective coping skills,” said Rachel. “I was immediately right back in the same cycle.” The second time she went to the treatment center, Rachel took it more seriously. She wanted to go to college and run. “Even when I was sick, and my head was all messed up, running would make me feel competent,” she told me. “As soon as I got out of rehab, I was like, all right, I still like running and I have got to get to a place where I can do this safely.” That would take years. One of the tools Rachel learned is a behavioral technique called opposite action. If you don’t want to do a thing, that is exactly the thing you should do. Now when she feels the urge to restrict, she knows she needs to eat something. On difficult runs, Rachel often opposite-actions herself into being stoked. “It’s like you gaslight yourself into having a good time and eventually you do,” said Rachel, who is a vegetarian, between mouthfuls of pizza. When Karen learned Rachel was running races in college, she was not supportive. She worried that Rachel had traded one addiction for another and was not mentally stable enough to put herself through that kind of rigor. She also grieved the years she had lost with her daughter. On the rare occasion Rachel was home, she wanted to spend time with her and resented the hours she spent training. “I did at one point use exercise in a very extreme way for a very bad reason, and I know that I gave my parents PTSD,” Rachel told me. “They were really resistant to me running and thought I was still doing it for unhealthy reasons.” But over the last few years, they have evolved. Now, when she goes home and tells her mom she is going for a three-hour run, instead of feeling like she is being guilt-tripped for it, she’s told to have a great time. Karen, who went back to school in her mid-50s to become a therapist, thinks Rachel has evolved, too. She no longer will only eat at “safe restaurants” and does not get defensive when Karen asks her if she is taking care of her health. Karen believes that while the mental aspect of Rachel’s illness may never fully go away, she has done the work and is using the techniques she learned in therapy. “That’s why Rachel’s capacity is so extraordinary,” said Karen, who also shares her daughter’s love for the piano. “I’ve always told people, if you can overcome an addiction or an eating disorder, you’re the toughest person on earth.” She watched Rachel cross the finish line for the first time in 2024 when she won Cocodona. This year, she and her husband were at nearly every aid station. When you listen to Rachel’s reflective interviews, her wise quips during a race, or read her Substack—she writes like she talks—you will notice that she continuously reflects on her races, both her wins and DNFs, and learns from them. When she won Cocodona in 2024, she said she had “dead fish energy” at the finish line and was embarrassed by the way she behaved. She had a hard time getting up the last climb on Mount Elden, got into a negative headspace, and without the knowledge or coping skills to get herself out, stayed there. The next year, her main goal at Cocodona was to have a better attitude at the finish. When she felt herself “hating her life and about to complain about the thing she chose to do,” she had a snack and chose to not let that spiral continue. “I think a lot of the time, people want their lives to be easy, but life isn’t easy,” she said. “You have to practice doing hard things in order to prepare yourself for when hard things come up. That’s what running is for me. Running helps me practice who I want to be when things get tough.” One of the aspects of Rachel’s run in Cocodona I wanted to understand most was what she told herself when she took the lead so early on in the race. Rachel has a doctorate degree, is specialty certified in three disciplines, and kept working more hours as an oncology physical therapist because she was continually promoted. She has won all four of the 200-mile mountain races she’s entered, but despite her success, both professionally and with running, she has always felt that she needed more proof that she was qualified. During Cocodona, when she took the lead early, she had a lot of doubts. That was when she told herself to zoom out. She was the most qualified person running the race and she needed to believe in herself and see what would happen. “I have spent a lot of time thinking about why it can’t be me,” she said. “I would prefer to wonder: ‘Why can’t it be me?’” The next time I saw Rachel after Sedona was the third morning of the race. I had just paced Megan Eckert 16 miles to the Walnut Canyon aid station at mile 227.9. Courtney was solidly in second place, Heather had left the aid station minutes before in third place, and Megan was in fourth about to grind another gear. All three women were on track to break the women’s course record. And at that exact moment, a marathon ahead in Flagstaff, at mile 253, Rachel was crossing the finish line. I watched her on the livestream from a laptop on a table covered with bowls of chips, pickles, and M&M’s as I poured water in my CamelBak. Volunteers embraced and thanked each other for being a part of history. We were not standing with the enormous crowd that had gathered to see Rachel cross the line, but we could feel them. Rachel was the first woman in the race’s history to finish first outright. She set a new overall course record and took almost eight hours off her previous time, finishing in 56:09:48. She also went globally viral, appeared on all the major networks, and further put what was once an obscure sport and an unthinkable distance into the zeitgeist. That evening at the finish line, I talked with Rachel for the first time. Her crew had applied sunscreen to her face throughout the race, but Rachel, who does not wear a hat, had what looked like a permanent suntan. Despite not sleeping for literal days and staying up that night to help Heather Jackson, who collapsed from exhaustion only four miles from the finish, she agreed to an interview the next morning. During the interview, the camerawoman asked her what she would tell her six-year-old self. “There were a couple of times when I tried to take my life,” she said, her voice breaking. “I wouldn’t have had any of this if that had gone according to plan. I’d tell her to just wait. Life is going to get really good.” When I met up with Rachel in Olympic Valley, California, the day before the Western States 100-Mile Endurance Run, in late June, she and John Kelly were trying to have a conversation that kept getting interrupted by people wanting a photo with her. John has finished the infamous Barkley Marathon three times, is known for his FKTs, and was running Western States. He sent Rachel a message on Instagram congratulating her after Cocodona and, to his surprise, she responded. The two had struck up a friendship, and this was the first time they were meeting in person. I found an empty high-end clothing boutique next to a restaurant in the valley and suggested that we do the interview there. John could sit on the couch and talk with Rachel afterward. We were five minutes in when a stocky black dog entered with his owner, and Rachel stopped the interview to pet the pup who obliged by rolling over for a belly rub. One of the first things I noticed about Rachel was the new colorful tattoo that took up the back of her left calf. She told me that as soon as she finished Cocodona, she knew that she wanted to get a tattoo to symbolize the encounter she had had with a Hopi woman on Mount Elden. Rachel had been looking forward to that section of the course because pacers were not allowed. She wanted to see who she could be alone, when things got hard, during the final 26 miles. Halfway up the mountain, there was a Hopi woman standing next to the trail waiting for her. They briefly talked, and the woman gave her cornmeal. “The gesture taught me that you never really do anything by yourself,” said Rachel, still emotional, remembering the interaction. When she got to the top of the mountain, she tossed the rest of the cornmeal for the runners who would traverse the trail after her. The tattoo was the Kachin Mana, the female figure associated with corn, fertility, and sustenance in Hopi tradition. After sleeping a total of 19 minutes, in two and a half days, via three dirt naps on the side of the trail, I thought it was possible the entire interaction was a hallucination. But two weeks later at Hardrock, Rachel talked with the woman again. After our interview, Rachel casually told John the procedure he needed to have done to his leg that had been ailing him for more than a year. Several weeks later, I saw on Facebook that after seeing multiple specialists, having multiple tests, exercises, and therapies, the one Rachel suggested worked. “She’s a very talented runner, but she’s much more than that,” said John, during a phone interview in late July. “Rachel has the mindset to do these enormously complex challenges, where things are absolutely going to go wrong, and she has the resilience to keep going, and the intelligence to figure out the best way around obstacles as they pop up.” He said that Rachel may have added years to his running career and had set the example for how he wants to show up when he has low moments during his Appalachian Trail FKT attempt, which he began this August. During our interview, I asked Rachel how she was recharging in the months since Cocodona, and she quickly replied, “I’m not.” That was on full display at Western States, where she was pacing Addie, her friend and the professional runner who had run alongside her at Cocodona. Rachel and I met again at Michigan Bluff, at the mile 55.7 aid station. She was there with her new boyfriend, Will, who she affectionately hugged. I had brought a cowbell with plans to cheer but was too tired. Rachel took up the mantle and rang that bell for hours. Between swings of the bell, she told me that Will was introverted and kept to himself, which was really nice for her because when she was done being out in the world, she could hang out with him and sit there without talking. Ann Trason, who won Western States 14 times and set 20 world records, was also at Michigan Bluff, sitting with a posse of women who had finished the race almost a half century ago. Now 65, Ann has rheumatoid arthritis and, until this January, when she completed 100 miles with her walker on a looped course, had not been in the public eye in nearly a decade. Thrilled to meet one of her heroes, Rachel chatted with Ann, who wore one of her belt buckles over a unicorn onesie. When Ann entered the sport in the 1980s, monetary sponsorship was extremely rare. Women had only been allowed to compete in the Olympic marathon that decade. The first running gels, which would later become GU Energy Labs, were still being tested in Ann’s neighbor and fellow ultrarunner Laura Vaughan’s father’s kitchen. Topics like mental health that Rachel so vulnerably discussed were even more taboo, especially for women. Ann, who has also struggled with disordered eating, told me that she hoped Rachel knew what had taken her decades to understand. “A race does not make a career, just like a day does not make a life.” Twelve hours later at midnight, Will was still by Rachel’s side at Robie Point, mile 98.9, where there was an all-night street party to cheer runners in. The two of them had been up since 3 A.M. Rachel had run 18 miles with Addie and was going back out to pace another runner to the finish line. I was in my car on my way to the Airbnb when I saw Rachel through my window. She looked so small and young and perhaps even tired, I had the thought, “How could one person possibly have this much energy? Wouldn’t she eventually crash?” It was Tara Dower and Ann who answered that for me. Tara, who finished sixth at Western States, was unsuccessfully trying to untangle her braided hair when I saw her at the finish line the following morning. Jennifer Lichter had broken the course record in her 100-mile debut the night before, and Tara, who is best known for the FKT she set on the Appalachian Trail in 2024, was processing what she had learned. She said that she struggled to mentally stay in the game when things got uncomfortable in a race. Rachel, who would pace her at Hardrock in two weeks, showed her what it meant to be “realistically positive.” “Rachel has the ability to stay positive in a race and keep looking at her progress,” said Tara. She recalled seeing Rachel run ten miles up a mountain, two days before they ran the Mammoth 200 miler last year. “If you’re out there and you love running the way Rachel does, you’re going to find so much more joy than looking for a result.” The first week of August, I talked with Rachel again. She was in France, preparing to run UTMB at the end of the month. Widely considered the Super Bowl of ultrarunning, the race follows a 106-mile loop through France, Italy, and Switzerland. With 32,940 feet of vertical gain, roughly the altitude at which commercial jets fly, the race may be better suited for mountain goats with oxygen masks than humans. Rachel, who does not have a coach and has said she is “not coachable,” was running consecutive eight-hour days and getting little sleep, as usual. It was already 9 P.M. She had an article due for UltraRunning Magazine that night and a photo shoot at 6:30 the next morning, but she was happy. She had figured out the bus system, was using the French she had learned in high school and college, and was familiarizing herself with the terrain and building her confidence. She had already run the entire course and the steepest sections twice. The first time she had run it, she was intimidated by how steep it was and dreaded the first 45 miles. But now she realized that she had built the climbs up in her mind to be much harder than they were. And it appeared she had learned that lesson Ann had offered. She didn’t always have to stick the landing on the first try. “I went to rehab and I faked it, and I had to go back,” she said. “And I went to Cocodona, and I didn’t have a good attitude. And I had to go back. You can have a day that doesn’t give you the result that you want, and that’s OK.” You can follow Rachel live at UTMB with real-time coverage from our sister publication, Trail Runner.

item.title: How SpaceX and Reflect Orbital Satellites Are Erasing the Stars Over National Parks
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.55
Taking in the night sky in Joshua Tree (Photo: Derek Sturman) On a chilly winter evening, deep in Yellowstone National Park, a group of people gathers in a geyser basin. Huddled together for warmth, they look upward, following the line of a green laser pointer as their guide uses it to trace the stars into the shapes of Orion the Hunter and the giant M forming the constellation Cassiopeia. Suddenly, someone spots something moving in the sky: a single, unblinking white light. The crowd gets excited, musing about what the object might be. But for stargazing guide Alexandra Trunnell, these white lights are a familiar and disheartening sight. Too small and steady to be airplanes and too slow to be meteors, they are satellites, including Starlink—thousands of which fly across the sky every night, interrupting the view of the stars. “My guests and I typically see our first satellite within minutes,” says Trunnell, who has been leading observatory tours and stargazing evenings across the country for more than a decade, including as the lead astronomer for Yellowstone Safari Company. “Many first-time stargazers assume that satellites are shooting stars, which breaks my heart because actual shooting stars [meteors] are so spectacular!” she shares. “Shooting stars are brief, brilliant flashes of light that streak across a small portion of sky for just a moment. Satellites, on the other hand, look like drifting stars—single points of light that plod across the entire sky for several minutes.” The growing number of satellites littering our skies is an increasingly serious problem highlighted by astronomers, cultural heritage experts and nature conservationists. In 2018, only a few thousand satellites were orbiting the Earth, mainly used for science and geopolitical reasons, such as weather forecasting and intelligence. But in May 2019, Elon Musk’s company, SpaceX, launched its first set of Starlink satellites, a so-called “megaconstellation” consisting of 60 satellites launched in a string-of-pearls formation. These were the first of 12,000 satellites that had been approved by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). Even back then, it was estimated that, by 2030, there would be more than 100,000 satellites in orbit, the vast majority owned and operated by private firms. That forecast is growing by the day. “When I was first leading stargazing tours over a decade ago, spotting satellites was a fun rarity,” says Trunnell. “I’d point out the International Space Station to my guests whenever possible, and I used to point out the very bright ‘flares’ from the old Iridium satellites. This was especially effective at warning guests about the potential impact of massive satellite constellations. It’s become so much worse in just a few years.” Trunnell explains that in 2019, there were fewer than 3,000 active satellites in orbit; today, that number has increased to more than 15,000. The majority of those are Starlink satellites, which have launched with unprecedented frequency. “Now, we see satellites crossing the sky constantly,” she says. Today, hundreds of private companies are operating satellites in low Earth orbit, the major players being SpaceX (Starlink), Eutelsat (formerly OneWeb) and Amazon’s Project Kuiper. In January 2026, SpaceX took its plans much further and applied for a license to launch one million satellites into orbit that would serve as AI data centers. The natural nighttime environment at parks like Yellowstone and Grand Canyon, which includes very dark skies, is crucial for functioning ecosystems, the food web and human health. Studies have shown that satellite-reflected light disrupts natural behavior patterns of migratory species, including birds, pollinators and sea turtles. Creatures that navigate by the stars use a ‘centre of rotation’ to identify stars around the pole star to find their way north. Studies already show that satellites are increasing the background sky brightness by reflecting sunlight at night. This can cause confusion and disorientation for migratory species. DarkSky International is an organization working to protect and restore our nights. For decades, this conservation work was focused on ground-based light pollution originating from infrastructure in cities and populated areas. But satellites represent an entirely new and far more unpredictable risk, because they are not confined to light-polluted areas or even to U.S. airspace. Satellites orbit the whole planet and frequently fly over otherwise protected places, national parks, heritage areas, Indigenous lands and dark sky preserves. Currently, the only existing legislation on satellites is the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which only governs weapons and very general concepts. This means that private space companies are free to do whatever they want as long as they get FCC clearance to launch from the United States, even if it disrupts the skies over a foreign country, a scientific telescope or a protected natural place. Michael Rymer, DarkSky International’s Dark Sky Communities Program Manager, says that, while the land within the boundaries of a national park is protected from damaging activities, the same is not true of the sky. “I couldn’t just build a gas station in the middle of Grand Canyon National Park,” explains Rymer. “What I could do if I had enough money is release 10,000 satellites that would fly above every national park at any given time of the night. Everything within the terrestrial boundaries of a national park is protected by law, but everything above the terrestrial plane seems to lack that level of protection.” While it’s true that some satellites are important and useful to the public, the mass numbers of satellites being sent up now are owned by private companies and used for commercial purposes, such as providing Internet in the backcountry or, in the case of Musk’s new plans, building AI data centers in low Earth orbit. Another company—Reflect Orbital—has just been granted permission from the FCC to begin testing a plan that would see them launch up to 50,000 new satellites that would be used as flying mirrors to reflect light down to the ground and create “sunlight on demand” for solar farms or urban street lighting at night. DarkSky has issued an open letter to Reflect Orbital and its investors urging them to pause their plans until an environmental impact assessment has been undertaken. According to park ranger Rader Lane, dark skies are a natural resource that allow visitors to experience the night environment in the same way people have for thousands of years. Lane is an interpretive ranger at Grand Canyon National Park, which is a certified International Dark Sky Park with a popular stargazing program. He has noticed a large uptick in the number of satellites over the world wonder in recent years. “As a ‘dark sky ranger’ for the National Park Service, I stand underneath pristine night skies for a living, connecting tens of thousands of visitors per year to the cosmos through constellation talks and telescope viewing. Over the last six years, the number of visible satellites in the sky has grown exponentially,” he says. Satellites are particularly noticeable in photography and telescope and radio images, where they leave streaks of light that mar photographs and ruin the images and radio signals that scientists use to study the cosmos. Bettymaya Foott is an astrophotographer whose work has been featured by National Geographic, Sky & Telescope and the National Park Service. She says the night sky “creates its own beautiful patterns and rhythms of light and dark, bright stars and dim stars, speckled against the dark night sky and the glowing dust lanes of the Milky Way.” She calls satellites “visible scars” that disrupt the natural rhythm that photographers are trying to capture. Alexandra Trunnell has had a similar experience with astrophotography in Yellowstone, but also emphasizes the negative impacts that satellites can have on science. “Ground-based observatories require very precise brightness measurements of various stars in a section of the sky,” says Trunnell. “Satellites affect these measurements, creating additional noise and reducing the precision of our data. It jeopardizes our ability to learn more about our universe.” So, is the future dark or bright for our night skies? Science and conservation organizations like DarkSky International, the International Astronomical Union and the American Astronomical Society continue to raise the alarm over the mass proliferation of satellites and are seeking solutions at the highest level. Regular meetings at the United Nations have brought together its Office of Outer Space Affairs with international astronomical institutions and private satellite companies for talks. However, to date, no international regulations have been implemented. Lane says that, until we begin to see the night sky as an intrinsic part of the wilderness experience, we won’t know what is at stake. “One of the reasons we preserve national parks is to connect with a sense of the sublime. The night sky is one of the foundational pillars of the natural world upon which humanity can achieve this sense of the sublime. Standing underneath the stars humbles us into greater understandings of ourselves, of the divine and of nature itself.”

item.title: The Best National Park for Every Travel Personality
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.05
(Photo: Getty / Canva ) It’s National Park Week, when the country takes a beat to celebrate the landscapes that have helped define this country and our culture. Each day has a theme, from Safety Sunday to Fee Free Tuesday, but the overall vibe for the week is love. Love for the grand views, love for the staff of these parks, love for the adventures that can be had inside these special places. As Outside’s national parks columnist, naturally I revel in any situation that brings attention to the greatest collection of landscapes on the planet. And the celebratory week got me thinking about the vast and diverse nature of the park system. No two parks are the same and there seems to be an ideal destination for every type of traveler out there. So in honor of National Park Week, I’ve decided to be a match maker and introduce the perfect park for specific personality types. Whether you’re an introvert who hates crowds, or a thrill-seeker looking for a rush, I have the perfect park for you. The least visited national park in the system is Alaska’s Kobuk Valley National Park, which saw just 7,700 visitors in 2025. Why? Access. No roads lead into the landscape, so you’ll need to take a propeller plane into the park. And once you’re inside the park, don’t expect to be pampered. There are no facilities whatsoever, so you’re on your own inside the two-million-acre expanse. Be prepared to traverse miles of sand dunes and see more caribou than people, but that’s what you want, right? Because caribou don’t force you to engage in small talk. Bring a packraft,]and you can float on a slice of the Kobuk River as it makes its way through the tundra, camping on sandbars along the way. Don’t want to make the trip to Alaska? Isle Royale National Park, which protects a series of islands in Lake Michigan, only received 29,000 visitors last year, making it the least-visited national park in the lower 48. You can only access it by boat or seaplane, but there is a full-service lodge on the main island. From there, you can strike out for the interior of the island where small, inland lakes offer the chance for more solitude. Strike out on a lonely dirt road and cover miles of backcountry terrain with everything you need to be self-sufficient in your 4WD vehicle. That’s the overlanding dream, and the dream is alive and well in Canyonlands National Park, which protects 337,000 acres of canyons, slickrock, and spires in Southeast Utah. Overlanders can explore endless miles of dirt and technical roads that traverse the park’s three distinct districts. The Needles District has rough, technical routes with plenty of rock crawling, while the Maze District has some of the most remote dirt roads in the contiguous United States. But the 100-mile White Rim Road is the classic route, traversing the park’s Island in the Sky district with cliffside, bench cut roads delivering big views of the Colorado and Green Rivers below. You’ll need an overnight permit for camping, and keep an eye out for mountain bikers who cherish the White Rim too. You need Egyptian cotton sheets and a post-dinner wine and chocolate pairing. There’s no shame in wanting to buffer a hard day’s adventure with a side of the finer things. Grand Teton National Park is the solution, largely because of Jackson Lake Lodge, one of only two Four-Diamond, full-service resorts inside a national park (the other is The Inn at Death Valley). The hotel operates on a historic ranch and features 28 individual log cabins adjacent to a large, communal lodge building, all within a short distance of Jenny Lake with views of the Grand Tetons on the horizon. A stay at Jenny Lake Lodge includes a daily gourmet breakfast and five-course dinner as well as afternoon lawn games on the lodge’s grand meadow. Cruiser bikes are included, as are interpretive walks and history talks. (From $1,149 a night; you can make reservations a year in advance). The location also makes it easy to drop into Jackson for a spa day or some retail therapy. No judgment here. There’s wildlife, and then there’s wildlife. Denali National Park has the latter, boasting five massive species of mammals that will make you question your place on the food chain. The big one is the grizzly bear, which reach up to 600 pounds and are best seen through a telephoto lens from very, very far away. Cruising Denali Park Road at dawn or dusk gives you a good chance to see grizzlies as they tend to roam the tundra and riverbanks within view of the road. You also have the chance to see massive moose, wolves, caribou, and adorable Dall sheep, which look like something out of a storybook. The odds of seeing all “Big Five” species are slim, but that’s what makes it an admirable goal. Can’t make the trek to Alaska? Yellowstone has grizzlies, bison, elk, and elusive wolves, too. For better or worse, the infrastructure of many of our national parks was designed around the car, with scenic roads taking a priority as many of these landscapes were set aside for protection. But that means there are some amazing drives that deliver awe-inspiring views inside our parks. Trail Ridge Road, inside Rocky Mountain National Park, takes the cake in my opinion because it gives motorists a chance to experience a true high-alpine environment without breaking a sweat. One of the highest paved roads in the country, Trail Ridge Road peaks out at 12,183 feet as it makes its way across the park between the towns of Estes Park and Grand Lake. You’ll be able to cruise above the tree line for eight miles while listening to your favorite podcast and adjusting your seat warmer. Make a point to stop at the Gore Range Overlook, near the crest of the road, where you’ll enjoy long- range views of the Never Summer Mountains on the western horizon. West Virginia’s New River Gorge National Park isn’t big—just 73,000 acres—but at its heart is a 1,000-foot-deep canyon that has become a multi-sport haven for the East Coast. The New, as locals call it, has 25 miles of Class IV whitewater at the bottom of the gorge, and more than 3,000 established climbing routes along its walls. It’s also one of the few national parks that allows legitimate mountain biking, with the 13-mile Arrowhead Trail system that is easily accessed from Fayetteville, the New’s main trail town. Oh, and show up in October, and you can jump off of a bridge. At 876 feet tall, the New River Gorge Bridge is the second tallest arch bridge in the world. For one day in the middle of October every year, BASE jumpers are allowed to leap from the bridge and land safely at the bottom of the gorge. It’s called Bridge Day, and it might be the ultimate celebration of adrenaline inside any of our national parks. Our national parks preserve a lot of key history, from the restored Civilian Conservation Corps camps of Shenandoah National Park to the massive sculptures that commemorate the country’s founding fathers at Mount Rushmore. Colorado’s Mesa Verde takes the cake, though, protecting more than 5,000 archaeological sites of the Ancestral Puebloans that date back to AD 600, well before the dudes on Mount Rushmore started cooking. The original residents of the area spent roughly 700 years building their homes into the sides of the cliffs, and visitors to the park today can actually explore these ancient structures firsthand. You can explore two of the archeological sites on your own, Step House and Wetherill Mesa, but to really engross yourself in the history, you need to sign up for a ranger-led tour of Cliff Palace, the largest cliff dwelling in North America with 150 rooms carved out of the tan sandstone wall. In addition to the individual rooms, Cliff Palace also has 23 kivas, which are larger communal spaces. A tour through this village gives you a chance to step back in time and experience how these ancient peoples literally carved out a life in the desert. While you can find exceptional meals at lodge restaurants inside many national parks, Cuyahoga Valley National Park is where food is actually grown. There are eight working farms within the national park’s boundaries, all of which are leased by local farmers who grow a variety of crops and animals, and all of which have programs where visitors can engage with the process. There’s a berry farm where you can pick your own sweet treats, a beef and pork farm with a market that allows you to buy bacon and burgers directly from the source, and farm stands where you can get seasonal veggies that were grown with regenerative principles. There’s even a vineyard that grows several different grape varieties. The park doesn’t have a sit-down restaurant of its own, but a few establishments in the town of Cuyahoga Falls focus on farm-to-table meals with an emphasis on locally-grown goods. Check out The Farmer’s Rail, which is part butcher shop, part restaurant owned by a local farmer. A relatively flat parking space and decent cell service…that’s all you need to live the digital nomad VanLife. Bonus points if those two amenities are located near some world–class adventure so you can explore the terrain between Zoom meetings. Joshua Tree might be the ultimate national park for the free-wheeling VanLife set. While the park itself has gorgeous campgrounds, getting a reservation can be tough, and cell service inside the park is spotty at best. But there’s a bevy of free dispersed camping on BLM land that borders the park on the south side, giving boondockers (those camping off-grid in an RV, van, or tent without utility hookups or official amenities) immediate access to the hiking trails and boulders that define this park, no reservations required. I pulled into the BLM tract on a crisp, fall Saturday night and had no trouble finding a spot to call home. And while cell service inside the park isn’t strong enough to send an email, the BLM land sits close enough to Interstate 10 to sport strong cell service. So you can log on just enough to keep your boss happy. There’s even a VanLife–specific campground just a few minutes outside of the park if you’re looking for more amenities. I was a proud minivan pilot for more than a decade, during which time I toted my wife and kids to countless national parks throughout the West and South. I firmly believe that the majority of parks in the system make for great family trips, but Arches, in Southeast Utah, is my favorite family park experience for a few reasons. First, arches are cool, and even the most jaded middle-school kid agrees. They may not admit it up front, but they will ask you to send them that photo you made them take where they are standing inside Delicate Arch. Second, Arches is a front-country park, with the vast majority of highlights accessible via short trails. This can be frustrating if you’re looking for a big, multi-day adventure through the landscape, but it’s a blessing if you’re marching little kids through the desert. You can walk around Balanced Rock in less than half a mile. You can walk through the massive towers of Park Avenue in under two miles. And third, the town of Moab is just outside the park boundary, so you have fast access to post-hike ice cream and inexpensive hotels with pools. Seriously, a lot of restaurants in Moab make their own ice cream. It’s a thing, and I’m here for it. Graham Averill is Outside magazine’s national parks columnist. He identifies as a minivan pilot and bougie prince. He recently wrote about how Bend, Oregon, is trying to harness tourism for the good of locals.

item.title: Meet Microduck, a $399 Open-Source Robot That Can Learn New Tricks
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 7.38
A new budget-friendly robot arriving later this year will let owners program it with new tricks. The $399 biped robot comes from Hugging Face, a company best known for hosting open-source and open-weight AI models. Hugging Face’s Pollen Robotics arm developed the Microduck, which weighs 1.8 pounds and stands 9.8 inches tall. The bot contains 15 motors, a microphone and speaker, a camera, LiDAR, and two motion sensors, along with a beak for picking up objects. The bot moves by waddling. A video shows the Microduck can walk, get up on its own, grab objects like your clothes, kick a ball, and even roller skate if you buy the attachable skates. Importantly, Microduck comes with seven pre-built capabilities out of the box, making it easy for consumers to use. The robot can also be controlled with the included game controller. Microduck can also “follow a laser dot, trigger movements, or let it react to its surroundings. The point is to make the first interaction immediate, even if you never write code,” Hugging Face wrote in a blog post. But the bot’s real selling point is its programmability. “The same robot becomes a complete development platform,” Hugging Face explains. “Its open-source software stack covers robot control, simulation, reinforcement learning, and sim-to-real deployment." The software is available today: the main Microduck repository contains the SDK and robot software, while Microduck RL contains the reinforcement learning and sim-to-real tools, Hugging Face says. As a result, Microduck should be able to learn new tricks through trial and error. Software developers also use the bot to "test how AI moves from simulation into the real world," the company adds. Hugging Face plans on sharing more about the software development aspect, but for now, the company says, “The important point is that the behaviors shipping with Microduck are not meant to define what the robot can do forever. They are a starting point.” For memory, the Microduck features 1GB of RAM and 32GB of storage. The bot also supports Wi-Fi and Bluetooth and comes with two NFC antennas. On the downside, Microduck’s battery life is estimated at about 1 hour with the 2,600mAh battery. Preorders for the Microduck are already open. “First deliveries targeted before Christmas 2026,” the site says. The product is currently only available in the US and Europe. The launch comes after reports that Nvidia is acquiring Hugging Face for an estimated $12.9 billion. Last month, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella released a public letter championing open-weight AI models. “The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models,” Huang wrote in his first post on X. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Here Are My Expert Tips on How to Photograph Tonight's Near-Total Lunar Eclipse
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 6.22
A near-total lunar eclipse is a spectacular event, and one that happens infrequently enough to warrant going outside to gaze at. This Thursday night into Friday morning, August 27-28, North and South America will be treated to an eclipse in which more than 96% of the moon will be immersed in the umbra, the darkest part of Earth's shadow. The eastern United States will experience the eclipse (weather permitting) in a midnight sky, but it's an early evening event on the West Coast. Interested in viewing the eclipse? Here's when to look and how to snap the best photographs. When Is the Near-Total Lunar Eclipse? When should you look up? The partial (umbral) eclipse begins at 10:34 p.m. ET, the mid-eclipse occurs at 13 minutes past midnight, and the partial umbral eclipse ends at 1:51 a.m. ET. On the West Coast, the partial phase starts at 7:34 p.m. PT, during evening twilight; mid-eclipse is at 9:13 p.m. PT, and the partial eclipse ends at 10:51 p.m. PT. The rest of North America will also see the full event; mid-eclipse occurs at 10:13 p.m. in the Central Time Zone, and 11:13 in the Mountain Time Zone. In Hawaii, the moon will rise partially eclipsed at 6:47 p.m. local time, already more than half an hour past maximum. Is It Safe to Watch a Lunar Eclipse? A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth lies between the sun and the moon, and the moon passes into Earth's shadow. During Thursday's eclipse, 96% of the moon will be immersed in the umbra, the dark, inner part of Earth's shadow. Its ruddy glow will contrast with the bright, crescent-like sliver of the moon that remains uneclipsed. But unlike a solar eclipse, which during its partial phases is far too bright to view safely with the naked eye, it's perfectly safe to look at all stages of a lunar eclipse without eye protection. It's also nice to remember that you will be in good company in your moon-gazing; the entire half of the Earth facing the moon will see it go through the same phases. Although you don't need any optical aid to enjoy the eclipse, using a telescope or binoculars will show a larger image and reveal details that may be invisible to your unaided eyes. Even a small pair of binoculars can greatly enhance your viewing experience. Just don't forget to look away from your camera from time to time to gaze at the changing appearance with the naked eye. A deep partial eclipse is a beautiful sight, and although it's great to get good images, it's no substitute for directly experiencing it. How to Snap a Good Photo of the Lunar Eclipse Although it can be challenging to get good eclipse photos because of the vast reduction of the moon's light around maximum eclipse, with a little preparation, it can be done. Here are some tips for snapping good pictures using a tripod-mounted camera. 1. Watch For the Light Photographing the early partial stages of the eclipse is much like photographing a non-eclipsed moon. Since a lunar eclipse always occurs at full moon, you will have plenty of light at the onset. Soon, though, you will have to compensate for the decrease in light as more and more of the moon slips into Earth's shadow. This is done by changing the ISO, f/ratio, and/or exposure time, while ensuring your camera remains in focus. The reduction in light will not be as dramatic as with a total eclipse, but the changing brightness and aspect of the moon will demand your attention. 2. Use a Tripod, If Possible Because you will be using relatively long exposures to shoot a total eclipse, you will need to keep your camera as steady as possible, ideally on a sturdy tripod that can remain rigid through wind gusts. With a compact camera, in the absence of a tripod, you may get some decent shots if you brace it against a solid flat surface. I took the below image, as well as the one showing the moon rising in deep twilight over the NYC skyline, with compact cameras, the first with a Sony Cyber-shot DSC-RX100 III, the latter with a Canon PowerShot, probably the SD600. I took the first image through a gap in the clouds during the near-total eclipse of November 21, 2021, in which 99% of the moon's surface was obscured at maximum. It should be a fair approximation of what this week's event will look like at mid-eclipse, although individual lunar eclipses may vary widely in how dark the obscured part of the moon may look. 3. Adjust the Exposure As the partial stage of the eclipse begins, settings should be what you might normally use to photograph a full moon. (Exact settings vary considerably between cameras; typical settings for my Sony Alpha 7R series cameras, using a lens with focal length set to 300mm, are an exposure of 1/250 seconds at f/8 and ISO of 200.) You should set the white balance to Daylight (the sun icon)—after all, what is moonlight but reflected sunlight? By the time that most of the moon is in shadow and its visible face has become a crescent, you should boost the ISO to 400 or 800 and lengthen your exposure to 1/100 seconds or longer. 4. Use Manual Focus The brightness of the moon's image in your viewfinder or LCD should be your guide; as the image dims, you will want to increase your exposure length. You should switch to manual focus because, for one thing, around the time of maximum eclipse, the moon's light may be too dim to trigger your autofocus. You should also lower your f/ratio to f/5.6 or smaller; this will let in more light but it will also decrease the depth of field, making it all the more important that you accurately focus the camera. Exposure bracketing can help ensure good shots in tricky lighting conditions. 5. Try Your Smartphone You can even enlist your smartphone in eclipse photography. These devices are great for shooting "mood" photos showing the moon through high clouds and can be used to capture a lunar eclipse as well. I've gotten good results in shooting total solar eclipses with iPhones, and I plan to use mine for this week's event. How to Shoot the Eclipse With a Smart Telescope In the past few years, smart telescopes—essentially self-contained astronomical cameras that you control through a smartphone or tablet—and even low-priced models, can take good images of the moon and other celestial objects. You can either take individual shots or, with most smart telescopes, run a time-lapse to create a sped-up movie sequence of the eclipse. To minimize file size in an event that will last several hours—up to about five hours if you want to include the penumbral phases, in which the Earth's shadow only partially eclipses a portion of the moon's surface—you will want to choose an interval of at least five seconds between shots. You may also want to compensate for the changing light levels during the eclipse. This is easy to do with Dwarflab scopes such as the Dwarf 3 and Dwarf Mini. First, you go to Solar System mode, select moon, slew to it manually or by using the joystick so that it is within the telephoto field of view, and press Track at the bottom of the screen. If you are satisfied with your test shot, you can switch to Time Lapse mode, and enable Auto Exposure (AE) in the exposure length settings. Then you should be good to go. If the image is too dark near maximum eclipse, you can increase the exposure length and gain; just be sure to switch back to AE after mid-eclipse. The process is similar with Seestar scopes; once the unit is properly aligned you enter Solar System mode and instruct it to GoTo the moon; when it is centered, check your focus and enter Auto Exposure. (If the Seestar has trouble finding the moon, make sure its compass is calibrated and instruct it to find a bright star. When this is done successfully, it should be much easier to find the moon.) You can set a time-lapse interval and start the shot. If the eclipsed part of the moon is too dark around mid-eclipse, you can switch to Manual mode and punch up the gain and increase the exposure length, and then return to Auto Exposure after the eclipse passes its peak. About Our Expert Since 2004, I have worked on PCMag’s hardware team, covering at various times printers, scanners, projectors, storage, and monitors. I currently focus my efforts on 3D printers, pro and productivity displays, and drives and SSDs of all sorts. Over the years, I have reviewed smart telescopes, iPad and iPhone science apps, plus the occasional camera, laptop, keyboard, and mouse. I've also written a host of articles about astronomy, space science, travel photography, and astrophotography for PCMag and its past and present sibling publications (among them, Mashable and ExtremeTech), as well as for the former PCMag Digital Edition.

item.title: 37 Secret Windows 11 Features Hiding in Plain Sight
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.94
Microsoft is always adding new features to Windows 11 in Insider builds, but you don't have to wait for the next stable release to take advantage of its best capabilities. The world's most popular operating system already has a wealth of useful tools just a few clicks away. Here, we've collected dozens of expert tips for boosting productivity, customizing your desktop, optimizing your PC, and securing your software so you can unlock your computer's full potential. 1. Realign the Start Button If you're new to Windows 11, the first thing that jumps out at you is the placement of the Start button. Long located in the lower-left corner of the screen, it's now centered with the rest of the icons on the taskbar. But don't worry, you can change it. Right-click the taskbar and open Taskbar Settings. From the Taskbar Behaviors drop-down menu, change the Taskbar Alignment to Left. Your taskbar icons move to the left, and the Start button goes back where it belongs. For more on personalizing the Windows 11 taskbar, check out our guide. 2. Download PowerToys Some of the best Windows 11 features don't come with the OS by default. Case in point: Microsoft's free PowerToys package includes 28 must-have extras for power users. For example, it has tools for renaming files in bulk and resizing images. You also get novel ways to manage windows, including the ability to create custom layouts and a shortcut for making windows always appear on top of others. An application for switching between light and dark modes based on the time of day and the option to control multiple PCs with a single keyboard and mouse round out the current offerings. Microsoft often adds new tools to this package as well. You can download PowerToys from the Microsoft Store or from other sources via the PowerToys website. 3. Optimize Your PC's Startup Apps Windows applications often configure themselves to start automatically when you sign in to your PC. These add clutter to your taskbar's notification area and slow down the startup process. Applications running in the background can also waste valuable system resources. I recommend tweaking your PC's startup apps and turning off anything you don't use. Simply head to Settings > Apps > Startup. If you don't want an application to launch when you sign in, flip its switch to Off. The same is possible via the Task Manager, where you can even see your last BIOS startup time. You can still launch any disabled application from a desktop shortcut or the Start menu; it just won't start when you sign in to Windows. 4. Upgrade Your Copy-Paste Experience Windows 11 has a Clipboard History feature that remembers text snippets and images you recently copied. To access it, press Windows+V. A pop-up will prompt you to enable Clipboard History if you haven't already. You can also click the little pin icon to pin copied items to the clipboard history for easy access later. 5. Get AI Assistance With Copilot Need to write a recommendation but don't know where to start? Have to spruce up the tone or grammar of an email? Or maybe you need a goofy image to spice up your newsletter. Copilot can help you with these things and more. Get to it by clicking the colorful, swirly icon on the right end of the taskbar or typing Windows Key-C. You can also now summon Copilot with the "Hey Copilot" wake word, like you would a smart speaker. Once you do, you hear a chime, and a convincingly human-sounding voice stands ready to answer any question you ask. Copilot is far smarter and more helpful than legacy voice assistants like Alexa and Google Assistant, though it doesn't (yet) allow you to control smart home devices. Copilot maintains your conversation's context, so you don't have to keep repeating yourself to refine results. One of Copilot's coolest, most unique features is Copilot Vision. This can point to parts of your screen to help you with completing a task in any app, including a complex one like Photoshop, while talking you through the process. Future updates will let you interact with it via text in this context, too. Otherwise, Copilot can write code, summarize a web page or PDF, and write a poem on a topic of your choice. Drag an image file onto it or select an area of the screen for it to explain. Copilot Daily is a custom, AI-generated podcast that catches you up with the day's happenings and fun facts. We have loads of advice on what to try with Copilot if you're new to this particular AI chatbot. Microsoft has been adding new Copilot features at a steady pace, including the ability to search your PC's files and invite someone else to a conversation for joint researching. Copilot has lots of features you can try. You can even assign it tasks. If you have a Copilot+ PC, you get even more capabilities, like an Agent in Settings, Click to Do for suggested actions, more image-enhancement tools, Recall for getting back to previous activities, and semantic search. 6. Customize the Quick Settings Panel Windows 11 separates the Quick Settings that appear in the Action Center in Windows 10 from that panel's notifications. Click the area of the taskbar that has Wi-Fi, speaker, and battery icons to open a menu that lets you control Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, projection to an external display, airplane mode, battery-saver mode, and more. As of the 24H2 update of Windows 11, you can no longer add or remove items (unless you're the type who likes to dig into the registry). Instead, the panel scrolls up and down to reveal all options, and you can place them to taste by clicking and dragging with your mouse cursor. Bonus tip: If you're using a Surface PC, you can switch between the gorgeous "Enhanced" mode and the standard sRGB color mode in this panel. 7. Create and Manage Multiple Desktops Microsoft replaces the old Task View button with a redesigned icon on the taskbar, which makes it easier to create and manage multiple desktops. Just hover over the icon to see any open virtual desktops or create a new desktop. You can then rearrange these desktops as necessary and drag apps from one desktop to another. You can use different wallpapers for each virtual desktop to better differentiate them. Right-click on the desktop, choose Personalize > Background, and then pick a distinct image. Note that this works only for the Background choice, not for Themes. If you choose a Theme, it applies to all virtual desktops. After applying a theme, however, you can change the background of each desktop. If you do, you see a cool cross-fade effect between the two backgrounds when you switch between them. 8. See Information at a Glance With Widgets While Windows 10 dabbled in widgets, Windows 11 goes all in. A new Widgets icon on the taskbar lets you check the weather, complete tasks on your to-do list, manage your Outlook calendar, read the latest news, see the latest sports scores, track stock prices, or watch nearby traffic. You can customize the widgets to suit your needs, rearrange them on the page, and manage your newsfeed preferences through Microsoft Start. You can also add third-party widgets to the panel, including those from Facebook Messenger and Spotify. It's possible to personalize the widgets on your lock screen now, too. 9. Learn New Ways to Snap Your Window Layouts Microsoft has supported snap-and-resize since Windows 7, but it gets a boost in Windows 11 with Snap Layouts. You can still drag windows to the sides and corners for half- and quarter-screen layouts, but Windows 11 adds a hover menu over the Maximize button that offers layout options. You can choose one large window on the left and two on top of each other on the right, or three in a row, for example. Your choices depend on the size of your display. The feature continues to get updates with more layout options and thumbnails for running apps in the layout choices. Click to select your preferred formation and then move your apps into place. You can turn off this behavior in Settings. Some keyboard shortcuts let you quickly snap windows, such as Windows Key-Left Arrow, to snap a window to the left half of the screen. 10. Connect Your Phone for Texts, Calls, and More Windows 11's Phone Link app enables you to wirelessly connect your smartphone, allowing you to view phone notifications on your PC, respond to text messages, and make calls. If you use an Android phone, you can also play music and, with select models, run multiple phone apps on your PC's screen. It's even possible to use your phone as a Wi-Fi hotspot or a webcam. The Start menu now offers a panel for quick access to your phone's activity. A recent update to the Settings app introduces the ability to toggle related functions, including displaying your phone in File Explorer and enabling cross-device copying and pasting. You can remotely lock your PC using your phone, and resume app activities between the devices. Unfortunately, Microsoft's Resume feature still has a long way to go to compete with Apple's Handoff capability. 11. Increase Security by Using Passkeys Passwords are so passé and not as secure as other options. Forward-minded websites and apps support more secure passkeys to log in, which are linked to a specific device.
