Windows 11 can now store your passkeys or use those you store on other devices, such as your smartphone. On Windows 11, passkeys take advantage of Windows Hello authentication via facial recognition, fingerprint, or PIN. 12. Send Files Between PCs Without the Cloud Windows 11 includes an AirDrop-style wireless file-sharing feature for moving files between PCs without using cloud storage or a USB drive. It works between PCs running either Windows 10 or Windows 11. Before using this feature, you must enable it on both the PC receiving the file and the one sending it. Simply head to Settings > System > Nearby Sharing on each PC. To use Nearby Sharing, right-click a file in File Explorer and select Share With > More Options. Then, select the Nearby Sharing icon. Note that this doesn't work if the file you want to send is synced with OneDrive; you will see a OneDrive file-sharing window instead. You can avoid this problem by moving files out of OneDrive before sharing them. For example, you might need to move it from your Desktop folder to your Downloads folder, which doesn't sync with OneDrive by default. Then, you can use the sharing menu. 13. Control Your PC and Type With Your Voice Windows 11's Voice Access feature lets you type with your voice and control your PC by speaking voice commands. For example, you can say "Launch Google Chrome" into your mic to open the browser or speak a sentence aloud to add it to a text field. Voice Access processes your voice on your PC to maintain privacy, rather than sending it to the cloud. Open the Voice Access app from your Start menu to get started. It will walk you through a quick setup process that explains the basics. A recent update to Windows 11 adds a Voice Isolation feature that helps Voice Access hear you more clearly in noisy environments, too. 14. Get Things Done With Focus Sessions With messages and video chats popping up throughout the workday, it's easy to get distracted. Focus Sessions in Windows 11 encourage you to set aside time for work that requires uninterrupted deep focus. It's in the Clock app. It quickly gives you at least 30 minutes of distraction-free work time. If you go beyond 45 minutes, the app automatically schedules a five-minute break about midway through your session. Here’s a step-by-step guide on setting it up for your PC. 15. Get the Most Out of the Updated File Explorer Explorer tabs save you from littering your desktop with multiple File Explorer windows when you need to view more than one at a time. Right-click on a folder and choose "Open in New Tab," just as you would in a web browser. You can even drag a file between tabs. Simply drag it to the desired tab and then drag it down into the file list. You can also drag tabs sideways to rearrange them and press Alt+Left Arrow to navigate back in a tab (but not Ctrl+PgUp and Ctrl+PgDn, as you can in a web browser). With the initial release of Windows 11, Microsoft streamlined the ribbon at the top of the File Explorer menu. Cut, Copy, Paste, Rename, Share, Delete, Sort, and View choices get prominent buttons at the top, saving you from having to wade through multiple menus you seldom use. Windows 11 also adds a New button for creating new folders and shortcuts, as well as documents based on installed programs. The buttons change based on context, too. So, for example, when you're searching in the right-hand search box, you get a Search Options button. A recent update added AI Actions in the context menu. For example, a "Remove Background" option appears when you right-click on an image file, and a "Summarize" choice is available if you click on a Microsoft 365 document. The latest File Explorer update further simplifies the context menu and enhances the consistency of dark mode. 16. See Closed Captions for Any Audio Windows can automatically generate closed captions for any audio playing on your system with the Live Captions feature, displaying them in a floating bar. To protect your privacy, the processing happens locally on your PC. Launch the Live Captions app from the Start menu to begin. Copilot+ PCs have an additional live translation feature. On these machines, Live Captions can automatically translate speech and display captions in another language. 17. View the Full App List Windows 11 adds an extra step to view your full list of installed apps. Instead of opening the Start menu and immediately seeing the App List next to the app tiles, you have to click the All button in the Pinned section of the Start menu. (A Windows update renamed this choice from All apps to just All.) Then, you can browse the list or search for a specific app. Of course, it might be quicker to type the first few letters of the app's name to search for it. Note that within the All list, you can still click on a letter of the alphabet to show a grid of the whole alphabet so you can zoom in on a particular letter. Bonus: Click on Search instead of Start to see your most recently used apps. Similarly, the More link in the bottom half of the Start menu shows more of your recent files and apps. Note that an update is rolling out that shows the full scrollable app list by default, though it hasn't arrived on our test PCs yet. 18. Pin Apps to the Start Menu Live Tiles are gone in Windows 11. In their place is a more simplistic Start menu where you can pin apps for easy access. Open the App List, right-click on an app, and select Pin to Start to move it to the Pinned section. Then, drag the app into the position you prefer. To remove apps, right-click and choose Unpin from Start. A newer option in Windows 11 is the ability to drag icons on top of each other to create folders, as you would on a mobile operating system. You can also adjust the relative sizes of Pinned and Recommended icon sections. 19. Use AI to Edit and Create Images Windows 11 includes three apps that work AI magic with images: the relatively recent Designer app, along with updated versions of the venerable Paint and Photos apps. Designer can create illustrations based on your text prompt, Photos can remove backgrounds or objects from photos, and Paint can do all three of those things. 20. Customize Your Interface With a Theme Themes return in Windows 11, but this time they work hand in hand with dark mode. Open Settings > Personalization and select one of the default themes to change the accent color, background image, color theme, cursor, and sounds all at once. Open Themes to edit current themes, add new themes from the Microsoft Store, or create your own. 21. Customize the Start Menu In Windows 10, the Settings button appears above the Start button when you tap it by default. Not so in Windows 11, but you can add it back via Settings > Personalization > Start > Folders. It's not only folders that you can add from here. You can also add Settings, File Explorer, and Network buttons, as well as folders for music, pictures, documents, and so on. 22. Replace the Start Menu With a Launcher Alternative launchers are faster and more customizable than the Start menu. They're better at finding files, launching apps, and even searching the web. Optional plug-ins even let you easily toggle dark mode, run custom actions, and search your notes. The best non-default launchers are free and easy to use, too. 23. Get Better App and File Recommendations The Start menu has a Recommended section for recent files and frequently used apps. To customize what appears here, open Settings > Personalization > Start, then tell Windows to stop showing recently installed apps, frequently used apps, or recently opened items in the Start menu, App List, and elsewhere. Another setting here is "Show recommendations for tips, shortcuts, new apps, and more." Some have characterized these as ads in Windows 11, but Microsoft claims that the suggestions are curated and from highly reputable software developers. I have them turned on and haven't noticed anything obnoxious or even objectionable. 24. Change the Default Apps With Windows 11, changing a default app is a bit complicated because you need to specify a default app for every file type rather than just setting an app as the default for every type of media it handles. Open the Settings app and tap on the Apps section in the left-hand menu. Once you choose Default Apps and click on the app you want to set as the default for a file type, you see the full list of file types that it can handle. Click on the file type you want and select an app from the menu that pops up. For a full rundown of the process, check out our guide. 25. Visualize Your Battery Better Windows 11 does a better job than its predecessor of helping you visualize your battery usage data. Go to Settings > System > Power & battery, then open the Battery usage tab. A chart shows how much power you have used over the last few days or hours. A list of apps below shows power usage by individual apps. If you find a program that's using too much power, you can shut down background usage and put it to sleep, just like with an Android phone or iPhone. 26. Quickly Pair Input/Output Devices Windows 11 now has a full-featured Sound menu with the ability to pair new input and output devices. Open Settings > System > Sound and click Add Device under the Output section to link external speakers or other devices. Or click Add Device under Input to connect an external microphone. You then have a choice to connect via Bluetooth, wireless docks, or other devices. Scroll down to the Advanced section and click All Sound Devices to view a full list of all input and output devices that you connected to your PC. The Windows 11 24H2 update added important support for the Bluetooth Low Energy Audio (LE Audio) assistive hearing devices. 27. Listen With New Sound Modes You get extra control over your audio output in Windows 11, including mono audio and enhanced audio modes. To go mono, open Settings > System > Sound, then enable Mono audio to combine the left and right audio channels. For enhanced audio—which includes bass boost, loudness equalization, room correction, and virtual surround—click All sound devices under the Advanced section of the Sound menu, choose a device to access the Properties menu, and enable Enhance Audio. 28. Get Used to the New Touch Gestures If you’re using a touch-screen PC convertible or tablet, you have to get used to a whole new set of touch gestures, many of which involve using multiple fingers. Swiping in from the left side no longer opens task switching mode, but rather the Widgets panel of news and information. To show the Task View, you now have to swipe up on the screen (anywhere) with four fingers. Swiping in from the right still thankfully opens notifications. Swiping down from the top no longer closes an app, but you can swipe down in an app window with three fingers to minimize an app and show the desktop. Swiping three fingers up opens all running windows. 29. Learn New Keyboard Shortcuts Windows 11 has new keyboard shortcuts, and they're worth learning: - Windows Key-W to open the Widgets panel - Windows Key-A to access the Quick Settings - Windows Key-Z to access Snap Layouts - Windows Key-K to cast media A couple of the best keyboard shortcuts are still in place from Windows 10, including Windows Key-V to show clipboard history and Windows Key-Shift-S for the screenshot tool. 30. Access Gaming Features Tapping Windows Key-G opens a panoply of utilities useful not only to gamers but to any Windows 11 user. The Game Bar lets you record screen activity and see system resources and performance stats, as well as chat with gamer pals and see your Xbox Achievements. It also offers audio and display settings such as Auto HDR. 31. Record Audio With the New Sound Recorder App Replacing the Voice Recorder is Windows 11's new Sound Recorder. The app has a redesigned interface that shows audio waveforms and more input options. It lets you output to a good selection of formats, including AAC, FLAC, MP3, WAV, and WMA. That said, it's pretty basic with no audio trimming. 32. Listen and Watch With the New Media Player Replacing the Groove app, the new Media Player in Windows 11 still lets you get your groove on while listening to music or watching videos. It's far more user-friendly than the old Media Player, which you still need to rip CDs. 33. Back Up Your PC With Windows Backup With the 23H2 version update of Windows 11 came a new Windows Backup app. This can save your files, settings, apps, and credentials (including Wi-Fi logins), syncing them to OneDrive cloud storage so that if you move to a new PC, you can simply sign in and have everything restored to your familiar setup. 34. Clear Your Desktop With Title Bar Shake The Windows Title Bar Shake setting is a favorite of ours. It's off by default, but you can enable it in Settings > System > Multitasking (or just search for "shake" in Settings). It lets you grab a window's top title bar and shake it to dismiss all other windows. We use it all the time to clear out a messy desktop and focus on the active window. 35. Compress Files to 7z, TAR, or Zip Formats in File Explorer With the 24H2 update, Windows 11 added the ability to compress in popular and efficient formats. TAR delivers higher compression ratios than ZIP, lets you split archives over multiple files, and offers strong error recovery. 7z has an even higher compression ratio than the other two and is open-source, to boot. 36. Project to Your PC Screen from Another Device Sure, you can project the screen of a PC, tablet, or phone to your TV, but you can also project from a device to your PC display. You first need to install the Wireless Display optional feature by going into Settings > System > Optional features. Then, head to Settings > System > Projecting to this PC and enable its functionality. If you're projecting from another PC (you can also project from an Android device), you can control the remote projecting PC with the local one's mouse and keyboard. For all the details, read our wireless display explainer. 37. Find Your Mouse Cursor More Easily In Windows, you can set your mouse cursor to not only be bigger or display movement trails but also to change colors so that it always appears in the inverse color of the background. This guarantees that your cursor or pointer (the setting applies to both) is always visible. Just go to Settings > Accessibility > Mouse pointer and touch. Then, choose the mouse pointer style that appears half black and half white. With this setting active, your mouse or pointer even appears in split colors if it's on the edge of two different-colored parts of the screen. Our explainer has all the details. Jason Cohen contributed to this story. About Our Experts I've been testing PC and mobile software for more than 20 years, focusing on photo and video editing, operating systems, and web browsers. Prior to my current role, I covered software and apps for ExtremeTech and headed up PCMag’s enterprise software team. I’ve attended trade shows for Microsoft, Google, and Apple and written about all of them and their products. I still get a kick out of seeing what's new in video and photo editing software, and how operating systems change over time. I was privileged to byline the cover story of the last print issue of PC Magazine, the Windows 7 review, and I’ve witnessed every Microsoft misstep and win, up to the latest Windows 11. I’m an avid bird photographer and traveler—I’ve been to 40 countries, many with great birds! Because I’m also a classical music fan and former performer, I’ve reviewed streaming services that emphasize classical music. I've been writing about technology for more than 15 years and using it in earnest for over twice as long. As a member of PCMag's software team, I focus on Windows coverage, but also write about other key desktop operating systems and system apps. (I used Windows 3.1 upon its release and have followed every subsequent release closely). Prior to joining PCMag, I wrote for How-To Geek starting in 2011, and my articles amassed over a billion page views. I went on to run the publication as editor-in-chief for four and a half years. I have also contributed to Computerworld, Fast Company, PCWorld, Reader's Digest, The New York Times, and many other outlets about everything from AI to PC hardware to Windows. I founded and ran my own direct-to-reader Windows-focused newsletters, Windows Intelligence and The Windows ReadMe, working in partnership with Thurrott.com.

item.title: 5G Home Broadband Is Soaring in Urban Areas, and This Carrier Comes Out on Top
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.54
New Ookla data suggests that neither slower speeds nor local competition has held back the fastest-growing segment of residential broadband: fixed-wireless access (FWA) 5G. Home 5G from AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon appear to be drawing more customers in urban areas than rural markets, even though the latter might seem like a more logical fit, according to the report, which covers FWA performance in the first half of 2026. Ookla found that “roughly 70%” of measurements uploaded from its Speedtest app came from urban areas as defined by the Census Bureau, though Ookla analyst Sue Marek acknowledges that “Speedtest sample volume does not directly equate to subscriber counts.” When T-Mobile began selling its 5G Home Internet back in 2021, the first widely available 5G FWA offering from the national carriers, the idea was to avoid competing with fiber-optic broadband, which is both faster and promises essentially unlimited capacity. (Verizon introduced home 5G service first, but its initial service relied on fast but extremely short-range millimeter-wave frequencies that limited it to isolated dots on maps in select cities.) For telecom firms, FWA does have the advantage of not coming with fiber’s buildout obstacles: “FWA is much easier to deploy and eliminates the headaches associated with urban fiber deployment, such as costly trenching, expensive municipal permits, and heavy construction fees," Ookla notes. Ookla’s data shows T-Mobile remains in a much faster lane than AT&T, which only launched its Internet Air service in 2023, and Verizon, whose 5G Home Internet now relies on that carrier’s fast and wide-ranging C-band spectrum. In the second quarter of 2026, T-Mobile offered by far the quickest median download speeds: 222.72Mbps, versus 160.43Mbps at AT&T and 126.53Mbps at Verizon. T-Mobile’s advantage was narrower with median uploads, none of which were that great: 18.12Mbps, compared with AT&T’s 12.2Mbps and Verizon’s 10.06Mbps. AT&T’s Q2 download speeds showed the biggest improvement compared with the year-ago quarter—a 46% jump from Q2 2025’s 109.76. Marek credits AT&T’s progress to the carrier lighting up the 5G spectrum it obtained from Echostar in a 2025 transaction. At all three carriers, rural users had a slower experience than customers in or near cities, with median downloads 24% slower for rural relative to urban at AT&T, 11% slower at T-Mobile, and a painful 33% pokier at Verizon. Relatively slow uploads everywhere meant that in every state, FWA flunked the definition of broadband the FCC set in 2024: 100Mbps down and 20Mbps up. Only DC, Hawaii, and New York saw more than 40% of Speedtest samples clear that bar; in California and Texas, meanwhile, only about a third did. The Ookla report includes fine-grained observations on performance changes by both time of day and time of year. In the former case, Speedtest data showed download and upload speeds declining in the afternoons, especially from 7 to 9 p.m., due to network congestion. In that evening peak period, T-Mobile’s median download speeds bottomed out at 165Mbps, while AT&T and Verizon’s slowed to roughly 125Mbps. On a seasonal scale, Ookla found performance declining from Q1 to Q2–downloads fell 4.1% at AT&T, 7% at T-Mobile, and 11.9% at Verizon, while uploads dropped 19.8% at AT&T, 21.5% at T-Mobile, and 14% at Verizon. Some blame falls on trees that fill out in the spring, ”with dense leaves that can weaken the FWA signals.” The rest goes to temperatures that rise and create more “thermal noise within electronic components,” Marek writes, which “causes networks to default to slower modulation schemes in order to maintain a stable connection.” Despite those fluctuating speeds, FWA has amassed a large customer base that Ericsson recently estimated at 17 million, almost 14% of the 123.75 million households with any kind of broadband, per Census Bureau stats. These services don’t impose data caps and are increasingly cheap, especially when sold by the prepaid brands of carriers. They routinely do well in customer satisfaction surveys conducted by J.D. Power and the American Customer Satisfaction Institute. In PCMag’s Readers’ Choice list, however, only Verizon’s home 5G shows up in the top 10—in 10th place with a 7.2 overall satisfaction score. About Our Expert Rob Pegoraro writes about interesting problems and possibilities in computers, gadgets, apps, services, telecom, and other things that beep or blink. He’s covered such developments as the evolution of the cell phone from 1G to 5G, the fall and rise of Apple, Google’s growth from obscure Yahoo rival to verb status, and the transformation of social media from CompuServe forums to Facebook’s billions of users. Pegoraro has met most of the founders of the internet and once received a single-word email reply from Steve Jobs.

item.title: Not Again: HP Says More Price Hikes Are Coming, Blames Memory Shortage
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.31
The worsening memory shortage is forcing HP to roll out more price hikes. "We have been increasing pricing. We expect to continue to increase pricing as input costs rise,” HP CFO Karen Parkhill said in an earnings call on Wednesday. HP warned about price hikes last year, but Parkhill says, “We use that as a last lever, after we have focused on demand shaping and product reconfiguration, and taking costs everywhere we can." The problem is that RAM and storage costs continue to climb, and HP is running out of its cheaper supply. It's been “working through the benefit of the lower cost of inventory on our balance sheets, that we had more [of] in the first half,” Parkhill said. “And now you're seeing inventory that is carrying higher costs working through our P&L [profit and loss] in the back half.” Parkhill added: “We continue to expect memory and storage costs to increase further as a percentage of the bill of materials.” In February, she estimated memory components will make up 35% of the bill of materials for this year, up from 15-18%. HP also agrees with research firms such as IDC that the PC market will contract, with shipments falling by the “high teens” through the second half of this year. That said, HP reported revenue growth in its May-to-July quarter. Sales for its personal systems business, which includes PCs, were up 18% year-over-year, even though unit shipments fell 16%. The result was a record $11.8 billion for the quarter. “While volume was down as expected, our continued prioritization of higher value unit placements, repricing for higher commodity costs, and services expansion more than offset the volume headwind,” Parkhill said. She added that the company has been gaining share in the premium PC category and capturing more revenue growth for HP’s AI PCs, which are more expensive. Still, this means consumers should brace for higher laptop prices, especially when looking for budget-friendly models. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Google's AI Mode Can Track Flight Prices, Help You Book With Points or Miles
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.20
Google’s latest update to its portfolio of AI travel tools includes one that can cut your expenses on a domestic flight to pocket change—if you fly on one of the three airlines that serve that route. This new set of AI Mode-based travel search options includes one to look up the cost of a mileage booking using Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines’ Atmos Rewards and American Airlines’ AAdvantage program. A video shows a user requesting mileage-booking options on American for a round-trip flight from Atlanta to Miami using the conversational AI interface, followed by Google returning mileage-booking rates ranging from 22,500 miles to 26,000 miles, plus $12 in federal taxes and fees. It does not show AA’s cash fares for that route, without which you can’t determine if you’re getting a better or worse-than-average return on your miles. With AAdvantage, you’ll see travel bloggers cite a range of 1.3 cents to 1.5 cents of cash value per mile as the minimum to aim for. This search also includes no information on mileage-booking options elsewhere; for that, you’d need to go to another airline’s site or use a specialized mileage comparison-shopping service like point.me. In addition to Alaska, Hawaiian, and American, Google is launching this search with three hotel chains: Choice Hotels International, Hilton, and Wyndham Hotels & Resorts. Its announcement says “the coming weeks” will bring support for Air France and KLM’s Flying Blue program, LATAM Airlines' LATAM Pass, and Lufthansa Group’s Miles & More, as well as the hotel groups Accor and Hyatt. Of those programs, Flying Blue can offer outsized value with occasional sales, while Hyatt redemptions continue to offer a better deal than competing hotel programs even after recent devaluations. (The absence of the two US airlines that have leaned most heavily into technology in their passenger experience, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines, is notable.) Google’s new additions to the travel tools genre also include the ability to set up a watch for airfare changes, something you can already do in Google Flights via its regular interface using AI Mode. Google’s video showcasing this option sees the user using Chrome on a phone, where chatting with a chatbot might be easier. The video does not indicate whether the chatbot supports Google Flights’ option to hide basic-economy airfares, but that feature should be available. Once you set up a fare-tracking alert, you’ll get an email advising you of any price changes Google has found. The last item to come off Google’s baggage carousel of new features also puts AI Mode as an alternative interface to its existing travel search site: in this case, for booking hotels. This AI front-end can connect you to the booking systems at Choice Hotels International, Hilton, IHG Hotels & Resorts, Marriott International, and Wyndham Hotels & Resorts, as well as the travel-booking sites Booking.com, Hotels.com, Expedia, Priceline, and Trip.com. (Pro tip from a frequent traveler: You may not get hotel-reward points if you book through a third party.) A Google video shows AI Mode offering to check points rates through Marriott’s Bonvoy program, even though that isn’t mentioned in the miles-and-points portion of today’s blog post. The hotel-booking tool is only available in the US. The other two new features are available everywhere you can use AI Mode, with notable exceptions found in the fine print: the very large destination that is the European Economic Area. AI flight price tracking won’t be available there or in Iceland, Liechtenstein, and Norway, nor will “some features” in miles-and-points search. item.title: Aiper Scuba V3 Review: Exceptional Pool Scrubbing Power With a Few Quirks
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.06
Armed with a dual-filtration system, AI-powered cleaning routines, two roller brushes, and four motors, the $1,099.99 Aiper Scuba V3 does an excellent job of keeping your pool looking its best. This cordless robot pool cleaner uses an AI camera to detect debris and avoid obstacles, and it has a pair of LED lights that enable it to operate at night. It will remove fine particles such as sand and dust by trapping them in a mesh filter, but cleaning the filter can get messy. Moreover, you can’t control the cleaner once it is submerged. For that, you should look to our Editors’ Choice for robot pool cleaners, the Dreame Z1 Pro. It lists for $1,499 but can be found for well under $1,000 if you shop around. Designed for pools of up to 1,614 square feet in size, the Scuba V3 measures 17.3 by 10.9 by 18.7 inches (HWD) and weighs 18.2 pounds. It uses four motors, two caterpillar treads, two roller brushes, and side-mounted JetAssist water nozzles to traverse and scrub the floor, walls, and waterline of your pool. It comes with a charging dock, a charging adapter, a retrieval hook, two foam inserts, a user guide, and a quick start guide. The foam inserts can be installed if the robot has trouble climbing tile walls. The top of the Scuba V3 features a handle, a drain cover, a control panel, and a removable debris basket. The debris basket has a screen that captures larger matter, such as leaves and twigs. If the pool contains sand, dirt, or other fine particles, you should install the included MicroMesh filter over the basket liner. The basket is easy enough to remove, but cleaning the MicroMesh filter can be challenging (more on this later). The Scuba V3 has a 4,800GPH suction rate, which is a bit stronger than the $1,599.99 Wybot S2 Pro (3,700GPH) but not quite as powerful as the $3,150 Beatbot AquaSense 2 Ultra (5,500GPH). The Dreame Z1 Pro has a very strong 8,000GPH suction rate. A built-in front camera on the cleaner powers Aiper’s AI Vision feature, which identifies debris and helps the robot avoid obstacles such as drain covers, pool toys, and pool lights. Also up front are a pair of LEDs for AI Vision cleaning at night and a Direct Time-of-Flight (DToF) sensor that works with the camera to help with smart navigation. The control panel on top is home to a power button, a Wi-Fi indicator, a status indicator bar that pulses green while charging and turns solid green when the battery is fully charged, and backlit icons for each cleaning mode (Floor, Walls, Waterline, and Auto). While in Auto mode, the robot will clean the entire pool. Press the Power button to toggle through each mode. There are additional cleaning modes that are only accessible from the mobile app: AI Patrol mode uses the camera to scan the floor for targeted cleaning; AI Navium mode uses local weather reports, historical cleaning patterns, and pool size to create a custom cleaning schedule; and Eco mode extends battery life but shortens cleaning time and is best suited to light cleaning tasks. You can also create your own schedules using the Schedule tool. The internal rechargeable battery provides up to 180 minutes of power in standard mode and up to 210 minutes in Eco mode, and it takes around five hours to fully charge a depleted battery. When the Scuba V3 runs out of battery power, it’ll head to the side of your pool and wait there for 10 minutes for easy retrieval, after which it will sink to the bottom (you’ll receive a low battery alert to your phone with a warning that the robot will sink after 10 minutes). At that point, you’ll have to use the included hook to remove the cleaner. The Aiper mobile app is the same app used to control the Ecosurfer S2 skimmer. It uses Wi-Fi to connect the robot to your home network, but it doesn’t offer underwater controls. The Dreame Z1 Pro and Polaris Freedom Plus cleaners both come with a physical remote that allows for underwater steering. The home screen displays a virtual pool graphic with icons for each installed Aiper device. The icons show the device name, its current status (battery life and cleaning mode), and the total running time. Below the graphic are icons for each device you have connected to the app. When you tap the Scuba V3 icon, you're taken to a screen where you can choose a cleaning mode (Auto, AI Patrol, Floor, Wall, Waterline), view your customized AI Navium cleaning schedule, and create your own. To access the robot’s settings screen, tap the gear icon in the upper-right corner. Here you can view a work log with total cleaning times and distances. Tap any work cycle to see which mode was used, the start time and duration, and the amount of battery life needed to complete the task. In the cleaning settings menu, you can choose to have the robot follow an S-shaped path or choose Adaptive mode, which uses the camera and sensor to target trouble areas. Use notification reminders to receive alerts when the robot starts or completes a task, or when an error occurs. Other settings allow you to configure network settings, enable Eco mode, update the firmware, and view the instruction manual. The Scuba V3 performed wonderfully in testing. In Auto mode, it did a great job of scrubbing the walls and waterline and removing debris, including fine sediment such as sand and dirt, from the floor of my 16-by-32-foot inground gunite pool. I enabled AI Navium mode, and it created a custom schedule, which had the robot clean the floor every other day and the floor and waterline once a week. This schedule kept my pool looking clean and fresh. I ran a handful of night cleaning sessions, and the LEDs and camera had no trouble zeroing in on leaves that had gathered in a corner of my pool. The Scuba V3 typically required between 160 and 180 minutes and used around 85% of its battery to clean my pool's floor, walls, and waterline during testing. It always returned to the side of the pool when the cleaning cycle was complete or when the battery level was low. My biggest gripe with this cleaner concerns emptying the debris basket. While larger particles are easy to wash out with a hose, cleaning the MicroMesh filter is another story. I had to remove it by hand and give it a good rinse, a process that always got my hands dirty with murky sediment. If you choose to use the MicroMesh filter, it’s a good idea to keep a pair of latex gloves handy. Final Thoughts Aiper Scuba V3 Pool Cleaner - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Aiper Scuba V3 takes the hassle out of pool care, leveraging smart AI navigation, dual filters, and night-vision LEDs to leave your floor, walls, and waterline spotless. It isn't without flaws—namely, a messy fine-mesh filter cleanup and a lack of underwater steering—but at $1,099.99, it delivers excellent, reliable cleaning power. However, if you prefer physical remote controls and higher suction, keep an eye out for sales on our Editors' Choice winner, the Dreame Z1 Pro, which frequently drops under $1,000. About Our Expert I’ve been working with computers for ages, starting with a multi-year stint in purchasing for a major IBM reseller in New York City before eventually landing at PCMag (back when it was still in print as PC Magazine). I spent more than 14 years on staff, most recently as the director of operations for PC Labs, before hitting the freelance circuit as a contributing editor.

item.title: iPhone 17 Is World's Best-Selling Phone Again, Samsung S26 Ultra Enters Top 4
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.00
While all the attention is on the next generation of iPhones Apple is about to unveil on Sept. 9, the company’s existing models continue to rule global sales. According to Counterpoint Research, the iPhone 17 was the world’s best-selling smartphone last quarter (Q2 2026), commanding 6% of global sales. Meanwhile, the iPhone 17 Pro Max and the iPhone 17 Pro came in second and third, respectively, to complete an all-Apple podium. The top three positions have now remained unchanged for two successive quarters. The same phones also led in Q4 2025, but the iPhone 17 Pro Max led that quarter, with the iPhone 17 coming in second. Per Counterpoint’s Q2 2026 report, Samsung's Galaxy 26 Ultra is the best-selling Android phone globally, and it’s the first time an ultra-premium phone has led the June quarter. The next two best-selling Android phones are also from the same maker: the Galaxy A07 4G and the Galaxy 17 5G. Surprisingly, the top 10 list only features phones from Apple and Samsung. The iPhone 17e and the iPhone 16 are the two other Apple devices on the list, while Galaxy A17 4G and Galaxy S26 are the two other Samsung phones. Combined, the top 10 phones accounted for 26% of global smartphone sales last quarter. For the iPhone 17e, support for MagSafe wireless charging and expanded storage from 128GB to 256GB at the same $599 price as the iPhone 16e played a crucial role in driving strong sales, Counterpoint says. The report arrives as Apple enters a new era. Tim Cook will step down as CEO on Sept. 1 and will be replaced by current hardware chief John Ternus. On Wednesday, Apple announced it is hosting an event on Sept. 9, where we expect Ternus to unveil the iPhone 18 Pro models and the company’s first-ever foldable iPhone. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Droplr Review: A Simple Screen-Capture App With Cloud Storage and a Few Limitations
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.97
There's no shortage of free and paid ways to capture images and recordings on your computer, thanks to screen-capture utilities. I know, I've tested many apps over the years. But even with that stiff competition, Droplr stands out from the pack. This low-cost tool makes it easy to capture and share images and recordings across a variety of devices, for yourself or with a team. Since I last reviewed the app, Droplr hasn't changed much, but competing tools have improved, such as Ashampoo Snap and ScreenPal, which is now an Editors' Choice winner for free screen capture. Still, Droplr is worth checking out, especially for business-focused teams. Droplr is a subscription-based screen capture utility, most similar to ScreenPal among the competitors I've tested. Unlike ScreenPal, Droplr lacks a free plan but offers a three-day trial to let you kick the tires. The Pro Plus plan lets individuals use Droplr for $6 per month (billed annually). For $7 per month (billed annually), up to 15 users can access Droplr's Team plan. This option also grants a handful of extra features, such as custom branding, domains, and team analytics. Enterprise customers receive even more features, such as larger team sizes, SSO account management, AI redaction and risk assessment tools, and unlimited bandwidth and storage. You’ll need to request a quote for that tier. Prices go up if you choose to get billed monthly rather than annually: $8 per month for Pro Plus and $9 per month for Team. Ashampoo Snap Pro 26 and Snagit sell their one-time-purchase software for $39.99 and $39, respectively (with low-cost upgrades if you're using the previous versions). The subscription-based ScreenPal starts at $4 per month for its paid plans. However, Windows Snipping Tool is a completely free app that has steadily expanded its capabilities. Alongside the base subscription, Droplr offers several premium add-ons. If you're willing to pay more money per year, you can access new features, such as logos for your uploaded files ($7 per year), a domain for your shared public page ($25 per year), and analytics tools ($24 per year). The tools are more targeted to professional users. As with Droplr itself, you can test these add-ons for free. Droplr works on a variety of platforms. I primarily used it as a Google Chrome extension. However, you can also download it for the Edge browser or as a desktop app for macOS and Windows. In addition, there are Android and iOS companion apps to use Droplr's screen recording features. Anything you record on one device syncs across all devices for easy cloud access. ScreenPal and Snagit sync with their respective mobile companion apps, but Snap Pro 26's Android app is standalone. As a Chrome extension, Droplr displays an unobtrusive window in your browser's corner with all your screen capture options. You can capture the selected area, the whole application, the whole screen, or use scrolling capture to take a screenshot of an entire long page. You can save the image to your desktop or to cloud storage (more on that in a bit). After capturing a screenshot, you use Droplr's image editor to mark it up. You can add text, draw colorful shapes, drop in emoji, and create links. You can change text size, but there's only one font style. So it’s not ideal for, say, filling out a form with a digital signature. Unfortunately, there's no optical character recognition (OCR) support, so Droplr can't recognize and edit text on the page like you can with Snagit and Snap Pro 26. Droplr's video recording is similarly easy. You can record just your screen, or turn on your webcam and microphone to record yourself along with your screen. I found the default icons a little small, but you can resize them. You can also modify what camera and microphone Droplr should use, record up to 4K video (maximum file size is 10GB), or turn your videos into unlimited animated GIFs (this must be done through the desktop apps). There are no real editing options, beyond trimming your video. ScreenPal offers a more substantial video editor as a premium add-on, with features including live video annotation, green-screen filters, and access to asset libraries. Droplr exports files in the PNG, MP4, and WebM formats. Those are pretty standard file types, but Snagit supports about 20. I found Droplr incredibly intuitive, but if you run into trouble, read its handy how-to guides to learn everything from recording on your phone to using screen recordings to supplement your hybrid work model. For more on grabbing items on screen, check out How to Capture Screenshots in Windows 11. Droplr doesn't just let you capture screenshots and recordings; it also lets you share and organize files for yourself, with your team, or publicly, depending on the privacy and collaboration settings you choose. Non-enterprise tiers enjoy 100GB of storage and 500GB of bandwidth per month. The dashboard displays all your files, pulled from all devices synced to your account. Here you can markup image files you still aren't pleased with, as well as download and share files with shortened URLs. To organize files, you can sort them into different themed "Boards," such as images for a mood board or videos for specific projects. You can also tag files with relevant metadata. For particularly sensitive files, you can schedule them to self-destruct after a set period. This kind of file-sharing functionality adds great utility to a paid screen capture utility, because many professional users who need to capture their screen are doing so to share information with other team members. It’s so much easier and faster to just share a video of what you’re doing than describe it step by step. Adding to the convenience, Droplr integrates with other programs such as Gmail, Google Docs, Photoshop, and Slack, and you can share files to social media. Although Droplr let me manually upload files outside of the file types it exports by default, those files didn’t always play back correctly. For example, two AVI videos I uploaded wouldn't play on my laptop, and when I tried to play them through Droplr’s mobile app, I only heard sound—no visuals. However, I could mark up the JPEG images I uploaded. Your mileage may vary, but you may want to stick to PNG and MP4 to ensure proper compatibility. Droplr lists all the file types it explicitly doesn't support. Final Thoughts Droplr - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. When it comes to paid screen-capture subscription services, Droplr is useful and intuitive, especially for professional users across a variety of devices. However, Editors' Choice pick ScreenPal, previously Droplr's closest rival, now surpasses it thanks to a free option and superior premium upgrades. Ashampoo Snap has also improved to a more capable premium utility. And for the best all-around screen-capture tool, check out Snagit, the reigning Editors' Choice pick for paid screen-capture utilities. STILL ON THE FENCE? About Our Expert My PCMag career began in 2013 as an intern. Now, I'm a senior writer, using the skills I acquired at Northwestern University to write about dating apps, meal kits, programming software, website builders, video streaming services, and video games. I was previously a senior editor at Geek.com and have written for The A.V. Club, Kotaku, and Paste Magazine. I'm the author of the gaming history book Video Game of the Year: A Year-by-Year Guide to the Best, Boldest, and Most Bizarre Games from Every Year Since 1977, and the reason everything you know about Street Sharks is a lie.

item.title: Ashampoo Snap Pro 26 Review: A High-Quality Screen Capture App With Live 4K Editing
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.63
Everyone from meme creators to CEOs must capture on-screen images—and sometimes video—to convey messages or share information. Snagit has been the face of screen capture utilities in the many years I've covered the category, but Ashampoo offers a serious alternative with Snap Pro 26. Like Snagit, the Editors' Choice winner for paid screen-capture utilities, Snap Pro 26 lets Windows users capture, annotate, edit, and publish images, and new live editing features expand the utility's video capabilities. Snap Pro 26 is a powerful app that has resolved its technical issues since our last review, even if a few remaining limitations keep it from becoming our top pick. Priced at $39.99 for a single-device license (or $12.99 if upgrading from a previous version), Snap Pro 26 is a relatively expensive screen-capture utility that costs roughly the same as Snagit ($39 per year). Fortunately, you get some unique tools for the money, which I detail later in this review. If you only need basic screen-capture features and want to save $40, the free Windows Snipping Tool is a sound option. Windows Snipping Tool lacks advanced features, such as GIF creation and Wi-Fi syncing, but it supports video recording. So, it will work in a pinch if you just need to capture images every now and then. ScreenPal, an Editors' Choice winner for free screen-capture utilities, offers video recording and generally more robust features. And with ScreenPal, you can upgrade to the Deluxe tier (GIF creation, green screen filter, and more) for a reasonable $4 per month. Grabbing a screen is simple. You select a capture method from the cool new radial menu at the top of the screen. There are shortcuts for numerous screen-capture options, including rectangular, freestyle, scrolling, timed capture, and full-window capture. You also use this menu to start a video recording or open the editor for the full suite of customization tools. Of course, you can simply tap the PrtSc key to capture the entire screen if you don't need to grab a specific area. In a nice touch, certain tools let you resize the capture area first before committing to a snap. Gamers can quickly capture screenshots of 2D and 3D games on their primary monitor without interrupting the action. That feature reminds me of the screenshot functionality in gamer-targeted software, such as Nvidia GeForce Experience, the Opera GX browser, and Steam. Snap Pro 26 continues to build on past iterations' strengths by keeping what worked and further polishing it. For example, with the new Live Edit feature, you can quickly mark up whatever you're seeing on your screen with notes and text before taking the shot. In essence, Live Edit makes capturing the screenshot the end of the process rather than the beginning. Ashampoo still offers many video-focused features, including timed video capture and live video editing. The latter is quite impressive, as it lets you annotate videos while you're recording, which reduces post-processing work. Snap also supports 4K resolution. You also get watermark options and video-capture capabilities, with numerous resolution and AVI/WMV options, that make creating tutorials and walkthrough clips a breeze. Like Snagit, Snap supports intuitive GIF creation and versioning, so you won't lose the original image after making tweaks. You can save images in the JPG, PNG, PDF, and PSD formats, and print from the app. Snap Pro 26 lets you lock the image capture tool to capture images in either 4:3 or 16:9 aspect ratio, which is handy if you favor certain dimensions. Snap conveniently saves your most recent captures in a row at the bottom of the interface for easy access. Snap Pro 26's OCR technology is yet another handy way to capture content. Suppose there's web page text you'd like to grab, but numerous on-page images make capturing it tricky. If you activate OCR mode, Snap Pro 26 scans the page, extracts the images, and presents clean text for capture. The app processes web pages with impressive speed. Snagit also offers this feature, but Snap has a slight edge in supporting multiple languages (English, French, German, Russian, Spanish, Turkish, Japanese, and more if you download additional languages on your device). The toolbar lets you add blur effects, color, arrows to highlight on-screen objects, and more. Editing images and adding effects (such as the outline options) proved effortless in testing. Overall, I found the redesigned interface very intuitive; it's easier to access the tools I want. After capturing video or a screenshot, your next step is to open the action bar tucked away on the right side of the screen. Depending on whether you captured a still or a video, you can email the content to others or upload it to various online destinations, including Ashampoo Web, Dropbox, Facebook, Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive, and X/Twitter. You can also send it to a printer or save it to your PC's hard drive. Snap Pro 26 lacks a companion app that lets you sync images between a PC and a handset on the same Wi-Fi network, as Snagit’s Fuse and ScreenPal's mobile apps do. Instead, Ashampoo offers a standalone Android screen capture app called Droid Screenshot. It lets you manually transfer images from your phone to your computer, and it isn’t as much of a hassle as you'd think. Unfortunately, just as Snap Pro 26 isn't on Mac, Droid Screenshot isn't on iOS. Snagit also lacks a dedicated Apple app, but you can at least use TechSmith Capture on mobile to send files to it. Final Thoughts Ashampoo Snap - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Ashampoo Snap Pro 26 has its weaknesses, from a lack of Apple options to the absence of the useful Wi-Fi Sync feature found in its main competitor, Snagit. However, live 4K video editing may be the feature that entices you away from our Editors' Choice winner among paid screen-capture utilities. In short, Snap Pro 26 is worth trying if you want to experience a screen-capture utility that does more than the average capture tool. STILL ON THE FENCE? About Our Expert My PCMag career began in 2013 as an intern. Now, I'm a senior writer, using the skills I acquired at Northwestern University to write about dating apps, meal kits, programming software, website builders, video streaming services, and video games. I was previously a senior editor at Geek.com and have written for The A.V. Club, Kotaku, and Paste Magazine. I'm the author of the gaming history book Video Game of the Year: A Year-by-Year Guide to the Best, Boldest, and Most Bizarre Games from Every Year Since 1977, and the reason everything you know about Street Sharks is a lie.

item.title: Rookie Mistake: Hacker's Attachment to Screen Name Made Him Easy to Catch
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.55
A hacker’s reuse of an online screen name likely helped investigators catch him. On Thursday, law enforcement arrested two men in Australia who are allegedly part of TeamPCP, a hacking gang that’s been spreading malware through open-source software tools. One of the reported suspects, 21-year-old Ruben Thomson, wasn’t hard to identify because of his association with the screen name DeadCatx3, cybersecurity provider Flare outlines in a new report. TeamPCP has been linked to the alias DeadCatx3 via an account on the software development platform GitHub, which the group used to host its tools. Flare looked to see if the DeadCatx3 handle was registered on any other platforms, and it popped up on HackerOne, a bug bounty platform security researchers use to submit software vulnerabilities. A user on HackerOne not only registered an account with the DeadCatx3 handle in June 2025 but also listed their full name on the profile. “The account in question had the name Ruben Thomson connected to it. It can’t be that easy, can it?” Flare said. It seems like it was. Flare uncovered a wider web of accounts traced back to Thomson, including a Steam account that featured a unique picture of a cartoon cat in a hoodie sitting in front of computer monitors. “We then found a screenshot of the TeamPCP Telegram account using the same profile picture as Thomson’s Steam account, signaling with high confidence that Ruben Thomson is the leader of Team PCP,” Flare concluded. The other reason TeamPCP was easier to investigate was that the group was “loud by choice,” Flare noted, and frequently posted on their Telegram channel and on X before their account was shut down. “A group that talks this much, this publicly, under this many aliases, doesn’t just invite scrutiny, but it hands you the first thread to pull,” the cybersecurity vendor added. Cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs did similar reporting on Thomson and even interviewed him last month before his arrest. Using the alias Ellis, Thomson "expressed no remorse over his cybercrime activities, and said he was grateful for the friendships and relationships built throughout his engagement with TeamPCP," Krebs wrote. "The young hacker also seemed resigned to his fate, and told KrebsOnSecurity that he’ll accept the consequences if he’s ever arrested." Australian Federal Police also reportedly arrested a 23-year-old named Louis Michael Gaebler. “It is estimated the malicious code potentially compromised more than 1,000 organizations globally, enabling the theft of more than 500,000 credentials, and the exfiltration of at least 300 gigabytes of data,” the agency added. Together, both suspects have been charged with 14 offenses and are scheduled to appear in a local court in Australia later today. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Switching to Claude? This Easy Trick Brings Your ChatGPT Memory With You
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.42
If ChatGPT isn't the AI chatbot for you, don't stick with it. You can easily jump ship to Claude and enjoy most of the same capabilities. Better yet, exporting your ChatGPT memories and bringing them into Claude takes only a minute. I walk you through the entire process below and explain exactly what will and won't survive the transfer. And if you're curious about how the two chatbots compare, check out our head-to-head matchup. What Can You Transfer From Claude to ChatGPT? You can transfer memory from ChatGPT to Claude, which includes a host of useful context and settings. Memory stores information about your career and identity, as well as the instructions you gave ChatGPT, the projects you worked on, and the preferences you expressed over the course of your chats. Some, but not all, of the above is self-explanatory. Your identity, for example, is a description of you based on your ChatGPT usage. For example, ChatGPT describes me as "highly engaged in gaming communities, including Warframe, Soulframe, Old School RuneScape, Nioh 3, and Where Winds Meet, often discussing builds, progression, and optimization.” Furthermore, I used ChatGPT as a tool when building my last computer, so “PC Watercooling Build Project” is one of my projects. Preferences cover a range of contexts based on your conversations. In my case, this means a bunch of information about what I want from certain computer components, as well as the specific components I chose for my build. My preferences also include taking screenshots on my phone when asking for fashion advice on my Warframes to avoid HDR-related color issues. It also notes that any such images I send still won’t perfectly represent how things look in the game. Generally, you should expect a fairly wide range of top-level information about you and how you use a chatbot to transfer from ChatGPT to Claude. What Won't Survive the Switch? Put simply, anything I didn't specifically mention above won't carry over. That includes apps you created, deep research reports, generated media, the text of your actual chats, and more. You can think of the process more like matching the settings of one app to another, rather than opening your music library in a different app. You should also remember that this process isn't perfect. For example, I talked with ChatGPT a lot about skincare, but those discussions didn't transfer. How to Transfer Memory and Settings to Claude All you need is a ChatGPT account and a Claude account, and not even a premium version of either. After you sign in to Claude, open its settings page, navigate to the Memory tab, and click the Start Import button to begin the process. Claude then walks you through a very short process: copy a prompt, feed it to ChatGPT, and paste its response back into the open window on Claude. Next, simply click the Add to Memory button, and the transfer completes nearly instantly. Afterward, you can prompt Claude to tell you what changed in its memory as a result of the transfer. In the aforementioned Memory section, you can also edit Claude’s memory. So, if there’s something that transferred from ChatGPT you don’t want in Claude’s memory or vice versa, you can tell Claude directly. As you use Claude, it will automatically continue to build out its memory of you. Moving to ChatGPT From Claude Isn't Quite So Seamless Transferring your memory from ChatGPT to Claude doesn’t remove anything from ChatGPT, so you can always resume using your ChatGPT account. However, ChatGPT doesn't offer a dedicated import memory function like Claude. Of course, ChatGPT’s memory isn’t set in stone. It’s entirely possible to view your memory in Claude, compare it with your memory in ChatGPT, and then tell ChatGPT to remember anything that Claude added to its memory as you used it. You really don't have to worry about losing anything permanently. About Our Expert I’ve been writing about consumer technology and video games for over a decade at a variety of publications, including Destructoid, GamesRadar+, Lifewire, PCGamesN, Trusted Reviews, and What Hi-Fi?, among many others. At PCMag, I review AI and productivity software—everything from chatbots to to-do list apps. In my free time, I’m likely cooking something, playing a game, or tinkering with my computer.

item.title: Four New Monthly Games Hit PlayStation Plus This September. Is It Time to Resubscribe?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.39
Is now the right time to re-up your PlayStation Plus subscription? The cost of gaming keeps getting more expensive with Sony hiking the price of its consoles. With the announcement that it plans to eliminate all physical games in the near future, does moving to a gaming subscription model make more sense? Like Microsoft's Xbox Game Pass, Sony's PlayStation Plus service adds new titles to its video game streaming service every month. To the uninitiated, PS Plus is a bit more complicated than Game Pass. While Sony grants subscribers access to monthly titles, depending on your tier, you'll also be able to play from its Game Catalog, Ubisoft+ Classics, and Classics Catalog. This month, you'll get Sony's premier baseball game, MLB The Show 26, Sniper Elite: Resistance, and two other games. Since PlayStation Plus saw price hikes earlier this year, is it still worth the cost? Here's everything new coming to PlayStation Plus this September and how to decide if this game streaming subscription is worth the money. New to PlayStation Plus for September 2026 Whether you subscribe to the Essential, Extra, or Premium tier of PS Plus, all subscribers gain access to the service's four monthly games. This round will be available from September 1 to October 5. They are: MLB The Show 26 (PS5) The latest edition of Sony's baseball video game series, MLB The Show 26, builds on the accomplishments of its predecessors. New for this release is an expanded single-player mode that includes high school and college baseball, a balls and strikes challenge system, an expanded card-collecting mode, and World Baseball Classic tournament formats and rosters. PS Plus members gain access to exclusive in-game content. Chained Echoes (PS4) Chained Echoes is a 16-bit style JRPG set in a fantastical world of magic and mech armor. On your journey to bring peace between three warring kingdoms, you will visit diverse landscapes, fight enemies, and collect up to a dozen party members before everything is said and done. Sniper Elite: Resistance (PS5, PS4) The latest entry in the long-running Sniper Elite franchise, Resistance is a third-person tactical shooter set in Nazi-occupied France. Your mission is to aid the ongoing resistance, and the game offers significant freedom in how to approach mission objectives. Wobbly Life (PS5, PS4) This online co-op game brings players together in an open-world sandbox filled with mini-games, collectibles, and tons of secrets. Additional game modes ensure there's always something to play, even if you want a break from the larger world. Members also have until August 31 to claim August's monthly games lineup, including Big Walk, Dying Light 2: Stay Human, and Signalis. New to PS Plus Game Catalog for August 2026 In addition to the monthly games, those who subscribe to the Extra or Premium tier gain new titles in the service's Game Catalog, a large collection of games that can be played with an active subscription. Here are the most recent additions: - Dying Light 2 (PS5, PS4) - August 25 - Hell Is Us (PS5) - August 25 - Helldivers 2 (PS5) - August 12 - Kingdom Come: Deliverance II (PS5) - August 18 - Metro Exodus (PS5, PS4) - August 25 - Two Point Museum (PS5) - August 25 - Umamusume Pretty Derby – Party Dash (PS4) - August 25 - Vampire Survivors (PS5, PS4) - August 18 New to PS Plus Classics Catalog for August 2026 If you subscribe to the Premium tier, you gain access to the Classic Catalog, which is loaded with PS1, PS2, and PS3 classics. These are the most recent additions: - Onimusha: Dawn of Dreams (PS5, PS4) - August 18 - Disney’s Atlantis: The Lost Empire (PS5, PS4) - August 18 What Games Are Leaving PlayStation Plus in August Here's what's leaving the service on September 15: - Madden NFL 26 - Persona 5 Tactica - Romance of The Three Kingdoms XIII - Toukiden 2 - Bubsy: The Woolies Strike Back - Toy Story 2: Buzz Lightyear to the Rescue - Toy Story 3 - Shadowrun Returns - Shadowrun Hong Kong: Extended Edition - Shadowrun Dragonfall: Director’s Cut What Do You Get With PlayStation Plus? In 2022, Sony merged its PlayStation Plus online multiplayer service and the PlayStation Now game subscription to create one platform that unlocks online gaming, cloud storage, exclusive offerings, and Share Play. Select additional games are also offered at no extra cost, with the exact details dependent on your subscription tier. Speaking generally, the higher the tier, the more games you can access. Here's how much each PS Plus membership tier currently costs and what you get for the money: - Essential: At $10.99 per month, Essential is PlayStation's cheapest plan, offering online multiplayer, cloud storage, and three games to play each month. - Extra: Increasing to $16.99 per month for the Extra plan will also gain you access to the Game Catalog and a collection of Ubisoft games. - Premium: For $19.99 per month, the Premium plan promises classic PlayStation games, game trials, PS5 cloud streaming, and access to a collection of films from Sony Pictures. Is PlayStation Plus Worth the Money? PlayStation Plus may make more sense for your wallet than buying games outright. It all comes down to what type of gamer you are, how often you play, and whether you care about owning your games. The monthly games that PlayStation adds to its Plus tiers only stick around for about four weeks, so make sure to claim them if you want them to stay in your library. The service also regularly adds and removes titles from its Game Catalog. You'll need to keep track of how long games will be available to make sure you get to play the titles you're most excited about. As an example, let's say you want to play all four of August's monthly games: MLB The Show 26 ($70), Sniper Elite: Resistance ($60), Chained Echoes ($25), and Wobbly Life ($25). That's $180 worth of games for just the $10.99 monthly service cost. That's a steal, as long as you claim them before the month is up. Once claimed, they'll appear in your library for however long you're subscribed. But if you're more interested in the service's giant Game Catalog, you'll want to pay attention to when titles leave so you can play them before they disappear and get your money's worth. And if you're not interested in a set of games one month or need to give your wallet a break, you can cancel the monthly plan at any time. You won't be able to access any games you claimed after you cancel, but they'll be available again once you restart the service. If you don't care about owning what you pay for or don't plan to replay games, PlayStation Plus might be the more affordable gaming option for you. Just make sure the games you're getting are actually worth the price of admission. If not, rotating subscriptions can be a good way to keep your monthly subscription costs low. About Our Expert As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: Nvidia CEO: We've Achieved AGI, But It Doesn't Really Matter
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.06
AI capable of matching or surpassing human intelligence remains a major goal for the tech industry. But to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, this artificial general intelligence (AGI) is a milestone that’s become irrelevant. “For many tasks, we could say that we have already achieved AGI. I think all of those milestones...are kind of senseless at this point,” Huang said in an earnings call on Wednesday. In contrast, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman tells Time in a new interview that his company will develop AGI internally by the end of this year. In OpenAI’s case, the company defines AGI as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work.” Huang didn’t define AGI on the earnings call. But he said it’s no longer people just prompting AI to execute tasks; more AI programs, called agents, can already run autonomously and improve “recursively," by running the task over and over again. “I think the most important thing that matters for the industry is that one, AI is doing productive and useful work,” he said. “Two, AI is generating profitable tokens. And three, if we had more compute, we could generate more profitable tokens, which results in more profit for all of the services. This is the exact phase where we are at.” The focus on productivity and profit might be in response to growing concern about an AI bubble amid unprecedented investment in AI data centers, even though the two leading players, OpenAI and Anthropic, still need to prove they’re profitable. Other critics say large language models will never achieve AGI because they lack persistent memory, struggle to understand logic, and remain prone to hallucinating incorrect information. In the meantime, Nvidia is raking in huge profits, generating $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2, up a staggering 106% year-over-year. The company also indicated it could grow even more, if not for the AI-driven memory shortage. Nvidia expects the shortage to remain a bottleneck at least through the early part of 2028. "We are experiencing extreme pricing conditions in memory," Nvidia CFO Colette Kress said on the call. "The magnitude of the price increase has exceeded our prior expectations, and [it's] headed even higher into next year." That doesn't bode well for the company's graphics cards, which have already seen a recent price increase. As for Huang, he indicated on Lex Fridman's podcast earlier this year that the tech industry had already reached AGI to a certain extent. “I think it’s now. I think we’ve achieved AGI,” he said, pointing to how today’s AI programs can create an app capable of going viral and attracting billions of users that later fizzles out. “Now, the odds of 100,000 of those agents building Nvidia [are] zero percent,” he added.
