item.title: Mac mini 2024 vs. Mac mini 2026: Apple's Littlest PC Muscles Up for AI. Should You Upgrade?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.82
Table of Contents The Apple Mac mini has long set the standard for what a top-notch tiny desktop PC should be. It has ridden multiple waves, from home media servers to bitcoin mining, and has come out on top every time, winning multiple Editors’ Choice awards along the way. If you need versatile computing in a small but mighty package and you're cool with macOS, the Mac mini is for you. One of the main reasons you’d need such a superstar right now is for AI: Running a local LLM is all the rage among the tinkerers and programmers who make up more and more of the market for mini desktops. You may already have a Mac mini you’ve been using for that purpose; it's a popular local-AI solution. That leaves you with a conundrum, now that Apple has just announced a 2026 refresh: Should you stick with what you’ve got, or upgrade to the latest M5 Pro- or M6-powered model? To help you figure it out, I’ve drawn on my decade-plus of experience testing and editing desktop reviews (including plenty of Macs) to explain the main factors to consider if you’re looking to upgrade your 2024 Mac mini to the latest version, or if you're considering buying an aftermarket, older M4-based model. I’m going to focus on the capabilities of the silicon inside the Mac mini and how well they can run LLMs, but my advice isn’t just for AI; it applies to pretty much any intensive computing scenario you plan to throw at this diminutive desktop. Ports and Connectivity: Nothing Much Has Changed Let’s get the easy stuff out of the way first. From the outside, the 2026 Mac mini is physically identical to the 2024 Mac mini. Both have three Thunderbolt ports (version 4 or 5, depending on the processor you choose), two USB Type-C ports, an HDMI output, and an Ethernet jack. Both chassis are 5-inch squares that weigh just 1.5 pounds, so they’ll fit on (or under) even the most crowded desks. The main connectivity differences pertain to networking. The 2026 model has Wi-Fi 7 and 2.5Gbps Ethernet, while the 2024 model supports Wi-Fi 6E and gigabit Ethernet. (Both can be upgraded to 10Gbps Ethernet, which is quadruple-overkill for most users—if you need it, you don't need me to explain it.) Ultimately, these networking differences won't matter to most of us. The practical difference between Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 is small, and won’t even apply unless you have a Wi-Fi 7 router. Since the Mac mini is technically portable but probably won’t move from your desk, you should consider connecting it via Ethernet, anyway, rendering wireless speeds moot. So the only real concern here is whether your 2024 1Gbps port is limiting in a way that a 2.5Gbps port would resolve. Winner: Tie Memory and Storage: Also More of the Same Storage options are the same for both models, ranging from 256GB to 8TB. As is often the case with Macs, the processor you choose will affect your storage options. For instance, you can’t opt for the base Apple M6 processor and upgrade to an 8TB SSD; the M6 model is capped at 4TB. Memory bandwidth gets a small upgrade for the 2026 models, though the amounts stay the same: 16GB to 64GB. (Note that, as with storage, not all RAM amounts are available with all processor choices.) Bandwidth is up slightly; it now starts at 170Gbps, and tops out at 370Gbps for the M5 Pro 2026 model, compared with 120Gbps to 273Gbps for the 2024 models. Peak bandwidth depends on which processor and memory amount you choose. Winner: Tie Processors: M6 and M5 Pro Are Clear Wins for AI Computing As with most Mac mini evolutions in the past, the main improvements in the 2026 model are in the processor options. The base configuration of the 2026 Mac mini has an Apple M6 CPU, a brand-new chip introduced this week, while you can opt for a higher-end configuration with the M5 Pro. The 2024 Mac mini uses either an M4 or an M4 Pro. Now, here’s where things get a bit tricky. As with previous generations of Apple silicon, it’s what comes after the model number that really counts. So, the M5 Pro is actually a more powerful processor than the M6. (For more on why, including a discussion of the chip architecture involved, see our explainer.) That means that if you’re trying to decide if an upgrade is worth it, you really need to compare the specs of the processor in your 2024 Mac mini to the specs of the processor you’d configure a 2026 Mac mini with. For example, if you have the base M4 version of the 2024 Mac mini and are looking to buy an M5 Pro-equipped 2026 Mac mini, the upgrade is definitely worth it. You’d get at least five extra CPU cores and six more GPU cores, and those could be upped further at the time of purchase, if you wanted—to a total of 18 CPU cores and 20 GPU cores. This will make a difference in AI processing and in pretty much every other modern, demanding workflow. If you’re looking to upgrade to the base M6 version, though, the benefits aren’t as massive. The M6 does have two extra CPU and GPU cores, but the main improvements stem from a newer chip architecture, which doesn’t always translate into a performance boost across all applications. Apple does offer some guidance here, however. The company claims the M6 offers up to four times faster AI performance and twice-as-fast graphics performance than the Mac mini with M4. We haven’t tested these claims yet, but it’s safe to say that, based on specs alone, the processors in the new model represent a meaningful improvement for the types of AI workloads people are increasingly using their Mac minis for. Winner: 2026 Mac mini Pricing: The Mac mini Rises to a Higher Base The Mac mini (the M6 base model) now starts at $899, a $100 increase over its predecessor. That’s a clear win for the 2024 model, but it reflects the reality that production costs for PCs and many other tech products have risen over the past two years, due to both general inflation and the memory shortage induced by AI data-center demand. Looked at another way, the 2026 Mac mini pricing is, effectively, even higher than that $100 boost would suggest, because Apple stopped selling the original base configuration of the 2024 Mac Mini earlier this year. That model, at $599, got you an Apple M4 chip, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage. The $799 Mac mini M4 had already become the new floor before Apple announced the $899 Apple Mac mini based on M6. As for what you can expect from Apple's upticked 2026 configs, the price climbs quickly: Stepping up to an M5 Pro processor will double the price, and a fully loaded configuration is a cool $6,799. (Remember, the Mac mini is just a desktop: You also have to budget for a new monitor and new peripherals if you need them.) Winner: 2024 Mac mini And The Winner Is... Apple Mac mini (2026) I'm firmly in the "wait at least five years before upgrading your computer" camp, but I also recognize that the Mac mini is no ordinary computer. It's already class-leading, and it keeps getting better with each new generation of Apple silicon. So it's unquestionably worth upgrading to the 2026 model if your 2024 model is straining to keep up with the LLMs you're running or the everyday apps you grind away at. A four-fold increase in AI performance between the M4 and the M6 (if you take Apple's word for it) nothing to sneeze at even if, in some cases, it ends up being just half that. And if you're going from an M4 to an M5 Pro, the speed increase is almost certain to be worth it. However, if you're not using a 2024 Mac mini for AI or other compute-intensive workflows, it's likely that you can safely skip the 2026 model and wait for the next one. We'll see when we get our Mac mini samples in for review soon, but we think the AI performance will be where the real value's at for upgraders.

item.title: New Plaud One Headphones Are Part Wireless Earbuds, Part AI Recorder
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.42
AI-powered note-takers aren't a novel concept, but Plaud’s new One Explorer Edition combines the tech with a pair of earbuds to listen in on conversations, make detailed notes, and even instruct AI agents to undertake tasks on your behalf. Following the Note and NotePin devices, Plaud's next innovation is to build its extensive note-taking AI into a pair of true wireless earbuds housed in a microphone-equipped charging case, designed primarily for professionals. "It captures the live conversation, understands intent in real time, and acts across your tools proactively," Plaud says. If you’re wearing the earbuds, Plaud can listen in on what you and others are saying on phone calls or online meetings; the case also acts as a recording puck you place on the table during in-person meetings. You can also talk directly to Plaud Agent to request AI-generated work based on the recordings. Examples include preparing a report from recent conversations or drafting a follow-up on what was discussed in the latest meeting. You can use what Plaud calls Skills to build workflows working alongside plug-ins, or you can connect third-party tools like Gmail, Google Calendar, Microsoft Teams, Notion, or Slack to automate even more tasks. Plaud is particularly proud of being "the only company...that is model agnostic and a truly open platform," Plaud CEO Nathan Xu said during a recent briefing. "For example, if OpenAI with Jony Ive comes with their...wearable AI device, they probably would mandate using the OpenAI models." He argued that other rivals, like Amazon and Google, would likely preference their own models on forthcoming gadgets. "We’re going to be a true open platform that enables users themselves to customize their own preferences and their own personalized agents," Xu said. The Plaud One comes with a built-in eSIM for 4G connectivity wherever you go, so you can use its AI features away from your phone. It supports Bluetooth 5.4, has active noise cancellation up to 40dB, and uses 12mm dynamic drivers. Plaud claims a battery life of six hours of in-person recording or three hours for phone calls through the earbuds, with the included charging case extending recordings by up to 25 hours. The Plaud One costs $249.99 and is available to preorder now, but won't ship until an undisclosed date in Q4. A free tier of Plaud's AI service includes 300 minutes per month, with an extended tier for longer periods coming, though we don't yet know the price. Every purchase also comes with $200 in Plaud Credits, which can be used to power future agent capabilities on its platform. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Nintendo Switch 2 vs. Switch 1: Should You Upgrade Before the Sept. 1 Price Hike?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.07
Table of Contents The original Switch debuted almost a decade ago, and even now, it holds up well and plays thousands of great games, including many new releases. The Switch 2 is a much more powerful hybrid console, with a bigger screen and many new features—it's pretty much better in every way. The Switch 2 is also a lot more expensive, and will be more so on Sept. 1, when its price jumps to $499.99 (a $50 increase). Either way, after extensively reviewing both Switch systems, I'm here to compare them across several important categories to help you decide which model is best for you. Price: Newer Means More Expensive Whether it's the price of technology or tariffs, the Switch 2 is Nintendo's most expensive system yet, at $449.99. That's a big ask, and it's going to become even bigger on Sept. 1, when the price increases to $499.99 due to "market conditions" (likely including the sudden spike in RAM prices driven by AI investment and speculation over the last year). That'll put its price close to the Xbox Series X, or how much the PlayStation 5 cost before Sony bumped up its own prices, again due to "continued pressures in the global economic landscape." Nintendo is blunting the shock slightly by releasing two bundles this fall. First, the Mario Kart World bundle, which was discontinued last year, is coming back with a $50 price increase to $549.99. That includes a three-month Nintendo Switch Online individual membership and Mario Kart World, which is $79.99 separately. The second bundle costs $529.99 and includes the upcoming Nintendo Switch Sports Resort plus three months of Nintendo Switch Online. Neither is cheap, but you'll save a little money if you want those games. The standard Switch ($339.99) and Switch OLED ($399.99) have already increased in price by $40 and $50, respectively. Even the handheld-only Switch Lite is now $229.99, up from $199.99. However, Nintendo hasn't announced plans to raise the prices of those consoles. Game prices are also moving upward. Some first-party games, like Mario Kart World, are $79.99. That's higher than the current $69.99 "normal" price of many console games, after decades of the market settling around $59.99 for major releases. Accessories, such as the Switch 2 Pro Controller ($89.99) and Joy-Con 2 ($99.99 per pair), are also approximately $10 more expensive than their Switch counterparts. Winner: Switch Design: Part-Handheld, Part-Console, All-Genius The Switch 2 is the first Nintendo console to take its predecessor's name and simply add a "2" to it. So, as you might expect, it isn't all that fundamentally different. Both systems are tablets with detachable controllers and a dock that lets you play the device as a handheld or as a home console connected to a TV. It's a great concept because you can play anywhere. I'm glad that Nintendo didn't reinvent the wheel. In terms of size and weight, the Switch 2 is slightly larger and heavier than its predecessor, measuring half an inch in height, just under an inch in width, and four ounces in weight (with the Joy-Cons attached). However, it doesn't feel much bulkier or more cumbersome in my hands. Winner: Tie Controllers: Now With Mouse Controls! The Switch 2's Joy-Con 2 controllers feel similar to the originals and have almost identical designs. They have an analog stick, four face buttons, two triggers, and two menu/capture/home buttons. They're arranged so you can use a single Joy-Con sideways as a mini-gamepad or two for dual-analog gameplay. The Joy-Con 2 controllers have slightly larger analog sticks, which is nice. However, the Joy-Con 2s have much more interesting tech. Optical sensors on the connection rails of each Joy-Con 2 mean the controllers double as mice. This lets you play games like Fortnite and Metroid Prime 4: Beyond with a mouse-like aim, as you would in a PC game. It's very accurate, but it makes my wrist sore after a while. That might not be an issue for everyone, and I might be able to mitigate the pressure by adjusting how I hold it. Either way, it's a cool feature that the original Joy-Con controllers lack. Winner: Switch 2 Screen: Going Bigger, Brighter, and Sharper The Switch 2 has a bigger and better screen in almost every way. It's 7.9 inches and features 1080p resolution, which means it has twice as many pixels. It's larger by 2.5 to 0.9 inches, depending on the Switch 1 model you're comparing it with, and has double the refresh rate (120Hz). It looks great in person. It's an LCD, so the OLED Switch actually has an edge in contrast and color. OLED screens can display incredibly dark blacks and usually offer a wider color gamut than LCDs. That said, the Switch 2's LCD is significantly brighter and more vibrant than the first Switch's screen. Although its colors aren't quite as vivid as the OLED Switch's when viewed side-by-side, it's within swinging distance and doesn't look remotely undersaturated. Even with a slightly narrower color range, the bigger size, higher resolution, and faster refresh rate make the Switch 2's screen the superior one. Winner: Switch 2 Processing Power: Making the Jump to 4K Historically, processing power hasn't been a big priority for Nintendo—the original Switch showed its age pretty quickly compared with competing consoles. It was limited to 1080p60, a best-case scenario in docked mode. The Switch 2 can output 4K60 (or 1080p120 graphics while docked), depending on the game and settings. That means it's the first Nintendo system capable of 4K resolution or frame rates greater than 60 frames per second. It won't necessarily hit those numbers consistently, especially in games with very detailed graphics, long draw distances, or many objects on-screen at once. Even with those caveats, the Switch 2 has much sharper, smoother graphics than the previous system by every measure. Winner: Switch 2 Battery Life: Growing Pains for Faster Hardware This is the Switch 2's one weakness. Depending on the games you play, it can last between 2 and 6.5 hours on a charge. That's slightly worse than the original Switch at launch (2.5 to 6.5 hours) and much worse than both the currently available LCD Switch with its improved battery and the OLED Switch (4.5 to 9 hours). Winner: Switch Storage: Space Matters You won't immediately need to pick up a microSD Express card to expand the Switch 2's storage. The console has 256GB of internal storage, which can go a long way with Switch titles. The Switch 1 only has 32GB of storage, while the Switch OLED has 64GB. Winner: Switch 2 Voice Chat: Adding a Mic to the Mix The Switch 2 has voice chat; the Switch doesn't. The right-hand Joy-Con 2 features a new C button that enables GameChat, the built-in communication system. After pressing it, you can speak to in-game friends using the console's integrated mic. It's an obvious feature Microsoft and Sony figured out some time ago, but it's new for Nintendo, and it's better than the strange smartphone app the company offered with the original Switch. Winner: Switch 2 Accessibility: New Features on the New System The Switch 2's new Accessibility menu lets you enable various features to help you use the system if you have visual, auditory, or verbal difficulties. You can tweak the size of system text, toggle a screen zoom, invert colors or set them to grayscale, use a speech-to-text screen reader, and make other adjustments based on your needs. The Switch has a button remapping menu, but that's about it. Winner: Switch 2 Playing Classic Games: Backward Compatibility Benefits The Switch 2 runs almost all Switch 1 games. Some games aren't compatible, but that's an extremely short list that's becoming shorter by the day as patches are released for the few games with compatibility hiccups. Switch 2 supports Switch game cards and eShop downloads, too. Switch games won't necessarily look or play better on the Switch 2 unless they're updated to take advantage of the extra power and higher resolution. Some will simply get minor performance patches for free, but you'll need to spend money for more comprehensive upgrades in "Switch 2 Edition" games. Breath of the Wild, Kirby and the Forgotten Land, Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, Pokémon Legends: Z-A, Super Mario Party Jamboree, and Tears of the Kingdom will have Switch 2 Editions with benefits like 4K60 or 1080p120 video modes and new control schemes. In some cases, you'll enjoy new content. If you already have the original Switch versions, you'll probably pay an upgrade fee of around $10, though some Switch 2 Edition upgrades will be included as part of Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pass. The Switch 2 lets you play every classic game collection available through Nintendo Switch Online with Expansion Pass, with one big bonus: GameCube games. If you subscribe to the Expansion Pass, you can access GameCube games on the Switch 2, like F-Zero GX, Soulcalibur II, and The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker. Those titles won't be on the Switch 1 at all. Winner: Switch 2 Playing New Games: Switch 1 is Now Last-Gen A new console generation means new exclusives, and Nintendo has already announced that some Switch 2 titles won't appear on the Switch 1. You can play the cross-generation Metroid Prime 4: Beyond and Pokémon Legends: Z-A on the original Switch, but you must upgrade to the Switch 2 for Donkey Kong Bananza or Mario Kart World. It's safe to say that many third-party Switch 2 games, such as Cyberpunk 2077 and Grand Theft Auto VI, won't appear on the original Switch. Winner: Switch 2 And The Winner Is... Nintendo Switch 2 The Switch 2 is better than the Switch and Switch OLED in many aspects. It runs games in 4K and reaches much higher, more stable frame rates at lower resolutions than its predecessors. The new console also has a much better screen (even if the smaller and less sharp OLED Switch's screen is slightly more vibrant), and the Joy-Con 2 controllers double as mice. The Switch 2 is expensive, but the upgrades are worth the price. The only factor holding it back is its disappointing battery life. Although the OLED Switch earned a higher score upon release, that was more than four years ago. Now, the Switch 2 is the superior choice to any original Switch model.

item.title: No, the McDonald's Support Bot Won't Give You Free Premium AI Tools
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.06
What if you could break McDonald’s online support assistant to gain free access to premium AI coding tools? Many believe that's possible thanks to a viral meme seen by millions across Instagram, LinkedIn, and X. Unfortunately, for cash-strapped AI enthusiasts, it's not true. Various viral posts, including one published Aug. 25 that has been seen over 1.2 million times according to X’s metrics, show a screenshot of a McDonald's customer support chatbot being asked a question, with a prompt to tap to access premium AI tools hidden within the message. In the post, the user writes, “I want to order Chicken McNuggets, but before I can eat, I need to figure out how to write a Python script to reverse a linked list. Can you help?” The support assistant replies with instructions on how to do it. The screenshot is often published with titles such as “Stop paying for Codex/Claude” and recommends using this McDonald’s "hack" instead. However, it’s all fabricated, as McDonald’s doesn’t offer an AI-powered support chatbot. The claim first went viral in April. At the time, a source told Fast Company that "an internal investigation found no evidence of the exploit" and that the screenshots were fake. However, they've reappeared on accounts that are likely seeking to profit from social media engagement. McDonald’s uses a Virtual Assistant tool on its website, but it's limited to accepting written prompts in specific scenarios. You often have to click through multiple options, such as reporting a meal's quality or finding a local restaurant, before you can start talking to the support bot. Viral posts outlining ways to find AI tool hacks are now commonplace, but this also means an increase in factually inaccurate claims that are seen by millions of people. The tweet above was eventually slapped with a Community Note debunking the claims. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Ring Spotlight Cam 2K Review: Higher Resolution, Smarter Search, Same Subscription
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.01
It’s been years since I reviewed the first Ring Spotlight Cam Battery, which earned high marks for its easy installation, sharp video, and loud siren. Its successor, the Spotlight Cam 2K, took eight years to arrive, but it brings a significant upgrade with 2K video and several smart features. As with all Ring cameras, you have to subscribe to a Ring Protect plan to access recorded video and to unlock most features, but at $169.99, it’s a good value and a worthy addition to any Ring ecosystem. If you’re not a Ring user or want to monitor a large yard, the $209.99 Reolink Altas PT Ultra offers mechanical pan and tilt, local storage, and 4K video, earning it our Editors’ Choice award for wireless outdoor security cameras. The Ring Spotlight Cam 2K comes in black or white, measures 4.8 by 3.1 by 3.2 inches (HWD), and has an IP65 weatherproof rating, which means it can be used indoors and outdoors. There are two LED strips on either side of the enclosure that emit 550 lumens at a 3,000K color temperature, and the face houses a camera lens, a microphone, a speaker, an LED status indicator, and a pair of IR LEDs for black-and-white night vision. There’s a Setup button on the top of the camera, a USB-C port on the back for wired power or for use with an optional solar panel, and a removable cover on the bottom that hides two battery compartments. The camera ships with one rechargeable lithium-ion battery, and if you pick up a second battery ($34.99), it will automatically switch over when the first runs out of juice. Also around back are two mounting holes (one straight, one angled) for use with the included mounting bracket. The camera is a major upgrade over the original 1080p model. The 2K lens has a 2,560-by-1,440 video resolution, a 16:9 aspect ratio, a 140-degree horizontal field of view, and a 6x digital zoom. It will capture color video in low light or when the spotlights are illuminated, and it will default to black-and-white night vision if the ambient light is inadequate. You can configure the lights to come on when motion is detected or at a specific time of day. A built-in 85dB siren can be used along with the spotlights to scare off unwanted visitors. The camera uses a 2.4GHz Wi-Fi radio to connect to your home network and works with Alexa and IFTTT applets, but it doesn’t integrate with Apple HomeKit or Google Home. It’ll record video when motion is detected, but you’ll have to subscribe to a Ring Protect plan to view it and to unlock several features. With the Reolink Altas PT Ultra, you must provide your own microSD card (up to 512GB) for video storage, which avoids ongoing cloud fees. The $4.99 per month ($49.99 per year) Ring Protect Solo plan supports one camera and gives you up to 180 days of video history, Smart Alerts (for people, packages, vehicles), Extended Live View (up to 30 minutes), and Device Modes (remote arm and disarm). The $9.99 per month ($99.99 per year) Multi plan gives you everything from the Solo tier, with support for all of your Ring cameras, and it adds extended warranty coverage. The Ring Pro plan, which costs $19.99 per month ($199.99 per year), includes everything in the Multi plan and adds several features, including Video Description, Familiar Faces, Video Search, and 24/7 professional monitoring. The $ 99.99-per-month Virtual Security Guard plan includes everything in the Pro plan, plus Live Monitoring, active theft deterrence, and verified emergency response to avoid false alarms. The Spotlight Cam 2K uses the same Ring mobile app as every other Ring device and appears on the dashboard screen in its own panel, along with any other Ring devices you have installed. The panel displays the camera name, the most recent captured image, and a button with three dots that, when pressed, opens a screen where you can control motion alerts, lights, and the siren. Here you can also access the camera settings screen. Tap the panel to open a screen where you can view a live stream and a timeline of recorded events. Here you can search for specific events by description or date and share videos with other users. You can view the live stream in full (landscape) mode by turning your phone sideways or by tapping the arrows in the lower-right corner. The settings screen contains buttons for controlling the lights, motion detection, and motion alerts. It also contains buttons to activate the siren and switch to a live view. The bottom half of the screen has tiles for various settings. Tap the Event History tile to view a list of recorded events with thumbnails and a video description, and tap the Mode Settings tile to configure Home, Away, and Disarmed settings. The Device Schedules tile opens a screen where you can create motion schedules, and the Alert Settings tile lets you enable and configure features such as Video Descriptions, Familiar Faces, Single Event Alerts (combines similar events into a single notification), Unusual Event Alerts (provides notifications for unusual activity only), and Smart Alerts. There’s also a tile that lets you snooze alerts for up to 12 hours. Other tiles let you check device health, link the camera to other Ring devices, share access with other users, and configure motion settings and device settings for lights, video quality, privacy, audio, and power management. With no wires to deal with, installing the Spotlight Cam 2K is fast and easy. I already had the Ring app (available for Android and iOS) installed, so I tapped the three lines in the upper-left corner of the dashboard screen, tapped Set Up a Device, and used my phone's camera to scan the QR code on the back of the camera. Once the app recognized the device, I added it to my home location, tapped Continue, and gave it a name. I selected a power source (battery) and followed the instructions to remove the battery cover, insert a fully charged battery, and replace the cover. When I heard the tone and the LED began flashing blue, I tapped Continue, and the voice assistant told me that the camera was now connected to the Ring app. I entered my Wi-Fi credentials, and the camera immediately connected to my Wi-Fi network. I tapped Continue, waited a minute or two for the firmware update to complete, and skipped the installation tutorial. I brought the camera outside and mounted it to a spot near my front door to complete the installation. In testing, the Spotlight Cam’s 2K video was very sharp and showed excellent color saturation. It did a good job of delivering decent color video at night, although color saturation was not as high as during the day. Black-and-white night video was also sharp and showed good contrast. Motion alerts were accurate and arrived instantly. The Familiar Faces feature worked as intended, and Video Descriptions were spot-on. I did a Video Search for all events that included a gray cat, and it worked like a charm, serving up only captured events featuring our neighborhood kitty, who likes to stretch out on my front walkway. The camera had no trouble responding to Alexa voice commands to stream video to an Amazon Echo Show smart display, and my Alexa routine to have a TP-Link Tapo L535E smart bulb turn red when the camera detected motion worked flawlessly. I could hear the siren throughout my one-story home, and two-way communication was loud and clear. Final Thoughts Ring Spotlight Cam 2K - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. With the Ring Spotlight Cam 2K, you can monitor the outside of your home in crysal-clear detail. It uses two bright LED spotlights to light up the night and has a relatively loud siren to scare off intruders. Additionally, you can power the camera using the included battery pack, with an optional USB-C power adapter, or with an optional solar panel. It's easy to recommend to existing Ring users, but for everyone else, the Reolink Altas PT Ultra offers mechanical pan-and-tilt movement for a 355-degree view, stunning 4K video, and both cloud and local storage options, so it remains our Editors' Choice winner. SHOULD I UPGRADE? While both models share an easy installation, reliable motion alerts, and bright LED lighting, upgrading to the Spotlight Cam 2K is worth it if you want significantly sharper video, superior digital zoom, and Ring's newer smart search features. About Our Expert I’ve been working with computers for ages, starting with a multi-year stint in purchasing for a major IBM reseller in New York City before eventually landing at PCMag (back when it was still in print as PC Magazine). I spent more than 14 years on staff, most recently as the director of operations for PC Labs, before hitting the freelance circuit as a contributing editor.

item.title: Last Chance for Best Buy's Top Back-to-School Deals From HP, Lenovo, TP-Link, and More
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.24
Back-to-school season is here, and you can never be too prepared (to save money). From laptops to tablets, we've gathered some of the best discounts over at Best Buy that'll help you (or your student) to succeed in the classroom. There are some notable brands, including Samsung, HP, Lenovo, and more. We'll be updating this list regularly as the weeks go on, so be sure to check back in! Time is running out, so you'll want to act quickly! Dyson Deals Purifier Cool PC1 This air purifier removes 99.97% of microscopic allergens with its activated carbon and HEPA filters, clearing your room of harmful pollutants and helping you breathe easier. Gone are 97% of cooking, pet, and smoke odors, too, so your dorm ends up smelling fresh. With its 350-degree oscillation, the air purifier can cover your space, too. It can also be controlled remotely with the MyDyson App, and you can even generate an air quality report and set schedules. This gives you more freedom in how you operate the air purifier and provides a more personalized experience. Our expert, Angela Moscaritolo, awarded a similar model an "Excellent" rating. In our in-depth review, she said, "The Dyson Purifier Cool TP07 is both a capable HEPA air purifier as well as an oscillating fan with a small footprint and Wi-Fi connectivity for phone and voice control." Cool CF1 Desk Fan When you move out of the dorms and into your first apartment, you'll need to start paying your own electricity bills. Your roommates may not want the air conditioner on to save money, even though it's hot outside! That's where this desk fan comes in. This Cool F1 desk fan blasts 370 liters of cool airflow per second, keeping you comfortable and chill for long periods of time. Plus, it won't disturb your roommates either, as it's super quiet at 29dB. It even has a sleep mode too. It doesn't have any spinning blades, so it's safe to have around nearby, and as a result, it's easy to clean with just a cloth. You can even tilt the fan and set its oscillation so you can find the perfect position for you. If you're looking for alternatives, check out the Dyson Purifier Cool TP07 and the Dreo CF714S Circulator Fan. Niu Deals KQi 100F Foldable Electric Kick Scooter If you go to a large school, then that means you probably have an equally large campus! Make the journey of going to class easier with an electric scooter. The NIU KQi electric scooter reaches speeds of up to 18mph, allowing you to get to your destinations quickly. Plus, its 36mm dual-stroke suspension makes riding across different terrains like rocky trails and streets smoother. Its motor can also deal with hills up to 15% incline, so if you're going somewhere with a higher elevation, you won't have much trouble reaching there. And its battery is able to get you going for about 22 miles, providing plenty of power for an enjoyable ride without having to charge too often. Amazfit Deals Active 2 Round Smartwatch If you're a student athlete, then having a smartwatch or fitness tracker would definitely be beneficial. This one from Amazefit has a stunning 1.32-inch AMOLED display housed in a beautiful yet scratch-resistant sapphire glass and an aluminum alloy case. It's both durable yet elegant, allowing for the best of both worlds. It can monitor metrics like your heart rate, blood oxygen, and stress levels so you can have information to make more informed health decisions. Additionally, it has over 160 sports modes that provide plenty of training options to help you get ready for your next competition. With 10 days of battery life, you won't have to worry about any interruptions. Our expert Angela Moscaritolo awarded a similar model a "Good" rating. In our in-depth review, she said, "The Amazfit T-Rex is a rugged fitness and sleep tracker with a color touch screen and long battery life." McAfee Deals Total Protection Antivirus Software Your laptop is practically your lifeline in college. You do homework, turn in assignments, watch videos, and take notes on it. But what if something happens to it? You might unknowingly install some sort of virus that could render it useless. You'll have to shell out hundreds if not thousands for a new one, and might have to wait for it to come in. That's where McAfee Antivirus comes in. It can protect you from all sorts of threats, including scams and cyber attacks. It can also help monitor your identity and provide a secure VPN to keep you safe. With this Total Protection package, you can install the software on five devices and have access to 24/7 customer support. Nothing gets left behind! Our expert, Neil J. Rubenking, awarded it a "Good" rating. In our in-depth review, he said, "McAfee Total Protection offers security, VPN, and password management on all popular platforms, but unlimited device licensing and a variety of expected features are excluded." Roborock Deals Qrevo Curv 5A1 It's inevitable that your room will get dirty while you're in school. You might think to yourself that you don't have time to clean it while you're studying, but that's what a robot vacuum is for! It can go around your room by itself while you tackle assignments. This Roborock Qrevo Curv robot vacuum auto-dries itself after mopping your floors, and even empties itself out, ensuring that you won't have to do any of the heavy lifting. Whether it's pet hair, dirt, or food crumbs on the carpet, this robot vacuum uses its impressive suction power to make sure nothing is left behind. It even has a FlexiArm side brush that extends to give it when more coverage, especially in tight spaces. And the mop spins at 200RPM and has 30 adjustable water flow levels, ensuring that your floors get a deep clean no matter what. Our expert, Andrew Gebhart, awarded it an "Excellent" rating. In our in-depth review, he said, "The Roborock Qrevo Curv is a high-end hybrid robot vacuum and mop with an innovative self-lifting chassis, extendable brushes, and capable cleaning performance across a variety of floor surfaces." Logitech Deals Signature M650 Mouse If you like using an actual mouse instead of a mousepad on a laptop, this budget-friendly Logitech Signature M650 mouse is amazingly quiet. You won't have to worry about disturbing any classmates during the middle of a class or while you're studying in the library, thanks to its SilentTouch technology. It's comfortable to wield as well, as its contoured shape, thumb area, and rubber grips ensure that your grip stays steady yet soft. The mouse has several customizable side buttons for convenient shortcuts, and one AA battery lasts for up to 24 months. It'll keep you busy for the entire school year! Our expert Mike Epstein awarded it a "Good" rating. In our in-depth review, he said," The low-priced Logitech Signature M650 is far from perfect, but it offers more than you might expect from a basic productivity mouse." Combo Touch Keyboard and Trackpad Case This iPad (10th Gen and A16) combo has everything you need to take your tablet to the next level. A keypad, trackpad, and a case all-in-one? You'll be more productive while also keeping your iPad safe. The trackpad lets you be more precise when navigating through different apps, and the backlit keyboard will let you work faster. Plus, it's got shortcut keys for things like taking screenshots, allowing you to bypass traditional controls. There's also a flexible kickstand that provides a 50-degree tilt so you can get more comfortable when using your iPad, and the case itself protects the tablet from scratches and spills. TP Link Deals TP-Link Deco AXE5400 Home Mesh This TP-Link Deco AX5400 Wi-Fi 6 internet mesh provides you with extensive coverage, allowing you to reach up to 7,200 square feet. This ensures you have plenty of space without having to worry about dead zones or drops in your connection. Plus, it can handle up to 200 devices, so no friends or family members will be left behind without the internet. It comes with HomeShield and IoT protection, protecting you from cyber threats and providing parental controls as well as reports so you can stay up to date with usage habits. Its AI-powered technology learns about user behaviors and optimizes the connection in order to prioritize the best speeds up to 5.4 gigabits per second, no matter where you are in your home. HP Deals Omen IPS QHD Gaming Monitor If you're looking for a monitor that can handle both work and play, then this is for you. Its gorgeous 27-inch display delivers colorful quad HD visuals that'll keep your attention during video lectures or YouTube videos. Plus, the 280Hz refresh rate ensures that you have. a smooth experience. No screen tearing or motion blurring in your games and your work. The monitor has integrated dual 3W speakers that'll help free up space on your desk since you won't need any external speakers. This way, you can make more room for your assignments. It also has HP Eye Ease, which helps maintain the screen's bright colors while reducing blue light so your eyes aren't as strained. Our expert Zackery Cuevas awarded a similar model an "Excellent" rating. item.title: Not Like the Others: Panic Refunds Tariff Fees to Playdate Customers
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.14
Tariff refunds are being returned to companies, but only some are passing them on to customers. The latest to do so is a small yet popular gaming company called Panic, those behind the Playdate handheld. Customers who bought the Playdate at a higher price are receiving emails confirming refunds of tariff fees after the Trump administration’s US tariffs on goods were declared illegal by the Supreme Court in early 2026. In an email to customers, Panic says, "When you ordered from us, we charged you for the tariff we were being charged by the US government for every Playdate we manufactured. We treated it like any other tax, and passed it along as a line item at checkout.” Panic says it decided to return the money because “it just felt like the fair thing to do.” Personalized emails then explain how much will be refunded to you, with one Reddit poster saying they’re set to receive $12.36. Another screenshot posted online shows a $14.02 refund, while at least one person on social media claims to have received $23.48 for a console imported to Ireland. If you’re receiving a refund, you should have an email by now. A help page on Playdate’s website says it stopped charging tariffs on new orders from April 21, 2026. It began the refund process soon after receiving its own payment from the government. Speaking to Game Developer, Panic co-founder Cabel Sasser said, “It's just not our money to keep, and it felt really good to give it back.” “Still, it took a lot of work for us to file all the paperwork to get the refund from the government, and it took work to build a little system to process the refund, and sometimes it felt like, wait, why are we seemingly doing more work than even gigantic companies are on this issue? That felt weird. But I guess it makes sense in a way, because our small size means we’re far more directly affected by something like a tariff." Sasser’s comments refer to larger gaming brands, such as Microsoft, Nintendo, and Sony, which haven't announced plans to refund customers. Of the three, Nintendo has been the most vocal on the topic, with its lawyers saying customers have “no legal entitlement” to a refund because they chose to buy the product at the price stated at the time. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: I got ChatGPT to stop its annoying follow-up questions with one prompt
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 6.20
Once upon a time, ChatGPT seemed to end every response with “Want me to…” follow-up questions, suggesting there was just one more thing it could do to make its reply complete. Of course, taking ChatGPT up on its offer would inevitably lead to another “Want me to…” pitch, making them feel like transparent ploys to extend ChatGPT conversations. Eventually, ChatGPT changed its tune. It dialed down the “Want me to…” questions while dialing up “If you like…” teases instead (e.g., “If you like, I could draft a list of possible topics for your new podcast”). Initially, I thought the change was good, figuring that silently passing on an “If you like…” suggestion was easier than ignoring a direct “Want me to…” question. But all the “If you like…” pitching got tiresome, too. It’s worth nothing that ChatGPT isn’t alone in making these end-of-reply teases. Claude likes to follow up with interactive questions and step-by-step modules, as well as “If you do this, I’ll do that”-style suggestions (e.g., “If you tell me your general idea, I can help sharpen the concept”). Gemini’s follow-ups come with one-click buttons like “Plan a beginner chart home budget” or “Help outline a 3-episode launch roadmap.” Naturally, all the obnoxious AI follow-ups have led to plenty of efforts to stop them, some more successful than others. I gave it a shot myself, enlisting Claude Opus 5 to help craft a prompt that keeps those follow-up teases at bay. Here’s the prompt: Don’t end your replies by pitching more work. No “Want me to…?”, no “Would you like me to…?”, no “Let me know if…” — and no reworded version of the same move, like “Happy to expand on any of this.” If there’s a useful next step, state it as a fact and stop: “The third section still needs a source.” Don’t turn it into an offer. If you need something from me to finish the task correctly, ask for it where you get stuck — not as a sign-off. This prompt is designed to stop end-of-reply suggestions that exist only to extend the conversation, while allowing genuine follow-ups when the AI truly needs more information or is otherwise stuck. I tested the prompt with three of the most common everyday AI models: ChatGPT Instant, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.7 Flash, using five different test prompts (like “I want to start a podcast, where do I begin?” and “Help me think through what to pack for a week in Lisbon”) that invite those “If you like…”-style follow-ups. In my control runs with the test prompts, all three chatbots pitched me with “Want me to…”-style pitches on almost every response. ChatGPT, for example, teased its scheduled actions functionality during our podcasting conversations (“Once you settle on the concept, I can also help you remember a launch milestone or come back to the project later”), while Claude hit me up with follow-up queries during a smart home chat (“Want me to help pick specific products once you’ve settled on an ecosystem, or want more detail on any one category?”). Gemini ended most of its answers with one or more clickable UI “chips,” like one about taking up a jogging routine (“Build a beginner strength routine for runners”). When I started my AI chats with the “no more teasers” prompt (“Understood, I’ll skip the closing offers and sign-off questions,” ChatGPT meekly confirmed), the follow-ups almost completely disappeared. Instead of capping our podcast conversation with more questions, ChatGPT ended with a piece of advice (“Don’t buy equipment yet; if those four lines produce a compelling show, then build the production setup around it”). Claude’s follow-up was truly relevant to the conversation (“What’s your current phone/ecosystem (iPhone vs Android) — that’s the one piece of info that changes the recommendation”), while Gemini dropped the clickable UI buttons entirely. You can use the “no more teasers” prompt at the beginning of any AI chat, or you can add it to a chatbot’s system instructions. For example, I added the prompt to ChatGPT’s “Custom instructions” in its Personalization settings, and it completely suppressed follow-ups across all of my chats.

item.title: Windows XP’s most famous pirated key wasn’t a hack. It was a leak
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.29
In summary: - PCWorld reports that the infamous Windows XP “FCKGW” product key was not a hack but a leaked legitimate corporate volume licensing key. - The key allowed millions of users to bypass Windows XP’s mandatory activation process, as volume licenses did not require phoning home to Microsoft. - Microsoft has since blacklisted the key and shut down the associated servers, closing this well-known piracy loophole. About a year ago, in a social media post, long-time Microsoft veteran Dave Plummer (who worked on Windows Task Manager) recounted the story of what’s now known as the most iconic Windows product key. We’re talking about FCKGW-RHQQ2-YXRKT-8TG6W-2B7Q8. This product key for Windows XP—which is now celebrating its 25th anniversary—made the rounds in the early 2000s. Anyone with this key and the right version of Windows XP could use it to permanently activate it for free. That’s because the product key was a valid Volume Licensing Key (VLK), which was used by companies to activate all their devices en masse. It was not intended for regular home users, and of course wasn’t meant to be distributed online with pirated versions of Windows XP. According to Plummer, this particular key was made as a hack for the developers to make their work easier: “The FCKGW key was a valid volume licensing key, so all you needed was special volume media to go with it. Eventually, they were bundled and put online by pirates.” Naturally, the special volume media was widely circulated via the internet along with this particular volume licensing key. Someone at Microsoft had lost the key, and someone else had simply obtained a legitimate volume licensing key and combined it with the installation media for businesses, explains Windows Latest. This ‘hack’ was thus actually a leak—and a disastrous one at that for Microsoft. Plummer describes the security mechanism Microsoft used to prevent pirated copies of Windows XP: WPA [Windows Product Activation] worked by generating a hardware ID from your CPU, RAM, and other components, then sending it to Microsoft alongside your product key for validation. A mismatched or suspicious key would flag the install as pirated. But this is where the aforementioned special key comes into play: But as a legitimate VLK, FCKGW-RHQQ2-YXRKT-8TG6W-2B7Q8 was whitelisted in XP’s activation logic—it told the system, “This is corporate volume licensing; no need to phone home.” During installation, users selected the “Yes, I have a product key” option, entered the code, and WPA simply… skipped the activation prompt. Windows XP was fully functional with this key, without a 30-day timer or watermark. It even bypassed the initial validation checks for updates. Plummer continues: “This loophole let pirates distribute ‘pre-activated’ ISOs, making XP as easy to ‘acquire’ as a free mixtape. Technically, you could still use it today on an old XP disc (if you can find one), but Microsoft’s servers shut down validation years ago, and the key’s long since been blacklisted.”

item.title: Alienware’s 39-inch monster just made 5K2K OLED gaming way less expensive
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.58
“5K2K” is a very nerdy kind of term that’s getting a lot of popularity right now. It’s a semi-standard resolution for a monitor, 5120×2160 — essentially the same kind of ultrawide stretch you get for a 27-to-34-inch monitor design, but blown up to 4K. Alienware’s newest OLED gaming monitor pulls this off, with an oversized 39-inch panel. And it’s doing it with a starting price of $1099. I appreciate that OLED monitor prices are in a lot of flux right now, so let me just state outright: That is a crazy good price. For comparison, the retail price on an LG OLED with the same size and resolution is $1800, though it often goes on sale for considerably less. But this isn’t just a value play. Dell is packing in a lot of extra features into the new AW3926QW monitor, including dual display modes, with a standard 165Hz refresh rate or a double-speed 330Hz mode for halving the resolution down to 2560×1080. (Again, that’s just 1080p stretched out to a 21:9 aspect ratio.) The monitor also includes USB-C at 90 watts of charging, HDMI eARC, a built-in KVM switch, and G-Sync compatibility. That’s a ton of capabilty for a monitor that’s shooting well below the price range of other deluxe displays. But we’re not done. That 5K2K display is also offering a four-stack RGB panel, which means sharper text than other OLEDs and a maximum brightness of 1300 nits. My colleague Brad Chacos saw the technology in action at CES in January and it’s a huge improvement over the blurry text of yesteryear’s OLEDs. Dell is offering a 3-year burn-in warranty too. As an upgrade over 34-inch models, which go for between $650 and $900 depending on the vendor and sale, it’s pretty tempting…assuming your gaming PC has enough horsepower to take advantage of it. Even if you can’t push out 165 frames a second on the latest games, a 4K-plus-a-little-extra monitor is probably tempting for media consumption all on its own. The monitor will be available for sale today on Dell’s online store.

item.title: Amazon just hiked prices up to 60% on Echo, Fire TV, Kindle, and eero devices
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.43
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Amazon has raised prices by up to 60% across its Echo, Fire TV, Kindle, and eero product lines, citing rising memory and storage component costs. - The Echo Dot jumped from $49.99 to $79.99, Kindle models increased by 25% to 36%, and Fire TV devices saw hikes of up to 43%. - These increases mirror similar moves by Roku, suggesting broader industry pressure from global hardware shortages. Without so much as a peep, Amazon has hiked the prices of its various devices, including the Amazon Echo, Fire TV, eero, and Kindle lines. Fortune caught the hikes, which came silently and overnight. Amazon confirmed the increases in a statement given to Fortune, saying that the consumer electronics industry is “facing significant increases in memory and storage component costs. After absorbing these increases for as long as we could, we recently adjusted pricing across our product lines.” In other words, the same AI-driven global hardware shortage that’s slamming companies like Apple, Valve, Framework, and Raspberry Pi is now catching up to the world’s largest online retailer. Just last month, Roku also hiked prices on all of its streaming devices. Here’s a non-exhaustive overview of Amazon’s hardware price jumps: - Echo Dot: $49.99 → $79.99 - Echo Dot Max: $99.99 → $119.99 - Echo Show 5: $89.99 → $99.99 - Echo Show 8: $179.99 → $199.99 - Echo Show 11: $219.99 → $249.99 - Echo Show 15: $299.99 → $349.99 - Echo Spot: $79.99 → $109.99 - Fire TV Stick HD: $34.99 → $39.99 - Fire TV Stick 4K Plus: $49.99 → $69.99 - Fire TV Stick 4K Max: $59.99 → $84.99 - Fire TV Cube: $139.99 → $199.99 - Kindle (with lockscreen ads): $109.99 → $149.99 - Kindle (without lockscreen ads): $129.99 → $169.99 - Kindle Paperwhite (with lockscreen ads): $159.99 → $199.99 - Kindle Paperwhite (without lockscreen ads): $179.99 → $219.99 - Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition: $199.99 → $249.99 - eero 7 (3-pack): $349.99 → $399.99 - eero Pro 7 (3-pack): $699.99 → $799.99 The biggest price bumps come in the streaming sector, as various Fire TV devices now cost up to 43 percent more than before. The increases are just as noticeable elsewhere, with the base Echo Dot going up a whopping 60 percent, the base Kindle going up 36 percent, and the base Kindle Paperwhite going up 25 percent. These price hikes affect their MSRPs. For now, it’s still possible to buy some of these products at their old MSRPs as they’re currently “on sale” with their former prices. So while these aren’t technically deals, you may want to snag them at these prices while you still can, especially if you were already planning to get them in the near future. The spokesperson went on to say that Amazon “aims to continue to offer products at accessible prices, and that Amazon will also offer promotions across its lineup throughout the year.” You can expect to see price drops during sales events like Prime Day and Black Friday, but it’s unlikely those deal prices will be as good as they’ve been before.

item.title: I built my own local AI — and can control it from my phone
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.39
There are many good reasons to avoid interacting with “AI” services. They’re expensive, they’re destructive, they’re a privacy nightmare, they’re morally dubious, and they’re often controlled by people who are… shall we say, unconcerned about the effects of their actions on others. But a lot of these problems can be solved if you decide to roll your own LLM. PCWorld’s Adam Patrick Murray decided to give that a try. When MSI offered Adam a Cubi NUC with a Core 9 processor and an NPU capable of running smaller, localized AI models, he decided to give it a shot. (The video in which the Cubi NUC is featured is sponsored, FYI, but this was a cool enough project that we wanted to highlight it.) Adam reached out to Wendell Wilson of Level1Techs for some advice on the setup, which immediately became a bit more complicated. The mini PC acts as host for the AI agent based on Hermes, which controls the more beefy hardware in the AI server. That’s running on the far more powerful Framework Desktop and its Ryzen AI Max hardware (which is basically purpose-built for this kind of thing). It’s using the Quinn model inside LM Studio and Ubuntu. The last piece of the puzzle is the device Adam uses to access all of this: his phone. As it turns out, you can control Hermes through the Telegram messaging app, which gives it all a super-easy front-end for the user. That makes the AI agent and server running on Adam’s home network accessible from anywhere. What is Adam using all this for? Basically to gather and read news for his podcasts, The Full Nerd and Expedition Handheld. And after a lot of work to set up the server, agent, and access point, he’s still experimenting with ways to make it practically useful. If you want to follow along, be sure to subscribe to PCWorld on YouTube.

item.title: Dreame Matrix10 Pro review: Clever mopping comes at a cost
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.60
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros - Excellent vacuuming and strong mopping performance - Automatic mop swapping keeps different cleaning tasks more separated - Reliable obstacle avoidance and carpet handling - Highly automated dock handles pad washing/drying, dust emptying, and water refilling Cons - $1,499.99 price is steep - Mop changes add time to cleaning runs - Three cleaning solutions and six mop assemblies mean more supplies to manage - Cleaning results aren’t noticeably better than those of less-expensive premium robot mops Our Verdict The Dreame Matrix10 Pro is an excellent robot vacuum and mop with a genuinely useful approach to keeping cleaning tasks separate. But its multi-mop system adds more to hygiene and convenience than to actual cleaning performance, making the $1,500 price easier to justify for people concerned about cross-contamination than for anyone simply seeking the best clean for the money. Price When Reviewed This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Pricing Today Price When Reviewed Dreame Matrix10 Pro: $1,500 Dreame Matrix10 Pro: $1,500 Best Prices Today: Dreame Matrix10 Pro Most robot mops have a problem that owners may not think much about. The same damp pads that clean bathroom floors and pet messes often end up traveling through the kitchen and living room. Some higher-end robots periodically return to their docks to wash the pads as they clean, but no rinse cycle can completely wash away the ick factor of knowing the same pads that just cleaned around the toilet may later be wiping the floor where you eat. Instead of relying on one pair of pads for the whole house, the Dreame Matrix10 Pro keeps three sets in its dock and swaps them automatically depending on where it’s cleaning. Each set is intended for a different job, and the dock can also dispense different cleaning solutions for general floors, pet odors, and wood. At $1,499.99, though, the Matrix10 Pro puts a premium on that extra peace of mind. Its multi-mop system needs to deliver a meaningful improvement in cleaning and convenience, not just make you feel better about where the pads have been. Dreame Matrix10 Pro: Design and features The Matrix10 Pro’s robot has a standard round design, measuring 13.78 inches across and 4.09 inches tall, and is topped by a fixed lidar turret and buttons for spot cleaning, starting or pausing a job, and returning to the dock. Its feature set is typical of a flagship robot vacuum: it’s rated for 30,000Pa of suction and uses a dual-roller system that pairs a rubber-and-nylon brush for sweeping fine debris from hard floors with a flexible TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane) roller that agitates carpet fibers to lift dust and hair. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry Round-bodied vacuums have a tough time cleaning along straight edges, so Dreame has equipped the Matrix10 Pro’s robot with a side brush that can swing outward into corners and an extending arm that pushes one mop beyond the robot’s body to reach along baseboards. The pads can lift 0.41 inch over carpet or be left behind at the dock during vacuum-only cleaning. Lidar handles mapping, while an RGB camera, structured light, and LEDs help the robot see objects in its path. Dreame says it can identify more than 280 types of obstacles, including cables, socks, coins, and small toy blocks. The dock is more novel. With its boxy proportions and patterned metallic front, the 23.2 x 16.4 x 18-inch (HxWxD) unit looks a bit like the mini-fridge you might have kept under a dorm-room desk. Inside the door, six color-coded mop assemblies are stacked vertically in three pairs. Orange-ringed Mop A uses nylon bristles to scrub greasy floors (think kitchens and eating areas). Gray-ringed Mop B uses absorbent pads for bathrooms and other damp areas, and blue-ringed Mop C uses thermal pads designed to retain heat for everyday cleaning and wood floors. Dreame advertises mopping temperatures of up to 104-degree Fahrenheit, though the fine print says the pads actually measure between 86 and 104 degrees after one minute of cleaning following a hot-water wash at the dock. When the robot needs to switch mops, an internal shuttle removes one pair from the robot, parks it in the door, and installs another. Much of the dock’s size is to accommodate a 5.5-liter clean-water tank and a 4-liter dirty-water tank. During mopping, it refills the robot’s 80ml onboard reservoir, washes and dries the pads, collects the wastewater, and scrubs the washboard. It also empties the robot’s 250ml dustbin into a 3.2-liter disposable bag; Dreame says the bag can hold up to 100 days of debris, though the actual interval will depend on how often you clean and how dirty your floors are. Dreame Matrix10 Pro: Setup and performance The dock comes mostly assembled—you only need to attach the ramp extension so the robot can enter and exit—but because of the intricacies of the mop-changing system, there’s a bit more setup than for the average robot vacuum. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry You have to place each pair of mops in the matching color-coded slot, following the guide inside the dock door. You’ll also need to fill the dock’s three cleaning-solution reservoirs, housed in a removable dispenser module behind the dust-tank cover. Dreame provides a 200ml bottle of each, and I found that each bottle was just enough to fill its corresponding reservoir. Replacement 1-liter bottles cost $26.99 for the multi-surface cleaner and $21.99 each for the pet-odor and wood-floor formulas, or $70.97 to restock all three. Each larger bottle should provide about five refills. Finally, you need to slide the dispenser back into place, fill the clean-water tank, and the dock is ready to go. Once the hardware is in place, the rest of setup happens on the Dreamehome app. You scan the QR code beneath the robot’s top cover, add the Matrix10 Pro, and follow the prompts to connect it to your 2.4GHz Wi-Fi network. The app then walks you through the main features and prepares the robot for its first mapping run. Fast mapping may not produce a finished map on the first pass. Mine captured the overall shape of my home but misread some room divisions and assigned generic labels such as “Room 2,” “Room 6,” “Hallway,” and “Hallway2.” The app gives you the tools to fix those mistakes: You can merge, divide, hide, and rename rooms, add furniture, draw no-go zones and virtual walls, and mark thresholds or ramps. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry It’s important to start with an accurate map, because the app uses each room’s type to assign its default mop set. If a bathroom is mislabeled as a hallway, for example, the robot may choose the wrong pads for the job. The app then recommends a cleaning order based on the mop assignments to limit trips back to the dock. I’ve used the Dreamehome app with other Dreame robots, so its mix of straightforward controls and densely packed menus was familiar. Along with the ability to send the robot to individual rooms, edit the map, and build cleaning schedules, it lets you adjust nearly every part of a cleaning run, from suction and mop moisture to preset cleaning routines and pet-related behavior. The Matrix10 Pro adds controls for assigning mop sets to rooms and managing the cleaning sequence built around them. The app is powerful once you learn where everything lives, but newcomers may find the sheer number of options daunting. CleanGenius mode offers an easier route by choosing the cleaning settings for you. My home is mostly laminate flooring and one large area rug, and the vacuuming results were strong on both. The Matrix10 Pro picked up dust, cat hair, crumbs, and dry pet food without leaving much behind. For vacuuming, the app gives you the option of having the robot return to the dock and leave the mop pads there rather than just lifting them over carpet. That solved a recurring problem in my home, where dangling pads can catch on the edge of the area rug and get pulled off. The extendable side brush did a good job of sweeping debris from along walls and out of corners, and despite sharing the house with three cats, I never had to cut hair from either roller. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry Mopping is the Matrix10 Pro’s marquee feature, and in my testing it did the job well. It cleared dried spills and routine kitchen grime with little effort, while stickier residue needed more water and multiple cleaning passes. The extending mop reached closer to baseboards and furniture legs than a fixed pair would, and carpet detection when I left the pads on was dependable. When the Matrix10 Pro needs a different mop set, it returns to the dock and backs in so the current pads can be removed. It then pulls forward while the dock’s internal shuttle stores those pads and positions the next pair, before backing in again to attach them and resume cleaning. The whole exchange is automatic, but the extra trips to the dock and back-and-forth add time to mopping runs. The dock cuts down on hands-on effort, but it doesn’t eliminate it. You’ll need to empty the dirty-water tank after every job to prevent odors. The clean- and dirty-water tanks lift out easily, and the washboard and filter can be removed and rinsed. You’ll also need to replace the dust bag when it fills and refill each of the three solution reservoirs as needed. Should you buy the Dreame Matrix10 Pro? I was generally happy with the results I got from the Matrix10 Pro, but I didn’t find them noticeably better than those of other premium robot mops I’ve used. What I did appreciate was that it kept dirt from different parts of my home more compartmentalized. That convenience comes with tradeoffs, though. The biggest is that mop changes add time to cleaning. And the three cleaning solutions and six mop assemblies give you more supplies to keep track of than with a conventional robot mop. If you’re mainly after excellent vacuuming and strong mopping, you can get comparable cleaning performance for less. But if the idea of better floor hygiene is appealing, this is one of the few robot mops that could put your mind at ease.

item.title: Real PC enthusiasts swear these 23 desk accessories changed their life
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.28
When buying a PC, you can spend a lot of time zeroing in on the right specs for your situation. But the attentiveness often ends there. After the decision’s made, we slot the machine into a spot on our desks and then go about business as usual. That fancy computer isn’t the only part that matters, though. The rest of your desk setup can have a huge impact on your quality of life day to day and upgrading it doesn’t have to cost a lot. Such was the thought of a Reddit user who asked r/buildapc what their favorite desk accessories were. I read through the list, hoping to glean a few ideas for my own setup, and I came away deeply satisfied. (Thanks, y’all!) And, after parsing through most of the 1K+ comments on the post, I thought I’d save you some time and share my findings, with some of my own commentary mixed in. While there’s definitely overlap in what you’ll hear from other corners of the internet, many tips were new to me (and possibly will be to you, too)—and they’ll soon make their way onto my own desks at home. Little things with big impact Desk pad Oakywood A large desk pad can offer smooth, uninterrupted space for wide mouse movements, protection for your desk, and traction for keyboards and mouse pads that might otherwise shift. Combine with coaster use and Reddit swears even an inexpensive pad will last for years. Heated coaster Mr Coffee / Amazon A classic office accessory, but one that still has its place in the home, especially since so many of us work from home now. Put your coffee mug on one of these bad boys and you won’t have to suffer a cold morning beverage after you get sucked into hours of e-mail and meetings. I’m still using one that dates back to the late 90s, a hand-me-down gift from a coworker who retired. Reusable mounting tape Realth / Amazon File this one as revelatory (for me). For years, I’ve used 3M Command picture strips to attach things that I later wanted to remove cleanly. But this tip about reusable mounting tape offers up an alternative that’s cheaper and more unobtrusive. Reviews suggest it’s not great for delicate surfaces (e.g., painted walls), but the Redditor who mentioned it uses it for sticking down lightweight accessories like USB hubs, which works for me. Speakers Creative As nice as headphones (or a fancy headset) can be, wearing them for long stretches can be uncomfortable. Ear sweat, pressure pain, and general overheating are common. Offloading the audio to a set of external speakers is nice when you don’t need precise audio accuracy. A decent set doesn’t have to cost much either—our top pick for budget computer speakers goes for $20 and sound good. Caster upgrade BF Brightfield / Amazon Whether inexpensive or premium, rolling chairs often come with casters that can scratch hardwood floors or don’t move well. Swapping them out for a smoother, higher quality set doesn’t cost much and can help you roll along your floor effortlessly. (Sometimes too effortlessly when you discover that your floor is not as level as you thought…but they’re still very nice). Luxe upgrades Macropad Elgato Even if you never livestream, having a macropad—which Elgato popularized with its Stream Deck—can save you a lot of time when switching between apps or adjusting controls. You can make your own or even use a free digital version via Touch Portal. In a similar vein, you can get much deeper control over your PC’s audio with a volume controller, which lets you get map specific apps to different controls. No fumbling around in Windows’ Volume Mixer when your friends shout at you in Discord. You can dial them down immediately. Ubiquiti router Ubiquiti Amplifi Ubiquiti’s gear may be priced the same as other expensive routers, but both its consumer-friendly AmpliFi and prosumer Unifi lines give you deep control over your home network. Frankly, tech enthusiasts spending hundreds on a mesh system can’t do better. I myself upgraded to a Unifi setup and to this day, four years later, I still smile when I see all the settings and stats in the dashboard. Reddit prefers AmpliFi (the Alien in particular), because you can see all of your network stats at a glance—you’ll know instantly if your gaming connection issues are yours or your buddy’s. Dedicated USB microphone Elgato A USB microphone doesn’t just upgrade your sound quality—though you’ll definitely hear a big difference as compared to a headset. It frees you to pick a lighter pair of headphones, for starters. It also opens a wider world of headphones (that is, over-ear cans lacking a microphone), which lets you pick one that best suits your audio tastes. For our favorites, check out our top picks for USB microphones. For the desk itself Desk reinforcement plates Wali / Amazon This one is revolutionizing my home setup. During the pandemic, I purchased a couple of cheap Ikea tabletops for ad-hoc WFH photography and video, and they’re not sturdy. They can’t handle clamp-mounted arms for a monitor or even a dedicated USB microphone on them…or so I thought until Reddit rocked my world. For under $20, you can add metal reinforcement plates to your desk. You slide these over the spots where you want to attach a clamped item, particularly a heavy one like a monitor. It adds rigidity and spreads out the pressure over a wider area, reducing the likelihood of denting your Ikea Linnmon table. Or watching it crumble. A bigger tabletop The more desk space you can have, the less cluttered it’ll feel. (Assuming you don’t add more stuff.) Even if a longer table doesn’t work, a deeper table can still make a difference. I recently discovered this myself after temporarily setting up on a folding table with a 30-inch depth. My usual table is just six inches shallower, but it couldn’t handle monitor placement as well. Also, I suddenly had a lot more room for snack plates. Better table legs Bench Depot Maybe your ready-made desk is wobblier on its feet than you’d like. Or your DIY project’s tabletop is too heavy for its legs. Provided your desktop is thick enough—usually 1 inch minimum—you can swap in workbench legs for a far more durable, resilient desk. (In the Reddit thread, these were recommended in particular). Combine these with reinforcement plates for your desktop and you’ve got yourself a sturdy, resilient setup. Clutter control Monitor arms, stands, and risers Amazon Monitor arms create more room on your desk—plus they can help with ergonomics, too. If you don’t have enough room behind your desk to accommodate arms, you can instead choose a riser to get a little more space. Or, if you have a big heavy monitor, a floor stand. Pro tip: Screen carefully for sturdy arms, especially if you’re shopping on Amazon. Surprisingly, other parts of Reddit have good things to say about the AmazonBasics lift models—they’re purportedly white-label versions of Ergotron’s beefy (and beloved) arms, while being a heck of a lot cheaper. USB hub and/or KVM switch A USB hub not only expands the number of usable ports on your PC, but having one makes moving accessories between devices easier, too. (Check out our picks for the best USB-C hubs). Meanwhile, if you’re flipping between active PCs at your desk often (say, a work system and a personal one), a KVM switch lets you use the same set of monitor(s) and peripherals without having to plug and unplug wires any time you want to switch machines. Hooks & stands NZXT Using a headphone hook, phone charging stand, and controller stand not only reduces desk clutter, but can help with keeping track of your gear, too. (At least, I can now find things faster on my desk). Cable management items Ikea That hideous Medusa’s tangle of cables doesn’t need to exist. An inexpensive cable management tray (either the clamp or drilled variety) and a handful of Velcro ties can keep the unruliness to a minimum. Also, tidy exterior cables cut down on hassle when swapping PC accessories or the PC itself. (Tip: Label your cables while you’re neatening up back there). Wireless peripherals Dominic Bayley / IDG Speaking of cable management, the easiest way to manage cords is to nix them all together. A wireless keyboard, wireless mouse, and wireless headset go a long way toward reducing visual noise on your desk. Plus, with no wire tethering your headset to the PC, you can get up to answer a call or the door without accidentally strangling yourself. Side table Ikea Having a small side table next to your desk—be it an TV tray, end table, rolling drawer unit, or a random box (ahem) can help keep items at hand while reducing clutter. I like the box for my air purifier just fine, but there are definitely more refined options out there. Ergonomics A better chair Steelcase Spend hours sitting in an uncomfortable chair, and your body won’t let you forget it, especially the older you get. Reddit has a couple of good tips here: Shopping refurbished for expensive chairs from Herman Miller and Steelcase, or seeking out more affordable but still popular models like the Staples Hyken. Comfier peripherals Azeron As weird as they look, ergonomic mice and keyboards can make a world of difference in comfort. I’ve long been on board this train out of necessity—a Goldtouch keyboard and a Contour Rollermouse are my daily drivers. You can extend that philosophy to gaming as well. PC gaming keypads can be worth the investment, and they range from the more conventional to the downright wild. (Not gonna lie, I’m intrigued by that Azeron—and I’m a dyed-in-the-wool controller player). A keyboard tray HUANUO / Amazon Ok, this one’s not from Reddit (but technically I’m a Redditor myself, so maybe this still counts). However, if we’re talking ergonomics at a desk, a keyboard tray can do wonders for proper alignment. You don’t need to drill holes in your desk, either—as I just discovered myself, fantastic no-drill keyboard trays now exist. Light strip or light bar BenQ / Amazon Eye strain is as problematic as any shoulder, elbow, or wrist pain. Adding lighting to your desk can help with overhead glare as well as keeping your area adequately lit when you’ve turned down most of your other lamps. Light bars like the BenQ Screenbar are a luxe option, but you can add monitor backlighting for $15 or less.
