The three men had become friends in New York, where they would gather in the evenings to sketch and discuss art at the Averys’ Lincoln Square apartment. “I cannot tell you what it meant for us during those early years to be made welcome in those memorable studios,” Rothko would later recall. In Gloucester, they explored the port, with its wharves and warehouses and fish-processing facilities, filling sketchbooks and painting small-scale works in watercolor. A total solar eclipse that August provided fodder for Avery, who made an amusing watercolor showing people on Good Harbor Beach looking at the celestial phenomenon through smoked glasses and colored film. That first summer together was bookended by major life events back in New York. The Depression had flooded the streets with the unemployed. Gottlieb married in June. In October, as memories of summer receded, Sally gave birth to a daughter, and a few weeks later, Rothko married. In those days, Rothko and Gottlieb would study Avery’s paintings and, according to Sally Avery, “take them apart.” On Cape Ann, they watched him treat the beach as a backdrop against which he placed monumental, thick-hipped figures, arranging areas of pattern (umbrellas, beachwear) against flat, colored shapes in compositions with shifting horizon lines. Following Avery’s example, they experimented with gouache and watercolor applied to colored construction paper. The Averys and Gottliebs returned in the summer of 1933, and were joined by the Rothkos in 1934. The Depression was biting hard, but the artists’ life in Gloucester remained simple and uncorrupted. “We saw each other day in and day out,” Sally recalled of those years. “Evenings we’d gather to have a cup of tea and look at our day’s work. There was no talk of selling—only of painting.” “I always thought Avery was a great artist,” Gottlieb would later say. “I always regarded him as a brilliant colorist and draftsman, a solitary figure working against the stream.” Gottlieb was right. Avery was one of the 20th century’s most original colorists. His expansive compositions were influenced by Pierre Bonnard and Matisse as well as by American folk art. Unlike Matisse, who loved bold, blatant colors, he favored unusual, in-between hues—mauves, browns, pale greens—all close in tonal value. He would often unify three or four slightly clashing varieties of the same color with a complementary hue elsewhere in the arrangement. Like spacious minor-key chords given a subtle major-key lift, these color combinations can arouse powerful emotions that are excruciatingly just short of fulfillment. When it came to being influenced by others, Matisse understood what was at stake. But, he said, “I have never avoided the influence of others. I would have considered it cowardice and a lack of sincerity toward myself.” To be open to influence is to risk being dislodged from your former self. It requires you to have the confidence to convert the ensuing upheaval to your own (still unknown) purposes. The process is complicated and rarely goes smoothly. Often, though not always, it involves some kind of betrayal. No one betrays anyone in this story. All three artists remained friends. But the two younger painters, Rothko and Gottlieb, although deeply affected by Avery’s original way of painting, eventually decided that they needed to go further—to change not just the colors, the shapes, or the subjects, but something more fundamental. In 1943, they broke away. Perhaps coincidentally, perhaps not, the breach happened just as Avery was beginning to thrive. He had been choosing larger canvases and distilling his paintings down to a few essential ingredients. The strategy was working. His work was selling. Dealers were fighting to represent him. He had a series of successful shows. The reviews were good. Rothko, meanwhile, experienced a creative crisis and, in 1940, stopped painting for a year. He had been digging into philosophy, reading Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, and Kierkegaard, as well as the Greek myths and tragedies. Gottlieb, at the same time, made works merging surrealism with imagery inspired by masks and ritual objects from Africa, the Pacific, and Native North American cultures. As the two younger men moved steadily closer to total abstraction, a tension that has in many ways defined American art—between the concreteness of the material world and the amorphousness of the sublime—was coming to a head. Avery, ever loyal to his sketchbook, remained committed to direct observation of particular people and places. His summer companions were about to throw in their lot with the sublime. The push toward abstraction in mid-century American art coincided with a surge of interest in existentialism, which had begun to displace the pragmatism that underlay Avery’s approach. A sense that even the closest ties might be loosened by what T. S. Eliot—who had himself summered for nearly two decades in Gloucester—had described (in a review of James Joyce’s Ulysses) as an “immense panorama of futility and anarchy” was lent gravity by the world wars. But the human predicament, as Albert Camus made clear in The Stranger (1942), went beyond man-made conflict. It was inextricable from all that was inhuman, arbitrary, and immense—from the blinding energy of the sun on an Algerian beach, for instance. On Cape Ann, Rothko and Gottlieb thought a lot about the sun, as well as the sea, the sky, and the smallness of human life. They were no doubt aware of the death-haunted history of Gloucester, where, between 1866 and 1890, more than 2,450 Gloucester men and 380 schooners failed to return from the fishing grounds. They wanted their art to communicate awe, and a sense of the insecurity and brutality of existence. It was as if the Atlantic were pulling them out to sea, away from both the harbor intimacy of Gloucester and the embrace of Milton and Sally Avery. In 1943, Rothko and Gottlieb co-authored a letter and sent it to The New York Times, which published it on June 13. The letter responded to the Times critic Edward Alden Jewell, who, in a review, had misjudged (they felt) paintings by Rothko and Gottlieb. It also doubled as a five-point manifesto: “To us,” they wrote, “art is an adventure into an unknown world, which can be explored only by those willing to take risks.” That was the first point. The fourth point ended: “We are for flat forms because they destroy illusion and reveal truth.” According to the fifth point, “only that subject matter is valid which is tragic and timeless.” A concluding salvo declared that for their work to succeed, “it must insult anyone who is spiritually attuned to interior decoration; pictures of the home; pictures for over the mantle; pictures of the American scene”—the list continues—“prize-winning potboilers; the National Academy; the Whitney Academy,” and so on. Avery could easily have felt personally targeted. He had exhibited, after all, at the first and second Whitney Biennials (in 1933 and 1936); he painted domestic interiors and American landscapes; and his pictures could be called “decorative” (at least in the sense Matisse meant when he described his more ambitious paintings as “decorations”). He was probably too magnanimous—or phlegmatic—to take umbrage, and the summer proceeded pleasantly enough. If the group dynamic had become awkward, it correlated, the art historian Robert Hobbs wrote in his monograph of Avery, “with the way rebellions between initiates and their mentors are frequently enacted: certain brash rejections are cushioned with compliments, and personal assurances attempt to heal the break that has in actual fact been made.” Which it had. Mentor and protégés went separate ways. They wouldn’t summer together again until 1957, when they reconvened in Provincetown on Cape Cod. Sometimes after a clear-cut break, a reciprocity gradually reemerges. Even as the abstract expressionists transformed American art, Avery wasn’t entirely left behind. The period’s most influential critic, Clement Greenberg, cast Avery as a sort of John the Baptist to the artists whom Greenberg had tried to deify. The new crop of abstract painters, he wrote in 1957, “has certain salutary lessons to learn” from Avery “that they cannot learn from any other artist on the scene.” In World War II’s immediate aftermath, Rothko painted abstract, colored shapes, beginning with what he called “multiforms” and shifting, around 1949, to his signature format of floating “lozenges” of soft-edged colors. He liked to layer warm and cool colors, so that in one lozenge a cooler purple might subdue a thin overlay of red while in its neighbor, a warm yellow rises like steam through the same red. The effect can be akin to music, and so intensely affecting that you’re almost willing to accept the artist’s preposterous rhetoric about his work. (“I would like to say to those who think of my pictures as serene,” Rothko once wrote, “that I have imprisoned the most utter violence in every inch of their surface.”) Meanwhile, Avery, working now on larger canvases, let particulars of the observed world dissolve into trembling fields of color. The paintings remained recognizable depictions of sea, land, and sky, but they, too, had as their true subject something closer to music. A gallery in the Cape Ann Museum exhibit (which will travel to the Phillips Collection, in Washington, D.C., in October) allows these late Avery paintings to share space with a sequence of mature Rothkos and similarly spare Gottliebs. The sense the gallery creates is of all three artists tenderly reunited and singing together in unison. If Rothko’s abstract paintings recall the ethereal, spatially ambiguous atmosphere of Caspar David Friedrich’s Monk by the Sea (painted between 1808 and 1810) or certain late works by J. M. W. Turner, they may also evoke the natural environment he observed on Cape Ann. His compositions are oriented vertically, but the lozenges nestled within each painting tend to be horizontal, so it’s tempting to see the thin strips dividing them as swaths of land hovering between sea and sky. Gottlieb, too, favored shapes that suggested the sun and moon—phenomena that he, a passionate sailor, had daily observed while out on the water. Despite all of this concordance, I came away sensing something unresolved about the relationship among these three powerful artists. The late Averys are good, but they’re simply not as strong as the best Rothkos, which hum with colors so richly resonant that they make Avery’s attempts to work on a larger scale look anemic. The Averys also lack the deep, metaphysical suggestiveness of the Gottliebs. Yet when you set aside the late works and consider Avery’s oeuvre, it seems to me that he was the better—more richly poetic, more generative—artist. The problem with the abstract expressionists’ relentless courting of the sublime was that the process of distillation produced too much bombast. And it led them into a cul-de-sac. As a skeptical character in John Updike’s novel Seek My Face put it, referring to the postwar generation of abstract expressionists, “they all still spoke of painting in terms of self-exploration and an agonized authenticity that would revolutionize the world and whatnot, but the results were a little like company logos, everybody working on the scale of 19th-century academic art but each of them having come up with some eye-catching simplification.” After Rothko settled on his signature manner, the level of repetition in his work became oppressive. Gottlieb, too, as he chased the sublime, seemed to shun the finer tendrils of the sensuous world, with results that felt fatally monotonous. To Greenberg, Avery was a prophet, his work a precursor to his younger peers’ more radical experiments. But maybe Avery was actually better than that. Rejecting Greenberg doesn’t mean claiming that abstraction was some kind of aesthetic mistake. But I would argue that, whereas Avery’s paintings continued to be aerated by the beautiful unruliness of the material world, Rothko and Gottlieb, especially later on, were relatively formulaic. True, if forced to choose, I might prefer to look at my favorite single Rothko over my favorite single Avery. But I would rather spend time with a dozen of Avery’s finest works than a dozen of Rothko’s. That’s because Avery understood that a deep canyon separates things in the world from their representations in art. The mystery of painting lies in what takes place in that shadowy, fertile zone, where what you thought was green foliage turns into the strangest dark purple, that body of gray water has flushed vivid turquoise, the blue sky is now flaming orange, and you don’t even know whether these transformations have taken place in life or on the canvas. Avery proved that figurative artists, in trying to represent the observable world, can be as free in their choices as any abstract painter. But their work is less likely to become clichéd, because any stale fixations will always be rinsed and refreshed by the real.

item.title: The Transcendence of Dolly Parton
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 2.31
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Dolly Parton transcended. It almost didn’t matter what: class, gender, region, musical genre, partisanship. She transcended boundaries in all of them. During an era when politicians act like pop stars, pop stars are expected to engage in politics, and politics divide fiercely, Parton was perhaps the only person in the United States who commanded nearly universal affection. Her death today, at 80, leaves an absence that no contemporary cultural figure could dream of filling. Parton’s origin story was, in the most literal sense, a rags-to-riches tale. She was born in a one-room cabin in the Appalachian Mountains of East Tennessee, one of 12 children of an illiterate sharecropper father. She memorialized her impoverished childhood in “Coat of Many Colors,” which tells of how her mother sewed a jacket from rags. When she wears it to school, “with patches on my britches / and holes in both my shoes,” her classmates mock and laugh at her. Rather than a hard-luck story, this is a triumph. Parton gets the last laugh: “But they didn’t understand it and I tried to make them see / That one is only poor only if they choose to be.” The song showcases one of the keys to Parton’s success: the ability to bare her soul while keeping a sense of humor and a smile. Her rise to fame began when she was hired by the rhinestone-adorned country singer Porter Wagoner as a “girl singer” in his act. Parton quickly demonstrated that she had more than an attractive face and voice, writing a string of successful songs, such as “Jolene” and “My Tennessee Mountain Home.” One indication of her songwriting talent was that her most famous song was a bigger hit for another singer. Parton had initially hoped that Elvis Presley would record “I Will Always Love You,” but she refused his manager’s demand to give Presley songwriting credit, and she cut the song herself. It topped the country charts twice, but after Whitney Houston rerecorded the song for The Bodyguard’s soundtrack in 1992, it was a No. 1 pop hit for weeks. Today, little separation exists between country music and the mainstream, but the genre garnered much less respect when Parton’s career began. She helped tear down old prejudices in an era when many music listeners might have professed to like “anything other than country.” Her success helped pave a path for later crossover stars such as Shania Twain and Taylor Swift. She pursued her own genre experimentation, too, collaborating with a range of artists. When she was nominated for the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, she protested that she wasn’t a rock musician and tried to withdraw from consideration. When the hall refused, she announced with appealing humility that she would earn the honor by making a rock album—her 49th and final—with guests including Joan Jett, Ringo Starr, and Paul McCartney. Parton always maintained her connection to rural southern music. Few country stars could claim a more authentic origin. She kept her down-home accent and platinum-bouffant hairstyle, and she spoke openly about her abiding Christian faith. These traits may have allowed her to take stands that might otherwise have been controversial. (She also avoided electoral politics, and declined Presidential Medals of Freedom from both Donald Trump and Joe Biden.) Like her predecessor Loretta Lynn, she cultivated a no-nonsense strain of feminism in her lyrics. In 1980, she starred alongside the outspoken liberals Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin in the movie 9 to 5, a workplace comedy in which three women conspire to get even with their sexist-pig boss. Parton agreed to take the role if she could write the theme song, and the track has proved even more enduring than the film. “It’s a rich man’s game no matter what they call it / And you spend your life puttin’ money in his wallet,” she sang. Was this working-class grievance or progressive economics? Radical feminism or mass-market entertainment? Why not both? Parton was beloved by the gay community, and she reciprocated that affection. She also quietly fostered change using her fortune. In 1986, she opened Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, and the theme park became the largest job provider in the area. In 1995, she launched Dolly’s Imagination Library. Starting first in her native Sevier County, and then expanding around the United States as well as in a few other countries, the program mails a book each month to children from birth to age 5, to encourage literacy and a love of reading. In 2020, she donated $1 million to help fund the development of a COVID-19 vaccine, then proudly received the shot. In her middle age, during a perhaps less enlightened time in American society, Parton was often a punch line. Her voluptuous chest and many plastic surgeries were frequent fodder for jokes, and Parton perfected the trick of playing along with the gags while also subverting them. One of her earliest singles is titled “Dumb Blonde,” but it warns, “This dumb blonde ain’t nobody’s fool.” In a 2002 New York Times interview, she said, “Hopefully people can see beneath the hair to know there’s a brain, beneath the boobs to know there’s a heart, and behind all the other stuff to know there’s some talent.” If that wasn’t always the case, Parton got her wish in the end. Admiration for her became an unshakable conviction across cultural lines. One sign of Parton’s status is that even Trump is on his best behavior, treating her death with a reverence he usually reserves only for his biggest public admirers, of whom she was not one. The president ordered flags flown at half-staff for a week to mark her death. It is a fitting farewell for an artist who united Americans in a way that few people ever have or will. Related: Here are three new stories from The Atlantic: Today’s News - Canada announced tariffs of up to 50 percent on imports of about 700 U.S. products after trade talks collapsed and new U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods took effect last week. The retaliatory tariffs—covering steel, aluminum, electronics, and appliances—will begin on September 8. - The Trump administration said in a court filing that the Kennedy Center could be demolished if it is not allowed to close for two years for renovations; a hearing is scheduled for Thursday. - Two unvaccinated people in Pennsylvania have died from measles, according to state health officials; they mark the first U.S. measles deaths reported this year. The deaths occurred amid an outbreak in Lancaster County that has infected more than 390 people and hospitalized 70. Evening Read Logging In Was Never Supposed to Be This Complicated By Will Oremus One afternoon earlier this month, I pulled up to the rec center and realized that I had a problem. It was not the three boisterous tweens in the back seat who were clamoring to be set loose in the basketball gym. It was my parking app. I had somehow gotten logged out of Passport Parking, which has become the only way to pay for a spot in much of my town, and it was demanding a four-digit PIN to let me back in. My first guess drew a warning message in red letters: “Invalid PIN. PIN cannot contain 4 sequential numbers, 2 repeated digits, or the last 4 digits of your phone number.” I searched my trusty password manager, which was supposed to spare me these predicaments, but it came up empty. By that point, the kids had run ahead and piled themselves against the gym door, waiting for me to let them in. Lately, the process of accessing apps and websites has grown dizzying. “I’m in password hell,” a colleague confided to me recently. More From The Atlantic Culture Break Explore. This summer’s pop hits from artists such as Slayyyter and Adéla are full of twisted nostalgia for a simpler era, Spencer Kornhaber writes. Read. Rachel Cusk’s newest book, Life of M, “takes autofiction’s familiar dance of authorial ambiguity and shakes it into something odd and unsettling,” Sophie Gilbert argues. Rafaela Jinich contributed to this newsletter. When you buy a book using a link in this newsletter, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

item.title: We’re Living in the World Dolly Parton Built
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 2.22
Dolly Parton’s death at age 80 comes at a time when her influence seems at its peak. Country music is surging, female singer-songwriters are on top, and audiences seem hungry for honest idiosyncracy—for figures who, like Dolly, transmit their inner truth to mass audiences in a voice that’s clear yet scraggly. But Parton’s greatest legacy is existential in nature. Piling on wigs and feathers, she showed that you can be yourself while playing a character. Parton’s self-construction project began in her childhood. She was born the fourth of 12 kids in a tiny cabin in Pittman Center, Tennessee. Her parents were so poor that they paid the doctor who delivered her with a sack of cornmeal. As a girl, she sang songs on her porch into a fake mic fashioned from a tin can and a tobacco stick, envisioning herself at the Grand Ole Opry. Her talent drew attention from local radio and TV personalities, and by age 13, she was singing on the real Opry stage. The craftiness and self-consciousness that came from growing up impoverished shaped her outlook for life. As she’d sing in her 1971 song “Coat of Many Colors”—her signature (and favorite) hit—her mother used to sew rags into garments that the young Parton would flaunt at school. Mockery from other kids taught her the lesson in self-determination that she’d turn into one of her defining lyrics: “One is only poor only if they choose to be.” As a young woman, she modeled her fashion off a “town tramp”—as she later put it—whom she’d grown up around. Her preacher grandfather whipped her for dressing that way, but to her, women with heels and push-up bras weren’t trashy; they were glamorous and confident. A fascination with stereotypes—with fulfilling them and subverting them—gave her an edge when she moved to Nashville. In 1966, her first solo hit, “Dumb Blonde” (written by Curly Putman), saw her singing that despite her looks, she “ain’t nobody’s fool.” On the TV variety series The Porter Wagoner Show, she played the aw-shucks second fiddle to the titular star even as she wrote songs that outcompeted Wagoner’s music. Her 1970 hit “Joshua” spun a tale in which the narrator approaches a mean-looking backwoods hermit, someone whom the rest of the town fears, only to realize that he has a heart of gold. It was an example of how her penchant for social criticism and her interest in flipping expectations made her songwriting stand out. She left Wagoner behind in 1974 to court an audience that transcended country music. Her songs sparkled with fun production touches, clever lyrical twists, and melodies that seemed at once as winding as a lazy river and as smartly constructed as good Levi’s. For 1980’s “9 to 5,” the sound of her fingernail clicks did as much work as the lyrics—and the movie the song accompanied—in celebrating the hustle of women at work. “Jolene,” her enduring ballad of jealousy, built itself around a chorus so plaintive that it seemed surely scraped from a harrowing chapter of Parton’s own life—but she was quick, in interviews, to say that the song’s story was more or less fiction. As she settled into icon status, she seemed to revel in the franchisability of her image: Dolly Parton was an idea that everyone could benefit from. She founded a theme park in her home state, selling a blend of rustic realness and fun kitsch. She only ever seemed tickled that Whitney Houston’s cover of “I Will Always Love You” eclipsed Parton’s original in eminence. She made childhood literacy the central focus of her philanthropic efforts—another subversion of the “dumb blonde” image (and one that channeled her upbringing by a father who couldn’t read). In recent years, Parton’s persona has come to take on political significance. She was, as my colleague David Graham has written, the rare public figure who seemed beloved by both red and blue America. She maintained that status through careful circumspection regarding partisan politics. But when it came to questions about sexuality and identity, she took a stand by repeatedly supporting gay, trans, and gender-nonconforming people. After all, she once told RuPaul, she herself was a drag queen. Many of the most important stories in music this decade owe a lot to Parton. Sabrina Carpenter has brought Dolly-style humor (and hair) back to the charts; Beyoncé enlisted Parton to play emcee on her 2024 album, Cowboy Carter; Ella Langley is blending backwoods scenery with wry, shrugging wisdom that recalls Parton’s catalog. But Parton set an example bigger than music—by showing how to take the scraps you were given and stitch them into something bright and new.

item.title: The good tourist: can we learn to travel without absolutely infuriating the locals?
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.61
Tourism has never had a great reputation, given that the very word “tourist” is pejorative. At best, it suggests someone whose interest is superficial and whose understanding of a place is nonexistent. What’s the first thing you think, when you hear the phrase, “They’re a bit of a tourist”? You think, that person is annoying. But the word’s reputation has plummeted further in recent years. Anti-tourism movements are springing up across the world: that might look like a protest march, as in Barcelona, where one placard bluntly pleaded “Tourists go home; you are not welcome here”. It might look like a visitor fee, as Venice introduced this year, or it might look like the mayor of Amsterdam simply closing the cruise ship terminal, as she did last year. Part of this is about sheer volume: the number of people crossing an international border as tourists (rather than displaced people or migrants) in 2023 was 1.3 billion, which is not only a complete bounceback post-Covid, but an almost 25-fold increase since the 1950s. Driven not only by flights becoming ever more affordable, but the online convenience of booking travel – from the launch of last-minute flight and hotel brokers in the late 90s, to Airbnb in the late 00s, followed by Google Flights and Trips – everything about travel has become easier and cheaper. But the difficulties and costs still exist, they’re just paid elsewhere. Tourism accounts for just over 8% of all global greenhouse gas emissions. Short-term holiday rentals distort housing markets until the locals are spending summer months living in car parks – as has happened in Ibiza. And that’s just the aggregate impact of tourism, before any of us have arrived and started doing anything. Dubrovnik in Croatia has new rules about not jumping in fountains or climbing on statues and not walking around shirtless. Amsterdam launched a “stay away” advertising campaign (specifically aimed at the British, shamingly). Budapest, Munich, Dusseldorf and Prague all banned “beer-bikes”, those 17-seat charabancs where stag parties pedal their way to oblivion. Split has introduced specific fines for vomiting and urinating in public (again, those signs are in English). The Italian culture minister, meanwhile, has simply had enough of people defacing the Colosseum. When you look at anti-tourism movements as a whole, it’s hard to escape the conclusion that travel is one of those nice things we no longer deserve. But into that sorry picture steps the travel journalist Paige McClanahan with her book The New Tourist. We can still travel, she says, and more than that, it’s important that we do; we just have to get a lot better at it. The old kind of tourist, she writes, is “a pure consumer who sees the people and places he encounters when he travels as nothing more than a means to some self-serving end: an item crossed off a bucket list, a fun shot for his Instagram grid, one more thing to brag about to his peers”. The new tourist, by contrast, is humbled by the unfamiliar, not unsettled by it, she “embraces the chance to encounter people whose backgrounds are very different to her own, and to learn from cultures or religions that she might otherwise fear or regard with contempt”. Maybe that doesn’t sound groundbreaking – in brief, when you’re away, try being your best self – but it cuts to the heart of a book that is part a modern history of international travel, part manifesto for it. Fundamentally, McClanahan sees travel as a social good. “When we think about the challenges humanity is going to face in the years and decades to come, whether it’s another pandemic, runaway AI or catastrophic climate change, each of these crises is completely ignorant of national borders,” she says. “Should we all just sit at home, is that going to prepare us? No, we need high-quality, meaningful interactions that are going to shift our perspectives and deepen our understanding of what it means to be a human being in such an interconnected world.” However, we can’t just carry on as we are. The term “overtourism” was popularised in 2016 by Skift, a travel news outlet, with Iceland as its poster child. After the country’s financial crash of the late 00s, the income from tourism became hugely important, partly as a way of paying off a massive IMF loan. But visitors come at a cost, whether it’s the destruction of moss and grassland from the footfall, or the new pressure on the road infrastructure when an island with a population of about 350,000 began seeing more than 2 million tourists by the end of 2017. McClanahan interviewed the former first lady of Iceland, Eliza Reid, for her book, who told her that she and her partner, the then president, Guðni Jóhannesson, walked through the middle of Reykjavik on a summer day in 2017. “And nobody recognised him, because there were no Icelanders there. It was all tourists.” That sense of heavily visited areas being denatured, left unrecognisable when the resident:visitor ratio is out of whack, was compounded after the pandemic. It wasn’t so much that tourists brought Covid (although they did); rather, that the international travel bans made people realise, as they did in other places such as Hawaii, “just how much they had been sacrificing for tourists for so long”, McClanahan says. It was assumed that people in tourism-heavy areas in Hawaii would be pining for travel bans to be lifted after so much income was lost during the pandemic, but the peace and quiet turned out to be much more valuable in some places. In polls, native Hawaiian community leaders and young people were the least likely to agree that tourism did more good than harm. At the end of a Hawaii tourism conference McClanahan attended, one participant stood up and said: “‘Tourism is colonialism. Tourists need to go home now,’” McClanahan remembers. “And I thought, ‘That’s my dude.’” It could be an Instagram post perpetuating colonial stereotypes (she is unflinchingly self-critical about this: “For example, Paige standing alone in a Cambodian ruin,” she cites as an example) or it could be visitor demand simply remaking the culture into a theme park, boom boxes and novelty penny farthings where real life should be happening. I suggest to McClanahan that, from Hawaii to Mallorca, what residents are rebelling against is as much late capitalism as it is tourists: historically, the inconvenience of having vastly more visitors a year than there are residents has been offset by what this does for the local economy. But, if the fruits, one way or another, aren’t evenly distributed – maybe the model drives a low-wage culture, maybe intermediaries such as cruise companies or Airbnb cream off the profit – that contract is bust and resentment creeps in on both sides. I remember this from going to Tulum in Mexico two years ago. It’s a chic tourist hotspot where a cab driver would happily relieve you of $30 to go 200 metres down the road. I felt pretty sour about that, but he probably felt pretty sour about me spending eight times as much on a single plate of food as the hourly rate of the person who served it to me. McClanahan agrees that “daytrippers to Venice, people coming off a cruise to buy a postcard and an ice-cream and then leave” might fit into that picture, but it’s possible to travel while staying “socially conscious and socially aware”: spend more time in a place, not at the height of the season, and spend money in local businesses. The first chapter of The New Tourist goes back to how we got here: 50 years ago, when newlyweds Tony and Maureen Wheeler set off from the south of England to drive to India. They weren’t the first to try the hippy trail, but they were the first to launch a publishing empire off the back of it: Lonely Planet. Many of us who took our first trips as adults holding one of these guides will remember the sensibility of them: it was all about budget travel, getting in and out of a place on a fiver. The Wheelers changed the terms of tourism entirely – the true traveller didn’t waltz in like Lady Muck, paying top dollar for everything. This new kind of tourist liked to be called a “traveller” and went to out-of-the-way places, craving the authenticity of the locals’ experience, not luxury. But this had its downsides, namely that these “travellers” had the same footprint but a lot less money. No offence – and this is my opinion, not McClanahan’s – the Wheelers made an absolute fortune off performative non-materialism and lauded being “off the beaten track”, while beating every track so hard you could see the tracks from space. Lonely Planet guides, by the turn of this century, had become more about the high end, but there is a broader tension, which McClanahan exemplifies with Bhutan – where you pay a really sizeable visitor sustainable development tax of $100 a person every day – versus Nepal, the “backpacker’s superhighway”. “In Bhutan,” she says, “you had to come with an organised tour and had to be led by a local tour guide. They were very explicitly going for lower volume, higher quality tourism.” She felt plugged in to Bhutan, “saw villages that felt untouched” (tourism in Bhutan has existed, in tiny numbers, since 1974); Nepal, heaving with visitors, didn’t come close, “although the landscapes were beautiful, of course”. It would be crude, though, to make that into a creed that you should only travel if you’re loaded. Maybe, rather, it means start by going to places where they want you. “For every Barcelona or Venice pushing back against tourism,” McClanahan says, “there are so many other places that are working as hard as they can to attract tourists.” Sri Lanka, Taiwan, Rwanda and Japan all have active state programmes to increase tourist numbers. McClanahan’s first law of new tourism is a simple one: “Travel to fewer places, and spend longer there. Understand that this might be the only time in your life that you have the opportunity to see this landscape, this wildlife, to come and meet these people.” Travel, as she describes it, comes with a “tinge of nostalgia, a bitter-sweetness” even while you’re doing it. “Part of its bliss is that you may never come back, and even if you do, you will never re-experience this moment.” But don’t go looking for bitter-sweetness: McClanahan talks about “last chance” tourism – people rushing to Victoria Falls, the Great Barrier Reef, Venice – which are all at risk, respectively from drought; marine debris and rising sea temperatures; and rising sea levels – looking for the last perfect selfie in front of the extremities of a dying planet. It sounds so self-defeating and, more than that, depressing, that it’s impossible to imagine people still doing that. But we can see that people are still doing that. And while many countries are entering into explicit contracts with visitors to meet the challenges of the climate crisis, not all of these are particularly helpful. In Palau in the western pacific, you will receive a pledge stamp in your passport that will give you special access to places if you buy reef-safe sunscreen. In Denmark, there’s a trial initiative called Copenpay, in which tourists might get a free boat trip for picking up litter, or a free drink if you cycle to a bar instead of driving. It’s a creative way to connect tourists to the place they’re in, but it all underlines how hard it is to truly mitigate your carbon footprint as a tourist: cycling through Copenhagen won’t make a lot of difference if you arrived there by plane. McClanahan is more plausible than most tech-optimists on the aviation front. “The technology for carbon-free travel already exists,” she says. “It’s not being deployed at anything like the scale needed, and we all need to educate ourselves, as consumers and as voters, about the transformation and the speed that we need. Whether it’s through electric flight, whether it’s hydrogen-powered flight, whether it’s through a hydrocarbon fuel that is made from carbon dioxide, extracted from the atmosphere, this technology exists, these planes have flown. It’s a question of being able to do it at the scale required to make an actual impact on the atmosphere.” On the climate crisis, as with all the ethical challenges tourism faces, McClahanan urges us to consider the counter-factual. There isn’t a simple fix, such as “stop doing it”. As the old TomTom satnav adverts used to say, you’re not in traffic, you are traffic. If you’ve travelled somewhere where you can see overtourism, you’re an overtourist. Yet “there’s a wonderful amount of humility that we gain from getting out of our comfort zone”, McClanahan says. “We just need to learn to do it differently.” The New Tourist by Paige McClanahan is out now published by Simon & Schuster.

item.title: Architourism in France: the retro futurist seaside town near Montpellier that’s out of this world
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.31
My dream holiday is a trip back in time. Not to see the results of seismic Pompeii or 15th-century Machu Picchu – although I love both – but somewhere created specifically between the mid 1950s and 1970s, when cities were getting weird. I love postwar architourism, exploring urban planning at its most frenzied and optimistic. I have relished trips to Niemeyer’s Brasília and Le Corbusier’s Chandigarh in India, where the monumental and visionary modernist architecture and interiors are at odds with the minimal population. So La Grande-Motte, the retro futurist folly of a resort town on the southern coast of France, a 30-minute drive from Montpellier, had long been on my “must visit” list. The tourist board of this Occitanie seaside town likes to flag up some superficial parallels between it and the aforementioned cities, but this isn’t a high-concept capital city or administrative hub. It was built in the late 1960s and early 1970s purely to persuade the French to stop going south to the Costa Brava in Spain. As part of an initiative by the French government, a stretch of windswept mosquito-infested coast between Montpellier and Perpignan, including Gruissan and Port Leucate, was reimagined as an alternative to the Côte d’Azur with several new-build beach towns. La Grande-Motte would be the weirdest project. It was made for fun. It’s also well positioned to visit the nearby salt marshes and 13th-century walled-in town of Aigues-Mortes, for when you want to feel as if you’ve ticked a few more holiday boxes. The mastermind behind the town’s architecture, Jean Balladur, took inspiration from temples and Mesoamerican pyramids from the first century, imagining what the 21st century would look like in the 1970s. Why shouldn’t modernist apartments be arranged in the shape of a Maya pyramid, or an intergalactic curve? I rented a tiny studio with my husband in the Incas building for part of my trip, and while there was nothing in the way of high design about the interior, being on that terrace immersed us in a timewarp. Walking around Point Zéro (named for being the site of the earliest construction), home to La Grande-Motte’s main beach, all looks fairly standard: families playing on the sand, couples drinking cocktails outside cafes. The beach gained a Blue Flag award for environmental management and water quality in 2025. But the place is unique: the ferris wheel is solar powered and the buildings suggest you’re on another planet entirely – there are no rectangular blocks and few right angles to be seen. The urban planning has been driven by pedestrian pathways and cycle routes, punctuated by thousands of trees. On the beach there are concrete sculptures by artist Joséphine Chevry, which look like the tips of the wartime sound mirrors in Dungeness, Kent. Chevry created them to help shape the dunes (AKA “the big mound”) but also to serve as functional wind breakers and shade when Point Zéro was created. They’re now mostly buried in the sand. Time has moved on but they will for ever be core to the town’s concept. The place has had cyclical fortunes. As with many seaside towns, it fell from grace in the 1980s. It was gauche. In 2014 the fashion designer Simon Porte Jacquemus created a nostalgic collection and book in homage to the town and talked to AnOther Magazine of its “trashy reputation”, but he also said he found it “inspiring and exciting” and remembered his holidays there as a child. And it seems a renaissance is under way as the grandchildren of people who first bought apartments here are discovering it. I’d recommend the fabulously vintage three-star Hotel Le Quetzal (doubles from €114 room-only) as an interesting base. It feels brilliantly 1970s, being part of the original wave of development in the town, but was refurbished a few years ago so the essentials are fresh and modern. Its design is as interesting as anywhere in town: the balconies jut out like theatre boxes and create an optical illusion of the building being slanted. There’s no restaurant but people microwave meals in the lobby or bring back a margherita from nearby L’Atelier de la Pizza to have on their balcony. A couple of days by the pool here are great, fending off seagulls from your pain au chocolate at breakfast and watching stray cats wander around the loungers; the same families have been coming for years. Nearby, L’innatendu is a better restaurant than anything on the seafront (I particularly recommend the squid with black rice), although the most enjoyable meal I had was a bunch of simple marinated skewers at La Guinguette des Alizés, opposite the seafront carousel on Avenue du Couchant that looks like a piece of pop art. Strolling around La Grande-Motte’s apartment blocks was as fascinating to me as a visit to the Colosseum. I walked through the open-air theatre that looks like a derelict World’s Fair site but is used for shows regularly, around the elegant white bow shape of Saint-Augustin’s church, down to the water and the Big Pyramid apartment complex facing the yachts on the dock, and to the low and curved buildings of Le Couchant. I spent hours photographing stairwells and walkways, and the hundreds of balconies that make the town the sum of its geometric parts – graphic beauty reminiscent of the Bauhaus, Saul Bass posters and Verner Panton furniture. La Grande-Motte is a sunny, gleaming white vision of a future that we could never live up to. Or perhaps deserve. Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: A local’s travel guide to Austin: what to eat, see and do in three days
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.90
Austin has become one of the most popular places in the US to move to, and also to visit. Droves of people descend on the city in March for the South by Southwest tech, film and music festival and in the fall for the Austin City Limits music festival. And Austin is one of the top five destinations in the US for bachelorette parties. Don’t let the bachelorettes scare you away, though. Austin is a great place to spend a few days, so long as you do it like a local. My family and I moved to Austin 12 years ago, after living in New York for many years. I’ve also lived in Washington DC, the San Francisco Bay Area and Philadelphia. Austin has a feel all of its own: it has a world-class music scene, great food that now goes well beyond Tex-Mex and barbecue, Texas history and fun shopping and museums – all with less hassle than bigger cities in the US. Here’s my guide to a long weekend there. In addition to picks for adults, I’ve included some recommendations for families that our kids (now teenagers) have loved through the years. And I’m vegetarian, so I’ve chosen some of the city’s best veggie eats options. Don’t worry, my meat-eating wife made sure that I included great barbecue choices, too. Day 1: Pool party & pickles Start your day with a walk or run on the trail at Town Lake (it’s officially labeled on maps as Lady Bird Lake, but locals refer to it as Town Lake). This 10-mile (16km) trail on both sides of a dammed portion of Texas’s Colorado River (a different Colorado River than the bigger and more famous one) is tree-shaded, beautiful and one of Austinites’ favorite places to exercise. If you have time, walk through Zilker Park, which is right next to the trail. If you have kids, go to the new and very fun playground at Butler Park, complete with a splash pad just up the path from the playground. Austin was one of the cities that started the food truck scene in the US several decades ago, and now there are more than 2,000 food trucks in the city. Some are located in trailer parks that have multiple truck options and picnic table seating. After your morning at Town Lake and Zilker Park, have lunch at the Picnic food truck park, or the nearby original location of local favorite Chuy’s (the Tex-Mex chain is now expanding throughout the US). Other great lunch options include Green Mesquite and Carpenters Hall. In the afternoon, go for a swim at Barton Springs Pool. Open year-round, this massive basin measures three acres and is fed by underground natural springs. It’s open throughout the day, and it’s free before 8am and after 9pm. Head back to your hotel or Airbnb for a rest, and then get ready for dinner. Tonight is casual: barbecue at Terry Black’s, or if you’re vegan, the food truck Rollin Smoke for a fantastic vegan barbecue sandwich made with baby portobello mushrooms, spicy slaw, barbecue sauce and pickles. It’s my favorite vegan barbecue sandwich in Austin (who says you can’t have barbecue if you’re veggie?), and it’s located in a food truck park with beautiful old trees shading the tables. Rollin Smoke has very good meat options, too (I’m told). If you have young children, head to Phil’s Icehouse. They have burgers and a full playground where the kids can play before or after dinner. Just don’t put them on the spinning flower after the meal. And be sure to get some ice-cream after dinner at Amy’s Ice Creams, a longtime favorite of Austinites. Amy’s is located next to Phil’s, and it’s so good we had an Amy’s truck serve dessert at our wedding. After dinner, head out to see some music at one of Austin’s many local music venues. One of our favorites is the Continental Club. There’s a main club downstairs and the intimate Continental Gallery upstairs, where you can see local musicians in a cozy space. Other great venues include C-Boy’s and the new Moody Amphitheater. For full local music listings on any night, check the Austin Chronicle. And if it’s summer, look to see if Blues on the Green has a free concert that night. If you have kids, take them to the free Rock the Park concert series, produced by local radio station KUTX. Day 2: Breakfast tacos, books & bats Start your day back at the lake with a rowing workout that’s almost, but not quite, on the lake. Rō Fitness is a local studio that has outdoor rowing classes by the water. It’s way more fun than working out at an indoor studio. You’ll need fuel after your workout. Grab a breakfast taco at Veracruz or Tacodeli or Tamale House East. Breakfast tacos are an Austin staple (they are to Austin as bagels are to New York), and all three of these places have delicious options. Today is a shopping day. Start out at BookPeople, one of the greatest bookstores in the US. It’s locally owned and independent, but the size of a superstore. BookPeople also dares to take a stand on issues, including being one of two bookstores that recently sued Texas state officials over a newly passed book ban law. It has an excellent kids section, and organizes live readings by kids’ authors. After you’ve gotten your book fix, head across the street to Waterloo Records, one of the best record stores in the US. Waterloo carries new and used vinyl, CDs and merchandise from rock to jazz to local Texas music. For more shopping options, head over to the stores along South Congress Avenue and South First Street (including Roadhouse Relics, a neon art store and gallery that is one of our favorites), and if you want to go thrifting, our teens say Austin Pets Alive Thrift and Texas Thrift are the best. After all of the shopping, it’s time for lunch. If you’re near BookPeople and Waterloo, head over to Soup Peddler, a local place for homemade soups, smoothies and fantastic grilled cheese sandwiches (trivia: Soup Peddler got its name because the founder started out delivering homemade soup by bike before opening full store locations). Or if you’re near South Congress and South First, go to the food trucks on South First or Underdog or Fresa’s. As you’re heading back to rest up, grab an ice-cream at Amy’s, a gelato at Dolce Neve or cupcakes at Sugar Mama’s. Some good dinner options for tonight include Loro, Suerte or Este. And if you’re looking for a vegetarian option, one of my favorite veggie restaurants is Bouldin Creek Cafe. It’s casual, with a great menu that includes vegan chips and queso. If it’s nice out, take a seat on the patio. Tonight’s activity could be going to see the bats at the Congress Street Bridge. Austin has the largest urban bat colony in North America, and in season they live in one of the bridges that crosses the Colorado River (they migrate to Mexico in the cooler weather). Bat-watching is a lot more fun than you might imagine from horror movies (and these bats look more like birds than vampire bats). If you’re not in the mood for bats, head to the legendary Broken Spoke. Get there early for dance lessons, then hoof it at this classic Texas honky-tonk. Day 3: Live oaks & Lady Bird wildflowers It’s your last day in Austin, and it’s a good one for visiting a museum. Some of our favorites include the Bullock Museum to learn all about the history of our state (bonus fact: Texas was once its own country, and some people want it to be its own country again). If you’re a fan of 1960s history, visit the excellent LBJ Presidential Library, which is the home of the 36th president’s papers. It has good exhibits on the US civil rights movement and 1960s US history in general. Another excellent museum option is the Blanton Museum of Art, or you could tour the Texas capitol (Austin is, after all, the capital of Texas). If you’re a nature fan, head to the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center. And if you have kids, the Thinkery is an excellent children’s museum. For lunch, it’s time for more barbecue (you’re in Austin, don’t fight it). Two terrific barbecue trucks are Mickelthwait and LeRoy and Lewis. And LeRoy and Lewis has another of my favorite vegetarian barbecue options: cauliflower burnt ends. In the afternoon, head back to Town Lake. This time, get out on the water by renting a kayak, stand up paddleboard or paddle boat (a kid-friendly option). If you have time and energy for a drink, head over to the ABGB for happy hour. They have a great beer selection, lots of outdoor seating and local bands playing music. For your farewell dinner, a few of our favorite restaurants that are a bit on the fancier end are Hestia, Uchi or the Lenoir wine garden, where dinner is served under live oak trees more than a hundred years old. And for a fantastic vegan option, go to Fabrik for a seven-course vegan tasting menu. You’ll need a reservation well in advance (they’re currently booking four to six weeks out). And for your final night in Austin, head out to another music venue. Or if you have kids, take them to the Austin favorite Peter Pan Mini Golf, which has been around for 75 years, or check Do512 Family for family events that are happening the dates you’re in town. Question Time When is the best time of year to visit Austin? There’s no dispute: it’s hot in the summer in Austin. A great time to visit is between October and May. From June through September, many days will be over 100F. If you’re here in the summer, spend lots of time at the Barton Springs pool. Is Austin expensive? Austin hotels can be expensive during big events like South by Southwest or the Formula One weekend. But for most dates, it’s less expensive than larger cities like New York, Los Angeles and San Francisco. Will I need a car to get around Austin? Most of the places that I’ve recommended are within walking distance from downtown. You can also rent bikes and scooters to get around. Austin’s public transportation is primarily through local buses, which can take you further out if needed. And car-share options are easy as well. - Steve Sachs is managing director of the Guardian US. He has worked at large and startup media companies for more than 20 years. He loves all kinds of music, and his most recent favorite concert, the Texas Songwriters Hall of Fame Show, featured a host of singer-songwriters including Lyle Lovett and Emmylou Harris

item.title: The best Christmas travel gifts: 38 presents for explorers and armchair travellers
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.18
Not sure what to get friends and family for Christmas? Fear not, we have plenty of ideas for a last-minute present. Our carefully chosen selection of travel-inspired gifts ranges from the practical to the indulgent, with great books for the armchair traveller and outdoor gear for the active. Maybe a cool new suitcase for weekends away would suit, or a stylish eco wash kit designed for travel? For those who have it all, perhaps opt for an experience to remember. Vouchers for vineyard visits, hotel breaks or afternoon tea may hit the spot. Happy shopping … and happy holidays! Travel books The Joy of Quiet Places In this era of overtourism, give the gift of 180 peaceful escapes in this Lonely Planet book. £22.99 lonelyplanet.com Why We Travel One for mindful travellers: Ash Bhardwaj asks what motivates us to venture out into the world and how we can do it better. The Tree Atlas Matthew Collins’ book spotlights 50 amazing trees, ideal for armchair adventurers as well as those who want to visit them in the wild. The Balkan Kitchen Irina Janakievska weaves together recipes, anecdotes and beautiful photography from her Balkan homeland. £24.30 guardianbookshop.com Cold Kitchen: A Year of Culinary Journeys Caroline Eden reflects on past global adventures and cooks recipes from her travels. £17.09 guardianbookshop.com Lamb’s London Fans of the hit spy show Slow Horses will love Herb Lester’s map and guide to Jackson Lamb’s London. Gift vouchers for getaways National Trust Treat a couple to a day out with the National Trust’s Unboxed gift experience, which includes entry to an NT property, parking and a cream tea. The Wine Garden of England These new gift vouchers allow recipients to choose one of eight Kent vineyards to visit for a discounted tour and tasting, with options including Chapel Down and Gusbourne. From £40 winegardenofengland.co.uk Kip Hideaways These beautiful gift cards can be put towards a self-catering escape in any of the collection’s 200-plus UK cabins and cottages. From £50 kiphideaways.com The Retreat Company These vouchers are valid for selected workshops and retreats, from art to yoga. From £25 theretreatcompany.com PoB Hotels This collection of independent hotels across the UK has monetary and experience vouchers to be redeemed against a meal, spa day or stay. Monetary vouchers from £75 pobhotels.com Experience vouchers from £50 pobhotels.com The best travel kit gifts Eye mask Gift a good night’s sleep on a long journey or in a bright tent with an eye mask from the British Red Cross, made in Nepal from recycled sari remnants. Phone wallet Help a teen (or adult) keep their valuables safe with a bright, wearable phone holder and card purse from the Tate, made from waterproof cotton canvas with a recycled cotton lining. Drop recycled wash kit Passenger has a great travel drop wash kit inspired by road trips. It has three drop-down compartments with a hanger – ideal for camping – and is made from recycled polyester. £29.95 passenger-clothing.com Packing cubes Packing cubes help organise and optimise space in a suitcase. Joules has a set of three with a lovely damask print and a drawstring bag. £40 joules.com Underseat suitcase The Jetset 15-inch underseat suitcase by Lugg is very stylish and spacious enough for long weekends. £29.74 lugg-online.com Activewear gifts for explorers Tulum recycled towel poncho Outdoor swimmers and water-sport enthusiasts will love Passenger’s Tulum towel poncho, made from recycled polyester. £29.98 passenger-clothing.com Brighton Water Shoes These unisex shoes are perfect for swimming and walking on pebbles. They come in a range of colours inspired by Brighton beach, from Palace Pier Pink to Sea Green. £18.99 brightonwatershoes.co.uk Floating keyrings Behaviour Change Cornwall makes a range of accessories, including floating keyrings, from ghost fishing gear such as buoys, floats and nets. £14.99 behaviourchangecornwall.co.uk Recycled plastic carabiner Climbers will treasure a unique Müll Club carabiner made from recycled household plastic – perhaps a yellow one from Marmite lids, or a purple one from Quality Street tubs. The best accessories gifts Handmade bracelets and necklaces El Camino allows travellers to show off their adventures on handmade bracelets and necklaces created to reflect the countries and cities visited and nature experiences such as the northern lights and dolphin-watching. From £32.99 elcaminobracelets.com Bobble beanie The National Gallery has a cosy merino wool bobble beanie in the colours of a hawfinch, designed to raise awareness of endangered birds. £45 shop.nationalgallery.org.uk Sustainable umbrella No sensible traveller leaves home without an umbrella. Kew Gardens has one made from recycled plastic bottles and sustainably sourced birch with a fun “magic of mushrooms” design. £38 shop.kew.org Cosy socks These are a must on most active holidays. Wild Wool sells pairs made in small family-run workshops in Spain, using offcuts from the textile industry (ie recycled wool and cotton). Lightweight slippers Another essential for travellers, the Baggu Puffy Slippers from Plastic Freedom are made from recycled nylon and fleece, with designs including constellations and flowers. £40.80 plasticfreedom.co.uk Wellness gifts for R&R Scented candles The Royal Academy has various scented candles made by sustainable brand Rekava in Ukraine, with aromas of the country, such as amber, herbs, honey and apricots. The container, lid and wick are all compostable. Festival essentials First-time festival-goers will love the eco travel toiletries and festival essentials kit from The Rosy Robin Company. It contains a compostable poncho, biodegradable wipes, organic sunscreen, bamboo toothbrush, travel toothpaste, natural deodorant and the all-important hand sanitiser, complete with a cotton mesh bag. Paddling in the Surf diffuser Bring the scent of the seaside into your home with a Happy Place diffuser rich in notes of seaweed, pear, grapefruit, lemon and mandarin. Hot-water bottles The National Trust has some lovely versions of this camping essential with covers made by Tweedmill Textiles. Patterns include autumn leaves. Not-a-Lavender bags Kalinko’s Not-a-Lavender bags are scented with agarwood and made from fabric offcuts by artisans in Myanmar. They keep clothes smelling fresh and protect them from moths. £14 kalinko.com The best food and drink gifts Limoncello spritz set Transport your recipient to the Amalfi coast with a spritz set, featuring the year’s hottest drink, limoncello, made by Three Wrens Gin in Cheshire. Four Seas by Salcombe Gin If gin is their tipple, get them a bottle of Four Seas by Salcombe Gin, celebrating 200 years of the RNLI and distilled with lemon peel smoked over Scottish whisky barrel woodchips, English sea buckthorn, sugar kelp from the Irish sea and elderberries from Wales. £39.50 shop.rnli.org Organic cold-pressed rapeseed oil Instead of olive oil, gift from closer to home with Riverford’s organic cold-pressed rapeseed oil, which is made in Aberdeenshire. £7.75 riverford.co.uk Truffle Hunter condiment gift box English Heritage has a truffle condiment set containing truffles found in the Sibillini mountains in Italy and other top truffle regions in Europe. It includes truffle-infused “dust”, salt, mustard, mayonnaise, ketchup and honey. £22 english-heritageshop.org.uk Home and garden ideas for travellers Penguin tea towels The UK Antarctic Heritage Trust has cute penguin tea towels that help support its conservation work. £25 for two shop.ukaht.org Custom pub portrait Immortalise a favourite holiday hangout with a custom pub portrait by Lancashire-based Hayley & Co. From £20 hayleyandco.co.uk Wildflower seedballs Kew Gardens and Transport for London have joined up to create a tin of six wildflower seedballs, containing poppy meadow, cranesbill, red clover, red campion, corn marigold, wallflower, common knapweed and marjoram. £10 shop.kew.org Canopy closed garden Create your own self-sustaining ecosystem in this dome-shaped planter, inspired by the biomes of Cornwall’s Eden Project. The 22cm high Canopy closed garden is mouth-blown from recycled glass.

item.title: Celebration Key: Everything we know about Carnival Cruise Line’s newest private beach destination
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 7.10
Celebration Key: Everything we know about Carnival Cruise Line’s newest private beach destination Editor's Note Celebration Key is Carnival Cruise Line's massive private sun-and-fun playground tucked into the southern coast of Grand Bahama Island. Following a massive $100 million pier expansion, up to four ships can now dock here at once — making it easier than ever to step off the gangway and directly onto the soft white sands, without ever needing a tender. What to expect on shore A day at Celebration Key serves up miles of white-sand beaches, two of the largest freshwater lagoons in the Caribbean, dozens of places to eat and drink, and a nonstop lineup of activities for toddlers, party-lovers and quiet-seekers alike. At the heart of it all stands the Suncastle — a towering, 10-story, sandcastle-like structure with twin racing waterslides that shoot riders directly into the lagoon waters. And getting around the area is easy. You can explore on foot via the wide paved walkways or hitch a ride on any one of the hop-on, hop-off trams. Which cruise ships go there? Nearly every Carnival ship in the fleet will dock at Celebration Key at some point, whether on a quick weekend trip to the Bahamas or a longer Caribbean sailing. Ships depart from 10 U.S. home ports, including Miami; Port Canaveral, Florida; Galveston, Texas; New Orleans; Baltimore; Jacksonville, Florida; Norfolk, Virginia; Mobile, Alabama; Tampa; and New York City. So, you won't have to look hard to find an itinerary that stops here. The lineup of Carnival ships includes: - Excel-class ships: Mardi Gras, Carnival Celebration and Carnival Jubilee - Vista-class ships: Carnival Horizon, Carnival Vista and Carnival Panorama - Venice-class ships: Carnival Venezia - Dream-class ships: Carnival Dream and Carnival Magic - Conquest-class ships: Carnival Conquest, Carnival Glory, Carnival Freedom, Carnival Liberty and Carnival Pride - Sunshine & Spirit-class ships: Carnival Sunrise, Carnival Sunshine, Carnival Legend and Carnival Spirit - Fantasy-class ships: Carnival Elation and Carnival Paradise Beginning in November 2026, Princess Cruises will also make a stop here, with Star Princess and Regal Princess first off the rank. In 2027, more ships will join, including: - Star Princess - Regal Princess - Sun Princess - Enchanted Princess - Sky Princess - Caribbean Princess Related: The ultimate guide to Carnival Cruise Line ships and itineraries German line AIDA Cruises will become the third Carnival Corporation line to stop at Celebration Key. AIDAluna is scheduled to make a visit Nov. 15, 2027, during a repositioning cruise from New York to the Dominican Republic. The 5 Celebration Key portals: Which spot is right for you? Celebration Key is divided into five color-coded areas known as "portals," each offering its own distinct atmosphere, family-friendly otto pool-party vibes to more laidback areas. While a lot is included — like basic beach access, sun loungers and some casual dining options — upgrades like cabanas, access to Pearl Cove Private Beach Club, waterslide passes, specialty food and drinks, kayaks, snorkel gear and guided shore excursions all cost extra. Here's what to know about each of Celebration Key's five portals and how to make the most of your day ashore. Paradise Plaza: Best for booking activities Every visit starts at Paradise Plaza. Step through the signature yellow sun arch and into a vibrant portal filled with music, a Bahamian-themed fountain and views of the Suncastle. Guest services and the shore excursions desk are in this area. Stop there first if you need to lock in an excursion, pick up a beach wheelchair (available on a first-come, first-served basis), ask questions or simply work out where to spend your day. You can also pick up an ice cream from Yumshine Scoops or last-minute beach supplies from the store. The plaza also hosts live entertainment. Look out for the high-energy Junkanoo performances featuring traditional Bahamian music, dancing and elaborate costumes. From here, paved paths fan out toward the rest of Celebration Key — the family-friendly Starfish Lagoon, the lively Calypso Lagoon, the exclusive Pearl Cove Beach Club and the shops at Lokono Cove. Starfish Lagoon: Best for families Starfish Lagoon is made for families, with shallow swimming areas, splash zones and plenty of space for kids to burn off energy. Claim a lounge chair on the white-sand beach or along the lagoon's gently sloping entry. Little ones naturally gravitate toward Guppy Grotto, a colorful splash playground complete with a tipping bucket and a shallow wading pool. There's shaded seating for parents taking a break from the sun. For action out of the water, Starfish Lagoon has volleyball, basketball and pickleball courts, as well as a gaming pavilion packed with foosball, table tennis and cornhole. Families looking to upgrade their beach day can splurge on a standard beachfront cabana or an overwater lagoon cabana that comes with a private waterslide and dedicated attendant service. You can even hire an AquaBana: a floating, shaded cabana anchored right near the Shoalmates Island Bar. When hunger strikes, Gill's Grill serves full-service Caribbean-style fish, lobster, crab and shrimp alongside burgers, chicken and kids meals. Captain's Galley Food Hall dishes up burgers, hot dogs, fried chicken, pizza, Mediterranean bowls, tacos and burritos from five different counters. Meanwhile, casual food trucks and snack shacks serve quick-grab chicken sandwiches, wraps, salads, Bahamian sushi and mini donuts. To quench your thirst, head to Lagoon Bar East on land or swim right up to the Parrotfish Swim-Up Bar for cocktails, mocktails and everything in between. Calypso Lagoon: Best for a party vibe If Starfish Lagoon is for families, Calypso Lagoon is where the volume gets turned up. Here you'll find DJs, a massive swim-up bar and an upbeat social scene that feels more resort pool than family beach day. Sports courts are shared with Starfish Lagoon, and cabanas are available for those who want their own space. Like Starfish Lagoon, the portal offers beach, lagoon and floating cabana options for an additional fee. Dining ranges from full-service to quick bites. Mingo's Tropical Bar and Kitchen serves fresh seafood, conch fritters, tacos, steak and sandwiches, while Surf N' Sauce BBQ and Brews specializes in slow-smoked meats and local Bahamian brews. Food trucks and snack shacks offer quick options like burgers, wraps and salads. Long Necks Bar is the star attraction. One of the Caribbean's largest swim-up bars, it boasts more than 100 seats both in and out of the water. Sunshine Swings Bar takes a more relaxed approach, with over-water swing seats and cocktails. Lagoon Bar West has beers, wine and mixed drinks. Pearl Cove Beach Club: Best for adults-only luxury For a quieter, VIP-style beach day, head straight for the western end of the resort to Pearl Cove Beach Club. This is Celebration Key's most exclusive sanctuary, a luxury retreat reserved for adults 18 and over. The mood shifts the minute you walk through the door. Gone are the loud party playlists and family splash zones. In their place, you'll find chilled lounge music, attentive staff and a sprawling 11,000-square-foot infinity pool overlooking a private stretch of sand. Days here revolve around poolside cocktails, ocean views and uninterrupted lounging on a private beach lined with plush sunbeds, cabanas and villas. An upscale restaurant and swim-up bar complete the resort-style experience. Access is limited to guests who purchase one of three admission packages, all of which are best booked before sailing. - Pearl Cove Beach Club Access: Club access plus welcome cocktail — $99.99 per person - Pearl Cove Beach Club Open Bar: Club access plus open bar (up to 10 drinks) — $139.99 per person - Pearl Cove Beach Club All Inclusive: Club access plus premium lunch at the Pearl Cove Beach Club Restaurant and open bar (up to 10 drinks) — $179.99 per person Additional food and beverages are available for purchase a la carte. Related: Carnival Rewards cruise loyalty program: The ultimate guide Lokono Cove: Best for shopping Lokono Cove offers a welcome break from the sun, blending shopping with local Bahamian culture. Here you'll find storefronts and kiosks selling locally made handicrafts and fine jewelry, duty-free goods and official Carnival merchandise. Colorful murals painted by local artists line the pathways, while a local Bahamian artisan market adds authentic local charm. Suncastle Grounds Coffee is the perfect pick-me-up with hot, iced or frozen coffee drinks and snacks. What costs extra at Celebration Key? While beach access, sun loungers and basic casual dining are included in the cruise fare, a few popular upgrades cost extra. - Included dining: Carnival's Island Eats program covers one meal at participating food trucks and snack shacks. Full-service, sit-down restaurants cost extra, but you'll get a 25% discount on entrees. - Extra-charge perks: Waterslide passes, cabana/villa rentals, Pearl Cove admission, motorized water sports, alcoholic beverages, and shore excursions (like island Jeep tours or glass-bottom boat rides). Does the Cheers! drink package work at Celebration Key? No, this Carnival beverage package is valid strictly onboard the ship. All drinks on the island must be purchased a la carte or bundled through a Pearl Cove Beach Club day pass. Does my Sail & Sign card work at Celebration Key? Yes, for food and drinks. Your card is accepted at Celebration Key's dining venues and is required for reboarding the ship. It's not accepted at retail outlets in Lokono Cove, so bring a credit card or cash for shopping and souvenirs. Is Celebration Key a private island? Technically, no. Celebration Key is a gated beach resort on the south coast of Grand Bahama Island, not a private island like Carnival's Half Moon Cay. Related: The 8 classes of Carnival Cruise Line ships, explained Is Celebration Key accessible for guests with mobility needs? Yes. Wide, paved paths connect the portals, open-air trams run continuously and beach wheelchairs are available at Paradise Plaza on a first-come, first-served basis. The main exception is Pearl Cove Beach Club, where loose sand pathways require guests to be fully mobile. Bottom line Celebration Key takes the hassle out of planning a port day, letting you easily tailor your time to match your vacation style — whether that means lounging by the lagoon, tackling giant waterslides or heading off on an island excursion. The key is deciding your game plan before walking off the ship: High-demand perks like cabanas, Pearl Cove Beach Club passes and popular tours sell out fast, so book them well in advance to secure your spot. Planning a cruise? Start with these stories: TPG featured card | 4X | Earn 4X Membership Rewards® points per dollar spent on purchases at restaurants worldwide, on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year, then 1X points for the rest of the year. | | 4X | Earn 4X Membership Rewards® points per dollar spent at US supermarkets, on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year, then 1X points for the rest of the year. | | 5X | Earn 5X Membership Rewards® points on prepaid hotel stays booked through AmexTravel.com or the Amex Travel App™. | | 3X | Earn 3X Membership Rewards® points on flights booked through AmexTravel.com, the Amex Travel App™, or purchased directly from airlines. | | 2X | Earn 2X Membership Rewards® points on prepaid car rentals booked through AmexTravel.com or the Amex Travel App™ and cruises booked and paid through AmexTravel.com. | | 1X | Earn 1X Membership Rewards® point per dollar spent on all other eligible purchases. |

item.title: Phantom award space: What it is and how to avoid it
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.84
Phantom award space: What it is and how to avoid it Editor's Note Imagine you set an award alert months ago for a flight you want to book. Your award alert finally pinged, so you searched, saw the award space and transferred rewards to book the award. But when you reach the final stage of the booking process, you get an error message because there actually isn't any available award space for your itinerary. You try again and get the same result. Unfortunately, you've discovered what is known as phantom award space. Phantom award space refers to award seats that appear in online searches but aren't actually bookable. This issue usually occurs when the inventory displayed by one loyalty program doesn't match what the operating carrier will actually confirm, often due to stale data or communication issues between reservation systems. Phantom award space is one of the most frustrating aspects of booking award flights. And, unfortunately, based on TPG staffers' experiences, phantom award space isn't all that rare. So, in this guide, we'll discuss some steps you can take before transferring your rewards to avoid being deceived by phantom award space. Why you should care about phantom award space Phantom award space is most troubling if you're looking to transfer rewards from a transferable rewards program to an airline to book an award. You'd likely do this because the airline you want to fly with isn't a transfer partner for the currency you're trying to redeem or because you can book through a partner airline loyalty program at a lower rate. For example, you might transfer Citi ThankYou Rewards points to American Airlines AAdvantage to book a Japan Airlines premium cabin flight. But the problem arises if you transfer your rewards and can't book the flights you want. You typically can't reverse a transfer, so your rewards become stuck in that program. Related: 6 no-annual-fee credit cards that earn transferable rewards Consider booking with the operating carrier The root cause of phantom award space is often stale data or a communication error between a loyalty program's booking engine and the partner airline's inventory management system. Therefore, you'll generally avoid the partner-related phantom award issues discussed in this guide when booking through the operating carrier. So, if you can book the award through the operating carrier at a competitive rate using points or miles that you have, this is usually the most straightforward option. However, there's often a compelling reason to book through a partner program. And just because a program offers award space for flights it operates to its own members doesn't mean it will make that space available to its partners. Related: The same flight, half the miles: Making this award booking mistake could cost you Do your homework on the airline Some airlines are known for showing more phantom award space than others. As such, it's important to familiarize yourself with the program you're trying to book through. For instance, TPG staffers have recently encountered phantom awards through several programs, including American Airlines AAdvantage, United MileagePlus, Air France-KLM Flying Blue and Air Canada Aeroplan. To this point, a message on Seats.aero recently noted Flying Blue has been experiencing increased phantom award space. It's equally important to research the airline you're hoping to fly. For example, TPG video producer Isabella Boccasino called Qantas to confirm premium cabin award space she was seeing through its program for a Japan Airlines flight from New York to Tokyo. During the call, the Qantas agent said the space wasn't actually available and told her phantom award space on Japan Airlines flights is a common issue for Qantas members. Try getting to the checkout page One of the easiest ways to check if the award space you see is real is to go through the booking process. After all, you'll get an error message at some point during the booking process if the award space isn't available. However, this method won't work for many travelers who must transfer rewards into their account before they can book the award. That's because many programs won't let you reach the final checkout page unless you have enough rewards in your account to book the flight. Related: The best credit cards for paying taxes and fees on award tickets Hold your award Some airlines let you put award tickets on hold before booking. A hold can provide additional reassurance that the program has found the award space and give you time to transfer rewards.
