However, a hold doesn't always guarantee the space is actually held for you. So, you should try to book the award as soon as possible after placing it on hold. Cross-check award availability One of the most important steps for verifying award space is to search for the same flight through multiple partners. If multiple partner programs independently show the same award space, that's a good sign the inventory is real. However, keep in mind that multiple partner programs may show the same phantom availability. Award space isn't necessarily phantom if you can't find it through another partner, though. After all, airlines often provide different inventory to different partners. Additionally, don't trust the availability you see through your favorite award search tool (such as Seats.aero or Point.me) to be real. Before transferring rewards, confirm the space directly with the loyalty program you plan to book through, rather than relying solely on an award search tool. Call the frequent flyer program Another useful option is to call the customer service desk for the mileage program you plan to book with and have it manually confirm whether the award space you found online exists before you transfer rewards into the program. However, even an agent's confirmation isn't foolproof, particularly for partner awards. Ask to reverse your transfer Suppose you've already transferred your rewards and determined there's no way to redeem them for your originally intended ticket. In that case, you could ask your credit card company and the mileage program to reverse the transfer. The chances of reversing a transfer are extremely slim, so don't be surprised if this doesn't work. However, there have been rare cases in which programs have worked with transferable currency programs to reverse transfers, such as after Flying Blue canceled awards it said it priced incorrectly. Bottom line Phantom award space can turn an exciting award find into a frustrating problem, especially if you've transferred valuable rewards into a program. Unfortunately, there's no foolproof way to verify partner award space before booking. But cross-checking with other programs, calling the loyalty program and placing the award on hold when possible can reduce your risk. And, most importantly, don't transfer rewards until you've done as much verification as you reasonably can. After all, transferable points are most valuable while they're still transferable. item.title: We raced from JFK to the Empire State Building — which mode of transportation was fastest?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.63
We raced from JFK to the Empire State Building — which mode of transportation was fastest? There are many ways to get from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Manhattan, but have you ever done a head-to-head test to determine the best option? Here at TPG, we decided to do just that. Staffers Liam Spencer, Medha Imam and Bella Boccasino recently headed to the Big Apple to put three modes of transportation to the test: - Train (JFK's AirTrain to the Long Island Rail Road) - Ride-hailing service - Blade helicopter You probably already have an educated guess as to which came out on top — but second place may surprise you. Check out the full video here — and keep reading for other considerations for your own trip from (or to) JFK. Other benefits to help with JFK transfers In the video, Liam, Medha and Bella all paid "retail" price for their assigned mode of transportation. However, there are several ways they could've maximized their purchases. AirTrain and Long Island Rail Road to Penn Station Liam's surprisingly strong showing on the train was the lowest-priced option, but there are a couple of possible avenues to make the most of these transit purchases. For starters, train travel typically triggers the $300 annual travel credit available on both the Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) and the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (see rates and fees). Alternatively, there are a handful of cards that offer bonus points on general travel purchases — including the Citi Strata Premier® Card (see rates and fees). Blade to Manhattan Bella's helicopter was pricey, especially with the added car transfer from Blade's 30th Street helipad to the Empire State Building — though surprisingly not all that much more than Medha's Uber. Nevertheless, there's one program that could've helped defray the cost: Bilt. As of Aug. 13, you can now redeem Bilt Cash for Blade flights up to twice per calendar year (up to $350 for each seat). Additionally, Bilt Platinum members receive one free Blade flight per year between Manhattan and either JFK or Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR). And all Bilt elite members can get 10% off Blade bookings through the Bilt app. Read more: What is Bilt Cash? How to earn and redeem this new reward currency Uber to the Empire State Building Medha came in last in our race, as traffic into Manhattan significantly delayed her arrival. Nevertheless, there are many avenues to save on ride-hailing purchases. With Uber, you can add select American Express cards to your account to unlock monthly Uber Cash for U.S. Uber rides and Uber Eats orders: - American Express Platinum Card®: Up to $200 in annual Uber Cash (up to $15 per month, plus an up to $20 bonus in December)* - American Express® Gold Card: Up to $120 in annual Uber Cash (up to $10 per month)* *Note: Uber Cash will only be deposited into one Uber account when you add the Amex Platinum or Amex Gold, respectively, as a payment method and redeem with any Amex card. Meanwhile, those with either the Sapphire Reserve or the Sapphire Reserve for Business will earn 5 points per dollar spent on Lyft rides, plus up to $10 monthly in-app credits (up to $120 annually) through Sept. 30, 2027. Finally, be sure to link your Uber and Lyft accounts with select loyalty programs to enjoy even more rewards on your rides: | Service | Loyalty partners | |---|---| | Uber | | | Lyft | | Just note that you must designate a specific earning partner in each app — you can't earn rewards in multiple programs on the same ride. Related: How to earn more points and maximize elite status benefits by double-dipping Bottom line Three TPG staffers raced from JFK to the Empire State Building, and, not surprisingly, Blade came out on top. However, the AirTrain to the Long Island Rail Road was surprisingly close — while also being the cheapest. And, unfortunately, the ride-hailing option was last by a wide margin due to the horrendous rush-hour traffic at the time. What's your favorite way to get to Manhattan from New York City's airports? Share your thoughts in the comments section below.

item.title: United's posh new Airbus A321XLR is headed overseas: Sneak peek on board
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.60
United's posh new Airbus A321XLR is headed overseas: Sneak peek on board United Airlines' newest plane will make its international debut right as the holiday season ramps up. On Dec. 1, right after Thanksgiving, the carrier's all-new Airbus A321XLRs will take off from Dulles International Airport (IAD) en route to Dublin and Amsterdam. Those flights will be the first of many to come for United — and will mark the hard launch of a plane that has been hailed for years as a potential game changer for the airline. This week, TPG got a sneak peek on board. Polaris business-class suites The A321XLR is a distinctive new aircraft for United because it's a single-aisle plane, but it sports many of the bells and whistles you'd normally expect to see on a large wide-body jet. Up front, instead of a traditional domestic-style first-class cabin, it's a bona fide international business class. Climbing on board, you'll find 20 of the airline's latest-generation Polaris suites, complete with lie-flat seats, sliding privacy doors and 19-inch 4K entertainment screens. Because this is a narrow-body jet, the suites are arranged in a 1-1 configuration (one seat on each side of the aisle). United notes it specifically designed the pods to give flyers more shoulder room — hoping to avoid the tighter quarters some flyers have complained about when flying lie-flat seats on single-aisle planes. Note that the XLR does not sport United's ultraluxe Polaris Studio suites that debuted earlier this year on its latest Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners. Those jumbo suites are just too big for a plane of this size! Premium Plus on the United Airbus A321XLR Moving to the middle of the aircraft, you'll arrive in Premium Plus. United has installed three rows of premium economy recliners arranged in a 2-2 configuration. The seats have privacy wings, cocktail trays and legrests. Like with most premium economy cabins, these most closely resemble a domestic first-class setup. And, unlike the premium economy on a lot of twin-aisle planes, there's no middle seat. Economy (with some new 'extras') In the back, close to 30% of the seats in coach are United's extra legroom Economy Plus seats. Among them is the airline's special row with a blocked middle seat. You can pay extra to avoid having someone sit next to you. As shown on the seat map for this jet, you'll find this seating option in row 32. United's economy seats feature 13-inch seatback screens, and each is equipped with Bluetooth connectivity for flyers with AirPods or similar wireless headphones. And as you head to the very back of the plane, you'll find one of the other new twists on this plane: a walk-up snack bar for passengers seated in economy. United chief commercial officer Andrew Nocella acknowledged the carrier could have outfitted that final row of the plane with three coach seats. But? "We know this is an eight-hour journey," he said. "We want to make sure it's comfortable." Long-haul vision for this single-aisle plane There's a reason United is outfitting its XLRs with features you'd expect on a much larger jet: The carrier plans to fly this plane back and forth across the Atlantic Ocean. While the XLR looks like a domestic airplane from the outside, it has long-haul range. Across the industry, airlines see this new aircraft as a way to open routes to smaller markets that might not have enough travel demand to justify flights with a larger, more expensive-to-operate jet. United's new XLRs were a big part of the blockbuster 2027 route drop revealed this week. The airline announced plans to fly the jet to five destinations in Europe next summer: - Luxembourg — from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) - Toulouse, France — from IAD - Ibiza, Spain — from EWR - Valencia, Spain — from EWR - Marseille, France — from EWR All of these are routes not currently served by any U.S. airline, which makes the "Born to Explore" livery on the plane's exterior a fitting slogan for the mission these jets will fly. United isn't alone in its big XLR plans To be fair, United is far from the only global carrier with big plans around these XLRs. European carriers Aer Lingus and Iberia have already used the aircraft to open up transatlantic flights from new U.S. cities. And, American Airlines debuted its version of the jet last December, featuring its new Flagship business-class suites and premium economy. American used the plane to launch a new route from New York City to Edinburgh, Scotland, earlier this year — a route I experienced firsthand in March. But unlike United, American is also using the XLR heavily on prime cross-country routes. Meanwhile, top rival Delta Air Lines has its own... thoughts... about leaning into single-aisle planes on long international flights. Bottom line United is all-in on this plane, though. The airline expects to take delivery of 50 XLRs by the end of this decade. So, expect to see the jet — Polaris suites and all — on many more long-haul routes to come. Related reading:

item.title: Explora Journeys loyalty program guide: The Explora Club, explained
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.54
Explora Journeys loyalty program guide: The Explora Club, explained Startup cruise line Explora Journeys hasn't had much time to build up a loyal following. It's only been operating since 2023. But that doesn't mean that it's not treating its most loyal customers right. The still relatively unknown luxury brand has a 1-year-old loyalty program, the Explora Club, that brings significant discounts for sailings after just a few cruises and, at its higher tiers, everything from onboard credits for wellness experiences and shore excursions to unlimited free laundry. At its top tier, the Explora Club program even offers what may be the ultimate perk in the cruise line loyalty program universe: a free cruise for two. Only a handful of other brands, such as Royal Caribbean, offer such a perk. Additionally, Explora Journeys recently enhanced its loyalty options for customers by expanding its partnership with Hilton. Here's a look at the Explora Journeys Explora Club loyalty program in detail. Ways to earn points There are two ways to earn points in the Explora Club: - Spending nights on an Explora ship - Spending money on an Explora ship In the first bucket of points earnings (points earned by spending nights on ships), you will earn a baseline amount of 100 points for every night that you sail on one of the line's three vessels. On top of that, you will get additional points for every night that you stay in a higher-end suite. Specifically, your points earnings on a per-night basis will correspond to the following chart (note that on Explora Journeys ships, all cabins are called suites, with Ocean Suites being the entry-level category that accounts for most rooms): | Type of cabin | Points earned per night | |---|---| | Ocean Suite | 100 | | Ocean Penthouse | 200 | | Ocean Residence | 300 | | Owner's Residence | 1,000 | As you can see, your earnings rate goes up considerably if you stay in a top suite. In the second bucket of earnings (points earned by spending money on ships), you will earn 100 points for every 1,000 euros or dollars you spend on most fee-based extras like spa treatments and premium drinks. Such points are earned in blocks of 100, so you won't earn any points through spending unless you spend more than 1,000 euros or dollars during a sailing (after which you'll get 100 points). Two other notable caveats to this type of earning are that you won't earn points for spending at several of the onboard boutiques on Explora ships, including Encore by Explora Journeys, Rolex, Cartier, Panerai, Piaget and Buccellati, and you won't earn points for spending at onboard casinos. In addition to the above, you will earn 100 points for every 1,000 euros or dollars you spend on shore excursions, whether they are booked in advance of sailing or on board. Program tiers and benefits There are five tiers to the Explora Club loyalty program: - Classic (upon joining the program) - Silver (1 to 5,000 points) - Gold (5,001 to 20,000 points) - Platinum (20,001 to 50,000 points) - Diamond (50,001 or more points) You are awarded status in each tier after you complete the sailing needed to reach the points threshold for that tier. For instance, you become a Silver member after completing your first sailing, when you earn your first points. You then become a Gold member after the sailing that puts you over the 5,001-point threshold for that tier. Points should appear in your account within 10 days of sailing. As is typical for cruise line loyalty programs, the entry-level tier of the program (Classic) doesn't bring all that much in terms of perks. The main benefit at this level is that you get access to exclusive Explora Club member offers. You'll also get a personalized welcome gift upon boarding. Additionally, at the Classic level, you will receive: - Priority access to new cruises when they're announced - Access to a dedicated area in the My Explora section of the line's website The next tier of the program, the Silver tier, brings several additional perks, including one that is quite valuable: a 5% discount when booking future sailings. That's real money in your pocket. In fact, given that Explora Journeys sailings can cost more than $1,000 per day, this one perk alone can be worth hundreds if not thousands of dollars when making a booking. This 5% savings, it should be noted, is only for the cruise portion of bookings. It does not apply to the cost of flights, transfers, port taxes, hotels, destination experiences, pre- and post-Journey services, prepaid services or insurance booked through Explora Journeys. On the positive side, this 5% discount can be combined with most other promotions and offers, with the exception of group booking rates and certain other promotional fares, such as those labeled as "Explora Journeys Travel Advisor Benefit," "MSC Family Benefit" and "Interline" fares. Related: Explora Journeys cruise ship review: Setting a new bar for luxury at sea In addition to all the perks of the Classic tier, the Silver tier also brings: - An exclusive Silver member welcome gift - A signature loyalty delight - A bottle of Champagne when sailing on your birthday - 5% savings on Explora Journeys merchandise at the Explora Journeys boutique - Priority assistance at the Explora Experience Centre - An invite to an exclusive cocktail event with ship leadership - A focus group invite - A personalized welcome from the general manager Once you reach the Gold tier of the program, you get three additional perks, none of which get us all that excited. The best extra perk at the Gold level, in our opinion, is an additional free bag of laundry once per cruise. (It's labeled "additional," as some categories of cabins already come with some free laundry services.) We always love free laundry as a perk when cruising, as it takes away one of the persistent pain points of such trips: keeping all your clothes clean. That said, a single free bag of laundry per cruise isn't really a game changer in the way unlimited free laundry would be. The two additional Gold member perks are an exclusive Gold member welcome gift and a surprise ritual or signature gift, distinct from turndown service. The first two tiers of the program, the Classic and Silver levels, may not bring all that much in terms of valuable perks. But on the flip side, they're super easy to achieve. To become a Classic member, all you have to do is sign up for the program. No cruise is necessary. And it only takes a single cruise to reach the Silver level. You also can reach the Gold level of the program in as few as one cruise if you stay in a top suite, given all the extra points you'll earn for such stays. But for the typical passenger who stays in an entry-level Ocean Suite, it'll likely take five to seven sailings to reach the Gold level, depending on your onboard and shore excursion spending level. The elite level that makes a difference In general, we find the first three tiers of the Explora Club loyalty program just so-so when it comes to perks. With the exception of the 5% discount on future cruise bookings, there really aren't all that many perks that are truly valuable in these three tiers. But the value of the program definitely steps up at the Platinum tier. At the Platinum tier, you get two more perks that bring real savings on every cruise: - A $100 credit for wellness experiences - A $100 credit for shore excursions Assuming you sign up for at least one treatment at the ship's spa and one shore excursion, that's $200 in value right there. Related: The 10 best luxury cruise lines for elegance and exclusivity Additionally, the Platinum tier of the program brings: - An exclusive Platinum member welcome gift - A daily complimentary laundry bag (maximum of one per day) - A behind-the-scenes bridge tour (upon availability) To reach the Platinum level, you'll need to take as many as 29 seven-night cruises, assuming you stay in entry-level Ocean Suites and don't spend much on board. But if you stay in higher category suites and/or spend a lot on board or on shore excursions, you could reach the Platinum tier far more quickly. Best elite perk The ultimate perk for Explora Club loyalty members, by far, comes upon reaching the top Diamond tier of the program. You'll get a complimentary weeklong cruise in an Ocean Suite. You heard that right: an entirely free cruise. And it's a cruise not just for you but for a guest, too. Just note that there is some fine print on this free cruise, the most notable of which is that it only becomes redeemable once you have spent 400 nights on an Explora ship. Additionally, while touted as a free "weeklong" cruise, the reward is technically only valid for a six-night cruise, not a cruise lasting a full week. That said, you can pay a little extra to book a longer journey. In the fine print for the reward, Explora Journeys notes that it "has a corresponding economic value and members can pay the difference for a higher-value Journey." Related: A beginners guide to picking a cruise line In addition to this free cruise, upon reaching the Diamond tier of the Explora Club program, you'll also become eligible for complimentary suite upgrades when making bookings — another truly valuable perk. Just note that these upgrades are subject to availability, and upgrades to an Owner's Residence (the highest category of rooms on Explora Journeys ships) are excluded. Another great perk at the Diamond level is that you will get a complimentary private transfer from your arrival airport or hotel to your ship on the day of embarkation. This private pickup service is assigned to the Diamond member and all the guests in the same reservation and can be requested once per cruise. The Diamond level also brings: - An exclusive Diamond member welcome gift - An exclusive embarkation area - A meet-and-greet experience with the line's president on Explora Journeys sailings - A complimentary culinary experience (e.g., Chef's Kitchen) - A private shopping adviser Note that, as is usually the case with cruise line loyalty programs, Explora Journeys customers do not have to requalify for status each year. That said, your status in the Explora Club is contingent upon booking and/or sailing with the line at least once every five years. If your last disembarkation date from a ship is more than five years (60 months) prior to your next sailing, all of your accrued points will expire, and you will be downgraded to the Classic level. Explora Club status match Do you have high-level status with another cruise line? The good news is that Explora Journeys is one of only a handful of cruise lines that offers a status match feature that will instantly catapult you to a high-level status in the Explora Club program, too. The Explora Club's status match program allows guests who hold loyalty status with more than a dozen other cruise lines, including Seabourn, Regent Seven Seas Cruises, Silversea Cruises, Crystal and Ponant Explorations, to match their status to equivalent tiers in the Explora Club prior to sailing. Members of the Seabourn Club loyalty program who are at the Silver level of status, for instance, can status match to the Silver level of the Explora Club program. Members of the Seabourn Club program at the Gold and Platinum levels can status match to the Gold level of the Explora Club program. A full list of loyalty programs you can status match to the Explora Club program is available here. Bottom line For the most part, the 1-year-old Explora Club loyalty program only offers modest perks at its lower tiers of status. But once you reach the higher tiers of the program, it brings real value, including onboard credits and, at its highest level, an entirely free cruise for two. Planning a cruise? Start with these stories:

item.title: American Airlines adds 3 new European destinations in 7-route expansion
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.29
American Airlines adds 3 new European destinations in 7-route expansion American Airlines will add three new destinations in Europe as it gets ready to roll out its 2027 travel schedule. The additions – Vienna, Austria; Reykjavik, Iceland; Porto, Portugal – were among seven new international routes American announced Thursday. Elsewhere, Amsterdam, Barcelona and Nice, France – cities American already serves – are each getting service to additional hubs. And, in the one transpacific route of the expansion, American will restore service from its Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) hub to Tokyo's Narita Airport (NRT). The carrier had first revealed plans return to Narita from Chicago earlier this summer. That route matches service that rival United Airlines announced earlier this year. American's new international routes for summer 2027 | Origin | Destination | Service begins | Aircraft | |---|---|---|---| | Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT) | Barcelona-El Pratt Airport (BCN) | May 27, 2027 | Boeing 777-200ER | | Chicago's O'Hare International Airport (ORD) | Tokyo's Narita Airport (NRT) | March 19, 2027 | Boeing 787-9 | | New York's JFK International Airport (JFK) | Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS) | March 28, 2027 | Airbus A321XLR | | JFK | Nice Côte d'Azur Airport (NCE) in France | May 6, 2027 | Airbus A321XLR | | JFK | London Heathrow Airport (LHR) | Fourth daily flight on March 28, 2027 | Boeing 787-9 (Flagship) | | Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) | Porto Airport (OPO) in Portugal | March 28, 2027 | Airbus A321XLR | | PHL | Reykjavik via Keflavík International Airport (KEF) in Iceland | May 27, 2027 | Airbus A321neo | | PHL | Vienna International Airport (VIE) | May 6, 2027 | Airbus A321XLR | Along with the O'Hare-Tokyo service, American had previously revealed Porto as one of the first European destinations for its new Airbus A321XLR aircraft, which entered service last year. Now, the airline has released the full details of the route, which launches from Philadelphia in March. 'Route drop' week It's the six European routes that make up the heft of American's "route drop. It comes just two days after United's — a high-profile spectacle that included a splashy press event inside a hangar at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR). United's reveal included 10 new international routes to an unconventional set of destinations, drawing headlines around the nation. Delta Air Lines summer 2027 route reveal is yet to come, though it remains to be seen if either it or American can match the buzz United has been able to build for its network updates in recent years. For Thursday, however, the stage is American's. Boeing, Airbus woes creep in Brian Znotins, American's senior vice president of network and schedule planning, said his carrier's announcement would have been much bigger on Thursday if not for issues at both Airbus and Boeing. Both have struggled to deliver new aircraft on schedule, disrupting fleet plans at airlines around the world. American has felt the disruptions significantly after the carrier returned several types of planes during the COVID-19 pandemic. Then, the arrival of new Boeing 787 Dreamliners and Airbus A321neos and A321 XLRs came much slower than expected, limiting American's long-haul options. "Boeing and Airbus are really letting us down," Znotins said. As of February Znotins expected American to have 13 newly delivered planes to incorporate into the schedule. But only five of those have arrived so far. "And so, we have a number of routes on the cutting room floor right now that we're having to defer for a year because of the lack of deliveries we're getting from our partners at Boeing and Airbus," he said. Regardless, the A321XLR is still poised to redraw airline route maps in the coming years. It's a smaller single-aisle plane, but has a remarkable range that allows U.S. carriers to fly it far into Europe. Couple that with the plane's small size and lower operating costs, and it opens up a slew of midsize markets that would be difficult to profitably serve with larger widebody jets. And that's just what American did, using its newly arrived XLRs to open up service to Nice and Porto – as well as to Vienna. Evaluating American's new destinations Vienna presents American with perhaps the biggest strategic opportunity in Thursday's route drop. When flights begin May 6, American is poised to become the only U.S. carrier flying to Vienna. The last U.S. airline to fly there was Delta Air Lines, which ended that route nearly two decades ago (2008). Now it will be up to American to make the Vienna service work – along with all the other new routes announced Thursday. The frequent flyer map Route planning has become something of an advanced science in the modern aviation industry. Vast amounts of data – market demographics, fare data and demand trends – help airline network chiefs like Znotins and his counterparts at other airlines help predict which new routes are likely to succeed. Increasingly, however, another factor has crept into the equation: where do frequent flyers want to go with their hard-earned points and miles? Perhaps that's no surprise given how much profit the industry mines from those frequent flyer programs – and the cobranded credit cards that support them. American's AAdvantage loyalty program is no exception. "When someone's buying groceries at their local grocery store, they're thinking about earning miles on their credit card to fly to Rome," Znotins said. "People get excited about earning miles and what trips they're going to take with those miles. That's something we really benefit from." And that's where Znotin's team comes in. "At the end of the day, it is about having a broad variety of destinations for customers to go to," he said. Related reading:

item.title: United's epic Greenland flight (and others) coming back in 2027; luxe new domestic plane delayed
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.61
United's epic Greenland flight (and others) coming back in 2027; luxe new domestic plane delayed United Airlines made a huge splash this week by announcing 10 all-new destinations as part of the carrier's largest international expansion ever. But the airline isn't just adding new routes for 2027. It's also bringing back every one of the ultra-unique destinations it flew this summer, from southern Europe to the Arctic. United's epic flight to Greenland? "We are planning to be back," chief network planner Patrick Quayle confirmed this week. Ditto for the new flights United launched this summer to off-the-beaten-path destinations in Croatia, Spain and Italy's Puglia region. "Everything is coming back," Quayle reiterated. "We're not dropping any routes." That's pretty remarkable. Many of the new destinations United has launched in recent years involve service to places seldom (or never) served by a U.S. airline. So drumming up enough demand to fill airplanes to these secondary cities is hardly a guarantee. That said, airline executives are increasingly willing to roll the (financial) dice on an ambitious new destination because of the excitement it drums up among their loyalty members. And United has often cited its bold international strategy as a major asset of its MileagePlus program. Don't expect bold routes to Scandinavia Not every gamble United has taken in recent years has paid off. For instance, a new route the airline launched to Dakar, Senegal, in 2025 didn't return this year — and the carrier this week said it has no plans to resume service. Also, don't expect a bunch of new routes to Scandinavia, any time soon. That region is home to two recent routes that United launched but then canceled. "We tried Bergen, Norway, and we previously had service into Stockholm," Quayle said this week. "And neither of those flights did particularly well." Instead, United is doubling down on southern Europe, where travelers have continually flocked in recent years. New routes to the region announced this week include Marseille and Toulouse, France; Valencia and Ibiza, Spain; and Olbia (Sardinia) and Catania (Sicily) in Italy. Luxe new domestic plane delayed Closer to home, United delivered one bit of less-than-positive news this week: It'll be a little while before we see its posh new domestic airplane. Earlier this year, the carrier announced plans to christen the fancy Airbus A321neo nicknamed the "Coastliner," which will have lie-flat Polaris suites and a premium economy cabin. This jet is expected to be a fixture on United's top transcontinental routes from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) and, eventually, John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). The Coastliner had been slated to debut this summer, but it's not here yet — and United confirmed the aircraft has faced delivery delays at Airbus. The carrier did not offer a timetable for when the first aircraft could arrive. "As soon as we get it, we will start flying it," Quayle said. A321XLR unlikely to sub-in, long-term Once delivered, it should offer a pretty luxe on-board experience, complete with 20 Polaris suites and 12 Premium Plus recliners. The layout is nearly identical to United's new long-haul variant of the A321neo, the A321XLR, which is a big part of the carrier's transatlantic plans going forward. While United awaits its Coastliners, Quayle said the airline "may" turn to its XLR for some limited cross-country service. But the airline has no long-term plans to use this long-haul-capable plane for domestic flying. Related reading:

item.title: These 6 business cards can help you stay under Chase’s 5/24 rule
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.14
These 6 business cards can help you stay under Chase’s 5/24 rule Editor's Note Chase issues some of the most sought-after rewards cards on the market, but the bank also has some of the strictest application policies. It limits cardholders to earning only one welcome bonus per consumer Sapphire card and has its infamous 5/24 rule. Chase has never officially commented on the existence of the 5/24 rule, but crowdsourced data confirm that applicants will almost certainly be denied new Chase cards if they have opened five or more accounts across issuers in the past 24 months. All personal credit card accounts count toward this rule, including cards with no preset spending limits and certain store cards. However, many business credit cards, including those issued by Chase, aren't considered when Chase determines your 5/24 standing. If you're trying to stay under 5/24, you can still rack up points and miles with business cards without affecting your ability to apply for Chase cards in the future. This isn't an exhaustive list, but it covers some of my favorite business cards available right now. All point and mile valuations in this article are based on TPG's August 2026 valuations. Comparing the best business cards to stay under 5/24 | Card | Best for | Annual fee | Welcome offer | |---|---|---|---| | | Everyday business spending | | Earn 15,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months of card membership. | | | Simple cash-back rewards | $0 | Earn $1,000 cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. | | | | $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $99 thereafter | Earn 65,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. | | | Business bonus categories | $95 | Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. | | | | | Earn up to 125,000 bonus points: 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership, plus 50,000 bonus points after spending an additional $3,000 ($9,000 total) on purchases in the first six months of card membership. | | | Premium business travel | $795 | Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first six months from account opening. | Related: The best business and personal credit card combinations The Blue Business Plus Credit Card from American Express Welcome offer: Earn 15,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months of card membership. Based on TPG's August 2026 valuations, this offer is worth $300. Annual fee: $0. Earning rates: - Earn 2 points per dollar spent on the first $50,000 spent each calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent thereafter. Why we like it: Reaching minimum spending requirements for welcome bonuses can be difficult for small businesses without high annual spending. However, The Blue Business Plus has a welcome offer that's attainable for most businesses, regardless of their typical budget. Additionally, if you value simplicity with earnings, this card is a great fit. You'll earn 2 points per dollar spent on all purchases for the first $50,000 in spending per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent thereafter. If your business spends less than $50,000 each year, this card is an excellent choice. Plus, you'll earn Membership Rewards points and have access to Amex's roster of 20 hotel and airline partners. Based on TPG's August 2026 valuations, this offer is worth $910. Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $99 thereafter. Earning rates: - Earn 2 miles per dollar spent on the following categories: cable and satellite providers, car rental merchants, eligible American Airlines purchases, gas stations and telecommunications merchants. - Earn 1 mile per dollar spent on all other purchases. Why we like it: Another solid option is the Marriott Bonvoy Business Amex Card, which includes a generous welcome offer. With the Bonvoy Business Amex, you'll get complimentary Marriott Gold Elite status, which includes perks like 25% bonus earnings on Marriott stays and 2 p.m. late checkout (subject to availability). Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Business American Express Card Related: Here's why you need both a personal and business Marriott Bonvoy credit card Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business Welcome offer: Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first six months from account opening. Based on TPG's valuations, this offer is worth $4,100. Annual fee: $795. Earning rates: - Earn 8 points per dollar spent on all purchases through Chase Travel℠, including The Edit (minimum two-night stay required for The Edit properties) - Earn 5 points per dollar spent on Lyft rides through Sept. 30, 2027. - Earn 4 points per dollar spent on flights and hotels booked direct. - Earn 3 points per dollar spent on social media and search engine advertising. - Earn 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases. Why we like it: The Sapphire Reserve for Business is a strong option for business owners who want premium travel perks without adding to their 5/24 count. Although you'll generally need to be under 5/24 to be approved, opening the card won't increase your 5/24 standing. The card's current welcome offer is especially noteworthy, with the ability to earn 200,000 bonus Ultimate Rewards points after meeting the spending requirement. You'll also get premium travel benefits that can help offset the card's hefty $795 annual fee, including airport lounge access and a $300 annual travel credit. If you can take advantage of its benefits and credits, the Sapphire Reserve for Business can be a valuable way to earn transferable Ultimate Rewards points while preserving your 5/24 slots for future personal card applications. Whether you walk dogs on the side, drive for Uber or run your own reselling business, you're usually eligible to apply for a business card. Additionally, you may be wondering why no Capital One business cards are on this list. That's because most Capital One business cards count toward your 5/24 status. Plus, some issuers frown on using your business card for personal expenses and may close your account if you do so. Related: Reasons to get a business credit card Bottom line While Chase cards offer real long-term value for cardholders, the issuer diligently monitors account applications. If you get approved for too many cards in a short period of time, you could risk getting future applications for Chase cards denied. Business cards can come in handy when you're trying to avoid the pitfall of Chase's 5/24 rule. item.title: Who is covered by credit card travel insurance?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.42
Who is covered by credit card travel insurance? Editor's Note No matter how carefully you plan your vacation, bad weather or mechanical delays can throw your trip off track without warning. That's why it's important to consider getting travel insurance to protect your trip. Thankfully, many of the top travel rewards cards on the market include various travel protections automatically when you use your card to pay for your trip. What is credit card travel insurance? Credit card travel insurance can come to the rescue when your carefully planned trip goes sideways. And as most travelers eventually learn, things don't always go according to plan. Depending on the card, coverage can kick in for illness, bad weather and other emergencies outside your control. Here's a list of common travel protections included with many travel credit cards: - Baggage delay coverage - Car rental coverage/auto collision damage waiver - Emergency medical and dental insurance - Lost and damaged baggage coverage - Travel accident insurance - Travel and emergency assistance - Trip cancellation and interruption coverage - Trip delay coverage Related: What's covered by credit card travel accident and emergency evacuation insurance? Which credit cards include travel insurance? Not all credit cards offer travel insurance, and the cards that do aren't created equal. Some offer a relatively basic set of protections, while others cover everything from delayed baggage to trip cancellations and emergency evacuations. Here are some of our favorite cards that offer travel protections: For more information, check out our list of the best cards with travel insurance. Having travel insurance is one thing. Having travel insurance that actually gives you the coverage you need is another. Here's how the protections on some of our favorite cards compare: | Card | Trip cancellation/interruption | Trip delay | Baggage delay | Emergency medical/evacuation | |---|---|---|---|---| | | Up to $10,000 per trip and up to $20,000 per eligible card per 12-month period* | Up to $500 per covered trip after a delay of more than six hours, with a maximum of two claims per eligible card per 12-month period* | None | Emergency medical transportation may be provided at no cost when coordinated through and approved by the Premium Global Assist Hotline** | | | None | Up to $300 per covered trip after a delay of more than 12 hours, with a maximum of two claims per eligible card per 12-month period* | None | No coverage; Global Assist Hotline can coordinate emergency medical assistance, but cardmembers are responsible for third-party costs** | | | Up to $2,000 per insured person for eligible nonrefundable common carrier tickets | Up to $500 per purchased ticket after a delay of more than six hours or an overnight stay | None | Not included | | | Up to $10,000 per covered traveler, $20,000 per trip and $40,000 per 12-month period per account | Up to $500 per covered traveler after a delay of more than 12 hours or an overnight stay | Up to $100 per day for up to five days after a delay of more than six hours | Up to $100,000 in emergency evacuation and transportation coverage | | | Up to $10,000 per covered traveler, $20,000 per trip and $40,000 per 12-month period per account | Up to $500 per covered traveler after a delay of more than six hours or an overnight stay | Up to $100 per day for up to five days after a delay of more than six hours | Up to $2,500 for emergency medical and dental expenses, subject to a $50 deductible, and up to $100,000 for emergency evacuation and transportation | | | Up to $5,000 per covered traveler, $10,000 per trip and $20,000 per 12-month period | Up to $500 per covered traveler after a delay of more than 12 hours or an overnight stay | Up to $100 per day for up to five days after a delay of six hours or more | Travel and emergency assistance is available for medical referrals and other assistance, but you're responsible for the cost of any services provided | *Eligibility and benefit level varies by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for details. Policies are underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. **Eligibility and benefit level varies by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for details. If approved and coordinated by Premium Global Assist Hotline, emergency medical transportation assistance may be provided at no cost. In any other circumstance, cardmembers are responsible for the costs charged by third-party service providers. Who is covered by credit card travel insurance? Credit card travel insurance can extend beyond just the cardholder. Depending on the coverage, your spouse or domestic partner, children, other family members and even traveling companions could be protected. Does credit card travel insurance cover my partner? Coverage can include a spouse or domestic partner. Take the Amex Platinum, for example. For trip cancellation and interruption insurance*, for example, a covered traveler includes a domestic partner, spouse or unmarried child under the age of 19 (or under 26 if they are a full-time college student). So, your partner doesn't necessarily need to be a cardmember to be covered. However, you'll still need to meet the requirements of the specific benefit for coverage to apply. Related: Should you get travel insurance if you have credit card protection? Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.* Does credit card travel insurance cover my family? Credit card travel insurance can extend to your family members, sometimes even when the cardholder isn't traveling with them. For example, trip cancellation and interruption insurance on the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve covers the cardholder and eligible family members. Chase's definition of family is surprisingly broad, extending beyond spouses and children to relatives such as parents, grandparents, siblings, aunts, uncles, nieces and nephews. Even better, those family members don't need to be traveling with the cardholder for this benefit to apply. Keep in mind that some credit card travel protections are secondary to other coverage or reimbursement available to you. That means your credit card coverage generally kicks in only after you've sought reimbursement elsewhere, like from the airline, hotel or another insurance policy. It may then cover eligible remaining expenses. Related: 7 times your credit card's travel insurance might not cover you Does credit card travel insurance cover friends or travel companions? Family members aren't the only people who can be covered by your credit card travel insurance. Some benefits also extend coverage to traveling companions. For example, the Amex Platinum's trip cancellation and interruption insurance* includes eligible traveling companions. Amex defines a traveling companion as someone who has made advanced arrangements with you or your family members to travel together for all or part of a covered trip. That means you don't necessarily need to be related to someone for them to qualify as a traveling companion under the benefit. * Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Bottom line Credit card travel insurance can offer valuable protection when the unexpected disrupts your trip, and that coverage can even extend beyond the cardholder. Spouses, domestic partners, family members and, in some cases, traveling companions may also be covered. Before relying on your card's travel protections, make sure you understand who qualifies for coverage and what requirements you need to meet for the benefit to apply. For Capital One products listed on this page, some of the benefits may be provided by Visa® or Mastercard® and may vary by product. See the respective Guide to Benefits for details, as terms and exclusions apply. For rates and fees of the Amex Platinum, click here. For rates and fees of the Amex Gold, click here.

item.title: IHG signs massive hotel deal in one of our favorite destinations in Japan
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 2.86
IHG signs massive hotel deal in one of our favorite destinations in Japan IHG One Rewards members will soon have more reasons to visit the Land of the Rising Sun — 14 more, to be exact. IHG Hotels & Resorts has signed a landmark deal to convert 14 hotels in Kyoto, one of Japan's most beloved tourist destinations, over the next year. The 1,063-room portfolio includes 12 Garner hotels (a midscale conversion brand within IHG's portfolio), a Holiday Inn Express and an unbranded hotel. All properties are located in "key districts in Kyoto," according to a press release, "ensuring guests are close to major transport hubs and some of the city's most popular cultural and tourism attractions." The deal — one of the largest of its kind that Japan has seen in recent years — is another step in Garner's already-rapid growth. The brand, which launched only three years ago, recently celebrated opening its 100th hotel globally. The deal also further solidifies IHG's longstanding partnership with GCP Hospitality (the hospitality arm of Gaw Capital Group), which has been appointed to lead the management team of the 14 new additions. IHG already boasts a varied portfolio in Kyoto, with properties ranging from budget-friendly Holiday Inn Kyoto Gojo and midscale Garner Hotel Kyoto Shijo Karasuma to the premium ANA Crowne Plaza Kyoto and ultra-luxurious Six Senses Kyoto. The 14-hotel conversion is set to position IHG as a major international player in Kyoto's hotel landscape, which has historically been dominated by domestic operators. Abhijay Sandilya, Managing Director, Japan & Micronesia, IHG Hotels & Resorts and CEO of IHG ANA Hotels Group Japan, said, "this deal demonstrates the growing interest from owners to rebrand hotels and benefit from quick access to IHG's leading enterprise, including our marketing, technology and distribution platforms, and the scale of IHG One Rewards globally." After renovations and rebranding, the 14 properties are slated for phased openings over the next 12 months — and we hope they will be available to book through IHG One Rewards soon after.

item.title: The gift card trick that helps me maximize my US restaurant credits while I'm abroad
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 2.69
The gift card trick that helps me maximize my US restaurant credits while I'm abroad I spent the first half of 2025 traveling through Europe and South America. Then, the month after I got back, I sold my house in Austin and moved to Spain, where I've been based for the past year. In that time, I've only made it back to the U.S. twice. That has created a problem: between my American Express Platinum Card® and Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees), I have up to $700 a year in restaurant credits that only trigger when I pay at a participating restaurant in the U.S.* I wasn't willing to let that value go to waste just because I wasn't going to be dining in the U.S. as often, so I researched a way to keep maximizing those credits from a distance. That's when I found UseYourCredits.com, a site that maps out participating restaurants for benefits on cards like these. It's also how I learned that a good chunk of those Resy and OpenTable restaurants sell their own gift cards online. Buy one directly from the restaurant's site, and it often triggers the statement credit just like paying your check would, even if you're thousands of miles away and don't have a reservation. I've been doing this for about a year now, and it's let me stay on top of these credits every single cycle without needing to be anywhere near the restaurant. Here's how I make it work. *Receive up to $400 per calendar year in Resy statement credits (distributed as up to $100 per quarter); simply pay with your Amex Platinum at an eligible U.S. Resy restaurant; no reservation required; enrollment required. How I find restaurants that work I rely on UseYourCredits.com, which maps out participating restaurants for both programs. The two credit pools look nothing alike. Resy's list includes almost 11,000 restaurants nationwide, but only about a third of them sell e-gift cards directly. (This cohort will expand when select Tock restaurants join starting Sept. 15.) Resy statement credits for use in the U.S. are available on select cards, including the American Express Platinum (up to $100 in statement credits quarterly; enrollment required) and the American Express® Gold Card (up to $50 in statement credits semiannually; enrollment required). Chase's Sapphire Reserve Exclusive Tables list, run through OpenTable, is much smaller (around 400 restaurants), with about a third selling e-gift cards. One detail that matters: buy the gift card through the restaurant's own website or ordering page, not a generic third-party gift card marketplace. It's usually fine if that page runs on a platform like Toast behind the scenes — what matters is that it's the restaurant's own official channel, not a marketplace that sells cards for dozens of different restaurants. If a restaurant doesn't sell gift cards online, calling the restaurant directly or buying one in person is also likely to trigger the credit, since the charge usually runs through the restaurant itself. Why I always test with a small purchase first I never try to use a full credit at an untested restaurant. I buy the smallest gift card the restaurant offers (usually $5) and wait to see whether the credit posts before I put another dollar toward it. That's exactly what I did at Austin restaurant Suerte last December: a $5 test on the Sapphire Reserve, followed by a $145 reload after the first credit posted. At nearby Launderette, I tested $25 on my Amex Platinum before reloading another $75. Every time, including for the third gift card I'm currently building up at Fresas (also an Austin staple), the statement credit has posted within two days of purchase. Testing small isn't just caution for caution's sake. Restaurants can change their gift card providers, and issuers can adjust how these transactions get coded. A $5 test protects you from finding out the hard way that $150 didn't trigger anything. How I stack multiple restaurant credits into one meal This is where the strategy really pays off. Chase splits its Sapphire Reserve dining credit into two $150 chunks: one for January through June and another for July through December (unused amounts don't roll over). Last December, I loaded that $150 test-and-reload combo onto a Suerte gift card to bank July-to-December 2025's credit before it disappeared. Then in February, I flew back to Austin and had dinner in person at Suerte. The bill came to $304 (tip included). I paid $150 of it with the gift card I'd already loaded, and charged the remaining $154 to my physical Sapphire Reserve. That $154 charge triggered a fresh $150 credit for the new January-to-June cycle. Between the banked credit and the newly triggered one, $300 of the $304 total was covered by the card, meaning I paid only $4 out of pocket. I used a similar approach with my Amex Platinum at Launderette: a $100 gift card that used my Q4 2025 credit (up to $100 in statement credits quarterly for U.S. Resy purchases; enrollment required), then a $100 charge on my physical card during that same February trip, which triggered my Q1 2026 statement credit. Two credit cycles, one meal, $200 covered. I'm doing it again at Fresas, where I've already used my Q2 statement credit to buy an e-gift card and reload with another $100 for Q3 before my next Austin trip. Related: The dining statement credits that save me over $1,000 every year Who should consider this strategy? You don't need to be living abroad full-time to get value out of this. It's worth considering if: - You're spending an extended stretch outside the U.S., whether that's a year abroad, a six-month posting or a quarter-long trip, and you don't want to watch your credits expire while you're gone. - You want to bank credits toward one bigger night out, a group dinner or a meal you're treating someone to, rather than trying to spend $50-$150 at a time. - You're holding a card with a smaller, more frequent statement credit, like on the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (up to $20 monthly credit for U.S. Resy purchases; enrollment required), and would rather consolidate several months into one gift card than remember to spend at a participating restaurant every single month. - You don't dine out often and are looking for a way to make a high annual fee feel less daunting. The Amex Platinum's $895 annual fee (see rates and fees) almost halves once you fully capture its up to $400 annual restaurant credit as U.S. Resy locations; the Sapphire Reserve's annual fee drops to an effective $495 once you factor in its $300 annual Exclusive Tables credit (up to $150 in credits biannually). Where this strategy falls short Not every card is worth the effort. I canceled my American Express Gold last year because I couldn't make the math work while living overseas: - Resy statement credit: Up to $50 in semiannual statement credits for U.S. Resy restaurants (enrollment required). You can use the same gift card strategy as with the Platinum and Sapphire Reserve cards, but with a much smaller payout relative to the effort. - $10 monthly dining statement credit: Up to $10 in monthly statement credits at select merchants (enrollment required). It's genuinely hard to use from abroad, since eligible merchants are mostly U.S.-based delivery and takeout brands. - Uber Cash: Up to $10 in Uber Cash each month toward U.S. Uber rides and Uber Eats orders when you add your Amex Gold as a payment method and pay with any Amex card. It doesn't work outside the U.S. at all. - Dunkin' statement credit: Requires reloading your Dunkin' app balance for just $7 every single month to maximize at U.S. Dunkin' locations (enrollment required) — a lot of upkeep for a small return. That's a lot of small, frequent maintenance for a card with a $325 annual fee (see rates and fees). Related: How to maximize Amex Gold credits when traveling abroad Compare that to the Platinum's statement credit (up to $100 in statement credits quarterly for U.S. Resy purchases; enrollment required) or the Sapphire Reserve's twice-yearly $150 credits, both of which only need one or two gift card top-ups a year, and it's clear why the larger, less frequent statement credits are easier to justify chasing. If you'd rather skip the gift card step entirely, the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card — which carries a $650 annual fee (see rates and fees) — offers a simpler alternative: up to $25 per month in statement credits worldwide at any restaurant that accepts Amex. It explicitly excludes gift card purchases, so there's no work-around, just the plain requirement that you remember to use it when you're actually eating out. Less to gain but also less friction. Related: Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Amex review: Marriott's most premium card Bottom line This strategy turned my restaurant credits into real, meaningful savings, including a $4 dinner in Austin that would have otherwise cost $304. It works best on cards with larger, less frequent statement credits, like the Amex Platinum and the Sapphire Reserve, and less well on smaller ones, which is why I stopped bothering with my Amex Gold. If you've got a restaurant credit sitting unused, it's worth five minutes to check whether that restaurant sells gift cards. Test small, confirm it posts and decide from there whether it's worth building into a monthly, quarterly or twice-yearly habit. Related: The credit card checklist that saves me hundreds on date nights For rates and fees of the Amex Platinum, click here. For rates and fees of the Amex Gold, click here. For rates and fees of the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Amex, click here.

Reviews Atmos Rewards Summit Visa card review: Stellar value for more than just Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines loyalists Augusta Stone is a credit cards writer for TPG. She joined the TPG team in 2023 and is excited to take points and miles beginners with her on a journey toward maximizing rewards. August 25, 2026 • 14 min read The cards we feature here are from partners who compensate us when you are approved through our site, and this may impact how or where these products appear. We don't cover all available credit cards, but our analysis, reviews, and opinions are entirely from our editorial team. Terms apply to the offers listed on this page. Please view our advertising policy and product review methodology for more information. Editorial note: This is a recurring post, regularly updated with new information and offers. TPG's Brian Kelly is a Bilt adviser and investor. Editorial disclaimer: Opinions expressed here are the author's alone, not those of any bank, credit card issuer, airline or hotel chain, and have not been reviewed, approved or otherwise endorsed by any of these entities. Related stories Limited-Time Offer Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card Rewards rate Rewards rate Rate Category 3 points Earn unlimited 3 points for every $1 spent on eligible dining, foreign transaction, Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases. 1 point Earn unlimited 1 point per $1 spent on all other purchases. Intro offer Limited-time online offer – 80,000 bonus points Annual fee $395 Regular APR 19.49% - 27.49% Variable APR on purchases and balance transfers Recommended credit 670-850 Excellent/Good Quick summary A premium airline card offers strong value for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines loyalists, while also appealing to those who frequently fly with Oneworld alliance members. The card provides valuable perks such as an annual companion award, free checked bags, preferred boarding and a faster path to elite status in the Atmos Rewards program. Atmos Rewards points are valued at 1.55 cents each as of August 2026 per TPG's valuations, with the best redemptions available for flights on Alaska, Hawaiian and Oneworld partners. Additional benefits include lounge passes, Wi-Fi passes, a Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit and high earning rates for purchases made abroad. What to consider Some benefits, like free checked bags and preferred boarding, are only available on Alaska and Hawaiian flights, limiting utility for travelers who rarely use these carriers. The card charges a premium annual fee and offers limited lounge access compared to other premium travel cards. Approval may be subject to specific application rules and a preference for applicants with an existing banking relationship. What you'll miss from the article A detailed comparison of this premium airline card with mid-tier and business alternatives, including which travelers might benefit most from each option. Generated by AI with support from our editorial team. Take it from me: I live in the southeastern U.S. (about as far from the Pacific Northwest as you can get), but I highly value Atmos Rewards points because I can use them to book tickets on American, the airline I fly most often, at an excellent value. Of course, the Atmos Rewards Summit is a stellar option for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines flyers and those based in the Pacific Northwest. But even if you're based outside of that footprint, there's a lot to love here — that's why the Atmos Summit won TPG's 2026 award for Best New Personal Credit Card. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐ *Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG's editors and is not influenced by the card issuer. Atmos Rewards Summit: The basics The is a cobranded airline card for Atmos Rewards members. Atmos Rewards is the joint loyalty program for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. The card earns Atmos Rewards points, which TPG's August 2026 valuations place at 1.55 cents apiece (one of the highest airline currency valuations). The card charges an annual fee of $395. The Atmos Rewards Summit provides a solid suite of airline-specific benefits when you fly Alaska or Hawaiian, including your first checked bag free and preferred boarding when you purchase airfare with your card.Cardholders also receive an annual 25,000-point Global Companion Award. Cardholders also have a faster path to Atmos Rewards elite status, as they earn 1 status point for every $2 spent (with no spending cap) and receive an anniversary status points boost. One of my favorite card perks is the Atmos Rewards Summit's standout earning rates, which are especially impressive compared to other airline cobranded cards. A top highlight is that cardholders earn 3 points per dollar spent on all foreign transactions, an unusual (and potentially quite lucrative) bonus category. The best way to redeem the Atmos Rewards points you'll earn on the Atmos Rewards Summit is for flights on Alaska, Hawaiian, Oneworld airlines and other partner airlines. Since Atmos Rewards retained Alaska Airlines' advantageous partner award chart, there are multiple sweet-spot redemption options. The provides multiple benefits when you fly Alaska and Hawaiian, but there are perks to enjoy in other parts of the travel journey as well. Airline-specific benefits These three benefits kick in when you purchase a fare on Alaska or Hawaiian with your Atmos Rewards Summit: Free checked bag: The cardholder and up to six guests on the same reservation get their first checked bag free. Free points sharing: Cardholders can send and receive Atmos Rewards points to and from up to 10 other Atmos Rewards members for no additional charge. Preferred boarding: The cardholder and up to six guests on the same reservation receive preferred boarding. The following perks are exclusive to Alaska Airlines flights, though they are expected to eventually be extended to Hawaiian Airlines flights as well: Departure delay voucher: Travelers will receive a $50 voucher if their Alaska Airlines flight is canceled or delayed more than two hours. No change fees: You won't pay a change fee for same-day changes with Alaska. Annual companion award The Atmos Rewards Summit provides an annual 25,000-point Global Companion Award that offers a discount on a second award ticket on Alaska, Hawaiian or a partner airline in any cabin class. When factoring in TPG's valuations, this perk is worth $388. High-spenders who put $60,000 or more on their Atmos Rewards Summit can earn a second 100,000-point Global Companion Award. Based on TPG's valuations, 100,000 Atmos Rewards points are worth $1,550. If you already spend a lot on your credit cards each year, it may be worth re-routing those purchases to your Atmos Summit card. Elite status boost Anniversary status points: Receive 10,000 status points every card anniversary. This points boost puts you halfway to earning Atmos Rewards Silver status. Faster path to elite status: Earn 1 status point for every $2 spent, with no spending cap. By spending $20,000 with the Summit card, you'll earn Atmos Rewards Silver status (which includes Oneworld Ruby status). If you spend $60,000 with the card, you'll earn Atmos Rewards Gold status (equivalent to Oneworld Sapphire status). Lounge passes Cardholders receive eight total Alaska Lounge passes each calendar year, earned as two passes each quarter. These passes can be shared with friends and family if you already have an Alaska Lounge membership. You must be traveling on a same-day ticketed flight on Alaska, Hawaiian, Oneworld or a partner airline to receive access with your lounge pass. A standard day pass costs $65 per person. Other benefits Other key perks include: Eight Wi-Fi passes (two passes each calendar quarter) While these perks certainly help offset the Atmos Rewards Summit's $395 annual fee, it's worth noting that this card doesn't offer a full Alaska Lounge membership or statement credits. This could be a downside for cardholders who want more benefits from a premium card. However, if you use the Global Companion Award and check one free bag each year, you'll come out ahead on the card's annual fee. 3 points per dollar spent on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases 3 points per dollar spent on eligible dining purchases and foreign transactions 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases Cardholders who have an eligible Bank of America account also earn a 10% rewards bonus on all points earned from card purchases. The Atmos Rewards Summit's bonus category for all foreign transactions will be attractive to many travelers who frequently take international trips, making this a standout card for a wide range of spenders. The earning rate for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases is standard for an airline cobranded card. Redeeming points There are many ways to redeem Atmos Rewards points, but you'll generally get the most value by using them for award flights on Alaska Airlines, Hawaiian Airlines, Oneworld carriers and other partner airlines. I frequently redeem Atmos Rewards points for short-haul domestic American Airlines flights, starting at 4,500 points one-way. I've flown from Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT) to New York's LaGuardia Airport (LGA) to visit friends for 4,500 Atmos Rewards points on multiple occasions. The Summit can make partner award redemptions even more valuable. Cardholders receive up to $25 per person in fee waivers on round-trip partner award flights. Plus, Atmos Rewards allows you to book multicity award itineraries at no additional cost. Transferring points The Atmos Rewards Summit offers a unique benefit in the world of cobranded airline cards, as you can transfer the Atmos Rewards points earned on this card to certain hotel partners. These are: However, you may not want to use your points this way unless you have a specific hotel redemption you're ready to book and need to top off your balance. Otherwise, your best use of Atmos Rewards points is to book award tickets for flights. The may not be the best fit for all types of travelers. Here are some downsides to consider: Some benefits, such as free checked bags and preferred boarding, are only usable on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines flights; that could be a deterrent if you aren't frequently flying with these carriers. The card does not provide broad lounge access and grants only two Alaska Lounge passes per quarter. You have to pay a high annual fee. Your rewards are limited to Atmos Rewards points, which have fewer redemption options than transferable credit card rewards. Atmos Rewards Summit vs. Atmos Rewards Ascent If you're interested in an Atmos Rewards card but don't want to pay a $395 annual fee for premium perks, I recommend considering the instead. The Atmos Rewards Ascent charges a $95 annual fee and offers perks similar to those of the Atmos Rewards Summit when flying on Alaska or Hawaiian, including free checked bags and preferred boarding. Atmos Rewards Ascent cardholders can earn an annual $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) upon each account anniversary after spending $6,000 or more within the prior anniversary year. The Atmos Rewards Summit doesn't include this perk, and it may be more enticing to certain travelers. However, it's worth noting that the Atmos Rewards Summit's 25,000-point Global Companion Award is a comparable benefit and is valued at a much higher $388, per TPG's valuations. The currently offers new cardholders the chance to earn 80,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening. Per TPG's valuations, the points and the Global Companion Award included in this bonus are worth $1,628. In terms of points awarded, this isn't the best offer we've ever seen in the Atmos Rewards Summit's offer history, but it meets our threshold of when to apply. Since Bank of America issues the Atmos Rewards Summit, you'll most likely be subject to the 2/3/4 rule. This means you can only get approved for two new Bank of America cards in a 30-day period, three cards in a 12-month period and four cards in a 24-month period. In addition, datapoints suggest Bank of America is inquiry-sensitive, so it may be worth waiting several months from your last hard inquiry before applying. TPG staffers have also found that Bank of America strongly prefers prospective cardholders to have an existing relationship with the bank, so it's likely worth opening and using a checking or savings account with it for a few months before applying. Other cards to consider instead of the Atmos Rewards Summit If the isn't the card for you, one of these competitors may be a better fit: If you prefer to earn transferable rewards: The (see rates and fees) earns transferable Bilt Points that can be moved to Atmos Rewards. It provides Priority Pass lounge access* and several perks for those ready to dive into Bilt's ecosystem. To learn more, read our full review of the Bilt Palladium. If you're considering another card in the Oneworld alliance: The Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Elite Mastercard® (see rates and fees) is a premium airline card that earns American Airlines AAdvantage miles to redeem with American Airlines, one of Atmos Rewards' Oneworld partners. It provides an Admirals Club membership for those interested in airport lounge access. To learn more, read our full review of the Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Elite. If you own a small business: The is an excellent choice for small-business owners who want to earn Atmos Rewards points. It earns a $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) after you spend $6,000 in the previous account anniversary year and charges a modest $95 annual fee ($70 for your company and $25 per card). To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Rewards Business. The Atmos Rewards Summit provides fantastic value for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines flyers ready to go all in on their joint loyalty program. The card's 25,000-point Global Companion Award, Alaska Lounge passes and high earning rate on foreign transactions are unique benefits that new cardholders should consider. However, if you're more of a casual traveler and aren't chasing Atmos Rewards elite status, you may be better off with its sister card, the mid-tier . Overall, Atmos Rewards points are a standout currency that can unlock redemptions across the Oneworld alliance, so the Atmos Rewards Summit is worth a look regardless of where you're flying from. Apply for the chance to earn 80,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening:

item.title: OpenAI’s executive exodus has one big winner
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 5.65
Today on Decoder, I’m talking to Verge senior AI reporter Hayden Field about some pure Decoder bait: the seemingly-endless org chart changes at OpenAI, and how all of them seem to consolidate power under cofounder Greg Brockman, the company’s president. OpenAI’s executive exodus has one big winner The Verge’s Hayden Field on how OpenAI president Greg Brockman has consolidated power as Sam Altman’s second-in-command. While Sam Altman is the CEO and still OpenAI’s most public face, Brockman has amassed enormous power and influence within the top ranks of the company as other senior leaders have left in rapid succession these past few months. Brockman now oversees the company’s entire consumer and enterprise product teams, including ChatGPT, Codex, and its major infrastructure build out. As Hayden recently reported, he is effectively now the day-to-day operational leader of OpenAI. This will have major effects on OpenAI as a company and its product strategy, at a time when it continues to cede ground to Anthropic in the enterprise and is preparing for a historic IPO. This is all against the backdrop of needing to turn a profit in the next few years and the company’s huge ambitions to replace both Google Search and the iPhone in the consumer market. So I wanted Hayden to break down for me what’s going on at OpenAI, and the increasingly important role Greg Brockman will play in its future. Okay: Verge senior AI reporter Hayden Field on Greg Brockman’s consolidation of power at OpenAI. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Hayden Field, you’re The Verge’s senior AI reporter. Welcome back to Decoder. Thanks. It’s great to be here. Always, always chaos when you’re here, Hayden. Absolutely. There’s never a calm week. If there’s a calm week coming up, I know something even crazier is coming the next week. We should just rename the show The Real Housewives of AI. [Laughs] Honestly, that would be fitting. Straight up, that’s what we should do. A lot of personalities, a lot of feelings, a lot of relationships that people have really come to value over a long period of time. And a lot of lore. A lot of lore that goes between all these people for years and years and years. It’s crazy. And now they’re even putting out profiles on some of their spouses. The circles and the people themselves are really interesting. Today the drama is about OpenAI and specifically Greg Brockman, who seems to be consolidating even more power at OpenAI. You just wrote a long story about this. It seems very clear that Greg is emerging as the central decision maker at OpenAI. Describe what’s going on. Greg has obviously been pretty influential at OpenAI for a really long time, but what’s different now is that he has so much control over the day-to-day operations in a way he didn’t before. He was always a cofounder. He was always heavily involved. It was him, Ilya Sutskever, and Sam Altman for a long time, all in these email threads that came out during the Musk v. Altman trial. We saw them all talking about the future of OpenAI, what it should look like, and all their strange dynamics with Elon Musk. But Brockman was in a big-picture role before, and now he’s increasingly taking on so much power in the day-to-day. Altman has been focusing more on the big picture, the IPO stuff, and the direction of the company at large. Meanwhile, Brockman is amassing all this power day-to-day as other executives leave. He’s been in control now of Codex, of its enterprise business, the consumer side. There are four arms of the company right now and he’s in control of all of them. It’s been really interesting to see how that’s happened over the last few months. Greg is a character in the AI story. Certainly inside of OpenAI, he’s been a central figure in a lot of the company’s drama over time. So if you’ve been paying attention to the AI industry, you’re familiar with him. But if someone haven’t, explain who Greg is and why he’s such a notable figure both in AI and at OpenAI. He has been on my radar for seven years now. He’s been on other people’s for even longer. He dropped out of MIT to join Stripe way back in the day. He was Stripe’s CTO during its really early explosive growth phase. He left in 2015 to cofound OpenAI. That’s how he came on the AI radar. Ever since then, he’s been a really influential figure.
